Those that have the antennae moniliform. 3. Those which have the antennae filiform. 4. Those which have the antennae fætaceous. A. Antennæ clavatis, extorsum incrassatis. a. Clava lamellata. 1. ECUERIES

Pages 284-284
or ECURRIES, popularly called Querries, are particularly used among us for officers of the king's stables, under the master of the horse, seven in number, who when his majesty goes abroad, ride in the leading coach, are in waiting one at a time monthly, and have a table with the gentlemen ushers during the time, and a salary of 300l. a-year each. They used to ride on horseback by the coach side when the king travelled; but that being more expensive to them than necessary to the sovereign, it has been discontinued. ECUERIES of the Crown Stable have that appellation, as being employed in managing and breaking the fadicle-horses, and preparing them for the king's riding. These are two in number; the first having an annual salary of 250l. and the second 200l., whereof one is, or always should be, in close waiting at court; and when his majesty rides, holds the stirrup, while the master of the horse, or one of the ecurers in his absence, assists in mounting him; and when his majesty rides, they usually attend him.

ECUES

Pages 284-284

in antiquity. See ECUESTRIAN Order and ECUTES. ECUES Auratus, is used to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>-bachelor, called auratus, q. d. gilt, because anciently none but knights might gilt <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> beautify their armour or other habiliments of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is not used, but instead of it miles, and sometimes chevalier.

ECUESTRIA

Pages 284-284

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> where the equites <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> sat.

ECUESTRIAN

Pages 284-285

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> chiefly used in the phrase equestrian statue, which signifies a statue representing a person mounted on horseback. The word is formed of the Latin eques, "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, horseman;" of equus, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>." ECUESTRIAN Games, among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, horse-races, of which there were five kinds, the prodromus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> plain horse <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, the chariot race, the decursory race about funeral piles, the ludi seviriates, and the ludi neptunales. ECUESTRIAN Order, among the Romans, signified their their knights or equites; also their troopers or horse- men in the field; the first of which orders <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> in con- tradistinction to the senators; as the last did to the foot, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, or infantry. Each of these distinctions was introduced into the state by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>.

EDSHEIMER

Pages 36-36
ADAM, a celebrated painter, born at Frankfort on the Main, in 1574. He was first a disciple of Philip Uffenbach, a German; but his desire of improvement carrying him to Rome, he soon became a most excellent artist in landscapes, history, and night-pieces, with small figures. His works are but few; and the great pains he bestowed in finishing them raised their prices so high, that they are hardly anywhere to be found but in the cabinets of princes. He was of a melancholy turn, and sunk under the embarrassments of his circumstances in 1610. James Ernst Thomas of Landau was his disciple; and imitated his style so nicely, that their performances are not easily distinguished.

ELECTRIDES

Pages 9-10

anciently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which received their name from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> (elektron) which they produced. They were at the mouth of the Po, according to Apollonius of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>; but some historians doubt of their existence. ELECTROMETER. In various parts of the article <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, we have described a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of instruments for ascertaining the presence of electricity, and measuring its quantity <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proportion. But there are several instruments of this kind that have not been described in that article; and as they are well deserving a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, either from the ingenuity of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, the reputation of their inventors, or the intrinsic value of the instruments themselves, we shall give an account of them here. Fig. 1. Plate CC. is a geometrical representation of Mr Cavallo's improved atmospheric electroscope, of half its real size. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is a glass tube CDMN, cemented at the bottom into the wooden piece <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, by which part the instrument is to be held when used for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; and it also serves to screw the instrument into its wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABO">ABO</a>, fig. 2, when it is not to be used. The upper part of the tube CDMN, is shaped tapering to a smaller extremity, which is entirely covered with sealing-wax, melted by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and not dissolved in spirits. Into this tapering part a small tube is cemented, the lower extremity G of which being also covered with sealing-wax, projects a short way within the tube CDMN. Into this smaller tube a wire is cemented, which with its lower extremity touches the flat piece of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> H, fastened to the tube by means of cork; the upper extremity of the wire projects about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch above the tube, and screws into the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> EF, which cap is open at the bottom, and serves to defend the waxed part of the instrument from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, &c. In fig. 3, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of this brass cap is represented, in order to show its internal shape, and the manner in which it is screwed to the wire, projecting above the tube L. The small tube L, and the upper extremity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tube CDMN, appear like one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> piece, on account of the sealing-wax, which covers them both. The conical corks P of this electroscope, which by their repulsion show the electricity, &c., are as small as can conveniently be made, and they are suspended by exceedingly fine silver wires. These wires are shaped in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> at the top, by which they hang very loosely on the flat piece of ivory H, which has two holes for that purpose. By this method of suspension, which is applicable to every sort of electroscope, the friction is lessened almost to nothing, and thence the instrument is sensible of a very small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of electricity. IM, and KN, are two narrow slips of tin-foil, stuck to the inside of the glass CDMN, and communicating with the wooden bottom AB; they serve to convey off that electricity, which, when the corks touch the glass, is communicated to it, and being accumulated, might disturb the free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the corks. In regard to its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, this instrument may serve to observe the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, as well as the atmospherical electricity. When it is to be used for artificial electricity, this electroscope is set upon a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> or other convenient support; then it is electrified by touching the brass cap EF with an electrified body, which electricity <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> sometimes be preserved for more than an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. Mr Cavallo had one of these electrometers which would remain electrical for more than twelve hours, though in a room without a fire. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> in an electrified state, any electrified substance be brought near the cap EF, the corks of the electroscope, by their converging, or by increasing their divergence, will show the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of that body's electricity. It is necessary to remark, that to communicate any electricity to this electroscope, by means of an excited electric, e.g., a piece of sealing-wax, (which we suppose is always negatively electrified), is not very readily done in the usual manner, on account of the cap EF being well rounded, and free from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or sharp edges. By the approach of the wax, the electroscope will be caused to diverge; but as soon as the wax is removed, the wires immediately collapse. The best method to electrify it, is to bring the excited wax so near the cap, that one or both the corks may touch the side of the bottle CDMN; after which, they will soon collapse and appear unelectrified: if now the wax be moved, they will again diverge, and remain electrified positively. When this instrument is to be used to try the electricity of the fogs, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, &c., the observer is to do nothing more than to unscrew it from its case, and, holding it by the bottom AB, to present it to the open Electrometer, open air, a little above his head, so that he may conveniently see the corks P, which will immediately diverge if there be any sufficient quantity of electricity; whose <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, i.e., whether positive or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, may be ascertained by bringing an excited piece of sealing-wax, or other electric, towards the brass cap EF. It is perhaps unnecessary to remark, that this observation must be made in an open place, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> out of town, the fields, the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, &c. The principal advantages of this electrometer, as stated by Mr Cavallo, are as follows: 1. The smallness of its size. Mr Cavallo made one so small, that its case, which was of brass, measured only three inches and a half in length, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>-tenths of an inch in diameter, and yet it acted perfectly well. 2. Its being always ready for experiments, without fear of entangling the threads, or having an equivocal result by the sluggishness of its motion. 3. Its not being disturbed by <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> or rain. 4. Its great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>; and, 5. Its keeping the communicated electricity longer than any other electrometer. II. Sauflure's Electrometer. M. de Saufure's electrometer, with which he made the observations on atmospheric electricity, that have been related in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Part V. of the article Electricity, and represented at fig. 4, is much the same with that of Mr Cavallo above described. The following are the most material circumstances in which they differ: First, the fine wires, by which the balls are suspended, should not be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to reach the tin-foil which is pasted on the inside of the glass, because the electricity, when strong, will cause them to touch this tin-foil twice consecutively, and thus deprive them in a moment of their electricity. To prevent this defect, and yet give them a sufficient degree of motion, it is necessary to use larger glasses than those that are generally applied to Mr Cavallo's electrometer; two or three inches in diameter will be found to answer the purpose very well. But as it is necessary to carry off the electricity which may be communicated to the inside of the glass, and thus be confounded with that which belongs to those substances that are under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>; four pieces of tin-foil should be pasted on the inside of the glass; the balls should not be more than one-twentieth of an inch diameter, suspended by silver wires, moving freely in holes nicely rounded. The bottom of the electrometer should be of metal; for this renders it more easy to deprive it of any acquired electricity, by touching the bottom and top at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In order to collect a great quantity of electricity from the air, the electrometer is furnished with a pointed wire, 15 inches or two feet long, which unscrews in three or four pieces, to render the instrument more portable; see fig. 4. When it rains or snows, the small parasol, fig. 5, is to be screwed on the top of the instrument, as by this its insulation is preserved, notwithstanding the rain.

ELEMENT

Pages 25-25

in a figurative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used for the principles and foundations of any art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> science; as Euclid's Elements, &c.

ELEMENTS

Pages 25-25

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, are those principles deduced from astronomical observations and calculations, and those <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> numbers which are employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of tables of the planetary motions. Thus, the elements of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, are his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and eccentricity, and the motion of the aphelia. The elements of the theory of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> are its mean motion; that of its node and apogee, its eccentricity, the inclination of its orbit to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the ecliptic, &c.

ELEPHANTA

Pages 25-26

a small, but very remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, about five miles from the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> in Elephanta, the East Indies. Of this we have the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> in Mr Grofe's Voyage to the East Indies. "It can at most be but about three miles in compass, and consists of almost all hill; at the foot of which, as you <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, you see, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> above the shore, on your <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, an elephant, coarsely cut out in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bigness, and at some little distance not impossible to be taken for a real elephant, from the stone being naturally of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of that beast. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of the same colour. On the back of this elephant was placed, standing, another young one, appearing to have been all of the same stone, but has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> broken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Of the meaning, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, of this image, there is no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> old enough to give any account. Returning then to the foot of the hill, you ascend an easy flight, which about half way up the hill brings you to the opening or portal of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cavern hewn out of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock into a magnificent temple: for such surely it may be termed, considering the immense workmanship of such an excavation; and seems to me a far more bold attempt than that of the pyramids of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. There is a fair entrance into this subterraneous temple, which is an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, in length about 80 or 90 feet, by 40 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is nothing but the rock cut flat at top, and in which I could not discern anything that did not show it to be all of one piece. It is about ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and supported towards the middle, at equidistance from the sides and from one another, with two regular rows of pillars of a singular order. They are very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a>, short in proportion to their thickness, and their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> bears some resemblance to a round cushion prefaced by the superincumbent mountain, with which they are also of one piece. At the further end of this temple are three gigantic figures; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of one of them is at least five feet in length, and of a proportionable breadth. But these representations have no reference or connection either to any known history or the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> of the Gentoos. They had <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a tolerable state of preservation and wholeness, considering the remoteness of their antiquity, until the arrival of the Portuguese, who made themselves masters of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> fury of their bigotry, not suffering any idols but their own, they must have even been at some pains to maim and deface them, as they now remain, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the stone. It is said they even brought field-pieces to the demolition of images, which so greatly deserved to be spared for the unequalled curiosity of them. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Catherine of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> was, it seems, so sensible, that she could not conceive that any traveller would return from that side of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> without visiting the wonders of this cavern; of which too the sight appeared to me to exceed all the descriptions I had heard of them. About two-thirds of the way up this temple, on each side, and fronting each other, are two doors or outlets into smaller grotts or excavations, and freely open to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Near and about the door-way, on the right <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, are several mutilated images, single and in groups. In one of the last, I remarked a kind of resemblance to the story of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> dividing the child, there standing a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> with a drawn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, holding in one hand an infant with the head downwards, which it appears in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> to cleave through the middle. The outlet Elephant outlet of the other on the left hand is into an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of about 20 feet in length and 12 in breadth; at the upper end of which, as you turn to the right, presents itself a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a> covered at top, of 10 or 12 feet deep, and in length answering to the breadth of the area: this joins to an apartment of the most regular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, an oblong square, with a door in perfect symmetry; and the whole executed in quite a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and manner from any of the oldest or best Grecian buildings anywhere extant. I took particular notice of some paintings round the cornices, nor for anything curious in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, but for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and freshness of the colouring, which must have lasted some thousands of years, on supposing it, as there is all reason to suppose it, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> itself. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the apartment is generally full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, its pavement or ground-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> not permitting it to be drawn off or to be soaked up. For it is to be observed, that even the cavern itself is not visitable after the rains until the ground of it has had <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to dry into a competent hardness."

ELEPHANTIASIS

Pages 26-26

called also the lepra of the Arabians, in Medicine, a chronic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, one of the two <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a> which affects the whole body, where even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> as well as the skin are covered with spots and tumours, which being <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, at last turn <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELEPHANTINE

Pages 26-26

in Roman antiquity, an appellation given to the books wherein were registered the transactions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and magistrates of Rome, of the emperors <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> generals of armies, and even of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> magistrates; the births and deaths of the people and other things relating to the census. They are supposed to have been so called, as being made of leaves of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> or elephants tusks. ELEPHANOMACHI. See ETHIOPIA.

ELEPHANTOPUS

Pages 26-26

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELEPHAS

Pages 26-26

the Elephant, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order of bruta. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELEUSINIA

Pages 26-28

in Grecian antiquity, a festival kept in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, every fourth year by some states, but by others every fifth. The Athenians celebrated it at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>: whence the name. Ceres, says an Athenian orator (Heracles), wandering in quest of her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Proserpine, came into Attica, where some good offices were done her, which is unlawful for those who are not initiated to hear. In return she conferred two unparalleled benefits; to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> is raised above the brute <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, from which the partakers derive sweeter hopes than other men enjoy, both as to the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and to eternity. It was the popular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the Eleusinian goddesses suggested prudent counsel to their votaries, and influenced their conduct; that these were respected in the infernal regions, and had precedence in the assemblies of the blest; while the unhallowed were in utter darkness, wallowing in mire, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> labouring to fill a leaky vessel. The Athenians were solicitous to secure these advantages to their children, by having them initiated as soon as was allowed. Ceres was supposed to be particularly partial to Eleusis and its vicinity. There were the memorials of her presence and of her bounty; the well named Gallichoirus, by which she had rested, in the reign of Erectheus; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on which the fat, named the sorrowful; the Rharian plain, where barley was sown; and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> and altar of Triptolemus, a husbandman whom she instructed in the culture of that grain, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of which succeeded to acorns. Her mysteries <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to possess a pre-eminence in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>, and to be accounted as much superior to all other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> festivals as the gods were to the heroes. Even the garments worn at the solemnity were supposed to partake of their efficacy, and to be endowed with signal virtues. It was usual to retain them until they were perishing; and then to dedicate them in the temple, or to reserve them for the purpose of wrapping newborn children. The mystic temple, as it was called, provided by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a> for the solemnity, created such awe by its sanctity as could be equalled only by the effect of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and magnitude, which excited astonishment in every beholder. The profane or uninitiated were forbidden to enter it on any pretence. Two young Arcadianians happened inadvertently to mix with the crowd. crowd at the season of the mysteries, and to go in; but the question suggested by their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> presently betrayed them, and their intrusion was punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, hierophant, or mystagogue, was taken from the Eumolpidae, a holy family flourishing at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and descended from Eumolpus, a shepherd and favourite of Ceres. He was enjoined celibacy, and wore a stole or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> garment, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and a wreath of myrtle. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> requisites in his character were strength and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, solemnity of deportment, magnificence, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>. Under him, besides many of inferior station, was the daduchus or torch-bearer, who had likewise his hair, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a>; the priest, who officiated at the altar; and the hiero-cervx or sacred <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALD">herald</a>; all very important personages. The latter was of a family which claimed the god <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> and Aglauros the daughter of Cecrops for its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The secrecy in which the mysteries were enveloped, served to enhance the idea of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, and to increase the desire of participation. It was so particular, that no person was allowed even to name the hierophant by whom he had been initiated. Public abhorrence and detestation awaited the babbler, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> directed he should die. The Athenians suffered none to be initiated into these mysteries but such as were members of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. This regulation, which compelled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, to become citizens of Athens, was strictly observed in the first ages of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, but afterwards all persons, barbarians excepted, were freely initiated. The festivals were divided into great and less mysteries. The less were instituted from the following circumstance. Hercules passed near Eleusis while the Athenians were celebrating the mysteries, and desired to be initiated. As this could not be done, because he was a stranger, and as Eumolpus was unwilling to displease him on account of his great power, and the services which he had done to the Athenians, another festival was instituted without violating the laws. It was called μεγάλη, and Hercules was solemnly admitted to the celebration and initiated. These less mysteries were observed at Agrae near the Ilissus. The greater were celebrated at Eleusis, from which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Ceres has been called Eleusinia. In later times the smaller festivals were preparatory to the greater, and no person could be initiated at Eleusis without a previous purification at Agrae. This purification they performed by keeping themselves pure, chaste, and unpolluted, during <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days; after which they came and offered sacrifices and prayers, wearing garlands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, called ευρέα or ευρέας, and having under their feet Διός κάρβον, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s skin, which was the skin of a victim offered to that god. The person who assisted was called ἐπιστήμης ἀπὸ ὕδατος <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which was used at the purification, and they themselves were called μυστικοί, the initiated. A year after the initiation at the less mysteries they sacrificed a sow to Ceres, and were admitted in the greater, and the secrets of the festivals were solemnly revealed to them, from which they were called ἑρώοι and ἐπιστήμης, inspectors. This festival was observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEDROMION">Boedromion</a> or September, and continued nine days from the 15th till the 23rd. During that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was unlawful Eleusinia, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or present any petition, on pain of forfeiting a thousand drachmas, or according to others on pain of death. It was also unlawful for those who were initiated to sit upon the cover of a well, to eat beans, mullets, or weasels. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any woman rode to Eleusis in a chariot, she was obliged by an edict of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a> to pay 6000 drachmas. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of this law was to destroy all distinction between the richer and poorer sort of citizens. When the season approached, the mystae or persons who had been initiated only in the lesser mysteries, repaired to Eleusis to be instructed in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> for the opening of the temple, with morning sacrifice, was performed. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> was then produced from the sanctuary. It was enveloped in symbolical figures of animals, which suggested words compendiously, in letters with ligatures, implicated, the tops huddled together, or disposed circularly like a wheel; the whole utterly inexplicable to the profane. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, which was called petroma, consisted of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> exactly fitted. The mysterious record was replaced after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, and closed up until a future festival. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rite was nocturnal, and confined to the temple and its environs. The mystae waited without, with impatience and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>. Lamentations and strange noises were heard. It thundered. Flashes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and of fire rendered the deep succeeding darkness more terrible. They were beaten, and perceived not the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. They beheld frightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a>, monsters, and phantoms of a canine form. They were filled with terror, became perplexed and unable to stir. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> then suddenly changed to brilliant and agreeable. The propylea or vestibules of the temple were opened, the curtains withdrawn, the hidden things displayed. They were introduced by the hierophant and daduchus, and the former showed them the mysteries. The splendor of illumination, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the temple and of the images, the fingering and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> which accompanied the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a>, all contributed to soothe the mind after its late agitation, and to render the wondering devotee tranquil and satisfied. After this inspection, or, as it was called, the εὐρέας, they retired, and others advanced. The succeeding days were employed in purification, in sacrifice, in pompous processions, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a>, at which they assisted, wearing mystic crowns. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> was called ἐπιστήμης ἀπὸ ὕδατος, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, you that are initiated; because they were commanded to purify themselves by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> in the sea. On the third day sacrifices, and chiefly a mullet, were offered; as also barley from a field of Eleusis. These oblations were called θύεις, and held so sacred that the priests themselves were not, as in other sacrifices, permitted to partake of them. On the fourth day they made a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, in which the παναγία, holy <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of Ceres, was carried about in a consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>, while on every side the people shouted Ἱερὸς Διός κάρβον, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">Hail</a>, Ceres! After these followed women, called ἐπιστήμης, who carried baskets, in which was saffron, carded <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, grains of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, a ferment, pomegranates, reeds, ivy boughs, certain cakes, &c. The fifth was called Ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιστήμης ἀπὸ ὕδατος, the torch day; because on the following night the people ran about with torches in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. It was usual to dedicate torches to Ceres, and contend which should offer the biggest. Eleusinia, biggeft, in commemoration of the travels of the god- drefs, and of her lighting a torch in the flames of Mount Ætna. The fifth day was called ἱακεῖς, from Iæchus, the fon of Jupiter and Ceres, who accompanied his mother in her fearch after Proferpine with a torch in his hand. From that circumference his statue had a torch in his hand, and was carried in solemn proceffion from the Ceramicus to Eleufis. The statue with thofe that accompanied it, called ἱακεῖον, was crowned with myrtle. In the way nothing was heard but finging and the noife of brazen kettles as the ve- taries danced along. The way through which they iffued from the city was called ἱερὸν ὁδός, the sacred way, the refuing place ἱερὸν ὄρος, from a fig-tree which grew in the neighbourhood. They alfo fopped on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Cephissus, where they derided thofe that paflèd by. After they had paflèd this bridge, they entered Eleufis by a place called ἐμπρὸς ἀνάλημα, the mystical en- trance. On thefeventh day were feports, in which the victors were rewarded with a meafure of barley, as that grain had been firft fown in Eleufis. The eighth day was called ἐπιβασίαις ἡμέρα, becaufe once Æfeclapius at his return from Epidaurus to Athens was initiated by the repetition of the lefs mysteries. It became cuftom- ary therefore to celebrate them a fecond time upon this, that fuch as had not hitherto been initiated might be lawfully admitted. The ninth and laft day of the festival was called Πληρωματική, corrihen veffels, becaufe it was ufual to fill two fuch veffels with wine; one of them being placed towards the caft, and the other to- wards the weft; which, after the repetition of fome myfical words, were both thrown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and the wine being fpilt on the ground, was offered as a libation. The story of Ceres and Proferpine, the foundation of the Eleufinian mysteries, was partly local. It was both verbally delivered, and repreffented in allegorical fhow. Proferpine was gathering flowers when she was stolen by Pluto. Hence the proceffion of the holy bafket, which was placed on a car dragged along by oxen, and followed by a train of females, fome carrying the myfical chefts, shouting, Hail, Ceres! At night a proceffion was made with lighted torches, to commemorate the goddef's fearching for her daughter. A meafure of barley, the grain which, it was believed, the had given, was the re- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> of the victors in the gymnic exercifes; and the tranflation at the temple had a reference to the le- gend. A knowledge of thefe things and places, from which the profane were excluded, was the amount of initiation; and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of it, which had been devised by craft, was fkillfully adapted to the reigning super- ftitions. The operation was forcible, and the effect in proportion. The priechood flourifhed as piety in- creafed. The difpensation was corrupt, but its ten- dency not malignant. It produced fandiety of man- ners and an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the focial duties; defire to be as distinguished by what was deemed virtue as by fihence. Some have fuppoled the principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> at this fef- tival to have been obfene and abominable, and that from thence proceeded all the myfierious fecrecy. They were carried from Eleufis to Rome in the reign of Adrian, where they were obferved with the fame ce- remonies as before, though perhaps with more free- dom and licentiousnefs. They lafted about 1800 years, and were at laft abolished by Theodosius the Great.

ELEUSIS

Pages 28-30

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town in Atti- ca, between <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a> and the Piraeus, celebrated for the feftivals of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>. See the preceding article.—Thofe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> were finally extinguifhed in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> upon the inva- fion of Alaric the Goth. Eleufis, on the overthrow of its goddef's and the ceftation of its gainful trafte, probably became foon an obfere <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, without cha- racter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. For fome ages, however, it was not entirely forfaken, as is evident from the vail conufumption of the ancient materials, and from the prefent re- mains, of which the following account is given by Dr Chandler*. "The port was finall and of a circular * Travels form. The flores of one pier are feen above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, into Greece, and the correffponding fide may be traced. About half-a- <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the fide is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> hill, which divides the plain. In the fide next the fea are traces of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and on the top are cutters cut in the rock. In the way to it, fome mafles of wall and rubble, partly ancient, are standing; with ruined churches; and beyond, a long broken aqueduct crofes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The Christian pirates had infefted the place fo much, that in 1676 it was abandoned. It is now a small village at the caltern extremity of the rocky brow, on which was once a caftle; and is inhabited by a few Albanian fa- milies, employed in the culture of the plain, and super- intended by a Turk, who resides in an old fquare tower. The proprietor was Achmet Aga, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> or prin- cipal perfon of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. "The myflic temple at Eleufis was planned by Ictinus, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> of the Parthenon. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a> was overfeer of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. It was of the Doric order; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> fo <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as to admit the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of a theatre. The columns on the pavement within, and their capi- tals, were raifed by Coroebus. Mentagenes of Xypete added the architraves and the pillars above them, which fustained the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. Another completed the edifice. This was a temple in antis, or without exterior columns, which would have occupied the room required for the victims. The affect was changed to Prothylos under Demetrius the Phaleræan; Philo, a famous architect, erecting a portico, which gave <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to the fabric, and rendered the entrance more commodious. The fite was beneath the brow, at the caft end, and encom- passed by the fortrefls. Some marbles, which are un- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> maflive, and fome pieces of the columns, remain on the fpot. The breadth of the cell is about 150 feet; the length, including the pronaos and por- tico, is 216 feet; the diameter of the columns, which are fluted, 6 inches from the bottom of the shafts, is 6 feet and more than 6 inches. The temple was a de- cafyle, or had 10 columns in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, which was to the caft. The peribolus or inclofure, which surround- ed it on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-eaft and on the fouth fide, meafures 387 feet in length from north to fouth, and 328 feet in breadth from caft to weft. On the weft fide it join- ed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of the weft end of the temple in a straight line. Between the weft wall of the inclofure and temple and the wall of the citadel was a paflage of 42 feet 6 inches wide, which led to the summit of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock at the north-weft <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the inclofure, on which are vifible the traces of a temple in antis, in length 74 feet 6 inches from north to fouth, and in breadth from the caft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUTHERIA">Eleutheria</a> east to the wall of the citadel, to which it joined on the west, 54 feet. It was perhaps that sacred to Tripolomus. This spot commands a very extensive view of the plains and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>. About three-fourths of the cottages are within the precincts of the mystic temple, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> tower stands on the ruined wall of the inclosure. "At a small distance from the north end of the enclosure is a heap of marble, consisting of fragments of the Doric and Ionic orders; remains, it is likely, of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> Propylea and of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, and of the Propyleum or gateway. Wheler <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> some large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> carved with wheat-ears and bundles of poppy. Near it is the butt of a colossal statue of excellent workmanship, maimed, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> disfigured; the breadth at the shoulders, as measured by Pococke, five feet and a half; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> on the head above two feet deep. It probably represented Proteusine. In the heap are two or three <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> pedestals; and on one are a couple of torches, crouched. We saw another fixed in the same stairs, which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> up the square tower on the outside. It belonged to the statue of a lady, who was hierophant or priestess of Proteusine, and had covered the altar of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> with silver. A well in the village was perhaps that called Callichorus, where the women of Eleusis were accustomed to dance in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Ceres. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> prevails, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the broken statue be removed, the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> cease. Achmet Aga was fully perplexed with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and declined permitting us to dig or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> there, until I had overcome his scruples by a present of a handsome snuff-box containing several zechins or pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>." Eleutheria, a festival celebrated at Platæa in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Eleutherius, or "the afforter of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>," by delegates from almost all the cities of Greece. Its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> originated in this: After the victory obtained by the Grecians under Paulus over Mardonius the Persian general, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Platæa, an altar and statue were erected to Jupiter Eleutherius, who had freed the Greeks from the tyranny of the barbarians. It was further agreed upon in a general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, by the advice of Ariftides the Athenian, that deputies should be sent every fifth year, from the different cities of Greece, to celebrate Eleutheria, festivals of liberty. The Platæans celebrated also an anniversary festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of those who had lost their lives in that famous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The celebration was thus: At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> was made with a trumpeter at the head, sounding a signal for battle. After him followed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, garlands, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bull, and certain free young men, as no signs of fertility were to appear during the solemnity, because they in whose honour the festival was instituted had died in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of their country. They carried libations of wine and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> in large-eared vessels, with jars of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and precious ointments. Last of all appeared the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, who, though not permitted at other times to touch <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, or wear garments of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, yet appeared clad in purple, and taking a water-pot out of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>-chamber, proceeded through the middle of the town, with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, towards the sepulchres. There he drew water from a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and washed and anointed the monuments, after which he sacrificed a bull upon a pile of wood, invoking Jupiter and infernal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, and inviting to the entertainment the souls of those happy heroes who had perished in the defence of their country. After this he filled a bowl with wine, saying, I drink to those who lost their lives in the defence of the liberties of Greece. There was also a festival of the same name observed by the Samians in honour of the god of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. Slaves also, when they obtained their liberty, kept a holiday, which they called Eleutheria. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELF">Elf</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> now almost obsolete, formerly used to denote a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAIRY">fairy</a> or hobgoblin; an imaginary being, the creature of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, superstition, and craft. See Fairy. Elf-Arrows, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given to the flints anciently fashioned into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>-heads, and still found fossil in Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and several other parts of the world; they are believed by the vulgar to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> by fairies, and that cattle are sometimes killed by them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Moray in Scotland, and formerly a bishop's see, is situated on the river Lossie, about six miles north from the Spey, in W. Long. 2° 25' N. Lat. 57° 40'. Mr Pennant says, it is a good town, and has many of the houses built over piazzas; but, excepting its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cattle-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, has little trade. It is principally remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> antiquities. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, now in ruins, has been formerly a very magnificent pile. The west door is very elegant and richly ornamented. The choir is very beautiful, and has a fine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> gallery running round it; and at the east end are two rows of narrow windows in an excellent Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is an octagon; the roof supported by a fine single <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> with neat carvings of coats of arms round the capital. There is still a great tower on each side of this cathedral; but that in the centre, with the spire and whole roof, are fallen in; and form most awful fragments, mixed with the battered monuments of knights and prelates. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> says, that Duncan, who was killed by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, lies buried here. The place is also crowded with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>-stones.—The cathedral was founded by Andrew de Moray, in 1224, on a piece of land granted by Alexander II.; and his remains were deposited in the choir, under a tomb of blue marble, in 1244. The great tower was built principally by John Innes bishop of this see, as appears by the inscription cut on one of the great pillars: "Hic Jacet in Xto, pater et dominus, Dominus Johannes de Innes, hujus ecclesiae Episcopus;—qui hoc notabile opus incepit et per septemnium aedificavit." Elgin is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough; and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Bruce. Elginshire, is the middle district of the ancient county of Moray. It is bounded on the north by that branch of the German ocean called the Moray Firth; on the east and south-east by Banffshire; on the south-west, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERNESS_SHIRE">Inverness-shire</a>; and on the west by the counties of Inverness and Nairn. It extends about 42 miles in length, and its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth is about 20. The southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is rocky and mountainous, called the district of Braemoray, which is occupied with extensive forests. The lower parts, towards the north, are rich and fertile; but might easily be rendered more productive. Elginshire, productive. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are, the Spey, Findhorn, and Lossie; all of which abound with salmon. It contains two royal boroughs, viz. Elgin, the county town, and Forres; and several considerable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, as Grantown, Garmouth, Lossiemouth, &c. The principal seats are Gordon-castle, the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Gordon; Castle <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">Grant</a>, the seat of Sir James Grant; Altyn, the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Cumming, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAYSHIRE">Morayshire</a> abounds with many remains of antiquity; the principal of which are the magnificent cathedral of Elgin, the priory of Pluscardine near the town of Elgin, the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Spynie, the castles of Lochindorb, Dunphail, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">dun</a> of Relugas, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Edenkellie. The ancient Scottish historians, particularly Fordun and Buchanan, give accounts of the Danes landing in Moray, about 1098, when Malcolm II. marched against them, and was defeated near Forres: after this they brought over their wives and children, and were in possession of the country for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; until they were finally expelled by that monarch, after the victories gained over them at Luncarty near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, at Barrie in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, and at Mortlach in the county of Banff. There are many monuments of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; the most remarkable of which is Sueno's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or pillar, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Nairn and Forres, in the parish of Rafford. Except freestone, <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a>, no mineral substance of value has been discovered. | Parish | <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> in 1755 | Population in 1790—1793 | |--------|-------------------|------------------------| | Alves | 1691 | 1111 | | Birnie | 525 | 402 | | Dallas | 700 | 888 | | Drainy | 1174 | 1040 | | Duffus | 1679 | 1800 | | Duthil | 1783 | 1110 | | Dyke and Moy | 1826 | 1529 | | Edenkellie | 1443 | 1800 | | Elgin | 6306 | 4534 | | Forres | 1993 | 2987 | | Kinloch | 1191 | 1031 | | Knockandoow | 1267 | 1500 | | Rafford | 1313 | 1072 | | Rothes | 1940 | 1500 | | St Andrews | 1132 | 777 | | Speymouth | 994 | 1347 | | Spynie | 865 | 602 | | Urquhart | 1110 | 1050 | Decrease, 28,934

ELEVATION

Pages 26-26

the same with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">Altitude</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> height. ELEVATION of the Hoft, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mats where the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> raises the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> above his head for the people to adore.

ELEVATOR

Pages 26-26

in Anatomy, the name of several muscles, so called from their serving to raise the parts of the body to which they belong.

ELEVATORY

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for raising depressed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fractured parts of the skull, to be applied after the integuments and periosteum are removed. See Surgery.

ELEVE

Pages 26-26

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> purely French, though of late used also in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Literally it signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scholar bred up under any one, being formed from the Italian allievo, an "apprentice" or "novice." It was first used by the French writers in speaking of painters; such a painter was an eleve of Da Vinci, of Raphael, &c. From <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> it came to be applied to such as studied or learned any other art under a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences, there were 20 eleves; and in that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, 10 eleves. The eleves are to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with the pensionaries. See Academy. The denomination eleve, however, has been fines suppremed, and that of adjoint substituted in its room; because every body did not know the tenie affixed to it by the academy; and now the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENSIONARY">pensionary</a> academists have not, as formerly, each of them an eleve; but the eleves are become adjoints, or affiliates of the academy.

ELI

Pages 30-30
high priest of the Israelites, and judge over them for forty years, was descended from Ithamar, a junior branch of the house of Aaron, and seems to have blended the priestly with the judicial character in the year 1156 before the commencement of the Christian era. It appears that the Jews were in a state of subjection or vassalage to the Philistines during the greater part of Eli's administration, and, what may at first appear singular, he contributed to the degeneracy of his countrymen, although his own piety and goodness were unquestionably great. He did not exert his magisterial authority in the exemplary punishment of vice, and even permitted his own sons with impunity to perpetrate the most atrocious acts of impiety and debauchery. This want of firmness, to give it no worse a name, was very reprehensible in one who filled such an important office, and peculiarly so in a man who was himself a faint. The celebrated Samson made his appearance during the administration of Eli, taking part in the management of public affairs for about twenty years, by whose astonishing deeds the independent spirit of that people was in some measure revived. The circumstances attending the death of Samson, which proved so calamitous to the nobility of the Philistines, might have induced the Jews to throw off the yoke; but they did not possess a sufficient degree of virtue and public spirit for such an exertion. Eli at this period was very far advanced in years, and, if possible, still more negligent in the discharge of his duty as a chief magistrate, allowing his two sons, Hophni and Phineas, to proceed to the most extravagant height of impiety and debauchery, whose example had a most powerful influence on the manners of the people. He was far from being unacquainted with their conduct, but he reproved them with such gentleness as was highly reprehensible, and but ill calculated to produce any change on the behaviour of his sons. The deity was so justly offended with this deportment of Eli, that a sacred seer was commissioned to upbraid him for his ingratitude and want of reformation. Young Samuel likewise was favoured with a vision of the approaching ruin of Eli's family, which he related to the otherwise venerable old man, on being solemnly adjured not to conceal a single circumstance. When Eli heard the declaration of the young prophet, being fully convinced that his conduct had been highly reprehensible, he exclaimed, "It is the Lord; let him do what seemeth him good." Soon after this the Israelites sustained a considerable loss in attempting to procure their emancipation, carrying the ark of God into their camp to animate the people, and intimidate their enemies; but the ark was captured by the Philistines, and Hophni and Phineas were slain. This intelligence having been brought to Eli, he no sooner heard that the ark of God was taken, than he fell backwards from his seat, broke his neck, and died in the 98th year of his age.

ELIAS

Pages 30-30

the prophet, memorable for having escaped the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> catastrophe of mankind; being taken up alive into heaven, in a fiery chariot, about 895 B.C. See the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>.

ELIJAH

Pages 30-31

who is sometimes denominated Elias, was one of the most distinguished of the Jewish prophets, and surnamed the Tishbite, probably from the district in which he was born. He began his prophetic office about 920 years before Christ, in the reign of wicked Ahab, by whom the Sidonian idolatry was introduced among the Israelites. The prophet was commissioned to appear before this impious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and threaten the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> drought as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for his crimes. The indignation of Ahab was so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> against the prophet for this prediction, that he resolved to punish him in a signal manner; but Elijah withdrew to a secret <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from his fury, at the divine command, where he was sustained in a miraculous manner. He was afterwards ordered to go to Saropta, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>, where a miraculous interposition of heaven, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of an indigent widow, sustained him for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, whose son the prophet restored to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. When the three years of famine, occasioned by the drought, were expired, the prophet was ordered to appear before the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and exhort him to that genuine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> which an interposition of the deity so very remarkable unquestionably demanded. He had an interview with Obadiah, the governor of the king's house, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and had frequently screened many from the vengeance of Jezebel the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, at the hazard of his own life. Fired with undaunted fortitude, the prophet said to Obadiah, "Go, tell thy <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, behold Elijah is here." The good man's regard for the prophet was so great, that he was afraid to deliver this message, since he knew that Ahab had used every effort to discover the prophet's retreat. The king was informed of his coming; and the first interview was distinguished by invectives on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the intrepid prophet and the proud sovereign, the former giving a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> on the following terms. The priests of the Sidonian gods, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the people of Israel, were to meet on Mount Carmel, where the prophet Elijah intended to give an incontrovertible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the almighty power of the God of Israel, and the total insignificance of the Sidonian divinities. For a detailed account of this memorable experiment, we must refer our readers to the book of Kings, as an abridgement of such a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> would do it manifest injury. It produced the fullest conviction in the minds of the Israelites, that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEHOVAH">Jehovah</a> alone was entitled to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>; and the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a> were instantaneously put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, as the most abominable perverters of the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. This was followed by abundance of rain, in answer to the devout prayers of the prophet; but his glorious triumph over idolatry so exasperated Jezebel, that she resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> the prophet, to avoid whose rage he fled into the wilderness, till the deity again employed him in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, but often hazardous, duties of a prophet. He afterwards foretold that Hazael should be king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, Jehu king over Israel; and he appointed Eliash the son of Shaphat to be his own successor. He denounced dreadful judgments against Ahab and his wicked queen Jezebel; but those which respected the king were not executed during his life, on account of the genuine repentance which he discovered. The successor of Ahab having been confined to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an accident, the god of Ekron was consulted relative to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, which induced the prophet to declare that he should assuredly die. The king being informed that it was Elijah who dared to send such a message, he dispatched a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> and fifty men to force him into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> presence; but they were destroyed by fire from heaven, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> shared the same fate. A third company confessed the visible interference of heaven in the prophet's behalf, and the captain throwing himself on the mercy of Elijah, went with him to the king. In the royal presence he undeniably repeated the same denunciation against the idolatrous monarch, which was very soon accomplished; and not long after this the holy prophet, at the divine command, divided under the waves of Jordan, dropped his prophetic mantle to the astonished Elisha, took the flaming chariot commissioned for his reception, and rode in majesty to heaven.

ELIQUATION

Pages 31-31

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, an operation by which a more fusible substance is separated from one that is less so, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> sufficiently intense to melt the former, but not the latter. Thus an alloy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> may be separated by a heat capable of melting the latter, but not the former. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIS">ELIS</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol6.html#article-ELEA">Elea</a>.

ELIS

Pages 31-32

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the district of that name in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, situated on the Peneus, which ran through it. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Phaedo the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, scholar of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, and friend of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>; who inscribes with his name the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. Pyrrho also was of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, at the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> called after him Pyrrhonists. The city of Elis owed its origin to an union of small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> after the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. It was not encompassed immediately with a wall; for it had the care of the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, and its territory was solemnly consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. To invade <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not protect it was deemed impiety; and armies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> marching through, delivered up their weapons, which, on their quitting it, were restored. Amid warring states the city enjoyed repose, was restored to by strangers, and flourished. The region round about it was called cale or hollow, from the inequalities. The country was reckoned fertile, and particularly fit for the raising of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. This, which grew nowhere else in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, equalled the produce of Judea in fineness, but was not so <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. Elis was a school, as it were, for Olympia, which was distant 37 miles. The athletic exercises were performed there, before the more solemn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, in a gymnasion, by which the Peneus ran. The helanodics or prefects of the games paired the rival combatants by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> called Plethron or The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a>. Within the wall grew lofty <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>-trees; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which was called the Xylios, were separate courses made for the foot-races. A smaller court was called the Quadrangle. The prefects, when chosen, resided for ten months in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> erected for their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, to be instructed in the duties of their office. They attended before sunrise to preside at the races; and again at noon, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> appointed for the pentathlum or five sports. The horses were trained in the agora or market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which was called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPODROME">Hippodrome</a>. In the gymnasion were altars and a cenotaph of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>. The women, besides other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> their bosoms in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, on a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> toward sunset. There also was the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, in which extemporary harangues were spoken and compositions recited. It was hung round with bucklers for ornaments. A way led from it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> through the Street of Silence; and another to the market-place, which was planned with streets between porticoes of the Doric order adorned with altars and images. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, one had a circular peristyle or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a>; but the image had been removed and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> was fallen in the time of Paeanias.
