The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was ancient as was also a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, one of the deities principally adored at Elis. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> had a temple in the citadel, with an image of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, made At the gate leading to Olympia was the monument of a person, who was buried, as an oracle had commanded, neither within nor without the city. The structures of Elis, Dr Chandler observes, seem to have been raised with materials far less elegant and durable than the produce of the Ionian and Attic quarries. The ruins are of brick, and not considerable, consisting of pieces of ordinary wall, and an octagon building with niches, which, it is supposed, was the temple with a circular peristyle. These stand detached from each other, ranging in a vale southward from the wide <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the river Peneus; which, by the margin, has several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, perhaps relics of the gymnasion. The citadel was on a hill, which has on the top some remnants of a wall. ELISHA the prophet, famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> he performed, died about 830 B.C. See the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>.

ELISION

Pages 32-32

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suppressing a vowel at the end of a word, for the sake of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the next word beginning with a vowel. Elisions are pretty frequently met with in English <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, but more frequently in the Latin, French, &c. They chiefly consist in suppressions of the a, e, and i, though an elision supposes any of the other <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>.

ELIXATION

Pages 32-32

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, the extracting the virtues of ingredients by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stewing.

ELIXIR

Pages 32-32

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> tincture extracted from many efficacious ingredients. Hence the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a tincture and an elixir seems to be this, that a tincture is drawn from one ingredient, sometimes with an addition of another to open it and to dispose it to yield to the menstruum; whereas an elixir is a tincture extracted from several ingredients at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

ELIZABETH

Pages 32-33
queen of England, daughter of Henry VIII. and Anne Boleyn, was born at Greenwich, September 7, 1533. According to the humour of the times, she was early instructed in the learned languages, first by Grindal, who died when she was about 17, and afterwards by the celebrated Roger Ascham. She acquired likewise considerable knowledge of the Italian, Spanish, and French languages. Dr Grindal was also her preceptor in divinity, which she is said to have studied with uncommon application and industry. That Elizabeth became a Protestant, and her sister Mary a Papist, was the effect of that cause which determines the religion of all mankind; namely, the opinion of those by whom they were educated: and this difference of opinion, in their tutors, is not at all surprising, when we recollect, that their father Harry was of both religions, or of neither. But the studies of Elizabeth were not confined merely to languages and theology: she was also instructed in the political history of the ancients; and was so well skilled in music, as to sing and play "artfully and sweetly." After the short reign of her brother Edward, our heroine being then about 20 years of age, her firebrand sister ascending to the crown, Elizabeth experienced a considerable degree of persecution, so as to be not a little apprehensive of a violent death. She was accused of nobody knows what; imprisoned; and, we are told, inhumanly treated. At last, by the intercession of King Philip of Spain, she was set at liberty; Elizabeth, which she continued to enjoy, till, on the death of her pious father, she, on the 17th of November 1558, ascended the throne of England. Her political history as a queen, is universally known and admired: but see (Hier attention to the government of her kingdom did glory of) not totally suspend her pursuit of learning. Ascham, in his Schoolmaster, tells us, that, about the year 1563, five years after her accession, she being then at Windsor, besides her perfect readiness in Latin, Italian, French, and Spanish, she read more Greek in one day than some prebendaries of that church did read Latin in a whole week, (p. 21.)—She employed Sir John Fortescue to read to her Thucydides, Xenophon, Polybius, Euripides, Aeschines, and Sophocles. (Ballard, p. 219.) That the Latin language was familiar to her, is evident from her speech to the university of Oxford, when she was near sixty; also from her spirited answer to the Polish ambassador in the year 1568. And that she was also skilled in the art of poetry, appears not only from the several scraps which have been preserved, but likewise from the testimony of a contemporary writer, Puttenham, in his Art of Engl. Poetry (a very scarce book). These are his words: "But, last in recital, "and first in degree, is the queen, whose learned, de- "licate, noble muse, easily furnishteth all the rest, "for satire, sweetness, or subtlety, be it in ode, elegy, "epigram, or any other kind of poem," &c. In this author are to be found only a specimen of 16 verses of her English poetry. "But," says Mr Walpole, "a "greater instance of her genius, and that too in La- "tin, was her extempore reply to an insolent prohibi- "tion delivered to her from Philip II. by his ambassa- "dor, in this tetralectic. Te vete ne pergas bello defendere Belgas: Quae Dracus erupit, nunc refittantur oportet: Quas pater everit, jubeo te condere collas: Religio papae fac refittatur ad unguaem. "She instantly answered him, with as much spirit as she used to return his invasions; Ad Graecas, bone rex, fient mandata kalendas." Being earnestly pressed by a Roman priest, during his persecution, to declare her opinion concerning the real presence of Christ's body in the wafer, she answered, Christ was the word that spake it; He took the bread, and brake it: And what that word did make it, That I believe, and take it. Fuller's Holy State. She gave the characters of four knights of Nottinghamshire in the following distich: Gervase the Gentle, Stanhope the stout, Markham the lion, and Sutton the loud. Walp. Cat. Coming into a grammar-school, she characterized three classic authors in this hexameter: Persius a crab-staff; bawdy Martial; Ovid a fine wag. Full. Worth. of Warw. 126. Sir. Sir Walter Raleigh having wrote on a window, Fain would I climb, yet fear I to fall; She immediately wrote under it, If thy heart fail thee, climb not at all. Worth. of Devon/b. 261. Doubtless, she was a woman of singular capacity and extraordinary acquirements; and, if we could forget the story of the Scottish Mary, and of her favourite Essex, together with the burning of a few Anabaptists; in short, could we forbear to contemplate her character through the medium of religion and morality, we might pronounce her the most illustrious of illustrious women. See further the articles ENGLAND, MARY, and SCOTLAND. She died in her palace at Richmond, the 24th of March 1602, aged 73, having reigned 44 years; and was interred in the chapel of Henry VII. in Westminster Abbey. Her successor James erected a magnificent monument to her memory.—She wrote, 1. The Mirror, or Glass of the Sinful Soul. This was translated out of French verse into English prose, when she was eleven years old. It was dedicated to Queen Catharine Parr. Probably it was never printed; but the dedication and preface are prefixed in the Spilge epistolae, in Hearne's edition of Livii Floridensis, p. 161. 2. Prayers and Meditations, &c. Dedicated to her father, dated at Hatfield, 1545. Manuscript, in the royal library. 3. A Dialogue out of Xenophon, in Greek, between Hiero a King, yet some time a private person, and Simonides a Poet, as touching the life of the Prince and Private Man. First printed, from a manuscript in her majesty's own handwriting, in the Gentleman's Magazine for 1743. 4. Two Orations of Isocrates, translated into Latin. 5. Latin Oration at Cambridge. Preserved in the king's library: also in Hollinshed's Chron. p. 1206; and in Fuller's Hist. of Camb. p. 138. 6. Latin Oration at Oxford. See Wood's Hist. and Antiq. of Oxf. lib. i. p. 289, also in Dr Jebb's Appendix to his Life of Mary Queen of Scots. 7. A Comment on Plato. 8. Boethius de consolatione philosophica, translated into English anno 1593. 9. Sallust de bello Jugurthino, translated into English anno 1595. 10. A play of Euripides, translated into Latin, (Cat. of Royal Auth.). 11. A prayer for the use of her fleet in the great expedition in 1596. 12. Part of Horace's Art of Poetry, translated into English anno 1593. 13. Plutarch de curiositate, translated into English. 14. Letters on various occasions to different persons: several speeches to her parliament; and a number of other pieces. Elizabeth Petrowna, (daughter of Peter the Elizabeth Great), the last empress of Russia, distinguished herself by her signal clemency. She made a vow, that no person should be put to death in her reign, and she strictly observed it. The example was followed, and confirmed by law, under the august sovereign of Russia, Catherine II. Elizabeth died in 1762, in the 21st year of her reign and 52d of her age.

ELL

Pages 33-33

(alua,) a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> which obtains, under different denominations, in most countries, whereby cloths, stuffs, linens, silks, &c. are usually measured; answering nearly to the yard of England, the canna of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the vara of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, the palm of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, &c. Servius <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the ell to be the space contained between the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> when stretched forth; but Suetonius makes it only the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a>. The ells most frequently used with us are the English and Flemish; the former containing three feet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one yard and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; the latter only 27 inches, or three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a yard; so that the ell English is to the Flemish ell as five to three. In Scotland, the ell contains 37\(\frac{1}{10}\) English inches. M. Ricard, in his Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, reduces the ells thus: 100 ells of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> are equal to 98\(\frac{1}{3}\) of Brabant, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>; to 58\(\frac{1}{2}\) of England and France; to 120 of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, Frankfort, Leipzig, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>; 125 of Brellaw; 110 of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRONTHEIM">Drontheim</a>; and 117 of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>.

ELLENCHUS

Pages 25-25

in Logic, by the Latins called argumentum et inquisitio, is a vicious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fallacious argument, which deceives under the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; the same with what is otherwise called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOPHISM">sophism</a>. ELEPHANT. See Elephas, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. American ELEPHANT: An animal only known in a fossil state, and that but partially, from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, some of the jaw-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, the thigh-bones, and vertebrae, found with many others five or six feet beneath the surface on the banks of the Ohio. But these bones differ in several respects from those of the elephant; for which, see Fossil Bones. As yet the living animal has evaded our search. Mr Pennant thinks it "more than probable, that it still exists in some of those remote parts of the vast new continent unpenetrated yet by Europeans. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> maintains and continues every created <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; and we have as much assurance that no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of animals <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> any more cease while the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> remains, than feed-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or night." See MAMMUTH. ELEPHANT-Beetle. See Scarabaeus, Entomology Index. Knights of the ELEPHANT, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, conferred upon none but persons of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and merit. It is also called the order of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> is said to have been owing to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> among the Danish croises having killed an elephant, in an expedition against the Saracens, in 1184; in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of which, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Canute instituted this order, the badge of which is a towered elephant, with an image of the holy virgin encircled with rays, and hung on a watered sky-colored ribbon, like the george in England.

ELLIOT

Pages 33-35

the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> George Augustus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Heathfield, was the youngest son of the late Sir Gilbert Elliot, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARONET">Baronet</a>, of Stobbs (A) in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROXBURGHSHIRE">Roxburghshire</a>; and was born about the year 1718. He received the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under a private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>; and at an early <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was sent to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, where he made considerable progress in classical learning, and spoke with fluency and elegance the German and French languages. Being designed for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> life, he was sent from thence to the celebrated Ecole Royale du Genie Militaire, conducted by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Vauban at La Fere in Picardy; where he laid the foundation of what he so conspicuously exhibited at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Gibraltar. He completed his military course on the continent by a tour, for the purpose of seeing in practice what he had studied in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some time as a volunteer in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Mr Elliot returned in the 17th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, Scotland; and was the same year, 1735, introduced by his father Sir Gilbert to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">Peers</a> of the 23rd regiment of foot, then lying at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, as a youth anxious to bear arms for (A) The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and honourable family of Elliot of Stobbs, as well as the collateral branch of Elliot of Minto in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and of Elliot of Port-Elliot in Cornwall, are originally from Normandy. Their ancestor, Mr Aliott, came over with William the Conqueror, and held a distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. There is a traditional anecdote in the family relating to an honourable distinction in their coat, which, as it corresponds with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, bears the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. When William set foot on English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, he flipped and fell on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. He sprung up, and exclaimed that it was a happy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>—he had embraced the country of which he was to become the lord. Upon this Aliott drew his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and swore by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a soldier, that he would maintain, at the hazard of his blood, the right of his lord to the sovereignty of the earth which he had embraced. On the event of the conquest, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William added to the arms of Aliott, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, on a field azure, an arm and sword as a crest, with the motto, Per fata, per ignes, fortiter et recte. for his king and country. He was accordingly entered as a volunteer in that regiment, where he continued for a year or more. From the 23rd regiment he went into the engineer corps at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOLWICH">Woolwich</a>, and made great progress in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; until his uncle Colonel Elliot brought him in his adjutant of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> grenadiers. With these troops he went upon service to Germany, and was with them in a variety of actions. At the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Dettingen he was wounded. In this regiment he bought the rank of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, and afterwards purchased the lieutenant-colonelcy from Colonel Brewerton, who succeeded to his uncle. On arriving at this rank, he resigned his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> as an engineer, which he had enjoyed along with his other rank, and in which service he had been actively employed very much to the advantage of his country. He received the instructions of the famous engineer Bellidor, and made himself completely <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the science of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUNNERY">gunnery</a>. Had he not so diffidently resigned his rank in the engineer department, he would <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, by regular progression, have been at the head of that corps. Soon after this he was appointed aide-de-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> to George II. and was distinguished for his military skill and discipline. In the year 1759, he quitted the second troop of horse grenadier guards, being selected to raise, form, and discipline, the first regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> horse, called after him Elliot's. As soon as they were raised and formed, he was appointed to the command of the cavalry in the expedition on the coasts of France, with the rank of brigadier-general. After this he passed into Germany, where he was employed on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, and greatly distinguished himself in a variety of movements; where his regiment displayed a strictness of discipline, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and enterprise, which gained them signal honour; and indeed they have been the pattern regiment both in regard to discipline and appointment, to the many light dragoon troops that have been since raised in our service. From Germany he was recalled for the purpose of being employed as second in command in the memorable expedition against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVANNAH">Havannah</a>; the circumstances of which conquest are well known. On the peace, his gallant regiment was reviewed by the king, when they presented to his majesty the standards which they had taken from the enemy. Graciously with their fine discipline and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> character, the king asked General Elliot what mark of his favour he could bestow on his regiment equal to their merit? He answered, that his regiment would be proud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his majesty should think, that, by their services, they were entitled to the distinction of Royals. It was accordingly made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> regiment, with this flattering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, "The 15th, or King's Royal Regiment of Light Dragoons." At the same time the king expressed a desire to confer some honour on the general himself; but the latter declared, that the honour and satisfaction of his majesty's approbation of his services was his best reward. During the peace he was not idle. His great talents in the various branches of the military art gave him ample employment. In the year 1775, he was appointed to succeed General A'<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> as commander-in-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the forces in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; but did not continue long in this station, not even long enough to unpack all his trunks; for finding that interferences were made by petty authority derogatory of his own, he resented the practice with becoming spirit; and not choosing to disturb the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the sister <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> personal to himself, he solicited to be recalled. He accordingly was so, and appointed to the command of Gibraltar in a fortunate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> for the safety of that important fortress. The system of his life, as well as his education, peculiarly qualified him for this trust. He was perhaps the most abstemious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the age; neither indulging himself in animal food or wine. He never slept more than four hours at a time; so that he was up later and earlier than most other men. He so inured himself to habits of hardiness, that the things which are difficult and painful to other men, were to him his daily practice, and rendered pleasant by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. It could not be easy to starve such a man into a surrender, nor possible to surprise him. The example of the commander in chief in a besieged garrison had the most persuasive efficacy in forming the manners of a soldiery. Like him his brave followers came to regulate their lives by the most strict rules of discipline before there arose a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for so doing; and severe <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, with short diet, became habitual to them by their own choice. The military system of discipline which he introduced, and the preparations which he made for his defence, were contrived with so much judgment, and executed with so much <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, that he was able with a handful of men to preserve his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> against an attack, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of which, even without the vigour, had been sufficient to exhaust any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> set of men. Collected within himself, he in no instance destroyed, by premature attacks, the labours which would cost the enemy time, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, and expense to complete; he deliberately observed their approaches, and seized on the proper moment, with the keenest perception, in which to make his attack with success. He never spent his ammunition in useless parade or in unimportant attacks. He never relaxed from his discipline by the appearance of security, nor hazarded the lives of his garrison by wild experiments. By a cool and temperate demeanour, he maintained his station for three years of constant investment, in which all the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> were employed. All the eyes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> were on this garrison; and his conduct has justly exalted him to the most elevated rank in the military annals of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. On his return to England, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> of the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> was as forward as the public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in giving him that distinguished mark his merit deserved. Both houses of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> voted an unanimous address of thanks to the general. The king conferred on him the honour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a> of the Bath, with a pension during his own and a second life of his own appointment; and on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 14, 1787, his majesty advanced him to the peerage, by the title of Lord Heathfield, Baron Gibraltar, permitting him to take, in addition to his family arms, the arms of the fortress he had so bravely defended, to perpetuate to futurity his noble conduct. His lordship died on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1790, at his chateau at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, of a second stroke of the palsy, after having for some weeks preceding enjoyed tolerable good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and an unusual flow of spirits. His death happened two days before he was to have set out for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a> in his way to Gibraltar; of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he was once more appointed to the defense, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>, in the view of an approaching <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He married <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Francis Drake of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>; and had by her (who died in 1769) Francis-Augustus, now Lord Heathfield, lieutenant-colonel of the 6th regiment of horse.

ELLIPOMACROSTYLA

Pages 35-35

an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, from the Greek, ἐλλιπος imperfect, παραγεν <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and ῥυμα a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>; which expresses an imperfect crystal with a long column, one end of the column being affixed to some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body, and composed of thin and slender hexangular columns, terminated by hexagonal pyramids.

ELLIPOPACHYSTYLA

Pages 35-35

an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, derived from the Greek, ἐλλιπος imperfect, παραγεν thick, and ῥυμα a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, and expresses a crystal of the imperfect kind with a thick column.

ELLIPSIS

Pages 35-35

in *<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>*, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNTAX">syntax</a>, where-in one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more words are not expressed; and from this deficiency it has got the name *ellipsis*.

ELLISIA

Pages 35-35

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 28th order, Luridae. See *<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*.

ELLYS

Pages 35-35

Dr Anthony**, who was born in 1693, and educated at Clarehall, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, after rising through many inferior degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, was, in 1752, promoted to the see of St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s. He died at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> in 1761, and is mentioned here only for the sake of his works, which are less known than they should in the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> opinions. They are, besides occasional sermons, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">Plea</a> for the Sacramental Test, as a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> security to the Church established, and very conducive to the welfare of the State. 2. Remarks on Hume's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>. 3. Tracts on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a> spiritual and temporal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in England, addressed to J. N. Esq., at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle; the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was printed in 1763, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1765. In these tracts, as the editors of them truly observe, he "discovers not only fine parts, extensive knowledge, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgment, but a heart overflowing with benevolence and candour, and a most Christian temper; for he always thought a person, though on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side of the question, with principles of perfection, to be a worse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> than he that was on the wrong." This amiable and respectable writer affords in his own conduct a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that a man may be steadily attached to a party, without wishing to encroach upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of others. **ELM.** See *Ulmus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*.

ELMACINUS

Pages 35-35

George**, author of a *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Saracens*, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> towards the middle of the 13th century. His history comes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from Mahomet to the year of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a> 512, answering to the year of our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> 1134; in which he sets down year by year, in a very concise manner, whatever regards the Saracen empire, intermixed with some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> relating to the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. His abilities must have been considerable; since, though he professed Christianity, he held an office of trust near the persons of the Mahometan princes. He was son to Yafer Al Amid, secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> under the Elmacinus sultans of Egypt for 45 years; and in 1238, when his father died, succeeded him in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. His history of the Saracens was translated from Arabic into Latin by Erpinius; and printed in these two languages in folio, at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in 1625. Erpinius died before the publication; but Golinus took care of it, and added a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>. It was dedicated to Erpinius's widow to Dr Andrews, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>. **ELOCUTION.** See *Oratory, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> III*.

ELOGY

Pages 35-35

a praise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> bestowed on any person or thing, in consideration of its merit. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of elogy consists in an expressive brevity. Eulogiums should not have so much as one epithet, properly so called, nor two words <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>: they should strictly adhere to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>: for extravagant and improbable elogies rather lessen the character of the person or thing they would extol. **ÉLOHI, Elohi, or Elohim**, in scripture, one of the names of God. But it is to be observed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, princes, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, judges, and even false gods, are sometimes called by this name. The sequel of the discourse is what afflicts us in judging rightly concerning the true meaning of this word. It is the same as *Eloha*. One is the singular, the other the plural. Nevertheless Elohim is often construed in the singular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, particularly when the true God is spoken of: but when false gods are spoken of, it is construed rather in the plural.

ELOINED

Pages 35-35

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>*, signifies restrained <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hindered from doing something: thus it is said, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> those within <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> be elained, so that they cannot sue personally, their next friend shall sue for them.

ELONGATION

Pages 35-35

in *<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>*, is an imperfect luxation, occasioned by the stretching <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lengthening of the ligaments of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>.

ELOPEMENT

Pages 35-35

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>*, is where a married woman departs from her husband, and cohabits with an adulterer; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the husband is not obliged to allow her any alimony out of her estate, nor is he chargeable for necessaries for her of any kind. However, the bare advertising a wife in the gazette, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, is not a legal notice to persons in general not to trust her; though a personal notice given by the husband to particular persons is said to be good.—An <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> lies, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> damages may be recovered, against a person for carrying away and detaining another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s wife.

ELOQUENCE

Pages 35-35

the art of speaking well, so as to affect and persuade. See *Oratory*.

ELPHINSTON

Pages 35-36

William**, a Scotch prelate and statesman of considerable eminence, who flourished in the end of the 15th and commencement of the 16th century, was born at Glasgow in the year 1431. At the university of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> he received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and in the learning which distinguished that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he made extraordinary proficiency. His studies being completed, he went over to France, to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of... Elphinston of the civil and canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he afterwards became a professor, and for the space of five years acquired considerable reputation in the discharge of his duty. On his return to Scotland, he entered into holy orders, was soon appointed official of Glasgow, and afterwards of St Andrews. He was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; and on a misunderstanding taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between James III. of Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. of France, his powerful mediation at the latter <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in conjunction with the bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNKELD">Dunkeld</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, effected an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> reconciliation. As Elphinston on this occasion displayed such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and eloquence, the king was so grateful for his meritorious services, that he rewarded him with the see of Rothes, from which he was translated to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Aberdeen about the year 1484, and also appointed to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> office of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which he managed with so much moderation and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, that all parties esteemed and admired him. When the civil wars broke out between James and the discontented <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, Bishop Elphinston appears to have declined all interference with public affairs of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and confined himself to the discharge of his ministerial duties. But when James IV. ascended the throne, his abilities as a statesman were again called forth, and he was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian, in order to bring about a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> between his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> master and the emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>; but he had been previously promised to another. Yet the bishop's mission was not without its salutary effects, as he was the means of terminating an enmity which had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> existed between the Dutch and Scots. This he conducted in such a masterly manner, that James never undertook any thing of importance, without first procuring the sanction of his approbation. He was equally the zealous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learning; and it is generally believed that the establishment of a university at Aberdeen was entirely owing to his influence with the Pope, from whom he obtained a bull for that purpose; and by his exertions was King's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> undertaken and completed. He bequeathed, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his decease, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for its support. He terminated his mortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> in 1514, about 83 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which advanced period his constitutional vigour was very little impaired, and all the faculties of his mind were in full force; but the serious losses at the memorable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Flodden had broken his heart. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which is among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> of Sir Thomas Fairfax, in the Bodleian library at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>.

ELSIMBURG

Pages 36-36

a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Gothland, and territory of Schonen, seated Elsinburg on the side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, over against Elsinore. It was formerly a fortress belonging to the Danes; but all the fortifications were demolished in 1679, and there is only one tower of a castle which remains undemolished. It now belongs to Sweden. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 20' N. Lat. 56° 2'.

ELSINORE

Pages 36-36
or ELINGOOR, a port town of Denmark, seated on the Sound, in the isle of Zealand. E. Long. 13° 23' N. Lat. 56° 0'.—It was a small village, containing a few fishermen's huts, until 1445, when it was made a trading town by Eric of Pommerania; who conferred upon the new settlers considerable immunities, and built a castle for their defence. From that period it gradually increased in size and wealth, and is now the most commercial place in Denmark next to Copenhagen. It contains about 5000 inhabitants, amongst whom are a considerable number of foreign merchants, and the conduits of the principal nations trading to the Baltic. The passage of the Sound is guarded by the fortress of Cronberg, which is situated upon the edge of a peninsulae promontory, the nearest point of land from the opposite coast of Sweden. It is strongly fortified towards the shore by ditches, bastions, and regular entrenchments; and towards the sea by several batteries, mounted with 60 cannon, the largest whereof are 45 pounders. Every vessel, as it passes, lowers her top-sails, and pays a toll at Elsinore. It is generally asserted, that this fortress guards the Sound; and that all the ships must, on account of the shoal waters and currents, steer so near the batteries as to be exposed to their fire in case of refusal. This, however, is a mistaken notion. On account indeed of the numerous and opposite currents in the Sound, the safest passage lies near the fortress; but the water in any part is of sufficient depth for vessels to keep at a distance from the batteries, and the largest ships can even sail close to the coast of Sweden. The constant discharge, however, of the toll, is not so much owing to the strength of the fortress as to a compliance with the public law of Europe. Many disputes have arisen concerning the right by which the crown of Denmark imposes such a duty. The kings of Sweden, in particular, claiming an equal title to the free passage of the Strait, were for some time exempted by treaty from paying it; but in 1720, Frederic I. agreed that all Swedish vessels should for the future be subject to the usual imposts. All vessels, before a small duty, rated at 1½ per cent. of their cargoes, except the English, French, Dutch, and Swedish, which pay only one per cent.; and in return the crown takes the charge of constructing light houses, and erecting signals to mark the shoals and rocks, from the Cattegat to the entrance into the Baltic. The tolls of the Sound, and of the two Belts, supply an annual revenue of above 100,000l.

ELUDING

Pages 37-37

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of evading <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rendering a thing vain and of no effect; a dexterous getting clear, or eloping out of an affair, difficulty, embarrassment, or the like. We say, to elude a proposition, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of chicaneery is, to elude the force of the laws; This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> has not resolved the difficulty, but studied it. Alexander, says the historian, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the Gordian knot, either eluded the oracle or fulfilled it: Ille neguicquam lucetatus cum latentibus nodis, Nikhil, inquit, intereft, quomodo folvatur; gladioque ruptis omnibus loris, oraculi forttem vel cludit, vel impiebit.

ELUTRIATION

Pages 37-37

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, an operation performed by washing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substances with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, stirring them well together, and hastily pouring off the liquid, while the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> remains suspended in it, that it may thereby be separated from the heavier part. By this operation metallic ores are separated from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and other unmetallic particles adhering to them.

ELVAS

Pages 36-37

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town, and one of the best and most important in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, seated in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>, a few miles from the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is built on a mountain, and is strongly fortified with works of free-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The streets of the town are handsome, and the houses neat; and there is a cistern so large, that it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> hold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> enough to supply the whole town six months. The water is conveyed to it by a magnificent aqueduct, three <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">ELY</a> three miles in length, sustained in some places by four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, one upon another. It was bombarded by the French and Spaniards in 1726, but without effect. It has generally a garrison of 1000 men. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> founded an academy here, in 1733, for young gentlemen. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 28. N. Lat. 38.

ELVELA

Pages 37-37

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the cryptogamia clas, and order of fungi. The fungus is turbinate, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> like an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> cone. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELY

Pages 37-37

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and bishop's see of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, situated about 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 51. N. Lat. 52. 24. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself, including the territory around; and has a judge who determines all causes civil and criminal within its limits. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> hath undergone various alterations since it was first established by Etheldreda, the wife of Egfride, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, who founded a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> here, and planted it with virgins, and became the first abbess of it herself. The Danes entirely ruined this establishment; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHELWOLD">Ethelwold</a>, the 27th bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, rebuilt the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, and filled it with monks; to whom King Edgar, and many succeeding monarchs, bestowed many privileges, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; so that this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> became in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the best of any in England. Richard, the 11th <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, wishing to free himself of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, within whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> his monastery was situated, and not liking so powerful a superior, he made great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with King Henry I. to get Ely erected into a bishopric; and spared neither purse nor prayers to bring this about. He even brought the bishop of Lincoln to consent to it, by giving him and his successors the manors of Bugden, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIGGLESWADE">Biggleswade</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPALDING">Spalding</a>, which belonged to the abbey, in lieu of his jurisdiction; but he lived not to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his industry and ambition, he dying before his abbey was erected into a see. His successor was the first bishop of Ely; but the great privileges the bishop enjoyed were almost wholly taken away, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> much restricted, by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, 27th Henry VIII. regarding the restoring to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> royalties: So, instead of being palatine of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Ely, the bishop and his temporal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> were by that act declared to be from thenceforth justices of the peace in the said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. This diocese contains all Cambridgeshire, and the isle of Ely, excepting Hellham, which belongs to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, and 15 other parishes, that are in the diocese of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>; but it has a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, viz. Emmeth. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of parishes in this diocese are 141, whereof 75 are inappropriate. It hath but one archdeacon, viz. of Ely. It is valued in the king's books at 2134l. 18s. 5d. The clergy's tenth amounting to the sum of 384l. 14s. 9½d. The bishopric is computed to be worth annually 4000l. The church is dedicated to St <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, as it now appears, has been the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of several of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. The west parts were rebuilt by Bishop Ridal; the choir and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a> were begun by Bishop Norwold, and finished by Bishop <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRODSHAM">Frodsham</a>. This see hath given two saints and two cardinals to the church of Rome; and to the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chancellors, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> lord treasurers, one lord privy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer, one chancellor to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, two masters of the rolls, and three almoners. To this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> belong a bishop, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, an archdeacon, eight prebendaries, with vicars, lay-clerks, choristers, a schoolmaster, usher, and 28 king's scholars.

ELYMAIS

Pages 37-37

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Elam, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. We are told (1 Mac. vi. 1.) that Antiochus Epiphanes, having understood that there were very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> treasures lodged in a temple at Elymais, determined to go and plunder it: but the citizens getting intelligence of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, made an insurrection, forced him out of the city, and obliged him to fly. The author of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a> (ix. 2.) calls this city Persepolis, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> because formerly it was the capital of Persia; for it is known from other accounts, that Persepolis and Elymais were two very different cities, the latter situated upon the Eulaeus, the former upon the Araxis.

ELYMUS

Pages 37-37

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the fourth order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELYOT

Pages 37-37

Sir Thomas, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of eminent learning in the 16th century, was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, travelled into foreign countries, and upon his return was introduced to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. His learning recommended him to Henry VIII. who conferred the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> on him, and employed him in several embassies: particularly in 1532, to Rome, about the divorce of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Catharine, and afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. about 1536. He wrote, The Castle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a>, the Governor, Banquet of Sapience, Of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">Education</a> of Children, De rebus memorabilibus Anglie, and other books; and was highly esteemed by all his learned contemporaries.

ELYSIUM

Pages 37-38

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the inferi or lower world, furnished with fields, meads, agreeable woods, groves, shades, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, &c. whither the souls of good people were supposed to go after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, and Æneas, were supposed to have have descended into Elysium in their life <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and to have returned again; (Virg. lib. vi. ver. 638, &c.) Tibullus (lib. i. eleg. 3.) gives us fine descriptions of the Elysian fields. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> opposes Elysium to Tartarus; which was the place where the wicked underwent their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. Illic locus est, partes ubi se via finit in ambas: Dextera, qua Ditis magni sub mania tendit: IIac iter Elysium nobis: at heva malorum Exercet panas, et <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> impia Tartara mittit. He assigns Elysium to those who died for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to those of pure lives, to truly inspired poets, to the inventors of arts, and to all who have done good to mankind. Some authors take the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Elysium to have been borrowed from the Phoenicians; as imagining the name Elysium formed from the Phoenician ἐλασ, or ἐλατις, or ἐλασ, "to rejoice," or "to be in joy;" the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> a being only changed into e, as we find done in many other names; as in Enakim for Anakim, &c. On which footing, Elysian fields should signify the same thing as a place of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; or, Locos lacivs, et amana vireta Fortunatorum nemorum, sedefique beatas. Virg. Others derive the word from the Greek ἀνασφορον, "I deliver, I let loose or disengage;" because here men's souls are freed or disencumbered from the fetters of the body. Beroaldus, and Hornius (Hist. Philo. lib. iii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 2.) take the place to have derived its name from Eliza, one of the first persons who came into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> after the deluge, and the author and father of the Ætolians. The Elysian fields were, according to some, in the Fortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the Atlantic. Others place them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Leucæ; and, according to the authority of Virgil, they were situated in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. According to Lucian, they were near the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; or in the centre of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we believe Plutarch. Olaus Wormius contends that it was in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> the Elysian fields were placed.

ELZEVIRS

Pages 38-38

celebrated printers at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, who greatly adorned the republic of letters with many beautiful editions of the best authors of antiquity. They fell somewhat below the Stephensens in point of learning, as well as in their editions of Greek and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> authors; but as to the choice of good books, they seem to have equalled, and in the neatness and elegance of their small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, greatly to have exceeded them. Their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Terence, and Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, have been reckoned their masterpieces; and are indeed so very fine, that they justly gained them the reputation of being the best printers in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. There were five of these Elzevirs, namely, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, Boaventure, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, Lewis, and Daniel. Lewis began to be famous at Leyden in 1595, and was remarkable for being the first who observed the distinction between the v consonant and u vowel, which had been recommended by Ramus and other writers <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before, but never regarded. Daniel died in 1680 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1681; and though he left children who carried on the business, passed nevertheless for the last of his family who excelled in it. The Elzevirs have printed several catalogues of their editions; but the last, published by Daniel, is considerably enlarged, and abounds with new books. It was printed at Amsterdam, 1674, in 12mo, and divided into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes.

EMANATION

Pages 38-38

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of flowing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proceeding from some source or origin. Such is the emanation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; or that of effluvia from odorous, &c., bodies; or of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> from God, &c.—The word is formed of the Latin e "out of," and manere "to flow or stream." EMANATION is also used for the thing that proceeds, as well as the act of proceeding. The power given a judge is an emanation from the regal power; the reasonable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is an emanation from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>.

EMANCIPATION

Pages 38-38

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the setting free a son from the subjection of his father; so that whatever moveables he acquires belong in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to him, and not to his father, as before emancipation. Emancipation puts the son in a capacity of managing his own affairs, and of marrying without his father's consent, though a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>. Emancipation differs from manumission, as the latter was the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in favour of a slave, whereas the former was that of a father in favour of his son. There were two kinds of emancipation: the one tacit, which was by the son's being promoted to some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, by his coming of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by his marrying; in all which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> he became his own master of course. The other, express; where the father declared before a judge, that he emancipated his son. In performing this, the father was first to tell his son imaginarily to another, whom they called pater fiduciarium, father in trust; of whom being brought back again by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> father, he manumitted him before the judge by a verbal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>. Emancipation formerly obtained in France with regard to minors or pupils, who were hereby set at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to manage their own effects, without the advice or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of their parents or tutors.

EMASCULATION

Pages 38-38

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of castrating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> depriving a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> of those parts which characterize his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTRATION">Castration</a> and Eunuch.

EMAUS

Pages 38-38

Emmaus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ammaus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a village, 60 stadia to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, or about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles: it afterwards became a town, and a Roman colony, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a>, (Jerome). Rehob has another Emmaus towards Lydda, 22 miles from Jerusalem, (Itinerary); a third, near Tiberias.

EMBALMING

Pages 38-39

is the opening a dead body, taking out the intestines, and filling the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with odoriferous and desiccative drugs and spices, to prevent its putrefying. The Egyptians excelled all other nations in the art of preserving bodies from corruption; for some that they have embalmed upwards of 2000 years ago, remain whole to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and are often brought into other countries as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> curiosities. Their manner of embalming was thus: they scooped the brains with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> scoop out at the nostrils, and threw in medicaments to fill up the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>: they also took out the entrails, and having filled the body with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, cappa, and other spices, except frankincense, proper to dry up the humours, they pickled it in nitre, where it lay. Embalming lay soaking for 70 days. The body was then wrapped up in bandages of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, to make it stick like <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>; and so was delivered to the kindred of the deceased, entire in all its features, the very hairs of the eye-lids being preserved. They used to keep the bodies of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, thus embalmed, in little houses magnificently adorned, and took great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in beholding them, alive as it were, without any change in their size, features, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. The Egyptians also embalmed birds, &c. The prices for embalming were different; the highest was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, the next 20 minae, and so decreasing to a very small <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>: but they who had not wherewithal to answer this expense, contented themselves with infusing, by means of a syringe, through the fundament, a certain liquor extracted from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>; and, leaving it there, wrapped up the body in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of nitre: the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> thus preyed upon the intestines, so that when they took it out, the intestines came away with it, dried, and not in the least purified: the body being enclosed in nitre, grew dry, and nothing remained besides the skin glued upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. The method of embalming used by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Egyptians, according to Maillet, is to wash the body several times with rose-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which he elsewhere observes, is more fragrant in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than with us; they afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a> it with incense, aloes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of other odours, of which they are by no means sparing; and then they <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the body in a winding sheet, made partly of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and partly of cotton, and moistened, as is supposed, with some sweet-scented water or liquid perfume, though Maillet uses only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> moistened; this they cover with another cloth of unmixed cotton, to which they add one of the richest suits of clothes of the deceased. The expense, he says, on these occasions, is very great, though nothing like what the genuine embalming cost in former times.

EMBARCADERO

Pages 39-39

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, much used along the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, particularly those on the side of the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which serves some other considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> farther within <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, for a port <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> place of shipping, i.e. of embarking and disembarking commodities. Thus Calao is the embarcadero of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARICA">Arica</a> the embarcadero of Potosi. There are some embarcaderos 40, 50, and even 60 leagues off the city which they serve in that capacity.

EMBARGO

Pages 39-39

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> on ships <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> merchandise, by public authority; or a prohibition of state, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> on foreign ships, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, to prevent their going out of port, sometimes to prevent their coming in, and sometimes both, for a limited time. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> may lay embargoes on ships, or employ those of his subjects, in time of danger, for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but they must not be for the private advantage of a particular trader or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and therefore a warrant to stay a single ship is no legal embargo. No inference can be made from embargoes which are only in war-time; and are a prohibition by advice of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and not at prosecution of parties. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> goods be laden on board, and after an embargo or restraint from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or state comes forth, and then the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the ship breaks ground, or endeavours to fail, if any damage accrues, he must be responsible for the same; the reason is, because his freight is due, and must be paid, even though the goods be seized as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRABAND">contraband</a>.

EMBARRASS

Pages 39-39

(Embarrassment), a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, though now naturalized; denoting a difficulty <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> obstacle which perplexes or confounds a person, &c. EMBASSADOR. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">AMBASSADOR</a>.

EMBER-WEEKS

Pages 39-39

are those wherein the ember <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> embering days <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. In the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred, and those of Canute, those days are called ymbren, that is, circular days, from whence the word was probably corrupted into ember-days: by the canonists they are called quatuor anni tempora, the four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> seasons, on which the circle of the year turns: and hence Henhaw takes the word to have been formed, viz. by corruption from temper, of tempora. The ember-days are, the Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, after Quadragesima <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, after Whit-funday, after Holy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOD">rood</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in September, and after St Lucia's day in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>: which four times answer well enough to the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the year, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">Spring</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">Summer</a>, Autumn, and Winter. Mr Sonnner thinks they were originally fasts, instituted to beg God's blessing on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Agreeable to which, Skinner supposes the word ember taken from the ashes, embers, then火烧ed on the head. These ember-weeks are now chiefly taken notice of, on account of the ordination of priests and deacons; because the canon appoints the Sundays next succeeding the ember-weeks, for the solemn times of ordination: Though the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they please, may ordain on any Sunday or holiday.

EMBERIZA

Pages 39-39

a genus of birds belonging to the order of paffiers. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EMBLEM

Pages 39-40
