a kind of painted ænigma, which, representing some obvious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, with reflections underneath, instructs us in some moral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of knowledge. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVISE">DEVISE</a>, ÆNIGMA, &c. Such is that very significant image of Scævola holding his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the fire; with the words, Agere et pati fortiter Romanum est, "To do and suffer courageously is Roman." The word is pure Greek, formed of the verb ἐπιβάλλων, "to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in, to insert." Suetonius relates, that Tiberius made the word be erased out of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, because borrowed from another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The emblem is somewhat plainer and more obvious than the ænigma. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">Gale</a> defines emblem an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, representing one thing to the eye, and another to the understanding. The Greeks also gave the name Emblems, εἰκονογραφία, to inlaid or mosaic works, and even to all kinds of ornaments of vases, moveables, garments, &c. And the Latins used emblem in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Accordingly, Cicero reproaching Verres with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and fine wrought works he had plundered from the Sicilians, calls the ornaments fixed thereto (and which on occasion might be separated from them) emblema. Add, that Latin authors frequently compare the figures and ornaments of discourse to these emblems. Thus, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin poet praising an orator, says, that all his words were ranged like the pieces in mosaic: Quam lepide nescio composita, ut tefferele omnes, At te pavimenti, atque emblemate vermiculato.

EMBOLISMUS

Pages 40-40

ἐμβολισμός, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, signifies "intercalation." The word is formed of ἐμβάλλων, "to inset." As the Greeks made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> year, which is only 354 days; in order to bring it to the solar, which is 365 years, they had every two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three years an embolism, i.e., they added a 13th lunar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> every two or three years, which additional month they called embolismicus, ἐμβολικός, because inserted, or intercalated.

EMBOSSING

Pages 40-40
or IMBOSING, in Architecture and Sculpture, the forming or fashioning works in relief, whether cut with a chisel or otherwise. Embossing is a kind of sculpture, wherein the figures stick out from the plane whereon it is cut: and according as the figures are more or less prominent, they are said to be in alto, mezzo, or basso, relievo; or high, mean, or low relief. See Engraving.

EMBOTHRIUM

Pages 40-40

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EMBRASURE

Pages 40-40

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the enlargement made of the aperture of a door <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> window on the inside of the wall; its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> being to give the greater play for the opening of the door or sashment, or to admit the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

EMBROCATION

Pages 40-40

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> kind of remedy, which consists in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRRIGATION">irrigation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> affected, with some proper liquor, as oils, spirits, &c., by means of a woollen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, or a sponge, dipped in the same.

EMBROIDERY

Pages 40-40

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> thread, wrought by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> upon cloth, stuffs, or muslin, into various figures. In embroidering stuffs, the work is performed in a kind of loom; because the more the piece is stretched, the easier it is worked. As to muslin, they spread it upon a pattern ready designed; and sometimes, before it is stretched upon the pattern, it is starched, to make it more easy to handle. Embroidery on the loom is less tedious than the other, in which, while they work <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, all the threads of the muslin, both lengthwise and breadthwise, must be continually counted; but, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, this last embroidery is much richer in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and susceptible of greater variety. Cloths too much milled are scarce susceptible of this ornament, and in effect we seldom fee them embroidered. The thinnest muslins are left for this purpose; and they are embroidered to the greatest perfection in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; in other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, however, they embroider very prettily, and especially in France. There are several kinds of embroidery: as, 1. Embroidery on the stamp; where the figures are raised and rounded, having cotton or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> put under them to support them. 2. Low embroidery; where the gold and silver <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> low upon the sketch, and are stitched with silk of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. 3. Guipure embroidery: this is performed either in gold or silver; they first make a sketch upon the cloth, then put on cut <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, and afterwards sew on the gold and silver with silk thread: in this kind of embroidery they often put gold and silver <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, tinsel, and spangles. 4. Embroidery on both sides; that which appears on both sides of the stuff. 5. Plain embroidery; where the figures are flat and even, without cords, spangles, or other ornaments. By stat. 22 Geo. II. c. 36. no foreign embroidery, or gold and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCADE">brocade</a>, shall be imported, upon pain of being forfeited and burnt, and penalty of 100l. for each piece. No person shall sell, or expose to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, any foreign embroidery, gold and silver thread, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, fringe, brocade, or make up the same into any garment, on pain of having it forfeited and burnt, and penalty of 100l. All such embroidery, &c. may be seized and burnt; and the mercer, &c. in whose custody it was found, shall forfeit 100l.

EMBRUN

Pages 40-40
or AMBRUN, a city of Dauphiny, in France, near the confines of Piedmont. E. Long. 6.6. N. Lat. 44. 35.

EMBRYO

Pages 40-40

in Physiology, the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of an animal in the womb, before the several members are distinctly formed; after which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it is denominated a fetus. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a> and Fetus.

EMDEN

Pages 39-39

a port-town and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, now in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; it is situated at the mouth of the river Ens. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 45'. N. Lat. 53. 50'.

EMENAGOGUES

Pages 43-44

in Medicine, such remedies as promote the menstrual discharge. They are thus called from μενος "in," μηνος "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>," ναυδος "I <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>," because their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> periods of flowing are once a-month.

EMERALD

Pages 40-41

a precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> belonging to the genus of siliceous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The word is derived, according to some, from the French smaragde, and that from the Latin smaragdus, signifying the same thing; by others it is said to be derived from the Italian smaraldo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Arabian zomorrad. According to Cronstedt the emerald is the loftiest of all the precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, though other naturalists <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it the next after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> in this respect. It is perhaps the most beautiful of all the gems, and, according to Wallerius, when heated in the fire, changes its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to a deep blue, and becomes phosphorescent; but recovers its green colour when <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. When pulverized it has a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> appearance, and, with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, melts to a very thin and colourless glass. It becomes electric by being rubbed, and some have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the tourmalin, viz. of being electrified by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and in that state attracting ashes or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> substances; though the emeralds are less powerful than the tourmalin, and after having attracted the ashes, they retain them without any signs of repulsion. Pliny mentions twelve different kinds of these precious stones; though it appears, from the vast size of some of them, that they must have been only certain kinds of green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, or other green stone, which at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Emeralds ready cut, or polished and not cut, being of good stone, and a fine colour, are worth— | Carats | Value | |--------|-------| | One carat, or four grains | 10 L. s. | | Two carats | 7 L. s. | | Three carats | 5 L. s. | | Four carats | 10 L. s. | | Five carats | 10 L. s. | | Six carats | 10 L. s. | | <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> carats | 15 L. s. | | Eight carats | 19 L. s. | | <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> carats | 23 L. s. | | Ten carats | 33 L. s. | To counterfeit Emeralds: Take of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> crystal, four ounces; of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, four ounces; verdigris, forty-eight grains; crocus martis, prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, eight grains: let the whole be finely pulverized and sifted; put this into a crucible, leaving one inch empty: lute it well, and put it into a potter's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and let it stand there as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as they do their plots. When cold, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the crucible; and you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of a fine emerald colour, which, after it is cut and set in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, will surpass in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> an oriental emerald. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERSION">Emersion</a>, in Physics, the rising of any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> above the surface of a fluid specifically heavier than itself, into which it had been violently immersed or thrust. It is one of the known laws of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">hydrostatics</a>, that a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> solid being forced <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into a heavier fluid, immediately endeavours to emerge; and that, with a force or moment equal to the excess of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the fluid above that of an equal bulk of the solid. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a solid be immersed in a fluid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> its specific gravity, it will emerge again till half its bulk or body be above the surface of the fluid. Emersion, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, or other planet, begins to re-appear, after its having been eclipsed, or hid by the interposition of the moon, earth, or other body. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> is sometimes found by observing the immersions and emersions of the first of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s satellites. The immersions are observed from the time of Jupiter's being in conjunction with the sun to its opposition; and the emersions, from the opposition to the conjunction; which two intervals are usually six months a-piece, and divide the year between them. But when Jupiter is in conjunction with the sun, and 15 days before and afterwards, there is nothing to be observed; the planet, with his satellites, being then lost in the light of the sun. Emersion is also used when a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> before hid by the sun, as being too near him, begins to re-appear and to get out of his rays.

EMERSON

Pages 41-42

William, an eminent mathematician, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1701, at Hurworth, a village about three miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARLINGTON">Darlington</a>; at least it is certain that he resided here from his childhood. His father <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a> Emerson was a tolerable proficient in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and without his books and instructions, perhaps his own genius (most eminently fitted for mathematical disquisitions) would have never been unfolded. He was instructed in the learned languages by a young clergyman, then curate of Hurworth, who... was boarded at his father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the earlier <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he attempted to teach a few scholars; but whether from his concise method (for he was not happy in explaining his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the warmth of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> temper, he made no progress in his school: he therefore soon let it off; and satisfied with a moderate competence left him by his parents, he devoted himself to a studious retirement. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 1781 (being sensible of his approaching <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>), he disposed of the whole of his mathematical library to a bookseller at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and on May 20th 1782, he died of a lingering and painful disorder at his native village, aged near 81 years. Mr Emerson in his person was rather short, but strong and well made, with an open countenance and ruddy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. He was exceedingly singular in his dress. He had but one coat, which he always wore open before, except the lower <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>; no waistcoat; his shirt quite the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVERIE">reverie</a> of one in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, no opening before, but buttoned close at the collar behind; a kind of flaxen wig which had not a crooked <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> in it, and probably had never been tortured with a comb from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its being made. He always walked up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> when he had anything to publish, revising sheet by sheet himself.—Trusting no eyes but his own, was always a favourite maxim with him. He never advanced any mathematical proposition that he had not first tried in practice, constantly making all the different parts himself on a small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, so that his house was filled with all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> instruments together or disjointed. He would frequently stand up to his middle in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> while <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, a diversion he was remarkably fond of. He used to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> incessantly for some time, and then for relaxation take a ramble to any pot-alehouse where he could get anybody to drink with and talk to. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a> was highly pleased with his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and used often to come to him in the fields and accompany him home, but could never persuade him to get into a carriage. On these occasions he would sometimes exclaim, "Damn your whim-wham! I had rather walk." He was a married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and his wife used to spin on an old-fashioned wheel, whereof a very accurate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> is given in his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. He was deeply skilled in the science of music, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of sounds, and the various scales both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, but was a very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> performer. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of Mr Emerson's works. 1. The Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a>. 2. The projection of the Sphere, orthographic, stereographic, and gnomical. 3. The Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">Trigonometry</a>. 4. The Principles of Mechanics. 5. A Treatise of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. 6. A Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, in two books. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> of Infinites, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> Method, illustrated by Examples. 8. Mechanics; or the Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a>. 9. The Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, in four books. 10. A System of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>. 11. The Laws of Centripetal and Centrifugal Force. 12. The Mathematical Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. 13. Tracts, 8vo. 14. Cyclomathesis; or an easy Introduction to the several branches of the Mathematics. 15. A short comment on Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's Principia; to which is added, A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of Sir Isaac against the objections that have been made to several Parts of his Works.

EMERY

Pages 42-43

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a rich <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses of no determinate shape <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> size, extremely hard, and very heavy. It is usually of a dusty brownish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> on the surface; but when broken, is of a fine bright iron-gray, but not without some tinge of redness; and is tangled all over with thinning streaks, which are small flakes of a foliaceous tale, highly impregnated with iron. It is also sometimes very red, and then usually contains veins of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. It makes no effervescence with any of the acid menstruums; and is found in some of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and some parts of Germany. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that some kinds of emery may contain the metal called <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PLATINA">platina</a>, and on this subject has the following curious observations. "Alonso Barba mentions a substance called clumpi; which is a hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of the emery kind, participating of iron, of a gray <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> shining a little, very hard to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, because it resists the fire much, found in Potosi, Chocaya, and other places, along with blackish and reddish ores that yield gold. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> platina is really found in large masses, either generally or only now and then, one might reasonably expect those masses to be such as are here described. "Of the same kind perhaps also is the mineral mentioned by several authors under the name of Spanish emery, smiris Hispanicus, which should seem, from the accounts given of it, to be no other than platina or its matrix. The smiris is said to be found in the gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> prohibited; to contain films or veins of native gold; to be in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> request among the alchemists; to have been sometimes used for the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERATION">adulteration</a> of gold; to stand, equally with the noble metal, cupellation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTATION">quartation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, and the regal cement; and to be separable from it by amalgamation with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, which throws out the smiris and retains the gold; properties strongly characteristic of platina, and which do not belong to any known substance besides. This debasement of gold per extracitum smiridis Hispanici is mentioned by Becher in his Minera arenaaria, and several times hinted at in his Physica subterranea. Both Becher and Stahl indeed call the substance which the gold receives from the emery an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, whereas platina is undoubtedly a metal; but this does not at all invalidate our supposition, for they give the name of earth also to the substance which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> receives from calamine in being made into bras, which is now known to be metallic. "From these observations I have been led to suspect, that the European emeries likewise might possibly participate of platina. If this was certain, it would account satisfactorily for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> which some of the alchemists are said to have made of emeries and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> ores; and we should no longer doubt, or wonder, that by treating gold with these kinds of minerals, they obtained a permanent augmentation; that this augmentation, though it refitted <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, antimony, aquafortis, and the regal cement, was separable, as Becher owns it was, by quicksilver; and that, when it exceeded certain limits, it rendered the gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> and brittle. "If emery contains platina, I imagined it might be discoverable by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the powdered mineral in melted lead, and afterwards working off the lead upon a telf or cupel. The experiment was made with eight ounces of the finest powder of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> emery, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of lead; which were covered with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> to prevent the scorching of the lead, and urged with a strong fire for two or three hours. The lead became hard, rigid, of a dark colour, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANULATED">granulated</a> texture, as if it had really imbibed some platinum from the emery; but in cupellation it worked almost entirely off, leaving only a head about the size of a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>'s head, which was probably no other than silver contained in the lead. "I repeated the experiment with some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>, thinking to obtain a more perfect <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the emery by vitrifying it with the lead. Two ounces of fine emery and six ounces of minium were well mixed together, and urged with a strong fire, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> crucible, for an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>: they melted into an uniform dark brownish glass. The glass was powdered, mixed with four ounces of fixed alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and some powdered <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, and put into a fresh crucible, with some common salt on the surface: The fire was pretty strongly excited; but the fusion was not so perfect as could be wished, and only about two ounces of lead were found revived. This lead had suffered nearly the same change as that in the foregoing experiment; and like it, gave no appearance of platinum on being cupelled. "It seems to follow from these experiments, that the emery employed in them contained no platinum; but as it is not to be supposed that all emeries are of one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, other sorts may deserve to be submitted to the same trials. As gold is contained in some parcels of common minerals, and by no means in all the individuals of any one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; platinum may possibly in like manner be found in some European ores, though there is not the least footprint of it in other parcels of the same kind of ore."

EMIMS

Pages 43-43
ancient inhabitants of the land of Canaan beyond Jordan, who were defeated by Chedorlaomer and his allies, Gen. xiv. 5. Moses tells us, that they were beaten in Shaveh Kirjathaim, which was in the country of Sihon conquered from the Moabites, Josh. xiii. 19.—21. The Emims were a warlike people, of a gigantic stature, great and many, and tall as the Anakims.

EMINENCE

Pages 43-43

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a little hillock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the adjoining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. EMINENCE is also a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> given to cardinals. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the Pope, whereby it was appointed that the cardinals should be addressed under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of eminence, bears <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1630. They then laid aside the titles of illu/brifimi and reverendifimi, which they had borne before. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> is likewise addressed under the quality of eminence. The popes John VIII. and Gregory VII. gave the same title to the kings of France. The emperors have likewise borne it. Eminentifimus, the superlative of eminent, has of late been attributed to the cardinals.

EMIR

Pages 43-43

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> among the Turks, signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. This title was first given to the caliphs; but when they assumed the title of Sultans, that of emir remained to their children; as that of Caesar among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. At length the title came to be attributed to all who were judged to descend from Mahomet by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Fatimah, and who wear the green turban instead of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. The Turks make an observation, that the emirs, before their fortieth year, are men of the greatest gravity, learning, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; but after this, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fools, they discover some signs of levity and stupidity. This is interpreted by the Turks as a sort of divine impulse in token of their birth and sanctity. The Turks also call the vizirs, bashaws, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governors of provinces, by this name.

EMISSARY

Pages 43-43

in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, a person employed by another to found the opinions of people, spread certain reports, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a spy over other people's actions. EMISSARY Vessels, in Anatomy, the same with those more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Excretory.

EMISSION

Pages 43-43

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used chiefly to denote the ejaculation of the semen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seed in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of coition. See Coition and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a>.

EMMANUEL

Pages 43-43
or Immanuel, a Hebrew word, which signifies 'God with us.' Isaiah (viii. 14.), in that celebrated prophecy, wherein he declares to Ahaz the birth of the Messiah, who was to be born of a virgin, says, This child shall be called, and really be, Emmanuel, that is, God with us. The same prophet (viii. 8.) repeats the same thing, while he is speaking of the enemy's army, which, like a torrent, was to overflow Judea. 'The stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Emmanuel.' The evangelist Matthew (i. 23.) informs us, that this prophecy was accomplished in the birth of Christ, born of the virgin Mary, in whom the two natures divine and human were united, and in this sense, he was really Emmanuel, or 'God with us.'

EMMERICK

Pages 43-43

a rich fortified town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>. It carries on a good trade with the Dutch, and both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Catholics have the free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The streets are neat and regular, and the houses tolerably built. It was taken by the French in 1672, and delivered to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> in 1673, under whose jurisdiction it now is. It is seated near the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 29. N. Lat. 52. 5.

EMMIUS

Pages 43-43

Ubro, born at Gretha in East Friesland in 1547, was a very learned professor, and chosen rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Nordcn in 1579. This seminary flourished exceedingly under his care; and declined as visibly after he was ejected, in 1587, for refusing to subscribe the Confession of Augsburg. The year after, he was made rector of the college of Leer; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a> confederated with the United Provinces, the magistrates appointed him rector of that college: which employment he filled with the highest repute near 20 years; until, the college being erected into an university, he was the first rector, and one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ornaments of it by his lectures, till his infirmities prevented his public appearance. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> was equal to his learning; so that the governor of Friesland and Groningen often consulted him, and seldom failed to follow his advice. He wrote...

EMOLLIENTS

Pages 44-44

in Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, are such remedies as sheath and soften the aperity of the humours, and relax and supple the solids at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

EMOLUMENT

Pages 44-44

is properly applied to the profits arising daily from an office <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> employ. The word is formed of the Latin emolumentum, which, according to some, primarily signifies the profits redounding to the miller from his mill; of molo, molere, "to grind."—The patent, or other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, whereby a person is preferred to an office, gives him a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to enjoy all the duties, honours, profits, and emoluments belonging thereto.—Emolument is also used, in a somewhat greater latitude, for profit or advantage in the general. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">EMOTION</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">PASSION</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, are thus distinguished by a celebrated writer*. An internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or agitation of the mind, when it passeth away without desire, is denominated an emotion: when desire follows, the motion or agitation is denominated a passion. A fine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, for example, raiseth in me a pleasant feeling: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that feeling vanishes without producing any effect, it is in proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> an emotion; but if the feeling, by reiterated views of the object, becomes sufficiently strong to occasion desire, it loses its name of emotion, and acquires that of passion. The same holds in all the other passions. The painful feeling raised in a spectator by a slight injury done to a stranger, being accompanied with no desire of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, is termed an emotion; but that injury raiseth in the stranger a stronger emotion, which being accompanied with desire of revenge, is a passion. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">External</a> expressions of distress produce in the spectator a painful feeling, which being sometimes so slight as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> away without any effect, is an emotion; but if the feeling be so strong as to prompt desire of affording relief, it is a passion, and is termed pity. Envy is emulation in excess: if the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> of a competitor be barely disagreeable, the painful feeling is an emotion; if it produce desire to depress him, it is a passion. See PASSION.

EMOY

Pages 44-45
or HIA-MEN, an island and port of China, under the jurisdiction of the province of FO-KIEN. The port is properly but an anchoring-place for ships, inclosed on one side by the island from which it takes its name, and on the other by the main-land: but it is so extensive, that it can contain several thousands of vessels; and the depth of its water is so great, that the largest ships may lie close to the shore without danger. In the beginning of the present century it was much frequented by European vessels; but few visit it at present, as all the trade is carried on at Canton. The emperor keeps here a garrison of 6 or 7000 men, commanded by a Chinese general. In entering this road, a large rock must be doubled which stands at the mouth of it, and divides it almost as the Mingant divides the harbour of Breft. This rock is visible, and rises several feet above the surface of the water. The island of Emoy is particularly celebrated on account of the magnificence of its principal pagod, consecrated to the deity Fo. This temple is situated in a plain, terminated on one side by the sea, and on the other by a lofty mountain. Before it the sea, flowing through different channels, forms a large fleet of water which is bordered with turf of the most beautiful verdure. The front of this edifice is 180 feet in length, and its gate is adorned with figures in relief, which are the usual ornaments of the Chinese architecture. On entering, you find a vast portico, with an altar in the middle, on which is placed a gigantic statue of gilt brass, representing the god Fo, sitting crook-legged. Four other statues are placed at the corners of this portico, which are 18 feet high, although they represent people sitting. Each of these statues is formed from a single block of stone. They bear in their hands different symbols which mark their attributes, as formerly in Athens and Rome the trident and caduceus distinguished Neptune and Mercury. One holds a serpent in his arms, which is twisted round its body in several folds; the second has a bent bow and a quiver; the two others present, one a kind of battle-axe, and the other a guitar, or some instrument of the same kind. After crossing this portico, you enter a square outer court, paved with large gray stones, the least of which is ten feet in length and four in breadth. At the four sides of this court arise four pavilions, which terminate in domes, and have a communication with one another by means of a gallery which runs quite round it. One of these contains a bell ten feet in diameter; the wooden-work which supports this heavy mass cannot be sufficiently admired. In the other is kept a drum of enormous size, which the bonzes use to proclaim the days of new and full moon. It must be observed, that the clappers of the Chinese bells are on the outside, and made of wood in the form of a mallet. The two other pavilions contain the ornaments of the temple, and often serve to lodge travelers, whom the bonzes are obliged to receive. In the middle of this court is a large tower, which stands by itself, and terminates also in a dome, to which you ascend by a beautiful stone stair-case that winds round it. This dome contains a temple remarkably neat; the ceiling is ornamented with mosaic work, and the walls are covered with stone figures in relief, representing animals and monsters. The pillars which support the roof of this edifice are of wood varnished; and on festivals are ornamented with small flags of different colours. The pavement of the temple is formed of little shells, and its different compartments present birds, butterflies, flowers, &c. The bonzes continually burn incense upon the altar, and keep the lamps lighted, which hang from the ceiling of the temple. At one extremity of the altar stands a brazen urn, which when struck sends forth a mournful sound: on the opposite side is a hollow machine of wood, of an oval form, used for the same purpose, which is to accompany with its sound their voices when they sing in praise of the tutelary idol of the pagod. The god Poussa is placed on the middle of this altar, on a flower of gilt brass, which serves as a base, and holds holds a young child in his arms; several idols, which are no doubt subaltern deities, are ranged around him, and show by their attitudes their respect and veneration. The bonzes have traced out on the walls of this temple several hieroglyphical characters in praise of Poulla; there is also to be seen an historical or allegorical painting in fresco, which represents a burning lake, in which several men appear to be swimming, some carried by monsters, others surrounded by dragons and winged serpents. In the middle of the gulf rises a steep rock, on the top of which the god is seated, holding in his arms a child, who seems to call out to those who are in the flames of the lake; but an old man, with hanging ears and horns on his head, prevents them from climbing to the summit of the rock, and threatens to drive them back with a large club. The bonzes are at a loss what answer to give, when any questions are asked them concerning this painting. Behind the altar is a kind of library, containing books which treat of the worship of idols. On descending from this dome you cross the court, and enter a kind of gallery, the walls of which are lined with boards; it contains 24 statues of gilt bronzes, representing the same number of philosophers, ancient disciples of Confucius. At the end of this gallery you find a large hall, which is the refectory of the bonzes; and after having traversed a spacious apartment, you at length enter the temple of Fo, to which there is an ascent by a large stone staircase. It is ornamented with vases full of artificial flowers (a work in which the Chinese excel); and here also are found the same kind of musical instruments as those mentioned before. The statue of the god is not to be seen but through a piece of black gauze, which forms a kind of veil or curtain before the altar. The rest of the pagod consists of several large chambers, exceedingly neat, but badly disposed; the gardens and pleasure grounds are on the declivity of the mountain; and a number of delightful grottoes are cut out in the rock, which afford an agreeable shelter from the excessive heat of the sun. There are several other pagods in the isle of Emouy; among which is one called The Pagod of the Ten Thousand Stones, because it is built on the brow of a mountain where there is a like number of little rocks, under which the bonzes have formed grottoes and very pleasant covered seats. A certain rural simplicity reigns here, which captivates and delights. Strangers are received by these bonzes with great politeness, and may freely enter their temples; but they must not attempt to gratify their curiosity fully, nor to enter these apartments into which they are not introduced, especially if they are not accompanied by suspicious persons; for the bonzes, who are forbid under pain of severe punishment to have any intercourse with women, and who often keep them in private, might, from fear of being discovered, revenge themselves for too importunate a curiosity.

EMPALEMENT

Pages 45-45

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, which consisted in thrusting a stake up the fundament. The word comes from the French empaler, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Italian impalare; or rather, they are all alike derived from the Latin palus, "a stake," and the preposition in, "in or into." We find mention of empaling in Ju- venal. It was frequently practised in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Nero, and continues to be so in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. EMPALEMENT of a flower, the same with CALYX. EMPANELLING. See IMPANELLING. EMPARLANCE. See IMPARLANCE.

EMPEDOCLES

Pages 45-45

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIGENTUM">Agrigentum</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. He followed the Pythagorean <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and admitted the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a>. He constantly appeared with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> on his head; to maintain, by this outward pomp, the reputation he had acquired of being a very extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Yet <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> says, that he was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lover of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, extremely averse to flatter and command, and that he even refused a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> that was offered him. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was a Treatise in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Principles of Things. Aristotle, Lucretius, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, make the most magnificent eulogiums on his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and eloquence. He taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>; and often alleviated the anxieties of his mind, as well as the pains of his body, with music. It is reported, that his curiosity to visit the flames of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> of Etna proved fatal to him. Some maintain that he wished it to be believed that he was a god; and that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> might be unknown, he threw himself into the crater and perished in the flames. His expectations, however, were frustrated; and the volcano, by throwing up one of his sandals, discovered to the world that Empedocles had perished by fire. Others report that he lived to an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and that he was drowned in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> about 440 years before the Christian era.

EMPEROR

Pages 45-46

(Imperator), among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, signified a general of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, who, for some extraordinary services, had been complimented with this appellation. Thus Augustus, having obtained no less than twenty famous victories, was as often saluted with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> emperor; and Titus was denominated emperor by his army after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Afterwards it came to denote an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> monarch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> supreme commander of an empire. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> Julius Caesar was called emperor: the same title descended with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to Octavius Augustus, Tiberius, and Caligula; and afterwards it became <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a>. In strictness, the title emperor does not, and cannot, add any thing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of sovereignty: its effect is only to give precedence and pre-eminence above other sovereigns; and as such, it raises those invested with it to the summit of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> greatness. It is disputed, whether or not emperors have the power of disposing of the regal title. It is true, they have sometimes taken upon them to erect kingdoms; and thus it is that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> are said to have been raised to the dignity: thus also, the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Bald, in the year 877, gave Provence to Bolon, putting the diadem on his head, and decreeing him to be called "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>," ut more priscorum imperatorum regibus videtur dominari. Add, that the emperor Leopold erected the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>; and though several of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> refused for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to acknowledge him in that capacity, yet by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> in 1712 they all came in. In the east, the title and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of emperor are more frequent than they are among us; thus, the fo- Emperor, sovereign princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, Mogul, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, &c., are all emperors of China, Japan, &c. In the year 1723, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> of Muscovy assumed the title of emperor of all Russia, and procured himself to be recognized as such by most of the princes and states of Europe. In the West, the title has been a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time restricted to the emperors of Germany. The first who bore it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, who had the title of emperor conferred on him by Pope Leo III, though he had all the power before. The imperial prerogatives were formerly much more extensive than they are at present. At the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, A.D. 1024, they exercised the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of conferring all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> benefices in Germany; of receiving the revenues of them during a vacancy; of succeeding to the effects of intestate <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>; of confirming or annulling the elections of the popes; of assembling councils, and of appointing them to decide concerning the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; of conferring the title of king on their vassals; of granting vacant fiefs; of receiving the revenues of the empire; of governing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> as its proper sovereigns; of erecting free cities, and establishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in them; of assembling the diets of the empire, and fixing the time of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; of coining <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and conferring the same privilege on the states of the empire; and of administering both <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and low <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> within the territories of the different states: but in the year 1437, they were reduced to the right of conferring all dignities and titles, except the privilege of being a state of the empire; of preces primariae, or of appointing once during their reign a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; of granting dispensations with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of majority; of erecting cities, and conferring the privilege of coining money; of calling the meetings of the diet, and presiding in them. To which some have added, 1. That all the princes and states of Germany are obliged to do them homage, and swear fidelity to them. 2. That they, or their generals, have a right to command the forces of all the princes of the empire when united together. 3. That they receive a kind of tribute from all the princes and states of the empire, for carrying on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> which concerns the whole empire, which is called the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. For the rest, there is not a foot of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> or territory annexed to his title: but ever since the reign of Charles IV, the emperors have depended entirely on their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> dominions as the only source of their power, and even of their subsistence. See Diet and Electors. The kings of France were anciently also called emperors, at the time when they reigned with their sons, whom they associated to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Thus Hugh Capet, having associated his son Robert, took the title of emperor, and Robert that of king; under which titles they are mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, by Gerbert, &c. King Robert is also called emperor of the French by Helgau of Fleury. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> le Gros, upon associating his son, did the same. In the First <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a> of the King's Charters, fol. 166, are found letters of Louis le Gros, dated in 1116, in favour of Raymond bishop of Maguelonne, wherein he styles himself, Ludovicus, Dei ordinante providentia, Francorum imperator augustus. The kings of England had likewise anciently the title of emperors, as appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of King Edgar: Ego Edgarus An- glorum basileus, omniumque regum infidelium oceani quae Britannium circumjacent, &c., imperator et dominus.

EMPESTRUM

Pages 46-46

BERRY-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">BEARING</a> HEATH; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monoecea class. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method this genus is ranked by Linnæus under the 54th order, Mifcellanea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EMPHASIS

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a particular stress of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, laid on such parts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> words of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> as the orator wants to inforce upon his audience. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECLAMATION">Declamation</a>; Oratory, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> IV.; and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>.

EMPHYSEMA

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a windy tumor, generally occasioned by a fracture of the ribs, and formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> infusing itself, by a small wound, between the skin and muscles, into the substance of the cellular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> adipose membrane, spreading itself afterwards up to the neck, head, belly, and other parts, much after the manner in which butchers blow up their veal.

EMPIRE

Pages 46-47

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, under the jurisdiction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. See Emperor. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> we read of four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> monarchies or empires, viz. that of the Babylonians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians; that of the Medes and Persians; that of the Greeks; and that of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The first subsisted from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Nimrod, who founded it in the year of the world 1800, according to the computation of Usher, to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDANAPALUS">Sardanapalus</a> their last <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> in 3257, and consequently lasted above 1450 years. The empire of the Medes commenced under Arbaces, in the year of the world 3257, and was united to that of the Babylonians and Persians under <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, in 3468, and it clofed with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Codomannus in 3674. The Grecian empire lasted only during the reign of Alexander the Great, beginning in the year of the world 3674, and terminating with the death of this conqueror in 3681, his conquests being divided among his captains. The Roman empire commenced with Julius Cæsar, when he was made perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, in the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> 708, and of the world 3956, 48 years before Christ. The seat of the empire was removed to Byzantium by Constantine, in the year of our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> 334; the east and west were then united under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Roman empire, till the Romans proclaimed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> emperor, A.D. 800. From this epocha the east and west formed two separate empires; that of the east, governed by Greek emperors, commenced A.D. 302; and being gradually weakened, terminated under Constantine Paleologus in 1453. The western empire was afterwards known by the appellation of the empire, or German empire. Antiquaries distinguish between the medals of the upper, and lower or bas, empire.—The curious only value those of the upper empire, which commences with Cæsar or Augustus, and ends in the year of Christ 260. The lower empire comprehends near 1200 years, reckoning <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the destruction of Constantinople in 1453.—They usually distinguish two ages, or periods, of the lower empire: the first beginning where the upper ends, viz. with Aurelian, and ending with Anastasius, including 200 years; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> beginning with Anastasius, and ending with the Paleologi, which includes 1000 years. Empire, or The empire, used absolutely and without any addition, signifies the empire of Germany; called also, in juridical acts and laws, The holy Roman empire. It had its beginning with the ninth century; Charlemagne being created first emperor by Pope Leo III, who put the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his head in St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTMAS_DAY">Christmas-<a </a>class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the year 800. Authors are at a loss under what form of government to range the empire. Some of them maintain it to be a monarchical state, because all the members thereof are obliged to ask the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of their states of the emperor, and to take an oath of fidelity to him. Others consider it as a republic, or aristocratic state, because the emperor cannot resolve or determine anything without the concurring suffrages of the princes. It is added, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they require investiture from, and swear fealty to him, it is only as head of the republic, and in the name of the republic, and not in his own; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> every thing is transacted in name of the doge. Others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the empire to be a monarcho-aristocratic state, i.e., a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> and aristocracy; because, though the emperor in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> seems to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> sovereignly, yet his decrees and resolves have no force, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the state refuse to confirm them. Lastly, it has been called an aristocratical state, because the diet, wherein the sovereignty is lodged, is composed of princes and the deputies of the cities; and is divided into three orders or bodies, called colleges, viz., the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of electors, the college of princes, and the college of cities. We say, diet of the empire, circles of the empire, fiefs of the empire, princes of the empire, estates of the empire, members of the empire, capitulations of the empire. See Diet, Circle, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">Capitulation</a>, &c. The states or estates of the empire are of two kinds, mediate and immediate. The immediate states are those who hold immediately of the empire: Whereof, again, there are two kinds; the first, such as have seats and voices in the imperial diet; the second, such as have none. The mediate states are those who hold of the immediate. The states which now compose the empire are, The princes of the empire, the counts of the empire, the free barons of the empire, the prelates of the empire, the princesses or abbesses of the empire, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> of the empire, and the imperial cities.

EMPIRIC

Pages 47-47

an appellation given to those physicians who conduct themselves wholly by their own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, without studying physic in a regular way. Some even <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, in a still worse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, for a quack who prescribes at random, without being at all acquainted with the principles of the art.

EMPIS

Pages 47-47

a genus of insects belonging to the order Diptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. EMPLASTER. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">Plaster</a>. EMPORIÆ, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, near the Pyrenees; separated by a wall; one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> occupied by the Greeks of Phocæa, whence originally are the Massilienses; the other, by native Spaniards, to whom was added by Augustus a Roman colony. Now Ampuriæ, in Catalonia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 50. N. Lat. 42. 15.

EMPORIUM

Pages 47-47

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, two cities near Emporium <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>; one well fortified, and guarded by a strong garrison, at which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> met a repulse; the other, Hannibal took and plundered. Now thought to be Pont-Nura, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Placentia.

EMPRESS

Pages 47-47

the spouse of an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a woman who governs an empire. See EMPEROR.

EMPYRAEMA

Pages 47-47

in Medicine, a disorder wherein purulent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is contained in the thorax <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, after an inflammation and suppuration of the lungs and pleura. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. EMPYREAL <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. So Dr Higgins denominates that which Dr Priestley calls <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> air, and other philosophers vital or pure air.

EMPYREUM

Pages 47-47

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by divines for the highest heaven, where the blest enjoy the beatific vision. The word is formed of ἐν and πυρ, fire, because of its splendour.

EMPYREUMA

Pages 47-47

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, signifies a very disagreeable smell produced from burnt oils. It is often perceived in distillations of animal as well as vegetable substances, when they are exposed to a quick fire. EMRODS. See Hemorrhoids.

EMULATION

Pages 47-47

a generous ardour kindled by the praiseworthy examples of others, which impels us to imitate, to rival, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, to excel them. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> involves in it esteem of the person whose attainments <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conduct we emulate, of the qualities and actions in which we emulate him, and a desire of resemblance, together with a joy springing from the hope of success. The word comes originally from the Greek αἰμιλία, dispute, contest; whence the Latin, emulatus, and thence our emulation. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> observes of emulation, that it is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of envy; if so, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the mother and the offspring; the one is a virtue and the other a vice. Emulation admires great actions, and strives to imitate them; envy refuses them the praises that are their due; emulation is generous, and only thinks of surpassing a rival; envy is low, and only seeks to lessen him. Perhaps, therefore, it would be more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> to suppose emulation the daughter of admiration: admiration, however, is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ingredient in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of it.

EMULGENT

Pages 47-47
or renal, arteries, those which supply the kidneys with blood; being sometimes single, sometimes double, on each side. See Anatomy Index.

EMULSION

Pages 47-47

a soft liquid remedy, of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and consistence resembling <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>.

EMUNCTORY

Pages 47-47

in Anatomy, a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for all those parts which serve to carry off the excrementitious parts of the blood and other humours of the body. Such more especially are the kidneys, bladder, and most of the glands.

ENALLAGE

Pages 47-47

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, is when one word is substituted for another of the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of speech: A substantive for an adjective; as exercitus victor, for victoriae; feculus, for sceleps; A primitive for a derivative; as Dardana arma, for Dardania: An <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOX">nox</a> humida calo precipitat, for precipitatatur, &c.

ENAMEL

Pages 47-48

in general, is a vitrified <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> betwixt Enamel, the parts of which is dispersed some unvitrified matter; hence enamel ought to have all the properties of glass except transparency. Enamels have for their basis a pure crystal glass <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> frit, ground up with a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and tin prepared for the purpose, with the addition usually of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of tartar. These ingredients baked together are the matter of all enamels, which are made by adding colours of this or that kind in powder to this matter, and melting or incorporating them together in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. For white enamel, Neri (De Arte Vitriar.) directs only manganese to be added to the matter which constitutes the basis. For azure, zaffer mixed with calx of bras. For green, calx of bras with scales of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, or with crocus martis. For <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, zaffer with manganese or with crocus martis; or manganese with tartar. For <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, manganese, or calx of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and red tartar. For purple, manganese with calx of bras. For <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, tartar and manganese. And for violet-coloured enamel, manganese with three-calced bras. In making these enamels, the following general cautions are necessary to be observed. 1. That the pots must be glazed with white glass, and must be such as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear the fire. 2. That the matter of enamels must be very nicely mixed with the colours. 3. When the enamel is good, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> well incorporated, it must be taken from the fire with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of tongs. 4. The general way of making the coloured enamel is this: Powder, sift, and grind, all the colours very nicely, and first mix them with one another, and then with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> matter of enamels; then set them in pots in a furnace; and when they are well mixed and incorporated, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> them into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and when dry, set them in a furnace again to melt; and when melted, take a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> too deep-coloured, add more of the common matter of enamels; and if too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, add more of the colours. Enamels are used either in counterfeiting or imitating precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in enamel; or by enamellers, jewellers, and goldsmiths, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. The two first kinds are usually prepared by the workmen themselves, who are employed in these arts. That used by jewellers, &c., is brought to us chiefly from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in little cakes of different sizes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> about four inches diameter, having the mark of the maker struck upon it with a punchcon. It pays 1s. 7½d. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> on importation, and draws back 1s. 5½d. at the rate of 4s. per pound.

ENAMELLING

Pages 48-54

the art of laying enamel upon <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, &c., and of melting it at the fire, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of making <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> curious works in it at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>. It signifies also to paint in enamel. The method of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in ENAMEL. This is performed on plates of gold or silver, and most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of copper, enamelled with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> enamel; whereon they paint with colours which are melted in the fire, where they take a brightness and lustre like that of glass. This painting is the most prized of all for its peculiar brightness and vivacity, which is very permanent, the force of its colours not being effaced or filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as in other paintings, and continuing always as fresh as when it came out of the workmen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. It is usual in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>; it being the more difficult the larger it is, by reason of certain accidents it is liable to in the operation. Enamelling should only be practised on plates of gold, the other metals being less pure: copper, for instance, teases with the application, and yields fumes; and silver turns the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> white. Nor must the plate be made flat; for in such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the enamel cracks; to avoid which, they usually forge them a little round or oval, and not too thick. The plate being well and evenly forged, they usually begin the operation by laying on a couch of white enamel (as we observed above) on both sides, which prevents the metal from swelling and blistering; and this first layer serves for the ground of all the other colours. The plate being thus prepared, they begin at first by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> out exactly the subject to be painted with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> vitriol, mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of spike, marking all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> very lightly with a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>.
