After this, the colours (which are to be before ground with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> extremely fine, and mixed with oil of spike somewhat thick) are to be laid on, observing the mixtures and colours that agree to the different parts of the subject; for which it is necessary to understand painting in miniature. But here the workman must be very cautious of the good or bad qualities of the oil of spike he employs to mix his colours with, for it is very subject to adulterations. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> care must likewise be taken, that the least dust imaginable come not to your colours while you are either painting or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> them; for the least speck, when it is worked up with it, and when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> comes to be put into the reverberatory to be made red hot, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> leave a hole, and so deface the work. When the colours are all laid, the painting must be gently dried over a slow fire to evaporate the oil, and the colours afterwards melted to incorporate them with the enamel, making the plate red hot in a fire like what the enamellers <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Afterwards that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the painting must be polished over again which the fire hath anything effaced, strengthening the shades and colours, and committing it again to the fire, observing the same method as before, which is to be repeated till the work be finished. Method of ENAMELLING by the Lamp. Most enamelled works are wrought at the fire of a lamp, in which, instead of oil, they put melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-grease, which they called caballine oil. The lamp, which is of copper, or white <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, consists of two pieces; in one of which is a kind of oval plate, six inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and two <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, in which they put the oil and the cotton. The other part, called the box, in which the lamp is inclosed, serves only to receive the oil which boils over by the force of the fire. This lamp, or, where several artists work together, two or three more lamps are placed on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of proper height. Under the table, about the middle of its height, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of organ-bellows, which one of the workmen moves up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with his foot to quicken the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of the lamps, which are by this means excited to an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of vehemence. Grooves made with a gauge in the upper part of the table, and covered with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, convey the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> of the bellows to a pipe of glass before each lamp; and that the enamellers may not be inconvenienced with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the lamp, every pipe is covered at five inches distance with a little tin plate, fixed into the table by a wooden handle. When the works do not require a long blast, Enamelling It is incredible to what a degree of fineness and delicacy the threads of enamel may be drawn at the lamp. Those which are used in making false tufts of feathers are so fine, that they may be wound on the reel like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> or thread. The fictitious jets of all colours, used in embroideries, are also made of enamel; and that with so much art, that every small piece hath its hole to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the thread through wherewith it is sewed. These holes are made by blowing them into long pieces; which they afterwards cut with a proper tool. It is seldom that the Venetian or Dutch enamels are used alone: they commonly melt them in an iron ladle, with an equal part of glass or crystal; and when the two matters are in perfect fusion, they draw it out into threads of different sizes, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the work. They take it out of the ladle while liquid, with two pieces of broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, which they extend from each other at arm's length. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the thread is required still longer, then another workman holds one end, and continues to draw it out, while the first holds the enamel to the flame. Those threads, when <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, are cut into what lengths the workman thinks fit, but commonly from 10 to 12 inches: and as they are all round, if they are required to be flat, they must be drawn through a pair of pinchers while yet hot. They have also another iron <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in form of pinchers, to draw out the enamel by the lamp when it is to be worked and disposed in figures. Lastly, they have glass tubes of various sizes, serving to blow the enamel into various figures, and preserve the necessary vacuities therein; as also to spare the stuff, and form the contours. When the enameller is at work, he sits before the lamp with his foot on the step that moves on the bellows; and holding in his left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> the work to be enamelled, or the bras or iron wires the figures are to be formed on, he directs with his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> the enamel thread, which he holds to the flame with a management and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> equally surprising. There are few things they cannot make or represent with enamel: and some figures are as well finished, as if done by the most skilful carvers. Enarthrosis, in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Diarthrosis. Encenida, the name of three several festivals celebrated by the Jews in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the dedication, or rather purification, of the temple, by Judas Maccabeus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, and Zorobabel. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is likewise used in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for the dedication of Christian churches. Encampment, the pitching of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>. Encanthis, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a tubercle arising either from the caruncula lachrymalis, or from the adjacent red skin; sometimes so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, as to obstruct not only the puncta lachrymalis, but also part of the sight or pupil itself. See Surgery. Encaustic and Encaustum, the same with enamelling and enamel. See Enamelling and Enamel. Encaustic Painting, a method of painting made use of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, in which wax was employed to give a gloss to their colours, and to preserve them from the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> art, after having been long lost, was encaustic restored by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Caylus, a member of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a> in France; and the method of painting in wax was announced to the Academy of Painting and Belles Lettres in the year 1753; though M. Bachelier, the author of a treatise De l'Histoire et du Secret de la Peinture en Cire, had actually painted a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in wax in 1749; and he was the first who communicated to the public the method of performing the operation of intuition, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> characteristic of the encaustic painting. The Count kept his method a secret for some time, contenting himself with exhibiting a picture at the Louvre in 1754, representing the head of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, painted in the manner of the ancients, which excited the curiosity of the public, and was very much admired. In the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of suspense, several attempts were made to recover the ancient method of painting. The first scheme adopted was that of melting wax and oil of turpentine together, and using this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> as a vehicle for mixing and laying on the colours. But this method did not explain Pliny's meaning, as the wax is not burnt in this way of managing it. In another attempt, which was much more agreeable to the historian's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of encaustic painting, the wax was melted with strong lixivium of tartar, and with this the colours were ground. When the picture was finished, it was gradually presented to the fire, so as to melt the wax; which was thus diffused through all the particles of the colours, so that they were fixed to the ground, and secured from the access of air or moisture. But the method of Count Caylus is much more simple: the cloth or wood which he designed for the basis of his picture, is waxed over, by only rubbing it simply with a piece of bees-wax; the wood or cloth, stretched on a frame, being held horizontally over, or perpendicularly before a fire, at such a distance, that the wax might gradually melt, whilst it is rubbed on, diffuse itself, penetrate the body, and fill the interstices of the texture of the cloth, which, when cool, is fit to paint upon; but as water colours, or those that are mixed up with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> water, will not adhere to the wax, the whole picture is to be first rubbed over with Spanish chalk or white, and then the colours are applied to it; when the picture is dry, it is put near the fire, whereby the wax melts, and absorbs all the colours. Mr J. H. Muntz, in a treatise on this subject, has proposed several improvements in the art of encaustic painting. When the painting is on cloth, he directs it to be prepared by stretching it on a frame, and rubbing one side several times over with a piece of beeswax, or virgin wax, till it is covered with a coat of wax of considerable thickness. In fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, this is the only operation necessary previous to painting; but coarse cloth must be rubbed gently on the unwaxed side with a pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, to take off all those knots which would prevent the free and accurate working of the pencil. Then the subject is to be painted on the unwaxed side with colours prepared and tempered with water; and when the picture is finished, it must be brought near the fire, that the wax may melt and fix the colours. This method, however, can only be applied to cloth or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, through the substance of which the wax may pass; but in wood, stone, metals, Encaustic or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, the former method of Count Caylus must be observed. Mr Muntz has also discovered a method of forming grounds for painting with crayons, and fixing these, as well as water-colours employed with the pencil. On the unwaxed side of a linen cloth, stretched and waxed as before, lay an even and thick coat of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> proper for the ground; having prepared this colour by mixing some proper pigment with an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of chalk, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERING">tempering</a> them with water. When the colour is dry, bring the picture to the fire, that the wax may melt, pass through the cloth, and fix the ground. An additional quantity of wax may be applied to the back of the picture, if that which was first rubbed on should not be sufficient for the body of colour; but as this must be laid on without heat, the wax should be dissolved in oil of turpentine, and applied with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, and the canvas be again exposed to the fire, that the fresh supply of wax may pass through the cloth, and be absorbed by the colour; and thus a firm and good body will be formed for working on with the crayons. If cloth and paper are joined together, the cloth must be first fixed to the straining frame, and then the paper must be pasted to it with a composition of paste made with wheaten flour, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STARCH">starch</a> and water, and about a twelfth part of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of common turpentine. The turpentine must be added to the paste when it is almost sufficiently boiled, and the composition well stirred, and left to simmer over the fire for five or six minutes: let wax be dissolved in oil of turpentine to the consistence of a thin paste; and when the cloth and paper are dry, let them be held near a fire; and with a brush lay a coat of the wax and turpentine on both sides the joined cloth and paper, in such a degree of thickness, that both surfaces may shine throughout without any appearance of dull spots. Then expose the cloth to the fire, or to the fun; by which means the oil will evaporate, and the wax become <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and be fit to receive any composition of colour for a ground, which is to be laid on as above directed in the case of cloth without paper. Almost all the colours that are used in oil-painting may be also applied in the encaustic method. Mr Muntz objects, indeed, to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pink, and unburnt terra di <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>; because these, on account of their gummy or stony texture, will not admit such a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> with the wax as will properly fix them; but other colours which cannot be admitted in oil-painting, as red <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, red <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>, crystals of verdigris, and red precipitate of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, may be used here. The crayons used in encaustic painting are the same with those used in the common way of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRAYON">crayon</a> painting, excepting those that in their composition are too tenacious; and the method of using them is the same in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. The encaustic painting has many peculiar advantages; though the colours have not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> or shining which they acquire with oil, they have all the strength of paintings in oil, and all the airiness of encaustic water-colours, without partaking of the apparent character or defects of either: they may be looked at in any light and in any situation, without any false glare; the colours are firm, and will bear washing; and a picture, after having been smoked, and then exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, becomes as clean as if it had been but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> painted. It may also be retouched at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> without any detriment to the colours; for the new colours will unite with the old ones, without spots, as is the case in common size painting; nor is it necessary to rub the places to be touched with oil as in oil pictures; it is not liable to crack, and easily repaired, if it should chance to suffer any injury. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of this painting is also a very material advantage; the colours are not liable to fade and change; no damp can affect them, nor any corrosive substance injure them; nor can the colour <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off in thivers from the canvas. However, notwithstanding all these and other advantages enumerated by the Abbe Mazeas and Mr Muntz, this art has not yet been much practised. Many of these properties belong to a much higher species of encaustic painting afterwards discovered in England, the colours of which are fixed by a very intense heat; nor are the colours or grounds on which they are laid liable to be dissolved or corroded by any chemical menstruum, nor, like the glassy colours of enamel, to run out of the drawing on the fire. What this method consists in will appear from the following account communicated in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Coleridge to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Macclesfield, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in 1756. "The art of painting with burnt wax (says he) has long been lost to the world. The use of it to painters in the infancy of the art of painting was of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. Drying oil being unknown, they had nothing to preserve their colours entire from the injury of damps and the heat of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>: a varnish of some sort was therefore necessary; but they being unacquainted with distilled spirits, could not, as we now do, dissolve <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> to make a transparent coat for their pictures: this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> therefore of burnt wax supplied that defect to them; and with this manner of painting the chambers and other rooms in their houses were furnished: this Pliny calls encaustum, and we encaustic painting. "The following experiments which I have the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to lay before your Lordship and the Society, were occasioned by the extract of a letter from the Abbe Mazeas, translated by Dr Parsons, and published in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part of the 49th volume of the Philosophical Transactions, No. 100. concerning the ancient method of painting with burnt wax, revived by Count Caylus. "The count's method was, 1. To rub the cloth or board designed for the picture simply over with beeswax. 2. To lay on the colours mixed with common water: but as the colours will not adhere to the wax, the whole picture was first rubbed over with (a) Spanish chalk is called by Dr Parsons, in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, Spanish white. This is a better kind of whitening than the common, and was the only white that had the name of Spanish annexed to it that I could procure, though I inquired for it at most if not all the colour shops in town." Eacautic nish chalk, and then the colours are used. 3. When painting, the picture is dry it is put near the fire, whereby the wax melts, and absorbs all the colours. "Exp. 1. A piece of oak board was rubbed over with bees-wax, first against the grain of the wood, and then with the grain, to fill up all the pores that remained after it had been planed, and afterwards was rubbed over with as much dry Spanish white as could be made to stick on it. This, on being painted (the colours mixed with water only), fo clogged the pencil, and mixed so unequally with the ground, that it was impossible to make even an outline, but what was so much thicker in one part than another, that it would not bear so much as the name of painting; neither had it any appearance of a picture. However, to pursue the experiment, this was put at a distance from the fire, on the hearth, and the wax melted by slow degrees: but the Spanish white (though laid as smooth as so soft a body would admit, before the colour was laid on), on melting the wax into it, was not sufficient to hide the grain of the wood, nor show the colours by a proper whitening of the ground; the wax, in rubbing on the board, was unavoidably thicker in some parts than in others, and the Spanish white the same: on this I suspected there must be some mistake in the Spanish white, and made the inquiry mentioned in the note (A). "To obviate the inequality of the ground in the first experiment. "Exp. 2. A piece of old wainscot (oak-board) th of an inch thick; which, having been part of an old drawer, was not likely to shrink on being brought near the fire: this was smoothed with a fifth skin; made quite warm before the fire; and then, with a brush dipped in white wax, melted in an earthen pipkin, smeared all over, and applied to the fire again. That the wax might be equally thick in all parts of the board, a ground was laid (on the waxed board) with levigated chalk mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water (viz. gum-arabic dissolved in water): When it was dry, I painted it with a kind of landscape; and pursuing the method laid down by Count Caylus, brought it gradually to the fire. I fixed the picture on a fire-screen, which would preserve the heat and communicate it to the back part of the board. This was placed first at the distance of three feet from the fire, and brought forwards by slow degrees, till it came within one foot of the fire, which made the wax swell and bloat up the picture; but as the chalk did not absorb the wax, the picture fell from the board and left it quite bare. "Exp. 3. I mixed three parts white wax, and one part white resin, hoping the tenacity of the resin might preserve the picture. This was laid on a board heated with a brush as in the former; and the ground was chalk prepared as before. This was placed horizontally on an iron box, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with a hot heater, shifting it from time to time, that the wax and resin might penetrate the chalk; and hoping from this position, that the ground, bloated by melting the wax, would subside into its proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but this, like the other, came from the board, and would not at all adhere. "Exp. 4. Prepared chalk four drams, white wax, white resin, of each a dram, burnt alabaster half a dram, were all powdered together and fitted, mixed with spirit of molasses instead of water, and put for a ground on a board smeared with wax and resin, as in Exp. 3. This was also placed horizontally on a box-iron as the former: the picture blistered, and was cracked all over; and though removed from the box-iron to an oven moderately heated (in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position), it would not subside, nor become smooth. When it was cold, I took an iron spatula made warm, and moved it gently over the surface of the picture, as if I were to spread a plaster. (This thought occurred, from the board being prepared with wax and resin, and the ground having the same materials in its composition, the force of the spatula might make them unite). This succeeded so well, as to reduce the surface to a tolerable degree of smoothness; but as the ground was broke off in many places, I repaired it with flake white, mixed up with the yolk of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and repainted it with molasses spirit (instead of water), and then put it into an oven with a moderate degree of heat. In this I found the colours fixed, but darker than when it was at first painted; and it would bear being washed with water, not rubbed with a wet cloth. "Exp. 5. A board (that had been used in a former experiment) was smeared with wax and resin, of each equal parts; was wetted with molasses spirit, to make whitening (or Spanish white) mixed with gum water adhere. This, when dry, was scraped with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, to make it equally thick in all places. It was put into a warm oven, to make the varnish incorporate partly with the whitening before it was painted; and it had only a small degree of heat; water was only used to mix the colours. This was again put into an oven with a greater degree of heat; but it flaked off from the board: whether it might be owing to the board's having had a second coat of varnish (the first having been scraped and melted off), and that the unctuous parts of the wax had so entered its pores, that it would not retain a second varnish, I cannot tell. "Exp. 6. Having miscarried in these trials, I took a new board, planed smooth, but not polished either with a fifth skin or rushes: I warmed it, and smeared it with wax only; then took ciniglia (tobacco-pipe clay) divested of its sand, by being dissolved in water and poured off, leaving the coarse heavy parts behind. After this was dried and powdered, I mixed it with a small quantity of the yolk of an egg and cow's milk, and made a ground with this on the waxed board: this I was induced to try, by knowing that the yolk of an egg will dissolve almost all unctuous substances, and make them incorporate with water; and I apprehended, that a ground thus prepared, would adhere too much the more firmly to the board than the former had done, as to prevent its flaking off. The milk, I thought, might "My friend M. da Costa showed me a piece of Spanish chalk in his collection, which seemed more like a ciniglia (tobacco-pipe clay) and was the reason of my using that in one of the experiments." Encaustic might answer two purposes; first, by uniting the ground with the wax; and secondly, by answering the end of size or gum-water, and prevent the colours from sinking too deep into the ground, or running one into another. When the ground was near dry, I smoothed it with a pallet knife, and washed with milk and egg where I had occasion to make it smooth and even: when dry I painted it, mixing the colours with common water; this, on being placed horizontally in an oven only warm enough to melt the wax, flaked from the board; but held so much better together than any of the former, that I parted part of it on paper. "Exp. 7. Flake-white (or the purest sort of white-lead) mixed with egg and milk, crumbled to pieces in the oven, put on the waxed board, as in the last experiment. "The bad success which had attended all the former experiments, led me to consider of what use the wax was in this kind of painting: and it occurred to me, that it was only as a varnish to preserve the colours from fading. "In order to try this: "Exp. 8. I took what the brick-layers call fine fluff, or putty, (b): to this I added a small quantity of burnt alabaster, to make it dry: this it soon did in the open air; but before I put on any colours, I dried it gently by the fire, lest the colours should run. When it was painted, I warmed it gradually by the fire (to prevent the ground from cracking) till it was very hot. I then took white wax three parts, white resin one part; melted them in an earthen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, and with a brush spread them all over the painted board, and kept it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the fire in a perpendicular situation, that what wax and resin the plaster would not absorb might drop off. When it was cold, I found the colours were not altered, either from the heat of the fire, or passing the brush over them. I then rubbed it with a soft linen cloth, and thereby procured a kind of glofs, which I afterwards increased by rubbing it with a hard brush; which was so far from scratching or leaving any marks on the picture, that it became more smooth and polished by it. "After I had made all the foregoing experiments, in conversation with my honoured and learned friend Dr Kidby, a fellow of this society, I said I had been trying to find out what the encaustic painting of the ancients was. Upon which he told me, that there was a passage in Vitruvius de Architectura relative to that kind of painting: and was so good as to transcribe it for me from the 7th book, chap. 9. De minii temperaturo. Vitruvius's words are: At si quis subtilior fuerit, et soluerit expositionem minuaceam suum colorem retinere, cum paries expolitus et aridus fuerit, tunc ceram Punicam liquefactam igui, paulo oleo temperatam, feta inducat, deinde polsa carbonibus in ferrea uafe composita, cum ceram opprime cum varietate, calefaciendo sudore evagat, fatique ut perequeratur, deinde cura candela lintece puris fibigat, ut signa marmoreo nuda curantur. Haec enim xavrii Graece dicitur. Iuolofans cerne Punicae loricae non patitur, nec <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> splendorem, nec folis radios lambendo eripere ex his pollutionibus colorum. "Which I thus translate: 'But if any one is more wary, and would have the polishing [painting] with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> hold its colour, when the wall is painted and dry, let him take Carthaginian [Barbary] wax, melted with a little oil, and rub it on the wall with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-pencil; and afterwards let him put live coals into an iron vessel [<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a>], and hold it close to the wax, when the wall, by being heated, begins to sweat; then let it be made smooth: afterwards let him rub it with a (c) <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> and (d) clean linen rags, in the same manner as they do the naked marble <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>. This the Greeks call xavrii. The coat of Carthaginian wax (thus put on) is so strong, that it neither suffers the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> by night, nor the sun-beams by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to destroy the colour.' "Being satisfied, from this passage in Vitruvius, that the manner of using wax in Exp. 8. was right, I was now to find if the wax-varnish, thus burnt into the picture, would bear washing. But here I was a little disappointed; for rubbing one corner with a wet linen cloth, some of the colour came off; but washing it with a soft hair-pencil dipped in water, and letting it dry without wiping, the colour stood very well. "A board painted, as in Exp. 8. was hung in the most smokey part of a chimney for a day, and exposed to the open air in a very foggy night. In the morning the board was seemingly wet through, and the water ran off the picture. This was suffered to dry without wiping; and the picture had not suffered at all from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> or the dew, either in the ground or the colours; but when dry, by rubbing it, first with a soft cloth, and afterwards with a brush, it recovered its former glofs. "Suspecting that some tallow might have been mixed with the white wax I had used, which might cause the colours to come off on being rubbed with a wet cloth, I took yellow wax which had been melted from the honeycomb in a private family, and consequently not at all adulterated: to three parts of this I added one part resin, and melted them together. "Exp. 9. Spanish-white, mixed with fish-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>, was put for a ground on a board, and painted with water-colours only. The board was made warm; and then the wax and resin were put on with a brush, and kept close to the fire till the picture had imbibed all the varnish, (b) "Putty is lime flaked, and while warm, dissolved in water, and strained through a sieve. (c) "The account of the method of polishing [painting] walls coloured with vermilion, gave me great satisfaction, as it proved the method I had taken in experiment 8. (which I had tried before I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> or knew of this passage in Vitruvius) was right. The use of the candle, as I apprehend, was to melt the wax on the walls where by accident the brush had put on too much, or afford wax where the brush had not put on enough, or had left any part bare. (d) "The rubbing the wall with a linen cloth, while warm, will do very well where there is only one colour to be preserved; but where there are many, as in a landscape, it will be apt to take off some, or render the colouring rather faint; which I found by wiping the wax off from a painting while it was hot." Encaustic varnish, and looked dry. When it was cold, I rubbed it first with a linen cloth, and then polished it with a hard brush. "In these experiments I found great difficulties with regard to colours. Many water colours being made from the juices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, have some degree of an acid in them; and these, when painted on an alkaline ground, as chalk, whitening, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, and plaster, are totally changed in their colours, and from green become brown; which contributes much to make the experiments tedious. I would therefore advise the use of mineral or metallic colours for this sort of painting, as most likely to preserve their colour; for although I neutralized Spanish white, by fermenting it with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and afterwards washed it very well with water, it did not succeed to my wish. "These experiments, and this passage from Vitruvius, will in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> explain the obscurity of part of that passage in Pliny which Dr Parsons, in his learned comment on the encaustic painting with wax, seems to despair of. "Caris pingere, was one species of encaustic painting. Exuvior, influm, may be translated, 'forced in by the means of fire; burnt in;' for whatever is forced in by the help of fire can be rendered into Latin by no other significant word that I know of but influm. If this is allowed me, and I think I have the authority of Vitruvius (a writer in the Augustan <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>) for it, who seems to have wrote from his own knowledge, and not like Pliny, who copied from others much more than he knew himself, the difficulty with regard to this kind of painting, is solved, and the encaustic with burnt wax recovered to the public. "What he means by the next kind he mentions, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EBRO">ebro</a> cefiro id gil viriculo, I will not attempt to explain at present. "The ship-painting is more easily accounted for, the practice being in part <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to this time; and is what is corruptly called breuning, for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> or burning. "This is done by reeds set on fire, and held under the side of a ship till it is quite hot; then resin, tallow, tar, and brimstone, melted together, and put on with a hair brush while the planks remain hot, make such a kind of paint as Pliny describes: which, he says, nec sole, nec <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a> ventique corruptitur. As they were ignorant of the use of oil-painting, they mixed that colour with the wax, &c., which they intended for each particular part of the ship, and put it on in the manner above described. "In the pictures painted for these experiments, and now laid before your lordship and the society, I hope neither the design of the landscape, nor the execution of it, will be too much taken into consideration as the varnish (which was the thing wanted in this inquiry); and I think that will evince, that the encaustic painting with burnt wax is fully restored by these experiments; and though not a new invention, yet having been lost for so many ages, and now applied further, and to other purposes, than it was by Vitruvius (who confined it to vermilion only), may also amount to a new discovery, the use of which may be a means of preserving many curious drawings to posterity; for this kind of painting may be on paper, cloth, or any other substance that will admit a ground to be laid on it. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is very simple, and is not attended with the disagreeable smell unavoidable in oil-painting, nor with some inconveniences inseparable from that art; and as there is no substance we know more durable than wax, it hath the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of being lasting." Still, however, there seem to have been some defects or inconveniences attending these and other subsequent attempts; for we find the ancient or some similar method of painting in wax remaining a defecratum upwards of 25 years after the publication of the preceding experiments; and when in 1787 a method was communicated to the Society of Arts by Miss <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, for which she was rewarded with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. The ground of her information she received at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, through the acquaintance of an amateur of painting, who procured her the satisfaction of seeing some paintings in the ancient Grecian style, executed by Signora Parenti, a professor at that place, who had been instructed by a Jesuit at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, the person who made the farthest discoveries in that art. Miss Greenland's friend knowing she was fond of painting, informed her what were the materials the painters used, but could not tell her the proportions of the composition; however, from her anxiety to succeed in such an acquisition, she made various experiments, and at last obtained such a sufficient knowledge of the quantities of the different ingredients as to begin and finish a picture, which she afterwards presented to the Society for their inspection. Her method is as follows: "Take an ounce of white wax, and the same weight of gum mastic powdered. Put the wax in a glazed earthen vessel over a very slow fire; and when it is quite dissolved, throw in the mastic, a little at a time, stirring the wax continually until the whole quantity of gum is perfectly melted and incorporated; then throw the paste into cold water; and when it is hard, take it out of the water, wipe it dry, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> it in one of Mr Wedgwood's mortars, observing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> it at first in a linen cloth to absorb some drops of water that will remain in the paste, and would prevent the possibility of reducing it to a powder, which must be so fine as to pass through a thick <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>. It should be pounded in a cool place and but a little while at a time, as after long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the friction will in a degree soften the wax and gum, and instead of their becoming a powder they will return to a paste. "Make some strong gum-arabic water; and when you paint, take a little of the powder, some colour, and mix them together with the gum-water. Light colours require but a small quantity of the powder, but more of it must be put in proportion to the body and darkness of the colours; and to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> there should be almost as much of the powder as colour. "Having mixed the colours, and no more than can be used before they grow dry, paint with fair water, as is practised in painting with water-colours, a ground on the wood being first painted of some proper colour prepared in the same manner as is described for the picture; walnut-tree and oak are the sorts of wood commonly made use of in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> for this purpose. The painting should be very highly finished; otherwise, when varnished, the tints will not appear united. "When the painting is quite dry, with rather a hard brush, passing it one way, varnish it with white wax, which is put into an earthen vessel, and kept melted over a very slow fire till the picture is varnished, taking Encaustic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> great care the wax does not boil. Afterwards hold the picture before a fire, near enough to melt the wax, but not make it run; and when the varnish is entirely cold and hard, rub it gently with a linen cloth. Should the varnish blister, warm the picture again very slowly, and the bubbles will subside. When the picture is dirty, it need only be washed with cold water. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> given by the Society upon the above is: The method made use of by Miss Greenland provides against all inconveniences; and the brilliancy of the colours in the picture painted by her, and exhibited to the Society, fully justifies the opinion, that the art of painting in wax, as above described, highly merited the reward of a gold pallet voted to her on this occasion.

ENCEINTE

Pages 54-54

in Fortification, is the wall <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rampart which surrounds a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, sometimes composed of battions or curtains, either faced or lined with brick or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or only made of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The enceinte is sometimes only flanked by round or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> towers, which is called a Roman wall.

ENCEPHALI

Pages 54-54

in Medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the head, where they cause so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a pain as sometimes to occasion distraction. The encephali are very rare; but there are some difficulties wherein they swarm: from whence we are told pestilential fevers have wholly arisen. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of one who died of this fever, a little, short, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> worm was found in the head, which malnecy wine, wherein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-radish had been boiled, could alone destroy. This medicine was afterwards tried on the sick, most of whom it cured. The like worms have also been taken out by trepanning, and the patient cured. Those worms that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> in the nose, ears, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, are also called encephali.

ENCHANTER

Pages 54-54

a person supposed to practice enchantment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fascination. See Fascination, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">Witchcraft</a>, &c. ENCHANTER'S Nightshade. See Circaea, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ENCHASING

Pages 54-54

Enchasing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Chasing, the art of enriching and beautifying <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and other metal-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, by some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> or figures represented thereon in low relief. Enchasing is practiced only on hollow thin works, as watch-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>-heads, tweezer-cases, or the like. It is performed by punching or driving out the metal, to form a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, from withinside, so as to stand out prominent from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> or surface of the metal. In order to this, they provide a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> blocks or punchers of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sizes; and the design being drawn on the surface of the metal, they apply the inside upon the heads or tops of these blocks, directly under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> or parts of the figures; then, with a fine hammer, striking on the metal, sustained by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, the metal yields, and the block makes an indentation or cavity on the inside, corresponding to which there is a prominence on the outside, which is to stand for that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the figure. Thus the workman proceeds to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> and finish all the parts by the successive application of the block and hammer to the several parts of the design. And it is wonderful to consider with what <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and justness, by this simple piece of mechanism, the artists in this kind <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> represent foliage, grotesques, animals, historical stories, &c.

ENCLITICA

Pages 54-54

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, particles which are so closely united with other words as to seem <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of them, as in virumque, &c.—There are three enclitic particles in Latin, viz. que, ne, ve.

ENCRATITES

Pages 54-54

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, heretics who appeared towards the end of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century: they were called Encratites, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Continentes, because they gloried in abstaining from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of wine and animal food.

ENCURECK

Pages 54-54

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a venomous insect found in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and said to be a kind of tarantula. According to Olearius, as quoted by Mr Boyle, it neither stings nor bites; but lets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> its venom like a drop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which causes insufferable pain in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and afterwards so profound a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, that, as report says, nothing can awake the patient except crushing one of the creatures on the part affected. It is nevertheless said, that the sheep eat these insects without damage. ENCYCLOPÆDIA, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> nearly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with Cyclopaedia; but adopted in preference to it in denoting the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as being more definite and of better authority. According to an observation of the late learned printer Mr Bower, the preposition en makes the meaning of the word more precise. For Cyclopaedia may denote "the instruction of a circle," as Cyclopædia is "the instruction of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>," whereas in Encyclopaedia, the preposition determines the word to be from the dative of cyclos, "instruction in a circle." And Vossius, in his book De vitis sermonis, has observed, "That Cyclopaedia is used by some authors, but Encyclopaedia by the best."

ENDEMIC

Pages 54-54
or Endemical, Diseases, those to which the inhabitants of particular countries are subject more than others, on account of the air, water, situation, and manner of living. ENDIVE. See Cichorium, Botany and Gardening Index.

ENDLESS

Pages 54-54

something without an end; thus authors mention endless rolls, the endless crew, &c.

ENDOR

Pages 54-54

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Galilee, four miles to the south of Mount Tabor, in the tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, where the Pythoness was consulted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>: at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, says Jerome, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> village.

ENDORSE

Pages 54-54

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, an ordinary, containing the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a> says is only used when a pale is between two of them.

ENDORSED

Pages 54-54

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is said of things borne back to back, more usually called Adosse.

ENDOWMENT

Pages 54-54

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes the settling a dowry on a woman; though sometimes it is used figuratively, for settling a provision upon a parson, on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the severing a sufficient portion of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, when the benefice is appropriated.

ENDYMION

Pages 54-55

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a shepherd, son of Athlius and Calyce. It is said that he required of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to him to be always young, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> as much as he would; whence came the proverb of Endymionis somnum dormire, to express a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> sleep. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him naked as he slept on Mount Latmos; and Endymion and was so struck with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, that she came <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven every night to enjoy his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. Endymion married Chromia <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Itonus; by whom he had three sons Paon, Epens, and Acolus, and a daughter called Eurydice. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Endymion's amours with Diana, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, arose from his knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>; and as he passed the night on some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain to observe the heavenly bodies, it came to be reported that he was courted by the moon. Some suppose that there were two of that name; the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, and the shepherd or astronomer of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>. The people of Heraclia maintained that Endymion died on Mount Latmos; and the Eleans pretended to show his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>.

ENEMY

Pages 55-55

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, an alien <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foreigner, who publicly invades the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>.

ENERGUMENS

Pages 55-55

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, persons supposed to be possessed by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, concerning whom there were many regulations among the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. They were denied <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and the eucharist; at least, this was the practice of some churches; and though they were under the care of exorcists, yet it was thought a becoming <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to let them have the public prayers of the church, at which they were permitted to be present. See EXORCISM.

ENERGY

Pages 55-55

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of Greek origin, signifying the power, virtue, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> efficacy of a thing. It is also used, figuratively, to denote emphasis of speech.

ENERVATING

Pages 55-55

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of destroying the force, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> office, of the nerves, either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them, by weakening them with debauchery, or by some other violence. Excess of wine, and other strong, hot, spirituous liquors, enervate or weaken the nerves. When they would render a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> useless, they enervate him, or cut his nerves.

ENFAILL

Pages 159-159

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies feetail, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fee entailed; that is, abridged, curtailed, or limited, to certain conditions. See Fee and Tail.

ENFIELD

Pages 55-55

WILLIAM, LL.D. an elegant and very justly admired writer, was born in the year 1741, at Sudbury. His original destination was for the sacred office of the ministry, and he was educated among the protestant dissenters at Daventry, where the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> polish which he gave to his compositions, distinguished him from many of his contemporaries. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of Benn's-garden of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a> made choice of him for their minister in the year 1763, when he was not more than 22 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and in this situation he was soon taken notice of as an amiable member of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and an engaging preacher. While he resided in Liverpool, he published two volumes of sermons, 12mo, as well as a collection of hymns and family prayers, which met with a very favourable reception. In the year 1770, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> and lecturer in the belles lettres at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRINGTON">Warrington</a> academy, which he filled for some years with general approbation and unwearied diligence. He was the compiler of many useful books, among the most popular of which we may <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> his "Speaker," composed of pieces of recitation from the best and most approved English authors. At the beginning of this collection there is an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on elocution. The Preacher's Directory; the English Preacher, a collection of sermons in 9 vols 12mo, from the most celebrated authors; Biographical Sermons on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in the Old and New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of single sermons on particular occasions, were also the productions of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>. The controversy relative to literary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> also engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and on this he wrote a quarto pamphlet. He likewise published in one volume 4to, Institutes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, theoretical and experimental; and during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his residence at Warrington, as teacher in the academy, the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> conferred on him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of LL.D. When that academy was dissolved in 1783, Dr Enfield <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for two years at Warrington in the capacity of a private tutor, after which he was chosen pastor of the Octagon meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, in the year 1785. He at length gave up his private tuition, and entirely devoted his time to literary labours, and the peculiar duties of his pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. About this time he lost his eldest son, who had been appointed to the office of town-clerk of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>. This event would have been productive of very serious effects on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and spirits, had it not been for the consolation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and philosophy, which are sufficient to support the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind under the prelude of the severest calamities. He undertook and executed the laborious task of abridging Brucker's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Philosophy, which in 1791 he published in 2 vols 4to. It has been allowed that the tenets of the different sects of philosophers were never before exhibited to the world with such perspicuity and elegance; qualifications for which Dr Enfield was undoubtedly eminent. He contributed largely to the Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, published under the inspection of Dr Aiken and others. An unexpected distemper hastened the termination of his useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and on the 3d of November 1797, he expired in the 57th year of his age. The general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of mankind which Dr Enfield possessed, falls to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of few; nor does it often happen that an individual dies so universally lamented. It was essential to him to be amiable in every station and condition of life. His posthumous sermons, in 3 vols 8vo, had a very numerous <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of subscribers, a strong <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the estimation in which he was held by all who knew him, either personally <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by report. In these discourses he treats, chiefly on moral topics, which he discusses with the nicest discrimination, and in a train of the most pleasing and manly eloquence.

ENFILADE

Pages 55-55

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, is used in speaking of trenches, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other places, which may be scoured by the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> along their whole length. In conducting the approaches at a siege, care must be taken that the trenches be not enfiladed from any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

ENFINE'

Pages 55-56

formerly ANTINOE, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, built by Adrian in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his favourite Antinous. It is situated towards the middle of the Said, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Upper Egypt, and still contains several stately monuments of antiquity. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times this city was very magnificent. It was about half a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in circumference, having two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets 45 feet wide, intersecting each other at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, and running through its whole length. The others were more narrow, but equally straight; the two largest having gates at each end, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which still remain. According to the Nubian geographer, it was called the city of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>, because <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> is said to have caused the magicians come from thence to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Near it were the ruins of Abydus, where there was an oracle of the god Befa, one of the most ancient in Egypt, and which was still famous in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Constantius; and hence some have derived the appellation <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, the neighbouring people coming in crowds to consult the oracle. The ruins of the gates are the most beautiful pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> to be met with in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The handsomest has three vaulted entries; the middle one being 40 feet in height, 22 wide, and 20 thick; the other two smaller. Each of the façades of this edifice is ornamented with four pilasters in bas relief, with Corinthian capitals, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACANTHUS">acanthus</a> leaves of which have a considerable projection. It was surrounded by eight Corinthian columns, of which only one now remains, but the pedestals of the rest are still entire. Besides these, there are heaps of rubbish in different parts of the town, apparently the remains of ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> or palaces. All these seem to have been bordered by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a>, forming a portico on each side, where the inhabitants might walk secure from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. One of the squares was ornamented with four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> Corinthian pillars, three of which are destroyed all but the bases. The fourth is quite entire, about 50 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the shaft composed of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. The pedestal has a Greek inscription, pretty much defaced, dedicating it to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Alexander Severus, to whom the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> had already dedicated the famous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> mentioned under that article. These four other columns were therefore probably raised in honour of that emperor after his victories over the Persians; for the foliage of the oak, with which the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of the shaft is decorated, was a sign of victory among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Towards the end of the fourth century the city was peopled by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALLADIUS">Palladius</a> assures us, that there were at that place 12 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of virgins, and several others inhabited by monks. In the convents there are still several Coptic monasteries possessed by monks equally miserable and ignorant. The Nubian geographer informs us, that the city was surrounded by a well cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and harvests; but these have now given place to sands and barren deserts. The ruins of Abydus above mentioned are still to be seen near this place.

ENFRANCHISEMENT

Pages 56-56

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the incorporating a person into any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body-politic.

ENGASTRIMYTHI

Pages 56-56

in Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, the Pythians, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> priestesses of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, who delivered <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> from within, without any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the mouth or lips. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, &c., are divided upon the subject of the engastrimythi. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> mentions it as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>. Others <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> it to the operation or possession of an evil spirit. And others to art and mechanism. M. Scottus maintains that the engastrimythi of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were poets, who, when the priests could not speak, supplied the defect by explaining, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> what Apollo dictated in the cavity of the basin on the sacred tripod.

ENGENDERING

Pages 56-56

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> sometimes used for the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of producing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> forming any thing: thus meteors are said to be engendered in the middle region of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> in the belly.

ENGINE

Pages 56-56

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> machine, made of one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL_POWERS"><a class="xref" h</a>ref="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> powers, as levers, pulleys, screws, &c., in order to raise, lift, or sustain any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, or produce any effect which could not be easily effected otherwise. The word is formed of the French engin, from the Latin ingenium, "<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>;" by reason of the ingenuity required in the contrivance of engines to augment the effect of moving powers. Engine for Extinguishing Fires. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">Hydrodynamics</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. [Merged from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEAM">STEAM</a>-ENGINE, p.56] a machine to raise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> by fire, or rather by the force of water turned into steam. See Steam-Engine.

ENGINEER

Pages 56-56

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, an able expert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who, by a perfect knowledge in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, delineates upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> marks upon the ground, all forts of forts, and other works proper for offence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. He should understand the art of fortification, so as to be able, not only to discover the defects of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but to find a remedy proper for them; as also how to make an attack upon, as well as to defend, the place. Engineers are extremely necessary for these purposes: wherefore it is requisite, that besides being ingenious, they should be brave in proportion. When at a siege, the engineers have narrowly surveyed the place, they are to make their report to the general, by acquainting him which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> they judge the weakest, and where approaches may be made with most success. Their business is also to delineate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of circumvallation and contravallation, taking all the advantages of the ground; to mark out the trenches, places of arms, batteries, and lodgments, taking care that none of their works be flanked or discovered from the place. After making a faithful report to the general of what is a-doing, the engineers are to demand a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of workmen and utensils, and whatever else is necessary.

ENGLAND

Pages 56-70

the southern <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Including <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, it is of a triangular form, and lies between the 50th and 55th degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, extending about 400 miles in length from south to north, and in some places it is 300 miles in breadth. It is bounded by Scotland on the north; by the English channel on the south, dividing it from France; by the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the east; and on the west by St George's, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Irish channel. At what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the island of Britain was peopled is Whence uncertain; nor do we know whether the southern or northern parts were first inhabited. We have no accounts that can be depended upon before the arrival of Julius Caesar, and it is certain he found the southern parts full of people of a very warlike disposition. These people, according to Caesar, were a colony of the Gauls; and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is embraced by most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as well as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers. It is chiefly founded on the agreement observed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> between the two nations in their customs, manners, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, way of fighting, &c. The more northern inhabitants, according to Tacitus, came from Germany. This he infers from the make of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>; but Caesar simply calls them <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>. England, including the principality of Wales, when first invaded by the Romans, was divided into 17 petty states. 1. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DANMONII">Danmonii</a>, called also Dunnonni and Danmonii, inhabiting the counties of Cornwall and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. 2. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUROTRIGES">Durotriges</a>, who inhabited the tract now called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>. 3. The Belgae possessed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, Wiltsire, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. 4. The Atrebati, or inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>. 5. The Regni, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> bordered on that of the Atrebati, and comprehended <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Hampshire. 6. The Cantii, inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. 7. The Dobuni are placed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> on the north side of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, near its head, in the counties of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. 8. The Catticuchlani, Calgenohlani, Catidadiaduni, or Cathidadiaduni, inhabited Buckinghamshire, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>. 9. The Trinobantes, who possessed the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>. 10. The Iceni, whose country comprehended <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and Huntingdonshire. These are by Ptolemy called Simeni, and by others Tigeni. Camden is of opinion, that they were the same whom Caesar calls Cenomagni. 11. The Coritani, whose country comprehended <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, Rutlandshire, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>. 12. The Cornubi possessed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, and Cheshire. 13. The Silures inhabited the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>, Brecknockshire, Glamorganshire, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>. 14. The Demetiae inhabited part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKESHIRE">Pembrokeshire</a>, and Cardiganshire. 15. The country of the Ordovices comprehended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a>, Caernarvonshire, Denbighshire, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>. 16. The Brigantes possessed the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, Westmorland, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>. 17. The county of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> was held by the Ottadini, Ottademi, or Ottalini. Their country, according to some, reached from the Tyne to the river Forth; though the most <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> opinion is, that it reached only to the Tweed. The above-mentioned names of these nations are plainly Roman, but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of them is not easily ascertained.
