ENTRY of an Heir, in Scots Law, that form of law by which an heir vests in himself a proper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to his predecessor's estate. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">Bill</a> of ENTRY, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. See BILL. In making entries inwards, it is usual for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to include all the goods they have on board the same ship in one bill, though sometimes they may happen to be upwards of 20 several kinds: and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the goods are short entered, additional or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> entries are now allowed; though formerly the goods so entered were forfeited. As to bills of entry outwards, or including goods to be exported, upon delivering them, and paying the customs, you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> receive a small piece of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> called a cocket, which testifies your payment thereof, and all duties for such goods. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> several sorts of goods are exported at once, of which some are free, and others pay customs; the exporter must have two cockets, and therefore must make two entries; one for the goods that pay, and the other for the goods that do not pay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. Entries of goods, on which a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRAWBACK">drawback</a> is allowed, must likewise contain the name of the ship in which the goods were imported, the importer's name, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of entry inwards. The entry being thus made, and an oath taken that the customs for those goods were paid as the law directs, you must carry it to the collector and comptroller, or their deputies; who, after examining their books, will <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> warrant, which must be given to the surveyor, searcher, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-waiter, for them to certify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of goods; after which the certificate must be brought back to the collector and comptroller, or their deputies, and oath made that the said goods are really shipped, and not landed again in any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

ENUMERATION

Pages 265-265

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERORATION">peroration</a>; in which the orator, collecting the scattered heads of what has been delivered throughout the whole, makes a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> and artful relation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> recapitulation thereof.

ENVELOPE

Pages 265-265

in Fortification, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, sometimes in form of a simple <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, and at others like a small rampart with a parapet: it is raised sometimes on the ditch, and sometimes beyond it.

ENVIRONNE

Pages 265-265

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, signifies surrounded with other things: thus, they lay, a lion environné with fo many bezants. See BEZANTS.

ENVOY

Pages 265-265

a person deputed to negotiate some affair with any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state. Those sent from the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, &c., to any petty prince or state, such as the princes of Germany, the republics of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, &c., go in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of envoys, not ambassadors; and such a character only do those persons bear, who go from any of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> courts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to another, when the affair they go upon is not very solemn or important. There are envoys ordinary and extraordinary, as well as ambassadors; they are equally under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nations, and enjoy all the privileges of ambassadors; only differing from them in this, that the same ceremonies are not performed to them.

EONIANS

Pages 265-266

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the followers of Eon, a wild fanatic of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bretagne, in the 12th century, whose brain was disordered. He concluded from the resemblance between eum, in the form for exercising malignant spirits, viz. Per eum, qui venturus est judicare vivos et mortuos, and his own name Eon, that he was the son of God, and ordained to judge the quick and dead. Eon, however, was solemnly condemned by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, in 1148, at which Pope Eugenius III. presided, and ended his days in a miserable Eonians, miserable prifon. He left behind him a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of followers and adherents, whom perfecution and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> so weakly and cruelly employed could not persuade to abandon his caufe, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to renounce an absurdity which, says Moheim, one would think could never have gained <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> but in such a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as Bedlam. EORIA; in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a feast celebrated by the Athenians in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Erigonus, who, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for their not avenging the death of his father <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICARUS">Icarus</a>, engaged the gods to inflict the curse on their daughters that they should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> men who never returned their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The feast was instituted by the order of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>.

EOSTRE

Pages 266-266

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> to whom they sacrificed in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April, called the month of Eoftra; and thence the name Easter, which the Saxons retained after their conversion to Christianity, applying it to the festival celebrated in commemoration of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>.

EPACRIS

Pages 266-266

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPACTS

Pages 266-266

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, the excesses of the solar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> month, and of the solar year above the lunar year of twelve synodical months; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of several solar months above as many synodical months, and several solar years above as many dozen of synodical months. The epacts, then, are either annual or menstrual. Menstrual epacts are the excesses of the civil or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> month above the lunar month. Suppose, e.g., it were new <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> on the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; since the lunar month is 29 days 12h. 44' 3"; and the month of January contains 31 days, the menstrual epact is 1 day 11h. 15' 57". Annual epacts are the excesses of the solar year above the lunar. Hence, as the Julian solar year is 365 days 6h. and the Julian lunar year 354 days 8h. 48' 38", the annual epact <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 10 days 21h. 11' 22"; that is, nearly 11 days. Consequently the epact of 2 years is 22 days; of 3 years, 33 days; or rather 3, since 30 days make an embolismic or intercalary month. Thus the epact of 4 years is 14 days, and fo of the rest; and thus, every 19th year, the epact becomes 30 or 0; consequently the 20th year the epact is 11 again; and so the cycle of epacts expires with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, or lunar cycle of 19 years, and begins with the same, as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: | <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>. Numb. | Epacts. | Gold. Numb. | Epacts. | Gold. Numb. | Epacts. | |-------------|---------|-------------|---------|-------------|---------| | 1 | XI | 8 | XXVIII | 14 | IV | | 2 | XXII | 9 | IX | 15 | XV | | 3 | III | 10 | XX | 16 | XXVI | | 4 | XIV | 11 | I | 17 | VIII | | 5 | XXV | 12 | XII | 18 | XIX | | 6 | VI | 13 | XXIII | 19 | XXX | | 7 | XVII | | | | | Again, as the new moons are the same, that is, as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the same day every 19 years, so the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the lunar and solar years is the same every 19 years. And because the said difference is always to be added to the lunar year, in order to adjust or make it equal to the solar year; hence the said difference respectively belonging to each year of the moon's cycle is called the epact of the said year, that is, the number to be added to the said year, to make it equal to the solar year; the word being formed from the Greek ἐπακτον, induco, intercalo. Upon this mutual respect between the cycle of the moon and the cycle of the epacts, is founded this rule for finding the Julian epact, belonging to any year of the moon's cycle. Multiply the year given of the moon's cycle into 11; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the product be less than 30, it is the epact sought; if the product be greater than 30, divide it by 30, and the remainder of the dividend is the epact. For instance, I would know the epact for the year 1712, which is the third year of the moon's cycle. Wherefore 3 is the epact for 1712; for 11 × 3 = 33, and 33 being divided by 30, there is left 3 of the dividend for the epact. But the difference of the Julian and Gregorian years being equal to the excels of the solar above the lunar year, or 11 days, it happens that the Gregorian epact for one year is the same with the Julian epact for the preceding year.

EPAMINONDAS

Pages 266-267

a celebrated Theban, the son of Polymnus, and one of the greatest captains of antiquity. He learned <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and music under Lyfis, a Pythagorean <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; and was from his infancy inured to all the exercises of body and mind. He was learned, generous, well-skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, brave, modest, and prudent; and had such a regard for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, that he would not tell a falsehood even in jest. He served first under the Lacedemonians; saved the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PELOPIDAS">Pelopidas</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who received in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight wounds; and contracted a strict friendship with that general, which lasted till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. At his persuasions, Pelopidas delivered the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thebes from the yoke of the Spartans, who had rendered themselves masters of Cadmea, which occasioned a bloody war between the two nations. Epaminondas was made general of the Thebans; on which he gained the celebrated battle of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEUCTRA">Leuctra</a>, in which Cleombrotus, the valiant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, was killed. He then ravaged the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and caused the city of Messina to be rebuilt and peopled. At length, the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was given to another, because Epaminondas had kept his troops in the field four months longer than he had been ordered by the people; but, instead of retiring in disgust, he now served as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldier, and distinguished himself by so many brave actions, that the Thebans, ashamed of having deprived him of the command, restored him to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, in order to carry the war into Thessaly, where his arms were always victorious. A war breaking out between the Elians and the inhabitants of Mantinea, the Thebans took the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the former. Epaminondas then resolved to endeavour to surprize Sparta and Mantinea; but not succeeding, he gave the enemy battle, in which he received a mortal wound with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>, the bearded <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> remaining in the wound. Knowing that it could not be drawn out without occasioning immediate death, he would not suffer it to be touched, but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to give his orders: and on his being told, that the enemy were entirely defeated, "I have lived <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough (he cried), cried), since I die without being conquered;" and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he plucked the javelin from his wound, and expired, 363 B.C. EPANALEPSIS. See ORATORY, No 73. EPANODOS. Ibid. No 75. EPANORTHOSIS. Ibid. No 75.

EPARER

Pages 267-267

in the manege, signifies the flinging of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his jerking and striking with his hindlegs.

EPAULEMENT

Pages 267-267

in Fortification, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> raised to cover sidewise, is either of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, gabions, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fascines loaded with earth. The epaulements of the places of arms for the cavalry, at the entrance of the trenches, are generally of fascines mixed with earth.

EPAULETTES

Pages 267-267

are a kind of shoulder-knots chosen for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, which are to be of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the facing, with a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> tape round it, and worsted fringe; those for the officers are made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, with a rich fringe; they are badges of distinction worn on one or both shoulders. Those of the dragoon-guards, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and dragoons, are worn on the left shoulder: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> dragoons, and officers of grenadiers, have one on each shoulder: those of the battalion wear one on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> shoulder only, which is to be made of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a> or lace with a gold or silver fringe. Those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> are to be gold and embroidery, with gold fringe or scarlet cloth, and worn on the right shoulder.

EPENTHESIS

Pages 267-267

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the interposition <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> insertion of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> in the middle of a word; as altium, for altum; religio, for religi; induperator, for imperator, &c.

EPEUS

Pages 267-267

of the line of Endymion, the inventor of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> ram, an engine of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in sieges to make a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>. He is thought to have built the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and to have founded the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> Metapontum.

EPHA

Pages 267-267
or Ephah, in Jewish antiquity, a measure for things dry, equal to 3 pecks and 3 pints. EPHEBÆUM, in antiquity, the place where the ephesoi or youth exercised; or, as some say, where those who designed to exercise met, and agreed what kind of exercise they should contend in, and what should be the victor's reward.

EPHANAY

Pages 274-274

a Christian festival, otherwise called Epiphany, the Manifestation of Christ to the Gentiles, observed on the sixth of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the appearance of our Saviour to the three <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">magi</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wise men, who came to adore him and bring him presents. The feast of epiphany was not originally a distinct festival; but made a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a> of Christ, which being celebrated 12 days, the first and last of which were <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> days of solemnity, either of these might properly be called epiphany, as that word signifies the appearance of Christ in the world. The word in the original Greek, επιφάνεια, signifies appearance or apparition; and was applied, as some critics <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, to this feast, on account of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> which appeared to the magi.—St Jerome and St Chrysostom take the epiphany for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, when he was declared to men by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." And accordingly it is still observed by the Coptic and Ethiopians in that view. Others contend, that the feast of Christmas, or the nativity of our Saviour, was held in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> churches on this day; which had the denomination epiphany, or appearance, by reason of our Saviour's first appearance on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. And it must be allowed, that the word is used among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek fathers, not for the appearance of the star to the magi, but for that of our Saviour to the world: In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> St Paul uses the word epiphanias in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> epistle to Timothy, i. 10. EPHONEMA. See ORATORY, No. 96.

EPHEBI

Pages 267-267

among the Athenians, a designation given to their young men when they arrived at 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they had their names entered in a public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>.

EPHEDEA

Pages 267-267

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the ditercia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the fifth order, Coniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPHEMERA

Pages 267-267

the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">Day</a>-fly, a genus of insects belonging to the order of neuroptera. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPHEMERIDES

Pages 267-267

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, tables calculated by astronomers, showing the present state of the heavens for every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> at noon; that is, the places where-in all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> are found at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. It is from these tables that the eclipses, conjunctions, and aspects of the planets, are determined; horoscopes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> celestial schemes constructed, &c. We have ephemerides of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, Kepler, Argoli, Heckerus, Mezzarachis, Wing, De la Hire, Parker, &c. S. Caffini has calculated ephemerides of the fixed medicinae or satellites of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, which are of good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in determining the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. In England, the Nautical <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">Almanack</a>, or Astronomical Ephemeris, published annually by anticipation, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the commissioners of longitude, is the most considerable. In France, celestial ephemerides have been published by M. Delplaces every ten years, from 1715 to 1745; they were afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by the Abbé Caille, with many additions; of which an account may be seen in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Academy of Sciences for 1743. The Academy of Sciences have likewise published annually, from the beginning of the present century, a kind of ephemeris under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Connaissance des Temps.

EPHESUS

Pages 267-269

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of antiquity, much celebrated on account of its temple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, and for being the most famous mart <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> staple town of Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Ephesus was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of all Asia. Stephanus gives it the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Epiphanesflates, or most illustrious; and Pliny styles it the ornament of Asia. The ancient city stood about 50 miles south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, near the mouth of the river Cayster, and the shore of the Icarian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the Aegean; but as it has been so often destroyed and rebuilt, it is no easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to determine the precise <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Most of our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> travellers are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the ancient city stood more to the south than the present; which they argue from the ruins that still remain. Ephesus was, in ancient times, known by the names of Alopece, Ortygia, Moger, Smyrna, Trachera, Samornion, and Ptolemaia. It was called Ephesus, according to Heracleides, from the Greek word ephesus, signifying permission; because <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> (says he) permitted the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a> to live and build a city in that place. Others tell us, that Ephesus was the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMAZON">Amazon</a> that founded the city; for Pliny, Justin, and Orosius, unanimously affirm that it was built by an Amazon; while others bestow this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> upon Androclus, the son of Codrus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, who was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Ionians that settled in Asia. But, in matters of early <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, it is impossible to come at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and therefore not worth our while to dwell on such fruitless inquiries. What we know for certain is, that the city, which in the Roman times was the metropolis of all Asia, acknowledged Lydmachus for its founder; for that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, having caused the ancient city to be entirely demolished, rebuilt, at a vast expense, a new one, in a place more convenient, and nearer the temple. Strabo tells us, that, as the inhabitants showed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reluctance to quit their ancient habitations, Lydmachus caused all the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> that conveyed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> into the neighbouring fens and the Cayster to be privately stopped up; whereby the city being on the first violent rains in great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> laid under water, and many of the inhabitants drowned, they were glad to abandon the ancient and retire. This new Ephesus was greatly damaged by an earthquake in the reign of Tiberius, but by that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> repaired and adorned with several stately buildings, of which there are now but few ruins to be seen, and scarce anything worthy of ancient Ephesus. The aqueduct, part of which is still standing, is generally believed to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the Greek emperors; the pillars which support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> are of fine marble, and higher or lower as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the water required. This aqueduct served to convey water into the city from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of Halites, mentioned by Paulusianus. The gate, now called by the inhabitants, for what reason we know not, the Gate of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">Persecution</a>, is remarkable for three bas-reliefs on the mould, of an exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The port, of which so many medals have been struck, is at present but an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and not much frequented. The Cayster was formerly navigable, and afforded a safe place for ships to ride in, but is now almost choked up with sand. But the chief ornament of Ephesus was the temple of Diana, built at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of all the states in Asia, and for its structure, size, and furniture, accounted among the wonders of the world. This great edifice was situated at the foot of a mountain, and at the head of a marsh; which place they chose, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we believe Pliny, as the least subject to earthquakes. This site doubled the charges; for they were obliged to be at vast expense in making drains to convey the water that came <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the hill into the morals and the Cayster. Philo Byzantius tells us, that in this work they used such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, as almost exhausted all the quarries in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and these drains or vaults are what the present inhabitants take for a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>. To secure the foundations of the conduits or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEWERS">sewers</a>, which were to bear a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of such a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, they laid beds of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, says Pliny, well rammed, and upon them others of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. Two hundred and twenty years, Pliny says 400, were spent in building this wonderful temple by all Asia. It was 425 feet in length, and 200 in breadth, supported by 127 marble pillars, 70 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, of which 27 were most curiously carved, and the rest polished. These pillars were the works of so many kings, and the bas-reliefs of one were done by Scopas, the most famous sculptor of antiquity; the altar was almost wholly the work of Praxiteles. Cheiromocrates, who built the city of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and offered to form Mount <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOS">Athos</a> into a statue of Alexander, was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> employed on this occasion. The temple enjoyed the privilege of an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, which at first extended to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURLONG">furlong</a>, was afterwards enlarged by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> to a bow-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, and doubled by Mark Antony, so that it took in part of the city: but Tiberius, to put a stop to the many abuses and disorders that attend privileges of this kind, revoked them all, and declared, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> guilty of any wicked or dishonest <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> should escape <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, though he fled to the altar itself. The priests who officiated in this temple were held in great esteem, and trusted with the care of sacred virgins, or priestesses, but not till they were made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>. They were called Epitiatores and Euphena, had a particular diet, and were not allowed by their constitutions to go into any private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. They were maintained with the profits accruing from the lake Scinthus, and another that fell into it, which must have been very considerable, since they erected a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> statue to one Artemidorus, who being sent to Rome, recovered them after they had been seized by the farmers of the public revenues. All the Ionians resorted yearly to Ephesus with their wives and children, where they solemnized the festival of Diana with great pomp and magnificence, making on that occasion rich offerings to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, and valuable presents to her priests. The affarcae, mentioned by St Luke, were, according to Beza, those priests whose peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> it was to regulate the public sports that were annually performed at Ephesus in honour of Diana: they were maintained with the collections made during the sports; for all Asia flocked to see them. The great Diana of the Ephesians, as she was styled by her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> adorers, was, according to Pliny, a small statue of ebony, made by one Canitius, though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> believed to have been sent down from heaven by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. This statue was first placed in a niche, which, as we are told, the Amazons caused to be made in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of an elm. Such was the first rise of the veneration that was paid to Diana in this place. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the veneration for the goddess daily increasing among the inhabitants of Asia, a most stately and magnificent temple was built near the place where the elm stood, and the statue of the goddess placed in it. This was the first temple; but not quite so sumptuous as that which we have described, though reckoned, as well as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, among the wonders of the world. The second, being that above described, was remaining in Pliny's time, and in Strabo's; and is supposed to have been destroyed in the reign of Constantine, pursuant to the edict by which that emperor commanded all the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of the heathens to be thrown down and demolished: the former was burnt the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> that Alexander was born, by one Erostratus, who owned on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a>, that the only thing which had prompted him to destroy so excellent a work, was the desire of transmitting his name to future ages. Whereupon the common <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Asia made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, forbidding any one to name him; but this prohibition served only to make his name more memorable, such a remarkable extravagance, or rather madness, being taken notice of by all the historians who have written of those times. Alexander offered to rebuild the temple at his own expense, provided the Ephesians would agree to put his name on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>; but they rejected his offer in such a manner as prevented the resentment of that vain prince, telling him, that "it was not fit one god should build a temple to another." The pillars, and other materials that had been saved out of the flames, were sold, and also the jewels of the Ephesian women, who on that occasion willingly parted with them; and the sum raised from thence served for the carrying on of the work till other contributions came in, which in a short time amounted to an immense <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. This is the temple which Strabo, Pliny, and other Roman writers speak of. It stood between the city and the port, and was built, or rather finished, as Livy tells us, in the reign of King Servius. Of this wonderful structure there is nothing at present remaining but some ruins, and a few broken pillars. The Ionians first settled at Ephesus under the conduct of Androclus, who drove out the Carians and Leleges, by whom those places were possessed at his arrival. The city, whether built by him, as Strabo affirms, or by Croesus or Ephesus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the Ionic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a>, as others maintain, became soon the metropolis of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>. It was at first governed by Androclus, and his descendants, who assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> title, and exercised the regal authority over the new colony; whence, even in Strabo's time, the posterity of Androclus were styled kings, and allowed to wear a scarlet robe, with a sceptre, and all the ensigns of the royal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. In process of time, a new form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was introduced, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> established; but when, or on what occasion, this change happened, we know not. This kind of government <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who lived before <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> the Great, and was one of the most cruel and inhuman tyrants we read of in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; for having driven out the senate, and taken all the power into his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, he filled the city with blood and rapine, not sparing even those who fled to the temple of Diana for shelter. Pythagoras was succeeded by Pindarus, who bore the same sway in the city; but treated the citizens with more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. In his time Ephesus being besieged by Croesus king of Lydia, he advised the inhabitants to devote their city to Diana, and fasten the wall, by a rope, to the pillars of her temple. They followed his advice, and were, from reverence to the goddess, not only treated with great kindness by Croesus, but restored to their former <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Pindarus being obliged to resign his power, retired to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. He was, according to Ælian, grandson to Alyattes king of Lydia, and Croesus's nephew. The other tyrants of Ephesus mentioned in history are, Athenagoras, Comes, Aristaarchus, and Hegesias; of whom the last was expelled by Alexander, who, coming to Ephesus, after having defeated the Persians on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANICUS">Granicus</a>, bestowed upon Diana all the tributes which the Ephesians had paid to the Persians, and established a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a> in the city. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between Mithridates and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, they sided with the former, and, by his directions, massacred all the Romans that resided in their city; for which barbarity they were severely fined, and reduced almost to beggary by Sylla, but afterwards treated kindly, and suffered to live according to their own laws, as is plain from several ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> and medals. The Ephesians were much addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, sorcery, and curious arts, as the scripture styles them; whence came the proverb "Ephesian letters," signifying all sorts of spells or charms. In the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> Paul, Ephesus retained a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of its ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. But it was a ruinous place, when the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> filled Constantinople with its <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and raised his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Sophia upon its columns. Since then it has been almost quite exhausted. Towards the end of the 11th century, a Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>, named Tangripermer, settled there. But the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, John Ducas, defeated him in a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and pursued the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Turks up the Maeander. In 1306, it was among the places which suffered from the exactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> Roger; and two years after, it surrendered to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Saylan, who, to prevent future insurrections, removed most of the inhabitants to Tyriaeum, where they were massacred. Ephesus appears to have subsisted as an inconsiderable place for some time. But now, the Ephesians are only a few Greek peasants, living in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> wretchedness, dependence, and infirmity; the representatives of an illustrious people, and inhabiting the wreck of their greatness; some, the subtractions of the glorious edifices which they raised; some, beneath the vaults of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, once the crowded <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of their diversions; and some, by the abrupt precipice, in the sepulchres which received their ashes. EPHETÆ from επινεῖν, "I send forth"), in antiquity, a sort of magistrates among the Athenians, instituted by King Demophoon, to take cognizance of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, manslaughter, and chance-medley. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was 100, whereof 50 were Athenians, and 50 Argians: they were not admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> till upwards of 50 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a> new-modelled it, excluded the Argians out of it, and made it to consist of 51 Athenians, each above 58 years of age: Ubbo Emmius de Rep. Athen. says, he transferred to them part of the jurisdiction of the Areopagites. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">AREOPAGUS</a>.

EPHOD

Pages 269-269

in Jewish antiquity, one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the priestly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; being a kind of girdle, which, brought from behind the neck over the two shoulders, and hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before, was put across the stomach, then carried round the waist, and made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of as a girdle to the tunic.—There were two sorts of ephods, one of plain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> for the priests, and the other embroidered for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>.

EPHORA

Pages 274-274

in Medicine, a preternatural defluxion of the eyes, when they continually discharge a sharp furred humour, which excoriates the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPHORI

Pages 269-269

in Grecian antiquity, magistrates established in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the regal power. The authority of the ephori was very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. They sometimes expelled and even put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the kings, and abolished <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suspended the power of the other magistrates, calling them to account at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. There were five of them, others say <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. They presided in the public shows and festivals. They were entrusted with the public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and peace; and were so <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> makes their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. They were established by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, according to the generality of authors: though this is denied by others, who <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> their origin 130 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. Thus Plutarch, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Cleomenes, ascribes their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to Theopompus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sparta; which is also confirmed by the authority of Aristotle.

EPHORUS

Pages 269-269

an orator and historian of Cumae in Æolis, about 352 years before Christ. He was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> to Isocrates, by whose advice he wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> which gave an account of all the actions and battles that had happened between the Greeks and barbarians for 750 years. It was greatly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; but is now lost.

EPHRAIM

Pages 269-269

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> by tribes: Ephraim and the half-tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a> are blended together by the sacred writer, and it only appears that Ephraim occupied the more southern, and the half tribe of Manasseh the more northern parts, but both seem to have extended from the Jordan to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Ephraim also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, on the separation of the 10 tribes from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, called also the kingdom of Israel and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>.

EPHRATA

Pages 269-270

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> settlement of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> called Dunkards <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tunkers. See Tunkers.

EPHREM

Pages 270-270

Syrus, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian writer, in the fourth century, deacon of Edessa, was born at Nisibis in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. He was greatly esteemed by St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, St Gregory Nyssen, and other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men. He wrote against the opinions of Sabellius, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a>, Apollonarius, the Manichæans, &c. and acquired such reputation by his virtue and his works, that he was called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> and the prophet of the Syrians. He died in 378. The best editions of his works are, that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in 1708, in folio, and that of Rome, from 1732 to 1738, in Syriac, Greek, and Latin, 6 vols folio.

EPHYDOR

Pages 270-270

in antiquity, an officer in the Athenian courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, who was to provide the plaintiff and defendant with equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>-glasses. When the glass was run out, they were not permitted to speak any farther; and, therefore, we find them very careful not to lose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mispend one drop of their water. Whilst the laws quoted by them were reciting, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any other business happened to intervene, they gave orders that the glass should be flopped. EPIBATÆ, ἐπιβάται, among the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who served on board the ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. They were armed in the same manner as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-forces, only that more of them wore full or heavy armour.

EPIBATERION

Pages 270-270

a poetical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks. When any person of condition and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> returned home after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> absence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> journey into another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he called together his friends and fellow-citizens, and made them a speech, or rehearsed them a copy of verses, wherein he returned solemn thanks to the immortal gods for his happy return; and ended with an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> by way of compliment to his fellow-citizens.—These verses made what the Greeks call ἐπιβατηρίον, epibaterium, of ἐπιβαίνω, "I go abroad." At going away they had another, called apobaterium.

EPIBATERIUM

Pages 270-270

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocotyledons. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPIC

Pages 270-270
or Heroic Poem, a poem expressed in narration, formed upon a story partly real and partly feigned; representing, in a sublime style, some signal and fortunate action, distinguished by a variety of great events, to form the morals, and affect the mind with the love of heroic virtue. We may distinguish three parts of the definition, namely, the matter, the form, and the end. The matter includes the action of the fable, under which are ranged the incidents, episodes, characters, morals, and machinery. The form comprehends the way or manner of the narration, whether by the poet himself, or by any persons introduced, whose discourses are related: to this branch likewise belong the moving of the passion, the descriptions, discourses, sentiments, thoughts, style, and verification; and besides these, the families, tropes, figures, and, in short, all the ornaments and decorations of the poem. The end is to improve our morals and increase our virtue. See Poetry.

EPICEDION

Pages 270-270

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a poem rehearsed during the funeral solemnity of persons of distinction.

EPICEDON

Pages 270-270

in the Greek and Latin <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a poem, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> poetical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a person.—At the obsequies of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, there were three kinds of discourses usually made; that rehearsed at his bustum or funeral pile, was called nemia; that engraven on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, epitaph; and that spoken in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of his funeral, epicedion. We have two beautiful epicedions in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, that of Euryalus and that of Pallas.

EPICHARMUS

Pages 270-270

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, was a scholar of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>. He is said to have introduced <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> in the reign of Hiero. Horace commends Plautus for imitating him, in following the chafe of the intrigue so closely as not to give the readers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spectators <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to trouble themselves with doubts concerning the discovery. He wrote likewise treatises concerning <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and medicine; but none of his works have been preserved. He died aged 90, according to Laertius, who has preserved four verses <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on his statue.

EPICHIROTONIA

Pages 270-270

among the Athenians. It was ordained by Solon, that once every year the laws should be carefully revised and examined; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any of them were found unsuitable to the present state of affairs, they should be repealed. This was called ἐπιχειροτονία τῶν νόμων, from the manner of giving their suffrages by holding up their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. See a farther account of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in Pott, Archæol. Græc. lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 26, tom. i. p. 242.

EPICOENE

Pages 270-270

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>, which, under the same gender and termination, mark indifferently the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Such in Latin is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">aquila</a>, vesperilio, &c., which signify equally a male <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> female eagle or bat. Grammarians distinguish between epicene and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. A noun is said to be common of two kinds, when it may be joined either with a masculine or a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a> article; and epicene, when it is always joined to some of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, and yet signifies both genders.

EPICRIT

Pages 273-273

in *<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>*, a short poem in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, treating only of one thing, and ending with some lively, ingenious, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> thought <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> point. The word is formed of επιγραφη, inscription, of επιγραφειν, to inscribe, or write upon. Epigrams then, originally signify <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, and they derive their origin from those inscriptions placed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> on their tombs, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, &c. These, at first, were only simple monograms: afterwards, increasing their length, they made them in verse, to be the more easily retained: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> and others have transmitted to us several of them. Such little poems retained the name of epigrams, even after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of their first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> was varied, and people began to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> them for the relation of little facts and accidents, the characterizing of persons, &c. The point or turn is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> much insisted on by the critics, who require the epigram constantly to clothe with something poignant and unexpected, to which all the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is only preparatory; while others, on the contrary, exclude the point, and require the thought to be equally disputed throughout the poem, without laying the whole stress on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>: the former is usually Martial's practice, and the latter that of Catullus. The Greek epigrams have scarce any thing of the point or briskness of the Latin one: those collected in the Anthology have most of them a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of ease and simplicity, attended with something <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and witty; such as we find in a sensible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, or a child that has <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. They have nothing that bites, but something that tickles. Though they want the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of Martial, yet to a good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> they are not insipid; except a few of them, which are quite flat and spiritless. However, the general faintness and delicacy of the pleasantry in them has given occasion for a Greek epigram, or *epigram à la Grecque*, to denote, among the French, an epigram void of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> or sharpness. The epigram admits of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of subjects: some are made to praise, and others to satirize; which last are much the easiest; ill-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> serving instead of point and wit. Boileau's epigrams are all satires on one or another; those of Des Reaux are all made in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his friends; and those of Mad. Scudery are so many eloges. The epigram being only a single thought, it would be ridiculous to express it in a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of verses.

EPICTETUS

Pages 270-271

a celebrated Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERAPOLIS">Hierapolis</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, in the first century, was the slave of Epaphroditus, a freedman and one of Nero's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>. Domitian banishing all philosophers from Rome, about the year 94, Epictetus retired to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a> in Epirus, where he died in a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the earthen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> he made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of sold for 3000 drachmas. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>; which was eminent in his own practice, as well as in his recommendation to others: hence he used to say, "That there is no need of adorning a man's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> with rich hangings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> paintings, since the most graceful furniture is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and modesty, which are lasting ornaments, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never be the worst for wearing." Of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, he seems to have made the nearest approaches to the Christian morality, and to have had the most <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of God and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>. He always possessed a cool and serene mind, unruffled by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; and was used to say, that the whole of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> was included in these words, support and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Epaphroditus trove in a frolic to wrench his leg; when Epictetus said, with a smile, and free from any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you go on, you will certainly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> my leg;" but the former redoubling his effort, and striking it with all his strength, he at last broke the bone; when all the return Epictetus made was, "Did Did not I tell you, Sir, that you would break my leg?" No man was more expert at reducing the rigour of the maxims of the Stoics into practice. He conformed himself strictly, both in his discourse and behaviour, to the manners of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> and Zeno. He waged continual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with fancy and fortune; and it is an excellence peculiar to himself, that he admitted all the severity of the Stoics without their furnaces, and reformed Stoicism as well as professed it; and besides his vindicating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> as strenuously as Socrates or any Stoic of them all, he declared openly against self-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, the lawfulness of which was maintained by the rest of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. Arrian, his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and death, which is lost; and preferred four books of his discourses and his Enchiridion, of which there have been several editions in Greek and Latin; and, in 1758, a translation of them into English was published by the learned and ingenious Miss Carter.

EPICUREAN PHILOSOPHY

Pages 271-271

the doctrine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> system of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> maintained by Epicurus and his followers. His philosophy consisted of three parts; canonical, physical, and ethereal. The first was about the canons or rules of judging. The censure which Tully passes upon him for his despising logic, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> hold true only with regard to the logic of the Stoics, which he could not approve of, as being too full of nicety and quirk. Epicurus was not acquainted with the analytical method of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> and argumentation, nor was he so curious in modes and formation as the Stoics. Soundness and simplicity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, assisted with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> reflections, was all his art. His search after <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> proceeded only by the senses; to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of which he gave so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a certainty, that he considered them as an infallible rule of truth, and termed them the first natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of mankind. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this philosophy he laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> atoms, space, and gravity, as the first principles of all things: he did not deny the existence of God, but thought it beneath his majesty to concern himself with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs: he held him a blest immortal Being, having no affairs of his own to take care of, and above meddling with those of others. As to his ethics, he made the supreme good of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to consist in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and consequently supreme evil in pain. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> itself, says he, teaches us this truth; and prompts us from our birth to procure whatever gives us pleasure, and avoid what gives us pain. To this end he proposes a remedy against the sharpness of pain: this was to divert the mind from it, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> our whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> upon the pleasures we have formerly enjoyed. He held that the wife man must be happy as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he is wife; the pain, not depriving him of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, cannot deprive him of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. There is nothing that has a fairer show of honesty than the moral doctrine of Epicurus. Gassendus pretends, that the pleasure in which this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> has fixed the sovereign good, was nothing else but the highest tranquillity of mind, in conjunction with the most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of body: but Tully, Horace, and Plutarch, as well as almost all the fathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, give us a very different account of it: indeed the nature of this pleasure, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> happiness is supposed to be seated, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> problem in the morals of Epicurus. Hence there were two kinds of Epicureans, the rigid and the remiss: the first were those who understood Epicurus's notion of pleasure in the purest sense, and placed all their happiness in the purest pleasures of the mind, resulting from the practice of virtue: the loose or remiss Epicureans, taking the words of that philosopher in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> sense, placed all their happiness in bodily pleasures or debauchery.

EPICURUS

Pages 271-271

the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at Gargettium in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, about 340 B.C., in the 90th Olympiad. He settled at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in a fine garden he had bought; where he lived with his friends in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tranquillity, and educated a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disciples. They lived all in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. The respect which his followers paid to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is admirable: his school was never divided, but his doctrine was followed as an oracle. His birthday was still kept in Pliny's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> he was born in was observed as a continual festival; and they placed his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> everywhere. He wrote a great many books, and valued himself upon making no quotations. He raised the atomic system to a great reputation, though he was not the inventor of it, but had only made some change in that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a>. As to his doctrine concerning the supreme good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, it was very liable to be misrepresented, and some ill effects proceeded from thence, which discredited his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with perverting the worship of the gods, and inciting men to debauchery; but he did not forget himself on this occasion; he published his opinions to the whole world; he wrote some books of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; recommended the veneration of the gods, sobriety, and chastity; and it is certain that he lived in an exemplary manner, and conformably to the rules of philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and frugality. Timocrates, a deceiver of his feet, spoke very scandalously of him. Gassendus has given us all he could collect from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> concerning the person and doctrine of this philosopher; who died of a suppression of urine, aged 72.

EPICYCLE

Pages 271-271

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, a little circle whose centre is in the circumference of a greater circle: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it is a small orb or sphere, which being fixed in the deferent of a planet, is carried along with it; and yet, by its own peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, carries the planet fastened to it round its proper centre. It was by means of epicycles that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> and his followers solved the various phenomena of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, but more especially their stations and retrogradations.

EPICYCLOID

Pages 271-271

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a curve <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the revolution of the periphery of a circle, along the convex <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> concave side of the periphery of another circle.

EPICYEMA

Pages 271-271

among physicians, denotes a superfluous secretion; being a false <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> happening after the birth of a regular fetus.

EPIDAURUM

Pages 271-271

Epidaurus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Epitaureum, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, on the Adriatic, built the same year, as is said, with Dyrrachium, 430 years after the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>: a considerable town formerly, but now reduced to a small village, called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAGUSA">Ragusa</a> Vecchio; distant six miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Ragusa. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19°. Lat. 42°. 20'.

EPIDAURUS

Pages 271-272

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Argolis, Epidauros. Argolis, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, on the Saronic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, to the south of the promontory Spireium; called Sacred, because of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> veneration paid to Æsculapius, whose temple stood at the distance of five miles from the town. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, during a pestilence, being advised to convey the god to Rome, sent a ship, with a solemn embassy, for his conveyance; but while the Epidaurians were in suspense to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with him, a huge <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> sailed to the ship; and being taken for the god, was carried to Rome in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnity. Epidaurus stood in a recess of the bay, fronting the east; and was fortified by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, being inclosed by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> reaching to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and rendering it difficult of access. It had several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and in the acropolis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> citadel was a remarkable statue of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. The site is now called Epithoros. The traces are indistinct, and it has probably been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> deserted. The harbour of Epidaurus is long. Its peripius or circuit was 15 stadia or near two miles. The entrance is between mountains, and on a small rocky <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> are ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> fortress. This, it seems, was the point on which a temple of Juno stood. It is frequented by vessels for wood or corn. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> of Æsculapius was inclosed by mountains, within which all the sacrifices as well of the Epidaurians as of strangers were consumed. One was called Titthion; and on this the god when an infant was said to have been exposed, and to have been suckled by a she-goat. He was a great physician, and his temple was always crowded with sick persons. Beyond it was the dormitory of the supplicants; and near it, a circular edifice called the Tholus, built by Polycletus, of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, worth seeing. The grove, besides other temples, was adorned with a portico, and a fountain remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> and decorations. The bath of Æsculapius was one of the benefactions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, while a Roman senator; as was also a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the reception of pregnant women and dying persons, who before were removed out of the inclosure, to be delivered or to expire in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The remains are heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, pieces of brick wall, and scattered fragments of marble; besides some churches or rather piles of rubbish miscalled, being destitute of doors, roofs, or any kind of ornament. The statue of Æsculapius was half as big as that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Olympus at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. It was made of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and, as the inscription proved, by Thrasymedes son of Arignotus of Paros.
