He was represented sitting, holding his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, with one hand on the head of a serpent, and a dog lying by him. Two Argive heroes, Bellerophon combating with the monster Chimera, and Perseus severing the head of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>, were carved on the throne. Many tablets described the cures performed by the deity, yet he had not escaped contumely and robbery. Dionysius deprived him of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, affirming that it was unseemly in him to appear in that manner when his father <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> was always seen with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> smooth. Sylla amassed the precious offerings belonging to him, and to Apollo and Jupiter, at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, to pay his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> before Athens. The marks in the walls testified that a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> had been plucked <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. A few fragments of white marble exquisitely carved occur in the heap of the temple. The inclosure of the temple once abounded in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century fix marbles remained, on which were written Epidaurus in the Doric dialect the names of men and women who had been patients of the god, with the distemper each had laboured under, and the remedies he had directed. Dr Chandler found only a couple of votive inscriptions, and two pedestals of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, one of which represented a Roman, and was erected by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Epidaurians. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a> was near the temple. It was of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, as most in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> were. At the upper end are seats of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, but these were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> along the sides only a few yards. A vaulted passage leading underneath into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, now choked up, was a private way by which the agonothete or presidents with the priests and persons of distinction entered. Two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cisterns or reservoirs remain, made by Antoninus for the reception of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Beyond them is a dry watercourse; and in the mountain-side on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand are the marble seats of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, overgrown with bushes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> by the ruins are supposed to possess many excellent properties. To these and a good air, Dr Chandler thinks, with the recreations of the theatre and of the stadium, and to the medicinal knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of the priests, may be attributed both the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the sick and the reputation of Æsculapius. Epidaurus, with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> Limera, to distinguish it from the Epidaurus of Argolis; called so, either from its meadows or its commodious harbours (Stephanus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>): a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, on the Ionian sea, to the south of the Sinus Argolicus, situated where now Molvaka stands, in the Morea. E. Long. 23.30° N. Lat. 35.40°

EPIDEMIA

Pages 272-272

in Grecian antiquity, festivals kept in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, at the stated seasons, when those deities, who could not be present everywhere, were supposed to visit different places, in order to receive the vows of their adorers.

EPIDEMIC

Pages 272-272

among physicians, an epithet of diseases which at certain times are popular, attacking <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

EPIDENDRUM

Pages 272-272

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the gynandra clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the seventh order, Orchidea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.—This is the plant which produces the fruit called vanilla, and which is used in perfuming chocolate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and snuff.

EPIDERMIS

Pages 272-272

in Anatomy, the cuticle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scarf-skin. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The word is formed of the Greek ἐπί, on, over; and δέρμα, skin.

EPIDICASIA

Pages 272-272

among the Athenians. Daughters inheriting their parents estate were obliged to marry their nearest relation; which gave occasion to persons of the same family to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> with one another, each pretending to be more nearly allied to the heiress than the rest. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> was called ἐπιδικασίας δική: and the virgin, about whom the relations contended, ἐπιδικασίας.

EPIDIDYMIS

Pages 272-273

in Anatomy, a little round body, on the back of each testicle; called alloparaflata. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. EPIGÆA, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the dendria clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 18th order, Bicornis. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. EPIDOTÆ, certain deities who presided over the growth growth of children. They were worshipped by the Lacedaemonians, and chiefly invoked by those who were persecuted by the ghosts of the dead, &c.

EPIGASTRIC REGION

Pages 273-273

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subdivision of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>. See **ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>**.

EPIGLOTTIS

Pages 273-273

in *Anatomy*, one of the cartilages of the larynx <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-pipe. See **ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>**.

EPIGONI

Pages 273-273

the sons and descendants of the Grecian heroes who were killed in the first Theban <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The war of the Epigoni is famous in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. It was undertaken ten years after the first. The sons of those who had perished in the first war, resolved to avenge the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of their fathers, and marched against Thebes, under the command of Thersander; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, of Alcmeon the son of Amphiaras, about 1307 years before Christ. The Argives were assisted by the Corinthians, the people of Messenia, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>. The Thebans had engaged all their neighbours in their quarrel, as in one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cause. These two hostile armies met and engaged on the banks of the Glifas. The fight was obstinate and bloody, but victory declared for the Epigoni, and some of the Thebans fled to Illyricum with Leodamas their general, while others retired into Thebes, where they were soon besieged, and forced to surrender. In this war Ægialus was the only one who was killed, and his father Adraetus was the only one who escaped alive in the first war. This whole war, as Paulanias observes, was written in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; and Callinus, who quotes some of the verses, ascribes them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> has been adopted by many writers. "For my <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> (continues the geographer), I own, that next to the Iliad and Odyssey of Homer, I have never seen a finer poem." The descendants of the veteran Macedonians, who served under Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and who had children by Aflatic women, were also called Epigoni. (Justin.)

EPIGRAPHE

Pages 273-273

among antiquarians, denotes the inscription of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, pointing out the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when, the persons by whom, the uses, and the like, for which it was erected.

EPILEPSY

Pages 273-273

in *Medicine*, the same with what is otherwise called the *falling-sickness*, from the patient's falling suddenly to the ground. See **MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>**.

EPILLOOMPHALON

Pages 274-274

in Medicine, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a> umbilicalis, proceeding from the omentum falling into the region of the umbilicus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> navel. EPILOON. See OMENTUM, ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPILOBUM

Pages 273-273

the Willow <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">Herb</a>; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the octandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 17th order, *Calycanthaceae*. See **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>**. **EPilogue**, in *Oratory*, the end <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conclusion of a discourse, ordinarily containing a recapitulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> matters delivered. **EPilogue**, in dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a speech addressed to the audience, after the play is over, by one of the principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> therein; usually containing some reflections on certain incidents in the play, especially those in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the person that speaks it; and having somewhat of pleasantry, intended to compose the palfines raised in the course of the representation; a practice which is ridiculed by the *Spectator*, and compared to a merry jig upon the organ after a good sermon, to wipe away any impressions that might have been made thereby, and send the people away <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they came.

EPIMEDIUM

Pages 273-273

Barren-wort; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tetrandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 24th order, *Corydalis*. See **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>**.

EPIMENIDES

Pages 273-274

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Gnosius in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. Contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he always wore his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; which, according to some, was because he was ashamed of being thought a Cretan; and indeed he does not seem to have had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his countrymen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> cited by St Paul be, as it is generally believed to be his; "The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, false bellies." Many stories are related of him, too wonderful to merit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; however, his reputation was so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> over all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, that he was there esteemed a favourite of the gods. The Athenians being afflicted with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, and commanded by the oracle to make a solemn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUSTRATION">lustration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, sent Nicias, the son of Niceratus, with a ship to Crete, to desire Epimenides to come to them. He accepted their invitation, Epimenides vitation, accompanied the messengers to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, performed the lustration of the city, and the plague ceased. Here he contracted an acquaintance with Solon, whom he privately instructed in the proper methods for the regulation of the Athenian commonwealth. Having finished his business at Athens, the citizens offered him many valuable presents and high honours, and appointed a ship to carry him back to Crete; but he returned their presents, and would accept of nothing except a little branch of the sacred olive preserved in the citadel; and desired the Athenians to enter into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Gnostics. Having obtained this, he returned to Crete; where he died soon after, aged 157 years; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as the Cretans, consistently with their character, pretended, 299. He was a great poet, and wrote 5000 verses on "the genealogy of the gods," 6500 "on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the ship <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> and Jason's expedition to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>," and 4000 "concerning <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHADAMANTHUS">Rhadamanthus</a>." He wrote also in prose, "Concerning sacrifices and the commonwealth of Crete." St Jerome likewise mentions his "book of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> and responses." The Lacedemonians procured his body, and preserved it among them by the advice of an oracle; and Plutarch tells us, that he was reckoned the seventh wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> by those who refused to admit Periander into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

EPIMETHEUS

Pages 274-274

a son of Japetus and Clymene, one of the Oceanides, who inconsiderately married Pandora, by whom he had Pyrrha, the wife of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>. He had the curiosity to open the box which Pandora had brought with her, and from thence issued a train of evils, which from that moment have never ceased to afflict the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Hope was the only one which remained at the bottom of the box, not having a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to escape, and it is the alone which comforts men under misfortunes. Epimetheus was changed into a monkey by the gods, and sent into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Pithecusa.

EPIPHANIUS

Pages 274-274

St., an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> father of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, born at Befanducan, a village in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, about the year 332. He founded a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, and presided over it. He was afterwards elected bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>; when he sided with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a> against Meletius, and ordained in Palestine Paulinus the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of St Jerome; on which a contest arose between him and John bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. He afterwards called a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, in which he procured a prohibition of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>'s writings; and made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all his endeavours to prevail on Theophilus bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> to engage St Chrysostom to declare in favour of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>: but not meeting with success, he went himself to Constantinople, where he would not have any conversation with St Chrysostom; and formed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of entering the church of the apostles to publish his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of Origen; but being informed of the danger to which he would be exposed, he resolved to return to Cyprus; but died at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in the year 403. His works were printed in Greek, at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, 1544, in folio; and were afterwards translated into Latin, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> they have been often reprinted. Petavius revised and corrected the Greek text by two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, and published it together with a new translation at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1622. This edition was reprinted at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in 1682.

EPIPLOCELE

Pages 274-274

in Medicine, is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rupture, in which the omentum subsides into the scrotum.

EPIRUS

Pages 274-275

a district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETOLIA">Etolia</a>, on the west by the Adriatic, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Thessaly and Macedon, and on the south by the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was anciently governed by its own princes, in which state it made a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The country, according to Josephus, was first peopled by Dodanim the son of Javan and grandson of Japhet. The people were very warlike; but they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> state <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after their neighbours were civilized; whence the illanders used to threaten their offenders with transportation to Epirus. Their horses were in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> request among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, as well as the dogs produced in one of the divisions called Molossus; and hence these dogs were called by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Molossi. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Epirus commences with the reign of Pyrrhus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> by Deidamia the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Lycomedes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Scyros. He is said to have behaved with great bravery at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; but it would appear that he behaved with no less barbarity. After the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was taken, he is said to have killed old king Priam with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; to have thrown Ajaxax the son Epirus of Hector and Andromache headlong from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower; and sacrificed Polyxena the daughter of Priam on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of his father. He carried Andromache with him into Epirus, where he settled by the advice of the famous soothsayer Helenus, one of Priam's sons, who had served during the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> both under his father and himself. The only remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the history of Epirus is the reign of Pyrrhus II, who made war upon the Romans. He was invited into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> by the Tarentines; and embarked about 280 B.C. After having escaped many dangers by sea, he landed in that country, and with great difficulty gained a victory over the Romans; but he was afterwards utterly defeated by them, and obliged to return into his own country. To retrieve his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, he then undertook an expedition against Macedon; where he overthrew Antigonus, and at last made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He then formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of subduing all the other Grecian states; but met with such an obstinate resistance at Lacedemon, that he was obliged to drop the enterprise; and was soon after killed at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> by a woman, who from the wall threw a tile upon his head, Deidamia, the granddaughter of Pyrrhus, was the last that sat on the throne of Epirus. She is said to have been murdered after a short reign; upon which the Epirots formed themselves into a republic. Under the new form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> Epirus never made any considerable figure, but seems rather to have been dependent on the kingdom of Macedon. The Romans having conquered <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> king of that country, restored the Epirots to their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; but they, forgetful of this favour, soon after took up arms in favour of Perseus. As a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for this ingratitude, the Romans gave orders to Paulus Emilius, after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Macedon, to plunder the cities of Epirus, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> them with the ground. This was punctually executed throughout the whole country on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The booty was sold, and each foot-soldier had 200 denarii, that is, five pounds <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings and twopence, and each of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of this sum. An hundred and fifty thousand men were made slaves, and sold to the best bidder for the benefit of the republic. Nor did the vengeance of Rome stop here; all the cities of Epirus, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 70, were dismantled, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men of the country carried to Rome, where they were tried, and most of them condemned to perpetual imprisonment. After this terrible blow, Epirus never recovered its ancient splendour. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the Achaean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, it was made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Macedon; but when Macedon became a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, Epirus was made a province of itself, called the province of Old Epirus, to distinguish it from New Epirus, another province lying to the east of it. On the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire, it fell to the emperors of the east, and continued under them till the taking of Constantinople by the Latins, when Michael Angelus, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> nearly related to the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, seized on Etolia and Epirus, of which he declared himself <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prince; and was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Theodorus, who took several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> from the Latins, and so far enlarged his dominions, that, disdaining the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of despot, he assumed that of emperor, and was crowned by Demetrius archbishop of Bulgaria. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, the last prince of this family, dying without lawful issue, bequeathed Epirus and Acarnania to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sons, who were driven out by Amurat the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. Great part of Epirus was afterwards held by the noble family of the Caftrioti; who, though they were masters of all <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, yet styled themselves princes of Epirus. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the famous George Caftriot, surnamed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDERBEG">Scanderbeg</a>, Epirus fell to the Venetians, who were soon dispossessed of it by the Turks; in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> it still continues, being now known by the name of Albania, which comprehends the Albania of the ancients, all Epirus, and that part of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> which is subject to the Turks.

EPISCOPACY

Pages 275-281

that form of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, in which diocesan <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> are established as distinct from and superior to priests <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> presbyters. We have already observed, that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> since the ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> have been distinguished into different orders, and that it has been much controverted whether the distinction be of divine or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; whether it was fettered in the apostolic <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> or afterwards. (See Bishop). This controversy commenced soon after the Reformation; and has been agitated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> warmth between the Episcopalian on the one side, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a> on the other. Among the Protestant churches abroad, those which were reformed by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> and his associates are in general episcopal; whilst such as follow the doctrines of Calvin have for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> thrown off the order of bishops as one of the corruptions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>. In England, however, the controversy has been considered as of greater importance than on the Continent; for it has there been strenuously maintained by one party, that the episcopal order is essential to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the church; and by others, that it is a pernicious encroachment on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of men, for which there is no authority in scripture. Though the question has for some time lain almost dormant, and though we have no desire to revive it; yet as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this kind might perhaps be deemed defective, did it contain no account whatever of a controversy which has employed some of the ablest writers of the past and present centuries, we shall give a fair though short view of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> arguments by which the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> of each contending party have endeavoured to support their own cause, leaving our readers to judge for themselves where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> lies. See Independents and Presbyterians. The Independent maintains, that under the gospel dispensation there is nothing which bears the smallest resemblance to an exclusive priesthood; that Christ and his apostles constituted no permanent order of ministers in the church; but that any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has a firm <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, a principle of sincere and unaffected piety, a capacity for leading <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and communicating instruction, and a fervent inclination to engage in the important employment of promoting the everlasting <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of mankind; is to all intents and purposes a regular minister of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he have an invitation to the pastoral office from some particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Against this scheme, which supposes the rights of Christians all equal and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and acknowledges no authority in the church except what may be derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of her members, the Protestant Episcopalian reasons in the following manner. He admits, arguments as an undoubted truth, that our blest <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> gave to none Episcopacy, none of his immediate followers authority or jurisdiction of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as could interfere with the rights of the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>; for all such authority was disclaimed by himself: "My <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> (said he to Pilate) is not of this world:" and to a certain person who asked him to decide a question of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> between him and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, he replied, "Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?" But when it is considered, that Christ came into this world to turn men from darkness to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and from the power of Satan to the living God; that he gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify to himself a peculiar people zealous of good works; that of these works many are such as unregenerate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> has no inclination to perform, and that the doctrines which he revealed are such as human reason could never have discovered; the advocate for episcopacy thinks it was extremely expedient, if not absolutely necessary, that, when he ascended into heaven, he should establish upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> some authority to illustrate the revelation which he had given, and to enforce obedience to the laws which he had enacted. There is nothing, continues he, more strictly required of Christians, than that they live together in unity, professing the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, joining in the same worship, and practising the same virtues. But as men have very different passions, prejudices, and pursuits, such unity would be impossible, were they not linked together in one society under the government of persons authorized to watch over the purity of the faith, to prescribe the forms of public worship, and to explain the nature, and inculcate the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the several virtues. The society of Christians, in respect of its unity and organization, is compared to the human body: for "as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office; so we being many are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another," (Rom xii. 4, 5). It is called the church, the kingdom of heaven, and the kingdom of God; and its affairs, like those of every other kingdom, are administered by proper officers in subordination to the one Lord, who, "when he ascended up on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and led <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> captive, gave some apostles, and some prophets, and some pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:" (Ephes. iv. 8—13.). That these various orders of ministers were vested with real authority in the church might be inferred from principles of reason as well as from the dictates of revelation. A society without some form of government, government without laws, or laws without an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> absurdity. Where there are laws, some must govern, and others be governed; some must command, and others obey; some must direct, and others submit to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of nature; it is likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of scripture. "Obey them (says the inspired author of the epistle to the Hebrews) who have the rule over you, and submit yourselves; for they watch for your souls as they that must give account." A text which shows that the authority of the ministers of religion was distinct from that of the civil magistrate, whose duty is to watch, not for the souls, but for the lives and properties, of his subjects. Of the society thus constituted, it was not, as of a philosophical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, left to every man's choice whether or not he would become a member. All who embrace Episcopacy, the faith of the Redeemer of the world are required to be baptized, under the pain of forfeiting the benefits of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>: but one great purpose for which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> was instituted, is to be the rite of initiation into the kingdom of heaven. For by one spirit are we all baptised into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free," (1 Cor. xii. 13.). Of baptism, whatever be the importance, it is evident, that to receive it, is not, like the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, or the veneration of the Supreme Being, a duty resulting from the relations of man to his Creator and fellow-creatures; that its whole efficacy, which in scripture is said to be nothing less than the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> of sins, is derived from positive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>; and therefore, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> rite can be of no avail, but when it is administered in the manner prescribed, and by a person authorized to administer it. That all Christians are not vested with this authority, as one of the common privileges of the faith, appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> which our Saviour after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> gave to his apostles. At that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, we are assured that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his followers was not less than five hundred; yet we find, that to administer eleven disciples only did "he come and speak, saying, 'Go ye, therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.'" Of the 500 disciples there is surely no reason to believe that there were not many well qualified to instruct either a Jew or a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> in the doctrines of the gospel; and it is certain, that any one of them could have washed his convert with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the name of the Holy Trinity as well as St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> or St John: but such an unauthorized washing would not have been Christian baptism, nor of equal validity with it, any more than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of a lawyer at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> is the judgment of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of justice, or of equal obligation. It is the commission of the sovereign which gives force to the judgment of the court; it is the commission of Christ which gives validity to baptism. The same reasoning is applicable to the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, which if it be not administered by those who have authority for such administration, cannot be deemed a sacrament of Christ's institution. These two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> are the external badges of our profession. By the one, we are incorporated into that society of which our Redeemer is the head and sovereign: in the celebration of the other, we have a right to join, whilst of that society we continue members. But if by an open and scandalous disregard of the precepts of the gospel, we should prove ourselves unworthy of its privileges, the same persons who are authorized to admit us into the church, are likewise vested with authority to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> us out of it: for to them were given "the keys of the kingdom of heaven (or the church), with assurance, that whatsoever they should bind on earth, should be bound in heaven; and whatsoever they should loose on earth, should be loosed in heaven," (Mat. xviii. 18.). As baptism is to be administered so long as there shall be persons to be enlisted under the banners of Christ, and the Lord's Supper to be celebrated so long as it shall be the duty of folders to adhere to the standard of their leader and their head; and as it is likewise to be feared that there <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never come a time when EPI [255] EPI When all Christians shall "walk worthy of the vocation wherewith they are called;" it follows, that this power of keys, which was originally given to the apostles, must continue in the church through all ages, even unto the end of the world. But as we have seen, that it was not at first intrusted to all the disciples in common, as one of the privileges inseparable from their number, and as no body of men can possibly transfer an authority of which they themselves were never possessed; it is certain, that even now it cannot, by the election of one class of Christians, be delegated to another, but must, by some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of succession, be derived from the apostles, who were sent by Christ as he was sent by his Father. To argue from the origin of civil to that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> government, although not very uncommon, the Episcopalian deems extremely fallacious. Of the various nations of the world, many of the sovereigns may indeed derive their authority from the suffrages of their subjects; because in a state of nature every man has an inherent right to defend his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and property; and what he possesses in his own person, he may for the good of society transfer to another: but no man is by nature, or can make himself, a member of the Christian church; and therefore authority to govern that society can be derived only from him by whom it was founded, and who died that he might "gather together in one all the children of God." Against such reasoning as this it hath been urged, that to make institutions, which like baptism and the Lord's supper are generally necessary to the salvation of all Christians, depend for their efficacy upon the authority or commission of a particular order, appears inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and goodness of God; as by such an economy an intolerable domination would be established over the souls of men, and the purpose for which the Saviour of the world died might be in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> defeated by the caprice of an ignorant and arbitrary priesthood. The objection is certainly plausible; but the Episcopalian affirms, that either it has no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, or militates with equal force against the wisdom of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> in the government of this world.—In every thing, he observes, relating to their temporal and to their spiritual interests, mankind are all subjected to mutual dependence. The rich depend upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and the poor upon the rich. An infant neglected from the birth would barely cry and cease to live; nor is it easily to be conceived, that in the more rigid climates of the earth a full grown man could provide even the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> animal life. Of religion, it is certain that in such a state nothing could be known; for there is not the smallest reason to imagine that any individual of the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>—an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, or a Newton, had he been left alone from his infancy, without culture and without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>,—could ever, by the native vigour of his own mind, have discovered the existence of a God, or that such speculations as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to that discovery would have employed any portion of his time or his thoughts. Even in civilized society it would be impossible, in the present age, for any man, without the assistance of others, to understand the very first principles of our common Christianity; for the scriptures, which alone contain those principles, are written in languages which are now nowhere vernacular. In the fidelity of translators, therefore, every illiterate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> must confide, for the truth of Episcopacy; those doctrines which constitute the foundation of all his hopes; and as no man ever pretended that the Christian sacraments are more necessary to salvation than the Christian faith, the Episcopalian fees no impropriety or inconsistency in making those persons receive baptism and the Lord's supper by the ministration of others, who by such ministration must of necessity receive the truths of the gospel. By such arguments as these does the Episcopalian endeavour to prove that Christ constituted some permanent order of ministers in the church, to whom in the constituted externals of religion the great body of Christians are by Christ commanded to pay obedience; and thus far the Presbyterian agrees with him; but here their agreement ends. They <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in hand attack the Independent with the same weapons, and then proceed to attack each other. The one maintains, that originally the officers of the Christian church were all presbyters or elders of one order, and vested with equal powers; whilst the other holds, that Christ and his apostles appointed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> orders of ministers in the church; that of these orders the highest alone was empowered to ordain others; and that therefore obedience, as to those that watch for our souls, can be due only to such as are episcopally ordained. In behalf of the Presbyterian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> it is urged, that the titles of bishop and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a>, being in the New Testament indifferently given to the same persons, cannot be the titles of distinct ecclesiastical officers; which appears still more evident from the ordination of Timothy, who, although he was the first bishop of Ephesus, received his episcopal character by the imposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the presbyter.—That one and the same man is, in the New Testament, styled sometimes a bishop and sometimes a presbyter, cannot be denied; but although every apostolic bishop was therefore undoubtedly a presbyter, it does not of course follow, says the Episcopalian, that every presbyterian was likewise a bishop. In the Old Testament, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and his sons are without any discrimination of order frequently styled priests; and in the New, both St Peter and St John call themselves presbyters, as St Paul, upon one occasion, styles himself a deacon—διάκονος (Eph. iii. 7): yet no man ever supposed those apostles to have been such ecclesiastical officers as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> presbyters and deacons; and it is universally known, that in the Jewish priesthood there were different orders, and that Aaron was of an order superior to his sons. This being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the presbyters, by the laying on of whose hands Timothy was made a bishop, may have been of the same order with arguments against it. St Peter and St John; and if so, it follows that his ordination was Episcopalian. At all events, we are certain, continues the advocate for Episcopacy, that it was not, in the modern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, Presbyterian; for the gift, which in the first epistle is said to have been "given by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyter," is in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> said to have been "in him by the putting on of the hands of St Paul." And here it is worthy of observation, that the preposition used in the former case is μετά, which signifies concurrence rather than instrumentality; but that in the latter is διά, which, as every Greek scholar knows, is prefixed to the instrumental cause by which any thing is effected: so that whatever may have been the order of the presbyters Episcopacy byters who concurred, St Paul appears to have been the sole ordainer. But by the confession of all parties, St Paul was a bishop in the highest sense in which that word is ever used; and the powers of the episcopate not being parcelled out among various partners, of whom each possessed only a share, the imposition of his hands was sufficient for every purpose which could have been effected by the hands of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of apostles. It appears, therefore, that from the promiscuous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the titles bishop and presbyter, and from the ordination of Timothy, nothing can with certainty be concluded on either side of this celebrated question. But if, instead of resting on mere words, which when taken alone and without regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEXT">context</a>, are almost all of ambiguous signification, we attend to some important facts recorded in the New Testament, the Episcopalian thinks we shall in them discover sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that the government of the primitive church was practical. During our Saviour's stay upon earth, it is undeniable that he had under him two distinct orders of ministers—the twelve, and the seventy; and after his ascension, immediately before which he had enlarged the powers of the eleven, we read of apostles, presbyters, and deacons, in the church. That the presbyters were superior to the deacons, and the apostles superior to both, is universally acknowledged; but it has been said, that in Scripture we find no intimation that the apostolic order was designed for continuance. A Quaker says the same thing of water-baptism; and the Episcopalian observes, that it would be difficult to point out by what passage of Scripture, or what mode of reasoning, those who upon this plea reject the apostolic order of Christian ministers, could overthrow the principles upon which the disciples of George Fox reject the use of that rite which our Saviour instituted for the initiation of mankind into his church. They were the eleven alone to whom Christ said, "Go ye therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost;" and therefore, although we frequently find presbyters and deacons administering the sacrament of baptism, we must conclude, that as a judge administers justice by authority derived from his sovereign, so those inferior officers of the church administered baptism by authority derived from the apostles. Indeed, had they pretended to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> by any other authority, it is not easily to be conceived how their baptism could have been the baptism instituted by Christ; for it was not with the external washing by whomsoever performed, but with the eleven and their successors, that he promised to be "always, even unto the end of the world." That the eleven did not consider this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, or the commission with which it was given, as terminating with their lives, is evident from their admitting others into their own order; for which they had competent authority, as having been sent by Christ as he was sent by his Father. When St Paul, to magnify his office and procure it from the Galatians due reverence, styles himself, "an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father," he must have known some who derived their apostolic mission by man; otherwise he could with no propriety have claimed particular respect, as he evidently does, from Episcopacy what was in his own apostleship no particular distinction. At that very early period, therefore, there must have been in the church secondary apostles, if they may be so called, upon whom, by imposition of hands, or by some other significant <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, the eleven had conferred that authority which was given to them by their Divine <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>. Such were Matthias and Barnabas; such likewise were Timothy, Titus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> churches in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, with many others whose names and offices are mentioned in the New Testament. That Matthias and Barnabas were of the apostolic order, has never been controverted; and that Timothy and Titus were superior to modern presbyters, is evident from the offices assigned them. Timothy was, by St Paul, empowered to preside over the presbyters Barnabas, of Ephesus, to receive accusations against them, to exhort, to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, and even to rebuke them; and Titus, the angel, was, by the same apostle, left in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> for the express purpose of setting things in order, and ordaining preachers-presbyters in every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. To exhort, to charge, and with Asia, bit authority to rebuke one's equal, is certainly incongruous; and therefore the Episcopalian thinks the powers conferred on Timothy altogether insufficient with that parity of order and of office for which his antagonists so strenuously plead. Even the commission given to Titus appears in his eyes by much too extensive for a Presbyterian minister, who, after having ordained in one city, could not have proceeded to ordain in another without the consent and assistance of his brother and fellow-labourer. With respect to the angels of the Asiatic churches, he observes, that in the Old Testament the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of angel is sometimes given to the Jewish high-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and particularly by the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a>, who calls him "the messenger (angelos) of the Lord of Hosts;" and that the angels of the churches mentioned by St John, were Christian high-priests, or bishops presiding over more than one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, as it is affirmed by all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, cannot, he thinks, be denied by any man who will take the trouble to compare Scripture with Scripture. We read (Acts xix. 10. and 20.), that "in the space of two years all they who dwelt in Asia heard from St Paul the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks; and that there the word of God grew mightily and prevailed;" but with what truth or propriety could this have been said, if at the time of St John's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the Apocalypse, which was 30 years after St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, all the Christians of Proconsular Asia were comprised in seven congregations, which assembled, each with its proper pastor, to perform, in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the duties of public worship? In a word, the advocate for Episcopacy insists, that no man, who reads without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the acts of the apostles, the epistles of St Paul, and the Apocalypse of St John, can seriously believe that Timothy, Titus, Euphroditus, Sophrones, and Silvanus, with the angels of the seven churches in Asia, were mere presbyters, or that the government of the church was, in those days, by a college of elders. When from the inspired penmen of the New Testament he proceeds to examine the succeeding writers of the Christian church, the Episcopalian finds such multiplied and concurring evidence of the apostolic institution of episcopacy, as he thinks it impossible to resist without Episcopacy, without denying the truth of all ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and even shaking the pillars of revelation itself; for "in the noble <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of martyrs," the witnesses of the episcopal government of the church are earlier, and by far more numerous, than those who testify that the gospel of St Matthew was written by that apostle, or that the book of the Apocalypse is canonical Scripture. The authority of the fathers indeed is at present very low; but should they be allowed to be as fanciful divines and as bad critics as their worst enemies are pleased to represent them, this would detract nothing from their evidence when they bear witness to the constitution of the church in their own times; for of their integrity there can be no doubt; and what the Episcopalian wants of them is only their testimony to matters of fact which fell under the cognizance of their own senses, and about which therefore they could not be deceived. It is here indeed chiefly that he triumphs over his antagonists. In the second and third centuries there was no general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, nor any Christian sovereign. A prelacy therefore, he urges, could not have been universally introduced, during that period, either by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> among the clergy, or by the authority of the civil magistrate. Yet that even then there was no church under heaven, of which the government was not episcopal, has been confessed by some of the most learned writers among the Presbyterians themselves; whence he concludes that episcopacy is of divine institution. The candid Episcopalian, however, allows, that in the apostolic age there may have been some churches which at first had only bishops and deacons to perform the offices of religion; for when the number of disciples in any place was so small that they could all meet in one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, there was no necessity for any other order of ministers; but it appears that, from the very beginning, bishops, presbyters, and deacons, were settled in all the larger cities of the Roman empire; and it was in those days an allowed maxim, that without a bishop there could be no church. The better to understand the original state and institution of episcopacy, it is necessary to observe, that the empire, which contained almost all the known part of the Christian world, was by Augustus Caesar divided into provinces, subjected each to the authority of one chief magistrate, who was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a praetor or proconsul, and who resided in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> or chief city of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. A province comprehended the cities of a whole region; and in the age of the apostles, each city was under the immediate government of certain magistrates within its own body, known by the name of boulē, or senatus, ordo and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CURIA">curia</a>, "the (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> and court of the city." Those magistrates were subordinate to the praetor or proconsul; but among them there was one superior to the rest, called sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> and sometimes defensor civitatis, whose jurisdiction extended not only over the city itself, but likewise over all the adjacent territory. That territory was denominated suburbium, or the suburbs, and often reached to the distance of 10 or 12 miles round the city, and sometimes much farther, containing within it many villages and small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> under the government of the city magistrates. From some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the New Testament, and from the concurring evidence of the earliest writers of the church, it appears to have been the purpose of the apostles to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> a bishop in every city where there was a civil magistracy; Episcopacy, but as they could not be personally present in all places at once, it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for them to enter upon the great work of converting the nations by first preaching the gospel in that city of each province which was the ordinary residence of the governor; because to it there must have been the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of people, who would carry the glad tidings with them into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> when they returned. Accordingly, having dispersed themselves over the empire, and made numbers of profelytes in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities, they fixed in each, where they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it necessary, a bishop, with a college of presbyters and deacons; and gave to those bishops, who were at first called apostles, a commission, as the other cities of the province should be converted, to fix in them bishops also. In some of the smaller cities, it is extremely probable that a bishop and a deacon were for a short time the only ecclesiastical officers, till the number of Christians increased so much as to make it impossible for them all to assemble in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the purposes of public worship. The bishop then ordained presbyters to officiate in those congregations where he himself could not be present, and to assist him in other parts of his pastoral office; but in all their ministrations the presbyters were subordinate to him, who was the chief pastor within the city, who composed the prayers which were offered up in public, and to whom all the other ministers of religion were accountable for their conduct. So long as the number of the faithful was confined within the walls of the city, it appears that the bishop with his presbyters and deacons lived together as in a college; that divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> was every Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, or oftener, performed in what was afterwards called the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> or mother-church, by the bishop himself, assisted by some of his clergy; and that the congregations which met in other churches, having no fixed pastors, were supplied by such presbyters as the bishop chose to send to them from his own church. Whilst matters <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in this state, the clergy had no other revenues than what arose from the voluntary oblations of the people; which were indeed so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as not only to support them with decency, but likewise to answer other ends of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> and munificence. They were commonly divided into four equal parts; of which one was allotted to the bishop, a second to the inferior clergy, a third to the poor, and a fourth to keep the churches in repair; and it was considered as a part of the bishop's duty to take care that the offerings should be faithfully applied to these purposes. When converts increased in number, and churches were built in the suburbs, each of those churches had a fixed pastor similar to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-priest among us; but still those pastors, as well as the city-clergy, ministered in subordination to the bishop, whose authority extended as far as the civil authority of the Roman magistrate, within which district or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> it was supreme over all orders of Christians. This every man knows who is acquainted with ecclesiastical history; for the bishop alone could ordain priests and deacons, administer the rite of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, absolve penitents who were under church censure, and exclude from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> heretics and notorious offenders; and from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> there lay no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> but to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of comprovincial bishops. Such synods were in each province convened by the bishop. Episcopacy, bishop of the chief city; for the apostles having been careful to place in those cities men of the most eminent gifts and abilities, the other bishops of the provinces applied to them for advice upon every emergency, and paid a particular deference to them upon every occasion. So that though all bishops were of equal authority as bishops, yet when they met to consecrate a new bishop, or to deliberate upon the affairs of the church, they yielded a precedence to the bishop of the metropolis, who called them together, and who was as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> or moderator of the synod. Hence the origin of metropolitans or archbishops; whose authority was so considerable, that though there is not a doubt but the election of bishops was anciently placed in the clergy and people of the vacant diocese, yet the bishop elected could not be consecrated without the consent of the archbishop of the province. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the extensive powers with which the primitive bishops were vested, they are commonly styled in the writings of those times presidents, provosts, or inspectors of the church, chief priests, princes of the clergy, and even princes of the people; but their authority was wholly spiritual. Those prelates, imitating the example of their Divine Master when on earth, neither possessed nor assumed to themselves any jurisdiction over the properties or civil rights of men. In consequence of St Paul's having reprimanded the Corinthians for going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> before the unbelievers, they were indeed often chosen as arbiters of such civil disputes as arose between individuals under their episcopal government; but on these occasions they could not act unless the submission was voluntarily made by both the contending parties, and then their decision was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a>. When the empire became Christian, this privilege was confirmed to them by law; for any civil cause depending before a court of justice could be withdrawn, and by the mutual consent of parties be submitted to the arbitration of the bishop, whose award, which in former times could be enforced only by the terror of church-censures, was then enforced by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> magistrate. In criminal causes, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> might be for life or death, they were prohibited both by the canons of the church and by the laws of the state from acting as judges; and therefore they never suffered such causes to come before them, except when it was necessary that the person accused, if found guilty, should be excluded from the communion of the faithful. But they had so many civil causes flowing in upon them, that they were soon obliged to devolve part of that care upon other persons, in whose knowledge, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and integrity, they could fully confide; and as the persons employed to act in the bishop's stead were often laymen, it has been conjectured that they gave rise to the office of lay-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> in the church, and to all that train of spiritual judges and spiritual courts against which such numbers are disposed to clamour. Be this as it may, it is certain that, through the piety and munificence of the Christian emperors, the bishops enjoyed large revenues and many valuable privileges; but it does not appear that they had any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or authority, as barons or temporal princes, till the Gothic nations, which subverted the Roman empire, had embraced the Christian faith. As Christianity incapacitated the leaders of those tribes from officiating as chief priests at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> rites which were usually celebrated at the opening of their public assemblies, the bishops came naturally to discharge that duty on such occasions, when they must have shared in the rank by sharing in the functions of the chief. The situation in which they thus appeared at the opening of all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> conventions, would enable them to join with much effect in the deliberations which ensued; and their superior knowledge, their sacred character, and their influence with the people, would soon acquire them power equal to their rank. They must therefore have been well entitled to demand admission into that council which was formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and the laychiefs at the national assemblies: and as they balanced the authority of those chiefs, we cannot doubt that the king would be disposed to give the utmost effect to their claim. Accordingly, we find the dignified clergy, who received large grants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> to be held on the same tenures with the lands of the lay-magistrates, presiding along with those magistrates in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> assemblies of every degree in all the Gothic nations, and enjoying every advantage in point of rank and authority in their national diets. Hence the bishop of Rome, and several bishops in Germany, have, like the dukes and marquises of that empire, been for a long time sovereign princes; and hence too the bishops of England and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> have always sat, and have an equal right with the lay-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> to sit, in the upper house of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is however obvious, that, so far as episcopacy is of apostolical institution, those peers and princes possess not the original character in any higher degree than the bishops in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who are barely tolerated, or than those in Scotland who do not enjoy that privilege; and that confirmation administered, or holy orders conferred, by a persecuted prelate, must be as effectual to the purposes of religion, as if given by a German <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or an English peer. In this short view of episcopacy, it has been our endeavour to do justice to the subject, without suffering ourselves to be influenced by partiality or prejudice. As we are not ourselves episcopalians, we have advanced nothing of our own; but have selected from English writers, who have at different times undertaken to defend the divine right of episcopacy, such facts and arguments as to us appear to be of the most importance, or to have the greatest weight, without remarking upon them, or offering any answer. The reasoning employed to prove that the order of bishops was instituted by the apostles, is taken from a work prepared for the press by Dr Berkeley prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, and son of the celebrated bishop of Cloyne. For the rest of the detail we are indebted chiefly to Bingham's Origines Ecclesiasticae; a performance in great estimation with those English divines who are commonly known by the appellation of high churchmen. As editors of a work of this kind, it is not our business to be of any party, or to support, in opposition to all others, a particular church, though that church should be our own: We shall therefore treat independency and prelacy as we have treated episcopacy, by employing some able writer of each society to plead his own cause. Meanwhile, we shall conclude this article with a few reflections, which, though they come from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of an obscure author, deserve to be engraved deep in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of every controversialist of every communion. On complicated questions (says a late apologist for the episcopal church in Scotland), men will always differ in opinion; but conscious each of the weakness of his own understanding, and sensible of the bias which the strongest minds are apt to receive from thinking long in the same track, they ought to differ with charity and meekness. Since unhappily there are still so many subjects of debate among those who name the name of Christ; it is doubtless every man's duty, after diverting himself as much as possible of prejudice, to investigate those subjects with accuracy, and to adhere to that side of each disputed question which, after such <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, appears to him to be the truth: but he transgresses the favourite precept of his divine master, when he casts injurious reflections, or denounces anathemas, upon those who, with equal sincerity, may view the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in a different light; and by his want of charity does more harm to the religion of the Prince of Peace, than he possibly could do good, were he able to convert all mankind to his own orthodox opinions. The following is a short history of the episcopal church of Scotland, extracted from a more detailed account by a member of that church. The real tenets of the Scotch episcopalians, or members of what was at one period the established church of Scotland, he observes, appear to be imperfectly understood. About the time of the reformation from popery, the want of order and decency in the worship of the reformed church was abolished in the reign of James VI. by the establishment of episcopacy on very liberal principles. This mode of worship obtained the sanction of the most respectable part of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and continued to flourish under the auspices of government, till it was overthrown by the sticklers for the national covenant. Its restoration was effected in the year 1662, and twenty-seven years afterwards it was again abolished by the advocates of the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>. It may be proper to observe, that the Scotch episcopal church had no public liturgy during her legal establishment. It is indeed true, that, the English book of common <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> was used by the first reformers, and there is reason to believe that John Knox himself was by no means inimical to set forms of prayer, nor to clerical subordination; but his successor, Andrew Melville, a man much inferior to him in point of erudition, introduced an equality among the clergy, and excited the odium of the people against the liturgy to such a degree, that an attempt to modify the prayer book for the use of the church of Scotland, was productive of the solemn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> and covenant, and the subsequent ruin of the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>. During the reign of William III. the episcopalians were treated with some degree of severity, because they could not transfer that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to him which they had sworn to King James. It is said that they were prohibited from officiating on the Sabbath day, except "in their own hired houses, where they received such friends as chose to come in unto them." In this manner was their worship conducted, praying either extempore, or from premeditation, till the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, when the English liturgy was introduced by degrees into Scotland, under the sanction of an act of parliament, passed on the 3d of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1712, "to prevent the disturbing of those of the episcopal communion in that part of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> called Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their religious worship, and in the use of the liturgy of the church of England."
