But as their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the house of Stuart was well known, they were, at the rebellion in 1715, laid under some restraints, yet neither severe in their nature, nor of any long continuance, since in 1729 their places of worship were as numerous as before, and frequented by numbers both of rank and respectability, many of whom held places under government. In England, Dr Sancroft, archbishop of Canterbury, with five other bishops, were deprived of their fees for refusing their allegiance to King William, which occasioned a schism in the church, as they were extremely popular. Different opinions were entertained respecting the nature and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the Lord's Supper, and the controversy infected the episcopalians of Scotland. The introduction of prayers into public worship in behalf of departed friends, was at least a very impolitic step at such a critical period, when every thing favouring of popery was held in the utmost abhorrence. On the death of Dr Rose, the proscribed bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, the diocesan form of church government was opposed by such of the presbyters as had been raised to the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and it was proposed to govern the whole church by a college of bishops. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> of which no precedent could be found in the annals of history, was successfully opposed by many of the most enlightened bishops, and it was of consequence abandoned. The Scotch episcopalians, it is well known, were always <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with an undue attachment to the Stuart family, which was even considered as their most distinguishing tenet; yet there is some reason to believe that the public opinion of this matter was rather exaggerated. They have invariably maintained that the Almighty, and not the people, is the ruler of princes, which fairly places them beyond the imputation of a republican or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a> spirit. The several restraints laid on Scotch episcopalians from time to time, with a view to eradicate their attachment to the Stuart family, were happily removed in the year 1792, and they enjoyed a free toleration like the rest of dissenters. It was about this time that the clergy of this church, with a very few exceptions, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of abjuration and allegiance. It is well known, it is added by the same writer, from whose account the above is taken, that in Scotland there are chapels quite distinct from the Scotch episcopal church, where clergymen who have been ordained either in England or Ireland, make use of the liturgy of the church of England; but as each of these is strictly and properly independent of the rest, and under the guardianship of no bishop whatever, those who attend them have, in every sense of the word, a much better claim to the appellation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGREGATIONALISTS">congregationalists</a> than to that of episcopalians.

EPISCOPALIANS

Pages 281-281

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an appellation given to those who prefer the episcopal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> to all others. See Episcopacy. By the test <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, none but episcopalians, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> members of the church of England, are qualified to enjoy any office civil or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>.

EPISCOPIUS

Pages 281-282

Simon, one of the most learned Epiphanus men of the 17th century, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> supporter of the Arminian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1583. In 1612, he was chosen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> professor at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in the room of Gomarus, who resigned; and the functions of his office, with his private studies, were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> burdens to him, compared with the difficulties he sustained on account of the Arminian controversy: which, though it began in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, soon flew to the pulpits, from whence it spread and inflamed the people. The States of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> having invited Epiphanus to take his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>, he went thither accompanied by some remonstrant ministers; but the synod would not allow them to fit as judges, nor to appear in any other capacity than as persons summoned before them: they submitted, were deposed from their functions, and banished the territories of the commonwealth. Epiphanus and his persecuted brethren retired to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>; but the times growing more favourable, he returned to Holland in 1626, and was made minister of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMONSTRANTS">Remonstrants</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>: in 1634 he was chosen rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> founded by the sect at Amsterdam, where he spent the remainder of his days. He died in 1643 of the same disorder which had killed his wife before, a retention of urine; having lost his sight some weeks previous to his end. The learned have bestowed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eulogiums on Epiphanus; but he did not always write with that moderation which might have been wished. His works make two volumes in folio, of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> consists of posthumous publications.

EPISODE

Pages 282-282

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a separate incident, story, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which a poet invents, and connects with his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> action, that his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> may abound with a greater diversity of events; though in a more limited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, all the particular incidents whereof the action or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> is compounded are called episodes. See Poetry.

EPISPASTIC

Pages 282-282

in Medicine, a topical remedy, which being applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> parts of the body, attracts the humours to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>.

EPISTATES

Pages 282-282

in the Athenian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the proedri. See Proedri.

EPISTEMONARCH

Pages 282-282

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, who had the care of everything relating to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of censor. His office answered very nearly to that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Rome.

EPISTOLARY

Pages 282-282

something belonging to an epistle, see Epistle. EPISTOLARY Compositions. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a>; and the article <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. EPITROPHE. See Oratory.

EPISTYLE

Pages 282-282

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the Greeks for what we call architrave, viz. a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wood, laid immediately over the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>. EPITAPH. (from επι, upon, and τάφος, sepulchre,) a monumental inscription, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of a person deceased. It has been disputed whether the ancient Jews <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> epitaphs on the monuments of the dead; but be this as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, epitaphs, it is certain, of very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, are found among them.—The Athenians, by way of epitaph, put only the name of the dead, with the epithet ἀγαθός, signifying "good," or ἑρωταῖος, "<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>," and the word ἁγίας, signifying their good wishes: the name of the deceased's father and his tribe were frequently added.—The Lacedemonians allowed epitaphs to none but those who had died in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> inscribed their epitaphs to the manes, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a> manibus; and frequently introduced the dead by way of propopoeia, speaking to the living; of which we have a fine instance, worthy the Augustan <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, wherein the dead wife thus bespeaks her surviving husband: Immatura peri; sed tu, felicior, annos Vive tuos, conjux optime, vivas meos. The epitaphs of the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> are generally crammed with fulsome compliments which were never merited, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in its best state could scarce lay claim to, and expressions of respect which were never paid in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the deceased. Hence the proverb with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> propriety took its rise, "He lies like an epitaph." Epitaph, is also applied to certain elogies, either in prose or in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, composed without any intent to be engraven on tombs; as, that of Alexander, Sufficit huic tumulus, cui non sufficeret orbis. and that of Newton, Isaacum

EPITAPH

Pages 282-282

denotes the same with a missive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>; but is now chiefly used in speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writings, as the epistles of St Paul, epistles of Cicero, epistles of Pliny, &c. EPITAPHS and Gospels, in the liturgy of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, are select portions of scripture, taken out of the writings of the evangelists and apostles, and appointed to be read, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, on Sundays and holidays. They are thought to have been selected by St Jerome, and by him put into the lectionary. It is certain they were very anciently appropriated to the days wherein we now read them, since they are not only of general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> throughout the western church, but are also commented upon in the homilies of several ancient fathers, which are said to have been preached upon those very days to which these portions of scripture are now affixed. The epistles and gospels are placed in an admirable order and method, and bear a special relation to the several days whereon they are read. The year is distinguished into two parts; the first being designed to commemorate Christ's living among us, the other to instruct us to live after his example. The former takes in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> from Advent to Trinity-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>; the latter, all the Sundays from Trinity to Advent. During the first of these seasons, the epistles and gospels are calculated to raise in us a grateful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of what our Saviour did and suffered for us, and set before our eyes his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, circumcision, and manifestation to the Gentiles; his doctrines and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>; his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, fasting, and temptation; his agony and bloody sweat; his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, and ascension; and his mission of the Holy Ghost. During the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> season of the year, the epistles and gospels tend to instruct us in the true paths of Christianity. See Collects.

EPITASIS

Pages 282-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a dramatic poem, wherein the plot, entered upon in the first part or protasis, was carried on, heightened, and worked up, till it arrived at its state or height, called cataclisis.

EPITHALAMIUM

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a nuptial song <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in praise of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> and bridegroom, praying for their prosperity, for a happy offspring, &c. Epithalamia were sung amongst the Jews, at the door of the bride, by her friends and companions, the evening before the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Psalm xlv. is an epithalamium. Among the Greeks the epithalamium was sung as soon as the married couple were gone to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and attended with shouts and stamping of the feet to drown the cries of the bride. They returned in the morning, and with the same song, a little altered, saluted them again. The evening song was called ἐπιθαλαμία νυκτὸς, the morning salute was called ἐπιθαλαμία πρωίς. This was the practice amongst the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> also, but their epithalamia were often obscene.

EPITHEIAS

Pages 283-283

in Medicine, the increase of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> beginning of a paroxysm, particularly in a fever.

EPITHEM

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a kind of fomentation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remedy of a spirituous or aromatic kind, applied externally to the regions of the heart, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, &c. to strengthen and comfort the same, or to correct some intemperance thereof.

EPITHET

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, an adjective expressing some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a substantive to which it is joined; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such an adjective as is annexed to substantives by way of ornament and illustration, not to make up an essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Nothing, says <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, tires the reader more than too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a redundancy of epithets, or epithets placed improperly; and yet nothing is so essential in poetry as a proper <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them. The writings of the best poets are full of them.

EPITRITUS

Pages 283-283

in prosody, a foot consisting of three <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> syllables and one short. Of these, grammarians reckon four kinds: the first consisting of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IAMBUS">iambus</a> and spondee, as filiūtantes; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, of a trocheus and spondee, as concitati; the third of a spondee and an iambus, as communicāns; and the fourth, of a spondee and trocheus, as incantārē. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> SPONDEUS, TROCHEUS, &c. EPITROPE. See ORATORY, No 83.

EPITROPUS

Pages 283-283

a kind of judge, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather an arbitrator, which the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, under the dominion of the Turks, elect in the several cities, to terminate the differences that arise among them, and avoid carrying them before the Turkish magistrates. See ARBITRATOR. Anciently the Greeks used the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> ἐπιτρόπος, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> as the Latins did procurator, viz. for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> or intendant. Thus the commissioners of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are called by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> and Xenophon ἐπιτρόποι. In the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, ἐπιτρόπος denotes the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, rendered in the vulgate procurator. EPIZEUXIS. See ORATORY, No 68.

EPOCHA

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fixed point of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> whence the succeeding years are numbered or counted. See ÆRA.

EPODE

Pages 283-283

in lyric <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> last <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ode, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ode being divided into strophe, antistrophe, and epode. See ODE, &c. The epode was sung by the priests, standing still before the altar, after all the turns and returns of the strophe and antistrophe, and was not confined to any precise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or kind of verses. The epode is now a general name for all kinds of little verses that follow one or more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ones, of what kindsoever they be; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> a pentameter is an epode after an hexameter. And as every little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which, being put after another, closes the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, is called epode; hence the fifth book of Horace's odes is entitled liber epodon, "book of epodes," because the verses are all alternately <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short, and the short ones generally, though not always, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the sense of the long one.

EPOPOEIA

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, which makes the subject of an epic poem. The word is derived from the Greek ἐπος, carmen, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>;" and ἐποιεῖν, facio, "I make." In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word, however, epopeia is the same with επος, or epic poem itself. See the article POETRY.

EPSOM

Pages 283-283

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, about 16 miles southwest from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> famous for its mineral waters. These were discovered in 1618; and though not in such repute as formerly, yet they are not impaired in virtue, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> made from them is famous all over <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, for gently cleansing and cooling the body. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, galleries, and other public apartments, are now run to decay; and there remains only one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on the spot, which is inhabited by a countryman and his wife, who carry the waters in bottles to the adjacent places, and supply the demands of dealers in London. On the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> are annually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races; but the inns, shops, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a>-greens are not near so much frequented as formerly. The market is on Friday; fair, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 25. The town is about one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in circumference, from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Durdans, which was burnt <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some years since, but has been rebuilt. It was once inhabited by his present majesty's father. In Hudson's Lane here was Epsom <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxon seat, long since converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>. Here are so many fields, meadows, orchards, gardens, and the like, that a stranger would be at a loss to know whether this was a town built in a wood, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a wood surrounded by a town. Epsom <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is easily imitated by art; i.e. by only dissolving half an ounce of Epsom salt in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of pure water, made somewhat brisk or quick by adding a little sulphuric acid and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, so as to let the alkali prevail.

EPULARES

Pages 283-284

in antiquity, an epithet given to those who were admitted to the sacred epulae <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> entertainments. EQUATORIAL <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">INSTRUMENT</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> Equatoria. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EQUANGULAR

Pages 285-285

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, an epithet given to figures whose <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> are all equal: such are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, an equilateral triangle, &c.

EQUERY

Pages 284-284
or Ecury, a grand stable or lodge for horses, furnished with all the conveniences thereof; as stalls, manger, rack, &c. The word is formed from the French ecure, which signifies the same thing. Some again derive ecure from the Latin curia, which not only denotes a place for beasts to be put up in, but also a grange or barn. But a more probable derivation is from equile, "a stable for horles," of equus, "horse." Some hold that the word stable, in propriety, relates only to bullocks, cows, sheep, hogs, &c. and ecury, to horses, mules, &c. A simple ecury is that provided for one row of horses; a double ecury that provided for two, with a passage in the middle, or two passages; the horses being placed head to head, as in the little ecury at Verfailles. Under ecury are sometimes also comprehended the lodgings and apartments of the ecurers, grooms, pages, &c. Ecury (ecuyer), is also an officer who has the care and management of the horses of a king or prince.

EQUIDISTANT

Pages 285-285

an appellation given to things placed at equal distances from some fixed point <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to which they are referred.

EQUILATERAL

Pages 285-285

in general, something that hath equal sides; as an equilateral triangle.

EQUILIBRIUM

Pages 285-285

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, is when the two ends of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> hang to exactly even and le- vel, that neither doth ascend or descend, but both keep in a position <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon; which is occasioned by their being both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with an equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>.

EQUIMULTIPLES

Pages 285-285

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, are numbers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities multiplied by one and the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. Hence, equimultiples are always in the same ratio to each other as the simple quantities before multiplication; thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> 6 and 8 are multiplied by 4, the equimultiples 24 and 32 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be to each other as 6 to 8.

EQUINOCTIAL

Pages 285-285

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. See Equator. The shadows of those who live under this circle are east to the southward of them for one half of the year, and to the northward of them during the other half; and twice in a year, viz. at the equinoxes, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at noon casts no shadow, being in their zenith. From this circle is the declination <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> latitude of pla- ces accounted in the degrees of the meridian. EQUINOCTIAL <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">Points</a>, are the two points wherein the equator and ecliptic intersect each other: the one being in the first point of Aries, is called the vernal point or equinox; and the other in the first point of Libra, the autumnal point or equinox. EQUINOCTIAL <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">Dial</a>, is that whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> lies <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the equinoctial. See Dial.

EQUINOX

Pages 285-285
or AEQUINOX, in Astronomy, the time when the sun enters one of the equinoctial points. The equinoxes happen when the sun is in the equi- noctial circle; when of consequence the days are equal to the night throughout the world, which is the case twice a-year, viz. about the 20th of March and the 23rd of September, the first of which is the vernal and the second the autumnal equinox. It is found by observation, that the equinoctial points, and all the other points of the ecliptic, are continually moving backward, or in antecedentia, that is, westward. This retrograde motion of the equinoctial points, is that famous and difficult phenomenon called the precession of the equinoxes. See Astronomy Index.

EQUIPAGE

Pages 285-285

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, denotes all sorts of utensils, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, &c. necessary for commencing and prosecuting with ease and success any military <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>- tions. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a> and field equipage consists of tents, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-furniture, saddle-horses, baggage, waggons, bat- horses, &c. To EQUIP, in naval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> borrowed from the French marine, and frequently applied to the business of fitting a ship for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> arming her for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

EQUIPOLLENCE

Pages 285-285

in Logic, is when there is an equivalence between any two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more terms or propo- sitions; i.e. when they signify one and the same thing, though they express it differently. Such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, &c. are said to be equipollent.

EQUIRIA

Pages 285-285

in antiquity, a festival instituted by Ro- mulus, and celebrated on the 27th of February, in ho- nour of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, at which there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races.

EQUISETUM

Pages 285-285
Horse-tail; a genus of plants belonging to the cryptogamia clas; and in the natural method ranking under the 51st order, Coniferae. See Botany Index.

EQUITES

Pages 285-285

amongst the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, were persons of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, immediately succeeding the senators in point of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The equites <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> knights were required to be possessed of 400 sesterces before they could be admitted into that order; and when the knights were so reduced as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of the pre- scribed revenue, they were expunged out of the eques- trian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>. The equitrian revenue <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned a- mounted to about 10,000 crowns. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> whereby the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>- hood was conferred amongst the Romans was the giving of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; for every eques or knight had a horse kept at the public <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, he received also the stipend of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> to serve in the wars, and wore a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> which was given him by the state. The equites composed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of men, and constituted the Roman cavalry; for there was always a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and nothing but a review was requisite to fit them for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The knights at last grew too powerful, were a bal- ance for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and people, neglected the exercises of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and betook themselves to civil employments. The equites were liable to be punished by the censors, and to suffer <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>. They were degraded by tak- ing from them the horse which was kept for each of them at the public charge; this was called equum adi- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a>.

EQUITY

Pages 285-286

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, is defined a correction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> qualification of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, generally made in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> wherein it faileth or is too severe. It likewise signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the words of the law to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> unex- pressed, yet having the same reason; so that where one thing is enacted by statute, all other things are enacted that are of the like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. For example, the statute of Glouce, gives <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of waste against him that holds lands for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or years; and by the equity thereof, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall have action of waste against a tenant that holds but for one year, or one half-year, which is with- out the words of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, but within the meaning of it; and the words that enact the one, by equity enact the other. So that equity is of two kinds. The one abridges and takes from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the law; the other enlarges and adds to it: and statutes may be con- strued according to equity, especially where they give remedy for wrong, or are for expedition of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Equity seems to be the interpolating law of reason, exerci- sed by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> in extraordinary matters to do equal justice; and by supplying the defects of the law, gives remedy in all cases. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>. Equity, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, sometimes confounded with Justice, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> among the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, re- presented with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> in the other. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">Equivalent</a>, is understood of something that is equal in value, force, or effect, to another. Equivalence is of various kinds, in proportions, in terms, and in things. Equivalent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">Propositions</a>. See Equifollence. Equivalent Terms, are where several words that differ in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> have yet one and the same signification; as every body was there, and nobody was absent, nihil non, and omne. Equivalent Things, are either moral, physical, or statistical. Moral, as when we say that the commanding or advising a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> is a guilt equivalent to that of the murderer. Physical, as when a man who has the strength of two men is said to be equivalent to two men. Sta- tistical, whereby a less <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> becomes of equal force with a greater, by having its distance from the centre increased. Equivocal terms or words, among logicians, are those which have a doubtful or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> meaning. According to Mr Locke, the doubtfulness or uncer- tainty of words has its cause more in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> them- selves, than in any incapacity of the words to signify them; and might be avoided, would people always <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> to denote the same idea or collection of ideas: but, adds he, it is hard to find a discourse on any subject where this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; a practice which can only be imputed to folly or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dishonesty; since a man, in making up his accounts, might with as much fairness use the numerical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> sometimes for one sometimes for another collection of units. Equivocal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a>, the production of animals without the intercourse between the sexes, by the in- fluence of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or stars, &c. This kind of generation is now quite exploded by the learned. Equivocation, the using a term or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> that has a double signification. Equivocations are ex- pedients to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> telling the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and yet without tell- ing a falsity. The fathers are great patrons of equivo- cations and mental reservations, holding that the use of such shifts and ambiguities is in many cases allow- able. Equuleus, or Eccluseus, in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> used for extorting a confession; at first chiefly practised on slaves, but afterwards made use of against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. The equuleus was made of wood, having holes at certain distances, with a screw by which the criminal was stretched to the third, sometimes to the fourth or fifth holes, his arms and legs being fastened on the equuleus with cords; and thus was hoisted aloft, and extended in such a manner, that all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- located. In this state <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot plates were applied to his body, and he was goaded in the sides with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called an ungula. Equuleus, Equiculus, and Equus <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s head, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>- ern hemisphere, whose stars in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue are four, in Tycho's four, in Hevelius's six, and in Mr Flamsteed's ten. Equus, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the class <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, and order of belluae. See Mamma- lia <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. And for the diseases of the horse, see Far- rier Index.

ERA

Pages 286-286

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>. See Era. Eranaarcha, a public officer among the an- cient Greeks, whose business was to preside over and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the alms and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> made for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Cor- nelius Nepos, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Epaminondas, describes his office thus: When any person was reduced to poverty, taken captive, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to marry, which he could not effect for want of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, &c., the eranarcha called an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of friends and neighbours, and tax- ed each according to his means and estate, to contri- bute towards his relief. Eranthemum, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERASISTRATUS">Erasistratus</a>, a celebrated physician, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>- son to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. He discovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> which Antiochus had conceived for his mother-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> Stratonice, and was re- warded with 100 talents for the cure by the father of Antiochus. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy to bleeding and vio- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> physic. Erasmus, Desiderius, born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> in 1467. He lost his father and mother at 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and was committed to the care of certain guar- dians, who would force him to be an ecclesiastic, which he refused for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. However, he was obliged to assume the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> among the canons regular in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Stein near Tergou; but afterwards obtained a dispensation from his vows. He was the most learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the age in which he lived; and contributed, by his example and his writings, to the reformation of learning in the several countries in which he occasionally resided, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, Hol- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, France, and England: with the last, he was most satisfied; and found the greatest encouragement from Henry VIII. Sir Thomas More, and all the learned Englishmen of those days. He published a great ma- ny books; and died at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1536. He was buried honourably, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is still held in veneration. He had, however, many enemies; and as he did not embrace the reformation, and yet confused many things in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, he hath been treated injuri- ously both by the Catholics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. The works of Erasmus in 10 vols folio were published at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>

ERASTIANS

Pages 286-287

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> which arose in England during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the civil wars in 1647, thus called from their leader Thomas Erastus, whose distinguishing doctrine it was, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> had no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, that is, no regular power to excommunicate, exclude, censure, abrogate, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, or the like.

ERATO

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, the name of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, who presided over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. To this muse some have ascribed the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the lyre and lute; and she is represented with a garland of myrtles and roses, holding a lyre in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a bow in the other, and at her side a Cupid with his torch. There is also a Nereid of the same name.

ERATOSTHENES

Pages 287-287

a Cyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, historian, and poet; called for his learning <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. He was keeper of the famous library at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; and was greatly in favour with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Euergetes, by whose order he wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Theban kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, which succession was entirely omitted by Manetho. He thus fixed the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, and his authority is by many preferred to that of Manetho. He wrote many other things, a catalogue of which is to be seen in Fabricius, Vollius, &c., but his only piece now remaining entire is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and fabulous account of the stars. He starved himself in old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> through grief for the dimness of his sight, about the 10th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12th year of Ptolemy Epiphanes, 194 B.C.

ERATOSTRATUS

Pages 287-287

an Ephesian who burnt the famous temple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> the same night that Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> was born. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, as some writers have observed, was not prevented <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seen by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, who was then present at the labour of Olympias, and at the birth of the conqueror of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. Eratostratus did this villany merely to eternize his name by so uncommon an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>.

ERCTION

Pages 287-287

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the art of raising <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> elevating any thing; as the erection of a perpendicular, &c. It is also used in a figurative sense; as the erection of a bishopric, marquise, &c. Erection is particularly used by medical writers for the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> when swelled and distended by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the muscles called erectores. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. There is also an erection of the clitoris, which is performed by muscles for that purpose. EREMIT. See Hermit.

EREBUS

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> denoting darkness. According to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, Erebus was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">Chaos</a> and the night, and the father of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. This was also the name of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the inferi among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>: they had a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a> for those who were detained in Erebus. Erebus was properly the gloomy region, and distinguished both from Tartarus the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of torment, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a> the region of bliss: according to the account given of it by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, it forms the third <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the invisible world beyond the Styx, and comprehends several particular districts, as the limbus infantum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the receptacle for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>; the limbus for those who have destroyed themselves; the fields of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>, full of dark groves and woods, inhabited by those who died for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>; and beyond these, an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for departed warriors.

ERETRIA

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Euboea, situated on the Euripus, in the south-west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. A very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the largest of the island, after Chalcis. After being demolished by the Persians, it was restored on an adjoining spot, according to Strabo, who mentions a school of Eretrian philosophers there. The Abantes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> were of Euboea.

ERFURT

Pages 287-287

a town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Thuringia, and subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>. It is defended by good ramparts; and has a castle on an eminence, which commands the town. Its inhabitants are almost all Lutherans, but its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> churches belong to the Catholics. There are several handsome structures, both public and private; but the houses in general are but indifferently built. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 14. N. Lat. 50. 49.

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a prison, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> house of correction, where slaves by the private authority of their masters were confined and kept for their offences to hard labour. The Greeks had a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of confinement of this sort called Σωφρονιστήριον.

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the southern hemisphere, in form of a river.—The stars in the constellation Eridanus, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are 34; in Tycho's, 19; and in the British catalogue, 84.

ERIGENA

Pages 287-288
or Scotus, John, a famous scholastic divine, born about the beginning of the ninth century; but where, is a matter of dispute among authors. Bale and Pits say he was born at St David's in Wales; Dempster, Mackenzie, and Henry, that he was born at Ayr in Scotland; which they infer from his names Erigena and Scotus, by the latter of which he was generally distinguished by his contemporary writers. But Du Pin and Sir James Ware assert that he was by birth an Irishman; Ireland being in those days called Scotia. and by the natives Erin. They agree, however, in relating that he travelled to Athens, where he acquired a competent knowledge of the Greek and other oriental languages; and that he afterwards resided many years in the court of Charles the Bald, king of France, who, on account of his singular abilities, treated him as his intimate friend and companion. He slept frequently in the royal apartment; and was constantly admitted to the king's table. "We may judge" (says a modern historian) of the freedom which he used with Charles, by the following repartee. As the king and Scotus were sitting one day at table, opposite each other, after dinner, drinking a cheerful glass, the philosopher having said something that was not quite agreeable to the rules of French politeness, the king in a merry humour asked him, Pray what is between a Scot and a fool? To which he answered, "Nothing but the table." See Henry's History of Great Britain, vol. i. p. 344, who quotes this story from Hoveden's Annals, ad an. 86. Quer. What language were they talking when this bon mot was uttered? During his residence with Charles, he wrote several books of scholastic divinity; which, though absurd enough, were at that time not sufficiently so to secure him from the imputation of heterodoxy; and on that account the pope commanded Charles the Bald to send him to Rome; but the king had too great a regard for his companion to trust him with his Holiness. One of the chief controversies in which Scotus was engaged, and with which the pope was much offended, was concerning the real presence and blood of Christ in the wafer. His opinion of this weighty matter is expressed in these few words: "What we receive corporally is not the body of our Lord; but that which feeds the soul, and is only perceived by faith." He was also engaged in two other controversies of equal importance, but of a somewhat less delicate nature. The first was, Whether any part of the eucharist be evacuated by stool? and the second, Whether Christ was born of the Virgin Mary aperta vulva? Patachius was of opinion, that this could not be without some injury to her perpetual virginity; and therefore believed that Christ came into the world per osuam clauam, as he came into the place where his disciples were assembled, through the door and not through the wall, without opening the door. Concerning the first of these delicate questions, Scotus with several others declared, that part of the eucharist was certainly evacuated by stool; for which they were honoured with the appellation of Stercorifici. And as to the second question, he said, that the vulva claua was a dangerous opinion: for it would thence follow, that he was not born, but issued; non eft nasci, sed erumpi. See MacKenzie, vol. i. p. 55. Whether this John Scotus returned to England; or ended his days in France, is a matter of doubt. Some of our historians tell us, that he left France in the year 864; and that, after residing about three years in Oxford, he retired to the abbey of Malmesbury, where his scholars stabbed him with their pen knives. There is no foundation for this story. Probably he died about the year 874; but whether in France or England, is uncertain, and of little importance. Some have related, that he was invited to England by King Alfred: but in this they confound him with John, abbot of Etheling, who was assassinated in 895; and to this mistake the various accounts concerning this author are to be attributed. Regardless of his history, he appears from his writings to have been a man of parts, and, in point of learning, superior to any of his contemporaries. He wrote, 1. De divisione naturae, lib. v. 2. De praedestinatione Dei. 3. Excerpta de differentiis et societatibus Graecis Latinique verbi. 4. De corpore et janguiine Domini. 5. Ambigua S. Maximi, seu scholia ejus in difficilis locos S. Gregorii Nazianzeni, Latine verba. 6. Opera S. Dionysii quattuor in Latinitate lingua conversa. All published. 7. De usu Dei, and several other works, in manuscript, preserved in different libraries.

ERISICHTHON

Pages 289-289

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Thessalian, son of Triops, who derided <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> and cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> her groves. This impiety irritated the goddesses, who afflicted him with continual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. He squandered all his possessions to gratify the cravings of his appetite, and at last he devoured his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> for want of food. Some say that his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> had the power of transforming herself into whatever animal she pleased, and that she made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of that artifice to maintain her father, who fed her, after which she assumed another shape, and became again his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. ERIVAN

Pages 288-288

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Persian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, dirty, ill-looking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in which are no handsome buildings, the houses being very <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, and raised with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mud; but it is full of gardens and vineyards. It is situated in a plain which is surrounded on all sides with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> near it, the Zengui to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west, and the Queer Boulac to the south-west. The fortres may pass for a town of itself; it is of an oval form, and is four miles in circumference, containing about 800 houses. It is inhabited by none but the native Persians. The Armenians have shops in it, where they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> and trade in the daytime, but at night return to their habitations in the city. The fortres is surrounded with three walls, made with bricks dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which have <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, and are flanked with towers, and defended with ramparts. On the north-east there is a dreadful precipice, above 200 yards in depth, at the bottom of which the river runs. The garrison usually consisted of 2000 men; but how many there are since the revolution is hard to say. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> is within the fortres. The city

EROTIA

Pages 289-289

a festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Eros the god of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. It was celebrated by the Thessalians every fifth year with sports and games, when musicians and others contended. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any quarrels <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seditions had arisen among the people, it was then usual to offer sacrifices and prayers to the god, that he would totally remove them.

EROTIC

Pages 289-289

is applied to anything which has a relation to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. In medicine we find the phrase delirium eroticum used for a kind of melancholy contracted through excess of love.

ERPENIUS

Pages 289-289

THOMAS, in Dutch Thomas of Erp, a celebrated professor of the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, was born at Gorcum in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in 1584, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>. He applied himself to the oriental languages at the persuasion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger; and afterwards travelled into England, France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Germany, and everywhere obtained the esteem of the learned. On his return to Holland, he was made professor of Arabic in the university of Leyden, and died there in 1624. He published a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many excellent works, which spread his reputation through the whole learned world. It is said, that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> admired so greatly the letters of Erpenius wrote to him in Arabic in the name of the United Provinces, that he could not cease <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> them, and showing them to those who spoke that language naturally.

ERPETOLOGY

Pages 289-291

INTRODUCTION. The animals of which we propose, under the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> Erpetology, to give the classification and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, belong to the class <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHIBIA">Amphibia</a>, and the order <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPTILIA">Reptilia</a>, in the Linnaean arrangement. The animals included under this class have obtained the denomination amphibious, from the supposed circumstance that they are equally capable of living both on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. But in this view, the application of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is inaccurate, for there are few, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perhaps no animals belonging to this class which can always exist, or even perform the functions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for any considerable length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in the water. Many of them, however, possess this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and therefore, the name has been extended to all which are distinguished by the same peculiarity of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> form, and a similar structure of internal organs. Some naturalists have denominated this order of animals oviparous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>. This denomination is undoubtedly sufficiently characteristic; for although some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are viviparous, and in this circumstance, as well as being furnished with four feet, exhibit some resemblance with the higher order of quadrupeds, the striking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> which is discovered by the anatomist and the physiologist affords unequivocal and decided marks of distinction. From the structure, habits, and general economy of this order of animals, we derive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which are sufficiently distinctive between it and the class of birds, to which the term oviparous is strictly applicable. This denomination, therefore, which is also employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de la Cepede, is sufficiently characteristic of the class of animals which are included under it. The word reptile, by which this order of animals has been distinguished by Linnaeus, seems not to be liable to much objection. All the individuals of which it is composed have very short legs, and these are placed at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from each other, so weak, that they are unable to support the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the body. The gray lizard, for instance, which is one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> of the tribe, is obliged to support itself on its belly, as soon as its progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is greatly diminished; so that it employs its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> rather for the purpose of crawling than that of walking. And indeed all the animals of the order, from the peculiar structure and disposition of their limbs, when their motions are slow, must drag the body along on the belly, other modifications of their locomotive powers depending only on the great length and relation of the instruments of motion. In this view, therefore, the Linnaean name of the order is not improperly applied to almost all the individuals which it comprehends. The term erpetology, which we have given to this treatise upon the order reptilia, was formerly employed by the Swedish naturalist Klein, in a more extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Under this title he included the order serpentes, as well as that of reptilia, thus comprehending the whole class of amphibia. Here we have adopted it in a more limited acceptation, and confined its meaning to the last order, pursuing the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of M. Bonnaterre, in his arrangement of the same order of animals in the Encyclopedie Methodique. Linnaeus has adopted as a mark of distinction of this order of animals, the peculiar structure of the heart, which in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the anatomist is said to be unicellular, or furnished only with one ventricle or cavity. This doctrine has been admitted by eminent anatomists, as well as by some of the greatest physiologists, such as Baerhaave, Haller, and some others; and called in question only when some exceptions have occurred, of animals belonging to this tribe, which have exhibited somewhat of a different structure. One instance of this is quoted in the heart of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> inland tortoise, which was examined by the French academicians of the 17th century, and in which they discovered three ventricles instead of one. But other physiologists are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the heart of this order of animals is really furnished with two ventricles, having an immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between them; they must therefore be considered as having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> heart. The lungs of the order reptilia, are, in their appearance and structure, widely different from those of other animals. They are in general composed of two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bladders, or membranaceous bags, which, in the different species are divided into a greater or smaller <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, or subdivisions; among which are distributed the pulmonary blood-vessels. These bear, but a small proportion to the venous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> through which the ramifications are carried; in this respect differing greatly from the lungs of the higher order of quadrupeds, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, in which the proportion of the blood-vessels is so much greater than that of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>-cells, that the lungs have more of a fleshy than of a membranaceous appearance. In this order of animals, therefore, in which the blood is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, the venous system far overbalances the venous; but in the class mammalia, which are warm-blooded animals, the venous system prevails over the venous. Of all the animals which occupy the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and which the Almighty creator has dispersed throughout his works, to fill up the void space, and to produce motion, the tribe of reptiles seems at first sight to have been least the objects of benevolence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. In their structure, habits, and modes of life, when compared with other orders of animals, they exhibit marks of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> and neglect. The body in general presents only a rude inactive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; their senses are extremely obtuse; their instincts are limited to the grossest sensations, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their enjoyments reaches only to the gratifications of appetite. On the boundaries of land and water, in those vast marshes, which are remarkable only for immense depictions of mud, few or scarcely any possess the graces or elegance of other terrestrial animals; like the latter they enjoy not the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of associating together for amusement or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, or of indulging in sporting tricks on the land or in the air. On the contrary, they crawl on the earth, on the margin of extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, surrounded with unwholesome vapors; or they live in the cavities of the rocks, or in the midst of barren deserts, undisturbed by other animals, and far retired from the habitations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Some delight in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> themselves to the rays of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; while others retire during the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to shady, moist, and sequestered places, proceeding from their retreats only during the night, as it were to conceal their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, and to spare man those feelings of fear, disgust, and horror, with which their presence inspires him. But as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of every part of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> chain of beings is worthy of our attentive consideration and regard, these animals, in the eyes of the careful observer of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, are far from being wanting in exciting his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and curiosity. He cannot fail to be highly gratified with contemplating the resources which they derive from the peculiar structure of their external form, as well as from the nature of their functions. Their manners, their habits, and the relations which they bear to beings of a higher order, on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the distance to which they are removed from brute <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> on the other, are objects worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of the naturalist. This study, properly directed and applied, unveils to our eyes the beneficent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. design and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, and raises our admiration to the wonderful and extensive variety of animated beings. The uses of some of the animals belonging to this class, as valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of food in those regions where they abound, or as furnishing the tables of the luxurious in other countries with a rich delicacy; the peculiarities of external form, and of internal structure, as well as of several of their functions, such as circulation and respiration; their great length of life; the reproductive power of some, and the long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> which others can undergo, give additional interest and importance to the natural history of these animals. In the following treatise, we propose to lay before our readers a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> but comprehensive view of the natural history of this order of animals; and for the sake of perspicuity we shall treat this subject under two general heads. We shall first consider the classification and natural history of the order reptilia; and secondly, we shall give a short sketch of their anatomy, with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> facts connected with their physiology. These <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> form the subjects of the two following chapters. CHAP. I. OF THE CLASSIFICATION AND NATURAL HISTORY OF REPTILES. In the Linnean arrangement, the order reptilia is divided into four genera. Other naturalists have adopted a different arrangement. De la Cepede, in his history of oviparous quadrupeds, has divided this order into two great classes. The first class includes those animals which are furnished with a tail, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> comprehends those which have no tail. The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> exhibits a view of the classification of this eminent naturalist. Class I. Animals furnished with a tail. Genus 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TORTOISES">Tortoises</a>, having the body covered with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> shield. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">Division</a> 1. The fingers very unequal, and lengthened out in the form of fins. Division 2. The fingers very short, and almost equal. Genus 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIZARDS">Lizards</a>: the body having no bony covering. Division 1. The tail flattened; five fingers on the fore feet. Division 2. The tail round; five fingers on each foot, and elevated scales on the back. Division 3. The tail round; five fingers on the fore feet; scaly bands under the belly. Division 4. The tail round; five fingers on the fore feet, without scaly bands under the belly. Division 5. The fingers furnished underneath with large scales, covering each other, like the slates on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Division 6. Three fingers on the fore and the hind feet. Division 7. Membranes in the form of wings. Division 8. Three or four fingers on the fore feet; four or five fingers on the hind feet. Class II. Animals which have no tail. Genus 1. Frogs: the head and the body lengthened out, and the one or the other angular. Genus 2. Tree-frogs: the body long, with soft viscid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> under the toes. Genus 3. Toads: the body thick and round. Appendix. Biped reptiles. Division 1. Two fore feet. Division 2. Two hind feet. Of this arrangement it may be observed, that, although it exhibits much minuteness and ingenuity, the distinctive characters upon which some parts of it are founded, are not always constant and fixed; for it has been found that these characters vary in the different individuals in which they have been observed. This variety, it has been conjectured, arises from the difference of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and peculiarities in their food and modes of life. M. Bonnaterre has adopted a different arrangement. He has also divided the whole order of reptiles into two classes, as will appear from the following table. Class I. Reptiles which have no tail.
