Genus 1. Frog. Genus 2. Tree-Frog. Genus 3. Toad. Class II. Reptiles which are furnished with a tail; Genus 1. Tortoise. Genus 2. Chameleon. Genus 3. Crocodile. Genus 4. Lizard. Genus 5. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">Flying</a> dragon. Genus 6. Salamander. Genus 7. Chalcis. This arrangement is undoubtedly, in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, convenient and proper; yet, as there seems to be in others an unnecessary multiplication of genera, we shall still adhere to the Linnean classification, which, though more simple, will in general be found not to be much less accurate; and the objects which it comprehends not being very numerous, it is sufficiently distinct. Linnaeus divided this order into four genera. The following are the characters of the genera, of which we give a translation, for the accommodation of the English reader.

ERPHYLE

Pages 288-289

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a sister of Adrastus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, who married Amphiarau. She was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Talus and Lysimache. When her husband concealed himself that he might not accompany the Argives in their expedition against Thebes, where he knew he was to perish, Eriphyle suffered herself to be bribed by Polynices with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> necklace which had been formerly given to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERMIONE">Hermione</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Venus, and she discovered where Amphiarau was. This treachery of Eriphyle compelled him to go to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; but before he departed, he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> his son Alcmaeon to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> his mother as soon as he was informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Amphiarau perished in the expedition; and his death was no sooner known than his last injunctions were obeyed, and Eriphyle was murdered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of her son.

ERRATIC

Pages 352-353

in general, something that wanders, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is not regular: hence it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> are called erratic flares.

ERRHINES

Pages 353-353

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines which when snuffed up the nose promote a discharge of mucus from that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Errhines prepared of cephalic herbs are of singular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in oppressive pains of the head, a hemicania, lethargic disorders, weaknesses of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, stuffings of the head, and coryza, mucous defluxions of the eyes, drowsiness, vertigoes, and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the malignant humours <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the lues venerae are lodged in the membranes of the nostrils.

ERROR

Pages 353-353

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, a mistake of our judgment, giving assent to that which is not true. Mr Locke reduces the causes of error to these four; first, want of proofs; secondly, want of ability to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> them; thirdly, want of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> to use them; and, fourthly, wrong <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>. He observes upon the first of these causes of error, that the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of mankind want conveniences and opportunities of making experiments and observations themselves, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of collecting the testimony of others, being prevented by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of their condition. Upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of these causes, he observes, that there are many, who, from the state of their condition, might bestow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in collecting proofs, but yet are not able to carry a train of consequences in their heads, nor weigh exactly the preponderancy of contrary proofs and testimonies, merely from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in men's understandings, apprehensions and reasonings. Thirdly, he remarks, that though some have opportunities and leisure enough, and want neither parts, learning, nor other helps, that they never come to the knowledge of several truths within their reach, either upon account of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or business; or otherwise because of their laziness or aversion to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The fourth cause of error, viz. wrong measures of probability, he imputes, 1. To the practice of taking for principles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> that are not in themselves certain and evident, but, on the contrary, doubtful and false. 2. To received hypotheses. 3. To predominant passions or inclinations. And, 4. To authority, or the giving up our assent to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> received opinions either of our friends or party, neighbours or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The causes of error in philosophy, or the reasons why all former philosophers have through so many ages erred, according to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, are these following: 1. Want of time suited to learning. 2. The little labour bestowed upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy. 3. Few entirely addicted to natural philosophy. 4. The end of the sciences wrong fixed. 5. A wrong way chosen. 6. The neglect of experiments. 7. Regard to antiquity and authority. 8. Admiration of the works in use. 9. The artifice of teachers and writers in the sciences. 10. Oftentimes promises of the moderns. 11. Want of proposing worthy tasks. 12. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a> and zeal being opposite to natural philosophy, as thinking philosophy dangerous, on account of the scholastic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that deep natural inquiries should subvert <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. 13. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">Schools</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> proving unfavourable to philosophy. 14. Want of rewards. And, 15. Despair, and the supposition of impossibility. ERROR Loci. Boerhaave is said to have introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, from the opinion that the vessels were of different sizes for the circulation of blood, serum, and lymph; and that when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>-sized globules were forced into the lesser vessels by an error of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, they were obstructed. But this opinion does not seem well grounded.

ERTHALIS

Pages 288-288

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERUCA

Pages 353-353

in general, denotes caterpillars of all kinds. The caterpillar state is that through which insects <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> before they arrive at perfection. See Larva, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERUDITION

Pages 353-353

denotes learning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> knowledge; and chiefly that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquity, of languages, and of books, which is the result of hard <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and extensive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>. The Scaligers were men of deep erudition; the writings of M. Launoy, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the Oratory, are full of erudition. Mr Locke says, it is of more <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to fill the head with reflections than with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of erudition. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the mind be not <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> is better than erudition, which only produces confusion and obscurity. M. Balzac calls a heap of ill-chosen erudition the luggage of antiquity.

ERUPTION

Pages 353-353

in Medicine, a sudden and copious excretion of humours, as pus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> blood: it signifies also the same with exanthema, any breaking out, as the pustules of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, small-pox, measles, &c. ERUPTION of Volcanoes. See Etna, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, and Volcano, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERVUM

Pages 353-353

the Lentil; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the diadelphia clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32nd order, Papilionacea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERYMANTHUS

Pages 353-354

ERYMANTHUS, a mountain, river, and town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> killed a prodigious boar, which he carried on his shoulders to Eryxitheus; who was so terrified at the fight, that he hid himself in a brazen vessel.

ERYNGIUM

Pages 354-354
Sea-holly, or Eryngo; a genus of plants, belonging to the pentandria clasps, and in the natural method ranking under the 45th order, Umbellatae. See Botany Index.

ERYSIMUM

Pages 354-354

Hedge mustard; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tetradyamia clasps, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 29th order, Siliqueae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERYSIPELAS

Pages 354-354

in Medicine, an eruption of a fiery <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> acid humour, from which no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body is exempted, though it chiefly attacks the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERYTHEA

Pages 354-354
or Erythia, an island adjoining, according to the ancients, either to or a part of Gades; nowhere now to be found by the description given of it by ancient authors. The poets feign this to be the habitation of the fabulous Geryon, disarmed by Hercules, who drove away his cattle. ERYTHRÆA, in Ancient Geography, a port-town of Aetolia, on the Corinthian bay. Another Erythrae of Bœotia, near Platæa and Mount Cithæron. A third Erythrae, a town of Ionia in the Hither Asia, situated in the peninsula, at its extremity, with a cognominal port. The Erythreans laid claim to the Sibyl Herochile, as their countrywoman, fumained thence Erythrea. Erythrae was famous for an ancient temple of Hercules. ERYTHRÆA, a town of Crete, situated in the south-east of the island, at the promontory Erythreum. ERYTHRÆUM MARE, erroneously called Rubrum by the Romans. Thus the ocean that washes Arabia and Persia, and extends a great way farther, is denominated. Hence it is, Herodotus says, that the Euphrates and Tigris fall into the Mare Erythreum. He also calls it the South Sea, on which the Persians dwell. It takes its name, not from its colour, the error of the Romans, who translated Erythreum "Rubrum;" but from Erythras, son of Perseus and Andromeda, whose kingdom lay on the confines of that sea; whence its name Erythreum.

ERYTHRINA

Pages 354-354

Coral Tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the diadelphia clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, Papilionaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERYTHROIDES

Pages 354-354

in Anatomy, the first of the proper tunics <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coats which cover the testicles.

ERYTHRONIUM

Pages 354-354

Dog's-tooth Violet; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandria clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 11th order, Sarmientoceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERYTHROXYLON

Pages 354-354

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the decandra clasps. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERYX

Pages 354-354

a son of Butes and Venus, who relying upon his strength, challenged all strangers to fight with him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> of the cestus. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> accepted his challenge after many had yielded to his superior dexterity; and Eryx was killed in the combat, and buried on the mountain, where he had built a temple to Venus. Virg. Æn. 5. v. 402. A mountain of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> near Drepanum, which received its name from Eryx, who was buried there. This mountain was so steep, that the houses which were built upon it seemed every moment ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. Daedalus had enlarged the top, and inclosed it with a strong wall. He also consecrated there to Venus Erycina a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> heifer, which resembled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> so much, that it seemed to exceed the power of art.

ERZERUM

Pages 354-354
or Erzeron, a city of Turkey in Asia, and capital of Armenia, or Turcomania. It is a pretty large town, five days' journey from the "xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black Sea, and ten from the frontiers of Persia. It stands in a delightful plain, at the foot of a chain of mountains, which hinder the Frat, or Euphrates, from falling into the Black Sea. A neighbouring hill supplies very fine springs, which not only water the fields, but the streets of the town. Erzerum is surrounded with double walls, defended by pentagonal towers; but the ditches are neither deep nor well kept up. The beglerbeg, or bailiff of the province, lives in the seraglio, which is very ill built. They reckon that there are 18,000 Turks at Erzerum, 6000 Armenians, and 10,000 Greeks. The Armenians have a bishop and two churches; and the Greeks have also a bishop, but the church is a miserable place. The lait are mostly braziers, inhabiting the suburbs, who work the copper brought from the neighbouring mountain. They drive a great trade in copper utensils and furs, particularly martins skins. Five or six days' journey from the town there are oaks that produce plenty of gall-nuts, which are brought hither. This place is the thoroughfare and resting place of all the merchants trading to the Indies, especially when the Arabs are watching for their prey round Aleppo and Bagdad. E. Long. 40° 50'. N. Lat. 29° 46'.

ESARHADDON

Pages 354-354

the son of Sennacherib, and his successor in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>. He is said to have reigned 29 years at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a>, from the year 3294 to 3322; besides which he reigned 13 years at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, in all 42 years. He died in the year of the world 3336, and was succeeded by Saaduichinus. Esarhaddon, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, seems to be the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDANAPALUS">Sardanapalus</a> who died, as Cæstarchus says, of old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, after the revolt of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; the name Sardanapalus being derived from Affarhadon Pul.

ESCALADE

Pages 354-355
or Scalade, a furious attack of a wall or a rampart, carried on with ladders, to pass the ditch or mount the rampart; without proceeding in form, breaking ground, or carrying on regular works to secure the men. When the troops are prepared to pass the ditch, either with the assistance of boards, hurdles, and fascines, when it is muddy, or with small boats of tin, or baskets covered with skins or oil cloth, when it is deep and filled with water, a party must be placed on the counterescarp, opposite to the landing-place, ready to fire at the garrison if they are alarmed, and oppose the mounting on the rampart. If the ditch is dry, the ladders are fixed in some place farthest distant from the centre; and as soon as they get upon the rampart, they put themselves in order to receive the enemy; if the centre should be surprised and filently overcome, the detachment hastens to break open the gate, and to let in the rest of the party. If the ditch is wet, the rampart high, and provided with a revetment, it will be difficult to surprize the town in this way; but if there is no revetment, the troops may hide themselves along the outside of the rampart till all are over. Since the invention and use of gunpowder, and the walls of cities have been flanked, they are seldom taken by escalade.

ESCALLONIA

Pages 355-355

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandria clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ESCAPE

Pages 355-355

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>; a violent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> privy evasion out of some lawful restraint, without being delivered by due course of law. There are two sorts of escapes, voluntary and negligent. Voluntary, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> arrests another for felony, or other crime, and afterwards lets him go freely by consent; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the party that permits such escape is held guilty, committed, and must answer for it. Negligent escape, on the contrary, is where one is arrested, and afterwards escapes against the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the person who arrested him, and is not pursued with fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, and retaken when the person pursuing hath lost sight of him. By stat. 8 and 9 Will. III. c. 26, the keepers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> conniving at escapes shall forfeit 100l.; and in civil <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> is answerable for the debt.

ESCHAR

Pages 355-355

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the crust <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scab occasioned by burns or caustic medicines.

ESCHARA

Pages 355-355

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of coralline, &c. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are these: they are of a flaky <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coral-like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, and resemble a woven cloth in their texture; and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> informs us, that they consist of arrangements of very small cells, whose surfaces appear much in that form. Linnaeus makes it a species of millepora, in the class of lithophytes.

ESCHEAT

Pages 355-355

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is that forfeiture which is incurred upon a person's being denounced a rebel. See ESHEAT LAW, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. No. clxvi. 12.

ESCHEVIN

Pages 355-355
or ECHEVIN (Scabinus), in the French and Dutch polity, a magistrate elected by the inhabitants of a city, to take care of their common concerns, the good order, conveniency, and decoration of the city, &c. At Paris there were formerly a prevôt and four eschevins; in most other cities a mayor and eschevins. In Languedoc, Provence, and Dauphiné, they were called consuls; at Toulouse, capitouls; and jurats at Bordeaux. Anciently the eschevins were the affleflors and counsellors of the comites or judges of cities; on which account they were called in some places pairs, pares; they even took cognizance of petty causes themselves. Du Cange observes, that the judges and their confessors, who were chosen by the inhabitants, were called seabinis, "eschevins," and their college seabinagium or "eschevinage." In Holland, the seabinis or eschevins judge of all civil affairs at first hand. They also take cognizance of criminal matters: and if the criminal confess himself guilty, they can see their sentence executed without appeal. They can even give torture. The number is not the same in all cities; at Amsterdam there are nine, at Rotterdam seven, &c.

ESCHRAKITES

Pages 355-355
or ESRAKITES, a sect of philosophers, among the Mahometans, who adhere to the doctrines and opinions of Plato. The word is derived from the Arabic word schraka, which in the fourth conjugation prwv af hrao, signifies "to shine, glitterlike the sun," so that Eschraotic seems to import "illumined." The Eschraotics, or Mahometan Platonists, place their highest good and happiness in the contemplation of the Divine Majesty; despising the gross imaginations of the Alcoran touching paradise. They are very careful in avoiding all vice; they preserve an equal and easy temper, love music, and divert themselves with composing little poems or spiritual songs. The shaicks or priests, and the chief among the preachers of the imperial mosques, are Eschraotics.

ESCLAIRISSEMENT

Pages 355-355

a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> adopted into our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifying the explaining <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clearing up of some difficulty or obscurity.

ESCORT

Pages 355-355

a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, sometimes used in English authors to denote a convoy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of armed men, attending some person or thing, in a journey or voyage, to defend or secure it from insults. Some derive the word from the Latin cohort.

ESCOUADE

Pages 355-355
or SQUAD, is usually the third or fourth part of a company of foot; so divided for mounting guards, and for the more convenient relieving of one another. It is equivalent to brigade of a troop of horse. See BRIGADE.

ESCUAGE

Pages 355-355

in our old customs, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, called service of the shield, by which the tenant was bound to follow his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> to the wars at his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> CHIVALRY, FEUDAL SYSTEM, and KNIGHT-SERVICE. ESCOLAPIUS. See ÆSCULAPIUS.

ESCULENT

Pages 355-355

an appellation given to such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the roots of them, as may be eaten; such are beets, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARROTS">carrots</a>, artichokes, leeks, onions, parsnips, potatoes, radishes, scorzonera, &c.

ESCURIAL

Pages 355-356

ESCURIAL, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated about 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. It is the largest and most superb structure in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and perhaps one of the finest in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The word is Arabic, meaning "a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> full of rocks." It is built in a dry barren spot, surrounded with rugged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, inasmuch that every thing which grows there is owing to art. This place was chosen, it is said, for the sake of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wherewith the fabric was built, which is got from a mountain <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> by, and is very durable; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of erecting it was to commemorate a victory which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. obtained over the French (but by the assistance of the English forces) at St Quintin, on St Laurence's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in the year 1557. The Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this structure forms a sizeable quarto volume, and it is said that its founder expended upon it six millions of ducats. The apartments are decorated with an astonishing variety of paintings, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, marble, jasper, gems, and other curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, surpassing all imagination. This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, besides its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, contains a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and richly ornamented; a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>; cloisters; a convent; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; and a library, containing about 30,000 volumes; besides large apartments for all kinds of artists and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, noble walks, with extensive parks and gardens, beautified with fountains and costly ornaments. The fathers that live in the convent are 200, and they have an annual revenue of 12,000l. It was begun by Philip in 1562, five years after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; and completed in 22 years. It consists of several courts and quadrangles, which altogether are disposed in the shape of a gridiron, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the martyrdom of St Laurence; the apartments where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> resides form the handle. The building is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of 640 by 580, and the height up to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is all round 60 feet, except on the garden side, where the ground is more taken away. At each <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> is a square tower 200 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of windows in the west <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is 200; in the east front 366. The orders employed are Doric and Ionic. There are three doors in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> front. Over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> entrance are the arms of Spain, carved in stone; and a little higher in a niche, a statue of St Laurence in a deacon's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, with a gilt gridiron in his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a book in his left. Directly over the door is a bas-relief of two enormous gridirons in stone. This vast structure, however, with its narrow high towers, small windows, and steep sloping roof, exhibits a very uncouth style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>: at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the domes, and the immense <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of its fronts, render it a wonderfully grand object from every point of view. The church, which is in the centre of all, is large, awful, and richly but not affectedly ornamented. The cupola is bold and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. The high altar is composed of rich marbles, agates, and jaspers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rarity, the produce of this kingdom. Two magnificent catafalques fill up the side arcades of this sanctuary: on one the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., his wife, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, are represented in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, larger than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, kneeling; opposite are the effigies of Philip II., and of his three wives, of the same materials, and in the same devout attitude. Underneath is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-place of the royal family, called the Pantheon. Twenty-five steps <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to this vault, over the door of which is an inscription denoting, that Hic locet, facer mortalitatis exuviae Catholicorum Regum, &c. was intended by Charles the emperor; refolved upon by Philip II., begun by Philip III., and completed by Philip IV. The mausoleum is circular, 36 feet diameter, incrustated with fine marbles in an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The bodies of the kings and queens <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in tombs of marble, in niches, one above the other. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of these sepulchres is grand, and executed with a princely magnificence; but, as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> traveller observes, in a style rather too gay, too light, and too delicately fitted up, for the idea we are apt to form of a chapel destined for the reception of the dead. The collection of pictures dispersed about various parts of the church, sacristy, and convent, has been considered as equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior, to any gallery in Europe, except that of Dresden. Formed out of the spoils of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the wasted cabinet of that unfortunate dilettante Charles I. of England, it contains some of the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> works of the greatest painters that have flourished since the revival of the art. In the sacristy is an altar called La Santa forma; this is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> custodia of gems, marbles, woods, and other precious materials, inlaid in gilt bronze; in which, rather than in the excellence of the workmanship or taste of the design, confers the merit of this rock of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. Before it hangs a curtain, on which Coello has represented Charles II. and all his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, coming to place this Forma. This is esteemed one of the most curious collections of portraits in the world; for all the persons are drawn with the greatest strength of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, and are said to be perfect resemblances not only of the monarch and grandees, but even of the monks, servants, and guards. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, busts, and medallions of the Escorial, are not in any great number, or very remarkable for their excellence: but the library contains a most precious collection of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, many fine drawings, and other curiosities. Notwithstanding the coldness of the exposure, the late king, for the sake of hunting, used to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> here several months in the year; and to make the place less inconvenient to his attendants and to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, he built an entire new town adjoining to it.

ESCUTCHEON

Pages 356-356
or SCUTCHION, in Heraldry, is derived from the French escuflon, and that from the Latin scutum, and signifies the shield whereon coats of arms are represented. Most nations of the remotest antiquity were wont to have their shields distinguished by certain marks painted on them; and to have such on their shields was a token of honour, none being permitted to have them till they had performed some honourable action. The escutcheon, as used at present, is square, only rounded off at the bottom.

ESDRAS

Pages 356-357

a Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Longimanus sent him with rich presents for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and ornament of the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, rebuilt under Zerubbabel; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> also ordered the neighbouring governors to provide him with what conduces to the pomp of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and to exempt the priests from paying taxes. He is supposed to be the collector of the Canon of Scripture; and that, by divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, he added some things which hap- pened after the deaths of the authors. It is guessed he wrote the Chronicles, besides those books which bear his name, the two last of which are exploded even by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome.

ESNE

Pages 357-357
or Esneh, a considerable sea-port town of Upper Egypt. It is governed by an Arabian prince, and by a cache, dependant on the bey of Girze. The Mahometans have several mosques here, and the Coptis a church served by two priests. "Esne (says Abulfeda), remarkable for its public baths and its commerce, is built on the westward of the Nile, between Assouan and Cous, but nearer to this latter. It acknowledges, adds the geographer of Nubia, the Coptis for founders. Its well cultivated territory abounds in grain and palm-trees. It is surrounded by gardens filled with fruit-trees. One admires here several ancient monuments constructed by the Coptis, and superb ruins." This description answers to Esne in our time, which is situated on the edge of a rich country, and shaded by groves of orange trees loaded with fruits and flowers. This town, formerly called Latopolis, revered Minerva and the fish Latus (Strabo). It contains within its boundary an antique temple; thick walls inclose it on three sides. Six large fluted columns, crowned by a capital ornamented with the palm leaf, form the façade of it; 18 others support the roof, which is composed of large squares of marble; the building is surrounded by a frieze, and innumerable hieroglyphics cover its exterior aspects. A little to the south of the town are seen the ruins of a monastery founded by St Helena, and near it the burying-place of the martyrs, adorned with tombs crowned by cupolas, supported by arcades. The inhabitants of Esne having revolted against the persecution of Diocletian, that emperor destroyed this town and put them to the sword. This place, consecrated by religion, is become a celebrated pilgrimage among the Coptis. They repair thither from the most distant provinces of the kingdom. In the chain of mountains which stretches to the eastward of the Nile, and nearly opposite Esne, are quarries of a soft stone, called Baram. It is made use of for kitchen utensils. It hardens in the fire, and forms excellent kettles and pans, which give no bad taste to the viands. This stone is probably the lapis ollaris, or pot-stone. "Esne (says Denon*) is the ancient Latopolis. Some remains are still visible of its port or quay on the bank of the Nile, which has been often repaired; but, notwithstanding all that has been done for it, still remains in a very miserable condition. This town also contains the portico of a temple, which appears to me to be the most perfect monument of ancient architecture. It is situated near the bazar in the great square, and would make an incomparable ornament to this spot, if the inhabitants had any idea of its merit; but instead of this they have defaced it by the most miserable ruined hovels, and have devoted it to the vilest purposes. The portico is very well preserved, and possesses a great richness of sculpture: it is composed of eighteen columns with broad capitals; these columns are noble and elegant, though they now appear in the most disadvantageous light: the rubbish should be cleared to find if any part of the cella remains. "The hieroglyphics in relief, with which it is covered within and without, are executed with great care; they contain, among other subjects, a zodiac, and large figures of men with crocodiles heads: the capitals, though all different, have a very fine effect; and as an additional proof that the Egyptians borrowed nothing from other people, we may remark, that they have taken all the ornaments, of which these capitals are composed, from the productions of their own country, such as the lotus, the palm-tree, the vine, the ruth, &c., &c."

ESPALIERS

Pages 357-357

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, are rows of trees planted about a whole garden <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> plantation, or in hedges, in such a manner as to enclose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> or separate parts of a garden; and are trained up regularly to a lattice of wood-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> hedge, for the defense of tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> against the injuries of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. They are of admirable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-garden, serving not only to shelter the tender plants, but screen them from the sight of persons in the walks. The trees chiefly planted for espaliers, are apples, pears, and some plums: some plant apples grafted upon paradise stocks; but as these are of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, it is better to plant those grafted upon crabstock, or upon what the gardeners call Dutch stocks; which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> both cause them to bear sooner, and prevent their growing too luxuriant. The best kinds of apple for this purpose, are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> pippen, nonpareil, renette, &c.; and the best sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, are the jargonelle, blanquette, &c. These last, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> designed for a strong moist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, should be grafted upon quince stocks; but if for a dry soil, upon free stocks. While the trees are young, it will be sufficient to drive a few stakes into the ground on each side of them; fastening the branches to these in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, as they are produced. This method will do for the first three years; after which an espalier should be made of ash-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, whereof there must be two sorts, larger and smaller; the former to be driven upright into the ground a foot asunder, and the latter, or slender poles, to be nailed across these, at about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches. Some prefer to this another sort of espalier, made of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> cut to any size; these are, indeed, more tightly, but withal vastly more expensive. When the espalier is thus framed, the branches are to be fastened to it with other twigs; observing to train them in a horizontal position, and at equal distances. Fruit trees thus managed are preferable to any others; not only as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> better-tasted fruit, but as taking up very little room in a garden, so as to be less hurtful to plants which grow in the quarters.

ESPLANADE

Pages 357-357

in Fortification, the sloping of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> of the covered-way towards the champaign.

ESPLEES

Pages 357-357

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the general products which lands yield, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the profit or commodity that is to be taken or made of a thing.

ESPOUSALS

Pages 357-358

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signify a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pro- mife made between a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and a woman to marry each other; and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where marriages may be consummated, espousals go before. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a> is termed an espousal de presenti. The espousals among the Jews were either by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, or by a piece of silver given and received, or by cohabitation. Amongst the Greeks, after the parents and friends of the young couple had finished their negotiation, the couple themselves pledged their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> to each other, the man swearing that he would be constant and true, the woman that she would marry him, and make him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all he had. Then they ratified their agreement by a kiss and joining <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Amongst the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> the espousals consisted in an engagement of friends on both sides, whether absent or present, in public or without witnesses. But the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way was by writings drawn up by common consent, and sealed by both parties: besides this, the man sent a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> to the woman, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>.

ESQUILLAE

Pages 358-358

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hills of Rome, which Varro <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have to be two, viz. Cilpias and Oppius; also Mons Esquilinus, softened from Exquilius; and this again from Excubinus, the watch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> kept here, from a jealousy he entertained of his colleague Titus Tatius. On the east side it reached the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> walls; on the south, the Via Lavicana; on the west, the wide valley between Mount Coelius and the Palatine; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the Mons Viminalis; on the east side was the Porta Esquilina. This hill by some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> was called Suburrana, from the street Suburra to the north of it: by the poets, Esquilus.

ESQUIMAUX

Pages 358-358

a people of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, inhabiting all that vast tract of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABRADOR">Labrador</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-NEW_BRITAIN">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. They differ very considerably, both in aspect and manners, from the other American nations; agreeing in most respects with the inhabitants of West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>. See New BRITAIN and GREENLAND.

ESQUIRE

Pages 358-358

was originally he who, attending a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, did carry his shield; whence he was called escuier in French, and scutifer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> armiger, i.e. armour-bearer, in Latin. Hotoman says, that those whom the French call esquires, were a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> kind of vassals, having jus scuti, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to bear a shield, and in it the ensigns of their family, in token of their gentility or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. But this addition hath not of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time had any relation to the office or employment of the person to whom it hath been attributed, as to carrying of arms, &c. but hath been merely a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of dignity, and next in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to a knight. For those to whom this title is now due, see the article COM-MONALTY. Officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s courts, and of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, counsellors at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, justices of the peace, are only esquires in reputation; and he who is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace has this title only during the time he is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, and no longer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he is not otherwise qualified to bear. A <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> being a superior officer, bears the title of esquire during his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; in respect of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trust he has in the commonwealth. The chiefs of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> families are esquires by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>; and in late acts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for poll <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, many wealthy persons <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reputed to be such, were ranked among the esquires of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. There is a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that every <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, who has 300l. a-year, is an esquire; which is a vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>: for no money whatsoever, or landed property, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> properly this title, unless he comes within one of the above rules: and no person can ascribe this title where it is not due, unless he pleases; there being no difficulty in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the line by the accounts given above and in the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">COMMONALTY</a>: but the meaner ranks of people, who know no better, do often badly prostitute this title; and, to the great confusion of all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and precedence, every man who makes a decent appearance, far from thinking himself any way ridiculed by finding the supercition of his letters thus decorated, is fully gratified by such an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. ESQUIRES of the king, are such as have that title by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, wherein there is some formality used, as the putting about their necks a collar of SS. and bestowing on them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of silver spurs, &c. ESRAKITES. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESCHRAKITES">ESCHRAKITES</a>.

ESSAY

Pages 358-358

in literature, a peculiar kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, the character whereof is to be free, easy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; not tied to strict order <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> method, nor worked up and finished like a formal system.

ESSAYING

Pages 358-358
or ASSAYING, in Chemistry and Metallurgy, signifies the examination of a small quantity of any ore or mineral by fire, in order to discover the quantity of metal it contains. This is very necessary for those who intend to deal largely in metallurgic operations, in order to avoid unnecessary expense, by becoming previously acquainted with the nature of the ore. See CHEMISTRY Index; and ORES, Reduction of. ESSAY-Hatch, is the miners term for a little trench or hole, which they dig to search for lead or ore.

ESSEDARII

Pages 358-358

a sort of gladiators, mentioned by Seneca, Suetonius, and Tully, who on some occasions engaged one another out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> called effedra. The effedrum was a sort of heavy chariot from which the Gauls and Britons engaged the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. See GLADIATOR.

ESSENCE

Pages 358-358

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, that which constitutes the particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of each genus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> kind, and distinguishes it from all others: being nothing but that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> idea to which this name is affixed, so that everything contained in it is essential to that particular kind. This Mr Locke calls the nominal essence; in contradistinction to the real essence, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of substances on which this nominal essence depends. Thus the nominal essence of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> is that complex idea the word gold stands for; let it be, for instance, a body, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, weighty, malleable, fusible, and fixed: but its real essence is the constitution of its infensible parts, on which these qualities and all its other properties depend, which is wholly unknown to us.

ESSENES

Pages 358-359
or ESSENJANS, in Jewish antiquity, They allowed a future state, but denied a resurrection from the dead. Their way of life was very singular: they did not marry; but adopted the children of others, whom they bred up in the institutions of their sect: they despised riches, and had all things in common, and never changed their clothes till they were entirely worn out. When initiated, they were strictly bound not to communicate the mysteries of their sect to others; and if any of their members were found guilty of enormous crimes, they were expelled. Pliny tells us, that they dwelt on the west side of the lake of Asphaltites; and that they were a solitary kind of men, living without women or money, and feeding upon the fruit of the palm-tree: he adds, that they were constantly recruited by new-comers, whom the surges of ill fortune had made weary of the world; in which manner the sect was kept up for several thousands of years, without any being born among them. The reason why we find no mention made of them in the New Testament, may be their recluse and retired way of life, no less than their great simplicity and honesty, whereby they lay open to no censure or reproof.

ESSENTIAL

Pages 359-359

something necessarily belonging to a thing, from which it cannot be conceived distinct: thus the primary qualities of bodies, as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, &c. are essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inseparable from them in all their changes and alterations. ESSENTIAL Oils are such as are really contained in a plant, and are drawn from it by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> in an alembic with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>: they are thus called, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to empyreumatic oils, which are raised by a naked fire without water.

ESSEX

Pages 359-359

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Stour, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>; on the east, by the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the west, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>; and on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. It extends 46 miles in length from east to west and about 42 in breadth from north to south, and 200 in circuit. This county is in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Capel. The county of Essex is divided into nineteen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, and contains twenty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 415 parishes, 125 vicarages, and 1100 villages. It sends eight members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; namely, two for the county, and two for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>, Harwich, and Malden. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> in the inland parts is healthy; but in the marshes near the sea it produces agues, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> called the Hundreds. However, the fertility of the unwholesome part is very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and even the higher grounds of this county are very fruitful. About Saffron Walden, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> saffron three years, it is said, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce good barley for 18 years successively without any manure. Its produce, which is very plentiful, consists of corn, most excellent saffron, cattle, fowl, fish, and particularly oysters. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this county are cloth, stuffs, and particularly baize. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, besides the Thames, are the Stour, which falls into the German sea at Harwich; the Lea, its western boundary, falls into the Thames below <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRATFORD">Stratford</a>; the Blackwater runs through the heart of the county, and passing by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHELMSFORD">Chelmsford</a> is joined by the Chelmer, and from thence runs into the German sea; the Coln runs by Halsted to Colchester, and so into the sea. The Roding which rises northwards, near Dunmow, runs into the Thames near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARKING">Barking</a>. All these rivers abound in most sorts of fish. In the year 1801, the total <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants in the county of Essex amounted to 226,437 persons. Of these 111,356 are males, and 115,081 are females. They are divided into 46,784 families, occupying 38,371 houses. The number employed in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> is 65,174; and in trade manufactures, &c., 25,283.

ESTATE

Pages 359-359

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> that a person has in lands, tenements, or other effects; comprehending the whole in which a person hath any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the same. Estates are either real or personal; otherwise distinguished into FREEHOLDS, which descend to heirs; or CHATTELS, that go to executors or administrators. A fec-simple is the amplest estate our law admits of. See Fee. Estates are obtained several ways; as, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from a father to a son; by conveyance or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> from one person to another; by gift or purchase; or by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> or will. See DESCENT, SUCCESSION, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">TENURE</a>, &c.

ESTATES

Pages 359-359

in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used either to denote the dominions of some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the general classes into which the people are divided. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the estates are the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, lords, and commons; or rather the lords and commons, who meet the king in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, for reforming abuses, and enacting good and wholesome laws.

ESTHER

Pages 359-359

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; containing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of a Jewish virgin, dwelling with her uncle Mordecai at Shushan, in the reign of Ahasuerus, one of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of this maid raised her to the throne of Persia; whereby she had an opportunity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her countrymen, whose destruction was plotted by Haman, a favourite of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The learned are not agreed who this Ahasuerus was. Archbishop Usher supposes him to be <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Hyttaipes, and Artyllona to be Esther. Scaliger makes him the same with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Hanethris to be Esther. Josephus, on the contrary, positively affirms, that the Ahasuerus of the scriptures, is the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Longimanus of profane story; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, throughout the whole book of Esther, translate Ahasuerus by Artaxerxes. Most people subscribe to this last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; and indeed the extraordinary kindness showed by Artaxerxes to the Jews, can scarcely be accounted for otherwise than by supposing that they had so powerful an advocate as Esther to solicit for them.

ESTOILE'E

Pages 359-359
or CROSS ESTOILLE'E, in Heraldry, a star with only four long rays in form of a cross; and, accordingly, broad in the centre, and terminating in sharp points.

ESTONIA

Pages 359-360

is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Russian empire, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>. It is bounded on the east by the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, on the west by Ingrin, and on the south by Lettonia. It is divided into six districts: 1. Harrien; 2. Wireland; 3. Alentakin; 4. Wich; 5. Jerven; and, 6. Odepoa. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are, Revel, Weifenberg, Borchholm, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, Nyfot, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HABSAL">Habsal</a>, Derpt, St Elin, Pernau, and Roderwick. In former times the inhabitants of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> carried on a good trade in corn, which was dried in stoves; but wars have much depopulated the country, inasmuch that not a fourth part of it is inhabited, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of gentlemen's seats <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in ruins.

ESTOPPEL

Pages 360-360

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, an impediment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, arising from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>; against which a man is forbidden, by law, to speak, though it be to say the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>.

ESTOVERS

Pages 360-360

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used, by Bracton, for that sufficiency which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, committed for felony, is to have out of his lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> goods for himself and his family during imprisonment. In Stat. 6 Edw. I. it is used for an allowance in meat or clothes. In some manors, the tenants have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> of estovers; that is, necessary botes or allowances out of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s wood: in which last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, estover comprehends <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-bote, hay-bote, and plow-bote; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a man have in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> these general words, de ratione habendi estoverio in bofcis, &c. he may thereby claim all three. Estovers is also used for alimony, which, if the husband refuses to pay, there is, besides the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>, a writ at common law, de effoveris habendis, in order to recover it.

ESTRAY

Pages 360-360
or STRAY, signifies any tame beast, as sheep, oxen, swine, and horses, or swans, found within a lordship, and not owned by any man; in which case being cried, according to law, in the church, and two market towns adjoining, if it be not claimed by the owner within a year and a day, it becomes the lord's of the field where found. If the owner claims it within the year and day, he must pay the charges of finding, keeping, and proclaiming them; and he may seize it, without telling the marks or proving his property, which may be done at the trial if contested. If the beast stray within the year to another lordship, the first lord cannot retake it. An estray must be fed and kept, uninjured, and without labour, till it is reclaimed or the limited time expires.

ESTREAT

Pages 360-360

EXTRACTUM, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used for the true copy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> duplicate of some original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, especially of amerements or penalties let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the rolls of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to be levied by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> or other officer, on every offender.

ESTREMADURA

Pages 360-360

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, near the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tajo, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEIRA">Beira</a>, on the east and south by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>, and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. It is about 88 miles in length, and 45 in breadth. This province is divided into six comarcas, viz. Litria, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, Tomar, Santarem, and Alanquar, to the north of the Tagus; and that of Setubal, to the south of this river. These are likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. Estremadura is equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not preferable, to any other province in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> or Portugal. The district of Santarem produces such plenty of corn, and feeds so many flocks of sheep, that it may enter into competition with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and the wines are all excellent; and it was here that the sweet oranges brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> were first planted, and of which there are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities transported to foreign parts, with the wines and other fruits. The fields are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> almost all the year, from which the bees collect large quantities of fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. The olive-tree are numerous, from which they have excellent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abound with good fish, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> have quarries of several kinds.

ETCHING

Pages 360-363

a method of engraving on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> strokes, instead of being cut with a tool or graver, are eaten in with aquafortis. See Engraving. Etching is of a later <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, though not very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, than engraving with the tool; of which it was at first only an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, that was practised by painters and other artists, who could much sooner form their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to, and attain a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of, working in this way, than with the graver. But being then nevertheless considered as a counterfeit kind of engraving, and therefore inferior to the other, it was cultivated in a very confined manner; the closeness of the resemblance of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to that performed by the tool, being made the test of its merit, and consequently the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of aim in those who pursued it. This servile confinement of the art of etching to the imitation of the original kind of engraving, was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cause of retarding its advancement towards perfection, as many of the most able masters cramped their talents with the observance of it: this may be seen in the instances of Sadelers, Swanenberg, Villamena, and particularly Le Boffe; who, in his treatise on engraving, has laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a principle, that the perfection of this kind consists in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> similitude of the work with that done by the tool. This absurd prepossession has been since worn out: and the method of working with aquafortis has been so far improved, that instead of being now deemed a spurious kind of engraving, it evidently appears, in many modern works, the foundation of an excellence that could never have been produced without it: since, though the neatness and uniformity of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a>, which attend the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the tool, is more advantageous with respect to portraits; yet the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and facility of the other manner give a much greater opportunity to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the force of genius and fancy in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-engraving; where the effect of the whole, and not the minute exactness in finishing all the parts, constitutes the principal value. There are two methods practised of engraving in this way; the one with a hard <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> or ground, the other with a soft. The first was formerly much used, being better accommodated to the intention of imitating the engraving with the tool; as the firmness of the body of the varnish gave more opportunity of retouching the lines, Etching lines, or enlarging them with the oval-pointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, called by the French échoppe, as was practised by Le Bossé and others for that purpose. The latter has now almost wholly superseded the use of the other, by the free manner of working it admits of; which affords a power of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> incompatible with the greater inflexibility of the hard varnish, that confines the lines and hatches to such a regularity and sameness, as gives a stiffness of manner and coldness of effect to the work. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of the use of the tool and aquafortis, which are now both employed in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, has, however, given that perfection to engraving which it possesses at present. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and spirit of the outline that the method of working with aquafortis affords, and the variety of shades which the different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> produce in this way, as well as other means of expressing the peculiar appearance and character of particular subjects, furnish what was defective in the sole use of the tool; while, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the exactness and regularity of the lines, which are required for finishing many kinds of designs, are supplied by the graver; and by a judicious application of both, that complete finishing is obtained, which either of them alone must necessarily want. The manner by which this art is performed, is the covering the surface of the plate with a proper varnish or ground, as it is called, which is capable of resisting aquafortis; and then scoring or scratching away, by instruments resembling needles, the parts of this varnish or ground, in the places where the strokes or hatches of the engraving are intended to be; then, the plate being covered with aquafortis, the parts that are laid naked and exposed by removing the ground or varnish, are corroded or eaten away by it; while the rest, being secured and defended, remain untouched. There are two methods of etching, as has been already observed; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of which from each other consists, as well in the difference of the varnish or ground, as in that of the aquafortis, adapted to each kind; but the general methods of performing them are alike in both. These varnishes or grounds are distinguished by the names of hard and soft: for in their consistence, or the resistance they give to the needles, lies their essential <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from each other. The hard varnish, it is with good reason conjectured, was not the first in use; but soon took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the other; and was, for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the most received in practice, on account of its admitting the work to be made more like that of the graver; the soft has, however, since, in its turn, prevailed to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of it in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, except in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of particular subjects; but not so entirely as to take away the expediency of showing how it is performed.
