The manner of etching with the soft varnish is now, however, one of the most important objects of the art of engraving; and it is at present in universal use, sometimes alone, but more frequently intermixed with the work of the tool, and in some cases with great advantage, even where the whole is intended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for being performed by the graver. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">Preparation</a> of the soft varnish; according to Mr Lawrence, an eminent English engraver at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. "Take of virgin wax and asphaltum, each two ounces; of black pitch and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> pitch, each half an ounce. Melt the wax and pitch in a new earthen-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> glazed pot; and add to them by degrees, the asphaltum finely powdered. Let the whole boil till such time as that, taking a drop upon a plate, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> when it is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> two or three times betwixt the fingers. The varnish being then enough boiled, must be taken off the fire; and letting it cool a little, must be poured into warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that it may work the more easily with the hands, so as to be formed into balls; which must be rolled up, and put into a piece of taffety for use." It must be observed, first, that the fire be not too violent, for fear of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the ingredients; a slight simmering will be sufficient; secondly, that while the asphaltum is putting in, and even after it is mixed with them, the ingredients should be stirred continually with the spatula; and thirdly, that the water, into which this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is thrown, should be nearly of the same degree of warmth with it, to prevent a kind of cracking that happens when the water is too cold. The varnish ought always to be harder in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> than in winter; and it will become so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be suffered to boil longer, or if a greater proportion of the asphaltum or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> resin be used. The experiment above mentioned, of the drop suffered to cool, will determine the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> or softness that may be suitable to the season when it is used. Preparation of the hard varnish used by Callot, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> varnish. Take four ounces of fat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> very clear, and made of good linseed oil, like that used by painters: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> it in a clean pot of glazed earthen-ware, and afterwards put to it four ounces of mastic well powdered; and stir the mixture briskly till the whole be well melted; then pass the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> through a piece of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> into a glass bottle with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> neck, that can be stopped very securely; and keep it for the use that will be below explained. Method of applying the soft varnish to the plate, and of blackening it. The plate being well polished and burnished, as also cleansed from all greasiness by chalk or Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, fix a hand-vice on the edge of the plate where no work is intended to be, to serve as a handle for managing it when warm; then put it upon a chafing-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a>, in which there is a moderate fire; observing to hold it so that it may melt; then cover the whole plate equally with a thin coat of the varnish; and while the plate is warm, and the varnish upon it in a fluid state, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the varnish gently with a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> or dauber made of cotton tied up in taffety; which operation smooths and distributes the varnish equally over the plate. When the plate is thus uniformly and thinly covered with the varnish, it must be blackened by a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a>, or of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> which affords a copious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; sometimes two, or even four, such candles are used together for the sake of dispatch, that the varnish may not grow cold; which if it does during the operation, the plate must then be heated again, that it may be in a melted state when that operation is performed; but great care must be taken not to burn it; which, when it happens, may be easily perceived by the varnish appearing burnt and losing its gloss. The following expedient is made use of for the more commodiously blackening... blackening the varnish, being particularly necessary where the plates are large: Fix a strong hook in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the room, through which pass four pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> of equal length, at the end of which are fixed four <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rings of about four inches diameter, for supporting the corners of the plate. The plate being thus suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, with the varnished side downwards, may be blackened with great convenience; but this is not, however, absolutely requisite, except in the case of large plates that could not, without difficulty, be held up, unless this or some other such contrivance were made use of. It is proper to be very cautious in keeping the flambeau or candle at a due distance from the plate, lest the wick touch the varnish, which would both foully and mark it. If it appear that the smoke has not penetrated the varnish, the plate must be again placed for some little time over the chafing-dish; and it will be found, that, in proportion as the plate grows hot, the varnish will melt and incorporate with the black which lay above it, in such a manner that the whole will be equally pervaded by it. Above all things, the greatest caution should be used in this operation, to keep all the time a moderate fire; and to move frequently the plate, and change the place of all the parts of it, that the varnish may be alike melted everywhere, and kept from burning. Care must also be taken, that during this time, and even till the varnish be entirely cold, no filth, sparks, or dust, fly on it; for they would then stick fast, and spoil the work. Method of applying the hard varnish. This is precisely the same as for the soft; being spread equally over the warm plate with the taffety-ball, and smoked in the same manner: only after it is smoked, it must be baked, or dried over a gentle fire of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, till the smoke from the varnish begins to decrease; taking care not to overheat the plate, which would both soften it and burn the varnish. The plate being thus prepared, and an exact <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of the outlines of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> made upon thin <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, the other side of the paper must be well rubbed with chalk or Spanish whitening, or, which is better, with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> chalk scraped to a powder; and the loose chalk is cleared off with a linen rag: then the stained side of the paper is laid upon the varnish, fixing the corners to the plate with wax or wafers, to prevent its shifting; and with a blunted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> or pointer the drawing is slightly traced, and communicates to the varnish an exact outline of the design to be etched. A variety of pointers is necessary for the work. Those used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> large strokes ought to be very blunt, exceeding round, and well polished at the point; the sole of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> answers very well for polishing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. The finest ought to be as sharp as a needle. If any scratches or false strokes happen in the working, they are to be stopped up with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipped in Venetian varnish, mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> black, by which means these places will be defended from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the aquafortis. The next operation is that of eating or corroding the plate with aquafortis; in order to which, a border of soft wax (being a composition of bees wax melted and tempered with a little <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> turpentine and tal- brothers that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> should be decided by single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. They both fell in an engagement conducted with the most inveterate fury on either side; and it is even said that the affections of these two brothers, who had been so inimical one to the other, separated themselves on the burning pile, as if sensible of resentment, and hostile to reconciliation.

ETERNITY

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who had neither <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> nor altars. They represented it under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a woman, who held the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> in the other: her symbols were a phoenix, globe, and elephant.

ETESIAC

Pages 363-363
or Etesian winds, are such as blow at stated times of the year, from what partsoever of the compass they come. They are so called from the Greek word ἑτερος, "year," being yearly or anniverary winds, such as our seamen call monsoons and trade-winds, which in some parts of the world continue constantly blowing for certain stated seasons of the year. Thus, the north winds, which, during the dog-days, constantly blow upon the coasts of Egypt, and hinder all ships from sailing out of Alexandria for that season, are called etesiac in Caesar's Commentaries. In other authors, the west and east winds are called etesiac, when they continue blowing for certain seasons of the year. Cellarius endeavours to prove that those winds are properly etesiac which blow from that part of the horizon which is between the north and west about the time of the solstice. In ancient writers, they are represented as of a very mild and gentle nature; and were called by mariners somnificogeti and delicati, from their sleeping or ceasing to blow in the night.

ETFU

Pages 363-363

a town of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, celebrated on account of the sublime temple of Apollinopolis, which, Denon observes,* is "the most beautiful of all Egypt, and, next to those of Thebes, the largest." Being built (he adds) at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when the arts and sciences had acquired all their splendour, the workmanship of every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is equally beautiful, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> are admirably executed, the figures more varied, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of a higher order than in the Theban edifices, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of which must be referred to an earlier <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. My first care was to take a general <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the building. "Nothing can be more simply beautiful than these outlines; nothing more picturesque than the effect produced in the elevation, by the various dimensions belonging to each member of the harmonious whole. This superb edifice is seated on a rising ground, so as to overlook not only its immediate vicinity, but the whole valley; and at the foot of this greater temple, but on a considerably lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, is a smaller one, at present almost buried. The only part still visible is in a hollow surrounded with rubbish, where may be seen a little portico of two columns, and as many pilasters, a peristyle, and the sanctuary of the temple inclosed within a pilastered gallery. A single <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, with its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> rising from the ruins, to the height of forty feet above the portico, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of a wall 100 feet beyond, shew that there formerly existed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the temple. It is remarkable of this monument, notwithstanding the skill displayed in its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, that the gates are not exactly in the middle of the sides. It seems to have been dedicated to the evil genius, for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of Typhon is seen in relief on the four sides of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PLINTH">plinth</a>, which surmounts each of the capitals. The whole frieze, and all the paintings within, appear descriptive of Isis defending herself against the attacks of this monster."

ETHERIDGE

Pages 363-363

Sir George, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and comic genius in the reigns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and James II., descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, and born in 1636. He travelled in his youth; and, not being able to confine himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, devoted himself to the gayer accomplishments. His first dramatic performance, the Comical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">Revenge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> in a Tub, appeared in 1664, and introduced him to the leading wits of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: in 1668, he produced a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> called She would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she could; and, in 1676, he published his last comedy, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">Mode</a>, or Sir Fopling Flutter; which is perhaps the most elegant comedy, and contains more of the real manners of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> than any one the English stage was ever adorned with. This piece he dedicated to the beautiful duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, in whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he then was; and who had so high a regard for him, that when, on the accession of James II. she came to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, she procured his being sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> first to Hamburgh, and afterwards to Ratibon, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till after his majesty quitted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Our author being addicted to certain gay extravagances, had greatly impaired his fortune; to repair which, he paid his addresses to a rich widow; but she, being an ambitious woman, had determined not to condescend to a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with any man who could not bestow a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> upon her; on which account he was obliged to purchase a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. None of the writers have exactly fixed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of Sir George's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, though all seem to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the Revolution. Some say, that on this event he followed his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James into France, and died there; but the authors of the Biographia Britannica mention a report, that he came to an untimely death by an unlucky accident at Ratibon; for that after having treated some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with a liberal entertainment at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> there, where he had taken his glass too freely, and being, through his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> complaisance, too forward in waiting on his guests at their departure, flushed as he was, he tumbled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> stairs and broke his neck, and so fell a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to mirth and jollity. As to Sir George's literary character, he certainly was born a poet, and seems to have been possessed of a genius whose vivacity needed no cultivation: for we have no proofs of his having been a scholar. His works, however, have not escaped censure on account of that licentiousness which in general runs through them, which renders them dangerous to young unguarded minds; and the more so, for the lively and genuine wit with which it is gilded over, and which has therefore justly banished them from the purity of the present stage.

ETHICS

Pages 363-364

the doctrine of manners, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the science of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. The word is formed from ἡρός, ἡρών, "mores," "manners;" because it is the object of ethics to investigate the manners or conduct of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. See MORAL Philosophy.

ETHMOIDES

Pages 364-364

in Anatomy, a bone situated in the middle of the basis of the forehead <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> os frontis, and at the top of the root of the nose, filling almost the whole cavity of the nostrils. It has its name from εὐεστής, cribrum, "sieve," and ἀδεια, "form," because all spongy and porous. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ETHNARCHA

Pages 364-364

ETHNARCH, (formed of ἐθνος, "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>," and ἄρχω, "command"), a governor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ruler of a nation. There are some medals of Herod I. surnamed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, on one side whereof is found Ἑρῴδου, and on the other Ἐθνάρχου, q. d. Herod the Ethnarch. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Philippi, we read that Antony, passing over into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, constituted Herod and Phasael his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> tetrarchs, and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> committed to them the administration of the affairs of Judea, (Jof. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">Ant</a>. lib. xiv. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 23.) Herod therefore had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> before ever the Parthians entered Syria, or before Antigonus's invasion, which did not happen till six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years after Herod was commander in Galilee, (Jof. lib. xiv. cap. 24, 25.) Consequently, Herod was then truly ethnarch, for he can be no otherwise denominated; so that it must have been in that space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the medals were struck, which only give him this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: which medals are a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of what we read in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the government which that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was intrusted with before he was raised to the royalty. Josephus gives Herod the appellation of tetrarch in lieu of that of ethnarch; but the two terms come so near to each other, that it is easy to confound them together. Though Herod the Great left by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> to Archelaus all Judea, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, and Idumea, yet Josephus tells us he was then only called ethnarch.

ETHNOPHRONES

Pages 364-364

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the seventh century, who made a profession of Christianity, but joined thereto all the ceremonies and follies of Paganism, as judicial astrology, fortresses, auguries, and other divinations.

ETIQUETTE

Pages 364-364

a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, primarily denoting a ticket <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> affixed to a bag or bundle of papers expressing its contents. It is also used, when applied to the Spanish and some other courts, to signify a particular account of what is to be done daily in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ceremonies relating to it. It likewise denotes those forms that regulate the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a> of conduct towards persons of various ranks and stations.

ETMULLER

Pages 364-364

MICHAEL, a most eminent physician, born at Leipzig in 1646. After having travelled through the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, he became professor of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, and anatomy, at Leipzig, where he died in 1683. He was a very voluminous writer, his works making no less than 5 vols folio, as printed at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in 1728. His son Michael Ernest Etmuller was also an ingenious physician, who published several pieces, and died in 1732.

ETOLIA

Pages 364-365

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, comprehending all that tract now called the Deppotat, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Little Greece. It was parted on the east by the river Evrenus, now the Fidari, from the Locrenses Ozoile; on the west, from Acarnania by the Achelous; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, it bordered on the country of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Epirus; and, on the south, extended to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Corinth. The Etolians were a restless and turbulent people; seldom at peace among themselves, and ever at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with their neighbours; utter strangers to all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of friendship or principles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; ready to betray their friends upon the least prospect of reaping any advantage from their treachery: in short, they were looked upon by the other states of Greece no otherwise than as outlaws and public robbers. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, they were bold and enterprising in war; inured to labour and hardships; undaunted in the greatest dangers; jealous defenders of their liberties, for which they were, on all occasions, willing to venture their lives, and sacrifice all that was most dear to them. They distinguished themselves above all the other nations of Greece, in opposing the ambitious designs of the Macedonian princes; who, after having reduced most of the other states, were forced to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them a peace upon very honorable terms. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the Eolian republic was copied from that of the Achaeans, and with a view to form, as it were, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>; for the Eolians bore an irreconcilable hatred to the Achaeans, and had conceived no small jealousy at the growing power of that state. The Cleomenic war, and that of the allies, called the social war, were kindled by the Eolians in the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, with no other view but to humble their antagonists the Achaeans. In the latter, they held out, with the assistance only of the Eleans and Lacedemonians, for the space of three years, against the united forces of Achaia and Macedon; but were obliged at last to purchase a peace, by yielding up to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> all Acarnania. As they parted with this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> much against their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, they watched all opportunities of wresting it again out of the Macedonian's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; for which reason they entered into an alliance with Rome against him, and proved of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in their war with him: but growing insolent upon account of their services, they made war upon the Romans themselves. By that warlike <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> they were overcome, and granted a peace on the following severe terms: 1. The majesty of the Roman people shall be revered in all Etolia. 2. Eolia shall not suffer the armies of such as are at war with Rome to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through her territories, and the enemies of Rome shall be likewise the enemies of Eolia. 3. She shall, in the space of 100 days, put into the hands of the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORCYRA">Corcyra</a> all the prisoners and deserters she has, whether of the Romans or their allies, except such as have been taken twice, or during her alliance with Rome. 4. The Eolians shall pay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in ready <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, to the Roman general in Eolia, 200 Euboic talents, of the same value as the Athenian talents, and engage to pay 50 talents more within the five years following. 5. They shall put into the hands of the con- ful 40 such hostages as he shall choose; none of whom shall be under 12, or above 40 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; the praetor, the general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and such as have been already hostages at Rome, are excepted out of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. 6. Etolia shall renounce all pretensions to the cities and territories which the Romans have conquered, though those cities and territories had formerly belonged to the Eolians. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Oenipolis, and its district, shall be subject to the Acaeanians. After the conquest of Macedon by Paulus Æmilius, they were reduced to a much worse condition; for not only those among them, who had openly declared for Perseus, but such as were only suspected to have favoured him in their hearts, were sent to Rome, in order to clear themselves before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. There they were detained, and never afterwards suffered to return into their native country. Five hundred and fifty of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men of the nation were barbarously assassinated by the partizans of Rome, for no other crime but that of being suspected to wish well to Perseus. The Eolians appeared before Paulus Æmilius in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> habits, and made loud complaints of such inhuman treatment; but could obtain no redress: nay, ten commissioners, who had been sent by the senate to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the affairs of Greece, enacted a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, declaring, that those who were killed had suffered justly, since it appeared to them that they had favoured the Macedonian party. From this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> those only were raised to the chief honours and employments in the Eolian republic who were known to prefer the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Rome to that of their country; and as these alone were countenanced at Rome, all the magistrates of Eolia were the creatures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> tools of the Roman senate. In this state of servile subjection they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the destruction of Corinth, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the Achaean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>; when Eolia, with the other free states of Greece, was reduced to a Roman province, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the province of Achaea. Nevertheless, each state and city was governed by its own laws, under the superintendence of the praetor whom Rome sent annually into Achaea. The whole nation paid a certain tribute, and the rich were forbidden to possess lands anywhere but in their own country. In this state, with little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, Eolia continued under the emperors, till the reign of Constantine the Great, who, in his new partition of the provinces of the empire, divided the western parts of Greece from the rest, calling them New Epirus, and subjecting the whole country to the praefectus praetorio for Illyricum. Under the successors of Constantine, Greece was parcelled out into several principalities, especially after the taking of Constantinople by the Western princes. At that time, Theodore Angelus, a noble Grecian, of the imperial family, seized on Eolia and Epirus. The former he left to Michael his son; who maintained it against Michael Paleologus, the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Greeks, after the expulsion of the Latins. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, the last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of this family, dying in 1430 without lawful issue, bequeathed Eolia to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s son, named also Charles; and Acarnania to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sons, Memnon, Turnus, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. But, great disputes arising about this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, Amurath II. after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Thessalonica, laid hold of so favourable an opportunity, and drove them all out in 1432. The Ma-

ETON

Pages 365-366

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, across which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> leading to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>. Eton has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> celebrated for its school and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, which were founded by Henry VI.; and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s college in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> admits none into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its fellows, who have not been brought up at Eton. It lies west from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, at the distance of about 20 miles. The scholars of Eton school have a festival which has been celebrated from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial, called the Montem, the observance of which was at first biennial, but is now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIENNIAL">triennial</a>, on the Whit Tuesday in every third year. It commences by a number of the older boys taking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> on the bridges, and guarding every other avenue around Windsor and Eton, as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> begins to dawn. They are generally selected on account of their fine figures and superior <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. Their dresses are all fantastic, composed of silks, satins, &c., some of them very richly embroidered, and chiefly in the appearance of running footmen, having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and denominated falt-bearers, who demand falt of every passenger they meet, by which they <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> a contribution, and peremptorily insist on receiving it. The contribution being given, which consists of whatever the person pleases to bestow, a printed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> is delivered, containing their motto, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the year; and this being produced to any other falt-bearer, exempts the passenger from the payment of any farther contributions during that day. The motto is, "Pro more et monte. Vivant rex et <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a>." They continue levying contributions in this manner from the dawn of day till about three o'clock in the afternoon, at which time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> closes. It commences at noon, and consists of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s and other bands of music;—several standards carried by different students;—all the boys of Eton, two and two, dressed in the uniform of officers; those belonging to the king's foundation, wear blue, the rest scarlet uniform, swords, &c.—the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> standard bearer;—the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> head boy of Eton school;—the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> boy;—his majesty, attended by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family on horseback, with their suite;—the queen and princesses in coaches, attended by their suite;—band of music, followed by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> concourse of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, and on horseback. The procession begins in the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at Eton proceeding through Eton to Slough, and round to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">Salt</a>-hill, where the whole of the boys <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> in review before the king and queen, and ascend the montem, where an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> is delivered, and the grand standard is displayed with much activity and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> by the standard-bear- er, who is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> selected from among the elder boys. Two extraordinary salt-bearers are chosen to wait upon their majesties, dressed in fanciful habits, and decorated in the most superb manner, carrying an embroidered bag, not only for the purpose of receiving what is denominated the royal salt, but also what may be collected by the other salt-bearers in different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. The donation of the king is 50 guineas, the queen's is the same sum; that of the prince of Wales is 30, and that of the other princes and princesses is 20 guineas each. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> being over, the royal family return to Windsor. A tumultuous entertainment is provided for the boys at the tavern at Salt-hill, and the beautiful gardens are laid out for ladies and gentlemen to take refreshments, where bands of music are constantly performing. At six o'clock in the evening, the boys return in the same order of procession as in the morning (but without the royal family), and after marching round the great square, are dismissed. After this the captain pays his respects to the royal family at the queen's lodge, Windsor, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to his departure for King's college, Cambridge; to defray the expenses of which, he is presented with the produce of the montem, which in the year 1796 amounted to more than 1000 guineas. This joyful day is terminated by a brilliant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and fashion; a promenade on the terrace of Windsor; bands of music performing, &c.; and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> is rendered still more interesting and delightful by the humble, affable deportment of the royal family, who readily mingle with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and walk on the terrace till it is almost dark. ETRURIA. See HETRURIA.

ETYMOLOGY

Pages 366-366

that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> which considers and explains the origin and derivation of words, in order to arrive at their first and primary signification, whence Quintilian calls it originatio.—The word is formed of the Greek ἀρχή, ἀρχεῖν, "true," and ἀρχαίος, ἀρχαῖος, "I speak;" whence ἀρχαῖος, ἀρχαῖος, &c., and thence Cicero calls the etymology notatio and veriloquium; though Quintilian chooses rather to call it originatio. A judicious inquiry into etymologies is thought by some of considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; because nations, who value themselves upon their antiquity, have always looked on the antiquity of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> as one of the best titles they could plead; and the etymologist, by seeking the true and original reason of the notions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> fixed to each word and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, may often furnish an argument of antiquity, from the traces remaining thereof, compared with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> uses. Add, that etymologies are necessary for the thorough understanding of a language. For, to explain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> precisely, there seems a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for recurring to its first imposition, in order to speak justly and satisfactorily thereof. The force and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of a word is generally better conceived when a person knows its origin and etymology. It is objected, however, that the art is arbitrary, and built altogether on conjectures and appearances; and the etymologists are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with deriving their words from where they please. And indeed it is no easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to go back into the ancient British and Gaulish ages, and to follow, as it were, by the track, the various imperceptible alterations a language has undergone from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> to age; and as those alterations have sometimes been merely owing to caprice, it is easy to take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> imagination <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conjecture for a regular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>: so that it is no wonder the public should be prejudiced against a science which seems to stand on so precarious a footing. It must certainly be owned, that etymologies are frequently so far fetched, that one can scarcely see any resemblance or correspondence therein. Quintilian has shown, that the ancient etymologists, notwithstanding all their learning, fell into very ridiculous derivations. The etymologies of our English words have been derived from the Saxon, Welch, Walloon, Danish, Latin, Greek, &c. In the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> the etymologies of terms are generally noted, where their obviousness does not render it unnecessary, or their dubiety or unimportance useless.

EUBAGES

Pages 367-367

an order of priests <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> philosophers among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Celts or Gauls: some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the enages to be the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> and saronides of Diodorus; and others, that they were the same with what Strabo calls EVATES.

EUBOEA

Pages 367-367

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, stretching out between <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> and Thessaly, opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>; from which it is separated by a narrow strait called Eurytus. This island, never exceeding 40, nor ever falling short of two miles in breadth, is in length 150 miles, and in compass 365, according to Pliny. Now NEROPONT, from its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town, which was anciently called Chalcis.

EUCHARIST

Pages 367-367

the sacrament of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, properly signifies giving thanks.—The word in its original Greek, Eucharistia, literally imports thanksgiving; being formed of ευ, bene, "well," and χαρις, gratia, "thanks." This sacrament was instituted by Christ himself; and the participation of it is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. As to the manner of celebrating the eucharist among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, after the customary oblations were made, the deacon brought <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and presbyters, standing round the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, to wash their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; according to that of the psalmist, "I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> wash my hands in innocency, and so will I compass thy altar, O Lord." Then the deacon cried out aloud, "Mutually embrace and kiss each other;" which being done, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> prayed for the uni- versal peace and welfare of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, for the tranquillity and repose of the world, for the prosperity of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, for wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and for all ranks and degrees of men. After this followed mutual saluta- tions of the minister and people; and then the bishop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> having sanctified the elements by a solemn benediction, he brake the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and delivered it to the deacon, who distributed it to the communicants, and after that the cup. Their sacramental wine was usually diluted or mixed with water. During the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a>- ministration, they sang hymns and psalms; and having concluded with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and thanksgiving, the people saluted each other with a kiss of peace, and so the as- sembly broke up.

EUCHITES

Pages 367-367
or EUCHITAE, a sect of ancient her- etics, who were first formed into a religious body to- wards the end of the fourth century, though their doc- trine and discipline subsisted in Syria, Egypt, and other eastern countries, before the birth of Christ; they were thus called because they prayed without ceasing, imagining that prayer alone was sufficient to save them. Their great foundation were those words of St Paul, (Thessalonians, v. 17.), Pray without ceasing. The word is formed of the Greek, ευχη, prayer, whence ευχαι, the same with the Latin, precatorer, "prayers." They were also called Enthufasts and Melissians; a term of Hebrew origin, denoting the same as Euchites. The Euchites were a sort of mystics, who imagined, according to the oriental notion, that two souls resided in man, the one good and the other evil; and who were zealous in expelling the evil soul or demon, and hastening the return of the good spirit of God, by contemplation, prayer, and singing of hymns. They also embraced the opinions nearly resembling the Ma- nichean doctrine, and which they derived from the ten- ets of the oriental philosophy. The same denomina- tion was used in the 12th century, to denote certain fanatics who infested the Greek and eastern churches, and who were charged with believing a double Trinity, rejecting wedlock, abstaining from flesh, treating with contempt the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's supper, and the various branches of external worship, and placing the essence of religion solely in external prayer, and maintaining the efficacy of perpetual sup- plications to the supreme Being for expelling an evil being or genius, which dwelt in the breast of every mortal. This sect is said to have been founded by a person called Lucoperus, whose chief disciple was named Tycheius. By degrees it became a general and invidious appellation for persons of eminent piety and zeal for genuine Christianity, who opposed the vicious prac- tices and insolent tyranny of the priesthood; much in the same manner as the Latins comprehended all the adversaries of the Roman pontiff under the general terms of WALDENSES and ALBIGENSES. St Cyril of Alexandria, in one of his letters, takes occasion to censure several monks in Egypt, who, un- der pretence of resigning themselves wholly to prayer, led a lazy, scandalous life. A censure likewise appli- cable to monasteries in general.

EUGENE

Pages 369-369

Francis, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Savoy, descended from Carignan, one of the three branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Savoy, and son of Eugene Maurice, general of the Swiss and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a>, governor of Champagne, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a>, was born in 1663. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. to whom he became afterwards so formidable an enemy, thought him so unpromising a youth, that he refused him preferment both in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and the state, thinking him too much addicted to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to be useful in either. Prince Eugene, in disgust, quitted France; and, retiring to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, devoted himself to the Imperial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and the Turks afforded the first opportunity of exerting his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> talents; and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> proved a new step in his advancement to the highest offices in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. He gave the Turks a memorable defeat at Zenta; commanded the German forces in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he foiled Marshal Villeroi in every engagement, and at length took him prisoner. Our limits do not allow a detail of his campaigns; but Prince Eugene distinguished himself greatly, when the emperor and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> united against the exorbitant power of Louis XIV. He died at Vienna in the year 1736; and was remarkable for his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and liberality, as for his abilities in the field and the cabinet.

EUGENIA

Pages 369-369

the YAMBOO; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the icofandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 19th order, Hesperideae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUHOLOGIUM

Pages 367-369

Ευχολογιον, a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, sig- nifying literally a discourse on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. The word is form- ed of ευχη, prayer, and λογος, discourse. The Euchologium is properly the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>, wherein are prescribed the order and manner of every thing relating to the order and administration of their ceremonies, sacraments, ordinations, &c. F. Goar has given us an edition of the Greek Euchologium in Greek and Latin, with notes, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. Euclid of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and logician, flourished about 400 B.C. The Athenians having prohibited the Megareans from entering their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> on pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, this philosopher disguised himself in women's clothes to attend the lectures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. After the death of Socrates, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and other philosophers went to Euclid at Megara, to shelter themselves from the tyrants who governed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. Euclid admitted but one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> good; which he sometimes called God, sometimes Spirit, and sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. Euclid of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, the celebrated mathematician, flourished in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Lagus, about 277 B.C. He reduced all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> principles of pure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, which had been delivered <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THALES">Thales</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, Eudoxus, and other mathematicians before him, into regularity and order, and added many others of his own discovering; on which account he is said to be the first who reduced <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> into the form of a science. He likewise applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of mixed mathematics, and especially to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, in which he also excelled. The most celebrated of his works is his Elements of Geometry, of which there have been a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of editions in all languages; and a fine edition of all his works was printed in 1703, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Gregory, Savilian professor of astronomy at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Eucrasy, (of εὖ, well, and κράσις, temperature), in Medicine, an agreeable well-proportioned mixture of qualities, whereby a body is said to be in good order, and disposed for a good state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. Eudiometer, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for ascertaining the purity of the atmospherical <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> or vital air contained in it, chiefly by means of its diminution, or the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of it by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> certain substances to its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Several kinds of eudiometers have been invented. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Eudosia, (Athena, before her conversion to Christianity), a celebrated lady, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Leonitus, a philosopher of Athens; who gave her such a learned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, that at his death, he left her only a small legacy, saying she was capable to make her own fortune; but pleading at Athens without success against her two brothers, for a share in her father's estate, she carried her cause personally by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to Constantinople; recommended herself to Pulcheria, the sister of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius the younger; embraced Christianity, was baptized by the name of Endofia, and soon after married to the emperor. Their union lasted a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> at last taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, on account of the emperor's jealousy, excited by Chrysapius the eunuch, she retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, where she spent many years in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and adorning churches and in relieving the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Dupin says, that she did not return thence till after the emperor's death; but Cave tells us, that she was reconciled to him, returned to Constantinople, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with him till his death; after which she went again to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, where she spent the remainder of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in pious works. She died in the year 460, according to Dupin; or 459, according to Cave: the latter observes, that on her deathbed she took a solemn oath, by which she declared herself entirely free from any stains of unchastity. She was the author of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> on the eight first books of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> in heroic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; and of a great number of poems, which are lost. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUDOXIANS">Eudoxians</a>, a party or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the fourth century, so denominated from their leader Eudoxius, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Antioch and Constantinople, a great defender of the Arian doctrine. The Eudoxians adhered to the errors of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> and Eumomians, maintaining, that the Son was created out of nothing; that he had a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> distinct and different from that of the Father, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a>. See Vigil. Eve, the mother of all mankind; who being deluded by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, occasioned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and all its dismal consequences. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>. Evelyn, John, a most learned and ingenious writer and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosopher, was born at Wotton in Surry, the seat of his father, in 1620. After making the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, he returned to England about the year 1651, and lived very retired at his rural retreat, Say's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; where his disgust at the violence and confusion of the times operated so far upon his studious disposition, that he actually proposed to Mr Boyle the establishing a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> for persons of the same turn of mind, where they might associate together without care or interruption. It was owing to Mr Evelyn's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to the place of his education, that Oxford became possessed of the famous Arundelian marbles; which he persuaded the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Henry Howard to bestow on that university. He was very affiduous in transmitting to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> whatever fell within the compass of his inquiries; and used humbly to style himself a pioneer in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. When the number of books he published is considered, the many he left behind him unfinished and unpublished, and the variety of subjects on which he employed his time, his industry and application are astonishing. "His life (says the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Mr Walpole) was a course of inquiry, study, curiosity, instruction, and benevolence. The works of the Creator, and the mimic labours of the creature, were all objects of his pursuit. He unfolded the perfections of the one, and afflicted the imperfections of the other. He adored from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>; was a courtier that flattered only by informing his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and by pointing out what was worthy for him to countenance; and was really the neighbour of the Gosfield, for there was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that might not have been the better for him. He was one of the first promoters of the Royal Society, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the ingenious and indigent, and peculiarly serviceable to the lettered world; for, besides his writings and discoveries, he obtained the Arundelian marbles for the university of Oxford, and the Arundelian library for the Royal Society: nor is it the least <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his praise, that he who proposed to Mr Boyle the erection of a philosophical college for retired and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> persons, had the honesty to write in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> life against Sir George Mackenzie's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Solitude. He knew that retirement in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> was industry and benefit to mankind; but in those of others, laziness and imutility." There are five small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s journey from Rome to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, drawn and etched by him; and among his published works are, 1. A Character of England; 2. The State of France; 3. An Essay on the the first book of Lucretius De rerum natura: 4. The French gardener; 5. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">Panegyric</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II.'s coronation; 6. Fumifugum, or the inconvenience of the air and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> dissipated; 7. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> and Art of Engraving on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a>; 8. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>; 9. Sylva, or a discourse of forest trees; and several others. This amiable gentleman died, full of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, in 1706. His son John Evelyn, born in 1654, distinguished himself by his elegant translations and poems; He was one of the commissioners of the revenue in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; but died early in life, in 1698.

EULER

Pages 370-372

LEONARD, professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, member of the imperial academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and fellow of the royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, as also correspondent member of the royal academy of sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, was born at Bafil, April 15, 1707, of reputable parents. The years of his infancy were passed in a rural retreat at the village of Richen, of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his father was minister.—Being sent to the university of Bafil, he attended regularly the different professors. As his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was prodigious, he performed his academical talks with uncommon rapidity; and all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he gained by this was consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, which soon became his favourite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The early progress he made in this science, only added new ardour to his application; and thus he obtained a distinguished place in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and esteem of Professor John Bernouilli, who was at that time one of the first mathematicians in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In 1723, M. Euler took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; and delivered on that occasion a Latin discourse, in which he drew a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of Newton and the Cartesian system, which was received with the greatest applause. He afterwards, at his father's desire, applied himself to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, and the oriental languages. Though these studies were foreign to his predominant propensity, his success was considerable even in this line: however, with his father's consent, he returned to geometry as his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to avail himself of the counsels and instructions of M. Bernouilli; he contracted an intimate friendship with his two sons Nicholas and Daniel; and it was in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these connexions that he became afterwards the principal ornament of the academy of Peterburgh. The project of erecting this academy, which had been formed by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, was executed by Catherine I.; and the two young Bernouillis being invited to Peterburgh in 1725, promised Euler, who was desirous of following them, that they would <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> their utmost endeavours to procure for him an advantageous settlement in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, by their advice, he applied himself with ardour to the study of physiology, to which he made a happy application of his mathematical knowledge; and he attended the medical lectures of the most eminent professors of Bafil. This study, however, did not wholly engross his time: it did not even relax the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of his vast and comprehensive mind in the cultivation of other branches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> science. For while he was keenly engaged in physiological researches, he composed A Dissertation on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Propagation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, and an answer to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> question concerning the making of ships; to which the academy of sciences adjudged the acephali, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, in the year 1727. From this latter discourse, and other circumstances, it appears that Euler had early embarked in the curious and important study of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, which he afterwards enriched with so many valuable discoveries. M. Euler's merit would have given him an easy admission to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> preferment, either in the magistracy or university of his native city, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> both civil and academical honours had not been there distributed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. The lot being against him in a certain promotion, he left his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, set out for Peterburgh, and was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> professor with his countrymen Messrs Hermann and Daniel Bernouilli in the university of that city. At his first setting out in his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, he enriched the academical collection with many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, which excited a noble emulation between him and the Bernouillis; and this emulation always continued, without either degenerating into a selfish jealousy, or producing the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in their friendship. It was at this time that he carried to new degrees of perfection the integral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a>, invented the calculation of sines, reduced analytical operations to a greater simplicity, and thus was enabled to throw new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on all the parts of mathematical science. In 1730, he was promoted to the professorship of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural philosophy</a>; and in 1733 he succeeded his friend D. Bernouilli in the mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>. In 1735, a problem was proposed by the academy which required expedition, and for the solution of which several eminent mathematicians had demanded the space of some months. The problem was solved by Euler in three days, to the great astonishment of the academy: but the violent and laborious efforts it cost him threw him into a fever, which endangered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and deprived him of the use of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> eye. The academy of sciences at Paris, which in 1738 had adjudged the prize to his memoir Concerning the Nature and Properties of Fire, proposed for the year 1740 the important subject of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>; a problem whose solution required the most arduous calculations, and comprehended the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the solar system. Euler's discourse on this question was adjudged a masterpiece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> and geometry; and it was more honourable for him to share the academical prize with such illustrious competitors as Colin Maclaurin and Daniel Bernouilli, than to have carried it away from rivals of less magnitude. Rarely, if ever, did such a brilliant competition adorn the annals of the academy; and no subject, perhaps, proposed by that learned body was ever treated with such accuracy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> and force of genius, as that which here displayed the philosophical powers of these three extraordinary men. In the year 1731, M. Euler was invited to Berlin to augment the lustre of the academy, that was there rising rising into fame. He enriched the last volume of the miscellanies (melanges), of Berlin with five memoirs, which make an eminent, perhaps the principal, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in that collection. These were followed with an astonishing rapidity by a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of important researches, which are scattered through the memoirs of the Prussian academy; of which a volume has been regularly published every year since its establishment in 1744. The labours of Euler <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear more especially astonishing, when it is considered, that while he was enriching the academy of Berlin with a prodigious number of memoirs, on the deepest parts of mathematical science, containing always some new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view, often sublime truths, and sometimes discoveries of great importance; he did not discontinue his philosophical contributions to the academy of Peterburgh, which granted him a pension in 1742, and whose memoirs display the marvellous fecundity of Euler's genius. It was with much difficulty that this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> obtained, in 1766, permission from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> to return to Peterburgh, where he desired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the rest of his days. Soon after his return, which was graciously rewarded by the munificence of Catherine II, he was seized with a violent disorder, which terminated in the total loss of his sight. A cataract, formed in his left eye, which had been essentially damaged by a too ardent application to study, deprived him entirely of the use of that organ. It was in this distressing situation that he dictated to his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, a tailor's apprentice, who was absolutely devoid of mathematical knowledge, his elements of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>; which by their intrinsic merit, in point of perspicuity and method, and the unhappy circumstances in which they were composed, have equally excited applause and astonishment. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, though purely elementary, discovers the palpable characteristics of an inventive genius; and it is here alone that we meet with a complete theory of the analysis of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOPHANTUS">Diophantus</a>. About this time M. Euler was honoured by the Academy of Sciences at Paris with the place of one of the foreign members of that learned body; and, after this, the academical prize was adjudged to three of his memoirs, Concerning the Inequalities in the Motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">Planets</a>. The two prize questions proposed by the same academy for 1770 and 1772 were designed to obtain from the labours of astronomers a more perfect theory of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. M. Euler, assisted by his eldest son, was a competitor for these prizes, and obtained them both. In this last memoir, he referred for further consideration several inequalities of the moon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, which he could not determine in his first theory, on account of the complicated calculations in which the method he then employed had engaged him. He had the courage afterward to review his whole theory, with the assistance of his son and Messrs Kraft and Lexell, and to pursue his researches until he had constructed the new tables, which appeared, together with the great work, in 1772. Instead of confining himself as before, to the fruitless integration of three <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> equations of the second degree, which are furnished by mathematical principles, he reduced them to the three ordinates, which determine the place of the moon; he divided into classes all the inequalities of that planet, as far as they depend either on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELONGATION">elongation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and moon, or upon the eccentricity, or the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a>, or the inclination of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> orbit.
