All these means of investigation, employed with such art and dexterity as could only be expected from analytical genius of the first order, were attended with the greatest success; and it is impossible to observe, without admiration, such immense calculations on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and on the other the ingenious methods employed by this great man to abridge them, and to facilitate their application to the real motion of the moon. But this admiration will become astonishment, when we consider at what <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> and in what circumstances all this was effectuated by M. Euler. It was when he was totally <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, and consequently obliged to arrange all his computations by the sole powers of his memory and his genius. It was when he was embarrassed in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> circumstances by a dreadful fire, that had consumed great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his substance, and forced him to quit a ruined <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, of which every corner was known to him by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, which, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, supplied the place of sight. It was in these circumstances that Euler composed a work, which, alone, was sufficient to render his name immortal. The heroic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and tranquillity of mind which he displayed here, need no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>; and he derived them not only from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of science, but from the power of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. His philosophy was too genuine and sublime to stop its analysis at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> causes; it led him to that divine philosophy of religion which ennobles <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, and can alone form a habit of true <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> and patience in suffering. Some time after this, the famous Wenzell, by couching the cataract, restored M. Euler's sight; but the satisfaction and joy that this successful operation produced, were of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Some instances of negligence on the part of his surgeons, and his own impatience to use an organ, whose cure was not completely finished, deprived him of his sight a second time; and this relapse was accompanied with tormenting pain. He, however, with the assistance of his sons, and of Messrs Kraft and Lexell, continued his labours; neither the loss of his sight, nor the infirmities of an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> could damp the ardour of his genius. He had engaged to furnish the academy of Peterburgh with as many memoirs as would be sufficient to complete its acts for 20 years after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In the space of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years he transmitted to the academy by Mr Golswin, above 70 memoirs, and above 200 more, which were revised and completed by the author of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. Such of these memoirs as were of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> were separated from the rest, and form a collection that was published in the year 1783, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Analytical Works. Euler's knowledge was more universal than could be well expected in one who had pursued with such unremitting ardour mathematics and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> as his favourite studies. He had made a very considerable progress in medical, botanical, and chemical science. What was still more extraordinary, he was an excellent scholar, and possessed what is generally called erudition in a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree. He had read, with attention and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the most eminent writers of ancient Rome; the civil and literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of all ages and all nations were familiar to him; and foreigners, who were only acquainted with his works, were astonished to find find in the conversation of a man, whose <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> life seemed solely occupied in mathematical and physical researches and discoveries, such an extensive acquaintance with the most interesting branches of literature. In this respect, no doubt, he was much indebted to a very uncommon memory, which seemed to retain every idea that was conveyed to it, either from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> or from meditation. He could repeat the Aeneid of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, from the beginning to the end, without hesitation, and indicate the first and last line of every page of the edition he used. Several attacks of a vertigo, in the beginning of September 1783, which did not prevent his calculating the motions of the aerostatical globes, were, nevertheless, the forerunners of his mild and happy passage from this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> to a better. While he was amusing himself at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">tea</a> with one of his grandchildren, he was struck with an apoplexy, which terminated his illustrious career at the age of 76. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was uncommonly strong and vigorous; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was good; and the evening of his long life was calm and serene, sweetened by the fame that follows genius, the public esteem and respect that are never withheld from exemplary virtue, and several domestic comforts which he was capable of feeling and therefore deserved to enjoy.

EULOGY

Pages 372-372

likewise means an encomium on any person, on account of some virtue <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>.

EUMARIDES

Pages 372-372

of εὐμάρις, "easy," among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a kind of shoes <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to men and women.—The eumarides were used for pomp and delicacy, being neat, and painted with various colours.

EUMENES

Pages 373-373

a celebrated orator of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> about the beginning of the fourth century. Some of his harangues and orations are extant. An historical writer in Alexander's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>.

EUMENIDES

Pages 373-373

a name given to the Furies by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. They sprang from the blood of the wound which Cœlus received from his son <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>. According to others, they were daughters of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, and conceived from the blood of Saturn. Some make them daughters of Acheron and Night, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pluto and Proserpine. According to the more received opinions, they were three in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, Tisiphone, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, and Alecto, to which some add Nemesis. Plutarch mentions only one called Adropha, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a>. They were supposed to be the ministers of the vengeance of the gods. They were stern and inexorable; and were always employed in punishing the guilty upon earth, as well as in the infernal regions. They inflicted their vengeance upon earth by wars, pestilence, and sufferings, and by the secret feelings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a> they punished the guilty by continual flagellation and torments. They were also called Furiae and Erinnys. Their worship was almost universal; and people dared not to mention their names or fix their eyes upon their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>. They were honoured with sacrifices and libations; and in Achaea they had a temple, which when entered by any one guilty of a crime, suddenly rendered him furious and deprived him of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his reason. In the sacrifices the votaries used branches of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> and of alder, hawthorn, saffron, and juniper; and the victims were generally turtle doves and sheep, with libations of wine and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. They were usually represented with a grim and frightful aspect, with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and bloody garment, and with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> writhing round their heads instead of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. They held a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> torch in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a whip of scorpions in the other; and were always attended by Terror, Rage, Paleness, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a>. In hell they were seated around Pluto's throne, as the ministers of his vengeance.

EUMENIDIA

Pages 373-373

festivals in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUMENIDES">Eumenides</a>, called by the Athenians εὐμενία ἱερά, "venerable goddesses." They were celebrated once every year, with sacrifices of pregnant <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a>, with offerings of cakes made by the most eminent youths, and libations of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wine. At <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> none but freeborn citizens were admitted, such as had led a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the most virtuous and unfulfilled.

EUMOLPIDES

Pages 373-374

the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> at the cele- Vol. VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a> of his own proper substance to another. He alone is unbegotten; and it is impossible that any other being should be formed of an unbegotten substance. He did not <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his own substance in begetting the Son, but his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> only: nor did he beget him in the likeness of his substance, but according to his own good <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He then created the Holy Spirit, the first and greatest of all spirits, by his own power indeed and operation immediately, yet by the immediate power and operation of the Son. After the Holy Spirit he created all other things in heaven and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, visible and invisible, corporeal and incorporeal, immediately by himself, by the power and operation of the Son," &c.

EUNOMIUS

Pages 374-374

a famous heresiarch of the 4th century, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Eulius, but abundantly more subtle than his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, as well as more bold in propagating the opinions of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, who after him are called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a>. He was ordained bishop of Cyzicus; but gave so much disturbance by the intemperance of his zeal, that he was deplored more than once. At last, tired with being tossed about, he petitioned to retreat to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, Dacora in Cappadocia; where he died very old about the year 374, after experiencing a variety of sufferings. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his works are lost. There is, however, besides two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three small pieces, a confession of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> remaining, which Cave inserted in his Historia Literaria, from a manuscript in Archbishop Tennison's library. See the preceding article.

EUNUCH

Pages 374-374

a castrated person. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTRATION">Castration</a>.—The word is formed from ευνούς, q. d. leōtē curam habet, "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> keeper of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>." In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, &c., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> are never made but upon occasion of some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which renders such an operation necessary; but in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> they make <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of children, from one to three years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, eunuchs, every year, to supply the operas and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> with singers. M. de la Lande, in his Voyage d'Italie, affirms, that there are public shops at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> where this cruel operation is performed, and that over the door of these shops is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> Quis faceret ragazzii. But Dr Burney informs us, that he was not only utterly unable to see or hear of any such shops during his residence in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but was constantly told, both by the natives and English settled there, that the laws against such a practice were so numerous and severe, that it was never performed but with the utmost secrecy. In the eastern parts of the world, they make eunuchs in order to be guards or attendants on their women. The feraglions of the eastern emperors are chiefly served and guarded by eunuchs; and yet, from good authority, we learn, that the rich eunuchs in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and other countries keep feraglions for their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Those who, out of an imprudent zeal to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> themselves from sensual pleasures, made themselves eunuchs, were, by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, condemned and excluded from holy orders. There are several severe prohibitions in Germany against the making of eunuchs; and in France an eunuch must not marry, not even with the consent of the woman. Though the practice of castration is detestable in every point of view; yet there appears no real foundation for the injurious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> generally entertained of eunuchs, viz. that they are all cowards, and devoid of genius for literature or any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. "As to genius (says the author last quoted), I never found those of the first class in music deficient in intellectual abilities for more serious studies. Indeed I have seen real genius and dispositions for literary pursuits, in more than one great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> singer; and as for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of music, not only the best fingers of the pope's chapel ever since the beginning of the last century, but the best composers, are among the sopranis in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>." With respect to the operation affecting the mind so much as to deprive it of all fortitude in times of danger, there is great reason to doubt the fact: most of the generals of eastern monarchs having been at all times of this class; and the bravest stand that ever was made against Alexander the Great was at Gaza, under the command of one of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>'s generals, who was an eunuch. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a> gives an account of Menophilus, a eunuch, to whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> intrusted his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>; which proves the possibility of such unfortunate persons possessing a heroism equal to that of the most determined Stoic. It is very certain, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> never supposed eunuchs to have been men of inferior intellects, or that they possessed less vigour of mind than other men. At least the Persians were not of this opinion; for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> relates, that when they had taken possession of some Ionian cities, παιδία τε τοῦ συνελευσθείς καὶ ἐκτελέσθεις, p. 451, ἐπὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς, καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐν τῇ ὁμοίως ἀναγκῇ. It is certain, however, Herodotus, in relating the melancholy story of Hermotimus, says, that μᾶλλον τοῦτο παρεξελευσθείς ἢ ἐπὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς, ἐπὶ τῆς ὁμοίως ἀναγκῇ, p. 665, ἐπὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς, ἐπὶ τῆς ὁμοίως ἀναγκῇ, "among the barbarians, the eunuchs are more valued than other men, on account of their universal fidelity." It appears from this passage of Herodotus, that in Persia eunuchs were far from being objects of contempt; and were even frequently promoted to the highest honours. This was indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with Hermotimus. We find in Agathias, who was one of the Byzantine historians, that a general in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, named Norzes, was a eunuch. This was in the latter ages. In Plutarch's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Arisides, Themistocles is related to have chosen an eunuch, whose name was Arnaes, from among his prisoners, to send on a secret embassy to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>. This surely may serve to show, that mental imbecility was not supposed by the Greeks to be the characteristic of eunuchism. The same story of the confidence placed in Arnaes, who was one of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s eunuchs, is related also in the life of Themistocles. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> paid such <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> respect to Hermias, who was a eunuch and governor of Atarnea, which is in Mytilene, that he even offered sacrifices in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of him; as Lucian informs us in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> entitled Eunuchus. This regard of Aristotle for Hermias has been often celebrated, and is mentioned by Suidas, Harpocration, and others. Eunuchs, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the third century, who were mad enough to castrate, not only those of their own persuasion, but even all others they could lay hold of. They took their rise from the example of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, who, misunderstanding the following words of our Saviour, "and eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of heaven," castrated himself.

EUODIA

Pages 375-375

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tetrantha clas; See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUONYMUS

Pages 375-375

the Spindle Tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 43rd order, Dumaee. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUPATORIUM

Pages 375-375
Hemp Agrimony; a genus of plants belonging to the syngenesia clas; and in the natural method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See Botany Index.

EUPATRIDAE

Pages 375-375

in antiquity, a name given by Theicus to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, as distinguished from the Geomori and Demiurgi. The Eupatridae, by Theicus's establishment, had the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of choosing magistrates, teaching and dispensing the laws, and interpreting holy and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in all other matters, was reduced to an equality. The Geomori were husbandmen, and inferior to the Eupatride in point of fortune; the Demiurgi were artificers, and fell short of the Eupatride in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

EUPHONY

Pages 375-375

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, an easiness, smoothness, and elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>. The word is formed of ὕψος, bene, “well;” and φωνή, vox, “<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>.” Quintilian calls euphonia, “vocatilis;” Scaliger, “facilis pronunciatio.” Euphonia is properly a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> whereby we suppress a too harsh <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convert it into a smoother, contrary to the ordinary rules. There are examples enough in all languages. EUPHYMISM. See Oratory.

EUPHORBIA

Pages 375-375

Spurge; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dodecandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricoccæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUPHORBIUM

Pages 375-375

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, a gummi-resinous substance, which exudes from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> oriental tree, (Euphorbia officinarum). See Materia Medica <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUPHORBUS

Pages 375-375

a famous Trojan, son of Panthous. He was the first who wounded <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, whom Hector killed. He perished by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of Menelaus, who hung his shield in the temple of Juno at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, the founder of the doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> transmigration of souls, affirmed that he had been once Euphorbus, and that his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> recollected many exploits which had been done while it animated that Trojan's body. As a further <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his affection, he showed at first sight the shield of Euphorbus in the temple of Juno. EUPHORION of Chalcis, a poet and historian, born in the 126th Olympiad. Suetonius says that Tiberius composed verses in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Euphorion, Rianius and Parthenius; with whom he was charmed to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he ordered their writings and their pictures to be kept in all the public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and celebrated authors.

EUPHRASIA

Pages 375-375

Eye-bright; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 40th order, Perforatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUPHRATES

Pages 375-376

a river universally allowed to take its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>; but in what particular spot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in what <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> it afterwards shapes its course, there is the greatest disagreement. Strabo says, that the Euphrates rises in Mount Abus, which he joins with, or accounts a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of, Mount Taurus; that its beginning is on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of Mount Taurus; and that running, first westward through Armenia, then striking off to the south, it forces its way through the mountain; and thus it rises in the south of Armenia, Mount Taurus being the boundary on that side; and runs through its south part, quite to Cappadocia, conterminous with Armenia <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>; or quite to this last, or to its south limit; to reach which, it must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> its west course a little north; because Taurus, from which it rose, lies lower, or more to the south, and almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with Melitene: and that then it turns to the south, in order Euphrates to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through Taurus, and escape to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; and then take a new bend to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. To this account of Strabo, Pliny runs quite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>; adverting eye-witnesses, who carry the Euphrates from north to south in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line, till it meets Mount Taurus; placing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> to the east, as Strabo does; whence, he says, it runs in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> course westward, before it <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> south, and that it rises not from Mount Taurus, but far to the north of it; and he makes it run straight west from its rise, then turn south spontaneously, without any interfering obstacle, in a manner quite different from Strabo, Mela, and others, who make Taurus the cause of this turn. The Euphrates naturally divides into two channels, one through Babylon, and the other through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, besides the several <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> cuts made between it and the Tigris about Babylon: and these cuts or trenches are what the Psalmist calls the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Babylon, on the willows of which the captives hung their harps. It is probable, that the Euphrates naturally poured into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at one particular mouth, before these cuts were made. A thing appearing so evident to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, that Pliny has set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the distance between the mouths of the Euphrates and the Tigris; and he says, some made it 25, and others 74 miles; but that the Euphrates being for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> back intercepted in its course by cuts, made for watering the fields, only the branch called the Positigris fell into the sea, the rest of it into the Tigris, and both together into the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>. Overflowing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> through which it runs, at stated times of the year, like the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, it renders it fertile.

EUPOLIS

Pages 376-376

an Athenian comic poet, flourished about the 83rd Olympiad. He took the freedom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> in satirizing the vices of the people. He lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fight between the Athenians and Lacedaemonians; and his fate was so much lamented, that after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> it was enacted that no poet should serve in the wars. Some say <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCIBIADES">Alcibiades</a> put him to death for his satirical freedom.

EURIPIDES

Pages 376-376

one of the Greek poets who excelled in tragedy, was born about 486 B.C. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, whither his father and mother had retired a little before <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> entered <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. He learnt <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> under Prodicus, morality under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a>; but at 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> abandoned philosophy, in order to apply himself to dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. He used to flout himself up in a cave to compose his tragedies, which were extremely applauded by the Greeks. The Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, commanded by Nicias, being defeated in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> purchased their lives and liberties by reciting the verses of Euripides; such esteem and veneration had the Sicilians for the pieces wrote by this excellent poet. Socrates, the wisest of the philosophers, felt such a value upon them, that they were the only tragedies he went to see acted: and yet his performances seldom gained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. Euripides frequently intersperses through them moral sentences, and severe reflections on the fair <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; whence he was called the Woman-hater. He was, nevertheless, married; but the scandalous lives of his two wives drew upon him the raillery of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, and other comic poets; which occasioned his retiring to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Archelaus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon, where he was well received. That <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was fond of learned men, and drew them to him by his liberality. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we may believe Solinus, he made Euripides his minister of state, and gave him other extraordinary proofs of his esteem. He had, however, pafled but a few years there, when an unhappy accident put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He was walking in a wood, and, according to his usual manner, in deep meditation; when, unfortunately happening upon Archelaus' hounds, he was by them torn in pieces. It is not certain whether

EURIPUS

Pages 376-377

a canal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> strait which divides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Euboea, now <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGROPONT">Negropont</a>, from the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. In one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it is so narrow, that a galley can scarcely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it. The agitations of the Euripus were much spoken of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Some say that the canal has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> and reflux six times in 24 hours; others, that it ebbs and flows <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but Livy does not allow this flux and reflux to be so regular. Father Babin, a Jesuit of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, who made many observations on the spot during his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> abode in the island of Negropont, tells us, that the Euripus is regular in its ebbing and flowing the first eight days of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>: the same regularity he observed from the 14th to the 25th day inclusive, and in the three last days: but in the other days of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, it is not so regular; for it sometimes ebbs and flows 11, 12, 13, and 14 times in the space of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> day. In this place, as the story <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> goes, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> drowned himself out of chagrin, for not being able to account for so unusual a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Euripus has since become a general name for all straits, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is in great motion and agitation. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> circuses had their euripi, which were no other than pits or ditches on each side of the course, into which it was very dangerous falling with their horses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> as they ran races. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> euripus was more particularly applied by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> or ditches which encompassed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> on three sides, and which were filled occasionally to represent naumachiae or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> battles. The same people called their smaller fountains or canals in their gardens <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">euripides</a>; and their largest, as cascades, &c., nilos.

EUROCLYDON

Pages 377-377

(of Εὔξεινος, east <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and κλαυδίω, wave,) is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of wind, of which we have an account only in Acts xxvii. 14, and concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of which critics have been much divided. Bochart, Grotius, Bentley, and others substitute another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> MS. and the Vulgate, viz. Εὐρακτών, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Euro-aquilo; but Mr Bryant defends the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> reading, and considers the Euroclydon, i.e. Εὔξεινος κλαυδίων, as an east wind that causes a deep <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or vast inundation. He maintains, in opposition to Dr Bentley's reasoning, who supposes that the mariners in the ship, the voyage of which is recited in this passage, were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, that they were Greeks of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and that the ship was an Alexandrian ship employed in the traffic of carrying corn to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>: and therefore, that the mariners had a name in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> for the particular typhonic or stormy wind here mentioned. He always flows from the passage itself, that the tempestuous wind called Euroclydon, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> (κλαυδίω) upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>; and therefore, as this is a relative <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, referring to the situation of the person who speaks of it, who was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> or south of it, the wind blew upon shore, and Euroclydon must have come from the south or south-east; which, he adds, is fully warranted by the point where the ship was, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> it ran in afterwards, which was towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-west.

EUROPA

Pages 377-377

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Agenor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Phoenicia and Telephaea. She was so beautiful that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> became enamoured of her; and the better to seduce her, he assumed the shape of a bull and mingled with the herds of Agenor, while Europa, with her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> attendants, were gathering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in the meadows. Europa caressed the beautiful animal; and at last had the courage to sit upon his back. The god took advantage of her situation; and with precipitate steps retired towards the shore, crossed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with Europa on his back, and arrived safe in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. Here he assumed his original shape and declared his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> consented, though she had once made vows of perpetual celibacy; and she became mother of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, Sarpedon, and Rhadamantus. After this distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> with Jupiter, she married Asterius, king of Crete. This monarch seeing himself without children by Europa, adopted the fruit of her amours with Jupiter, and always esteemed Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamantus, as his own children. Some suppose, that Europa lived about 1552 years before the Christian era.

EUROPE

Pages 377-381

one of the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the world. This is considerably the smallest of the four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> divisions of the terraqueous globe. Its length, from east to west, according to the most authentic accounts, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> about 3300 miles British <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, and its breadth 2350. The continental <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is bounded on the south by the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, comprehending the most distant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Europe, viz. that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> is now considered as constituting a part of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Many geographers of eminence have given the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZORES">Azores</a> to Europe, from their greater <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> than to any other continental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and have considered the Madeiras as a constituent part of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> for a similar reason. Europe is bounded on the north by the Arctic ocean and the new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; while its eastern limits appear to be more uncertain in the estimation of geographers. It appears evident, however, that a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> limit might be ascertained by tracing the river Oufa from its source to its confluence with the Belaia; and thence from the Kama to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>, which would make its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> extremely natural to the town of Sarepta; it requiring only an imaginary line of very small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a>, which would satisfactorily ascertain its western boundary. The western and southern parts of Europe anciently consisted of the people called Celts; the Fins occupied the north-east, and the Laplanders, a people equally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> with the Samoeds of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, possessed its remotest parts towards the north, who rendered their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> less uncouth and barbarous by assimilating it to that of the Fins. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> from Asia seem to have driven those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants towards the east and north, whose descendants occupy the greater part of Europe. From the Slavonic tribes, who also came from Asia, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, Russians, &c., were descended. They were accompanied by the Heruli, who made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of what is now denominated the Lettic speech, to be met met with in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, Lithuania, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOGITIA">Samogitia</a>, and nearly allied to the Sclavonic language, according to the account of Tooke in his view of Russia. At an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the colony of Iberi and northern Mauritani came over into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and at a later period both the Hungarians and Turks emigrated from Asia. Notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> character of d'Anville as a geographer, we believe that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> reflecting the geographical knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> is greatly exaggerated. It appears evident that nothing more of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a> was known to the ancients than the southern part as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of Weter and Wener. It is no doubt true that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, by means of their shipping, even in the imperfect state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> at that period, traversed the southern shores of the Baltic, as far as to the river Rubo, ascertaining the names of various tribes along that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the maps of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> are admitted as decisive proofs in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is certain that they were wholly unacquainted with the interior of Germany; and consequently the tribes of which he makes mention, may rather be considered as having dwelt along the northern shores of the Baltic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the southern parts on the left of the Danube. They were no doubt acquainted with the Carpathian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; but their knowledge of Europe towards the north-east was undoubtedly circumscribed by the 50th or 52nd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of north latitude. In many barbarous languages, the same word was often used indiscriminately either for a mountain or a forest, the want of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to which has frequently been the prolific source of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, and placed mountains of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had planted trees. It has been supposed that the Riphean mountains were the Uralian chain, of which the ancients knew nothing, instead of a forest of prodigious extent from east to west. It is also well known that the Venedici Montes of Ptolemy have no existence upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and therefore must once have been a very extensive forest with which the moderns are unacquainted, and perhaps no traces of it are now anywhere to be met with. Christianity is the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> all over Europe, except in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; and even there it has been computed, that about one-half of the inhabitants are members of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The Christian religion has always been accompanied in its progress with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of knowledge, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of industry, and the civilization of manners, whereas the barbarous tribes in the northern parts of Europe advanced by very slow degrees, and the Scandinavians <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a state of pagan <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> till the eleventh century. Some tribes of Sclavonia to the south of the Baltic, were not converted to Christianity till the thirteenth century, and of course were for many ages in a state little superior to brutality; and the people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a> were not converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> till about a century ago, by means of missionaires sent from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. The people of Europe, as to matters of religion, are divided into catholics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">protestants</a>, the former being chiefly confined to the southern parts of it, where the imagination requires the gratifications arising from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> pomp and parade; and the latter in the northern parts of it, the simplicity of which is much better calculated to please the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the judgment. The Christian religion being thus diffused all over Europe, that division of the globe has hence become a kind of republic in respect of literature, every scientific <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and discovery being transmitted from one portion of it to another with the utmost dispatch. For this reason Europe has been sometimes compared to ancient <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and it is to be hoped that Russia <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never prove another Macedon. The greater part of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe lies within the northern temperate zone, a distinction which is now nearly annihilated by the interesting discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">Climate</a> is found to depend very frequently on causes which are purely local, since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> in a southern latitude, exhibit mountains of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> which are not known even in Lapland, while the torrid zone is plentifully supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and habitations, and for any thing which can be determined to the contrary, it may contain mountains which are covered with snow. As it is happily delivered from those intense heats which are peculiar to Asia and Africa, the inhabitants are in general blest with greater bodily vigour and intellectual strength. One of the most striking features of Europe in a general point of view is its inland seas which give it a decided superiority over the other more extensive divisions of the earth, and contribute powerfully to the extension of its industry, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and civilization. If such blessings had been enjoyed by Africa, it is more than probable that the consequences of her industry would have been diffused far and wide. Of these inland seas, the Mediterranean holds the most distinguished place, as the centre of civilization both to the ancient and modern inhabitants of Europe. It is about 2000 miles in length to its farther extremity in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, but the maps of antiquity make it 300 more. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and the Archipelago open on its northern side, formerly denominated the Adriatic and Egean seas, from the last of which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the sea of Marmora, or the Propontis, by means of the Hellespont; and the strait of Constantinople leads into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Sea, to the north of which is the sea of Azof (Palus Maeotis), or utmost <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> boundary of Europe in that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. This vast expanse of water is beautifully ornamented with numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and an opulent sea coast, exhibiting delightful specimens of almost every thing in nature which is sublime and beautiful. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">Tides</a> cannot be perceived except in straits of very small dimensions, although naturalists have observed, that a current sets along the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> from west to east, while its direction is from east to west towards the coast of Africa. In the gulf of Venice the current runs along <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> in a north-west direction, and returns by the opposite shore of Italy. There is abundance of fish to be met with in the Mediterranean, some of which are but rarely to be found in more northern latitudes. This sea in particular abounds with coral, now certainly known to be the production of marine insects. This imaginary plant is tri-coloured, composed of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and does not exceed eleven inches in height. It is hard in the sea, and in this respect undergoes not the smallest change by exposure to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and the nets made use of for procuring it, measure from 60 to 125 feet. From the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of its rocks or perilous navigation, the Black Sea is said to have derived its name. As the sea of Azof Azof almost always exhibits a muddy appearance, it was for that reason denominated Palus by the ancients, and it is united to the Euxine or Black Sea by the strait of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a>. The next inland sea of Europe is the Baltic, to which the Germans have given the name of the Eastern Sea, which accounts for the people denominated Eastlings in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of England, who undoubtedly came from the shores of the Baltic. It opens from the German Sea by a gulf trending north-east, known by the name of the Skager Rock, from whence it passes southward in the Cattgat, to the south-east of which we meet with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of Eldinore, where vessels become in some degree tributary to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Denmark. It is afterwards divided into two branches of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> extent, called the gulfs of Bothnia and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, both of which are covered with ice for nearly five months in the year. The greatest depth of the Baltic is said not to exceed 50 fathoms; and according to the opinion of naturalists, its extent suffers a diminution of four feet every century. It has been affirmed that its waters do not contain above one-thirtieth of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, while other sea-waters frequently contain one-tenth, which has been ascribed to the vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ice; and when the north <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows, these waters, it is also said, may be employed for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy. There are no tides in the Baltic, but very few fish. The White Sea, in the northern parts of Russia, is the last inland sea of Europe, which was well known to the English in particular, before the commerce of Archangel was transferred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>. It went by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Sea in the reign of Alfred the Great; and the writers of Iceland called it the sea of Gauvik, on the shores of which stood their Biarmia. There are a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of islands in the White Sea, but the accounts which geographers have hitherto given us, are neither circumstantial nor satisfactory. The German Sea deserves to be mentioned among the other maritime divisions of Europe, which has received the appellation because it waters the western shores of ancient Germany, from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> to the farthest boundary of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>. It may properly be regarded as constituting a part of the Atlantic Ocean, ending at the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, from whence the British Channel extends to the west. Another extensive inlet of the Atlantic is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>; for the British Channel is rather to be considered as the wide frith of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>. St George's Channel lies on the south between Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and the Irish Sea leading to the North Channel, is situated in the centre. What the ancients called the Deucalionian Sea, lies to the north of Scotland, which was likewise denominated the Sarmanian, as extending throughout the Baltic. The Arctic Ocean lies to the north of Europe, the dismal receptacle of countless miles of ice, piled up in mountains, the hoary majesty of which, while it captivates the eye, can scarcely fail to strike terror into the heart of the mariner. Yet from those dreary regions, which at first appear only as a prodigious waste in the works of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, the benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">Parent</a> of the universe diffuses innumerable millions of herrings for the use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. This is worthy of the divine being whose goodness is whispered to us in every breeze, which glows in the starry moment of heaven, and is diffused through the whole creation. The Goodwin Sands in the vicinity of the Kentish coast, are as dangerous to the mariner as uninviting to the fisher; but excellent fish are to be found on many banks on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, among which may be ranked the cod, the soal, and the plaice. What are called the silver-pits of the mariners, lying between the Dogger and Well <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, supply the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> market with cod, which discovers a predilection for the deep waters in the vicinity of the banks. The Hornriff, a narrow strip extending to Jutland, is situated towards the north-east of the Dogger bank. The Juttriff extends from the mouth of the Baltic to the German Sea, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>. The Man Bank takes its rise opposite to Berwick, which is little more than 15 miles in length. To the eastward of this lies the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> Forties, extending from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a> Ness to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, and from between 40 and 100 miles from the shore; and a bank reaches across the German Sea towards Juttriff, from the coast of Buchan. It was thought necessary, in this concise account of Europe, to mention some of the most considerable banks or comparative shoals, which have often been regarded as the summits of lofty mountains beneath the surface of the deep; and which, as the haunts of fishes of different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, have arrested the attention of national industry. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Europe will be given in our account of the countries through which they respectively flow. The greater part of the Volga is considered as belonging to Europe; the next highly celebrated river is the Danube, after which we may <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> the Nieper, the Rhine, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>. The Alps are the loftiest mountains; next the Pyrenees; and that vast ridge by which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> is divided from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. The Carpathian Mountains, the chain called Emineh, and the Apennines, are of inferior magnitude. The European states and kingdoms may properly be divided into three classes; 1. Despotic monarchies, of which Russia and Turkey may serve as specimens. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">Absolute</a> monarchies, such as Spain and Denmark. And 3. Those of a limited nature, as the Germanic empire, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Great Britain. Since the governments of Venice, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and Holland were subverted by the French, few, if any traces of a permanent aristocracy are to be met with, or any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. In some of the Swiss cantons we may perhaps find the shadow of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a>; and France is at present a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> despotism called an empire, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession being hereditary indefeasible. It is customary with some geographers to divide the constituent parts of Europe into first, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and third orders, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> importance; the first order including the united kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, France, Russia, the Austrian dominions, Prussia, Spain, Turkey. In the second order stand the United Provinces, Denmark, Sweden, Portugal and Switzerland; and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> states of Germany and Italy constitute the third, a detailed account of which our readers will find in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> under their proper names.

EURYALE

Pages 381-381

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, one of the Gorgons, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Phorcys, and sister of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>; she was subject neither to old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

EURYANDRA

Pages 381-381

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EURYDICE

Pages 381-382

Eurydice, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the wife of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, who, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> from Aristaeus that endeavoured to ravish her, was slain by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>. Her husband went <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the shades, and by the force of his music persuaded Pluto and Proserpine to give him leave to carry back his wife; which they granted, provided he did not look on her till he came to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>: but he breaking the condition, was forced to leave her behind him. See Orpheus.

EURYMEDON

Pages 382-382

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a noble river running through the middle of Pamphylia; famous for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> fight on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in which the Athenians under Cimon the son of Miltiades, defeated the Persians. The sea fight happened first in the sea of Pamphylia, towards Cyprus; the land engagement, the following night on the Eurymedon. Cimon, after defeating the Persian fleet, armed his men with the armour of the captives, and set sail for the enemy, who lay on the banks of the Eurymedon, in the ships taken from the Persians; who on seeing their own ships and their own people in appearance, were off their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and thus became an easy conquest.

EURYSTHEUS

Pages 382-382

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> and Mycenæ, son of Sthenelus and Nicippe the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPS">Pelops</a>. Juno hastened his birth by two months, that he might come into the world before <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> the son of Alcmena, as the younger of the two was doomed by order of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> to be subservient to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the other. (See Alcmena). This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> was cruelly exercised by Eurystheus, who was jealous of the fame of Hercules; and who to destroy so powerful a relation, imposed upon him the most dangerous and uncommon enterprises, well known by the name of the twelve labours of Hercules. The success of Hercules in achieving those perilous labours alarmed Eurystheus in a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and he furnished himself with a brazen vessel, where he might secure himself a safe retreat in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of danger. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hercules, Eurystheus renewed his cruelties against his children, and made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEYX">Ceyx</a> king of Trachinia, because he had given them support, and treated them with hospitality. He was killed in the prosecution of this war by Hyllus the son of Hercules. His head was sent to Alcmena the mother of Hercules; who, mindful of the cruelties which her son had suffered, insulted it, and tore out the eyes with the most inveterate fury. Eurystheus was succeeded on the throne of Argos by Atreus his nephew. The death of Eurystheus happened about thirty years before the Trojan war.

EURYTHMY

Pages 382-382

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, is a certain majesty, elegance, and easiness, appearing in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> members <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> parts of a body, painting, or sculpture, and resulting from the fine proportion of it.

EUSDEN

Pages 382-382

Laurence, an Irish clergyman, rector of Conely in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, and poet laureat after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mr Rowe. His first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> was the eminent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>; whose poem, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>, he translated into Latin, and dedicated to his lordship. He was esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, who rewarded an epithalamium he wrote on his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of poet laureat. He was the author of many poetical pieces, though but little known before his premature death; he died in 1730.

EUSEBIANS

Pages 382-382

a denomination given to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, on account of the favour and countenance which Eusebius, bishop of Caesaria, showed and procured for them at their first rise. See Arians and Eusebius.

EUSEBIUS

Pages 382-382

surnamed Pamphilus, a celebrated bishop of Caesarea in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, and one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born in Palestine about the latter end of the reign of Gallienus. He was the intimate friend of Pamphilus the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>; and, after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, took his name in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. He was ordained bishop of Caesarea in 313. He had a considerable share in the contest relating to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a>; whose cause he, as well as several other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Palestine, defended, being persuaded that Arius had been unjustly persecuted by Alexander bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. He assisted at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice in 325; when he made a speech to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine on his coming to the council, and was placed next him on his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He was present at the council of Antioch, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a> bishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was deposed; but though he was chosen by the bishop and people of Antioch to succeed him, he absolutely refused it. In 335, he assisted at the council of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> held against Athanasius; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of bishops at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, at the time of the dedication of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> there. By these bishops he was sent to the emperor Constantine to defend what they had done against Athanasius; when he pronounced the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> made on that emperor during the public rejoicings in the beginning of the 30th year of his reign, which was the last of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Eusebius survived the emperor but a short time, for he died in 338. He wrote, 1. An <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, of which Valetius has given a good edition in Greek and Latin; 2. The Life of Constantine; 3. A treatise against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROCLES">Hierocles</a>; 4. Chronicon; 5. Preparations Evangelicae; 6. De demonstratione Evangelica, of which there are but 10 books extant out of 20; and several other works, some of which are lost.

EUSTACHIUS

Pages 382-382

Bartholomew, physician and anatomist at Rome, flourished about the year 1550. His anatomical plates were discovered there in 1712, and published in 1714.

EUSTATHIANS

Pages 382-384

a name given to the Catholics of Antioch in the 4th century, on occasion of their refusal to acknowledge any other bishop beside St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a>, deposed by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>. The denomination was given them during the episcopate of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a>, whom the Arians substituted for St Eustathius, about the year 339, when they began to hold their assemblies apart. About the year 350, Leontius of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, called the eunuch, who was an Arian, and was put in the fee of Antioch, defied the Eustathians to perform their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; which they accepting, the church of Antioch served indifferently both the Arians and Catholics. This, we are told, gave occasion to two institutions, which have subsisted in the church ever since. The first was psalmody in two choirs; though M. Baillet thinks, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they instituted an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> psalmody between two choirs, it was between two Catholic choirs, and not by way of response to an Arian choir. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was the doxology, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a> be to the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost. See Doxology. This conduct, which seemed to imply a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the Arians, gave <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence to abundance. Eustathians dance of Catholics, who began to hold separate meetings; and this formed the schism of Antioch. Upon this, the rest, who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to meet in the church, ceased to be called Eustathians, and that appellation became refrained to the dissenting party. St Flavianus, bishop of Antioch in 381, and one of his successors, Alexander, in 482, brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a coalition, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reunion, between the Eustathians and the body of the church of Antioch, described with much solemnity by Theodoret, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, iii. c. 2. Eustathians were also a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the fourth century, denominated from their founder Eustathius, a monk so foolishly fond of his own profession, that he condemned all other conditions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Whether this Eustathius was the same with the bishop of Sebastea and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Semi-Arians, is not easy to determine. He excluded married people from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>; prohibited his followers from praying in their houses; and obliged them to quit all they had, as incompatible with the hopes of heaven. He drew them out of the other assemblies of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> to hold secret ones with him, and made them wear a particular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; he appointed them to fast on Sundays; and taught them, that the ordinary faiths of the church were needful, after they had attained to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity which he pretended to. He showed great horror for chapels built in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of martyrs, and the assemblies held therein. Several women seduced by his reasons, forsook their husbands; and abundance of slaves deserted their masters' houses. He was condemned at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Gangra in Paphlagonia, held between the years 326 and 341. Eustathius, bishop of Thessalonica, in the 12th century, under the reigns of the emperors Emmanuel, Alexander, and Andronicus Comnenus. He was a very eminent grammarian; and wrote commentaries upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, and Dionysius the geographer. The best edition of his Commentaries on Homer is that of Rome, printed in Greek, in 1542, in four volumes folio. His Commentaries on the Periegesis of Dionysius were printed by Mr Hudson at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in 1697, 8vo. Eustathius appears to have been alive in the year 1194. Eustatia, St Eustatia, or Eustatius, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, belonging to the Dutch, and situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 62° 56' N.
