Lat. 17° 29'. It is little else than a huge mountain, which formerly has, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, been a volcano. Its situation is so strong, that it has but one landing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and that is fortified in such a manner as to be almost impregnable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a> is the chief product of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; and it is cultivated to the very top of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, which terminates in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain surrounded with woods, but having a hollow in the middle, which serves as a large den for wild beasts. No fewer than 5000 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> people and 15,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> subsist on this spot, where they rear hogs, kids, rabbits, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, in such abundance, that they can supply their neighbours, after having served themselves. The first Dutch colony sent to this island consisted of about 1600 people. They were dispossessed by the English from Jamaica in 1665. Soon after, the Dutch and French becoming confederates, the English were expelled in their turn. The French continuing to hold a garrison in the island till the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>, when it was restored to the Dutch. Soon after the revolution, the French drove out the Dutch, and were in their turn driven out by the English under Sir Timothy Thornhill, with the loss of no more than eight men killed and wounded, though the fort they took mounted 16 guns, and was in every other respect very strong. Sir Timothy found it necessary for the protection of the Dutch, to leave a small English garrison in the fort; but he granted the French no terms of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, except for their lives and baggage. By the peace of Ryswick, the entire <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this island was restored to the Dutch. This island was reduced by the British in the year 1781. Though not 20 miles in circumference, it abounded at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, by reason of the vast influx of trade from every other island in these seas. Being a free port, it was open to all the subjects of the belligerent powers; and thus a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> was established among them, through which they were enabled to carry on a commercial correspondence, which greatly mitigated the inconveniences of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The greatest benefit, however, was reaped by the Dutch; who, by transacting all trading business for other nations, were thus intrusted with numberless commissions, and likewise enjoyed vast profits from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the merchandises to which they were entitled. At the time the attack was made upon them, they were so little under the apprehensions of such an event, that their warehouses were not sufficient to contain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of commercial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> imported for sale, and the beach and streets were covered with hogsheads of tobacco and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. In this situation, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Rodney having received orders to commence hostilities against the Dutch, suddenly appeared before the island with such an armament of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> forces, as in its defenceless situation was not only useless but ridiculous. The governor could scarcely <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> the officer who summoned him to surrender; but being convinced how matters stood, the only possible step was taken, namely, to surrender the whole island and everything in it, at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Along with the island there fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the captors a ship of 60 guns, with 250 sail of merchantmen, while the value of property on the island was estimated at no less than four millions <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. This capture became afterwards a subject of discussion in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, where the conduct of the British commanders was severely scrutinized by Mr Burke. The admiral and general made their defense in person; but the minority at that time were far from being satisfied; and it was supposed that on the change of ministry a rigid inquiry would have been set on foot, had not the splendour of Admiral Rodney's victory over de Grasse put an end to all thoughts of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The island of St Eustatius is naturally of such difficult access, as already observed, that it is almost impossible for an enemy to effect a landing if proper care is taken by those who are in possession of it. This very circumstance proved the ruin of the new possessors. The British, secure in their inaccessible situation, conducted themselves in such a manner as induced the Marquis de Bouille to make an attempt to regain it. Having failed from Martinique at the head of 200 men, he arrived on the 26th of November 1781, off one of the landing places. places of the island, which was deemed so inaccessible that it had been left without a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>. With much loss and difficulty, however, he landed here with four or five hundred of his people during the night. The appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> put an end to his landing any more; and he now <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself obliged either to relinquish the enterprise or to attack the garrison, which was almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those he had on the island. He chose the latter; and was favoured in his enterprise by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> negligence of his antagonists. A difficult pass, which a few men might have occupied with success against a great number, was left unguarded, which the marquis secured in time, and then pushed forward with the utmost expedition. The British, mistaking a body of Irish troops which attended the French commander for their own comrades, suffered them to approach without thinking of opposing them. They were then exercising on the parade; but were soon made sensible of their fatal mistake by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> discharge from their supposed friends, by which many were killed and wounded. The surprise occasioned by this sudden attack was so great, that no resistance could be made; especially as their commanding officer, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Cockburn, who happened at that instant to come upon the parade, was made prisoner. A number of them, however, hastened to the fort with a view of making head against the enemy; but the French had already taken possession of the gate, and prevented the drawbridge from being raised. They entered the fort; which, being surrendered by those who had taken shelter in it, the rest of the garrison, dispersed in various places, and imagining the number of the enemy to be much greater than it really was, submitted without any opposition. The French commander took this opportunity of showing his disinterestedness in pecuniary matters. Among the spoils that fell into his hands a large sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was claimed by the British commanding officer as being his private property, which was generously restored to him: in like manner the property of the Dutch inhabitants was referred to them, and nothing was allowed to be seized but the produce arising from the sale of prizes that had been taken by the English when they captured the island.

EUSTYLE

Pages 384-384

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in which the pillars are placed at the most convenient distance one from another, the intercolumniations being <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> two diameters and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, except those in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, before and behind, which are three diameters distant.

EUTERPE

Pages 384-384

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Mnemosyne. She presided over music, and was looked upon as the inventor of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>. She is represented as crowned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and holding a flute in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>: Some mythologists attributed to her the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of tragedy, more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed to be the production of Melpomene.

EUTHYMYIA

Pages 384-384

among the Greeks, signified such a disposition <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state of the mind, as could not be ruffled either by good or bad fortune, by sickness or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, good or evil.

EUTROPIUS

Pages 384-384

FLAVIUS, a Latin author, in the 4th century, was secretary to Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and afterwards bore arms under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, and followed that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in his expedition against the Persians. He wrote an Abridgement of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, from the foundation of Rome to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a>; the best edition of which is that of Miss Le Fevre, afterwards Madame Dacier, published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Dauphin, in 4to, in the year 1683.

EUTYCHIANS

Pages 384-385
ancient heretics, who denied the duplicity of natures in Christ; thus denominated from Eutyches, the archimandrite, or abbot of a monastery at Constantinople, who began to propagate his opinion A.D. 428. He did not, however, seem quite steady and confident in his sentiments: for he appeared to allow of two natures, even before the union; which was apparently a consequence he drew from the principles of the Platonic philosophy, which supposes a pre-existence of souls: accordingly, he believed that the soul of Jesus Christ had been united to the divinity before the incarnation; but then he allowed no distinction of natures in Jesus Christ since his incarnation. This heresy was first condemned in a synod held at Constantinople by Flavian, in 448, approved by the council of Ephesus, called convivus latronum, in 499, and re-examined, and confirmed, in the general council of Chalcedon in 451. The legates of Pope Leo, who assisted at it, maintained, that it was not enough to define, that there were two natures in Jesus Christ; but insisted strenuously, that, to remove all equivocations, they must add these terms, without being changed, or confounded, or divided. The heresy of the Eutychians, which made a very great progress throughout the east, at length became divided into several branches. Nicephorus makes mention of no fewer than twelve: some called Schematists, or Apparentists, as only attributing to Jesus Christ a phantom or appearance of flesh, and no real flesh; others, Theodofians, from Theodolius bishop of Alexandria; others, Jacobites, from one James (Jacobus), of Syria; which branch established itself principally in Armenia, where it still subsists. Others were called Acaphists, q.d., without head; and Severians, from a monk called Severus, who seized on the see of Antioch in 513. These last were subdivided into five factions, viz. Agnoeists, who attributed some ignorance to Jesus Christ; the followers of Paul; Mitraists, that is, the black Angelites, thus called from the place where they were assembled; and lastly, Adrites and Cononites. EUTYCHIANS was also the name of another sect, half Arian half Eunomian; which arose at Constantinople in the fourth century. It being then a matter of mighty controversy among the Eunomians at Constantinople, whether or not the Son of God knew the last day and hour of the world, particularly with regard to that passage in the gospel of St Matthew, chap. xxiv. ver. 36, or rather that in St Mark, xiii. 32, where it is explicated, that the Son did not know it, but the Father only; Eutychius made no scruple to maintain, even in writing, that the Son did not know it; which sentiment displeasing the leaders of the Eunomian party, he separated from them, and made a journey to Eunomius, who was then in exile. That heretic acquiesced fully in Eutychius's doctrine, and admitted him to his communion. Eunomius dying soon after, the chief of the Eunomians at Constantinople refused to admit Eutychius; who, upon this, formed a particular sect of such as adhered to him, called Eutychians. This same Eutychius, with one Theopronius, as was all in Sozomen's time, were the occasions of all the changes made by the Eunomians in the administration of baptism; which consisted, according to Nicephorus, in only using one immersion, and not doing it in the name of the Trinity, but in memory of the death of Jesus Christ. Nicephorus calls the chief of that sect, not Eutychius, but Euphychius, and his followers Eunomian/Eunuchians.

EUTYCHIUS

Pages 385-385
patriarch of Alexandria, lived about the ninth age; and wrote annals in the Arabic language, printed in Oxford in 1658, with a Latin version by Mr Pococke. Selden had printed something of his before. EUXINE or "xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black Sea, forms part of the boundary between Europe and Asia. It receives the Neiper, the Danube, and other large rivers; and extends from 28 to 40 degrees of E. Long. and from 40 to 46 of N. Lat. The ancients imagined this sea to have been originally only a lake or standing pool which broke first into the Propontis, and then into the Egean, washing away by degrees the earth which first kept it within bounds, and formed the two channels of the Bosphorus Thraceus and Hellespont, now the Dardanelles.—It was anciently called the Aenus, supposed to be from Athenea the son of Gomer, who is said to have settled near it. This original being forgotten in length of time, the Greeks explained it by inhoptable, which the word Axenos literally signifies; and therefore, when they came to consider the inhabitants of these coasts as more civilized and hospitable, they changed the name into Euxinus, which it still retains.

EVACUANTS

Pages 366-366

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, are properly such medicines as diminish the animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, by throwing out some morbid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> redundant humor; or such as thin, attenuate, and promote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and circulation thereof.

EVACUATION

Pages 366-366

in Medicine, the art of diminishing, emptying, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> attenuating, the humours of the body.

EVAGRIUS SCHOLASTICUS

Pages 366-366

a famous historian, born at Epiphania, about the year 536. He practised the profession of an advocate, from which he was called Scholasticus, which name was then given to the pleaders at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. He was also tribune and keeper of the prefect's dispatches. He wrote an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which begins where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> and Theodoret ended theirs; and other works, for which he was rewarded by the emperors Tiberius and Mauricius. M. de Valois published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> a good edition of Evagrius's ecclesiastical history, in folio; and it was republished at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> in 1620, in folio, by William <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, with additional notes of various authors.

EVANDER

Pages 366-366

a famous Arcadian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, called the son of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, on account of his eloquence, brought a colony of his people into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, about 60 years before the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; when Faunus, who then reigned over the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>, gave him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in which he settled with his friends. He is said to have taught the Latins the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of letters, and the art of husbandry. He kindly received <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> when he returned from the conquest of Geryon, and he was the first who raised him altars. He gave Æneas assistance against the Rutuli, and distinguished himself by his hospitality. It is said that he first brought the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> into Italy, and introduced there the worship of the Greek deities. He was honoured as a god after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and his subjects raised him an altar on Mount Aventine.

EVANGELISTS

Pages 366-367

the inspired authors of the gospels. The word is derived from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον, formed of εὖ, bene, "well," and αγγέλος, "angel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> messenger." The denomination evangelists was likewise given in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to such as preached the gospel up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, without being attached to any particular church, being either commissioned by the apostles to instruct the nations, or of their own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> abandoning every worldly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, and consecrating themselves EUC [339] EUC Evangelists to the sacred office of preaching the gospel. In which some interpreters think it is that St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, who was one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> deacons, is called the evangelist, in the 21st <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Acts of the Apostles, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> 8. Again, St Paul <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to Timothy, ep. ii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. iv. ver. 5, bids him do the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of an evangelist. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, Eph. iv. 11, ranks the evangelists after the apostles and prophets.

EVANID

Pages 367-367

a name given by some authors to such colours as are of no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, as those in the rainbow, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> before and after sunset, &c. Evans colours are also called fantastic and emphatic colours.

EVANTES

Pages 367-367

in antiquity, the priestesses of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, thus called, because in celebrating the orgia they ran about as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> distracted, crying, Evan, evan, oh evan. See BACCHANALIA.

EVAPORATION

Pages 367-367

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, signifies the conversion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> into vapour, so that it becomes specifically <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">METEOROLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EVASION

Pages 367-367

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used for any subtle endeav- our to set aside <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to escape the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the law, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be endured. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a per- son says to another that he will not strike him, but will give him a pot of ale to strike him first, and according- ly he strikes, the returning of it is punishable; for no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall evade the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the law by such a pretence to cover his malice.

EVATES

Pages 367-367

a branch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Celtic philosophers. Strabo divides the British and Gaulish philosophers into three sects; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BARDS">bards</a>, evates, and druids. He adds, that the bards were the poets and musicians; the evates, the priests and naturalists; and the druids were moralists as well as naturalists: But Marcellus and Hornius reduce them all to two sects, viz., the Bards and Druids.

EVEHAM

Pages 369-369
or EVESHOLM, commonly called Evesham, a town of Worcestershire, seated on a gentle ascent from the river Avon, over which there is a bridge of seven arches. It is 9½ miles from London, 14 miles from Worcester, and has a harbour for barges. It is an old borough, reckoned the second in the county; and sends two members to parliament. It had formerly an abbey with a mitred abbot; which abbey when standing was one of the largest and most stately of any in the kingdom. It was governed by a bailiff, till King James I. at the request of his son Prince Henry, gave it a charter for a mayor, 7 aldermen, 12 capital burgesses, a recorder, and chamberlain, who are all of the common council, with 24 other burgesses called assistants. Four of the aldermen, and the mayor for the time being, are justices of the peace; and of oyer and terminer, and of gaol delivery, for all offences in the corporation, except high treason; and the corporation has power to try and execute felons within the borough. Here are two parish churches; but the bells of both have been removed to a beautiful old tower which was one of the gates of the abbey. The town is noted for the great victory obtained near it by Prince Edward, afterwards King Edward I., over Simon Montfort, the great earl of Leicester, who was killed in the battle. There is an open prospect from hence of the spacious valley called the vale of Evesham or vale of Gloucester, which so abounds with the best of corn, as well as pasture for sheep, that it is reckoned the granary of all these parts. The vale runs all along the banks of the Avon, from Tewkesbury to Pershore, and Stratford in Warwickshire, and the river is so far navigable. It has a weekly market and four fairs. The market-house built by Sir Edward Hobby has its upper apartments used by the corporation for a sessions-house, and formerly for the affizes of the county. There are considerable garden grounds around the place, the produce of which supplies the adjacent towns.

EVERGETES

Pages 369-369

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> signifying benefactor, given to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon, and to Antigonus Doson, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It was also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given to the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and Pontus, and we often see among the former an Alexander Evergetes, and among the latter a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> Evergetes. Some of the Roman emperors also claimed that epithet of Benevolent and Humane.

EVERGREEN

Pages 369-369

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of perennials, which continue their verdure, leaves, &c. all the year: such are hollies, phyllreas, lauriflumines, bays, pines, firs, cedars of Lebanon, &c. EVERLASTING <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LATHYRUS">Lathyrus</a>, Rotany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. EVES DROPPERS. See EAVES-Droppers.

EVICTED

Pages 369-369

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements by law.

EVIDENCE

Pages 369-369

that perception of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> which arises either from the testimony of the senses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from an induction of reason. Evidence, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> by testimony of men upon oath, or by writings or records. It is called evidence, because thereby the point in issue in a cause to be tried is to be made evident to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>; for probatio debet esse evidenter et perspicue. The system of evidence, as now established in our courts of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, is very full, comprehensive, and refined; far different from, and superior to, anything known in the middle ages;—as far superior in that as in all other improvements and refinements in science, arts, and manners. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of evidence during the ages of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> was extremely imperfect, and the people were incapable of making any rational improvement. Thus it was the imperfection of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> reason that caused the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and introduction of the ORDEAL, as an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the Supreme Being. As men are unable to comprehend the manner in which the Deity carries on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the universe, by equal, fixed, and general laws, they are apt to imagine, that in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> which their passions or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> render important in their own eyes, the Supreme Ruler of all ought visibly to display his power in vindicating innocence, and punishing vice.

EVIL

Pages 369-369

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, &c. is either moral <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. Moral evil is the disagreement between the actions of a moral <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, and the rule of those actions, whatever it is.—Natural evil is, whatever destroys or any way disturbs the perfection of natural beings: such as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BLINDNESS">blindness</a>, diseases, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s Evil, or Scrofula. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EVIL-MERODACH

Pages 369-370

the son and successor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>. nezzar the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in the year of the world 3443; but governed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> during the indisposition of his father, who, after <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, having recovered his understanding, once more ascended the throne; and, as some believe, imprisoned his son Evil-Merodach. In this confinement it is supposed that Evil-Merodach made an acquaintance and friendship with Jehoiachim king of Judah, who had been carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar. However that was, it is certain, that, soon after his succession to the throne, he delivered the king of Judah out of prison, after a confinement of 37 years, heaped many favours on him, and placed him above all the other kings who were at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Babylon, (2 Kings xxv. 27. Jer. lii. 31.). Evil-Merodach reigned but one year, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of Archbishop Usher; but Dr Prideaux <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have him to have reigned two years; and was succeeded by Neriglissar his father's husband, who having been at the head of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> that put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, reigned in his stead. Others will have it, that this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was immediately succeeded by his son <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BELSHAZZAR">Belshazzar</a>.

EVOCATI

Pages 374-375
soldiers among the Romans, who having served their full time in the army, went afterwards volunteers at the request of some favourite general; on which which account they were called by the honourable names of Emeriti and Beneficiarii.

EVOCATION

Pages 375-375

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> always observed by them at the undertaking a siege, wherein they solemnly called upon the gods and goddesses of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to forfayce it and come over to them. Without the performance of this ceremony, they either thought that the place could not be taken, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that it would be a sacrilege to take the gods prisoners. They always took it for granted that their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> was heard, and that the gods had deserted the place and come over to them, provided they were able to make themselves matters of it.

EVOLUTION

Pages 375-375

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> made by a body of troops, when they are obliged to change their form and disposition, in order to preserve a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> occupy another, to attack an enemy with more advantage, or to be in a condition of defending themselves the better. It consists in doublings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-marches, conversions, &c. A battalion doubles the ranks, when attacked in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> or rear, to prevent its being flanked or surrounded; for then a battalion fights with a larger front. The files are doubled, either to accommodate themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a narrow ground, or to resist an enemy that attacks them in flank. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ground <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow it, conversion is much preferable; because, after conversion, the battalion is in its first form, and opposes the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>-leaders, which are generally the best men, to the enemy; and likewise, because doubling the files in a new or not well-disciplined regiment, they may happen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into disorder. See Doubling.

EVOLVULUS

Pages 375-375

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 29th order, Campanaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EVREMONT

Pages 376-376
CHARLES DE ST DENIS, a polite scholar and soldier, was born at St Denis le Guant in Lower Normandy in 1613. He was intended for the profession of the law, and entered on the study; but he soon quitted it, and was made an ensign before he was 16. A military life did not hinder him from cultivating polite literature; and he signalized himself by his politer and wit as much as by his bravery. The king made him a marshal de camp, and gave him a pension of 3000 livres per annum. He served under the duke of Candale in the war of Guienne; and in Flanders, till the suspension of arms was agreed on between France and Spain: he afterwards accompanied Cardinal Mazarine when he went to conclude the peace with Don Lewis de Haro, the king of Spain's first minister. He wrote, as he had promised, a long letter to the marquis de Crequi, of this negotiation; in which he showed, that the cardinal had sacrificed the honour of France to his own private interest, and rallied him in a very satirical manner. This letter falling into the hands of the cardinal's creatures some time after his death, was represented as a base crime, and he was obliged to fly to Holland. He had too many friends in England (whither he had taken a tour the year before with the count de Soiffons, sent to compliment Charles II, upon his restoration) to make any long stay in Holland; and therefore passed over into England, where he was received with great respect, and admitted into intimate friendship with several persons of distinction. The king gave him a pension of 300l. a-year. He had a great desire to return to his native country; and, after the peace of Nimeguen, wrote a letter in verse to the king of France to ask leave, but in vain. Upon the death of King Charles, he lost his pension. He did not rely much on King James, though that prince had shown himself extremely kind to him. The Revolution was advantageous to him. King William, who had known him in Holland, gave him substantial marks of his favour. He died of a strangury in 1703, aged 90; and was interred in Westminster abbey, where a monument is erected to his memory. His behaviour was engaging, his humour cheerful, and he had a strong disposition to satire: he professed the Roman religion, in which he was born; but at the bottom was certainly a freethinker. He always spoke of his disgrace with the resolution of a gentleman; and whatever strong desire he had to return to his country, he never solicited the favour with meanness; therefore, when this leave was signified to him unexpectedly in the decline of his life, he replied, that the infirmities of age did not permit him to leave a country where he lived agreeably. There have been many editions of his works: but the best is that of Amsterdam in 1726, in 5 vols. 12mo, to which is prefixed his life by Doctor Des Maizeaux; who has also given an accurate English translation of them in 3 vols. 8vo.

EWERY

Pages 385-385

in the British customs, an office in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, to which belongs the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, of laying the cloth, and serving up <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in silver ewers after dinner.

EX

Pages 385-385

a river that rises in a barren tract of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, called Exmore, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>; and after being joined by several little streams, runs by Tiverton, where there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river. About <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles below Tiverton, it is joined by a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stream called the Colomtton; and about two miles lower, by another stream formed by the junction of the Horton and Credy. With these additions, it washes the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOPSHAM">Topsham</a>, above four miles below Exeter, it receives another considerable addition to its stream; two miles farther, it is joined by the Ken, and falls into the ocean at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXMOUTH">Exmouth</a>, after a course of about 45 miles. Ships of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> burden go up to Topsham, from whence vessels of 150 tons are conveyed to the quay at Exeter, by means of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> canal. The Ex is navigable for vessels of considerable burden to Topsham. The passage, however, at the mouth of the river is but narrow, having rocks on the east side and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> sands on the west; nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> more than six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet deep at low water, but the tide rises 14 or 15 feet, so that it is deep enough at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water. When ships are within the bar they may ride abreast at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Starcross, about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from the river's mouth; but those that go to Topsham <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a> on the goze at low water.

EX OFFICIO

Pages 385-385

among lawyers, signifies the power a person has, by virtue of his office, to do certain acts without being applied to. Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace may, ex officio, at his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, take surety of the peace, without complaint made by any person whatsoever. There was formerly an oath ex officio, whereby a supposed offender was compelled in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to confess, accuse, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clear himself of a crime; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> is repealed.

EX POST FACTO

Pages 385-385

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, something done after another: thus an estate granted may be good by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> ex <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> facto, that was not so at first, as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. EXACERBATION. See PAROXYSM.

EX-POST-FACTO

Pages 421-421

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes something done after another thing that was committed before. An estate granted may be made good by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> ex-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-facto, that was not so at first by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, &c.

EXACITION

Pages 385-385

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a wrong done by an officer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a person in pretended authority, in taking a reward or fee that is not allowed by law. A person guilty of exactation may be fined and imprisoned. It is often confounded with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTORTION">EXTORTION</a>.

EXACUM

Pages 385-385

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 20th order, Rotaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. EXÆRESIS, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the operation of extracting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> taking away something that is hurtful to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body.

EXAGGERATION

Pages 385-385

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, a method by which the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, in representing things, changes them too much, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> makes them too strong, either in respect of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> or colouring. It differs from caricaturing, in that the latter perverts or gives a turn to the features of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, &c., which they had not, whereas exaggeration only heightens or improves what they had.

EXALTATION

Pages 385-386
or ELEVATION, is chiefly used in a figurative sense, for the raising or advancing a person to some ecclesiastical dignity; and particularly to the papacy. EXALTATION of the Cross is a feast of the Romish church, held on the 14th of September; in memory, as is generally supposed, of this, that the emperor Heraclius brought back the true cross of Jesus Christ on his shoulders, to the place on Mount Calvary from which it had been carried away 14 years before by Cosroes king of Persia, at his taking of Jerusalem, under the reign of the emperor Phocas. The cross was delivered up by a treaty of peace made with Siroe, Cosroes's son. The institution of this treaty is commonly said to have been signalized by a miracle; in that Heraclius could not stir out of Jerusalem with the cross while he had the imperial vestments on enriched with gold and precious stones, but bore it with ease in a common dress. But long before the reign of Heraclius there had been a feast of the same denomination observed both in the Greek and Latin churches, on occasion of what our Saviour said in St John xiii. 32. And I, if I be exalted, or lifted up, will draw all men unto me. And again, in chap. viii. ver. 28. When you have exalted, or lifted up the Son of Man, then shall ye know that I am he. The feast of the dedication of the temple built by Constantine was held, says Nicephorus, on the 14th of September, Exaltation September, the day on which the temple had been consecrated, in the year 335; and this feast was also called the exaltation of the cross, because it was a ceremony therein, for the bishop of Jerusalem to ascend a high place, built by Constantine for that purpose, in manner of a pulpit, called by the Greeks the sacred mysteries of God, or the holiness of God, and there hoist up the cross for all the people to see it. Exaltation, in Physics, denotes the act, or operation, of elevating, purifying, sublimizing, or perfecting any natural body, its principles and parts; also the quality or disposition which bodies acquire by such operation. The term exaltation has been peculiarly affected by the chemists and alchemists; who imagining it to have some extraordinary emphasis, are employing it on every occasion. Exaltation, in Astrology, is a dignity which a planet acquires in certain signs or parts of the zodiac; which dignity is supposed to give it an extraordinary virtue, efficacy, and influence. The opposite sign, or part of the zodiac, is called the dejection of the planet. Thus the 1st degree of Cancer is the exaltation of Jupiter, according to Albumazar, because it was the ascendant of that planet at the time of the creation; that of the sun is in the 19th degree of Aries, and its dejection in Libra; that of the moon is in Taurus, &c. Ptolemy gives the reason of this in his first book De Quadrup. Examination, an exact and careful search or inquiry, in order to discover the truth or fallacy of a thing. Self-Examination, is a point much insisted on by divines, and particularly the ancient fathers, by way of preparation to repentance. St Ignatius reduces it to five points; viz. 1. A returning thanks to God for his benefits. 2. A begging of grace and light, to know and distinguish our sins. 3. A running over all our actions, occupations, thoughts, and words, in order to learn what has been offensive to God. 4. A begging of pardon, and conceiving a sincere sorrow for having displeased him. And, 5. Making a firm resolution not to offend him any more; and taking the necessary precautions to preserve ourselves from it. Examiners, in chancery, two officers of that court, who examine, upon oath, witnesses produced in causes depending there, by either the complainant or defendant, where the witnesses live in London or near it. Sometimes parties themselves, by particular order, are examined. In the country, above 20 miles from London, on the parties joining in commission, witnesses are examined by commissioners, being usually counsellors or attorneys not concerned in the cause. Example, in a general sense, denotes a copy or pattern. Example, in a moral sense, is either taken for a type, instance, or precedent, for our admonition, that we may be cautioned against the faults or crimes which others have committed, by the bad consequences which have ensued from them; or example is taken for a pattern for our imitation, or a model for us to copy after. That examples have a peculiar power above the naked precept, to dispose us to the practice of virtue and holiness, may appear by considering, 1. That they most clearly express to us the nature of our duties in their subjects and sensible effects. General precepts form abstract ideas of virtue; but in examples, virtues are most visible in all their circumstances. 2. Precepts instruct us in what things are our duty; but examples assure us that they are possible. When we see men like ourselves, who are united to frail flesh, and in the same condition with us, to command their passions, to overcome the most glorious and glittering temptations, we are encouraged in our spiritual warfare. 3. Examples, by secret and lively incentive, urge us to imitation. We are touched in another manner by the visible practice of good men, which reproaches our defects, and obliges us to the same zeal which laws, though wise and good, will not effect. The example of our Saviour is most proper to form us to holiness; it being absolutely perfect, and accommodated to our present state. There is no example of a mere man that is to be followed without limitation: But the example of Christ is absolutely perfect; his conversation was a living law: "He was holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners." Example, in Rhetoric, denotes an imperfect kind of induction or argumentation; whereby it is proved, that a thing which happened on some other occasion will happen again on the present one, from the similitude of the cases. As, "The war of the Thebans, against their neighbours the Phocians, was ruinous; consequently, that of the Athenians against their neighbours, will likewise be fatal." Exanthema, among Physicians, denotes any kind of efflorescence or eruption, as the measles, purple spots in the plague, or malignant fevers, &c. Exarch, in antiquity, an appellation given, by the emperors of the east, to certain officers sent into Italy, in quality of vicars, or rather prefects, to defend that part of Italy which was yet under their obedience, particularly the city of Ravenna, against the Lombards, who had made themselves masters of the greatest part of the reft. The residence of the exarch was at Ravenna; which city, with that of Rome, was all that was left the emperors. The first exarch was the patrician Boetius, famous for his treatise, De Consolatione Philosophiae; appointed in 568 by the younger Justin. The exarchs subsisted about 185 years, and ended in Eutychius: under whose exarchate the city of Ravenna was taken by the Lombard king Astulphus, or Alolophus. The emperor Frederic created Heraclius, archbishop of Lyons, a descendant of the illustrious house of Montboissier, exarch of the whole kingdom of Burgundy; a dignity till that time unknown anywhere but in Italy, particularly in the city of Ravenna. Homer, Philo, and other ancient authors, give likewise the name exarchus to the choragus or master of the fingers, in the ancient choruses, or him who sung first; the word αρχων or αρχηται, signifying equally to begin, and to command. Exarch of a Diocese was, anciently, the same with primate. This dignity was inferior to the patriarchal, yet greater than the metropolitan.

EXARCH ALSO

Pages 386-387

h also denotes an officer, still subsisting in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; being a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> legate à latere of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, whose office it is to visit the provinces allotted him, in order to inform himself of the the lives and manners of the clergy; take cognizance of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> causes; the manner of celebrating divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; the administration of the sacraments, particularly confession; the observance of the canons; monastic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; affairs of marriages, divorces, &c., but above all, to take an account of the several revenues which the patriarch receives from several churches; and, particularly, as to what regards the collecting the same. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXARCH">exarch</a>, after having greatly enriched himself in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, frequently rises to the patriarchate itself. Exarch is also used, in the eastern church antiquity, for a general or superior over several monasteries; the same that we otherwise call archimandrite; being exempted, by the patriarch of Constantinople, from the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>; as are now the generals of the Roman monastic orders.

EXAUCTORATIO

Pages 387-387

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, differed from the missio, which was a full discharge, and took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> after they had served in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> 25 years; whereas the exauctoratio was only a partial discharge: they lost their pay indeed, but still kept under their colours <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vexilla, though not under the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">aquila</a> (or eagle), which was the standard of the legion: whence, instead of Legionarii, they were called Subsignarii, and were retained till they had either served their full <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> or had lands assigned them. The exauctoratio took place after they had served 17 years.

EXCALCEATION

Pages 387-387

among the Hebrews, was a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, whereby a widow, whom her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> refused to marry, had a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to summon him to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and, upon his refusal, might excalceate him, that is, pull off one of his shoes, and spit in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>; both of them actions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ignominy.

EXCELLENCY

Pages 387-387

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> anciently given to kings and emperors, but now to ambassadors, generals, and other persons who are not qualified for that of highness, and yet are to be elevated above the other inferior dignities.

EXCENTRIC

Pages 387-387

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to circles and spheres which have not the same centre, and consequently are not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>; in opposition to concentric, where they are parallel, having one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre.

EXCENTRICITY

Pages 387-387

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is the distance of the centre of the orbit of a planet from the centre of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; that is, the distance between the centre of the ellipse and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> thereof.

EXCEPTION

Pages 387-387

something reserved, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> set aside, and not included in a rule. It is become proverbial, that there is no rule without an exception; intimating, that it is impossible to comprehend all the particular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, under one and the same maxim. But it is dangerous following the exception preferably to the rule. Exception, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes a stop or stay to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; and is either dilatory or peremptory, in proceedings at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; but in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> it is what the plaintiff alleges against the sufficiency of an answer, &c. An exception is no more than the denial of what is taken to be good by the other party, either in point of law or pleading. The counsel in a cause are to take all their exceptions to the record at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> has delivered any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of it.

EXCESS

Pages 387-387

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between any two unequal numbers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities, or that which is left after the lesser is taken from or out of the greater.

EXCHANGE

Pages 397-399

e signifies also a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in most considerable trading cities, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, negotiants, a- gents, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, brokers, interpreters, and other persons concerned in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, meet on certain days, and at certain times thereof, to confer and treat together of matters relating to exchanges, remittances, payments, adventures, assurances, freightments, and other merca- ntile negotiations, both by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and several cities of France, these places are called burfs; at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and Lyons, places de change; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, colleges of merchants. These assemblies are held with so much exactness, and merchants and negotiants are so indispensably required to attend at them, that a person's absence alone makes him to be suspected of a failure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bankruptcy. The most considerable exchanges in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, are that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>; and that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Exchange. Even in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, there were places for the merchants to meet, in most of the consid- erable cities of the empire. That said by some to have been built at Rome in the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> 259, 493 years before our Saviour, under the consulate of Appius Claudius and Publius Servilius, was called col- legium mercatorum; wherefore it is pretended there are still some remains, called by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Romans oggia, the lodge; and now usually the place of St. George. This notion of a Roman exchange is supposed to be founded Exchange, founded on the authority of Livy, whose words are as follows: viz. Certamen confutatus incidet uter dedicaret Mercurii aedem. Senatus a se rem <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> populum rejicit: utri eorum dedicatio jusfa populati <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">data</a> est, eum praecipuam annona, mercatorum collegium instituire jusfa. Liv. lib. ii. But it must be here remarked, that collegium never signified a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in the purer ages of the Latin tongue; so that collegium mercatorum instituire must not be rendered to build an exchange for the merchants, but to incorporate the merchants into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. As <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> was the god of traffic, this aedes Mercurii seems to have been chiefly designed for the devotions of this company or corporation. Exchange, Bills of. The following information concerning the origin of bills of exchange is extracted from Beckmann's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Inventions. "I shall not here repeat (says he) what has been collected by many learned men respecting the important history of this noble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, but only lay before my readers an ordinance of the year 1394, concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of bills of exchange, and also two bills of the year 1424, as they may serve to illustrate farther what has been before said on the subject by others. These documents are, indeed, more modern than those found by Raphael de Turre in the writings of the jurist Baldus, which are dated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> the 9th 1328; but they are attended with such circumstances as sufficiently prove that the method of transacting business by bills of exchange was fully established so early as the fourteenth century; and that the present form and terms were even then used. For this important information I am indebted to Mr Von Martens, who found it in a book which, as far as I know, has never been noticed in any literary journal, though it is much more deserving of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> than many others better known. It is a history, written in Spanish, of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> trade and other branches of commerce at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, taken entirely from the archives of that city, and accompanied with documents from the same source, which abound with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> highly interesting (a). Among these is an ordinance issued by the city of Barcelona in the year 1394, that bills of exchange should be accepted within twenty-four hours after they were presented; and that the acceptance should be written on the back of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. "In the year 1424, the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, in Flanders, requested the magistrates of Barcelona to inform them what was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice, in regard to bills of exchange, when the person who presented a bill raised <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> on it in an unusual manner, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of its not being paid, and by these means increased the expenses so much that the drawer would not consent to sustain the loss. The bill which gave occasion Exchange, to this question is inserted in the memorial. It is written in the short form still used; which certainly seems to imply <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. It speaks of advance; and it appears that first and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> bills were at that time drawn, and that when bills were not accepted, it was customary to protest them. "As this article is of great importance I shall here transcribe it, from vol. ii. p. 203: "Cum de mensibus Aprilis et Maii ultimo elapsi, Antonius Quarti, mercator Lucanus rhedens in villa Brugenfi, Joanne Colom, mercatore civitatis Barchinonae, etiam rhedente in praedicta villa Brugenfi, duo milia scutorum Philippi, quolibet feuto pro xxii grosfi computato, solvendi per Franciscum de Prato mercatorem Florentiae, more solito, in Barchinonae, mediatis Petro Gilberto et Petro Olivo, et mediatis Petro Scorpi, et supradicto Petro Gilberto, mercatoribus Cardonae: prout de dictis cambiis apparet quattuor litteris papireis, quarum tenores sequentur. "Superscriptio autem prime litterae fuit talis: Franciscus de Prato et comp. a Barcelone. Tenor vero eiudem ad intra fuit talis: Al nome de Dio, Amen, à xxviii. Aprile 1404. Pagate per quefa prima di camb. à ufanza à Piero Gilberto, è Piero Oavò feuti mille à fold. x. Barfelonefi per feuto, i quali feuti mille fono per cambio che con Giovani Colombo à grossi xxii., di g. feuto: et pag. à noftro conto: et Christo vi guardi. Subtus vero erat scriptum: Antonio Quarti Sal de Bruggias. "Superscriptio vero secunda litterae fuit talis: Franciscus de Prato et comp. a Barcelone. Et <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> intra fic habebatur: Al nome de Dio, Amen, à di xviii. di Magio 1424. Pagate per quefa prima di camb. à ufanza à Piero Gilberto et à P. de Scorpo feuti mille de Felippo à fold. x. Barfelonefi per feuto: i quali feuti mille fono per cambio che con Giov. Colombo à grossi xxii., di g. feuto: et pag. à noftro conto: et Christo vi guardi. Subtus vero erat sic scriptum: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">Ant</a>. Quadri Sal de Bruggias.* Bills of exchange are justly considered as of the greatest importance to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of commerce; but several queries have been proposed respecting them, which do not as yet appear to have received a satisfactory solution. It still seems to be a disputed point, whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> ought to consider them as nothing more than a deposit belonging to the drawer, and successively confided to the remitters; or as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> capable of being transferred, and entirely vested in the holder at all times, who should be alone responsible for neglecting it, when its value is vitiated. Professor Busch of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> thought that bills of exchange should always be viewed as the exclusive property of the person holding them, which, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> published (a) "Memorias históricas sobre la marina comercio y artes de la antigua ciudad de Barcelona, por D. Antonio de Capmany y de Montpalau." <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> 1799, 2 vol. 4to. As a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of what I have said above, I shall mention the following important article, which may be found in this work. A <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> tariff, written in Latin, of the year 1221, in which occur a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of remarkable names and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of merchandise not explained. Another of the like kind in the year 1252. Letters of power to appoint consuls in distant countries, such as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, &c. dated in the years 1266, 1268, and 1321. An ordinance of the year 148, respecting insurances, which required that underwriting should be done in the presence of a notary, and declared policies à feriatures privadas to be null and void. A privilegium of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Andronicus II. to the merchants of Barcelona, written in Greek and Spanish, in 1290. Account of the old Spanish trade with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and saffron; and of the oldest guilds or incorporated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of tradesmen at Barcelona," &c. Exchange, published in 1792, is defended by a number of plausible arguments. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> was applied to the difficult and fluctuating case of the holder of a bill which has several indorsements, where the drawer, the drawee, and persons early indorsing it, have all become bankrupts. Should the person holding it under each bankruptcy prove the entire amount of said bill, it is manifest that he must receive much more than he can in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> claim as his due. It seems most equitable that he should be forced to prove his debt against none but his immediate predecessor, the assignees of such predecessor being allowed a similar proof up to the drawer. To such as are frequently in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of discounting bills, from their commercial situations in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, this becomes a matter of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; for farther information concerning which, we refer our readers to the ingenious work of Professor Busch already alluded to, and to Additions to the Theoretical and Practical Delineation of Commerce, published in 1798 (B).

EXCHEQUER

Pages 399-401

in the British <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of record, in which all causes concerning the revenues and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> are heard and determined, and where the crown revenues are received. It took this name from the cloth that covered the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the court, which was party-coloured, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chequered. This court is said to have been erected by William the Conqueror, its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> being taken from a like court established in Normandy <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Anciently its authority was so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that it was held in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and the acts thereof were not to be examined or controlled in any other of the king's courts; but, at present, it is the last of the four courts at Westminster. In the exchequer, some reckon <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> courts, viz., those of pleas, accounts, receipts, exchequer-chamber (which is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of all the judges on difficult matters in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>), errors in the exchequer, errors in the king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, and, lastly, the court of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> in the exchequer. But the exchequer, for the dispatch of business, is generally divided into two parts; one of which is chiefly conversant in the judicial hearing and deciding of all causes relating to the king's coffers, formerly termed the exchequer of accounts: the other is called the receipt of the exchequer, as being principally employed in receiving and paying of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Vol. VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. Officers of the receipt may take one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> in the Exchequer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, as their fee, for funds issued out; and they are obliged, without delay, to receive the money brought thither; and the money received is to be put into chests under three different locks and keys, kept by three several officers. All sheriffs, bailiffs, &c., are to account in the exchequer; and in the lower part, termed the receipt, the debtors of the king, and persons in debt to them, the king's tenants, and the officers and ministers of the court, are privileged to sue one another, or any stranger, and to be sued in the like actions as are brought in the courts of king's bench and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas. The judicial part of the exchequer, is a court both of law and equity. The court of law is held in the office of pleas, according to the course of common law, before the barons: in this court, the plaintiff ought to be a debtor or accountant to the king; and the leading <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is either a writ of subpeona, or quo minus, which last goes into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, where no process out of courts of law ought to run, except a capias utlagatum. The court of equity is held in the exchequer chamber, before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and barons; but generally, before the barons only: the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> baron being the chief judge to hear and determine all causes. The proceedings of this part of the exchequer are by English <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> and answer, according to the practice of the court of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> that the plaintiff here must set forth, that he is a debtor to the king, whether he be so or not. It is in this court of equity that the clergy exhibit bills for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, &c. Here too the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a> exhibits bills for any matters concerning the crown; and a bill may be exhibited against the king's attorney by any person aggrieved in any cause prosecuted against him on behalf of the king, to be relieved therein; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the plaintiff is to attend on the attorney-general, with a copy of the bill, and procure him to give an answer thereto; in the making of which he may call in any person interested in the cause, or any officer, or others, to instruct him, that the king be not prejudiced thereby; and his answer is to be put in without oath. But, besides the business relating to debtors, farmers, receivers, accountants, &c., all penal punishments, intrusion, and forfeitures upon popular actions, are matters (b) In Vol. III. p. 613, under the article BILL, the old duty on stamps is mentioned, and the new entirely omitted. Bill of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, draft, order, or promissory or other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, payable to the bearer on demand, for 40s. and not exceeding 5l. 5s.; 8d.—Otherwise than to the bearer on demand, when the sum shall amount to 40s. and shall not exceed 1l. 5s.; 1s. Foreign bills of exchange drawn in sets, where the sum shall not exceed 100l. for each bill in each set, 1s. Exceeding 100l. and not 200l.; 2s. Exceeding 200l. and not 500l.; 3s. Exceeding 500l. and not 1000l.; 4s. Exchequers likewise cognizable by this court; where there <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">Excise</a>, also sits a puisne-baron, who administers the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> sheriffs, bailiffs, auditors, receivers, collectors, comptrollers, surveyors, and searchers of all the customs, &c. The exchequer in Scotland has the same privileges and jurisdiction as that of England; and all matters competent to the one are likewise competent to the other. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Book of the Exchequer, is a book under the keeping of the two chamberlains of the exchequer; said to have been composed in 1175 by Gervais of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TILBURY">Tilbury</a>, nephew of King Henry II, and divided into several chapters. Herein is contained a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the court of England, as it then stood, its officers, their ranks, privileges, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, perquisites, power, and jurisdiction; and the revenues of the crown, both in money, grain, and cattle. Here we find, that for one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a>, as much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> might be bought as would serve 100 men a whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; that the price of a fat bullock was only 12 shillings, and a sheep four, &c. Chancellor of the Exchequer. See Chancellor. Exchequer Bills. By statute 5 Ann. c. 13, the lord treasurers may cause exchequer bills to be made of any sums not exceeding 1,500,000l. for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and the duties upon houses were made chargeable with 4l. 10s. per cent. per annum to the bank for circulating them. The bank not paying the bills, actions to be brought against the Company, and the money and damages recovered: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any exchequer bills be lost, upon affidavit of it before a baron of the exchequer, and certificate from such baron, and security to pay the same if found, duplicates are to be made out: also when bills are defaced, new ones shall be delivered.
