The king, or his officers in the exchequer, by former statutes, might borrow money upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of bills, payable on demand, with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> after the rate of 3d. per diem for every 100l. bill. And by 8 and 9 W. III. c. 20, an interest of 5d. a day was allowed for every 100l. But 12 W. III. c. 1, lowered the interest on these bills to 4d. a-day per cent. And by 12 Ann. c. 11, it is sunk to 2d. a-day. Forging exchequer bills, or the indenturements thereof, is felony. Excise, (from the Belgic acciisse, tributum, "tribute,") an inland duty or imposition, paid sometimes upon the consumption of the commodity, or frequently upon the wholesale, which is the last stage before the consumption. This is doubtless, impartially speaking, the most economical way of taxing the subject; the charges of levying, collecting, and managing the excise duties, being considerably less in proportion than in other branches of the revenue. It also renders the commodity cheaper to the consumer, than charging it with customs to the same amount would do; for the reason <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now given, because generally paid in a much later stage of it. But, at the same time, the rigour and arbitrary proceedings of excise laws seem hardly compatible with the temper of a free <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. For the frauds that might be committed in this branch of the revenue, unless a strict watch is kept, make it necessary, wherever it is established, to give the officers a power of entering and searching the houses of such as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in excisable commodities, at any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the day, and, in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, of the night likewise. And the proceedings, in case of transgressions, are so summary and sudden, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may be convicted in two days' time in the penalty of many thousand pounds, by two commissioners or justices of the peace; to the total <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, and disregard of the common law. For which reason, though Lord Clarendon tells us, that to his knowledge the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> (who was made lord treasurer by King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., to oblige his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>) intended to have let up the excise in England, yet it never made a part of that unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s revenue; being first introduced, on the model of the Dutch prototype, by the parliament itself after its rupture with the crown. Yet such was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of its general unpopularity, that when in 1642 "affusions were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> by malignant persons upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons, that they intended to introduce excises, the house for its vindication therein did declare, that these rumours were false and scandalous, and that their authors should be apprehended and brought to condign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>." Its original establishment was in 1643, and its progress was gradual; being at first laid upon those persons and commodities where it was supposed the hardship would be least perceivable, viz. the makers and vendors of beer, ale, cider, and perry; and the royalists at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> soon followed the example of their brethren at Westminster, by imposing a similar duty: both sides protesting that it should be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> no longer than to the end of the war, and then be utterly abolished. But the parliament at Westminster soon after imposed it on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and such a multitude of other commodities, that it might be fairly denominated general: in pursuance of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Mr Pymme (who seems to have been the father of the excise), in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Sir John Hotham, signifying, "that they had proceeded in the excise to many particulars, and intended to go on farther; but that it would be necessary to use the people to it by little and little."—And afterwards, when the nation had been accustomed to it for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years, the succeeding champions of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> boldly and openly declared "the impost of excise to be the most easy and indifferent levy that could be laid upon the people;" and accordingly continued it during the whole usurpation. Upon King Charles's return, it having then been long established, and its produce well known, some part of it was given to the crown, in 12 Car. II. by way of purchase for the feudal tenures and other oppressive parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> revenue. But, from its first origin to the present time, its very name has been odious to the people. It has, nevertheless, been imposed on abundance of other commodities in the reigns of King William III. and every succeeding prince, to support the enormous expenses occasioned by our wars on the continent. Thus brandies and other spirits are now excised at the distillery; printed silks and linens, at the printers; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STARCH">starch</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> powder, at the makers; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver wire, at the wiredrawers; all plate whatsoever, first in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the vender, who pays yearly for a licence to sell it, and afterwards in the hands of the occupier, who also pays an annual duty for having it in his custody; and coaches and other wheel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, for which the occupier is excised; though not with the same circumstances of arbitrary strictness with regard to plate and coaches as in the other instances. To these we may add coffee and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, chocolate and cocoa paste, for which the du- ty is paid by the retailer; all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> wines, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called *sweets*; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> and pasteface, first when made, and again if stained or printed; malt, as before mentioned; vinegars; and the manufacture of glas; for all which the duty is paid by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a>; hops, for which the person that gathers them is answerable; candles and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, which are paid for at the makers; malt liquors brewed for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, which are specified at the brewery; cider and perry at the vendors; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> and skins, at the tanner's; and, lately, tobacco, at the manufacturer's: A <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>, which no friend to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> would wish to see farther increased. The excise was formerly farmed out; but is now managed for the king by commissioners in both kingdoms, who receive the whole product of the excise, and pay it into the exchequer. These commissioners are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in England, and five in Scotland. The former have a salary of £1000 a-year, the latter £600. They are obliged by oath to take no fee or reward but from the king himself; and from them there lies an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to five other commissioners called commissioners of appeals.

EXCISION

Pages 401-401

in a scripture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off of a person from his people, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for some sin by him committed. The Jews, Selden informs us, reckon 36 crimes, to which they pretend this punishment is due. The Rabbins reckon three kinds of excision; one, which destroys only the body; another, which destroys the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> only; and a third, which destroys both body and soul. The first kind of excision they pretend is an untimely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is an utter extinction of the soul; and the third, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the two former: thus, making the foul mortal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> immortal, says Selden, according to the degrees of misbehaviour and wickedness of the people. **EXCLAMATION.** See Oratory, No 85.

EXCLUSION

Pages 401-403
or Bill of Exclusion,** a bill proposed about the close of the reign of King Charles II., for excluding the duke of York, the king's brother, from the throne, on account of his being a Papist. **EXCLUSIVE,** is sometimes used adjectively, thus; *A patent carries with it an exclusive privilege.* Sometimes adverbially: as, *He sent him all the numbers from No 145 to No 247 exclusive;* that is, all between these two numbers, which themselves were excepted. **EXCOECARIA,** a genus of plants belonging to the dioecia clas, and in the natural method ranking under the 38th order, Tricocceae. See Botany Index. **EXCOMMUNICATION,** an ecclesiastical penalty or censure, whereby such persons as are guilty of any notorious crime or offence, are separated from the communion of the church, and deprived of all spiritual advantages. Excommunication is founded on a natural right which all societies have, of excluding out of their body such as violate the laws thereof; and it was originally instituted for preserving the purity of the church; but ambitious ecclesiastics converted it by degrees into an engine for promoting their own power, and inflicted it on the most frivolous occasions. The power of excommunication, as well as other acts of ecclesiastical discipline, was lodged in the hands of the clergy, who distinguished it into the greater and lesser. The lesser excommunication, simply called *aphorismos,* "separation or suspension," consisted in excluding men from the participation of the eucharist, and the prayers of the faithful. But they were not expelled the church; for they had the privilege of being present at the reading of the Scriptures, the sermons, and the prayers of the catechumens and penitents. This excommunication was inflicted for lesser crimes; such as neglecting to attend the service of the church, misbehaviour in it, and the like. The greater excommunication, called *panteles aphorismos,* "total separation and anathema," consisted in an absolute and entire exclusion from the church and the participation of all its rites. When any person was thus excommunicated, notice of it was given by circular letters to the most eminent churches all over the world, that they might all confirm this act of discipline, by refusing to admit the delinquent to their communion. The consequences of this latter excommunication were very terrible. The excommunicated person was avoided in civil commerce and outward conversation. No one was to receive him into his house, nor eat at the same table with him; and when dead, he was denied the solemn rites of burial. The Romish pontifical takes notice of three kinds of excommunication. 1. The minor, incurred by those who have any correspondence with an excommunicated person. 2. The major, which falls upon those who disobey the commands of the holy see, or refuse to submit to certain points of discipline; in consequence of which they are excluded from the church militant and triumphant, and delivered over to the devil and his angels. 3. Anathema, which is properly that pronounced by the pope against heretical princes and countries. In former ages, these papal fulminations were most terrible things; but at present, they are formidable to none but a few petty states of Italy. Excommunication, in the Greek church, cuts off the offender from all communion with the 318 fathers of the first council of Nice, and with the saints; configns him over to the devil and the traitor Judas; and condemns his body to remain after death as hard as a flint or piece of steel, unless he humbles himself and makes atonement for his sins by a sincere repentance. The form abounds with dreadful imprecations; and the Greeks assert, that if a person dies excommunicated, the devil enters into the lifeless corpse; and therefore, in order to prevent it, the relations of the deceased cut his body in pieces, and boil them in wine. It is a custom for the patriarch of Jerusalem annually to excommunicate the pope and the church of Rome; on which occasion, together with a great deal of idle ceremony, he drives a nail into the ground with a hammer, as a mark of malediction. The form of excommunication in the church of England anciently ran thus: By the authority of God the Father Almighty, the Son and Holy Ghost, and of Mary the blessed mother of God, we excommunicate, anathematize, and sequestrate from the pale of holy mother church," &c. The causes of excommunication in England are, contempt of the bishop's court, hereby, neglect of public worship and the sacraments, incontinency, adultery, simony, &c. It is described to be twofold. The less is an ecclesiastical censure, Excommunicate, excluding the party from the participation of the sacraments; the greater proceeds farther, and excludes him not only from these, but from the company of all Christians. But if the judge of any spiritual court excommunicates a man for a cause of which he hath not the legal cognizance, the party may have an action against him at common law, and he is also liable to be indicted at the suit of the king. Heavy as the penalty of excommunication is, considered in a serious light, there are, notwithstanding, many obstinate or profligate men, who would despise the brutum fulmen of mere ecclesiastical censures, especially when pronounced by a petty surrogate in the country, for railing or contumelious words, for non-payment of fees or costs, or other trivial cause. The common law, therefore, compassionately steps in to their aid, and kindly lends a supporting hand to an otherwise tottering authority. Imitating herein the policy of the ancient Britons, among whom, according to Caesar, whoever were interdicted by the druids from their sacrifices, "In numero impiorum ac seculerorum habentur: ab his omnes decedunt, aditum eorum fermonemque defugiant, ne quid ex contagione incommodi accipiant: neque eis potentibus jus reddatur, neque homos illus communicetur." And so with us, by the common law, an excommunicated person is disallowed to do any act that is required to be done by one that is probus et regularis homo. He cannot serve upon juries; cannot be a witness in any court; and, which is the worst of all, cannot bring an action, either real or personal, to recover lands or money due to him. Nor is this the whole; for if, within 40 days after the sentence has been published in the church, the offender does not submit and abide by the sentence of the spiritual court, the bishop may certify such contempt to the king in chancery. Upon which there issues out a writ to the sheriff of the county, called from the bishop's certificate a significavit; or from its effect, a writ de excommunicato capiendo: and the sheriff shall thereupon take the offender and imprison him in the county jail, till he is reconciled to the church, and such reconciliation certified by the bishop; upon which another writ de excommunicato deliberando, issues out of chancery to deliver and release him. Excommunication was also practised among the Jews, who used to expel from their synagogue such as had committed any grievous crime. See the Gospel according to St John, ix. 22. xii. 42. xvi. 2. And Joseph, Antiquities, lib. ix. cap. 22. and lib. xvi. cap. 2. Godwin, in his Moses and Aaron, distinguishes three degrees, or kinds, of excommunication among the Jews. The first he finds intimated in John ix. 22. The second in 1 Cor. v. 5. And the third in 1 Cor. xvi. 22. See Niddah. The rule of the Benedictines gives the name excommunication to the being excluded from the oratory, and the common table of the house, in our inns of court called discomuning. This was the punishment of such monks as came too late. Excommunication, or a being secluded from a participation in the mysteries of religion, was also in use under paganism. Such as were thus excommunicated were forbidden to assist or attend at the sacrifices, or to enter within the temples; and were afterwards delivered over to the demons and furies of hell, with certain imprecations; which was called among the Romans diris devovere. See Excruciation. The Druids among the ancient Britons and Gauls, likewise, made use of excommunication against rebels; and interdicted the communion of their mysteries to such as refused to acquiesce in their decisions. See Druids. Excoriation, in Medicine and Surgery, the galling or rubbing off the cuticle, especially of the parts between the thighs and about the anus. In adults, it is occasioned by riding, much walking, or other vehement exercise, and may be cured by vulnerary applications. In children there is often an excoriation, not only of the parts near the pudenda, chiefly of the groin and scrotum, but likewise in the wrinkles of the neck, under the arms, and in other places; proceeding from the acrimony of urine and sweat; and occasionally itching pains, crying, watching, restlessness, &c. To remedy this, the parts affected may be often washed with warm water, and sprinkled with drying powders, as chalk, hartshorn, but especially tutty, lapis calaminaris, and cerus, which may be tied loosely in a rag, and the powder shook out on the parts. Excrement, whatever is discharged out of the body of animals after digestion; or the fibrous part of the aliment, mixed with the bile, saliva, and other fluids. Urine and the feces are the gross excrements that are discharged out of the bladder or belly. Other excrements are the various humours that are secreted from the blood through the different sinews in the body, and which serve for several uses; such as the saliva, sweat, bile, the pancreatic juice, lymph, the semen, nails, the hair, the horns and hoofs of animals. Alchemists, who have fought everywhere for their great work, as they called it, have particularly operated much on the excrements of men and other animals; but philosophical chemistry has acquired no knowledge from all these alchemical labours, from the obscurity with which their authors have described them. The philosophic chemists have not much examined animal excrements. Of these Homberg is the only one who has particularly analyzed and examined human ordure; and this was done to satisfy an alchemical project of one of his friends, who pretended that from this matter a white oil could be obtained, without smell, and capable of fixing mercury into silver. The oil was found by Homberg, but mercury was not fixed by it. The labours of this able chemist were not, however, useless, like those of the alchemists; because he has clearly related the experiments he made on this matter, in the memoirs of the Academy of Sciences. These experiments are curious, and teach several essential things concerning the nature of excrements. The result of these experiments is as follows: Fresh human feces, being distilled to dryness in a water bath, furnish a clear, watery, insipid liquor, of a disagreeable smell, but which contains no volatile alkali; which is a proof that this matter, although nearly in a putrefactive state, is not however putrefied; for all substances really putrid furnish with this degree of heat a manifest volatile alkali*. The dry residuum of the foregoing experiment, being distilled in a retort with a graduated fire, furnishes a volatile alkaline spirit and salt, Human feces, diluted and lixiviated in water, furnish by filtration and evaporation of the water an oily salt of a nitrous nature, which deflagrates like nitre upon ardent coals, and which inflames in close vessels when heated to a certain degree. The same matter yielded to Homberg, who treated it by a complete fermentation or putrefaction, excited by a digestion during 40 days in a gentle water-bath heat, and who afterwards distilled it, an oil without colour, and without bad smell, and such as he endeavoured to find; but which did not, as we said before, fix mercury into silver.

EXCRESSENCE

Pages 403-403

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, denotes every premature tumour which arises upon the skin, either in the form of a wart <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tubercle. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they are born with a person, as they frequently are, they are called navi materni, or marks from the mother; but if the tumour is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, so as to depend from the skin, like a fleshy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, it is then called a sarcoma. See Surgery.

EXCRETION

Pages 403-403
or SECRETION, in Medicine, a separation of some fluid, mixed with the blood, by means of the glands. Excretions, by which we mean those that evacuate superfluous and heterogeneous humours, purify the mass of blood; the humours which are generated in the blood are excreted by the glands, and are replaced by a sufficient quantity of aliment.

EXCRETORY

Pages 403-403

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to certain little ducts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessels, destined for the reception of a fluid, secreted in certain glandules, and other viscera, for the excretion of it in the appropriated places.

EXCUBIAE

Pages 403-403

in antiquity, the watches and guards kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> by the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. They are contradistinguished from the vigiles which were kept in the night. The excubiae were placed either at the gates and intrenchments <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; for the latter there was allowed a whole manipulus to attend before the praetorium, and four soldiers to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> of every tribune. The excubiae at the gates of the camp, and at the intrenchments, were properly called flationes. One <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of foot and one troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> were assigned to each of the four gates every day. To <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, or abandon their corps of guards, was an unpardonable crime. The triarii, as the most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> order of soldiers, were excused from the ordinary watches; yet being placed opposite to the equites, they were obliged to have an eye over them.

EXCUSATI

Pages 403-403

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote slaves, who, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> to any church for sanctuary, were excused and pardoned by their masters; but these were obliged to take an oath to that purpose before they could have them again; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they broke the oath, they were punished and fined as persons guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>.

EXEAT

Pages 403-403

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, used for a permission which a bishop grants a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> to go out of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> to go out of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>.

EXECRATION

Pages 403-403

in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, consisting of direful curses and marks of infamy: such was that used against <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon by the Athenians. A general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the people being called, they made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, that all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and images of that king, and of all his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, should be demolished, and their very name razed; that all the festivals, sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, priests, and whatever else had been instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of him, should be profaned; that the very places where there had been any monument <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inscription to his honour, should be detestable; that nothing should be set up, or dedicated in them, which could be done in clean places; and, lastly, that the priests, as often as they prayed for the Athenian people, allies, armies, and fleets, should as many times detest and execrate Philip, his children, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> forces, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> and name of the Macedonians. At the taking and demolishing of cities, it was usual among the Jews, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, to pronounce curses upon, and load with direful execrations, the rebuilders of them.

EXECUTION

Pages 403-405

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the completing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> finishing some <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, as of judgment, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, &c. and it usually signifies the obtaining possession of any thing recovered by judgment of law. Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> observes, that there are two sorts of executions: the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a>; and the other a quoique, that tends to an end. An execution final is that which makes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of the defendant's goods, or extends to his lands and delivers them to the plaintiff, who accepts the same in satisfaction; and this is the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, and the whole that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s writ requires to be done. The writ of execution with a quoique, though it tends to an end, yet is not final, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> capas <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> satisfac. where the defendant's body is to be taken, in order that the plaintiff may be satisfied for his debt. See CAPTAS. Executions are either in personal, real, or mixed actions. In a personal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, the execution may be made three ways, viz. by the writs of capas ad satisfaciendam, against the body of the defendant; fieri facias, against his goods; or elegit, against his lands. See FIERI Facias and ELEGIT. In a real and mixed action, the execution is by writ of habere facias satisfaciam, and habere possessionem*. Writs of execution bind the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of goods only from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of delivery of the writ to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is bound from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the judgment obtained; and here the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of any goods for valuable consideration, after a judgment, and before the execution awarded, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be good. It is otherwise as to lands, of which execution may be made, even on a purchase after the judgment, though the defendant fell such land before execution. Likewise, sheriffs may deliver in execution all the lands whereof others shall be seized in trust for him against whom execution is had on a judgment, &c. When any judgment is signed, the execution may be taken out immediately thereon; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be not inflicted within a year and a day after, where there is no fault Execution, fault in the defendant, as in the case of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>, writ of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, &c., there must be a *seire facias*, to revive the judgment; though, if the plaintiff files out any writ of execution within the year, he may continue it after the year is expired. After judgment against the defendant, in an action wherein special bail is given, the plaintiff is at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to have execution against such defendant, or against his bail: but this is understood where the defendant does not render himself, according to law, in safeguard of the bail; and execution may not regularly be sued forth against a bail, till a default is returned against the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>: also if the plaintiff takes the bail, he shall never take the principal. It is held that an execution may be executed after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the defendant: for his executor, being privy thereto, is liable, as well as the testator. The executor is an entire thing, so that he who begins must end it; therefore, a new sheriff may distrain an old one, to sell the goods seized on a distressing, and to bring the money into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. **Execution**, in criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the completion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. This follows judgment†; and must in all cases, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> as well as otherwise, be performed, by the legal officer, the sheriff or his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>; whose warrant for so doing was anciently by precept under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the judges, as it is still practised in the court of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, upon the execution of a peer: though, in the court of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, it is done by writ from the king. Afterwards it was established, that in case of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the judge may command execution to be done without any writ. And now the usage is, for the judge to sign the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of all the prisoners names, with their separate judgments in the margin, which is left with the sheriff. As, for a capital felony, it is written opposite to the prisoner's name, "let him be hanged by the neck;" formerly in the days of Latin and abbreviation, "suf. per col." for "suspendatur per collum." And this is the only warrant that the sheriff has for so material an act as taking away the life of another. It may certainly afford <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of speculation, that in civil causes there should be such a variety of writs of execution to recover a trifling debt, issued in the king's name, and under the seal of the court, without which the sheriff cannot legally stir one step; and yet that the execution of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, the most important and terrible task of any, should depend upon a marginal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. The sheriff, upon receipt of his warrant, is to do execution within a convenient time: which in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is also left at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, indeed, a more solemn and becoming exactness is used, both as to the warrant of execution and the time of executing thereof: for the recorder, after reporting to the king in person the case of the several prisoners, and receiving his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, that the law must take its course, issues his warrant to the sheriffs, directing them to do execution on the day and at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> assigned. And in the court of king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, if the prisoner be tried at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, or brought there by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABEAS_CORPUS">habeas corpus</a>, a rule is made for his execution; either specifying the time and place, or leaving it to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the sheriff. And, throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, by statute 25 Geo. II. c. 37, it is enacted that, in case of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, the judge shall in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> execution to be performed on the next day but one after sentence passed. But, otherwise, the time and place of execution are by law no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the judgment. It has been well observed, that it is of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance that the punishment should follow the crime as early as possible; that the prospect of gratification or advantage, which tempts a man to commit the crime, should instantly awake the attendant idea of punishment. Delay of execution serves only to separate these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; and then the execution itself affects the minds of the spectators rather as a terrible sight, than as the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of transgression. The sheriff cannot alter the manner of the execution, by substituting one death for another, without being guilty of felony himself.† It is held also by Sir Edward Coke and Sir Matthew Hale, that even the king cannot change the punishment of the law, by altering the hanging or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> into beheading; though, when beheading is part of the sentence, the king may remit the rest. And, notwithstanding some examples to the contrary, Sir Edward Coke strongly maintains, that *judicandum est legibus, non exemptis*. But others have thought, and more justly, that this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, being founded in mercy, and immemorially exercised by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, is part of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law. For hitherto, in every instance, all these exchanges have been for more merciful kinds of death; and how far this may also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> within the king's power of granting conditional pardons (viz. by remitting a severe kind of death, on condition that the criminal submits to a milder) is a matter that may bear consideration. It is observable, that when Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a> was executed for the popish plot in the reign of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, the then sheriffs of London, having received the king's writ for beheading him, petitioned the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords, for a command or order from their lordships, how the said judgment should be executed: for, he being prosecuted by impeachment, they entertained a notion (which is said to have been countenanced by Lord Ruffell), that the king could not <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> any part of the sentence. The lords resolved, that the scruples of the sheriffs were unnecessary; and declared, that the king's writ ought to be obeyed. Disappointed of raising a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, they immediately signified to the house of commons by one of the members, that they were not satisfied as to the power of the said writ. That house took two days to consider of it; and then fully resolved, that the house was content that the sheriff do execute Lord Stafford by severing his head from his body. It is farther related, that when afterwards the same Lord Ruffell was condemned for high <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, the king, while he remitted the ignominious part of the sentence, observed, "That his lordship would now find he was possessed of that prerogative, which in the case of Lord Stafford he had denied him." One can hardly determine (at this distance from those turbulent times), which most to disapprove of, the indecent and languid zeal of the subject, or the cool and cruel sarcasm of the sovereign. To conclude: It is clear, that if, upon judgment to be hanged by the neck till he is dead, the criminal be not thoroughly killed, but revives, the sheriff must hang him again. For the former hanging was no execution of the sentence; and, if a false tenderness were to be indulged in such cases, a multitude of collusions might ensue. Nay, even while abjurations were in force, such Execution, in the law of Scotland. See Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Execution, in the French music, is used to denote the manner of fingering, or of the performance of a fong. "As to the manner of fingering, called in France execution, no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> may, with any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> dispute it with the French. If the French, by their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the Italians have gained a bolder <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, the Italians have made their advantage of the French, in learning of them a more polite, moving, and exquisite execution." St Evremond. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">EXECUTIVE POWER</a>. The supreme executive power of these kingdoms is vested by our laws in a single person, the king or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> for the time being. See the article KING. The executive power, in this state, hath a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> in parliament, i.e., to refuse assent to any acts offered; otherwise the two other branches of legislative power would, or might, become despotic.

EXECUTOR

Pages 405-405

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies either the person entitled to succeed to the moveable estate of one deceased, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who by law or special appointment is intrusted with the administration of it.

EXECUTORY

Pages 405-405

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is where an estate in fee, that is, made by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fine, is to be executed afterwards by entry, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>, or writ. Leafe for years, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a>, conditions, &c., are termed inheritances executory.

EXECUTRY

Pages 405-405

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the moveable estate falling to the executor. Under executry, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> moveables, is comprehended every thing that moves itself, or can be moved; such as corns, cattle, furniture, ready <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, &c.

EXEDRAE

Pages 405-405

in antiquity, denoted halls with many seats, where the philosophers, rhetoricians, and men of learning, met for discourse and disputation. The word occurs in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers as a general name for such buildings as were distinct from the main body of the churches, and yet within the limits of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> taken in its largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Among the exedrae the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISTERY">BAPTISTERY</a>.

EXEGESIS

Pages 405-405

a discourse by way of explanation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> comment upon any subject. In the Scotch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, there is an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> among the students in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, called an exegesis, in which a question is stated by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESPONDENT">respondent</a>, who is then opposed by two or three other students in their turns; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the professor moderates, and solves the difficulties which the respondent cannot overcome.

EXEGETES

Pages 405-405

(formed of ἐξηγέομαι, "I explain,") among the Athenians, persons learned in the laws, whom the judges used to consult in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> causes.

EXEGETICA

Pages 405-405

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, the art of finding, either in numbers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, the roots of the equation of a problem, according as the problem is either numerical or geometrical.

EXEMPLAR

Pages 405-405

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> original, to be imitated, or copied. See MODEL.

EXEMPLAR ALSO

Pages 405-405

R also denotes the idea, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> image, conceived or formed in the mind of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, whereby he conducts his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Such is the idea of Cæsar, which a painter has in his mind when he goes to make a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Cæsar. EXEMPLIFICATION of Letters Patent, denotes an exemplar, or copy of letters patent, made from the enrolment thereof, and sealed with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of England. Such exemplifications are as effectual to be showed or pleaded, as the letters patent themselves.

EXEMPTION

Pages 405-405

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a privilege to be free from some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appearance: thus, barons and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of the realm are, on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, exempted from being sworn upon inquests; and knights, clergymen, and others, from appearing at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s turn. Persons of 70 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, apothecaries, &c., are also by law exempted from serving on juries; and justices of the peace, attorneys, &c., from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> offices.

EXERCISE

Pages 408-408

may also be applied with propriety to the forming our fleets into orders of failing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, &c., an art which the French have termed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVOLUTION">evolution</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> exercise may be defined, the execution of the movements which the different orders and disposition of fleets occasionally require, and which the several ships are directed to perform by means of signals. See Tactics.

EXERCISES

Pages 408-408

are also understood of what young gentlemen learn in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> and riding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, riding the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, &c. How useful, how agreeable forever, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> may be to the mind, it is very far from being equally salutary to the body. Every one observes, that the Creator has formed an intimate connexion between the body and the mind; a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a>, by which the body instantly feels the disorders of the mind, and the mind those of the body. The delicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of our frail <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> lose their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and become enervated, and the vessels are choked by obstructions, when we totally desist from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and the consequences necessarily affect the brain; a more studious and sedentary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is therefore equally prejudicial to the body and the mind. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> likewise become stiff; we <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> an awkward constrained manner; a certain disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> attends all our actions, and we are very near being as disagreeable to ourselves as to others. An inclination to study is highly commendable; but it ought not, however, to inspire us with an aversion to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is to live among his fellows: and whatever may be the condition of our birth, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> our situation in life, there are a thousand occasions where a man must naturally desire to render himself agreeable; to be <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and adroit; to dance with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; to command the fiery steed; to defend himself against a brutal enemy; to preserve his life by dexterity, as by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>, &c. Many rational cauls have therefore given rise to the practice of particular exercises; and the most sagacious and benevolent legislators have instituted, in their academies and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, proper methods of enabling youth, who devote themselves to study, to become expert also in laudable exercises.

EXERCITOR

Pages 408-408

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, he who employs a ship in trade, whether he be owner, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> only freights her from the owner. EXERGIA. See Oratory, No. 92.

EXERGUM

Pages 408-408

among antiquarians, a little space around <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> without the figures of a medal, left for the inscription, cipher, device, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, &c.

EXETER

Pages 408-410

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, situated on the river Exe, ten miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the British channel: W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 40' N. Lat. 50° 44'. Anciently the name of this city was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ILEX">Ilex</a>, and Itha Dunniorum. The present name is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of Excester, that is, a city upon the Exe. It is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and wealthy, with gates, walls, and suburbs: the circumference of the whole is about three miles. It is the see of a bishop, transferred hither from Crediton, by Edward the Confessor; and is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, for its buildings, wealth, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its inhabitants. It had six gates, besides many turrets, several of which are now pulled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. It had formerly so many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, that it was called Monkton, till <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Athelstan changed its name to Exeter, about the year 940; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he also fortified the city (which had before been only enclosed with a ditch and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>) with circular walls, embattlements, towers, and turrets of squared <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, encircling the whole, except the western side, with a deep <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>. Besides chapels and five large meeting houses, there are now fifteen churches within the walls, and four without. St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, is a magnificent pile; though little now remains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fabric of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, except that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which is called Our Lady's Chapel. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> of twelve bells, reckoned the largest ring of the largest bells in England; as is also its organ, whose largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> are fifteen inches in diameter. In 1763 the cathedral was repaired, beautified, and new paved; when, in removing the old pavement, was found the leaden <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> of Bishop Bitton, who died in 1373; the top of which, being decayed, afforded an opportunity of viewing the skeleton lying in its proper form; near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the finger was found a sapphire ring set in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; the stone considerably large, but of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value, on account of several flaws in it. Near this stood a small neat chalice and paten of silver gilt, but the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> had destroyed the greatest part of the gilding. In the centre of the paten was engraved a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with two forefingers extended in the attitude of benediction. The top of the crozier was also found, but totally decayed. A most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> painted glass window has been lately erected at the western end of the cathedral, the eastern end having before a remarkable fine antique one. In the other windows there is much fine ancient painted glass. The altar is remarkable for its beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and execution. On the left hand side of it there yet exists the seat where Edward the Confessor and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> sat and installed Leofricus, his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, the first bishop of Exeter; and in the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> aisle is the monument of the same Leofricus, who died 1073, which at the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> was a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, but by the enlarging of the church by his successors, became nearly the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> western end of the church is most magnificently adorned with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the patriarchs, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was built in 1439. Exeter. The beautiful throne for the bishop was constructed about 1466, and is said to be the grandest of the kind in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The great north tower was completed in 1485, which contains a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> that weighs 12,500 pounds; and exceeds the great Tom of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> by 2500 pounds. This city has had <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> charters granted, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> confirmed by most of our kings; but it was made a mayor town in the reign of King John, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself by King Henry VIII. It is governed by a mayor, 24 aldermen, four bailiffs, a recorder, chamberlain, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, town-clerk, &c. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-bearer, and four stewards, four sergeants at mace wearing gowns, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>-bearers in liveries with silver badges. It had anciently a mint; and in the reigns of King William III. and Queen <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, many pieces of silver <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> were coined here, which have the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> E under the bust. Here are 12 or 13 incorporate city companies. All pleas and civil causes are tried by the mayor, recorder, aldermen, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; but criminal causes, and those relating to the peace, are determined by eight aldermen, who are justices of the peace. Here are four principal streets, all entering in the middle of the city, which is therefore called Carfax, from the old Norman word Quatre voix, i.e. the four ways. Near it is a conduit, lately removed from the centre to the side of the principal street, which was first erected by William <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a>, mayor of the city, in the reign of Edward IV. and there are others well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> brought in pipes from the neighbourhood. There is an old castle in the north-east part of the city, called Rougemont, from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> foil it stands on; from thence there is a pleasant prospect from the walls. It is supposed to have been built by the West Saxon kings, and that they resided here, as did afterwards the earls and dukes of Cornwall. This castle was remarkably strong both by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art. The gate which originally led into it, was walled up by order of William the Conqueror, in token of his having reduced it to his obedience after a very obstinate resistance; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by it an inferior gate was made in the wall in which state they both remain. The outward stone facing is kept in tolerable repair; but the inside being but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, is gradually crumbled down. Here yet remains the ancient chapel, built in 1260, and kept in good repair, where prayers are read, and a sermon preached in sessions weeks. The city itself is healthy, and pleasantly situated on the sides of a hill, having other hills to its N.W. and S. by which it is sheltered from the force of storms. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> which sustained the ditch that in a great part surrounded the castle, is planted and gravelled, and accommodated with seats, it being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for walking for the inhabitants; and the ditch between it and the castle being filled up, is now thickly planted with elms, which form a delightful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. The old <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is now entirely demolished, and an elegant session house erected, where the assizes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-sessions, and county courts are held. In the city and suburbs are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> both for debtors and malefactors; a workhouse, almshouses, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>; an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for the sick and lame <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of the city and county, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the infirmaries of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and Westminster; and two free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-schools. It has <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> on Wednesdays and Fridays; and four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year. Great trade is carried on here in ferges, perpetuanas, long ells, and other woollen goods, in which it is computed that at least 600,000l. a year is traded for: yet no markets were erected here for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, yarn, and kerseys, till the 30th of Henry VIII. Before that time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> drove a considerable trade to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and France: they were incorporated in the reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> I. by the name of "The Governor, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">Consul</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Merchant-adventurers, trading to France." Here is also a weekly ferge market, the greatest in England, next to the Brigg market at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. It is said that some weeks as many ferges have been sold here as amount to 80,000l. or 100,000l.; for besides the vast quantities of their woollen goods shipped for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, Spain, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the Dutch give large commissions for buying up ferges, perpetuanas, &c. for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and Germany. It is particularly remarked of this city, that it is almost as full of gentry as of tradesmen; and that more of its mayors, and bailiffs have descended from, or given rise to good families, than in any other city of its size in the kingdom: for the great trade and flourishing state of this city tempted gentlemen to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> their sons in it, contrary to the practice of many of the inland as well as northern counties, where, according to the vain and ruinous notion of the Normans, trade was despised by the gentry, as fit for only <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> and the vulgar. This city was under the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, whose coins have been frequently dug up in and about it. After they left England, the Saxons drove the Britons out of it into Cornwall, and encompassed it with a ditch, besides bulwarks. The Danes attacked and spoiled it in 875; and afterwards in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> of the general massacre of the Danes by the English, Swyn, one of their kings, came hither with a great force, put the men to the sword, ravished the women, massacred the children, burnt the city, and defaced the walls. A long time after this, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as it was reviving, William the Conqueror besieged and took it; and it was again besieged in the reigns of King Stephen and Edward IV. In the reign of Henry VII. it was again besieged by Perkin Warbeck, and battered furiously: but the citizens forced him to raise the siege; which pleased the king, that he came hither, and presented a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">mantua</a>-ce to the city, and gave the very sword from his side to be borne always before the mayor. In the reign of Edward VI. in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1544, it was smartly cannonaded by the rebels of Cornwall and Devon, who almost starved it by breaking down its bridges, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off its water, and stopping up all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>; but it held out till the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> John Ruffel came with a force and raised the siege on the 6th of August, which was then appointed as an anniversary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of thanksgiving by the city, and is still observed as such. King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.'s queen, to whom this city gave shelter in the civil wars, was here delivered of Henrietta, afterwards duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>; whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> is in its guildhall, as are also General Monk's and George I.'s, &c. In the south-east quarter of the city was a house called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> house, wherein the above queen was delivered of the princess. This having lately been taken down, an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> is built on the spot, with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> adjoining it; and for the convenience of the inhabitants, a paillage has been made through the town wall to Southern Hay, on which green stands the county hospital, already spoke of, besides a considerable number of new buildings. There Exeter are remains of several ancient structures, which are daily giving way to modern erections; among the rest, an old building, said to have been a palace of King Athelstan. The guildhall is a spacious and convenient building, whose <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> or portico projects a great way into the street, and was first erected in 1330, to which its present front was rebuilt in 1593, and repaired in 1720. An arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> formerly flowed nearly up to the city's wall, till 1316, when Hugh Courtenay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Devon, in revenge for an affront, ruined the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, by constructing weirs and dams in the river; but to remedy it, in 1539, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> passed for making a navigable canal, for the better conveyance of goods in barges to and from the city to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOPSHAM">Topsham</a>. This was carried into execution in 1581, but not completed till 1675; nor was it after all found sufficient, till the present haven was constructed in 1697, when it was rendered capable of bringing ships of 150 tons quite to the quay, constructed near the walls of the city. In short, Exeter, by a constant adherence to its motto, *Semper fidelis*, has been applauded by all historians for its inviolable fidelity to its sovereigns, whether they held their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> or parliamentary <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. The city sends two members to parliament; and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the Cecils. The number of houses in Exeter, according to the return ordered by act of parliament in 1801, was 2836, and the number of inhabitants amounted to 17,383.—The see of Exeter was once one of the most wealthy in the kingdom; but its revenues were most shamefully wasted by Bishop Voysey, who alienated its lands. What little he left was so much encumbered, that the see has never been able to recover its former <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>; and so small are its present revenues, that it has been found necessary for the bishop to hold some other preferment for the better support of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> contains the entire counties of Devonshire and Cornwall, wherein are 64 parishes, whereof 239 are inappropriate. It hath four archdeacons, viz. of Cornwall, Exeter, Barnstaple, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOTNES">Totnes</a>. The diocese was formerly valued in the king's books at £550l. 14s. 6d.; but, since Bishop Voysey's time, it is lowered to £500l. and is computed to be worth annually £200l. The clergy's tenth is £200l. 15s. 2½d. To the cathedral belong a bishop, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, four archdeacons, a chancellor, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, a cantor, 24 prebendaries, and other inferior officers and servants.

EXFOLIATION

Pages 410-410

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by surgeons for the scaling of a bone, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the separation of the dead <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a bone from the living part.

EXHALATION

Pages 410-410

a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for all effluvia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> steams raised from the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in form of vapour.

EXHAUSTIONS

Pages 410-410

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>. Method of exhaustions, is a way of proving the equality of two magnitudes, by a *reductio <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> absurdum*; showing, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one be supposed either greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less than the other, there <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> arise a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>. The method of exhaustions was of frequent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> mathematicians; as Euclid, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>, &c. It is founded on what Euclid says in his tenth book; viz. that those quantities whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is less than any assignable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, are equal; for if they were unequal, be the difference never so small, yet it may be so multiplied, as to become greater than either of them; if not so, then it is really nothing. This he assumes in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of Prob. I. book x. which imports, that if, from the greater of two quantities, you take more than its half, and from the remainder more than its half, and so continually, there will, at length, remain a quantity less than either of those proposed. On this foundation it is demonstrated, that if a regular polygon of infinite sides be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> in, or circumscribed about, a circle; the space, which is the difference between the circle and the polygon, will, by degrees, be quite exhausted, and the circle become equal to the polygon.

EXHEREDATION

Pages 410-410

in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, with us ordinarily called *disinheriting*, is the father's excluding his sons from inheriting his estate. There are 14 causes of exheredation, expressed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>'s Novellæ; without some one of which causes, he decrees the exheredation null, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a> insufficient, as the civilians call it. Indeed, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman law, the father might pronounce exheredation without any cause; but the rigour of this law was restrained and moderated by Justinian.

EXHIBIT

Pages 410-410

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is where a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, being produced in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> to be proved by witness, the examiner, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> appointed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of any such, certifies on the back of the deed or writing, that the same was shewn to the witness at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his examination, and by him sworn to.

EXHIBITION

Pages 410-410

in our old writers, is used for an allowance of meat and drink, such as was customary among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> appropriators of churches, who usually made it to the depending <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>. The benefactions settled for the maintaining of scholars in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, not depending on the foundation, are also called *exhibitions*.

EXHORTATION

Pages 410-410

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, differs only from *suasion*, in that the latter principally endeavours to convince the understanding, and the former to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the affections.

EXHUMATION

Pages 410-410

(of *ex*, "out of," and *humus*, "ground"), the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> up a body interred in holy ground, by the authority of the judge. In France, the exhumation of a dead body is ordered, upon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that he was killed in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>. By the French laws a parson has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to demand the exhumation of the body of one of his parishioners, when interred out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> without his consent.

EXIGENCE

Pages 410-410
or **EXIGENCY**, that which a thing requires, or which is expedient and suitable thereto.

EXIGENT

Pages 410-410

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ which lies where the defendant in a personal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> cannot be found, nor any effects of his within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, by which he might be attached <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distrained.

EXIGENTERS

Pages 410-410

four officers in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, who make all exigents and proclamations, in all actions where <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of outlawry lies. Writs of supersedeas, as well as the prothonotaries, upon exigents, are likewise drawn up in their office.

EXILE

Pages 410-411

EXILE. See BANISHMENT. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the word *exilium* properly signified an interdiction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and fire; the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which was, that the interdicted person must betake himself into some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, since there was no living without fire and water. Thus Cicero, *<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Herenn.*, observes, that the form of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> did not express *exilium*, but only *aque et ignis interdictio*. The same author remarks, that exile was not properly a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, but a voluntarily fleeing or avoiding the punishment decreed: *Exilium non est supplicium, sed per fugium, partique supplicii*. He adds, that there was no crime among the Romans, as among other nations, punished with exile; but exile was a resource to which people flew voluntarily, in order to avoid chains, ignominy, starving, &c. The Athenians frequently sent their generals and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men into exile, out of envy of their merits, or distrust of their too great authority. See OSTRACISM.

EXISTENCE

Pages 411-411

that whereby anything has an actual essence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is said to be. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>.

EXITERIA

Pages 411-411

in antiquity, oblations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prayers to any of the gods for a prosperous expedition or journey. There were also feasts under this denomination, which were celebrated by the Greeks with sacrifices and prayers, when their generals undertook expeditions against an enemy.

EXOCETUS

Pages 411-411
