the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">FLYING</a> FISH, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXODIARY

Pages 411-411

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman tragedy, was the person who, after the drama <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> play was ended, sung the EXODIUM.

EXODIUM

Pages 411-411

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, signifies the end <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conclusion of a feast. Particularly, it is used for the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the feast of tabernacles, which, it is said, had a special view to the commemoration of the exodus or departure out of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>.

EXODUS

Pages 411-411

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; being the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five books of Moses: It is so called from the Greek ἐξόδος, the "going out" or departure of the children of Israel from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of which is delivered in this book, together with the many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> wrought on that occasion.

EXOMPHALUS

Pages 411-411

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, called also omphalocele and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a> umbilicalis, is a supernatural tumor of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, at the navel, from a rupture <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of the parts which invest that cavity.

EXORCISM

Pages 411-411

the expelling of devils from persons possessed, by means of conjurations and prayers. The Jews made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pretences to this power. Josephus tells several wonderful tales of the great success of several exorcists. One Eleazer, a Jew, cured many demons, he says, by means of a root set in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>. This root, with the ring, was held under the patient's nose, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> was forthwith evacuated. The most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of conjurors of this class were impostors, each pretending to a secret nostrum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, which was an overmatch for the devil. Our Saviour communicated to his disciples a real power over demons, or perhaps over the diseases said to be occasioned by demons. See DEMONIAC. Exorcism makes a considerable part of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, the rituals of which forbid the exorcising any person without the bishop's leave. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is performed at the lower end of the church, towards the door. The exorcist first signs the possessed person with the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, makes him kneel, and sprinkles him with holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Then follow the litanies, psalms, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; after which the exorcist asks the devil his name, and adjures him by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> not to afflict the person any more; then, laying his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> on the demoniac's head, he repeats the form of exorcism, which is this: "I exorcise thee, unclean spirit, in the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ: tremble, O Satan! thou enemy of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, thou foe of mankind, who hast brought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> into the world; who hast deprived men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and hast rebelled against <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>: thou seducer of mankind, thou root of evil, thou source of avarice, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, and envy." The Romanists likewise exorcise houses and other places, supposed to be haunted by unclean spirits; and the ceremony is much the same with that for persons possessed.

EXORCISTS

Pages 411-411

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an order of men, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church, whose employment it was to exorcise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out devils. See the preceding article.

EXORDIUM

Pages 411-411

in Oratory, is the preamble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> beginning, serving to prepare the audience for the rest of the discourse. Exordiums are of two kinds; either <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and formal, or vehement and abrupt. The last are more suitable on occasions of extraordinary joy, indignation, or the like. See ORATORY, No. 26.

EXOSTOSIS

Pages 411-412

in Anatomy, an acute eminence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> excrescence, putting preternaturally above the bone. EXOTERIC and ESOTERIC, are terms denoting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> and internal, and applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers; the one was public or exoteric; the other secret, or esoteric. The first was that which they openly professed and taught to the world; the latter was confined to a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of chosen disciples. This method was derived originally from the Egyptians; who, according to the united testimony of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Plutarch, &c. had a twofold <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, one secret and sacred, another public and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. The same practice also obtained among the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a> of the Gauls, and the Brachmans of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The Egyptian priests, with whom it originated, sustained the character of judges and magistrates, and probably introduced this distinction with a view to the public welfare, and to serve the purpose of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Clement of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> informs us, that that they communicated their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> principally to those who were concerned in the administration of the state; and Plutarch confirms the same <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>. However, others have supposed that they invented the fables of their gods and heroes, and the other external ceremonies of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> and conceal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and moral truths; but whatever was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of their practice, it was certainly applied to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> purposes.

EXOTIC

Pages 412-412

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> properly signifying foreign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> extraneous, i.e., brought from a remote or strange <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we sometimes say exotic or barbarous terms or words, &c. The word is derived from the Greek ἐξωτικός, ἐξωτερικός, extra, "without, on the outside." Exotic, is chiefly applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which are natives of foreign countries, particularly those brought from the East and West Indies, and which do not naturally grow in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The generality of exotics, or exotic plants, do not thrive in England without some peculiar care and culture: they require the warmth of their own climates; whence the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of hot beds, glass frames, green houses, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXPANSION

Pages 412-412

among metaphysicians, denotes the idea which we have of lasting distance, all whose parts exist together. Expansion, in Physics, the enlargement <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> increase of bulk in bodies, chiefly by means of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. This is one of the most general effects of that subtle principle, being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all bodies whatever, whether <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> or fluid. In some few <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, indeed, bodies seem to expand as they grow <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of freezing: but this is found to be owing to a new arrangement of the particles, or to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>; and is not at all a regular and gradual expansion like that of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, or any other solid or fluid substance by means of heat. In certain metals also, an expansion takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> when they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from a fluid to a solid state: but this too is not to be accounted any proper effect of cold, but of the arrangement of the parts of the metal in a peculiar manner; and is therefore to be ascribed to a kind of crystallization. The expansion of bodies by heat is very various, and in solids does not seem to be guided by any certain rule. In the 48th volume of the Phil. Trans. Mr Smeaton has given a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the expansions of many different substances. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXPECTANCY

Pages 412-412

estates in, are of two sorts; one created by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the parties, called a remainder; the other, by act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a>.

EXPECTATION

Pages 412-412

in the doctrine of chances, is applied to any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINGENT">contingent</a> event, and is capable of being reduced to the rules of computation. Thus a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in expectation when a particular event happens, has a determinate value before that event happens; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a person is to receive any sum, e.g., £10l. when an event takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which has an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of happening and failing, the value of the expectation is half that sum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> £5l.; and in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the expectation of obtaining any sum is estimated by multiplying the value of the sum expected by the fraction which represents the probability of obtaining it. The expectation of a person who has three chances in five of obtaining £10l. is equal to $\frac{3}{5} \times 100$ or £60l. and the probability of obtaining £10l. in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is equal to $\frac{3}{5}$. EXPECTATION of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, signifies, in the doctrine of life <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a>, that share or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the years of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life, which a person of any given <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> may expect to enjoy on an equality of chance. According to Mr Simpson, by the expectation of life we are not to understand that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> which a person may have an equal chance of surviving, which is a different and more simple consideration; but the number of years at which the purchase of an annuity ought to be valued, granted on it without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a> of money. There <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be a greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in this number of years, in proportion to the various degrees of mortality to which the different stages of human life are exposed. Thus, it is more than an equal chance that an infant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> come into the world, will not reach the age of 10 years; yet the expectation of life, or share of existence due to it, is almost 20 years upon an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>. The reason of this vast difference is the excess of the probability of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in the first tender years of existence above that which respects the more advanced stages. If the numbers of those who die at every assignable period were always found to be on an equality, the two quantities already mentioned would be the same; but when these numbers constantly become less and less, the expectation must of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> become the greater of the two.

EXPEDITION

Pages 412-412

the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to some distant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with a view of hostilities. Such were the expeditions of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> and Alexander into the Indies. Expeditious for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a> were called crofades.

EXPERIENCE

Pages 412-412

a kind of knowledge acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> without any teacher. It consists in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of things we have seen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> read, which the judgment has reflected on, to form for itself a rule or method. Authors make three kinds of experience: The first is the simple uses of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses, whereby we perceive the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> things without any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> thereto, or making any application thereof. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is, when we prudently and diligently make trials of various things, or observe those done by others, attending closely to all effects and circumstances. The third is that preceded by a foreknowledge, or at least an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the event, and

EXPERIMENTAL PHILOSOPHY

Pages 415-416
action, to produce heat, inflammation, and dissolution, in bodies; or if its essence consists in motion only, or in the fermentation of those particles which we call inflammable, and which enter as principles, in greater or less quantities, in the composition of mixed bodies. The most learned inquirers into nature incline to the former opinion; and have recourse to a matter which they regard as the principle of fire. They suppose that there is in nature a fluid adapted to this purpose, created such from the beginning, and that nothing more is necessary than to put it in action. The numberless experiments which are daily made in electricity seem to favour this opinion, and to prove that this matter, this fluid, this elementary fire, is diffused through all nature, and in all bodies, even ice itself. We cannot say what important knowledge this great discovery of electricity may lead if we continue our inquiries concerning it. It appears, however, that we may believe, without any inconvenience or absurdity, that fire and light, considered in their first principle, are one and the same substance differently modified. XIV. Be this matter however as it may, experimental philosophy is employed in making the most ingenious and most useful researches concerning the nature of fire, its propagation, and the means by which its power may be excited or augmented; concerning the phosphorus and its inflammation; fire excited by the reflection of the sun's rays from a mirror; and on the effects of fire in general; concerning lightning and its effects; the fusion of metals; gunpowder and its explosion; flame and the aliment of fire; and an infinity of like objects which it explains, or concerning which it makes new discoveries, by the aid of experiments. XV. By the word light, we understand that agent by which nature affects the eye with that lively and almost constantly pleasing sensation, which we call seeing, and by which we discern the size, figure, colour, and situation of objects, when at a convenient distance. All philosophers agree, that the light which is diffused in any place, is a real body. But what this body is, and by what means it enters that place where it is perceived, is a question about which philosophers are divided. XVI. Experimental philosophy is applied in discovering or proving, by an infinity of experiments, what is the nature of light, in what manner it is propagated, what its velocity and progressive motion. It also investigates and explains the principles of optics properly so called, and shows the directions which light observes in its motions. From thence it proceeds to the examen of the principles of catoptries, and describes the laws and effects of reflected light. It next treats of the principles of dioptries, and explains the laws of refracted light; and lastly, it teaches, from the principles of natural and artificial vision, the construction of optical instruments, as lenses, concave mirrors, prisms, telescopes, &c., &c., and the uses to which they are applied. XVII. By revolving or separating the rays of light, philosophy has obtained true and clear discoveries of the nature of colours. We are naturally led to imagine that colours, and their different degrees, make a part of the bodies that present them to our sight; that white is inherent in snow, green in leaves and grass, and red in a stuff dyed of that colour. But this is far from being true. If an object, which presents any colour to our sight, be not illuminated, it presents no colour whatsoever. In the night all is black. Colours therefore depend on light; for without that we could form no idea of them; but they depend also on bodies; for of several objects presented to the same light, some appear white, others red, blue, &c. But all these matters being separate from our own bodies, we should never acquire any ideas of them, if the light, transmitted or reflected by these objects, did not make them sensible to us, by striking upon the organs of our sight, and if these impressions did not revive in us those ideas which we have been used to express by certain terms. For these reasons philosophy considers colours from three points of view, 1. As in the light; 2. In bodies, as being coloured; and, 3. From the relation they have to our visual faculties, which they particularly affect, and by which we are enabled to distinguish them. It is unnecessary in this place to say more either on colour in particular or experimental philosophy in general. The different subjects of this collective article are particularly treated under their proper names, in the order of the alphabet: the reader will therefore turn, as he has occasion, to Acoustics, Catoptries, Chromatics, Dioptries, Hydrodynamics, Mechanics, Optics, Pneumatics, Electricity, Magnetism, &c., &c., &c. Also, Aerostation, Atmosphere, Burning Glass, Chemistry, &c., &c. ---

EXPERIMENTUM CRUCIS

Pages 416-420

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, leading, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> decisive experiment; thus termed, either on account of its being like a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> placed in the meeting of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, guiding men to the true knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of that thing they are inquiring after: or, on account of its being a kind of torture, whereby the nature of the thing is as it were extorted by force. **EXPHORESIS.** See Oratory, No 85. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">EXPIATION</a>,** a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, by which satisfaction or atonement is made for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of some Expia: crime, the guilt done away, and the obligation to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> cancelled. Expiations among the Heathens, were of several kinds; as sacrifices and religious washings. They were used for effacing a crime, averting any calamity, and on numberless other occasions, as purifying <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and sacred places, and armies before and after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. And they were performed for whole cities as well as particular persons. The method of expiation among the Jews was chiefly by sacrifice, whether for sins of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, or to purify themselves from certain pollutions. Feast of Expiation, among the Jews, called by our translators the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of atonement, was held on the tenth day of Tisri, or the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Jewish year, answering to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our September and October. It was instituted by God himself, Levit. xxiii. 27, &c. On that day the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, entered into the most holy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and confessed his sins; and, after several ceremonies, made an atonement for all the people, to wash them from their sins. Lev. chap. xvi. See SCAPE-GOAL. Expiation, in a figurative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is applied by divines to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> procured to the sins of the penitent by the merit of Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. See the article CHRISTIANITY. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">Expiration</a>, in Medicine. See Expiration. Expiration, is also used figuratively, for the end of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> granted, agreed on, or adjudged. Explicit, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, something clear, distinct, formal, and unfolded. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">Explosion</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, a sudden and violent expansion of an aerial or other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> fluid, by which it instantly throws off any obstacle that happens to be in the way, sometimes with incredible force, and in such a manner as to produce the most astonishing effects upon the neighbouring objects. Explosion differs from expansion, in that the latter is a gradual and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> power, acting uniformly for some time, whereas the former is always sudden, and only of momentary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The expansions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substances do not terminate in violent explosions, on account of their slowness, and the small space through which the metal, or other expanding substance, moves; though their strength may be equally <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> with that of the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> aerial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>. Thus we find, that though wedges of wood, when wetted, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> cleave solid blocks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, they never throw them to any distance, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it is seldom that the expansion of any elastic fluid bursts a solid substance without throwing the fragments of it to a considerable distance, the effects of which are often very terrible. The reasons of this may be comprised in the two following particulars: 1. The immense velocity with which the aerial fluids expand, when affected by a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and, 2. Their celerity in acquiring heat and being affected by it, which is much superior to that of solid substances. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, heated as much as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> when brought to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> heat, is expanded to four times its bulk; but the metal itself will not be expanded the sixtieth part of the space. In the case of gunpowder, which is a violent and well-known explosive substance, the velocity with which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> moves is calculated by Mr Robins, in his Treatise upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, to be no less than 7000 feet in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, or little less than 79 miles per minute. Hence the impulse of the fluid is inconceivably great, and the obstacles on which it strikes are hurried off with vast velocity, though much less than that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned; for a cannon bullet, with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of powder that can be conveniently given, does not move at a greater rate than 2400 feet per second, or little more than 27 miles per minute. The velocity of the bullet again is promoted by the sudden propagation of the heat through the whole body of air, as soon as it is extricated from the materials of which the gunpowder is made; so that it is enabled to strike all at once, and thus greatly to augment the momentum of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. It is evident that this contributes very much to the force of the explosion, by what happens when powder is wetted or mixed with any substance, which prevents it from taking fire all at once. In this case the force of the explosion, even when the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of powder is made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, cannot be compared to that of dry powder. Upon these principles we may conclude that the force of an explosion depends, 1. On the quantity of elastic fluid to be expanded; 2. On the velocity it acquires by a certain degree of heat; and, 3. On the celerity with which the degree of heat affects the whole of the expansive fluid. These three take place in the greatest perfection where the electric fluid is concerned; as in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, earthquakes, and volcanoes. This fluid, as is shown in many parts of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, differs not from elementary fire or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; it pervades the whole system of nature; its expansion is nothing else than its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> from a centre towards a circumference, for it does not seem capable of any proper expansion by a separation of its parts like any other fluid. Hence, when it begins to expand in this manner, the motion is propagated through it with a velocity far exceeding that of any other fluid whatever. Thus, even when the quantity is excessively small, as when an electric spark is sent through a glass full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, the expansion is so violent as to dissipate the glass into innumerable fragments with great danger to the bystanders, as is observed under the article <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a>. In violent lightning, where the electric fluid collects itself into balls, the strength of the explosion is proportionate to the quantity. Every one has heard of the prodigious effects of lightning when it happens to strike buildings, trees, or even the most solid rocks; and in some cases, where the quantity of electricity is still greater than in any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAIL">flail</a> of lightning, we hear of still more tremendous consequences ensuing. Dr Priestley gives an instance of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fire ball (undoubtedly a quantity of electric <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>) rolling on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which after rising up to the topmast of a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, burst with such violence that the explosion resembled the discharge of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of cannon fired at once. Great damage was done by it; but there is not the least doubt that most of its force was spent on the air, or carried <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the sea by the mast and iron work of the ship. Indeed, considering that in all cases a great part of the force of electric explosions is dissipated in this manner, it may justly be doubted whether they can be measured by any method applicable to the measurement of other forces. Even in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> electricity the force is prodigiously great; inasmuch that Dr Van Marum calculated that of the great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> belonging to the machine in Teyler's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> to be upwards of 900 pounds. In those cases where the electrical matter acts like volcanic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fire, the force of the explosions, though exceedingly great, is capable of measurement by comparing the distances to which the bodies are thrown with their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. This is most evident in volcanoes, where the projections or the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> rocks and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> manifest the greatness of the power, at the same time that they afford a method of measuring it. These explosions, as is shown under the article Volcano, are owing to extrication of aerial vapors, and their rarefaction by intense heat. In all of them the air is originally in a state of decomposition, viz., its invisible and solid part is joined with some terrestrial substances. Thus, when fixed air, for instance, is exposed to any pure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> which attracts it, as calcined <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, a decomposition instantly takes place. All these vapors are composed of elementary fire and some invisible substance capable of assuming a solid form. The decomposition just mentioned is therefore easily explained; the solid part of the air joins itself to the magnesia, while the elementary fire or latent heat is dissipated, and passes through the sides of the vessel. Were it now in our power suddenly to restore the latent heat to the whole of the fixed air, so that it would at once assume its former expansion, a violent explosion would follow. This seems to be precisely the case with the volcanic explosions. An immense quantity of the fixed part of different aerial fluids is united to the various substances found below the surface of the earth. By means of the electric fire which kindles the volcanoes, the aerial fluids are suddenly restored to their elastic state; and not only so, but their natural elasticity is greatly augmented, so that the explosions take place with great violence. The case is the same with gunpowder; only that the condensed air in this case is at first of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> kind, but is quickly phlogisticated by reason of the combustible matters mixed with the nitre, while the heat produced by the inflammation augments the elasticity of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> air to four times what it usually is, so that the whole force of the explosion is calculated at 1000 times the pressure of the common <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. Thus the explosions of gunpowder and of volcanoes are essentially the same. The reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> quickness of those of gunpowder is, that it takes fire so readily by the intimate mixture and combustibility of all the materials. In volcanoes the explosions likewise follow one another very quickly, and are by no means inferior in strength to those of gunpowder; but here the quantity of vapor makes up for the comparative slowness with which it is affected by the heat. Thus, though we could not by any means contrive to fire cannon in quick succession by means of calcareous earth as we can do with gunpowder, yet in the huge <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> of a volcano the elastic matter is supplied in such quantities, that the explosions are in a manner unremitting; that even in ordinary experiments the confinement of aerial vapors has often occasioned violent explosions in chemical vessels. In one case too the extrication of fixed air adds excessively to the force of an explosion, viz., in that of pulvis fulminans. This is compounded of sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of tartar. The latter we know contains much fixed air; and it is probable that the violence of the explosion is occasioned by this air; for the greater quantity of it that the alkaline salt contains, the greater force does it explode with. Fulminating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> emits a quantity of phlogisticated air, to which its explosive power is supposed to be owing, as is explained under the article <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>; but that of fulminating silver is so extraordinary, that scarce any force of aerial vapor that can be extricated is likely to produce it, and it seems probable that electricity itself is concerned. Next in strength to the aerial vapors are those of aqueous and other liquids. The most remarkable effects of these are observed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> engines; but there is one particular case from which it has been inferred that aqueous steam is vastly stronger than the flame of gunpowder. This is when water is thrown upon melted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; for here the explosion is so strong as almost to exceed imagination; and the most terrible accidents have been known to happen from such a flight cause as per. one of the workmen spitting in the furnace where copper was melting. Here, however, it is most probable that a decomposition of the water takes place. That owing to this element can be decomposed, or reformed into elastic fluid of the vapors, has been completely established by the most satisfactory experiments, and is now, we believe, universally admitted by chemical philosophers. See Water, Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The position is indeed denied by the phlogitists; but their arguments appear not to be conclusive; nor is it a fact which militates in the least against their principles. On the supposition that the water is decomposed in the present case, however, the phenomenon in question is easily solved. The water being thrown in substance upon the melted copper, is decomposed by the violent heat; and one part of it adheres to the metal, thus converting it into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a>, or oxide, while the other is converted into inflammable air, or hydrogen <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, which expanding suddenly, throws the melted metal all about with the greatest violence by means of its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a>. To understand the manner in which this is accomplished, we must consider some of the principles of Gunnery laid down by Mr Robins, and related under that article. One of these is, that though the air, in cases of ordinary velocity, makes no great resistance, it is far otherwise where the velocity of the moving body becomes very great. In all cases of explosion also there is in the first instance a resisting <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> made by the exploding fluid; and consequently the weight of the atmosphere is to be overcome, which amounts to about 14 pounds on every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inch of surface. Supposing the surface of the exploding fluid, then, on that of melted copper, to contain an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 4 square inches, it meets with a resistance of 60 pounds from the atmosphere, and consequently communicates an equal pressure to the fluid metal. Even this must of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> throw it about, unless the same pressure was exactly diffused over every part of the surface. But much more must this effect be increased by the immense velocity with which the fluid moves, and by which the resistance of the atmosphere is augmented in a prodigious degree, as is explained under the article Gunnery. The elastic fluid generated is then confined not only by the fluid metal and sides of the furnace, but by the air itself, which cannot get out of the way; so that the whole resembles a cannon closed at the mouth, and filled with inflamed gunpowder. Hence not only the melted metal, but the furnace itself and the adjacent walls of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, are hurried off as they would be by the firing of a great quantity of gunpowder in a small space, and which is well known to produce analogous effects. In explaining the phenomenon in question, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> supposes that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> heat of the metal applied to the Explosion. aqueous steam produces the explosion; and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this alleges, that copper imbibes a greater quantity of heat during fusion than any other metal. Aqueous steam, however, seems to be too slow for producing such sudden and violent effects. Explosions, it is true, will be occasioned by it, but then it must be confined for a very considerable time; whereas the effects of water thrown upon melted copper are instantaneous. It may now be asked, Why such explosions do not take place with any other metal, iron for instance, when water is thrown upon its surface in fusion? In answer to this we must observe, That though water is decomposed by being applied to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot iron in the form of steam, yet there is a possibility, that when the same element is applied in substance to the fluid metal, no decomposition may ensue. Something like this indeed happens with copper itself; for notwithstanding the violent effects which take place on the contact of water in substance with the melted metal, no explosion happens though aqueous steam be blown upon its surface. On the contrary, the upper part of the metal is thus cooled, and forms itself into cakes, which are afterwards taken off, and new ones formed in the same manner; neither does aqueous steam affect red-hot copper in the manner that it does iron in the same state. A decisive proof that the explosion is not occasioned by the mere heat of the aqueous steam may be deduced from the example of melted glass, which produces no explosion though we pour water upon it in that state; and yet the heat of melted glass is undoubtedly equal at least to that of melted copper. It must be observed, however, that in all cases where a very hot body is thrown upon a small quantity of water in substance, an explosion will follow; but here the water is confined and suddenly rarefied into steam, which cannot get away without throwing off the body which confines it. Examples of this kind frequently occur where masons or other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> are employed in fastening cramps of iron into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> where, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there happens to be a little water in the hole into which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> is poured, the latter will fly out in such a manner as sometimes to burn them severely. Terrible accidents of this kind have sometimes happened in foundries, when large quantities of melted metal have been poured into wet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>. In these cases, the sudden expansion of the aqueous steam has thrown out the metal with violence; and if any decomposition has taken place at the same time, so as to convert the aqueous into an aerial vapour, the explosion must be still greater. To this last kind of explosion we must refer that which takes place on pouring <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> oil or burning oil or tallow. Here the case is much the same whether we pour the oil on the water, or the water on the oil. In the former case, the water which lies at the bottom is rarefied into steam, and explodes; in the latter, it sinks down through the oil by its superior specific gravity, and explodes as it passes along. In either case, however, the quantity of aqueous fluid must be but small in proportion to that of the oil: a very great quantity would put out the flame, or destroy the heat, in whatever way we applied it. Another kind of explosion is that which takes place in solid substances, where we can scarcely suppose either aqueous or aerial vapours to be concerned. The most remarkable of these are the volcanic bombs mentioned by Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> in the great eruption of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a> in 1779. They were large pieces of lava which burst in pieces like bombs as they fell to the ground; but he does not inform us whether their bursting was attended with any great violence or not. Indeed, amidst such scenes of horror, and the continual tremendous explosions of the volcano, smaller phenomena of this kind would probably be overlooked. Other examples are the Glass Tears, of which an account is given under that article; the bursting of electrical globes, when put in motion; of other glass vessels spontaneously, and seemingly without any cause; and lastly, the bursting of large <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> metal vessels in the act of cooling. These are all so similar to one another, that it is probable they depend on one general cause. All of them agree in this respect, that the extreme parts of them are considerably cooled, while the internal remain very hot. Thus, in the volcanic bombs, the current of air, formed by their swift passage through it in falling, necessarily carries off a great quantity of heat from the parts which are in contact with it, while the rest are scarce at all cooled. The glass tears are artificially cooled on the outside by dropping them upon water; and in consequence of this, their explosion is probably more violent in proportion to their bulk than that of the volcanic bombs. Glass vessels only burst spontaneously when they have not been well annealed; and we know that this bad <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNEALING">annealing</a> consists only in applying cold too suddenly to the outside. Something like this probably takes place when cast-iron vessels explode; and we are certain it does so with electrical globes, for these last are not apt to burst if they have been well annealed. In all cases, therefore, there is a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the outward surface by the cold, while the internal parts remain as much expanded as ever. In this case there must be a continual effort of that subtle fluid called elementary fire, from the internal to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> part, as the contraction gradually proceeds the contrary way. Thus, when a volcanic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>, for instance, is cooled on the outside, its parts are consolidated so that the internal fluid has not such an easy passage through it as is necessary. In consequence of this it makes a greater effort, which is still farther augmented by the cooling and contraction of the internal parts squeezing the fluid out from among themselves, and forcing it to recoil upon that in the centre, as well as to exert itself against the external part; from which united operation the effect already mentioned at last takes place. This explanation, however, does not hold with respect to electrical globes, glass tears, or ill annealed glass: but in order to accommodate it to all these, we have only to remember, that fire, and the electric fluid acting from a centre to a circumference, are not in the least different; so that from whatever cause the electric matter is disposed to act in this manner, the same effect will follow, i.e., an explosion will take place if the substance does not afford an equally ready passage through all its parts, and that whether any sensible heat is felt in it or not. The only other kind of explosion we have to take notice of is that produced by inflammable and dephlogisticated air, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> and hydrogen gases, when mixed together and set on fire. This differs from any of those hitherto considered, because in reality there is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> Explosion. Iute condensation rather than an expansion throughout the whole of the operation; and the result is the formation of water; and could the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> be made to take fire throughout their whole substance absolutely at the same instant, there would be no explosion, but only a sudden production of heat. From this cause also is derived a very singular phenomenon taken notice of by Dr Priestley in his experiments on that subject, recorded in the Phil. Transl. Having enclosed several quantities of inflammable and dephlogisticated air in a copper vessel, firing them afterwards by the electric sparks, he found that the force of the explosion was directed more towards one part of the vessel than another; least on that part where the electrical discharge was made, and most upon that which was farthest from it. This inequality was very considerable; insomuch that he could not repeat his experiment any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of times without injuring the vessel in that part which was farthest from the discharge. The reason he gives for this is, that the mixture was not fired at the same instant, but first at the place where the discharge was made. This first explosion would have acted equally upon all parts of the vessel, had it not been for the intervention of the air. By the first momentary explosion, however, the air in the farthest part of the vessel was condensed, so that the next explosion was made stronger, while the copper in the forcible part of the vessel had the whole of this strong explosion to resist, the hinder part being but little concerned, as the air in it was condensed and reduced almost to a vacuum. Though the phenomena of explosions are sometimes very destructive, they are likewise of considerable use in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, by removing obstacles which could scarcely be got the better of by any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> power whatever. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these are the blowing up of rocks, the separating of stones in quarries, and other purposes of that kind. The destruction occasioned by them in times of war, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> formed upon the principle of explosion for the destruction of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, are well known; and if we cannot call these useless, we must allow them at least to be necessary evils. For the production of explosions, gunpowder is the only substance that has yet been found to answer; nevertheless, as its use is attended with considerable expense, several attempts have been made to find out a cheap substitute for it. One of the most remarkable of these was by mixing small quantities of water, enclosed in little bladders or some easily destructible vehicles, along with a charge of powder. By this contrivance it was hoped that the water being converted into vapour when the powder was inflamed, would augment the force of the explosion; but instead of this, it was found greatly to diminish it. The reason was evident, viz. that the conversion of the water into steam required much of the latent heat of the inflamed gunpowder, that enough was not left to give the necessary expansion to the aerial fluid produced. A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases has also been tried; but the explosion here has always been found too weak. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, indeed, very terrible effects are produced by such a mixture, but in these the quantity is immense; so that the comparative weakness of the mixture cannot be discovered. Electricity therefore seems to be the only resource we have; except by adding ingredients to gunpowder which may increase the strength of it. There can be no doubt indeed that the electric fluid is possessed of sufficient strength to perform every thing we could desire; and electricians have supposed, perhaps justly enough, that a cannon <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with water might, by means of electricity, become more dangerous than one charged with gunpowder; but this fluid is so exceedingly capricious, so imperceptible and unmanageable, that the use of it cannot as yet be thought practicable, nor in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> ever will be so. The effects of explosions, when violent, are felt at a considerable distance, by reason of the concussions they give to the atmosphere; for, as has been already hinted, all of them act upon the atmospherical fluid with extraordinary force, which they exert upon terrestrial substances subjected to their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Sir William Hamilton relates, that at the explosions of Vesuvius in 1767, the doors and windows of the houses at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> flew open if unbolted, and one door was burst open though it had been locked. A great quantity of gunpowder being put into the ditch of a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and set on fire, destroyed part of the wall, and broke down one of the gates. The blowing up of powder magazines or powder <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> will destroy buildings and kill people, though certainly without the reach of the flame, and untouched by any part of the shattered <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> or mill. But the most curious effect is, that they electrify the air, and even glass windows, at a considerable distance. This is always observable in firing the guns of the Tower at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and some years ago, after an explosion of some powder mills in the neighbourhood of that city, a great number of people were alarmed by a rattling and breaking of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; which by the vulgar was taken for a supernatural phenomenon, but undoubtedly was owing to some commotion in the electrical fluid from the violent concussion of the atmosphere. In this respect, however, the effects of electrical explosions themselves are most remarkable, though not in the uncommon way just mentioned; but it is certain, that the influence of a flash of lightning is diffused for a great way round the place where the explosion happens, producing many very perceptible changes both on the animal and vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. **EXPO**NENT, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, the same with index. See **ALGEBRA**. Exponential is also used in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, in the same sense as index or logarithm.

EXPONENTIAL CALCULUS

Pages 420-420

the method of differencing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> finding the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a> of exponential quantities, and of summing up those differences, or finding their fluents.

EXPONENTIAL CURVE

Pages 420-420

is that whose <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is defined <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> expressed by an exponential equation; as the curve denoted by $a^x = y$, or by $x^y = y$.

EXPONENTIAL EQUATION

Pages 420-420

is one in which is contained an exponential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>; as the equation $a^x = b$, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> $x^y = <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a>$, &c.

EXPONENTIAL QUANTITY

Pages 420-420

is that whose power is a variable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>; as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> $a^x$, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> $x^y$. Exponential quantities are of several degrees and orders, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of exponents or powers, one over another.

EXPORTATION

Pages 420-420

the shipping and carrying out of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> wares and commodities for other countries. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> **<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">COMMERCE</a>**, **TRADE**, and **SHIPPING**.

EXPOSING

Pages 420-421

EXPOSING, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of setting a thing to public view. In the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the sacrament is said to be exposed when it is shown in public uncovered on festival days, and during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of plenary indulgences. Exposing is also used with a farther latitude; thus we say, It is prohibited to expose false and clipped <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Such a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> stands very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and has a delicious prospect; but it is exposed to all the four winds. Such a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> being on the frontiers, and not fortified, is exposed to the insults of every party of forces. EXPOSING of Children, a barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> practised by most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> excepting the Thebans, who had an express <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the contrary, whereby it was made <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> to expose children; ordaining at the same time, that such as were not in a condition to educate them should bring them to the magistrates, in order to be brought up at the public expense. Among the other Greeks, when a child was born, it was laid on the ground; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the father designed to educate his child, he immediately took it up; but if he forbore to do this, the child was carried away and exposed. The Macedonians indeed had a different custom; for with them all new-born children were brought before certain triers, who were some of the gravest men in their own tribe, by whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> were carefully viewed; and if they were found likely and well favoured, they gave orders for their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and allotted a certain proportion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> for their maintenance; but if weakly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> deformed, they ordered them to be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into a deep cavern in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, near the mountain Taygetus, as thinking it neither for the good of the children themselves nor for the public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, that defective children should be brought up. Many persons exposed their children only because they were not in a condition to educate them, having no intention that they should perish. It was the unhappy fate of daughters especially to be thus treated, as requiring more charges to educate and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> them in the world than sons. The parents frequently tied jewels and rings to the children they exposed, or any other thing whereby they might afterwards discover them, if <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> took care for their safety. Another <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in adorning these infants was either to encourage such as found them to nourish and educate them, if alive, or to give them <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> if dead. The places where it was usual to expose children were such as people frequented most. This was done in order that they might be found, and taken up by compassionate persons who were in circumstances to be at the expense of their education. With this intention the Egyptians and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> chose the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and the Greeks the high-ways.

EXPOSITION

Pages 421-421

in a literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the explaining an author, passage, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, and setting their meaning in an obvious and clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

EXPOSITOR

Pages 421-421
or EXPOSITORY, a title which some writers have given to a lesser kind of dictionaries or vocabularies, serving to expound or explain the meaning of the obscure or difficult words of a language. It is also used in the same sense with commentary and paraphrase.

EXPOSTULATION

Pages 421-421

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a warm <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to a person who has done another some injury, representing the wrong in the strongest terms, and demanding redress.

EXPOSURE

Pages 421-421

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, the situation of a garden wall, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass, as south or east. See Gardening.

EXPRESSED OILS

Pages 421-421

such oils as are obtained from bodies only by pressing. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXPRESSION

Pages 421-421

in Medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, &c. the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of expression <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> extracting the juices or oils of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, or other matters, by squeezing, wringing, or pressing them in a press. After having let the herbs infuse a due <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, their juice must be drawn by expression in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth or by a press.

EXPULSION

Pages 421-421

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of violently driving a person out of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, &c. Expulsion, in Medicine, the act whereby any thing is forcibly driven out of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which it is: thus we say, the expulsion of the fetus in delivery.

EXSICCATION

Pages 421-421

(formed of ex and siccar, "dry,") in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, &c. the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of drying up <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> evaporating the moisture of a thing.

EXSPIRATION

Pages 421-421

in Physics, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of respiration by which the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is expelled <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> driven out of the lungs. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> and Respiration.

EXSUDATION

Pages 421-421
or Exudation, the act of sweating out. In which manner, gums, balsams, &c. are usually produced from trees.

EXTANT

Pages 421-421

something that still subsists, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is in being. It is but <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Livy, of the writings of Cicero, Caesar, &c. that are extant, the rest are lost. We have nothing extant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, though he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>.

EXTASY

Pages 421-421

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of catalepsy, when a person perfectly remembers, after the paroxysm is over, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> he conceived during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it lasted.

EXTENATION

Pages 422-422

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, opposite to the hyperbole. The Greeks call it ἀλογίας.

EXTENSION

Pages 421-421

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and essential properties of body; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that by which it possesses or takes up some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of universal space, which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of that body. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>.

EXTENT

Pages 421-422

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Sometimes it signifies a writ <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> command to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> for the valuing of lands or tenements; and sometimes the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the sheriff, or other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>, upon this writ. Old and New EXTENT, in Scots Law. See Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXTENUATION

Pages 422-422

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of diminishing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lessening the bulk or substance of a thing, especially of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. Fevers, agues, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> abstinences, &c., occasion <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> extenuations or emaciations.

EXTERMINATION

Pages 422-422

in general, the exterminating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> destroying something. EXTERMINATION or EXTERMINATING, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, is used for taking away. Thus algebraists speak of exterminating surds, fractions, and unknown quantities out of equations. See MacLaur. Algebr. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. Chap. 12 where we have some general theorems for the exterminating unknown quantities in given equations.

EXTERNAL

Pages 422-422

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation applied to the surface <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> outside of a body, or that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which appears or presents itself to the eye, touch, &c., in contradistinction to internal. EXTERNAL is also used to signify any thing that is without side a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or that is not within himself, particularly in his mind; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say, external objects, &c.

EXTINCTION

Pages 422-422

in general, denotes the putting out <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> destroying something, as a fire or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. See Extinguishing of FIRE.

EXTINGUISHMENT

Pages 422-422

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a consolidation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> union, as where one has due to him a yearly rent out of lands, and afterwards purchases the lands out of which the rent arises; in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, both the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and the rent being united in one possessor, the rent is said to be extinguished. EXTIRPATION (formed of ex and stirps, "root,") the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of pulling up or destroying a thing to the very roots. Among the prayers of the Romish jubilee, there is one for the extirpation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>. EXTIRPATION is also used, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> entirely; as a wen, &c., or the eating it away, as a wart, &c., by corrosive medicines.

EXTISPICES

Pages 422-422

in antiquity, the person who drew prelages from viewing the entrails of animals offered in sacrifice.

EXTORTION

Pages 422-422

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is an illegal manner of wresting any thing from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, either by force, menace, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> authority. It is also the exaction of unlawful usury, winning by unlawful games, and taking more than is due under pretence of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, as excessive tolls in millers, &c. At the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, extortion is punishable by fine and imprisonment; and the statute of 3 Eliz. I.c. 30. has enacted, that officers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> guilty of extortion for the expedition of businets, &c., shall render to the party treble value. There are likewise <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> other statutes for punishing extortions of sheriffs, bailiffs, gaolers, clerks of the assize and of the peace, attorneys, solicitors, &c.

EXTRACT

Pages 422-422

in matters of literature, is something copied <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> collected from a book or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>.

EXTRACTION

Pages 422-422

in genealogy, implies the stock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> family from which a person is descended. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">DESCENT</a>. EXTRACTION of Roots, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, the methods of finding the roots of given numbers or quantities. See ALGEBRA and ARITHMETIC.

EXTRACTOR

Pages 422-422

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> forceps for extracting children by the head.

EXTRAJUDICIAL

Pages 422-422

something done out of the proper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the ordinary course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. As when judgment is given in a cause, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, not depending in that court where such judgment is given, or wherein the judge has no jurisdiction.

EXTRAORDINARIUS

Pages 422-422

amongst the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a body of men consisting of a third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and a fifth of the foot, which was separated from the rest of the forces borrowed from the confederate states with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> policy and caution, to prevent any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> that they might possibly entertain against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> forces. A more choice body of men were drawn from among the extraordinarii under the name of ablesti. See ABLESTI.

EXTRAORDINARY

Pages 422-422

something out of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> course. EXTRAORDINARY Couriers, are those sent express on some urgent occasion. EXTRAORDINARY <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">Ambassador</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> envoy, is such a one as is sent to treat or negotiate some special and important affair, as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, confederacy, &c., or even on occasion of some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, as condolence, congratulation, &c. A gazette, journal, or other newspaper extraordinary, is that published after some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and notable event, containing the detail or particulars thereof, which are not found in the ordinary papers.

EXTRAVAGANTES

Pages 422-422

those decretal epistles which were published after the CLEMENTINES. They were so called, because at first they were not digested <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ranged with the other papal constitutions, but seemed to be, as it were, detached from the canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. They <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be called by the same name when they were afterwards inserted in the body of the canon law. The first extravagantes are those of John XXII, successor of Clement V. The last collection was brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the year 1483, and was called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> extravagantes, notwithstanding that they were likewise incorporated with the rest of the canon law.

EXTRAVASATION

Pages 422-423

in contusions, fissures, depressions, fractures, and other accidents of the cranium, is when one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more of the blood-vessels, that are distributed EXU attributed in the dura mater, is broken or divided, where- by there is such a discharge of blood as greatly oppres- ses the brain, and disturbs its office; frequently bring- ing on violent pains and other mischiefs; and at length <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> itself, unless the patient is timely relieved. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">SURGERY</a> and MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXTREME

Pages 423-423

is applied to the last and outermost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of any thing; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which finishes and terminates it on that side.

EXTREMES

Pages 423-423

in Logic, denote the two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> terms of the conclusion of a syllogism; viz. the predicate and subject. They are called extremes, from their relation to another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, which is a medium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> between them. The predicate, as being likewise had in the first proposition, is called the majus extremum, greater extreme; and the subject, as being put in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> proposition, is called the minus extremum, lef- ter extreme. Thus, in the syllogism, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is an ani- mal; <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> is a man, therefore Peter is an animal; the word animal is the greater extreme, Peter the less ex- treme, and man the medium. See SYLLOGISM.
