A certain portion of land, burdened with the service of one soldier or knight, was called a knight's fee; and thus an estate, furnishing any service, number of soldiers, was said to contain as many knight's fees; so that now the manors, baronies, &c., became powerful according to the number of soldiers they were bound to furnish. In the grants from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, the nobility were obliged to furnish a certain number of soldiers for the service of the sovereign; and in those from the nobility to their vassals, the like service was required. Even the commons who had grants from the crown furnished a certain proportion of knights. The force of the nation was called into action by grants in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a>, or from the sovereign and nobility. A numerous and powerful army was instantly assembled, and at once ready for action. Of this army the king was the general, the nobility the officers, and the vassals soldiers; the whole being exactly arranged, and capable of entering upon any expedition without the least delay. Thus a remedy was found in some measure for the weakness of the feudal sovereigns; but though the knights tenure could accomplish this, it could not bring back the former affection and cordiality which subsisted between the various ranks of people. On the contrary, by uniting them more firmly to one another by legal ties, it rendered matters rather worse. The oppression originating from the operation of the feudal incidents, still continued with unremitting violence. The grants of knights tenure were attended with the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of homage and fealty; the same incidents of relief, wardship, marriage, aid, and efcheat, with the feudal tenures. The princes promised to abate somewhat of their rigour in demanding the feudal perquisites, but did not keep their word. Laws were occasionally promulgated, and for some time had an effect; but palliatives soon became ineffectual, and a new state of weakness began to commence. The two remarkable eras in the feudal history are, two eras in the time before the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of knight-service (D), and the history that during which it continued. Fiefs were in a state of fluctuation from the destruction of the Roman empire till the ninth century; but they were rendered perpetual in France about the year 877, and were generally become so in every country of Europe about the beginning of the tenth. Du Cange, voce Militia, gives us an example of a knight fee in the year 880. By the year 987, when Hugh Capet was raised to the throne Doubtcon of France, knight service was become general all over Europe, and was introduced into England after having made its appearance in other countries (E). In England, however, there have been several doubts and inquiries. inquiries among the learned concerning the introduction of the feudal laws. Many are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that they were first introduced by William the Conqueror; and, consequently, that they were entirely unknown to the Anglo-Saxons: but others think, that they existed among the latter in the same form under which they were continued by the Normans. Dr Stuart is of opinion that the Saxons who settled in England could not be strangers to fiefs. He supposes the conformity of manners, which undoubtedly prevailed between the Saxons and other barbarians, a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the hereditary grant of land, as well as the fluctuating state of feudal tenures which preceded it, were known to the former. Collateral proofs are derived from the spirit and tenure of the Anglo-Saxon laws, but especially from the grants of hereditary estates on condition of military service (f). The condition of fiefs under the Anglo-Saxons was very different from what it was afterwards. In their times we find no mention made of these oppressions of which so much notice has already been taken; and this may easily be accounted for from the alteration of the feudal spirit in different ages. During the time that a warm and generous affection subsisted between the feudal superiors and vassals, the incidents were marks of generosity on the one part, and gratitude on the other; but as soon as a variance had taken place, by reason of the interested disposition which the introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> produced, the same incidents became sources of the most flagrant oppression. This was remarkably the case in the time of William the Conqueror; and, during the reign of King John, matters were come to such a crisis, that the people everywhere complained loudly, and demanded the restoration of the laws of Edward the Confessor (c). "What these laws of Edward the Confessor were (says Mr Hume), which the English every reign during a century and a half desired so passionately to have restored, is much disputed by antiquarians; and our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of them seems one of the greatest defects of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English history." Dr Stuart has offered insufficient explanation; but this is in fact no more than a confusion of jargon, that "by the laws or customs of the Confessor, they by that condition of felicity was expressed which had been enjoyed during the fortunate state of the feudal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>. The cordiality, equality, and independence, which then prevailed among all ranks in society, continued to be remembered in less prosperous times, and occasioned an ardent desire for the revival of those laws and usages which were the sources of so much happiness." Besides the great distinction (of which an account Distinction has already been given) between the state of fiefs under the Anglo-Saxons and under the Normans, they were Anglo-Saxon, no less distinguished by the introduction of knight-fee and the service. Hitherto the refinement of the English had Anglo-Saxon been obstructed by the invasion of the Danes, and the Norman infaral situation of the kingdom; but after the Norman conquest the fiefs were made perpetual. Still, however, the knight-fee and knight-service were altogether unknown. William, the fifth prince who enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Normandy, was well acquainted with every thing relating to fiefs; for that duchy had experienced all the variety incidental to them from the time of its being granted to Rollo by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Simple in the year 912, to the year 1066, when William was put in possession of England by the battle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>. On his accession to the throne, a number of forfeitures took place among those who had followed the fortune of Harold. Their estates were to be disposed of at the pleasure of the conqueror; and it was natural to suppose that he would follow the method practised in was known in Scotland, and that it was not a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> at that time. The same author thinks it even probable, that it was known in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. (f) The use of entails was known to the Anglo-Saxons; and this practice, as well as the succession to allodial estates, must have contributed very much to establish hereditary fiefs. This opinion seems also to be confirmed by the accounts we have of the great power of many of the nobility among the Anglo-Saxons, and the natural tendency that fiefs must have, in the course of things, to become perpetual, though analogical arguments cannot entirely be depended upon in this case. There is indeed positive <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that the territory which anciently constituted the kingdom of Mercia belonged to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a> as an hereditary fief and earldom. The grant was given him by Alfred when he married his daughter Ethelfleda; and it is likewise attested by Camden, that in the time of Ethelred the earldom of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a> was an inheritance, and the regular succession of its earls is still known. We are informed also by creditable historians, that Bernicia and Deira were feudal and inheritable earldoms among the Saxons. The same was true of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> when possessed by the Scottish monarchs. This last appears from the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>: in which the grant was conveyed by Edmund king of England to Malcolm of Scotland in the following terms: "Edmundus rex totam Cumberland praedavit et contrivit, et commendavit eam Malcolmo regi Scoticie; hoc pacto, quod in auxilio fibi foret terra et mari." From the use of the word commendavit, indeed, Spelman takes occasion to say, that a feudal homage was not intended; but the contrary may be proved by the original Saxon from which the foregoing is a Latin translation; and the word, according to several learned critics, signifies feudal homage with the most strict propriety. Thus Du Cange informs us, that commendare se aliqui was the general <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> for faire Phommage a un suzerain. (c) The laws which are now extant under the name of Edward, are generally allowed to be of doubtful authenticity; nor are they, even supposing them to be genuine, of any use in answering the present question. They determine indeed the existence of fiefs among the Anglo-Saxons; and Dr Stuart is of opinion, that the compilation which goes under the name of this prince, though <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> it bears, nevertheless merits greater attention than has usually been bestowed upon it. M. Honard, a foreign lawyer, is the latest writer who has made it his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; but he is better acquainted with the Norman than the Anglo-Saxon customs. in his own country. Hence the origin of knight service in England. A grant of land, to any person whatever, was estimated at a certain number of knights fees; and each of these required the service of a knight. The grants of lands were even renewed to the old tenants under this tenure; so that by degrees the whole military people in the kingdom acquiesced in it. To accomplish this, Domesday Book is supposed to have been compiled, which contained an exact account of all the landed property of the kingdom.—Hence it is to be concluded, not that William introduced fees into England, as some have imagined, but that he brought them to their ultimate state of perfection by the introduction of knight-service. This is evident from the laws enacted during his reign. In these it is not only mentioned that knight-service was enacted, but that it was done expressly with the consent of the common <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the nation; which at that time was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> (n). The invention of knight-service proved generally agreeable: for, as only a few of the Anglo-Saxon fees were hereditary, the advancement of the rest to perpetuity, under the tenure of knight-service, must have been accounted an acquisition of some importance; as not only augmenting the grandeur and dignity of the sovereign, but securing the independence of the subject, and improving his property. In the happy state of the feudal association, there was indeed no necessity for the knight's fee; but when the discordance and oppression so often mentioned began to take place, it became then necessary to point out particularly every duty of the vassal, as well as of the lord; and this was fully done by the invention of knight-service. The nobles possessed duchies, baronies, and earldoms; which extensive possessions were divided into as many fees, each of them to furnish a knight for the service of the king, or of the superior; so that every feudal state could command a numerous army and militia to support and defend it in case of any emergency. The knights were also bound to assemble in complete armour whenever the superior thought proper to call, and to hold themselves in readiness for action whenever the king or superior found it convenient to take the field; so that thus the militia might be marched at the shortest notice to defend or support the honour of the nation. The knights were usually armed with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>, and shield; and each was besides obliged to keep a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. This last requisite was owing to the contempt into which the infantry had fallen through the prevalence of tournaments and luxuries of various kinds, though it was by means of the infantry that the barbarians had originally distinguished themselves in their wars with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and became able to cope with these celebrated warriors. All proprietors of fees or tenants by knight-service fought on foot: the cavalry were distinguished by the name of battle; and the success of every encounter was supposed to depend on them alone. They only were completely armed; the infantry, being furnished by the villages under the jurisdiction of the barons, had at first only bows and flings; though afterwards they were found worthy of much greater attention. While the feudal association remained in perfection, its inefficiency the superior could at any time command the military service of his vassals; but in the subsequent degeneracy, this service could neither be depended upon when wanted, nor was it of the same advantage when obtained as formerly. The invention of knight-service tended in a great degree to remedy this inconvenience. Those who were possessed of knights fees were now obliged to remain 40 days in the field at their own expense; and this without exception, from the great crown vassals to the smallest feudatories; but if longer service was required, the prince was obliged to pay his troops. In those times, however, when the fate of nations was frequently decided by a single battle, a continuance in the field for 40 days was sufficient for ordinary occasions. Thus matters seemed once more to be restored nearly to their former state. It was now, as much as ever, the interest of the nation to act with unanimity in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, not only against foreign enemies, but against the tyranny of the prince over his subjects, or of one part of the subjects over the other. New inconveniences, however, soon began to take place, owing to the gradual improvements in life and the refinement of manners. From the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of military service, a fine had been accepted instead of actual appearance in the field. In the times of barbarity, however, when men accounted rapine and bloodshed their only <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, there were but few who made an offer of this compensation; but as wealth and luxury increased, and the manners of people became softer, a general unwillingness of following the army into the field became also prevalent. A new tenure, called scutage, was therefore introduced, by which the vassal was only obliged to pay his superior a sum of money annually, instead of attending him into the field.* Hence originated taxes and their misapplication; for as the king was lord paramount of the whole kingdom, it thence happened that the whole scutage money collected throughout the nation centred in him. The princes, article then, instead of recruiting their armies, frequently filled their coffers with the money, or dissipated it otherwise, hiring mercenaries to defend their territories when threatened with any danger. These being composed of the dregs of the people, and disbanded at the armistice end (n) The following law of William the Conqueror not only makes express mention of the knight's fee and service, but alludes to a former law of William and his parliament, by which this tenure was actually established. "Statutum etiam et firmiter praecipimus, ut omnes comites, et barones, et milites, et servientes, et universi liberi homines totius regni nostrì praedìci, habeant et teneant se semper bene in armis et in equis, ut decet et oportet, et quod sint semper prompti et bene parati <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> servitium suum integrum nobis explendum, et peragendum, dum, cum semper opus adfuerit, secundum quod nobìs debent de feodis et tenementis suis de jure facere, et si cut illis statutum per commune consilium totius regni nostri praedìci, et dedimus et concedimus in fendo jure hæreditario." LL. Guill. c. 58. end of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>, filled all Europe with a disorderly banditti, who frequently proved very dangerous to society. To avoid such inconveniences, standing armies were introduced, and <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> began to be raised in every European kingdom. New inconveniences arose. The sovereigns in most of these kingdoms, having acquired the right of taxation, as well as the command of the military power, became completely despotic: but in England the sovereign was deprived of this right by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">Magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">Charta</a>, which was extorted from him, as related under the article ENGLAND, No [153]; so that, though allowed to command his armies, he could only pay them by the voluntary contributions of the people, or their submitting to such taxations as were virtually imposed by themselves.

FEOFFMENT

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, (from the verb feoffare <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> infestuare, "to give one a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEUD">feud</a>"); the gift or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of any corporeal hereditament to another. He that so gives, or enfeoffs, is called the feoffer, and the person enfeoffed is denominated the feoffee. This is plainly derived from, or is indeed itself the very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> feudal donation; for though it may be performed by the word "enfeoff," or "grant," yet the aptest word of feoffment is do or dedi. And it is still directed and governed by the same feudal rules; inasmuch that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rule relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and effect of the feudal grant, tenor eft qui legem dat feudo, is in other words become the maxim of our law with relation to feoffments modus legem dat donationi. And therefore, as in pure feudal donations, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, from whom the feud moved, must expressly limit and declare the continuance or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of estate which he meant to confer, ne quis plus donatfe praefumatur, quam in donatione exprimatur; so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one grants by feoffment lands or tenements to another, and limits or expresses no estate, the grantee (due ceremonies of law being performed) hath barely an estate for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. For, as the personal abilities of the feoffee were originally presumed to be the immediate or principal inducements to the feoffment, the feoffee's estate ought to be confined to his person, and subsist only for his life; unless the feoffer, by express provision in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the estate, hath given it a longer continuance. These express <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are indeed generally made; for this was for ages the only conveyance, whereby our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were wont to create an estate in fee-simple, by giving the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> to the feoffee, to hold to him and his heirs for ever; though it serves equally well to convey any other estate of freehold.

FER DE FOURCHETTE

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a crois having at each end a forked <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, like that formerly used by foldiers to rest their muskets on. It differs from the crois-fourche, the ends of which turn forked; whereas this has that sort of fork fixed upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> end. See HERALDRY.

FER DE MOULIN

Pages 643-643

Milrinde, Inke de Moulin, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> supposed to represent the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ink of a mill, which sustains the moving millstone. FERDINAND V. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, called the Catholic, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to his successors. He married Isabella of Castile, by which that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was united to the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. This illustrious couple laid the foundation of the future <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and power of Spain. The conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, and the discoveries of Christopher Columbus, made this reign a celebrated era in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Spain. He died in 1516, aged 63. See (History of) SPAIN.

FERAE

Pages 643-643

an order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, belonging to the class <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a>. See MAMMALIA <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FERALIA

Pages 643-643

in antiquity, a festival observed among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> on February 21st, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to Ovid, on the 17th of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the manes of their deceased friends and relations. Varro derives the word from inferi, or from fero; on account of a repast carried to the sepulchres of such as the last offices were that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> rendered to. Festus derives it from ferio, on account of the victims sacrificed. VOL. VIII, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. Vossius observes, that the Romans called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> fera, "cruel," and that the word feralia might arise thence. —Macrobius, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>. lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 13, refers the origin of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> to Numa Pompilius. Ovid, in his Fasti, goes back as far as Æneas for its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. He adds, that on the same day a sacrifice was performed to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Muta, or Dumb; and that the persons who officiated were an old woman attended with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of young girls. During the continuance of this festival, which lasted eleven days, presents were made at the graves of the deceased, marriages were forbidden, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of the gods shut up. While the ceremonies <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, they imagined that the ghosts suffered no punishments in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, but that their tormentors allowed them to wander round their tombs, and feast upon the meats which their surviving friends had prepared for them.—For a more particular account of the offerings and sacrifices and feasts for the dead, see INFERIE and SILLICERNIUM. Sometimes at the feralia public feasts were given to the people, at the tombs of the rich and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, by their heirs or particular friends.

FERENTARI

Pages 643-643

in Roman antiquity, were auxiliary troops, lightly armed; their weapons being a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, bow, arrows, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLING">sling</a>.

FERENTINUM

Pages 643-643

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Hernici in Latium, which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, after subduing that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, allowed to be governed by its own laws. Now Feretino, an episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 5. N. Lat. 41. 45.

FERENTUM

Pages 643-643
or FORENTUM, in Ancient Geography, a town of Apulia in Italy. Now Forenza, in the Basilicata of Naples.

FERETRIUS

Pages 643-643

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, à ferendo, because he had afflicted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> à feriendo, because he had conquered their enemies under <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>. He had a temple at Rome built by Romulus. It was there that the spoils called opima were always carried.

FERETRUM

Pages 643-643

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the bier used in carrying out the bodies of the dead, which duty was performed by the nearest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> relations of the deceased: thus, sons carried out their parents, brothers their fathers, &c.

FERG

Pages 643-644
or FERGUE, FRANCIS PAUL, a charming landscape-painter, was born at Vienna in 1689, and there learned the first principles of his art. He successively cursively practised under Hans Graf, Orient, and Thiele. This last, who was painter to the court of Saxony, invited him to Dresden to infert small figures in his landscapes. Ferg thence went into Lower Saxony, and painted for the duke of Brunswick and for the gallery of Salzdahl. From Germany he went to London, where he might have lived in the highest esteem and affluence, if, by an indireet marriage, he had not been so effectually deprived, that he was ever after involved in difficulties. The necessities which arose from his domestic troubles compelled him to diminish the prices of his paintings in order to procure an immediate support; and as those necessities increased, his pictures were still more sunk in their price, though not in their intrinsic value. By a series of misfortunes he was overrun with debts, and to avoid the pursuit of his creditors, he was constrained to secrete himself in different parts of London. He died suddenly in the street one night as he was returning from some friends, about the year 1738, before he had attained his 50th year; and left four children. This pleasing artist, Mr Walpole observes, had formed a manner of his own from various Flemish painters, though resembling Poelemburg most in the enamelled softnesses and mellownesses of his colouring; but his figures are greatly superior; every part of them is sufficiently finished, every action expressive. He painted small landscapes, fairs, and rural meetings, with the most agreeable truth; his horses and cattle are not inferior to Wouwermans; and his buildings and distances seem to owe their respective softnesses to the intervening air, not to the pencil. More faithful to nature than Denner, he knew how to omit exactness, when the result of the whole demands a less precision in parts. The greatest part of his works are in London and Germany; and the price they now bear is the best proof of their real merit. He also etched well with aquafortis; and his prints of that kind are generally esteemed by the curious.

FERGUS

Pages 644-644

the name of three kings of Scotland. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) SCOTLAND.

FERGUSON

Pages 644-645

Robert, a Scottish poet, who acquired a considerable share of celebrity at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> on the 5th of September 1752, of which we are assured from unquestionable authority, although some have placed it in 1751. His father's name was William, who, as well as the son, likewise paid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>; but he wisely relinquished the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> for the more certain emoluments of trade and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, being employed in different mercantile houses both in Edinburgh and Aberdeen. He was an accountant in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">Linen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> when he died, but never acquired anything like an independent fortune. The subject of the present sketch was of a weak and delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> during infancy,—indeed to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that small hopes were entertained of his ever reaching the years of manhood. Yet such were the care and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of his parents, that he was able to attend an English school by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was six years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when his progress was considered as very extraordinary. It was no less rapid at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> school of Edinburgh, which he attended four years, acquiring a competent knowledge of the Latin tongue with very little labour <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> exertion. From that he went to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a>, and in two years after to the university of St Andrews, which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his father preferred to Edinburgh, because a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the name of Ferguson had left two bursaries for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of two boys of the same name. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was never impaired at any time by severe study; yet he kept alive at the university the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which had been entertained of him while at school, and he was decidedly the first mathematician of the same standing. He was patronized by Dr Wilkie, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, who was perhaps as much attached to him for his poetical as his mathematical talents, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> himself being a poet, and author of the Epigoniad. This kindness was repaid by Ferguson, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dr Wilkie, by a beautiful elegy to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, written in the Scottish dialect. A little before he left the university, Ferguson had conceived the idea of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a tragedy on the death of Sir William Wallace, for which he had collected materials; but as he afterwards met with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the same subject, he abandoned the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, after he had completed two acts. His own reason for doing so he thus expressed: "Whatever I publish shall be original, and this tragedy might be considered as a copy." He returned to Edinburgh when he had finished his studies, without having fixed on any particular employment; for although he was destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> by his father, on his death he paid little attention to the expectations of his mother. He declined also the study of physic, affirming this as a reason, that when he read the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of diseases, he believed that he felt the symptoms of them all in himself. He was then induced to attempt the study of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, in which, as was natural to expect, he made no proficiency. He seems to have turned a wishful eye to some fine place, to obtain which he paid a visit to an uncle who resided at Aberdeen, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of literature and opulence, hoping that through his influence he might be settled in some place suited to his merit. In this rational hope he was completely disappointed; for although his uncle shewed him every mark of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, his fondness decayed by degrees, and in six months he desired him in an abrupt manner to leave his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, without attempting to procure for him any kind of living. It would perhaps be rash and uncandid to reprobate this conduct of his uncle, whose penetration probably beheld, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the actual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, at least the germinating seeds of these too fashionable vices and follies into which he afterwards plunged. We only give this as a conjecture of our own; but it seems to derive considerable countenance from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> between the manner in which his uncle received him, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their separation. Be this as it may, the conduct of his uncle operated powerfully on the mind of Ferguson, which, with the fatigue of his journey back to Edinburgh, brought on him a severe illness, on his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> from which he composed two elegies; one on the decay of friendship, and the other against repining at fortune; both which were suggested by this adventure at Aberdeen. The disappointment of his hopes, and the effect it produced on his mind, are very evident from the following stanzas. But, ah! these youthful sportive hours are fled, The scenes of jocund mirth are now no more; No healing slumber 'tide my humble <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, No friends console the sorrows of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. And what avail the thoughts of former joy? What comfort bring they in the adverse <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>? Can they the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANKER">canker</a>-worm of care destroy, Or brighten fortune's discontented lour? So <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> were his necessities at this period, that he Ferguson copied papers in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> clerk's office for so much per sheet, which employment he soon left in disgust. So boundless was his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, which was only equalled by his good nature, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, and goodness of heart, that all who knew him received him with affection; but his powers of song and talents for mimicry often led him into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the dissipated, whose example could not fail of doing him essential injury, but who had neither the power nor inclination to provide for him through life. The irregularities into which he was thus frequently led, often awakened upon him the dictates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>; and the conversation of a minister who understood his manner of life, made a deep <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on his mind. In short, his remorse soon assumed the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> despair. His sprightliness entirely forsook him: but he gradually recovered from his despondency, and his health was fully restored. Soon after he cut his head so dreadfully in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, that from the loss of blood he became delirious, in which condition he remained for some months, till the want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> and perpetual talking put a period to his existence on the 16th of October 1774. He was buried in the Canongate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>. Over his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> his admirer Robert Burns has since erected a monument. Had he joined <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> to his bright genius and good heart, he would have no doubt risen to distinguished eminence in the literary world. His poems in the Scottish dialect have been universally admired by his countrymen; and when we reflect that they were composed in a round of dissipation, they must be considered as unequivocal evidences of his genius and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>.

FERIA

Pages 646-646

in the Roman breviary, is applied to the several days of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; thus Monday is the feria secunda, Tuesday the feria tertia; though these days are not working days, but holidays. The occasion of this was, that the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were used to keep the Easter week holy, calling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> the prima feria, &c., whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> feria was given to the days of every week. But besides these, they have extraordinary feriae, viz. the three last days of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">Passion</a> week, the two following Easter <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> feriae of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">Rotation</a>.

FERIAE

Pages 645-646

in Roman antiquity, holidays, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> days upon which they abstained from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">Proclamation</a> was generally made by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALD">herald</a>, by command of the Rex Sacrorum or Flamines, that all should abstain from business; and whoever transgressed the order was severely fined.—The feriae were of two kinds, public and private. The public feriae were fourfold. 1. Stativae, which were kept as public feasts by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> upon certain immovable days appointed by their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>;—such were the Compitalia, Carmentalia, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUPERCALIA">Lupercalia</a>, &c. 2. Feriae Consecratae, which were moveable feasts, the days for the celebration of which were fixed by the magistrates or priests; of this sort were the Feriae Latinae, Paganalia, Compitalia, &c., which happened every year, but the days for keeping them were left to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the magistrates or priests. 3. Feriae Imperatae, which were fixed and instituted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> command of consuls, praetors, dictators, upon the gaining of some victory or other fortunate event. 4. Nundinae. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> NUNDINAE, AGONALIA, CARMENTALIA, &c. The private feriae were holidays observed by particular persons or families on several accounts, as birthdays, funerals, &c. The feriae belonged to, and were one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the dies festi. See FESTI. FERIAE Latinae, a festival at which a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bull was sacrificed, and the Latin and Roman <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> provided each a set <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of meat, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; and during the celebration, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and Latins swore eternal Feria eternal friendship to each other, taking home a piece of the victim to every town. The festival was instituted by Tarquinius Superbus when he overcame the Tuscans and made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with the Latins, proposing to build a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> temple to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Latialis, at which both nations might meet and offer sacrifices for their common safety. At first the solemnity lasted but one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, but it was at different times extended to ten. It was held on the Alban mount, and celebrated with chariot races at the Capitol, where the victor was treated with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> draught of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a> drink.

FERIANA

Pages 646-646

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thala in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, taken and destroyed by Metellus in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Jugurtha. It was visited by Mr Bruce in his late travels through Africa, who expected to have found many magnificent ruins in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but was disappointed. The only remarkable objects he met with were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, which are excessively warm. These are without the town, and flow from a fountain named El Tarmid. Notwithstanding the excessive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the fountain is not destitute of fishes. They are of the shape of a gudgeon, above four inches in length; and he supposed that there might have been about five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six dozen of them in the pool. On trying the water with a thermometer, he found the heat so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that he was surprised the fish were not boiled in it. That fish should exist in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat, is very surprising; but it seems no less wonderful that Mr Bruce, while standing naked in such water, should leisurely make observations on its heat, without suspecting that he himself would be boiled by continuing there. We have to regret that the accidental wetting of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> on which he wrote <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his remarks has deprived the public of the knowledge of the precise degree to which the thermometer is raised by this water. The fish are said to go down the stream to some distance during the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and to return to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> or warmest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> at night.

FERMANAGH

Pages 646-646

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster; bounded by Cavan on the south, Tir-Oen on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-east, by Tyrconnel on the north-west, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEITRIM">Leitrim</a> on the south-west, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONAGHAN">Monaghan</a> on the west. It is 38 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is taken up with bogs; and the great lake called Lough-Erne, which is near 20 miles in length and in some places 14 in breadth, diversified with upwards of 300 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, most of them well wooded, inhabited, and covered with cattle. It abounds also with great variety of fish, such as huge pike, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">bream</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROACH">roach</a>, eels, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, and salmon. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of the lake in some places is said to have a particular softness and limpidity, that bleaches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> much sooner than could be done by other water. The lake is divided into the upper and lower, between which it contracts itself for five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six miles to the breadth of an ordinary river. In one part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are marble rocks 50 or 60 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. This county formerly sent four members to the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. two for the shire, and two for Inniskillen the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Fermanagh gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of vicount to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Verney.

FERMENT

Pages 646-646

any body which being applied to another, produces <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>. Ferments are either matters already in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of fermentation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that soon run into this act. Of the first kind are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of wine, yeast, fermenting beer, or fermenting wine, &c. and of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> are the new expressed vegetable juices of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> fruit. Among distillers, ferments are all those bodies which, when added to the liquor, only correct some fault therein, and, by removing some obstacle to fermentation, forward it by secondary means: as also such as, being added in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of fermentation, make the liquor yield a larger proportion of spirit, and give it a finer flavour.

FERMENTATION

Pages 646-646

may be defined a sensible internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the constituent particles of a moist, fluid, mixed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> body; by the continuance of which motion, these particles are gradually removed from their former situation or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, and again, after some visible separation is made, joined together in a different order and arrangement, so that a new compound is formed, having qualities very sensibly different from those of the original fluid. Fermentation, properly so called, is confined to the vegetable and animal kingdoms; for the effervescences between <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, however much they may resemble the fermentation of vinous liquors, are nevertheless exceedingly different. It is divided into three kinds; or rather, there are three different stages of it, viz. the vinous, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACETOUS">acetous</a>, and the putrefactive. To these has been added a fourth, the panary, or the fermentation of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. Of the first, vegetables alone are susceptible; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of young animals is in some slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> susceptible of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> (A); but animal substances are particularly susceptible of the third, which vegetables do not so easily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into without previously undergoing the first and second. The produce of the first stage is wine, or some other vinous liquor; of the second, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>; and of the third, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">ammonia</a> or volatile alkali. (A) Under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">CHINA</a>, No 115, a fact is mentioned which seems to show that animal substances are likewise capable of the vinous fermentation; viz. that the Chinese make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a certain liquor called lamb wine, and likewise that they use a kind of spirit distilled from sheep's flesh. This is related on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of M. Grolier; but as he does not mention the particulars of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, we are at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to suppose that the flesh of these animals has been mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, or some other ingredients naturally capable of producing a vinous liquor; so that instead of contributing anything to the fermentation in question, they may in reality be detrimental, and furnish only that strong and disagreeable smell complained of in the liquid.

FERN

Pages 646-647

Filix. See Filices, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fern is very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in dry and barren places. It is one of the worst weeds for lands, and very hard to destroy where it has any thing of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> to root in. In some grounds, the roots of it are found to the depth of eight feet. One of the most effectual ways to destroy it is often mowing the grass; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the field is ploughed up, plentifully dunging thereof is very good: but the most certain remedy for it is urine. However, fern, cut while the sap is in it, and left to rot upon the ground, is a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> improver of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. In some places of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the inhabitants mow it green; and, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> it to ashes, make those ashes up into balls, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They then dry them in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them to clean their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> with; looking upon it to be near as good as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> for that purpose. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">Male</a> Fern. See Polypodium, Botany Index. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> Fern. See Pteris, Botany Index.

FERNANDO

Pages 647-647
or Fernandes, an island in the Pacific ocean. See Juan Fernandez.

FERNELIUS

Pages 647-647

John, physician to Henry II. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, was born in Picardy, in the latter end of the 15th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the beginning of the 16th century. Being sent to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, he applied himself in a most intense manner. All other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> was insipid to him. He cared neither for play nor for walking, nor for entertainments, nor even for conversation. He read Cicero, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of Cicero procured him this advantage, that the lectures he read on philosophical subjects were as eloquent as those of the other matters were barbarous at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He also applied himself very earnestly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. This continual study drew upon him a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> fit of sickness, which obliged him to leave Paris. On his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, he returned thither with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to study physic; but before he applied himself entirely to it, he taught philosophy in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARBARA">Barbara</a>. After this, he spent four years in the study of physic; and taking a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, confined himself to his closet, in order to read the best authors, and to improve himself in the mathematics; that is, as far as the business of his profession would suffer him. Never was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> more diligent than Fernel. He used to rise at four o'clock in the morning, and studied till it was time either to read lectures or to visit patients. He then examined the urine that was brought him; for this was the method of those times, with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people, who did not send for the physician. Coming home to dine, he shut himself up among his books till they called him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Rising from table, he returned to his study, which he did not leave without necessary occasions. Coming home at night, he did <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as at noon: he staid among his books till they called him to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>; returned to them the moment he had supped; and did not leave them till eleven o'clock, when he went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. In the course of these studies he contrived mathematical instruments, and was at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> charges in making them. But his wife murmuring at the expense, he dismissed his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>-makers, and applied himself in good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> to practice physic. But as visiting patients did not employ his whole time, he read public lectures upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> and Galen. This soon gained him a great reputation through France and in foreign countries. His business increasing, he left off reading lectures; but as nothing could make him cease to study in private, he spent all the hours he could spare in composing a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of physic, entitled Phyllologia, which was soon after published. He was prevailed with to read lectures upon this new work, which he did for three years: and undertaking another work which he published, De venae sectione, he laid himself under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of reading lectures some years longer, in order to explain this new book to the youth. While he was thus employed, he was sent for to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in order to try whether he could cure a lady, whose recovery was despaired of. He was so happy as to cure her; which was the first cause of that esteem which Henry II. who was then but dauphin, and was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with that lady, conceived for him. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> offered him, even then, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of first physician to him; but Fernel, who infinitely preferred his studies to the hurry of a court, would not accept the employment. When Henry came to the throne, he renewed his entreaties: but Fernel represented that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which was offered to him was due, for several reasons, and as an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, to the late king's physician; and that, as for himself, he wanted some time to make experiments concerning several discoveries he had made relating to physic. The king admitted this: but as soon as Francis I.'s physician died, Fernel was obliged to go and fill his place at Henry II.'s court. And here just the contrary of what he dreaded came to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>; for he enjoyed more rest and more leisure at court than he had done at Paris; and he might have considered the court as an agreeable retirement, had it not been for the journey which the new civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> obliged the king to take. He died in 1558, leaving behind him a great many works, besides what have been mentioned; as, De abditis rerum caufis, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> books of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATHOLOGY">Pathology</a>, a book on Remedies, &c. They have been printed several times with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> prefixed, written by William Plantius his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>.

FERONIA

Pages 647-647

the Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of woods and orchards. This deity took her name from the town Feronia, situated at the foot of Mount Soraëtæ in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where was a wood and temple consecrated to her. That town and wood are mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, in the catalogue of Turnus's forces. Strabo relates, that those who sacrificed to this goddess, walked barefoot upon <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coals, without being hurt. She was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> deity of freed men, who received their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> at her temple.

FERRARA

Pages 647-648

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of the pope, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name. It is seated in an agreeable and fertile plain; watered by the river Po, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> on one side; and on the other is encompassed by a strong wall and deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> ditches full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as well as by a good citadel, finished by Pope Paul. In the middle of the city is a magnificent castle, which was formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the dukes, and is not now the least ornament of Ferrara. It is quite surrounded with water; and the arsenal, which is near it, deserves the observation of travellers. Over against the palace is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>'s garden; with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELVEDERE">Belvedere</a>. Ferrara Belvidere on account of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Behind the garden there is a palace, built with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, called the palace of diamonds, because all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> fashion. Ferrara had formerly a considerable trade; but it is now almost deserted, being very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, inasmuch that there is hardly a person to be seen in the streets. This is owing to the exactions of the popes. The fortifications are now neglected, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> university is dwindled into a wretched <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the Jesuits. However, in 1755, it was advanced to an archbishopric by Pope Clement XII. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about it is so marshy, that a shower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> almost impassable. It is 24 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, 38 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, 70 north-by-west of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and 190 north of Rome. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 14'. N. Lat. 44° 36'. Ferrara, the duchy of; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in the pope's territory, bounded on the north by the state of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the west by the duchies of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIRANDOLA">Mirandola</a>, on the south by the Bolognese and by Romagna, of which it was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice. It is 50 miles in length, and 43 in breadth along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; but grows narrower and narrower towards the Mantuan. This country is almost surrounded by the branches of the Po, which often overflow the country, and form the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> morass of Comacchio, which has a bad effect on the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It is thin of people, and indifferently cultivated, though fit for corn, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. The Po and the lake of Comacchio yield a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fish. Ferrara is the capital town; besides which there are Arano, Comacchio, Magnavacca, Belriguardo, Cento, Buendeno, and Fichera. This duchy was formerly possessed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>. But the pope took possession of it in 1598, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Alfonso II, duke of Ferrara, it being a fief of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>.

FERRARIA

Pages 648-648

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the gynandrae class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the fifth order, Enateae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FERRARS

Pages 648-648

GEORGE, a lawyer, poet, historian, and accomplished <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, and born about the year 1570, in a village near St Albans. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and thence removed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn; where applying with uncommon diligence to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he was soon distinguished for his elocution at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. Cromwell, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> minister of Henry VIII., introduced him to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, who employed him as his menial <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, and in 1535, gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Flamstead, in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. This is supposed to have been a profitable estate; nevertheless, Mr Ferrars being a gay courtier, and probably an expensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years after was taken to execution by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s officer for a debt of 200 merks, and lodged in the compter. Being at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> member for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons immediately interfered, and he soon obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in favour with the king to the end of his reign, and in that of Edward VI. he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> protector Somerset as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in his expedition to Scotland in 1548. In the same reign, the young king being then at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, Mr Ferrars was proclaimed lord of misrule, that is, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of sports and pastimes; which office he discharged during 12 days, in Christmas holidays, to the entire satisfaction of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. This is all we know of Mr Ferrars; except that he died in 1579, at Flamstead in Hertfordshire, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He is not less celebrated for his valour in the field, than for his other accomplishments as a gentleman and a scholar. He wrote, 1. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; published in Grafton's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a>, 1569, fol. 2. Six tragedies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dramatic poems; published in a book called the Mirror for Magistrates, first printed in 1559, afterwards in 1587, and again in 1610. FERRET. See MUSTELA, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FERRETO

Pages 648-648

in glas-making, a substance which serves to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> glas. This is made by a simple calcination of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, but it serves for several colours: there are two ways of making it. The first is this. Take thin plates of copper, and lay them on a layer of powdered brimstone, in the bottom of a crucible; over these lay more brimstone, and over that another layer of the plates, and so on alternately till the pot is full. Cover the pot, lute it well, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it in a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and make a strong fire about it for two hours. When it is taken out and cooled, the copper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found calcined, that it may be crumbled to pieces between the fingers like a friable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It will be of a reddish, and, in some parts, of a blackish colour. This must be powdered and sifted fine for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Another way of making ferreto is as follows. Make a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stratifications of plates of copper and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> vitriol alternately in a crucible; which place on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the glas furnace near the eye; and let it stand there three days; then take it out, and make a new stratification with more fresh vitriol; calcine again as before. Repeat this operation six times, and a most valuable ferreto will be obtained.

FERRETS

Pages 648-648

among glasfakers, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> with which the workmen try the melted metal, to see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be fit to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>.—It is also used for those irons which make the rings at the mouth of the bottles.

FERRO

Pages 648-650

(W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19°, N. Lat. 28°), the most westerly of the Canary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, near the African <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, where the first meridian was lately fixed in most maps; but now, the geographers of almost every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> make their respective capitals the first meridian, as we do <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a dry and barren spot, affording no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> except what is supplied in a very surprising manner by a tree which grows in these islands, called the Fountain-Tree. Ferro, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Feroe Islands; a cluster of little islands lying in the Northern ocean, between 61° 15', and 62° 21' N. Lat. and between 5° and 8° W. Long. They belong to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. There are 17 which are habitable; each of which is a lofty mountain arising out of the waves, divided from the others by deep and rapid currents. Some of them are deeply indented with secure harbours; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> seeming to have favoured mankind with the safest retreats in the most boisterous seas. All are very steep, and most of them faced with most tremendous precipices. The surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> consists of a shallow foil of remarkable fertility; for barley, the only corn grown here, yields above 20 for one; and the grass affords abundant pasture for sheep. The exports are, salted mutton and tallow, goose quills, feathers, and eider <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; and, by the industry of the inhabitants, knit woollen waistcoats, caps, and stockings. No trees beyond the size of juniper or stunted willows <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow here, nor are any wild <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> to be met with except rats and mice, originally escaped from the shipping. Vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fowl frequent the rocks; and the taking of them furnishes a very perilous employment to the natives, as described under the article <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>-Catching. The sea which surrounds these islands is extremely turbulent. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> vary greatly on the western and eastern sides. On the first, where is received the uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> of the ocean from the remote <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, the tide rises <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> fathoms; on the eastern side it rises only three. Dreadful whirlwinds, called by the Danes aer, agitate the sea to a strange <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; catch up a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water, so as to leave a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> temporary chain in the spot on which it falls, and carries away with it, to an amazing distance, any fishes which may happen to be within the reach of its fury. Thus great shoals of herrings have been found on the highest mountains of Feroe. It is equally restless on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; tearing up trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and animals, and carrying them to very distant places. Among the numerous whirlpools of these seas, that of Suderoe, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the same name, is the most noted. It is occasioned by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> 61 fathoms in depth in the centre, and from 50 to 55 on the sides. The water forms four fierce circumjurgations. The point they begin at is on the side of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basin, where commences a range of rocks running spirally and terminating at the verge of the crater. This range is extremely rugged, and covered with water from the depth of 12 to 8 fathoms only. It forms four equidistant wreaths with a channel from 35 to 20 fathoms in depth between each. On the outside beyond that depth, the sea suddenly sinks to 80 and go. On the south border of the basin is a lofty rock, called Sumbøe Munk, noted for the multitude of birds which frequent it. On one side, the water is only 3 or 4 fathoms deep; on the other 15. The danger at most times, especially in storms, is very great. Ships are irresistibly drawn in; the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a> loses its power; and the waves <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>; so that an escape is almost miraculous; yet at the reflux, and in very still <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, the inhabitants will venture in boats for the sake of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>.
