Innumerable flocks of aquatic birds are continually to be seen perched on the extremities of the rocks, which make their nests in the clefts above the precipices; and vast numbers of them may be killed by the discharge of a single musket, and the rest will not stir, so little are they accustomed to be disturbed. One of the islands contains but a single habitation, which can be visited by the curate only in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. In the southern parts of these islands coal-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> were discovered about the beginning of the eighteenth century, and trials of the coals were only made in 1777, when it was judged that working them would be of sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> was determined by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> to be about 12,000 feet long, 4000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> on a medium, and five feet deep; but so great did the difficulty of working it appear, that the idea was abandoned. The coals were analyzed by the celebrated professor Kratzenstein of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, who found that they were superior to those of England, as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> longer, and giving a more intense <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, but not so easily kindled. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of them has been made in Scotland, and they are allowed to be of a superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. It is a favourable circumstance to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of the produce of those islands, that their harbours are never frozen, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of consequence could meet with no interruption during the winter. The measles and smallpox never attack the inhabitants but when they are brought there by strangers, when the ravages they make are almost as terrible as those of the pestilence; but for 70 years back they have not been subjected to this dreadful visitation. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, and neither too hot in summer, nor extremely <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in winter. There are frequent mists on these islands, but they do not seem to be injurious to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> often blows with such violence, that the people on horseback are obliged to dismount at its approach, which is announced by a whistling across the rocks; and persons on foot must throw themselves flat on their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, to avoid the dreadful consequences of the irresistible hurricane. So sudden is its approach at some times, that a burning <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> might be carried in the open air but a few seconds before it. There is seldom any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> on these islands; but when the phenomenon does happen, its awful and incessant roar among the rocks is truly alarming. Potatoes, the cultivation of which is rapidly advancing, thrive well, and the same is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with radishes and turnips. Corn is not much cultivated, which would require excessive labour in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> so mountainous, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> fishery requires all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> that can be spared. Trees cannot be made to grow upon them, and of consequence there is no wood. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants does not exceed 3000; and they are in general well made, with fair complexions, and their whiteness is very seldom impaired by the influence of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. They are not deficient in understanding; and although phlegmatic, yet they are benevolent and hospitable, and are seldom known to quarrel. They are fond of brandy, and yet it is said that they are very rarely seen in a state of intoxication. They are frugal and upright, yet extremely credulous, and much addicted to superstitious practices. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> among them, as parents educate their own children, and their knowledge of consequence is very circumscribed. They abound in skilful players at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>, but are wholly unacquainted with instruments of music, and dance to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERROL">Ferrol</a>, a sea port town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. It has a good harbour, and is frequented by the Spanish fleet in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. W. Long. 8° 46'. N. Lat. 43° 26'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">Ferruginous</a>, any thing pertaining of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, or which contains particles of that metal. Ferrugo, Rust, or oxide of iron. See Iron, Oxide of, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Ferrum, Iron. See Iron, Chemistry Index. Ferry, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, or by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, to have a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> for passage, on a river or river, for carrying passengers, horses, &c. over the same for a reasonable toll. Fertility, that quality which denominates a thing fruitful or prolific. Nothing can produce fertility in either <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, but what promotes Fertility promotes perhaps health; nothing but good blood, spirits, and perfect animal functions, that is, high health, can beget perfect fecundity; and therefore, all means and medicines, all nostrums and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECIFICS">specifics</a>, to procure fertility, different from those which procure good blood and spirits, are arrant quackery. Dr Cheyne says, that water-drinking males are very rarely infertile; and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any thing in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> can prevent infertility, and bring fine children, it is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and feed diet persevered in by both parents. To increase the fertility of vegetables, says <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, we must not only increase the vigour of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and of the plant, but also preserve what would otherwise be lost; whence he infers that there is much saved by setting, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of sowing. It is reported, continues he, that if nitre be mixed with water to the thickness of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and after a vine is cut, the bud be anointed therewith, it will sprout within eight days. If the experiment be true, the cause may be in the opening of the bud, and contiguous parts, by the spirit of the nitre; for nitre is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of vegetables. How far this may be true, is not perhaps sufficiently known, notwithstanding the experiments of Sir Kenelm Digby and M. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a>. Consult Mr Evelyn's Sylva, the Philosophical Transactions, the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, and Dr Stahl's Philosophical Principles of Chemistry; but a proper set of accurate experiments seems still wanting in this view.

FERULA

Pages 650-650

Fennel-giant, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 45th order, Umbellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The drug asafoetida is obtained from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ferula.

FESCENNIA

Pages 650-650
or Fescennium, in Ancient Geography, a town of Etruria, above Falerii; where the Fescennine verses were first invented. Now Gallo, in the Ecclesiastical State, near the Tiber.

FESCENNINE VERSES

Pages 650-650

in antiquity, were a kind of satirical verses, full of wanton and obscene expressions, sung <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rehearsed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, with many indecent gestures and dances, at the solemnization of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; (Hor. lib. v. ep. i. 145.). The word is borrowed, according to Macrobius, from facinum, "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>;" the people taking such songs to be proper to drive away witches, or prevent their effect; but its more probable origin is from Fescennium, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Campania, where such verses were first used.

FESSE WAYS

Pages 650-650
or in FESSE, denotes anything borne after the manner of a fesse; that is, in a rank across the middle of the shield. [Merged from PARTY PER FESSE, p.650] implies a parting across the middle of the shield, from side to side, through the fesse point.

FESTI DIES

Pages 650-650

in Roman antiquity, certain days in the year devoted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods. Numa, when he distributed the year into 12 months, divided the same into the dies festi, dies profesti, and dies intercisi. The festi were again divided into days of sacrifices, banquets, games, and feriae. See FERIE. The profesti were those days allowed to men for the administration of their affairs, whether of a public <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> private <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: these are divided into fasti, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a>, &c. See FASTI, COMITIALES, &c. The intercisi were days <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> both to gods and men, some parts of which were allotted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the one, and some to that of the other.

FESTINO

Pages 650-650

in Logic, the third mood of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the syllogism, the first proposition whereof is an universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, the second a particular affirmative, and the third a particular negative; as in the following example: FES No bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can be happy. TI Some rich men are bad men. NO Ergo, Some rich men are not happy.

FESTIVAL

Pages 650-650

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of feasting. See Feast.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is particularly applied to anniversary days of civil <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> joy.

FESTOON

Pages 650-650

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, &c. an ornament in form of a garland of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and leaves, intermixed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twisted together. It is in the form of a string or collar, somewhat bigger in the middle, where it falls <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>; being extended by the two ends, the extremities of which hang down perpendicularly. Festoons are now chiefly used in friezes, and other vacant places which want to be filled up and adorned; being done in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> clusters of flowers, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> placed on the doors of their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and houses on festival occasions.

FESTUCA

Pages 650-650

Fescue Grass, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandra clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FESTUS POMPEIUS

Pages 650-650

a celebrated grammarian of antiquity, who abridged a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Verrius Flaccus, De Significatione Verborum; but took such liberties in citation and criticism, as Gerard Vossius observes, are not favourable to the reputation of his author. A complete edition of his Fragments was published by M. Dacier in 1681, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Dauphin. Scaliger says, that Festus is an author of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> use to those who would attain the Latin tongue with accuracy.

FETLOCK

Pages 650-650

in the manege, a tuft of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> growing behind the pastern <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of many horses; for those of a low size have scarce any such tuft.

FETTI

Pages 650-651

FETTI, Domenico, an eminent painter in the style of Julio Romano, was born at Rome in 1589, and educated under Ludovico Civioli of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. He painted but little for churches, but excelled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; his pictures are much sought after, and are scarce. He abandoned himself to disorderly courses; and put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by excesses, in the 35th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. FETUS. See Foetus.

FEU-DUTY

Pages 651-651

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the annual rent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> duty which a vassal, by the tenor of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, becomes bound to pay his superior. Feu-Holding, in Scots Law, is that particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> by which a vassal is taken bound to pay an annual rent or feu-duty to his superior. FEVER. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> deified the diseases, as well as the passions and affections of men. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> places them in the entrance into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, Æn. vi. 273. Among these Fever had a temple on Mount Palatine, and two other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome; and there is still extant an inscription to this goddes. FEBRI. DIVÆ. FEBRI. SANCTÆ. FEBRI. MAGNÆ. CAMILLA. AMATA. PRO. FILIO. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">MALE</a>. AFFECTO. Fever, in Farriery. See Farriery Index. FEVERFEW. See Matricaria, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

FEUD

Pages 651-651

in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> customs, is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> quarrel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enmity, not to be satisfied but with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the enemy: and thence usually called deadly feud. Feud, called also feida, and faida, in the original German, signifies guerran, i.e. bellum, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>." Lambert writes it feith, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> it signifies capitallis inimicitia, or "implacable hatred." In Scotland, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, feud is particularly used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of kindred, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the death of any of their blood, against the killer and all his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy. Feud (Feodo), the same with Fief, or Fee. See Feodal System.

FEUDAL

Pages 651-651
or Feodal, of or belonging to a feud or fee. See Feodal.

FEUDATORY

Pages 651-651
or Feodatory, a tenant who formerly held his estate by feudal service. See Feodal Tenure.

FEVERSHAM

Pages 651-651

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England, situated on a branch of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, which is navigable for boys. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> demeine A.D. 811, and called in Kenulf's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s little Town, though it is now a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one. It was inhabited by the Britons <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the invasion of Caesar. In 923, King Athelstan held a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> here. King Stephen erected a stately <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, 1147, whose <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> sat in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and he was buried in it, together with Maud his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, and Euflace his son; but of this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, two <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> gate-houses are all that now remain. The town was first incorporated by the name of the barons of Feversham; afterwards by Henry VIII. with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the mayor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>; and lastly, by that of the mayor and jurats and commonalty. It is a populous flourishing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, consisting chiefly of two long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets, with a market-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the centre, built 1574. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was rebuilt in 1754, at the expense of 2300l. but was originally built in Edward II.'s reign. There Feversham is a free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school in this place, built and endowed by Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> in 1582; also two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. It is a member of the cinque-port of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, and has a manufactory of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are supplied from hence with abundance of apples and cherries, and the best oysters for stewing. These last were at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> carried away in such quantities by the Dutch, that many men and boats were employed in the winter to dredge for them; and it is said they carried home as many as amounted to above 2000l. a-year. The fishermen admit none to take up their freedom but married men.

FEVILDEA

Pages 651-651

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dircia clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, Cucurbitaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FEVRE

Pages 651-651

Cloud le, an eminent French painter, was born at Fontainbleau in 1633, and studied in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> there, and then at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> under Le Sueur and Le Brun; the latter of whom advised him to adhere to portraits, for which he had a particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, and in his style equalled the best masters of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He died in England in 1675, aged 42.

FEZ

Pages 651-652

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name in Barbary, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is described as a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls, within which there are hills and valleys, only the middle being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> and flat. The river which runs through the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, is divided into two streams, from which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are cut into every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town: so that the mosques, colleges, palaces, and the houses of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, are amply supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They have generally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> marble basins in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of their houses, which are supplied with water by marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the walls. They constantly run over, and the stream returns back into the street, and so into the river. The houses are built with brick <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and are adorned on the outside with fine mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, or tiles like those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The wood work and ceilings are carved, painted and gilt. The roofs are flat; for they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on the tops of the houses in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Most of the houfes are two stories high, and fome three. There are piazzas and galleries running all round the court on the inside, fo that you may go under cover from one apartment to another. The pillars are of brick, covered with glazed tiles, or of marble, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> between. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> work is carved and painted with gay colours, and moft of the rooms have marble cifters of water. Some of the great men build towers over their houfes feveral flores high, and fpare no expence to render them beaufiful; from hence they have a fine profept all over the city. There are in this city 700 moftques, great and fmall, 50 of which are magnificent, and fupported with marble pillars and other ornaments. The floors are covered with mats, as well as the walls to the height of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Every moftque has a tower or minaret, like thoife in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, with a gallery on the top, from whence they call the people to prayers. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> moftque is near a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in circumference. The middle <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is 150 yards in length, and 80 in breadth, with a tower proportionably high. Round this to the eafh, weft, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, there are great colonnades 30 or 40 yards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. There are 900 lamps lighted every night; and in the middle of the moftque are large branches, which are capable of holding 500 lamps each. Along the walls are feven pulpits, from which the doctors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> teach the people. The buflnels of the prieft is only to read prayers, and diftribute alms to the people; to support which, there are large revenues. Besides the moftques, there are two colleges built in the Moorifh manner, and adorned with marble and paintings. In one of them there are 150 rooms, besides a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. In this there is a great marble vafe full of water, adorned with marble pillars of various colours, and finely polifhed. The capitals are gilt, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> fhines with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, azure, and purple. The walls are adorned with Arabic verfes in gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. The other colleges are not near fo beaufiful, or rather are all gone to ruin fince the neglect of learning. There are hofpitals in the city, where formerly all strangers were maintained three days gratis. But the eftefts belonging to them have been confiscated for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s ufe. There are above 100 public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, many of which are ftately buildings. People of the fame trade or buflnel live in streets by themfelves. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about Fez is pleasant and fertile, and in many places abounding with corn and cattle, yet a great part of it lies waite and uncultivated, not fo much for want of inhabitants as from the opprefion of the governors; which makes the people choofe to live at fome diftance from the high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, where they cultivate juft as much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> as is neceffary for their own fubfiftence. Round the city there are fine marble tombs, monuments, and gardens full of all manner of fruit trees. Such are the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> accounts of this city. The following are given by M. Chenier, in his Recherches Historiques fur les Maures. Fez was built in the end of the eighth century by Edris, a defendant of Mahomet and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>; whose father, in order to avoid the procriptions of the caliph <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDALLA">Abdalla</a>, retired to the extremity of Africa, and was proclaimed fovereign by the Moors. Sidy Edris, having fucceeded to the throne of his father, built the city of Fez in the year 793. He caufed a moftque to be erected, in which his body was interred, and the city ever afterwards became an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> for the Moors, and a place of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. In the firft moments of fervour, which a new worfhip inspires, another moftque was built called carubin, which is perhaps one of the largest and moft beaufiful edifices in Africa. Several others were fucceffively built, besides colleges and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>; and the city was held in fuch veneration, that when the pilgrimage to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> was interrupted in the fourth century of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, the western Mahometans substituted that of Fez in its flead, while the eastern people went to Jerufalem. When the Arabs had overpread <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Africa, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, they brought to Fez the little knowledge they had acquired in the sciences and arts; and that capital conjoined, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> where philofophy was taught, together with medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. This laft gradually degenerated; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> brought astrology into repute, and this quickly engendered the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>. Fez soon became the common refort of all Africa. The Mahometans went thither for the purpofes of devotion; the affluence of strangers introduced a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for pleafure; libertinifm quickly followed; and, as its progrefs is moft rapid in warm countries, Fez, which had been the nurfe of sciences and arts, became a harbour for every kind of vice. The public baths, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, cleanliness, and cuftom, had rendered neceffary, and which were everywhere refpefted as sacred places, became fenes of debauchery; where men introduced themfelves in the habits of women: youths in the fame difguife, with a diftaff in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, walked the fleets at funfet in order to entice strangers to their inns, which were lefs a place of repofe than a convenience for profition. The ufurpers who difputed the kingdom of Fez after the 16th century overlooked these abuses, and contented themfelves with subjefting the masters of the inns to furnish a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COOKS">cooks</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It is to this laxity of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> that Fez owed its firft splendour. As the inhabitants are beaufiful, the Africans flocked thither in crowds; the laws were overturned, morals defpifed, and vice itfelf turned into an engine of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> refoerce. The fame spirit, the fame inclinations, the fame depravity, still exift in the hearts of all the Moors. But libertinifm is not now encouraged; it wears there, as in other places, the mark of hypocrify; and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> not venture to show itfelf in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The Mahometans of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, thofe of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a> and Cordova, migrated to Fez during the different revolutions that agitated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; they carried with them new cuftoms and new arts, and perhaps fome flight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of civilization. The Spanish Moors carried from Cordova to Fez the art of staining goat and fheep fkins with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which were then called Cordova <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and now <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> leather, from that city where the art is lefs perfeft. They manufacture gauzes at Fez, filk ruffles, and girdles elegantly embroifered with gold and filk, which fhew how far their ingenuity might be carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> induftry were more encouraged. There is ftill fome taste for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> preferved at Fez, and the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is fpoken there in greater purity.

FEZZAN

Pages 652-654

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, about 300 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and 200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> from east to west. It is bounded on the east by the Harutsch and line of the deserts; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Tibboes on the south and south-east; by that of the Nomadic Tuaregs on the south-west; and the country which forms the western boundary is inhabited by Arabs. It contains 101 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, of which Mourzouk is the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this kingdom is neither temperate nor agreeable at any season whatever; for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is almost intolerable, even to the inhabitants, especially when the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the south; and the prevalence of the north wind during winter makes the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> so intense, as not only to chill the natives, but those also who visit it from northern Fezzan regions. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">Rain</a> falls but seldom in this country, and in very small quantities. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a> is also a rare phenomenon; Mr Horneman affirms us that there was not a single storm from November 1798 to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1799; and that on the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1799 there were some faint flashes of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> unaccompanied by any claps of thunder. Winds, however, blow very frequently, both from the north and south, whirling up the dust and sand in such a manner as to give the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> a yellowish appearance. There is neither river nor rivulet of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the whole country, according to Mr Horneman, who informs us that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is a deep sand, beneath which is found calcareous rock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and sometimes a stratum of an argillaceous substance. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">Date</a> trees may be considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> production of Fezzan, in the western parts of which some senna grows, of a superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that which is imported from the country of the Tibboes. Culinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and almost every vegetable peculiar to the garden, are met with in abundance. Wheat and barley seem well adapted to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the soil, as well as to the climate; yet corn is not raised in sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> for home consumption, which is brought from those parts of Africa bordering on the northern parts of the kingdom. This is most probably owing to the native indolence of the people, the despotism of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the difficulties inseparable from their peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of tillage. They bestow little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on the rearing of cattle, which are only found in the most fertile parts of the country, and even in these their numbers are but small. They are made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to draw <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and are never killed but in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animal is the goat; and although sheep are reared in the southern parts of the country, the most abundant supply is furnished by the Arabs on the borders. They make coarse cloths of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, which constitute the apparel of the inhabitants in general. Their horses are not numerous, as they make most use of asses, either for carriage, draught, or burden. Camels bear a most extravagant price, being only made use of by the higher ranks, or by opulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and the common food of all these animals is the fruit of the date tree. Although the trade of Fezzan consists entirely of foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, it is nevertheless considerable. Mourzouk is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> market and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, Bengasi, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and other places, between the months of October and February. The caravans which come to Mourzouk from the west or south, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in ostrich feathers, tiger skins, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> dust, and also in slaves of both sexes as articles of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a> and snuff, with other articles manufactured in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, are brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> by the merchants from Bengasi; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, firearms, sabres, knives, and woollen cloth, are conveyed to it from Tripoli. Fezzan is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, a descendant of the family of the Sheerefs; and according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the country, his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> came from the western parts of Africa, invaded and made a conquest of it about 500 years ago. He reigns over his dominions with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a>- Fezzan. Solute power, but is at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> tributary to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a> of Tripoli, who annually receives from him the sum of 4000 dollars by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an officer appointed for that purpose. The sultan who was upon the throne when Mr Horne <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in 1798 visited the country, assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Sultan Muhammed ben Sultan Manfur," engraved on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> which is applied to all public acts, and also to correspondence within his dominions; but he makes use of a smaller seal when he writes to the bashaw of Tripoli. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>; yet it descends not in all cases from father to son, for when the heir apparent dies, a nephew may succeed in preference to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son, which is frequently the occasion of much bloodshed, when the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession comes to be warmly contested. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the sultan is within the walls of the fortress of the capital, where he leads a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of retirement attended by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>. The harem is near the palace, into which he never enters, as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> whom he inclines to see is conducted to his apartment. The harem consists of the sultana and about 40 female slaves, which last he frequently dispose of, and replaces them by others, unless they bear him children, or become the objects of his ardent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, either by their personal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> or other accomplishments. Those who wish for an audience with the sultan, approach the throne, which is an old elbow <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> raised a few steps from the ground, kiss his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and raise it so as to touch their forehead, and then kneel before him to give a statement of their business in common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, taking care, however, to intermix it with such exclamations as these: "God prolong thy life, God protect thy country," and to offer him some small present. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the sultan consists of a first and second minister, the general of his forces, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and a few <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> slaves. Some of the black slaves who are purchased while boys, and educated according to their distinctions and talents, often acquire considerable influence with the sultan. The dress of the sultan, when he appears in state, consists of a white frock of stuff, ornamented with gold and silver, and sometimes of satin interwoven with silver. The appearance of his turban is remarkable, which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> not less than three feet from the fore to the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and two feet in breadth. His revenue arises from certain taxes on all gardens and cultivated lands, and from fines and requisitions imposed in an arbitrary manner. The slaves who are employed in collecting these are often rigorous in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, but it is often possible to procure their lenity by means of a bribe. The expenditure of this revenue is chiefly confined to the support of the sultan, his court and palace; for the cadi and department of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers of government, are supported by the produce of date-tree woods and gardens. The administration of justice is vested in the hands of a cadi, whose decisions are guided by the Mohammedan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by antiquated customs, and established practice; but judgment in all criminal cases is purely arbitrary, or is referred to the sultan. The office of cadi has been hereditary in one family, ever since the conquest of the country by the ancestors of the present sultan; and when he dies, his place is filled by one who is the most eminent for learning, or who can best read and write, which is all the learning that he is ever possessed of. It is difficult to ascertain anything like an accurate statement of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Fezzan; but Mr Horne man conjectures that they may amount to about 75,000, all of them professing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Mahomet. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of the people varies considerably; those in the northern parts <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> in this respect a striking resemblance to the Arabians, while those in the southern districts are very much like the Tibboes and Tuaregs. Those who are strictly indigenous are of ordinary stature, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> far from being muscular; of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, short black <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, with their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> formed like the people of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and their nose not so flat as that of the negro. Their walk, mien, and gesture, indicate a total want of energy, either of body or mind. The women of this country are in general fond of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and the wanton manners and public freedoms in which they are permitted to indulge, are frequently astonishing, even to Mahometans from other countries; and the men are very much addicted to the vice of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>, using the juice of the date-tree, or a drink that is called bufa, which is of an intoxicating nature. Different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> prevail in this country, but that which is brought from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUDAN">Soudan</a> is reckoned the most inveterate. The common lues venerea is called franzzi, for the cure of which they make use of falts and colocynth as powerful cathartics, healing the fores with natron water or dissolved soda. They are sometimes afflicted with haemorrhoids, the cure of which is no doubt rendered more difficult by the too liberal use of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>; and a fever and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGUE">ague</a> which are very pernicious to foreigners. They are entirely unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHLEBOTOMY">phlebotomy</a>, yet they sometimes draw blood by means of cupping; and some are as much acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> as to be able to cure a simple fracture. Their houses are miserable structures, composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> or bricks mixed with clay, and dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and the hands of the labourer are all the tools which are employed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. When the walls are finished, they are covered over with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> made of calcareous earth, which is also done with the hand. Their houses are extremely low, and there is no other entrance for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> but by the door. They are uncommonly abstemious in respect of diet. Indeed they can never abstain from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> meat when it is placed before them; but this is not an article of food with the generality, and their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> for a rich man is, "that he eats <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and meat every day." FEWEL. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">FUEL</a>.

FIASCONO

Pages 654-654

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territories of the pope, remarkable for its good wine. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 12. N. Lat. 42. 20.

FIBRARIAE

Pages 654-654

an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to minerals of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> structure.

FIBRE

Pages 654-656

in Anatomy, a perfectly simple body, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least as simple as any thing in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> structure; being fine and slender like a thread, and serving to form other parts. Hence some fibres are hard, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> ones; and others soft, as those destined for the formation of all the other parts. The fibres are divided also, according to their position and and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, into such as are straight, oblique, transverse, annular, and spiral; as they are arranged in these directions in different parts of the body. Fibre is also used to denote the slender filaments which compose other bodies, whether animal, vegetable, or mineral; but more especially the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> roots of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Fibrose, or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">Fibrous</a>, something consisting of fibres, as the roots of plants. See Root. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIBULA">Fibula</a>, in Anatomy, the outer and smaller of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the leg. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fibula, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> for the closing of gaping wounds.—Celsus speaks of the fibula as to be used when the wound was so patent as not easily to admit of being sewed. (Op. lib. vii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 25. apud <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIN">fin</a>.). Fibula, in Antiquity, was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>, buckle, or clasp, made use of by the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> for keeping clothe or tying up some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their clothes. They are of various forms, and often adorned with precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Men and women wore them in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and at their shoes. Players and musicians, by way of preserving the voices of children put under their care to learn their arts, used to keep <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the prepuce with a fibula, lest they should have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with women. Ficinus, Marsilius, a celebrated Italian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1433, and educated at the expense of Lawrence de Medicis. He attained a perfect knowledge of the Greek and Latin tongues, and became a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a great physician, and a great divine. He was in the highest favour with Laurence and Cosmo de Medicis, who made him a canon of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Florence. He applied himself intensely to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and while others were striving who should be the deepest read in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, who was then the philosopher in fashion, he devoted himself wholly to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. He was indeed the first who restored the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosophy in the west; for the better effecting of which, he translated into Latin the whole works of Plato. There goes a story, but we know not how true it is, that when he had finished his translation, he communicated it to his friend Marcus Musurus, to have his approbation of it; but, that Musurus disliking it, he did it all over again. He next translated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOTINUS">Plotinus</a>; and afterwards the works, or part of them at least, of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a>, Jamblicus, Porphyrius, and other celebrated Platonists.—In his younger years, Ficinus lived like a philosopher; and too much so, as is said, to the neglect of piety. However, Savonarola coming to Florence, Ficinus went with everybody else to hear his sermons; and while he attended them for the sake of the preacher's eloquence, he imbibed a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and devoted himself henceforward more especially to the duties of it. He died at Correggio in 1499; and as Boronius affirms us upon the testimony of what he calls credible authors, appeared immediately after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to his friend Michael Mercatus: to whom, it seems, he had promised to appear, in order to confirm what he had taught concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. His writings, sacred and profane, which are very numerous, were collected and printed at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in 1566, at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1561 and 1576, and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1641, in two vols folio. Twelve books of his Epistles, among which are many treatises, were printed separately in folio at Venice 1495, and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, 1497, in 4to. Ficoides, the specific name given to several plants, as the mesembryanthemum, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">musa</a>, and opuntia. See Mesembryanthemum, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Fiction. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">Fable</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. Ficus, the Fig-tree; a genus of plants, belonging to the polygamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 53rd order, Scabridae. See Botany Index. The ficus religiosa, or Banian tree, is a native of several parts of the East Indies. It has a woody stem, branching to a great height and vast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, with heart-shaped entire leaves ending in acute <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. Of this tree the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> contain a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> equally beautiful and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>: There soon they choose The fig-tree: not that tree for fruit renown'd; But such as, at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to Indians known In Malabar or Decan, spreads her arms, Branching so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, that in the ground The bended twigs take root, and daughters grow: About the mother tree, a pillar'd <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">High</a> overarch'd, and echoing walks between; There oft' the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> herdsman, shunning <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, Shelters in cool, and tends his pasturing herds At loop-holes cut through thickest shade. Par. Lost, Book ix. l. 1100. The Banian tree, or Indian fig, is perhaps the most beautiful of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>'s productions in that genial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, where she sports with the greatest profusion and variety. Some of these trees are of amazing size and great extent, as they are continually increasing, and, contrary to most other things in animal and vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, they seem to be exempted from decay. Every branch from the main body throws out its own roots; at first, in small tender fibres, several yards from the ground; these continually grow thicker until they reach the surface; and then striking in, they increase to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trunks, and become <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> trees, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out new branches from the top; these in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> suspend their roots, which, twining into trunks, produce other branches; thus continuing in a state of progression as long as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, the first parent of them all, contributes her sustenance. The Hindoos are particularly fond of the Banian tree; they look upon it as an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the Deity, from its long <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, its outstretching arms, and overhanging beneficence; they almost pay it divine honours, and Find a fane in every sacred <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. Near these trees the most esteemed pagodas are generally erected; under their shade the Brahmins spend their lives in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> solitude; and the natives of all castes and tribes are fond of recreating in the cool recesses, beautiful walks, and lovely vistas of this umbrageous canopy, impervious to the hottest beams of a tropical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. A remarkable large tree of this kind grows on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the river Nerbudda, ten miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Baroche in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guzerat; a flourishing settlement lately in possession of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, but ceded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace concluded with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a> in 1783, to to Mahdajee Scindia a Mahratta <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. It is distinguished by the name of Cubbeer Burr, which was given in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a famous saint. It was once much larger than at present; but high floods have carried away the banks of the island where it grows, and with them such parts of the tree as had thus far extended their roots: yet what remains is about 2000 feet in circumference, measured round the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> stems; the overhanging branches, not yet struck <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, cover a much larger space. The chief trunks of this single tree (which in size greatly exceed our English elms and oaks), amount to 350; the smaller stems, forming into stronger supporters, are more than 3000; and every one of these is casting out new branches, and hanging roots, in time to form trunks, and become the parents of a future progeny. Cubbeer Burr is famed throughout Hindoostan for its great extent and surpassing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>: the Indian armies generally encamp around it; and, at stated seasons, solemn jatarras, or Hindu festivals, are held there, to which thousands of votaries repair from various parts of the Mogul empire.—It is said that 7000 persons find ample room to repose under its shade. The English gentlemen, on their hunting and shooting parties, used to form extensive encampments, and spend weeks together under this delightful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>, which is generally filled with green wood pigeons, doves, peacocks, and a variety of feathered songsters; crowded with families of monkeys performing their antics tricks; and shaded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATS">bats</a> of a large size, many of them measuring upwards of six feet from the extremity of one wing to the other. This tree not only affords shelter, but sustenance, to all its inhabitants, being covered amid its bright foliage with small figs of a rich scarlet, on which they regale with as much delight, as the lords of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> on their more costly fare in their parties.

FIDDES

Pages 656-656

RICHARD, a learned divine and polite writer, was born in 1671, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He was presented to the living of Hallham in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, where he was so admired for the sweetness of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and the gracefulness of his delivery, that the people for several miles round flocked to his sermons. Coming to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1712, he was by the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Swift, introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Oxford, who made him one of his chaplains, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> soon after appointed him chaplain to the garrison at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">Hull</a>: but losing his patrons upon the change of the ministry, he lost his chaplainship; and being obliged to apply himself to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, composed, 1. A body of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>; 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey; 3. A Treatise of Morality, &c. He died in 1725. FIDDLE. See VIOLIN. FIDDLE-Wood. See CITHAREXYLON, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FIDE-JUSSORES Affidivi. See ASIDUUS.

FIDE-JUROR

Pages 656-656

in the Civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a surety, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one that obliges himself in the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, for the greater security of the creditor or stipulator.

FIDEI COMMISSUM

Pages 656-656

in Roman antiquity, an estate left in trust with any person, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of another. See TRUSTEE.

FIDENA

Pages 656-656
or FIDENÆ, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Sabines, five miles to the north of Rome, where traces of it are still to be seen. Fidenates, the people (Livy).

FIDES

Pages 656-656
FAITH or FIDELITY, one of the virtues deified by the Pagans. She had a temple near the Capitol, founded by Numa Pompilius; but no animals were offered, or blood spilt, in her sacrifices. During the performance of her rites, her priests appeared in white vestments, with their heads and hands covered with linen, to show that fidelity ought to be sacred.

FIDUS

Pages 656-656

in Pagan worship, a god who presided over alliances and promises. This deity, which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> borrowed from the Sabines, was also called Sanctus, Semon, and Semi Pater.

FIELD

Pages 656-656

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is the whole surface of the shield <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the continent, so called because it containeth those achievements anciently acquired in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. It is the ground on which the colours, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, furs, charges, &c. are represented. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> heralds, field is less frequently used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> than shield or escutcheon. See SHIELD, &c. FIELD Book, in Surveying, a book in which the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, stations, distances, &c. are set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. FIELD-Colours, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>-Colours, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, are small flags of about a foot and a half <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, which are carried along with the quartermaster general, for marking out the ground for the squadrons and battalions. FIELD Fire, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>. See TURDUS, ORNITHOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FIELD-Officers, in the art of war. See OFFICER. FIELD-Pieces, small cannons, from three to twelve pounders, carried along with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the field. FIELD <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">Staff</a>, a weapon carried by the gunners, about the length of a halbert, with a spear at one end; having on each side ears screwed on, like the cock of a matchlock, where the gunners screw in lighted matches when they are upon command; and then the field-staffs are said to be armed. FIELD-Works, in Fortification, are those thrown up by an army in besieging a fortress, or by the besieged to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Such are the fortifications of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, highways, &c. Elysian Fields. See ELYSIAN.

FIELDING

Pages 656-657

HENRY, a well-known writer of the present <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>-general Fielding who served under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, was born in 1707. He had four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>; of whom Sarah is well known, as writer of The Adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Simple. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his mother, his father married again; and Sir John Fielding, who succeeded him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of the peace for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, is his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> by this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Henry was sent to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; but a failure in his remittances obliged him to return in two years, when his own propensity to gaiety and profusion drove him to write for the stage at 20 years of age. His first dramatic piece, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> in several Masques, which was well received, appeared in 1727; and all his plays and farces, to the amount of 18, were written before before the year 1737, and many of them are still acted with applause. While he was thus employed, he married a young lady with £500 in fortune, and inherited an estate of £200 a-year from his mother; all which, though on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of retiring into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he contrived to dissipate in three years; and then applied himself to the study of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> for a maintenance. In losing his fortune, he acquired the gout; which, rendering it impossible for him to attend the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he with a shattered <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> had recourse to many extempore applications of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> for immediate supplies; until, soon after the rebellion in 1745, he accepted the office of acting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> for Middlesex, an employment much more profitable than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> in the public esteem. Reduced at length by the fatigues of this office, and by a complication of disorders, he, by the advice of his physicians, went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, where he died in 1754. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fugitive pamphlets and periodical essays; but is chiefly distinguished by his Adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Andrews, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Tom Jones. His works have been collected and published, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> prefixed, by Mr Murphy.

FIERI FACIAS

Pages 657-657

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ that lies where a person has recovered judgment for debt <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> damages in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s courts against one, by which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> is commanded to levy the debt and damages on the defendant's goods and chattels.

FIFESHIRE

Pages 657-658

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, lying between the friths of Tay and Forth; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-east by the frith of Tay, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>; on the south by the frith of Forth, which separates it from the Lothians; the German ocean bounds it on the east; and on the west it borders with the counties of Perth and Kinros, and a small corner of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLACKMANNAN">Clackmannan</a>. It extends about 60 miles in length from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULROSS">Culross</a> to Fifehead, and is about 18 in breadth; comprehending a superficies of nearly 480 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is agreeably diversified; towards the west it is mountainous, and a ridge of hills extends eastward almost its whole length, occupying the central district; towards the north and south the surface gradually descends to the friths, exhibiting the most beautiful and enlivening prospect of fertile and well cultivated fields. It is watered by several streams, none of which deserve the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, except the Eden and Leven; the former empties itself into the ocean at St Andrews, and the latter at the village of Leven: both these rivers abound with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a> and salmon; and on no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Scotland is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> more productive than on the Fife coast. From its situation, it appears to have been very early inhabited; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, coal-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, harbours, and other advantages for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, attracted settlers, and the coast was first peopled and best cultivated; this appears to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, when <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James VI. compared the county to a grey mantle with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> fringe. The whole coast is covered with small burghs, which that monarch regarded with particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and very early in his reign endeavoured to render them subservient to his wishes, by raising Scotland <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the world as a commercial <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; he granted them many privileges and immunities, and encouraged the inhabitants by every means in his power, to prosecute the advantages which, by their local situation, they possessed; indeed, the municipal privileges which they received from that monarch, though rendered unimportant by the union with England, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> remain a monument of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> sagacity and discernment. The county can boast of possessing several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> seats of royalty: at Dunfermline, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALKLAND">Falkland</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGHORN">Kinghorn</a>, and at St Andrews, vestiges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> splendour are still to be seen. It contains 13 royal boroughs, which possess parliamentary representation, and several which have lost that privilege from their being unable to defray the expense which attended the sending a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> to the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. To the county also belong the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of May, on which there is a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>, and Inchgarvie. Fifeshire is divided into 60 parishes, and contains, by the enumeration in 1801, 93,743 inhabitants, being nearly 196 to the square <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>; a much greater proportion than is to be found in any other county in Scotland. It was anciently an earldom in the Macduff family, created by Malcolm III. for the services performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THANE">thane</a> of Fife, in restoring him to the throne of Scotland, when usurped by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>. That <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> having expired, it was lately revived in the Duffs of Braco, lateral descendants of the ancient family: the ruins of the residences of that powerful nobleman are still evident in many parts of the county.
