A subscription of 500,000l. was immediately filled in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, by a body of men who were incorporated for 21 years by the name of The Society of the Free British Fishery. Every encouragement was held out by government, both to the society, and to individuals who might embark in this national business. A bounty of 36s. per ton was to be paid annually out of the customs, for 14 years, to the owners of all decked vessels or buffes, from 20 to 80 tons burden, which should be built after the commencement of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, and fitted out and employed in, the laid fisheries, whether by the society or any other persons. At the same time numerous pamphlets and newspaper essays came forth; all pretending to elucidate the subject, and to convince the public with what facility the herring fisheries might be transferred from Dutch to British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. This proved, however, a more arduous task than had been foreseen by superficial speculators. The Dutch were frugal in their expenditures and living; perfect masters of the arts of fishing and curing, which they had carried to the greatest height and perfection. They were in full possession of the European <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>; and their fish, whether delivering or otherwise, had the reputation of superior qualities to all others taken in our seas. With such advantages, the Dutch not only maintained their ground against this formidable company, but had also the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of seeing the capital gradually sinking, without having procured an adequate return to the adventurers; notwithstanding various aids and efforts of government from time to time in their favour, particularly in 1757, when an advance of 20s. per ton was added to the bounty. In 1786 the public attention was again called to the state of the British fisheries, by the suggestions of Mr Dempster in the house of commons, and by different publications that appeared upon the subject; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the minister suffered a committee to be named, to inquire into this great source of national wealth. To that committee it appeared, that the best way of improving the fisheries was to encourage the inhabitants living nearest to the seat of them to become fishers: And it being found that the north-western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the kingdom, though abounding with fish and with fine harbours, was utterly destitute of towns, an act was passed for incorporating certain persons therein named, by the style of "The British Society for extending of the fisheries and improving the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coasts of the kingdom;" and to enable them to subscribe a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> stock, and therewith to purchase lands, and build thereon free towns, villages, and fishing stations, in the Highlands and islands in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Great Britain called Scotland, and for other purposes. The isle of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, Loch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">Broom</a>, the isles of Sky and of Cannay, have already been pitched upon as proper situations for some of these towns. The progress of such an undertaking from its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> must be slow, but still flower when carried on with a limited capital arising from the subscriptions of a few public-spirited individuals. But it is not to be doubted but that it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ultimately tend to the increase of our fisheries, and to the improvement of the Highland part of this kingdom. Its tendency is also to lessen the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> of a brave and industrious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of inhabitants, too many of whom have already removed with their families to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. 1. Anchovy FISHERY. The anchovy is caught in the months of May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, on the coasts of Catalonia, Provence, &c., at which season it constantly repairs up the straits of Gibraltar, into the Mediterranean. Fisher. Collins says they are also found in plenty on the western coasts of England and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The fishing for them is chiefly in the night time; when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> being put on the stern of their little fishing vessels, the anchovies flock round, and are caught in the nets. But then it is asserted to have been found by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that anchovies taken thus by fire, are neither so good, so firm, nor so proper for keeping, as those which are taken without fire. When the fishery is over, they cut off the heads, take out their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a> and guts, and then lay them in barrels and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> them. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of eating anchovies is with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, &c. in order to which they are first boned, and the tails, fins, &c. clipped off.—Being put on the fire, they dissolve almost in any liquor. Or they are made into a sauce by mincing them with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, &c. Some also pickle anchovies in small delft or earthen pots, made on purpose, of two or three pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, more or less, which they cover with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> to keep them the better. Anchovies should be chosen small, fresh pickled, white on the outside and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> within. They must have a round back; for those which are fat or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> are often nothing but sardines. Besides these qualities, the pickle, on opening the pots or barrels, must be of a good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and not have lost its flavour. 2. Cod FISHERY. There are two kinds of cod fish; the one green or white cod, and the other dried or cured cod; though it is all the same fish, differently prepared; the former being sometimes salted and barrelled, then taken out for use; and the latter having lain some competent time in salt, dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. We shall therefore speak of each of these apart; and first of the Green. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> fisheries for green cod are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, on the great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of Newfoundland, and on the isle of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and the isle of Sable; to which places vessels <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts both of Europe and America. They are from 100 to 150 tons burden, and will catch between 30,000 and 40,000 cod each. The most essential part of the fishery is, to have a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> who knows how to cut up the cod, one who is skilled to take off the head properly, and above all a good falter, on which the preserving of them, and consequently the success of the voyage depends. The best season is from the beginning of February to the end of April; the fish, which in the winter retire to the deepest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, coming then on the banks and fattening extremely. What is caught from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> to June keeps well; but those taken in July, August, and September, when it is warm on the banks, are apt to spoil soon. Every fisher takes but one at a time: the most expert will take from 350 to 400 in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but that is the most; the weight of the fish and the great coldness on the bank fatiguing very much. As soon as the cod is caught, the head is taken off; they are opened, gutted, and salted; and the falter flows them in the bottom of the hold, head and tail, in beds a fathom or two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; laying layers of salt and fish alternately, but never mixing fish caught on different days. When they have lain thus three or four days to drain off the water, they are replaced in another part of the ship, and salted again; where they remain till the vessel is loaded. Sometimes they are cut in thick pieces, and put in barrels for the conveniency of carriage. Dry. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fishery for this article is, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Rose to the Bay des Exports, along the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, in which compass there are divers commodious ports for the fish to be dried in. These, though of the same kind with the fresh cod, are much smaller, and therefore fitter to keep, as the salt penetrates more easily into them. The fishery of both is much alike; only this latter is most expensive, as it takes up more time and employs more hands, and yet scarce half so much salt is spent in this as in the other. The bait is herrings, of which great quantities are taken on the coast of Placentia. When several vessels meet and intend to fish in the same part, he whose falter first touches ground becomes entitled to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and privileges of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>: he has the choice of his station, and the refusal of all the wood on the coast at his arrival. As fast as the masters arrive, they unrigg all their vessels, leaving nothing but the throats to fasten the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the mates provide a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> on shore, covered with branches of trees, and sails over them, with a scaffold of great trunks of pines, 12, 15, 16, and often 20 feet high, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> from 40 to 60 feet long, and about one-third as much in breadth. While the scaffold is preparing, the crew are a-fishing; and as fast as they catch, they bring their fish ashore, and open and salt them upon moveable benches; but the main salting is performed on the scaffold. When the fish have taken salt, they wash and hang them to drain on rails; when drained, they are laid on kinds of stages, which are small pieces of wood laid across, and covered with branches of trees, having the leaves stripped off for the passage of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. On these stages, they are disposed, a fish thick, head against tail, with the back uppermost, and are turned carefully four times every 24 hours. When they begin to dry, they are laid in heaps 10 or 12 thick, in order to retain their warmth; and every day the heaps are enlarged till they become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> their first bulk; then two heaps are joined together, which they turn every day as before: lastly, they are salted again, beginning with those first salted; and being laid in huge piles, they remain in that situation till they are carried on board the ships, where they are laid on the branches of trees disposed for that purpose, upon the ballast, and round the ship, with mats to prevent their contracting any moisture. There are four sorts of commodities drawn from cod, viz. the sounds, the tongues, the roes, and the oil extracted from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>. The first is salted at the fishery together with the fish, and put in barrels from 600 to 700 pounds. The tongues are done in like manner, and brought in barrels from 400 to 500 pounds. The roes are also salted in barrels, and serve to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the sea to draw fish together, and particularly pilchards. The oil comes in barrels, from 400 to 500 pounds, and is used in dressing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. In Scotland they catch a small kind of cod on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a> and all along the Murray frith on both sides; as also in the friths of Forth, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, &c. which is much esteemed. They salt and dry them in the sun upon rocks, and sometimes in the chimney. 3. Coral FISHERY. See CORAL. 4. Herring Fishery. Our great stations for this fishery are off the Shetland and Western Isles, and off the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, in which the Dutch also share. There are two seasons for fishing herring; the first from June to the end of August; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in autumn, when the fogs become very favourable for this kind of fishing. The Dutch begin their herring fishing on the 24th of June, and employ a vast number of vessels therein, called buffets, being between 45 and 60 tons burden each, and carrying three or four small cannon. They never stir out of port, without a convoy, unless there be enough together to make about 18 or 20 cannon among them, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they are allowed to go in company. Before they go out they make a verbal agreement, which has the same force as if it were in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. The regulations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> of Holland are partly followed by the French and other nations, and partly improved and augmented with new ones; as, that no fisher shall cast his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> within 100 fathoms of another <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>: that while the nets are cast, a light shall be kept on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> part of the vessel: that when a boat is by any accident obliged to leave off fishing, the light shall be cast into the sea; that when the greater part of a fleet leaves off fishing, and casts <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, the rest shall do the same, &c. Mr Anderson * gives to the Scots a knowledge of great antiquity in the herring fishery. He says that the Netherlanders resorted to these coasts as early as A.D. 836, to purchase salted fish of the natives, but, imposing on the strangers, they learned the art, and took up the trade, in after-times of such immense emolument to the Dutch. Sir Walter Raleigh's observations on that head, extracted from the same author, are extremely worthy the attention of the curious, and excite reflections on the vast strength resulting from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of well-applied industry. In 1603, he remarks, the Dutch sold to different nations as many herrings as amounted to 1,759,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. In the year 1615, they at once sent out 2000 buffets, and employed in them 37,000 fishermen. In the year 1618, they sent out 3000 ships, with 50,000 men to take the herrings, and 9000 more ships to transport and sell the fish; which by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> employed 150,000 men, besides those first mentioned. All this wealth was gotten on our coasts, while our attention was taken up in a distant whale fishery. The Scottish monarchs for a long time seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> all their attention to the preservation of the salmon fishery, probably because their subjects were such novices in sea affairs. At length James III. endeavoured to stimulate his great men to these patriotic undertakings; for by an act of his third parliament, he compelled "certain lords spiritual and temporal, and burrows, to make ships, buffets, and boats, with nets and other pertinents, for fishing. That the same should be made in each burgh; in number according to the substance of each burgh, and the least of them to be of twenty tons: and that all idle men be compelled by the sheriffs in the country to go on board the same." Numerous indeed have been the attempts made at different periods to secure this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> to ourselves, but without success. In the late reign, a very strong effort was made, and bounties allowed for the encouragement of British adventurers: the first was of 30s. per ton to every butt of 70 tons and upwards. This bounty was afterwards raised to 50s. per ton, to be paid to such adventurers as were entitled to it by claiming it at the places of rendezvous. The buffets are from 20 to 90 tons burden, but the best size is 80. A vessel of 80 tons ought to take ten lasts, or 120 barrels of herrings, to clear expenses; the price of the fish to be admitted to be a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> a barrel. A ship of this size ought to have 18 men, and three boats: one of 20 tons should have six men; and every five tons above require an additional <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. To every ton are 280 yards of nets; so a vessel of 80 tons carries 20,000 square yards: each net is 12 yards long, and 10 deep, and every boat takes out from 20 to 30 nets, and puts them together so as to form a long train; they are sunk at each end of the train by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which weighs it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the full <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>: the top is supported by buoys, made of sheepskin, with a hollow stick at the mouth fastened tight: through this the skin is blown up, and then stopped with a peg, to prevent the escape of the air. Sometimes these buoys are placed at the top of the nets: at other times the nets are suffered to sink deeper, by the lengthening the cords fastened to them, every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> being for that purpose 10 or 12 fathoms long. But the best fisheries are generally in more shallow water. Of the Scots fishery in the Western Isles, the following account is given by Mr Pennant †. "The fishing is always performed in the night, unless by accident. The buffets remain at anchor, and send out their boats a little before sunrise: which continue out, in winter and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, till day-light; often taking up and emptying their nets, which they do 10 or 12 times in a night, in case of good success. During winter it is a most dangerous and fatiguing employ, by reason of the greatness and frequency of the gales in these seas, and in such gales are the most successful captures: but by the Providence of heaven the fishers are seldom lost; and, what is wonderful, few are visited with illness. They go out well prepared, with a warm great coat, boots, and skin aprons, and a good provision of beef and spirits. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> attends the buffets, which in the tempestuous season, and in the darkest nights, are continually shifting in these narrow seas, from harbour to harbour. Sometimes 80 barrels of herrings are taken in a night by the boats of a single vessel. It once happened in Loch Slappan, in Sky, that a butt of 80 tons might have taken 200 barrels in one night, with 10,000 square yards of net; but the master was obliged to desist, for want of a sufficient number of hands to preserve the capture. The herrings are preserved by salting, after the entrails are taken out. This last is an operation performed by the country people, who get three halfpence per barrel for their trouble; and sometimes, even in the winter, can <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> fifteen pence a day. This employs both women and children; but the salting is only intrusted to the crew of the buffets. The fish are laid on their backs in the barrels, and layers of salt between them. The entrails are not lost, for they are boiled into an oil: 8000 fish will yield ten gallons, valued at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> the gallon. A vessel of 80 tons, takes out 144 barrels of salt; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRAWBACK">drawback</a> of 2s. 8d. is allowed for each barrel used by the foreign or Irish <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of the fish; but there is a duty of 1s. per barrel for the home consumption, and the same..." for those sent to Ireland. The barrels are made of oak staves chiefly from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>; the hoops from several parts of our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and are either of oak, birch, hazel or willow; the last from Holland, liable to a duty. The barrels cost about 3s. each, they hold from 500 to 800 fish, according to the size of the fish; and are made to contain 32 gallons. The barrels are inspected by proper officers; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COOPER">cooper</a> examines if they are statutable and good; if faulty, he destroys them, and obliges the maker to stand to the loss. "Loch Broom has been celebrated for three or four centuries as the resort of herrings. They generally appear here in July; those that turn into this bay are part of the brigade that detaches itself from the western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of that great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> which annually deserts the vast depths of the arctic circle, and comes, heaven-directed, to the seats of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, offered as a cheap food to millions, whom wasteful <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-hearted avarice hath deprived, by enhancing the price, of the wonted supports of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> of the fish from their northern retreat is regular; their visits to the Western isles and coasts certain; but their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to one particular loch extremely precarious. All have their turns; that which swarmed with fish one year, is totally deserted the following; yet the next loch to it may be crowded with the shoals. These changes of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> give often full employ to the buffes, who are continually shifting their harbour in quest of news respecting these important wanderers. They commonly appear here in July; the latter end of August they go into deep water, and continue there for some time, without any apparent cause: in November, they return to the shallows, when a new fishery commences, which continues till <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>: at that time the herrings become full of roe, and are useless as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of commerce. Some doubt, whether those herrings that appear in November are not part of a new migration; for they are as fat, and make the same appearance, as those that composed the first. The signs of the arrival of the herrings are flocks of gulls, who catch up the fish while they skim on the surface, and of gannets who plunge and bring them up from considerable depths. Both these birds are closely attended to by the fishers. Cod fish, haddock, and dog fish, follow the herrings in vast multitudes; these voracious fish keep on the outsides of the columns, and may be a concurrent reason of driving the shoals into bays and creeks. In summer, they come into the bays generally with the warmest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and with easterly gales. During winter, the hard gales from north-west are supposed to assist in forcing them into shelter. East winds are very unfavourable to the fishery." Herrings are cured either white or pickled, or red. Of the fish, those done by the Dutch are the most esteemed, being distinguished into four sorts, according to their sizes; and the best are those that are fat, fleasty, firm, and white, salted the same day they are taken, with good salt, and well barrelled. The British cured herrings are little inferior, if not equal, to the Dutch: for in spite of all their endeavours to conceal the secret, their method of curing, lasting, or casking the herrings, has been discovered, and is as follows. After they have hauled in their nets, which they drag in the stern of their vessels backwards and forwards in traversing the coast, they throw them upon the ship's deck, which is cleared of every thing for that purpose: the crew is separated into sundry divisions, and each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> has a peculiar task; one part opens and guts the herrings, leaving the milts and roes; another cures and salts them, by lining or rubbing their inside with salt; the next packs them, and between each row and division they sprinkle handfuls of salt; lastly, the cooper puts the finishing hand to all, by heading the casks very tight, and stowing them in the hold. Red herrings must lie 24 hours in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRINE">brine</a>, inasmuch as they are to take all their salt there; and when they are taken out, they are spitted, that is, strung by the head on little wooden spits, and then hung in a chimney made for that purpose. After which, by a fire of brushwood, which yields a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of smoke, but no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, being made under them, they remain there till sufficiently smoked and dried, and are afterwards barrelled up for keeping. 5. Lobster FISHERY. Lobsters are taken along the British channel, and on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, whence they are brought to London for sale; and also in the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>. By 10 and 11 W. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 24, no lobster is to be taken under eight inches in length, from the peak of the nose to the end of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIN">fin</a> of the tail; and by 9 Geo. II. cap. 33, no lobsters are to be taken on the coast of Scotland from the 1st of June to the 1st of September. 6. Mackerel FISHERY. The mackerel is a summer fish of passage, found in large shoals, in divers parts of the ocean, not far north; but especially on the French and English coasts. The fishing is usually in the months of April, May, and June, and even July, according to the place. They enter the English channel in April, and proceed up to the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> as the summer advances; so that by June they are on the coasts of Cornwall, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, Normandy, Picardy, &c. where the fishery is most considerable. They are an excellent food fresh; and not to be despised, when well prepared, pickled, and put up in barrels; a method of preserving them chiefly used in Cornwall. The fish is taken two ways; either with a line or nets: the latter is the more considerable, and is usually performed in the night-time. The rules observed in the fishing for mackerel are much the same as those already mentioned in the fishery of herrings. There are two ways of pickling them: the first is, by opening and gutting them, and filling the belly with salt, crammed in as hard as possible, with a stick; which done, they range them in firata or rows, at the bottom of the vessel, trewelling salt between the layers. In the second way, they put them immediately into tubs full of brine, made of fresh water and salt; and leave them to steep, till they have imbibed salt enough to make them keep; after which, they are taken out, and barrelled up, taking care to press them <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> down. Mackerel are not cured or exported as merchandise, except a few by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> and Leoftoff merchants, but are generally consumed at home; especially in the city of London, and the sea-ports between the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> and Yarmouth, east, and the Land's End of Cornwall, west. 7. Oyster FISHERY†. This fishery is principally carried on at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>; Feverham and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; the Isle of Wight; the Swales of the Medway; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENBY">Tenby</a> on the coast of Wales. From Feverham, and adjacent parts, the Dutch have sometimes loaded a hundred large hoyes with oysters in a year. They are also taken in great quantities near <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, and in all the creeks and rivers between Southampton and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>: many of which are carried about by sea to London and to Colchester, to be fed in the pits about Wavenhoe and other places. 8. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a> FISHERY. See Pearl, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and Ceylon. 9. Pilchard FISHERY. The chief pilchard fisheries are along the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, on the coast of Bretagne, and along the coasts of Cornwall and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. That of Dalmatia is very plentiful: that on the coasts of Bretagne employs annually about 300 ships. Of the pilchard fishery on the coast of Cornwall the following account is given by Dr Borlase: "It employs a great number of men on the sea, training them thereby to naval affairs; employs men, women, and children, on land, in salting, pressing, washing and cleaning; in making boats, nets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, casks, and all the trades depending on their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and sale. The poor are fed with the offals of the captures, the land with the refuse of the fish and salt; the merchant finds the gains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> and honest commerce, the fisherman the gains of the fish. Ships are often freighted hither with salt, and into foreign countries with the fish, carrying off at the same time part of our tin. Of the usual produce of the great number of hogheads exported each year for ten years, from 1747 to 1756 inclusive, from the four ports of Fowey, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a>, and St Ives, it appears that Fowey has exported yearly 1732 hogheads; Falmouth, 14,631 hogheads and two thirds; Penzance and Mounts Bay 12,149 hogheads and one-third; St Ives, 1280 hogheads: in all amounting to 29,795 hogheads. Every hoghead for ten years last past, together with the bounty allowed for each hoghead exported, and the oil made out of each hoghead, has amounted, one year with another at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, to the price of £1, 13s. 3d.; so that the cash paid for pilchards exported has, at a medium, annually amounted to the sum of £49,532l. 10s."—The numbers that are taken at one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out of the nets are amazingly great. Mr Pennant says, that Dr Borlase assured him, that on the 5th of October 1767, there were at one time enclofed in St Ives's Bay 7000 hogheads, each hoghead containing 35,000 fish; in all 245 millions. The pilchards naturally follow the light, which contributes much to the facility of the fishery; the season is from June to September. On the coasts of France they make use of the roes of the cod fish as a bait; which, thrown into the sea, makes them rise from the bottom, and run into the nets. On our coasts there are persons poled ashore, who, spying by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the water where the shoals are, make signs to the boats to go among them to cast their nets. When taken, they are brought on shore to a warehouse, where they are laid up in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> piles, supported with backs and sides; and as they are piled, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> them with bay salt; in which lying to soak for 30 or 40 days, they run out a deal of blood, with dirty pickle and bitter: then they wash them clean in sea water; and, when dry, barrel and press them hard down to squeeze out the oil, which flows out at a hole in the bottom of the cask. 10. Salmon FISHERY†. The chief salmon fisheries in Europe are in England, Scotland, and Ireland, in the rivers, and sea coasts adjoining to the river mouths. The most distinguished for salmon in Scotland are, the river Tweed, the Clyde, the Tay, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a>, the Spey, the Nefs, the Bewly, &c. in most of which it is very common, about the height of summer, especially if the weather happens to be very hot, to catch four or five score salmon at a draught. The chief rivers in England for salmon are, the Tyne, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, and the Thames. The fishing is performed with nets, and sometimes with a kind of locks or weirs made on purpose, which in certain places have iron or wooden <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> to diposed, in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, that being impelled by any force in a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to the course of the river, they may give way and open a little at the point of contact, and immediately shut again, closing the angle. The salmon, therefore, coming up into the rivers, are admitted into these grates, which open, and suffer them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through, but that again, and prevent their return. The salmon is also caught with a spear, which they dart into him when they see him <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> near the surface of the water. It is customary likewise to catch them with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> and lanthorn, or wip of straw fet on fire; for the fish naturally following the light, are struck with the spear, or taken in a net spread for that purpose, and lifted with a sudden jerk from the bottom. "The capture of salmon in the Tweed, about the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of July (says Mr Pennant †) is prodigious. In a good fishery, often a boat load, and sometimes near two, are taken in a tide: some few years ago there were above 700 fish taken at one haul, but from 50 to 100 is very frequent. The coopers in Berwick then begin to salt both salmon and grilfe in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> and other large vessels, and afterwards barrel them to send abroad, having then far more than the London markets can take off their hands. "Most of the salmon taken before April, or to the setting in of the warm weather, is sent fresh to London in baskets: unless now and then the vessel is disappointed by contrary winds of failing immediately; in which case the fish is brought ashore again to the coopers offices, and boiled, pickled, and kitted, and sent to the London markets by the same ship, and fresh salmon put in the baskets in lieu of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STALE">stale</a> ones. At the beginning of the season, when a ship is on the point of failing, a fresh clean salmon will sell from a shilling to eighteen pence a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>; and most of the time that this part of the trade is carried on, the prices are from five to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings per stone; the value rising and falling according to the plenty of fish, or the prospect of a fair or foul <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Some fish are sent in this manner to London the latter end of September, when the weather grows cool; but then the fish are full of large roes, grow very thin bellied, and are not esteemed either palatable or wholesome. "The season for fishing in the Tweed begins November 30th, but the fishermen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> very little till after Christmas: it ends on Michaelmas day; yet the corporation of Berwick (who are conservators of the river) Fisher. river) indulge the fishermen with a fortnight past that time, on account of the change of the style. "There are on the river 41 considerable fisheries, extending upwards about 14 miles from the mouth, (the others above being of no great value), which are rented for near 5400l. per annum: the expense attending the servants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, nets, boats, &c. amount to 3000l. more; which together makes up the sum 10,400l. Now, in consequence, the produce must defray all, and no less than 20 times that sum of fish will effect it; so that 28,000 salmon must be caught there one year with another. "Scotland possesses great numbers of fine fisheries on both sides of that kingdom. The Scotch in early times had most severe laws against the killing of this fish; for the third offence was made capital, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of James IV. Before that, the offender had power to redeem his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. They were thought in the time of Henry VI. a present worthy of a crowned head: for in that reign the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Scotland sent to the duchess of Clarence 10 casks of salted salmon; which Henry directed to pass duty free. The salmon are cured in the same manner as at Berwick, and a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is sent to London in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; but after that time, the adventurers begin to barrel and export them to foreign countries; but we believe that commerce is far less lucrative than it was in former times, partly owing to the great increase of the Newfoundland fishery, and partly to the general relaxation of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. "Ireland (particularly the north) abounds with this fish: the most considerable fishery is at Cramna, on the river Ban, about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from Coleraine. When I made the tour of that hospitable kingdom in 1754, it was rented by a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> for 620l. a-year; who assured me, that the tenant, his predecessor, gave 1600l. per annum, and was a much greater gainer by the bargain, for the reasons before mentioned, and on account of the number of poachers who destroy the fish in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> months. "The mouth of this river faces the north; and is finely situated to receive the fish that roam along the coast in search of an inlet into some fresh water, as they do along that end of the kingdom which opposes itself to the northern ocean. We have seen near Ballicafla, nets placed in the sea at the foot of the promontories that jut into it, which the salmon strike into as they are wandering close to shore; and numbers are taken by that method. "In the Ban they fish with nets 18 score yards long, and are continually <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> night and day the whole season, which we think lasts about four months, two sets of 16 men each alternately relieving one another. The best drawing is when the tide is coming in: we were told, that at a single draught there were once 840 fish taken. "A few miles higher up the river is a wear where a considerable number of fish that escape the nets are taken. We were lately informed, that, in the year 1760, about 320 tons were taken in the Cranna fishery." Curing Salmon. When the salmon are taken, they open them along the back, take out the guts and gills, and cut out the greatest part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, endeavouring to make the inside as smooth as possible: they then salt the fish in large tubs for the purpose, where they lie a considerable time soaking in brine; and about October they are packed close up in barrels, and sent to London, or exported up the Mediterranean. They have also in Scotland a great deal of salmon salted in the common way, which after soaking in brine a competent time, is well pressed, and then dried in smoke: this is called kipper, and is chiefly made for home consumption; and if properly cured and prepared, is reckoned very delicious. Sturgeon + Fishery. The greatest sturgeon fishery is in the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>, on the Caspian sea; where the Muscovites employ a great number of hands, and catch them in a kind of inclosure, formed by huge stakes representing the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> Z repeated several times. These fisheries are open on the side next the sea, and close on the other; by which means the fish ascending in its season up the river, is embarrassed in these narrow angular retreats, and so is easily killed with a harping iron. Sturgeons, when fresh, eat deliciously; and in order to make them keep, they are salted or pickled in large pieces, and put up in casks from 30 to 50 pounds. But the great object of this fishery is the roe, of which the Muscovites are extremely fond, and of which is made the caviar, or kavia, so much esteemed by the Italians. See CAVIAR. Tunny Fishery. The tunny (a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Scomber), was a fish well known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and made a great article of commerce: And there are still very considerable tunny fisheries on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, as well as several other parts of the Mediterranean. The nets are spread over a large space of sea by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> fastened to anchors, and are divided into several compartments. The entrance is always directed, according to the season, towards that part of the sea from which the fish are known to come. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> placed upon the summit of a rock high above the water, gives a signal of the fish being arrived; for he can discern from that elevation what passes under the waters infinitely better than any person nearer the surface. As soon as notice is given that the shoal of fish has penetrated as far as the inner compartment, or the chamber of death, the pallage is drawn close, and the slaughter begins. The undertakers of these fisheries pay an acknowledgment to the king, or the lord upon whose land they fix the main stay or foot of the tonnara; they make the best bargain they can: and, till success has crowned their endeavours, obtain this leave for a small consideration; but the rent is afterwards raised in proportion to their capture. The tunny enter the Mediterranean about the vernal equinox, travelling in a triangular phalanx, so as to cut the waters with its point, and to present an extensive base for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> and currents to act against, and impel forwards. These fish repair to the warm seas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to spawn, steering their course thither along the European shores, but as they return, approach the African coast; the young fry is placed in the van of the squadron as they travel. They come back from the east in May, and abound on the coast of Sicily and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> about that time. In autumn they steer northward, and frequent the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; but during the whole season stragglers are occasionally caught. When taken in May, the usual time of their appearance in the Calabrian bays, they are full of spawn, and their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is then esteemed unwholesome, apt to occasion headaches and vapours; the milts and roes are particularly so at that season. To prevent these bad effects, the natives fry them in oil, and afterwards salt them. The quantity of this fish consumed annually in the Two Sicilies almost exceeds the bounds of calculation. From the beginning of May to the end of October it is eaten fresh, and all the rest of the year it is in use salted. The most delicate part is the muzzle. The belly salted was called tarantillum, and accounted a great delicacy by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; its present name is Surra. The rest of the body is cut into slices, and put into tubs. Turbot Fishery. Turbot grows to a large size, some of them weighing from 23 to 30 pounds. They are taken chiefly off the north coast of England, and others off the Dutch coast. The large turbot (as well as several other kinds of flat fish) are taken by the hook and line, for they lie in deep water; the method of taking them in weirs or flaked nets being very precarious. When the fishermen go out to fish, each person is provided with three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, which are coiled on a flat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> piece of wicker work; the hooks being baited, and placed regularly in the centre of the coil. Each line is furnished with 14 score of hooks, at the distance of six feet two inches from each other. The hooks are fastened to the lines upon heads of twisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> 27 inches in length. When fishing, there are always three men in each coble, and consequently nine of these lines are fastened together, and used in one line, extending in length near three miles, and furnished with 2520 hooks. An anchor and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUOY">buoy</a> are fixed at the first end of the line, and one more of each at the end of each man's lines; in all four anchors, which are common perforated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and four buoys made of leather or cork. The line is always laid across the current. The tides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> and ebb continue an equal time upon our coast, and, when undisturbed by winds, run each way about six hours; they are so rapid that the fishermen can only shoot and haul their lines at the turn of tide, and therefore the lines always remain upon the ground about six hours; during which time the myxine glutinosa of Linnaeus will frequently penetrate the fish that are on the hooks, and entirely devour them, leaving only the skin and bones. The same rapidity of tides prevents their using hand lines; and therefore two of the people commonly wrap themselves in the sail, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> while the other keeps a strict look-out, for fear of being run down by ships, and to observe the weather. For storms often rise so suddenly, that it is with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> difficulty they can sometimes escape to the shore, leaving their lines behind. Besides the coble, the fishermen have also a five-men boat, which is 40 feet long and 15 broad, and 25 tons burden; it is so called, though navigated by six men and a boy, because one of the men is commonly hired to cook, &c., and does not share in the profits with the other five. This boat is decked at each end, but open in the middle, and has two large lug sails. All our able fishermen go in these boats to the herring fishery at Yarmouth in the latter end of September, and return about the middle of November. The boats are then laid up till the beginning of Lent, at which time they go off in them to the edge of the Dogger, and other places to fish for turbot, cod, ling, skates, &c. They always take two cobsles on board; and when they come upon their ground, anchor the boat, throw out the cobsles, and fish in the same manner as those who go from the shore in a coble; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> only, that here each man is provided with double the quantity of lines, and instead of waiting the return of the tide in the coble, return to their boat and bait their other lines; thus hauling one set and shooting another every turn of tide. They commonly run into harbour twice a-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> to deliver their fish. The best bait is fresh herring cut in pieces of a proper size; the five-men boats are always furnished with nets for taking them. Next to herrings are the lesser lampreys. The next baits in esteem are small haddocks cut in pieces, sand <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and limpets, here called flidders; and when none of these can be had, they use bullock's liver. The hooks are two inches and a half long in the shank, and near an inch wide between the shank and the point. The line is made of small cording, and is always tanned before it is used. Turbots are extremely delicate in their choice of baits; for if a piece of herring or haddock has been 12 hours out of the sea, and then used as bait, they will not touch it. Whale Fishery. See Baleena, Cetology Index. Whales are chiefly caught in the north seas; the largest sort are found about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> or Spitzbergen. At the first discovery of this country, whales not being used to be disturbed, frequently came into the very bays, and were accordingly killed almost close to the shore; so that the blubber being cut off was immediately boiled into oil on the spot. The ships in these times took in nothing but the pure oil and the whalebone, and all the business was executed in the country; by which means a ship could bring home the product of many more whales than she can, according to the present method of conducting this trade. The fishery also was then so plentiful, that they were obliged sometimes to send other ships to fetch off the oil they had made, the quantity being more than the fishing ships could bring away. But time and change of circumstances have shifted the situation of this trade. The ships coming in such numbers from Holland, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, Hamburgh, and other northern countries, all intruders upon the English, who were the first discoverers of Greenland, the whales were disturbed, and gradually, as other fish often do, forsaking the place, were not to be killed so near the shore as before: but are now found, and have been so ever since, in the openings and spaces among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, where they have deep water, and where they go sometimes a great many leagues from the shore. The whale fishery begins in May, and continues all June and July; but whether the ships have good or bad success, they must come away, and get clear of the ice by the end of August; so that in the month of September at farthest they may be expected home; but a ship that meets with a fortunate and early fishery in May may return in June or July. But, for the manner of taking whales, and for a farther account of the whale fishery, as a trade, see Cetology.

FISHGARD

Pages 700-700
or FISGARD, a town of Pembroke-shire, situated on a steep cliff on the sea shore, 254 miles from

FISHING

Pages 700-702

in general, the art of catching fish, whether by means of nets, of spears, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the line and hook. FISHING in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, spear, or harpoon, for fish that go in shoals, has been explained in the preceding article. That performed by the rod, line, and hook, for solitary fish, is usually termed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANGLING">ANGLING</a>: See that article; and for the particular manner of angling for the different kinds of fish, see their respective names, as DACE, EEL, PERCH, under <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a>. Here we shall give an account of the following: 1. The Barbel (†), (so called on account of the barb or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> that is under his chaps), though a coarse fish, gives considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> to the angler's ingenuity. They swim together in great shoals, and are at their worst in April, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they spawn, but come soon in season; the places whither they chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, are such as are weedy and gravelly rising grounds, in which this fish is said to dig and root with his nose like a swine. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> he frequents the stronger, swiftest currents of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; as deep bridges, weirs, &c., and is apt to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> himself among the piles, hollow places, and mofs or weeds; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> remain there immoveable; but in the winter he retires into deep waters, and helps the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> to make a hole in the sands to hide her spawn in, to hinder its being devoured by other fish. He is a very curious and cunning fish; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his baits be not sweet, clean, well scoured, and kept in sweet mofs, he will not bite; but well ordered and curiously kept, he will bite with great eagerness. The best bait for him is the spawn of a salmon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, or any other fish; and if you would have good sport with him, bait the places where you intend to fish with it a night or two before, or with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> cut in pieces; and the earlier in the morning or the later in the evening that you fish, the better it will be. Your rod and line must be both strong and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, with a running plummet on the line; and let a little bit of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> be placed a foot or more above the hook, to keep the bullet from falling on it; so the worm will be at the bottom, where they always bite; and when the fish takes the bait, your plummet will <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> and not choke him. By the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> of your rod you may know when he bites, as also with your <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> you will feel him make a strong snatch; then strike, and you will rarely fail, if you play him well; but if you manage him not dexterously, he will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> your line. The best time for fishing is about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in the morning, and the most proper season is the latter end of May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and the beginning of August. 2. The Bleak (†), is an eager fish, caught with all sorts of worms bred on trees or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; as also with flies, paste, sheep's blood, &c. They may be angled for with half a score of hooks at once, if they can be all fastened on; he will also in the evening take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> fly. If the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> be warm and clear, there is no fly so good for him as the small fly at the top of the water, which he will take at any time of the day, especially in the evening; but if the day is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and cloudy, gentles and caddis are the best; about two feet under water. No fish yields better sport to a young angler than the bleak. It is so eager, that it will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> out of the water for a bait. There is another way of taking bleak, which is by whipping them in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, or on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> side in fresh water in a summer's evening, with a hazel top about five or six feet long and a line twice the length of the rod. But the best method is with a drabble, thus: Tie eight or ten small hooks across a line two inches above one another; the biggest hook the lowermost, (whereby you may sometimes take a better fish), and bait them with gentles, flies, or some small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> worms, by which means you may take half a dozen or more at a time. 3. For the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">Bream</a> [†], observe the following directions, which will also be of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in carp fishing.—Procure about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of large red worms; put them into fresh mofs <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> well washed and dried every three or four days, feeding them with fat mould and chopped fennel, and they will be thoroughly scoured in about three weeks. Let your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, but all silk is the best; let the floats be either swan-quills or goose-quills. Let your plumb be a piece of lead in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, with a small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> at the little end of it; fasten the lead to the line, and the live hook to the lead, about ten or twelve inches space between lead and hook will be enough; and take care the lead be heavy enough to sink the float. Having baited your hook well with a strong worm, the worm will draw the hook up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the bottom, which will provoke the bream to bite the more eagerly. It will be best to fit up three or four rods or lines in this manner, and set them as will be directed, and this will afford you much the better sport. Find the exact depth of the water if possible, that your float may swim on its surface directly over the lead; then provide the following ground bait. Take about a peck of sweet groat-ground malt; and having boiled it a very little, strain it hard through a bag, and carry it to the water side where you have founded; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where you suppose the fish frequent, throw in the malt by handfuls squeezed hard together, that the stream may not separate it before it comes to the bottom; and be sure to throw it in at least a yard above the place where you intend the hook shall lie, otherwise the stream will carry it down too far. Do this about nine o'clock at night, keeping some of the malt in the bag, and go to the place about three the next morning; but approach very warily, lest you should be seen by the fish; for it is certain that they have their sentinels watching on the top of the water, while the rest are feeding below. Having baited your hook so that the worm may crawl to and fro, the better to allure the fish to bite, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> it in at the place where you find the fish to stay most, which is generally in the broadest and deepest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the river, and so that it may rest about the midst of your bait that is on the ground. Cast in your <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> line so that it may rest a yard above that, and a third about a yard below it. Let your rods lie on the bank, with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> to keep them down at the great ends; and then withdraw yourself, yet not so far but that you can have your eye upon... Fishing upon all the floats; and when you see one bitten and carried away, do not be too hasty to run in, but give time to the fish to tire himself, and then touch him gently. When you perceive the float sink, creep to the water side, and give it as much line as you can. If it is a bream or carp, they will run to the other side; which strike gently, and hold your rod at a bent a little while; but do not pull, for then you will spoil all; but you must first tire them before they can be landed, for they are very shy. If there are any carps in the river, it is an even wager that you take one or more of them; but if there are any pike or perch, they will be sure to visit the ground bait, though they will not touch it, being drawn thither by the great resort of the small fish; and until you remove them, it is in vain to think of taking the bream or carp. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, bait one of your hooks with a small bleak, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROACH">roach</a>, or gudgeon, about two feet deep from your float, with a little red worm at the point of your hook; and if a pike be there, he will be sure to snap at it. This spot is good till nine o'clock in the morning; and in a gloomy day, till night; but do not frequent the place too much, lest the fish grow shy. 4. The Carp. A person who <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> for carp must arm himself with abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, because of its extraordinary subtlety and policy; they always choose to lie in the deepest places, either of ponds or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, where there is but a small running stream. Further, observe, that they will seldom bite in cold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and you cannot be too early or too late at the spot in hot weather; and if he bite, you need not fear his hold; for he is one of those <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-mouthed fish that have their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in their throat. Neither must you forget, in angling for him, to have a strong rod and line; and since he is so very wary, it will be proper to entice him, by baiting the ground with a coarse paste. He seldom refuses the red worm in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the caddis in June, or the grasshopper in June, April, and September. This fish does not only delight in worms, but also in sweet paste; of which there is great variety; the best is made of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and ought to be thrown into the water some hours before you begin to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>; neither will small pellets thrown into the water two or three days before be worse for this purpose, especially if chickens' guts, garbage, or blood mixed with bran and cow dung, be also thrown in. But more particularly, as to a paste very proper for this use, you may make it in the manner following: Take a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of flour, and mingle it with veal, cut small, making it up with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of honey; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> all together in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> till they are so tough as to hang upon the hook without wafing off. In order to effect which the better, mingle whitish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> with it; and if you keep it all the year round, add some virgin wax and clarified honey. Again, If you fish with gentles, anoint them with honey, and put them on your hook, with a deep scarlet dipped in the like, which is a good way to deceive the fish. Honey and crumbs of wheat <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, mixed together, make also a very good paste. In taking a carp either in pond or river, if the angler intends to add profit to his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, he must take a peck of ale-grains, and a good quantity of any blood to mix with the grains, baiting the ground with it where he intends to angle. This food will wonderfully attract the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>-fish, as carp, tench, roach, dace, and bream. Let him angle in a morning, plumbing his ground, and angling for carp with a strong line; the bait must be either paste or a knotted red worm; and by this means he will have sport enough. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of proper Bait for the several sorts of Fish referred to in the annexed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. Flies. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a> fly, found under hollow stones at the sides of rivers, is of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> streaks on the back and belly, has large wings, and is in season from April to July. 2. Green drake, found among stones by river sides, has a yellow body stripped with green, is long and slender, with wings like a butterfly, his tail turns on his back, and from May to Midsummer is very good. 3. Oak-fly, found in the body of an oak or ash, with its head downwards, is of a brown colour, and excellent from May to September. 4. Palmer fly or worm, found on leaves of plants, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called a caterpillar, and when it comes to a fly is excellent for trout. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">Ant</a> fly, found in ant hills from June to September. 6. The May fly is to be found playing at the river side, especially against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> fly is to be found upon every hawthorn after the buds are come off. Paste. 1. Take the blood of sheep's hearts, and mix it with honey and flour worked to a proper consistence. 2. Take old cheese grated, a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it, and colour it with saffron: in winter use rufly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> instead of butter. 3. Crumbs of bread chewed or worked with honey or sugar, moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> icy water. 4. Bread chewed, and worked in the hand till stiff. Worms. 1. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> bob, found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> ground after ploughing; it is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, with a red head, and bigger than a gentle; another is found in heathy ground, with a blue head. Keep them in an earthen vessel well covered, and a sufficient quantity of the mould they harbour in. They are excellent from April to November. 2. Gentles to be had from putrid <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>: let them lie in wheat bran a few days before used. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">Flag</a> worms, found in the roots of flags; they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow colour, are longer and thinner than a gentle, and must be covered like them. 4. Cow-turd bob, or clap bait, found under a cow turd from May to Michaelmas; it is like a gentle, but larger. Keep it in its native earth like the earth bob. 5. Caddis worm, or cod bait, found under loose stones in shallow rivers; they are yellow, bigger than a gentle, with a black or blue head, and are in season from April to July. Keep them in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> bags. 6. Lob worm, found in gardens; it is very large, and has a red head; a streak down the back, and a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> tail. 7. Marsh-worms, found in marshy ground; keep them in moss ten days before you use them: their colour is a bluish red, and are a good bait from March to Michaelmas. 8. Brandling red worms, or blood worms, found in rotten dunghills and tanners bark; they are small red worms, very good for all small fish, have sometimes a yellow tail, and are called rag-tails.

FISHING BY

Pages 703-705

G by means of birds, a method peculiar to the Chinese, who train certain birds for the purpose in the same manner as falcons are taught to pursue <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>. For this purpose they have trained a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of pelican, resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> corvortant, which they call the Leu-tse, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. Sir George Staunton, who, when the embassy was proceeding on the southern branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> canal, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> those birds employed, tells us, that on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the east side of the canal, are thousands of small boats and rafts, built entirely for this species of fishery. On each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or raft are ten or a dozen birds, which, at a signal from the owner, plunge into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and it is astonishing to see the enormous size of fish with which they return, grasped within their bills. They appeared to be so well trained, that it did not require either <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> about their throats to prevent them from swallowing any portion of their prey, except what their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was pleased to return to them for encouragement and food. The boat used by these fishermen is of a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> make, and is often carried to the lake, together with the fishing birds, by the men who are there to be supported by it. The same author saw the fishermen busy on the great lake Wee chaung-hee; and he gives the following account of a very singular method practised by them for catching the fish of the lake without the aid of birds, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, or of hooks. To the one side of a boat a flat board, painted <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, is fixed, at an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of about 45 degrees, the edge inclining towards the water. On moonlight nights the boat is so placed that the painted board is turned to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, from whence the rays of light striking on the whitened surface, give it the appearance of moving water; on which the fish being tempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> on their element, the boatmen raising with a string the board, turn the fish into the boat. Water-fowl are much sought after by the Chinese, and are taken upon the same lake by the following ingenious device. Empty jars or gourds are suffered to float about upon the water, that such objects may become familiar to the birds. The fisherman then wades into the lake with one of these empty vessels upon his head, and walks gently towards a bird; and lifting up his arm, draws it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> below the surface of the water without any disturbance or giving alarm to the rest, several of whom he treats in the same manner, until he fills the bag he had brought to hold his prey. The contrivance itself is not so singular, as it is that the same exactly should have occurred in the new continent, as Ulloa affirms, to the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, upon the lake Cienega de Tesias. Of these there are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds; some made of Mulcovy duck quills, which are the best for flow waters; but for strong streams, found cork, without flaws or holes, bored through with a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, into which is put a quill of a fit proportion, is preferable: pare the cork to a pyramidal form, and make it smooth. *Fishing Hook,* a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> made of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wire, of a proper form to catch and retain fish. The fishing hook in general ought to be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the shank, somewhat thick in the circumference, the point even and straight; let the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> be in the shank. For setting the hook on, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> strong but small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, laying the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on the inside of your book; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be on the outside, the silk <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fret and cut it asunder. There are several sizes of these fishing hooks, some big, some little; and of these, some have peculiar names; as, 1. Single hooks. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> hooks; which have two bendings, one contrary to the other. 3. Snappers, or gorgers, which are the hooks to whip the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> fly upon, or bait with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fly. 4. Springers, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> hooks; a kind of double hooks, with a spring, which flies open upon being struck into any fish, and so keeps its mouth open. FISHING-Line, is either made of hair twisted; or silk; or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> grass. The best colours are the furred, white, and gray; the two last for clear waters, the first for muddy ones. Nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> watery green despisable; this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is given artificially, by steeping the hair in a liquor made of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, root, and the juice of walnut leaves, boiled together. FISHING-Rod, a long slender rod or wand, to which the line is fastened, for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANGLING">angling</a>.—Of these there are several sorts; as, 1. A troller, or trolling rod, which has a ring at the end of the rod, for the line to go through when it runs off a reel. 2. A whipper, or whipping rod; a top rod, that is weak in the middle, and top heavy, but all slender and fine. 3. A dropper; which is a strong rod and very light. 4. A snapper, or snap rod; which is a strong pole, peculiarly used for the pike. 5. A bottom rod; being the same as the dropper, but somewhat more pliable. 6. A fingling or procking stick; a forked stick, having a short strong line, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, baited with a lob worm: this is only for eels in their holes. FISHING-Frog, or Angler. See Lophius. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> of FISHING, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of fish.
