It has been held, that where the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> hath the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on both sides of the river, it is good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that he hath a right of fishing; and it puts the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> upon him who claims liberam piscariam: but where a river ebbs and flows, and is an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, there it is common to all, and he who claims a privilege to himself must prove it; for if the trespass is brought for fishing there, the defendant may justify, that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where is brachium maris, in quo unumquoque subditus domini regis habet et habere debet liberam piscariam. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> the soil belongs to the owners of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> on each side; and the soil of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> is in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, but the fishing is common to all. He who is owner of the soil of a private river, hath liberam piscariam; and he that hath liberam piscariam, hath a property in the fish, and may bring a possession <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> for them; but communis piscaria is like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of all other commons. One that has a clofe pond in which there are fish, may call them piscis suos, in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, &c. but he cannot call them <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">bona</a> et catalle, if they be not in trunks. There needs no privilege to make a fish pond, as there doth in the case of a warren. See Franchise.

FISHING FLIES

Pages 702-703

a bait used in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANGLING">angling</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds of fish. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">FISHING</a>. The fly is either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>. I. Natural flies are innumerable. The more usual for this purpose are mentioned in the preceding page. There are two ways to fish with natural flies; either on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or a little underneath it. In angling for chevin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROACH">roach</a>, or dace, move not your natural fly twitly when you see the fish make at it; but rather let it glide freely towards him with the stream; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be in a still and slow water, draw the fly slowly sidewise by him, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make him eagerly pursue. II. The artificial fly is seldom used but in blustering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, when the waters are so troubled by the winds, that the natural fly cannot be seen, nor rest upon them. Of this artificial fly there are reckoned no less than 12 sorts, of which the following are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>. 1. For <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">dun</a> fly; made of dun <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and the feathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>'s wing; or the body made of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> wool, and the feathers of a black drake. 2. For April, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> fly; the body made of black wool, dyed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> under the wings and tail. 3. For the beginning of May, the ruddy fly; made of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wool, and bound about with black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, with the feathers of a black <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPON">capon</a> hanging dangling on his sides next his tail. 4. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, the greenish fly; the body made of black wool, with a yellow <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> on either side, the wings taken off the wings of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUZZARD">buzzard</a>, bound with black broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. 5. The moorish fly, the body made of darkish wool, and the wings of the blackish mail of a drake. 6. The tawney fly, good till the middle of June; the body made of tawney wool, the wings made contrary one against the other of the whitish mail of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> drake. 7. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the wafly fly; the body made of black wool, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> about with yellow silk, and the wings of drakes feathers. 8. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> fly; good in the middle of July; the body made with greenish wool, cast about with the feathers of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s tail, and the wings made of those of the buzzard. 9. For August, the drake fly; the body made with black wool cast about with black silk; his wings of the mail of a black drake, with a black head. The best rules for artificial fly fishing are, 1. To fish in a river somewhat disturbed with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>; or in a cloudy <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when the waters are moved by a gentle breeze: the south <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is best; and if the wind blow <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, yet not so but that you may conveniently <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> your tackle, the fish will rise in plain deeps; but if the wind be small, the best angling is in swift streams. 2. Keep as far from the water side as may be; fish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the stream with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at your back, and touch not the water with your line. 3. Ever <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> in clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, with a small fly and slender wings; but in muddy places, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a larger. 4. When, after rain, the water becomes brownish, use an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> fly; in a clear day, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-colored fly; a dark fly for dark waters, &c. 5. Let the line be twice as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the rod, unless the river be encumbered with wood. 6. For every sort of fly, have several of the same differing in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with the different complexions of several waters and weathers. 7. Have a nimble eye, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, to strike presently with the rising of the fish; or else he will be apt to spue out the hook. 8. Let the fly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> first into the water, and not the line, which will scare the fish. 9. In slow rivers, or still places, cast the fly across the river, and let it sink a little in the water, and draw it gently back with the current. Salmon flies should be made with their wings standing one behind the other, whether two or four. This fish delights in the gaudiest colours that can be; chiefly in the wings, which must be long, as well as the tail.

FISSURES

Pages 705-705

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a>, certain interruptions, that in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> manner divide the several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of which the body of our globe is composed. See Geology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fissure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">Bones</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, is when they are divided either transversely or longitudinally, not quite through, but cracked after the manner of glass, by any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force. See Surgery.

FISTULA

Pages 705-706

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind, resembling our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flageolet. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> wind instruments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, were the tibia and the fistula. But how they were constituted, wherein they differed, or how they were played upon, does not appear. All we know is, that the fistula was at first made of reeds, and afterwards of other matters. Some had holes, some none; some again were single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>; others a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of several; witness the syringa of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. Fistula, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a deep, narrow, and callous ulcer, generally arising from abscesses. It differs from sinus, in its being callous, the latter not. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fistula, in Farriery. See Farriery Index. Fistularia, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>-Pipe Fish; a genus of fishes, belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. FIT. See Paroxysm. Dr Cheyne is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that fits of all kinds, whether epileptic, hysterical, or apoplectic, may be cured solely by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> diet, of about two quarts of cows milk a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, without any other medicine. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FITCHES">Fitches</a>, in Husbandry, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, more generally known by the name of chick-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>. See Cicer, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. Fitches are cultivated either for feeding cattle, or improving the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. They make a wholesome and nourishing food, whether given in the straw or thrashed out. When sown only to improve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, they are ploughed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they begin to blossom, by which means a tough stiff clay soil is much enriched. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FITCHET">Fitchet</a>, a name used in some places for the weasel, called also the feumart. See Mustela, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FITCHY">Fitchy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, (from the French fiche, i.e., fixed); a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to a crois when the lower branch ends in a sharp point: and the reason of it Mackenzie supposes to be, that the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were wont to carry crosses with them wherever they went; and when they flopped on their journey at any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, they fixed those portable crosses in the ground for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>'s sake. Fitz, makes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sons of the kings of England, as Fitz-roy; which is purely French, and signifies the "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s son." Fitzherbert, Sir Anthony, a very learned lawyer in the reign of King Henry VIII, was descended from an ancient family, and born at Norbury in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>. He was made one of the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas in 1523; and distinguished himself by many valuable works, as well as by such an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> discharge of the duties of his office, as made him esteemed an oracle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. His writings are, The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Abridgement; The Office and Authority of Justices of Peace; the Office of Sheriffs, Bailiffs of Liberties, Escheators, Constables, Coroners, &c.; Of the Diversity of Courts; The New Natura Brivium; Of the Surveying of Lands, and The Book of Husbandry. He died in 1538. Fitz-Stephen, William, a learned monk of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, of Norman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, but born of respectable parents in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He lived in the 12th century; and being attached to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Archbishop Becket, was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. In the year 1774, he wrote in Latin, *The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of St. Thomas, archbishop and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>*; in which, as Becket was a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, he introduces a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the city of London, with a miscellaneous detail of the manners and usages of the citizens: this is deservedly considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> curiosity, being the earliest professed account of London extant. Fitz-Stephen died in 1191.

FIVES

Pages 706-706
or VIVES.** See Farriery. **FIXATION,** in Chemistry, the rendering any volatile substance fixed, so as not to fly off upon being exposed to a great heat: hence, **FIXED BODIES,** are those which bear a considerable degree of heat without evaporating, or losing any of their weight. Some of the most fixed bodies are diamonds, gold, &c. **FIXED or Fixable Air,** an invisible and permanently elastic fluid, superior in gravity to common atmospheric air and most other aerial fluids, exceedingly destructive to animal life; produced in great quantities, naturally from combustible bodies, and artificially by many chemical processes. From its acid properties it has obtained the name of *aerial acid*, *cretaceous acid*, and *carbonic acid*; from its noxious qualities, it has been called *mephitic air*, or *mephitic gas*; and, from the circumstance of being produced in vast quantities during the combustion of charcoal, it first obtained from Van Helmont the name of *gas sygnetire*. The term fixed air has been given from its property of readily losing its elasticity, and fixing itself in many bodies, particularly those of the calcareous kind; and though some objected to the propriety of the term, the fluid in question is so well known by the name of fixed air, that we choose still to retain it. See Chemistry Index. For an account of the apparatus for impregnating water with fixed air or carbonic acid, see Materia Medica Index. **FIXED Stars,** are such as constantly retain the same position and distance with respect to each other; by which they are distinguished from *erratic* or *wandering* stars, which are continually shifting their situation and distance. The fixed stars are properly called *flora*; the rest have the peculiar denomination of *planet* and *comet*. See Astronomy Index. **FIXITY,** or **FIXEDNESS,** in Chemistry, is in a peculiar manner used for the affection opposite to volatility; i.e., the property whereby bodies bear the action of the fire, without being dissipated in fumes.

FIXMILLNER

Pages 706-707

PLACIDUS,** an eminent astronomer, was born at Achleiten near Linz, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, on the 28th of May, 1720. He received the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Kremsmünster, of which his uncle Alexander was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. Here he studied during five years, and delighted so much in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> straight and curve-line figures, that his mother called him the *<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">almanack</a>-maker*. He went afterward to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>, where he studied a regular course of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and particularly turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> under a professor Stuard, whose method of teaching that science was truly extraordinary, as he never made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of any figures, and yet conveyed such a clear idea of every proposition as made it perfectly easy. He was admitted as a novice into Kremsmünster in 1737, and the next year he took the solemn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> in presence of his uncle. After being two years in this monastery, during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he devoted every leisure <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of mathematics and philosophy, he went to Fixmillner, Salzburg to finish his studies in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, acquiring at that time a competent knowledge of oriental and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquities. In the year 1745, he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of L.D., after which he received <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>'s orders in his own monastery, and was created professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which office he held for 40 years, discharging the duties belonging to it till within a few days of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was also chosen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and regent of the young <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, which he retained during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the *Jus Canonicum*, notwithstanding his extensive epistolary correspondence, and the management of the whole business of the monastery; but this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was never published. He was, by the intrigues of his friends, induced to publish his *Reipublicae sacrae origines divinae, seu Ecclesiae Chrifti exterorior junctura, imperium, et hierarchia, ex primigenia ejus institutione eruta et demonstrata*. His commendable diligence procured him universal esteem, but it was his knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> which rendered him illustrious. His uncle Alexander fitted up an apartment for containing the instruments necessary for the dissemination of mathematical knowledge, and he also erected an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, which was begun in 1748, and completed in 1758, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Anfelm Dering of Emdorf, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>. While the observatory was <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, Fixmillner led a life of retirement and severe study, his favourite subject during these ten years being astronomy. When it was finished, one Dobler, a celebrated mathematician, was appointed first astronomer; but the successors of Fixmillner's uncle having discovered his extensive mathematical knowledge, made him an offer of the astronomical department, and the sole direction of the observatory. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he accepted in the year 1762, still retaining his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> as professor of ecclesiastical law. He was not yet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the learning which practical astronomy requires, to remedy which defect he attentively perused Lalande's *Exposition du Calcul Astronomique*, soon after which he obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> astronomical work of the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and in 1766 he published his *Meridianus Speculæ Astronomicæ Cremsenensis*, by which he acquired considerable reputation. Ten years after this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he gave the world his *Decennium Astronomicum*, containing many curious and important particulars respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of astronomy. His *Acta Astronomicæ Cremsenensis*, which did not appear till after his decease, still farther increased his astronomical reputation; and he was a large contributor to many periodical publications in different countries. He made and collected a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of observations of the planet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, which were at that period both scarce and difficult, the importance of which was publicly acknowledged by Lalande, as they greatly assisted him in constructing his tables of that planet. Fixmillner was one of the first astronomers who calculated the orbit of the new planet Uranus (Georgium Sidus), and his tables respecting it may be seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> almanack for 1789. He also proved the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what was formerly conjectured, that the 34th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> of Taurus, which Flamsteed observed in 1690, was the new planet. It may be said of most philosophers, that they observe a great Fixmilliner great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, and calculate little, but the conduct of Fixmilliner was exactly the reverse. He turned his attention to the observation of the solar spots more than any of his predecessors, which he noticed in the years 1767, 1776, 1777, 1778, and 1782, from which he deduced important inferences respecting the revolution of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> on his axis. He had a genius uncommonly adapted to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, by which he was enabled to invent a new micrometer, and a machine for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> concentric circles. As an additional <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his profound inventive genius, he resided in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, by which means he was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> deprived of literary assistance, yet to the very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of life he was a singular instance of the most indefatigable zeal, diligence, and perseverance. He was little subject to the influence of the turbulent passions;—perhaps less so than most other men. Like the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which it was his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> delight to study, he was simple, uniform, and constant; and such were the mildness and integrity of his character, that he could not fail to acquire the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and esteem of mankind. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation never inspired him with vanity, and he rather wished to conceal than to propagate what was written in his praise. It gave general joy to his monastic brethren to celebrate the anniversary of the fiftieth year of his residence in it, which he did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> survive. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was very much impaired by his intense application, and he finished his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> on the 27th of August 1791, in the 71st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

FLACCUS

Pages 707-707
CAIUS VALERIUS, an ancient Latin poet, of whom we have very imperfect accounts remaining. He wrote a poem on the Argonautic expedition; of which, however, he did not live to finish the eighth book, dying at about 30 years of age. John Baptista Pius, an Italian poet, completed the eighth book of the Argonautics; and added two more from the fourth of Apollonius; which supplement was first added to Aldus's edition in 1523.

FLAG

Pages 707-707

in the marine, a certain banner <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> standard, by which an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> is distinguished at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from the inferior ships of his squadron; also the colours by which one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is distinguished from another. See Plate CCXVIII. In the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, flags are either <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, or blue; and are displayed from the top of the main-mast, fore-mast, or mizen-mast, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the admiral. When a flag is displayed from the flag-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> on the main-mast, the officer distinguished thereby is known to be an admiral; when from the foremast, a vice-admiral; and when from the mizen-mast, a rear-admiral. The first flag in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> standard, which is only to be hoisted when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> are on board the vessel: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is that of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> of hope, which characterizes the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> admiral, or lords commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>: and the third is the union flag, in which the crosses of St George and St Andrew are blended. This last is appropriated to the admiral of the fleet, who is the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> officer under the lord high admiral. The next flag after the union is that of the white squadron at the main-mast head; and the last, which characterizes an admiral, is the blue, at the same mast head. For a vice-admiral, the first flag is the red, the second the white, the third the blue, at the flag staff on the fore-mast. The same order proceeds with regard to the rear-admirals, whose flags are hoisted on the top of the mizen-mast: the lowest flag in our navy is accordingly the blue on the mizen-mast. To Lower or Strike the FLAG, in the marine, is to pull it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, or to take it in, out of respect, or submission, due from all ships or fleets inferior to those any way justify their superiors. To lower or strike the flag in an engagement is a sign of yielding. The way of leading a ship in triumph is to tie the flags to the shrouds, or the gallery, in the hind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship, and let them hang down towards the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and to tow the vessels by the stern. Livy relates, that this was the way the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> used those of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. To Hoist out the FLAG, is to put out or put abroad the flag. To Hang out the White FLAG, is to ask <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; or it flows when a vessel is arrived on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, that it has no hostile intention, but comes to trade or the like. The red flag is a sign of defiance and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. FLAG is also used for a sedge, a kind of rush. Corn-FLAG. See GLADIOLUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Sweet-scented FLAG. See ACORUS, BOTANY Index. FLAG-Officers, those who command the several squadrons of a fleet; such are the admirals, vice-admirals, and rear-admirals. The flag officers in our pay, are the admiral, vice-admiral, and rear-admiral, of the white, red, and blue. See ADMIRAL, FLAG, and FLEET. FLAG-Ship, a ship commanded by a general or flag-officer, who has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to carry a flag, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the secondary vessels under the command thereof. FLAG-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-SAND_STONE">sand-stone</a> of a flat structure, on account of which it is much employed for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> foot-paths or the floors of apartments in which wood is unsuitable.

FLAGELLANTES

Pages 707-708

a set of wild fanatics who chastised and disciplined themselves with whips in public. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Flagellantes had its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the year 1260; its author was one Rainier a hermit; and it was propagated from hence through almost all the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It was in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> no more than the effect of an indiscreet zeal. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons of all ages and sexes made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, walking two by two with their shoulders bare, which they whipped till the blood ran <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, in order to obtain mercy from God, and appease his indignation against the wickedness of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. They were then called the devout; and having established a superior, he was called the general of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. Though the primitive Flagellantes were exemplary in point of morals, Flagellants, yet they were joined by a turbulent rabble who were infected with the most ridiculous and impious opinions; so that the emperors and pontiffs thought proper to put an end to this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> frenzy, by declaring all devout whipping contrary to the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and prejudicial to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>'s eternal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. This fact revived in Germany towards the middle of the next century, and rambling through many provinces, occasioned great disturbances. They held, among other things, that flagellation was of equal virtue with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and the other sacraments; that the forgiveness of all sins was to be obtained by it from God without the merits of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; that the old law of Christ was soon to be abolished, and that a new law enjoining the baptism of blood to be administered by whipping was to be substituted in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; upon which Clement VII, by an injudicious as well as unrighteous policy, thundered out anathemas against the Flagellants, who were burnt by the inquisitors in several places; but they were not easily extirpated. They appeared again in Thuringia and Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> in the 15th century, and rejected not only the sacraments, but every branch of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> worship, and placed their only hopes of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and flagellation, to which they added other strange doctrines concerning evil spirits. Their leader <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> Schmidt and many others were committed to the flames by German inquisitors in and after the year 1414.

FLAGEOLET

Pages 708-708
or FLAGEOLET, a little flute, used chiefly by the shepherds and country people. It is made of box or other hard wood, and sometimes of ivory; and has six holes besides that at the bottom, the mouthpiece, and that behind the neck.

FLAGS

Pages 707-707

in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, are small banners of distinction stuck in the baggage waggons to distinguish the baggage of one brigade from another; and of one battalion from another; that they may be marshalled by the waggon-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> general according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of their brigades, to avoid the confusion that might otherwise arise.

FLAIL

Pages 708-708

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for thrashing corn. It consists of the following parts. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> piece held in the thrasher's hand. 2. The twiple, or that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which strikes out the corn. 3. The caplins, or strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> leathers, made fast to the tops of the hand-staff and twiple. 4. The middle band, being the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> thong or fish skin that ties the caplins together.

FLAIR

Pages 708-708

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The seamen say that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> doth flair over, when a ship is housed in near the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, so that the work hangs over a little too much, and this is let out broader aloft than the due proportion <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow.

FLAKE

Pages 708-708

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a name given by the florists to a sort of carnations which are of two colours only, and have very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stripes, all of them going quite through the leaves. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> FLAKE, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> corroded by means of the pressing of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a ceruse prepared by the acid of grapes. It is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and far surerfies, both with regard to the purity of its whiteness and the certainty of its standing, all the ceruse or white lead made with us in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. It is used in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> painting for all purposes where a very clean white is required. The white flake should be procured in lumps as it is brought over, and levigated by those who <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it; because that which the colourmen sell in a prepared flake is levigated and mixed up with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, and often with white lead, and worse sophistications.

FLAMBEAU

Pages 708-708
or FLAMBOY, a luminary made of several thick wicks, covered over with wax, serving to burn at nights in the streets; as also at funeral processions, illuminations, &c. Flambeaux differ from links, torches, and tapers.—They are made square, sometimes of white wax and sometimes of yellow. They usually consist of four wicks or branches near an inch thick, and about three feet long, made of a sort of coarse hempen yarn half twisted. They are made with the ladle much as torches or tapers are; viz. by first pouring the melted wax on the top of the several suspended wicks, and letting it run down to the bottom. This they repeat twice. After each wick has thus got its proper cover of wax, they lay them to dry; then roll them on a table, and to join four of them together by means of a red hot iron. When joined, they pour on more wax till the flambeau is brought to the size required, which is usually from a pound and a half to three pounds. The last thing is to finish their form or outside, which they do with a kind of polishing instrument of wood by running it along all the angles formed by the union of the branches. The flambeaux of the ancients were different from ours. They were made of woods dried in furnaces or otherwise. They used divers kinds of wood for this purpose; the wood most usually was pine. Pliny says, that in his time they frequently also burnt oak, elm, and hazel. In the seventh book of the Aeneid, mention is made of a flambeau of pine; and Servius on that passage remarks, that they also made them of the cornel-tree.

FLAMBOROUGH HEAD

Pages 708-708

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> promontory on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, five miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a>, and 215 from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.—E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26°. N. Lat. 54°. 15.—This was the Fleamberg of the Saxons; so called, as some think, from the lights made on it to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the landing of Ida, who in 547 joined his countrymen in these parts with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> reinforcement from Germany, and founded the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Edward the Confessor, Flamborough was one of the manors of Harold, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of the West Saxons, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England. On his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the Conqueror gave it to Hugh Lupus; who, in perpetual alms, bestowed it on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITBY">Whitby</a>.—The town is on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side, and consists of about 150 small houses, entirely inhabited by fishermen; few of whom, as is said, die in their beds, but meet their fate in the element they are so conversant in. The cliffs of the Head are of a tremendous height and amazing <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. Beneath are several vast caverns; some closed at the end, others pervious, formed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>. In some places the rocks are infilled, and of a pyramidal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, soaring up to a vast height. The bases of most are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, but in some pierced through and arched. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of all these rocks is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, from the dust of the innumerable flocks of migratory birds, which quite cover the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of them, filling every little projection, every hole that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> give them leave to rest.

FLAME

Pages 708-709

is a general name for every kind of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> vapour, provided the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> it emits hath any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of intensity. The name flame, how- ever, is most generally applied to such as are of a conical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, like those rising from our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fires; without this they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called luminous vapours, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> simple lights. According to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, flame is only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or the vapour of any substance raised from it by fire, and heated to such a degree as to emit light copiously. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> seems to be the most accurate and expressive of any. It is certain, that bodies are capable of emitting flame only in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of vapour that rises from them. Thus wood, coals, &c., which emit a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantity of vapour, flame violently; while <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, tin, &c., which emit but a small fume, can scarce be perceived to flame at all. This rule, however, is by no means to be depended upon in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Some vapours seem to be in their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> uninflammable, and capable of extinguishing flame; as those of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the mineral <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, sal-ammoniac, arsenic, &c.; while others take fire on the slightest approach of a flaming substance; such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>, spirit of wine, &c. These last-mentioned substances also exhibit a remarkable phenomenon; namely, that they cannot be made to flame without the approach of some substance actually in flames beforehand. Thus, spirit of wine poured on a red-hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, though instantly dissipated in vapour, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not flame; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> touch its surface, the whole is set in a flame at once. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is otherwise with oils, especially those of the grocer's kind; for the vapours will readily be changed into flame by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> increase of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, without the approach of any flaming substance. There is, however, no kind of vapour, perhaps, that is incapable of being converted into flame, provided it is exposed to a sufficient degree of heat. Thus the vapour of water made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through burning coals produces an exceedingly strong and bright flame. It is remarkable, that this kind of vapour seems to be more powerful than almost any other in absorbing heat, and detaining it in a latent state. When any quantity of aqueous vapour is condensed, more heat will be separated from it than would have been sufficient to heat an equal bulk of iron red hot. It is most probably to this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which all vapours have of absorbing heat, and detaining it in a latent state, that we are to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the phenomena of flame, and also the exceeding great elasticity of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>. It is certain, that vapours, of water at least, have a much greater power of absorbing and retaining heat, than the water from which they are raised. In open vessels, water cannot be heated more than 212 degrees of Fahrenheit's thermometer; but in Papin's digester, where the vapour is forcibly confined, it has been heated to 400 of the same degrees; and, no doubt, might have been heated a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more, had the vessel been strong enough to bear the expansive force of the steam. On opening the vessel, however, the excess of heat was found to have resided entirely in the vapour; for the water in the vessel very soon sunk <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to 212, while the steam issued forth with great violence. From these experiments it appears, that the steam of water, after it has absorbed as much heat in the latent state as it can contain, continues to absorb or detain among its particles, an unlimited quantity of sensible heat; and if the steam could be confined till this quantity became great enough to be visible by emission of light, there cannot be the least doubt that the vapour would then be converted into flame. In what manner the heat is detained among the particles of steam, is perhaps impossible to be explained; but to this heat we must undoubtedly ascribe the violent expansive force of steam of every kind. It seems probable, that when smoke is converted into flame, the latent heat with which the vapour had combined, or rather that which made an essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, breaks forth, and adds to the quantity of sensible heat which is already present. This seems probable, from the sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> with which all flames <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out. If a vessel full of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is set over the fire, a smoke or vapour begins to arise from it; which grows gradually thicker and thicker; and at last begins to shine in some places very near the surface of the oil, like an electric light, or sulphur <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> kindled. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the oil is very hot, as well as the steam which issues from it. But this last is continually giving off its sensible heat into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; so that at the distance of an inch or two from the surface of the oil, the heat of the steam will not exceed 400 degrees of Fahrenheit, or perhaps may not be so much; but if a burning candle is held in the steam for a moment, the whole is immediately converted into flame, with something like an explosion; after which the oil burns quietly until it is all consumed. The flame, as soon as it appears, is not only much hotter than the steam from whence it was produced, but even than the oil which lies below it. Whence, then, has this sudden and great increase of heat arisen? It could not be the sensible heat of the vapour, for that was greatly inferior; nor could it be communicated from the oil, for that could communicate no more than it had to itself. The candle, indeed, would communicate a quantity of heat to the vapour which touched its flame; but it is impossible that this quantity should extend permanently over a surface perhaps 100 times larger than the flame of the candle, in such a manner as to make every part of that surface equally hot with the flame of the candle itself; for this would be to suppose it to communicate 100 times more heat than really was in it. The heat therefore must have originally resided in the vapour itself; and as, in the freezing of water, its latent heat is extricated and becomes sensible, and the water thereupon loses its fluidity; so, in the ascension of vapour, the latent heat breaks forth with a bright flash, and the vapour is then totally decomposed, and converted into foot, ashes, or water, according to the different nature of the substances which produce it, or according to the intensity of the heat. Several other hypotheses have been invented to solve the phenomena of burning and flaming bodies; for an account of which, see <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNITION">Ignition</a> and Heat, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flames are of different colours, according to the substances from which they are produced. Thus, the flame of sulphur and spirit of wine is blue; the flame of nitre and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; that of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, of a greenish blue, &c. These varieties afford an opportunity of making a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of agreeable representations in fireworks, which could not be done if the flame produced from every different substance was of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. See Pyrotechnics.

FLAMEN

Pages 709-710

in Roman antiquity, the name of an order order of priests, instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Numa; authors not being agreed on this head. They were originally only three, viz. the Flamen Dialis, Flamen Martialis, and Flamen Quirinalis. The Flamen Dialis was sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and a person of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> and authority in the state. He discharged several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> duties which properly belonged to the kings, and was honoured with many eminent privileges beyond all other officers, but was obliged to observe several superstitious restraints. The Flamen Martialis was sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, and was ordained to inspect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of that god. The Flamen Quirinalis was sacred to, and superintended the rites of, Quirinus Romulus. The Flamines last mentioned, though of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> authority, were much inferior to the Flamen Dialis. All three were chosen by the people, and consecrated by the Pontifex Maximus. In latter times several priests of the same order and name were added to them, but inferior in power. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> at last amounted to 15; the three first of whom were senators, and called Flamines maiores; the other 12 taken from among the people, being denominated Flamines minores.—Some authors tell us the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had a Flamen for every deity they worshipped. The greater Flamines wore the robe edged with purple, like the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> magistrates; had an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and a seat in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. They wore a little band of thread about their heads, whence their name is said to be derived, quasi Filamines.—The wife of the Flamen Dialis was called Flaminica, and wore a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, on which was painted a thunderbolt, and above her head-dress she had green oak boughs, to indicate that she belonged to Jupiter the thunderer, to whom the oak was sacred. The Flamines wore each of them a hat or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> called Flammum or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">Apex</a>.

FLAMINIUS

Pages 710-710
or FLAMINIO, Mark Antony, one of the best Latin poets in the 16th century, of Imola in Italy, son and grandson of very learned men. The pope had chosen him secretary to the council in 1543; but he refused that employment, because, favouring the new opinions, he would not employ his pen in an assembly where he knew these opinions were to be condemned.—He paraphrased 38 of the psalms in Latin verse, and also wrote notes on the Psalms; and some letters and poems which are esteemed. He died at Rome in 1550.

FLAMSTEED

Pages 710-711

John, an eminent English astronomer, and the first who obtained the appointment of astronomer-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a> in the year 1646. He was educated at the free school of Derby, where he was head scholar at 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, naturally tender and delicate, was much tried by a severe illness. When some of his companions went to the university, the state of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> prevented him from accompanying them. He afterwards met with a book De Sphera, written by John Sacrobosco, which was perfectly suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> turn of his genius, and therefore he perused it with uncommon satisfaction, translating as much of it into English as he thought would be necessary for him; and from the Astronomia Carolinae of Strut he learned the method of calculating eclipses, and ascertaining the places of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. Mr Hatton, a mathematician, sent him Kepler's Tabulae Rudolphinae, and Riccioli's Almagestum Novum, together with some other astronomical works to which he was as yet a stranger. In 1669 he calculated an eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which had been omitted in the Ephemerides for the following year, together with five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> to fixed stars, and sent them to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Brouncker, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, who submitted them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of that learned body, by which they were greatly applauded, and he received a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of thanks from Mr Oldenburg the secretary. He likewise received a letter of thanks from Mr Collins, one of the members. In 1670 he was invited to come up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by his father, that he might become personally acquainted with his learned correspondents, of which he gladly accepted, and had an interview with Mr Oldenburg and Mr Collins, by the latter of whom he was introduced to Sir Jonas Moore, who became the warm friend and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of Mr Flamsteed. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this journey he became acquainted with many astronomical instruments, and was presented by Sir Jonas Moore with Townley's micrometer, who also assisted him in procuring glasses at a moderate rate for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of telescopes. On his way home again he returned by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he paid a visit to the celebrated Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, Barrow and Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, then Mr Newton, and entered a student of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. In the year 1672, he made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> extracts from the letters of Galileo and Crabtree, by which his knowledge of dioptries was very much improved; and during the same year he made a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of celestial observations when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> would permit, which were afterwards published in the Philosophical Transactions. In 1673 he composed a treatise on the true and apparent diameters of the planets, when at their greatest and least distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which even the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Newton did not scruple to borrow, and made some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it in his Principia in 1685. He published an Ephemeris in 1674, in which he exposed the folly and absurdity of astrology, and the same year he drew up a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> for the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, with an astronomical account of their ebbing and flowing, which Sir Jonas Moore assured him would be well received by his majesty. Sir Jonas received from Mr Flamsteed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of barometers, with directions how to use them, which he presented to the king and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, to whose notice he embraced every opportunity of introducing Mr Flamsteed. Having taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. at Cambridge, he formed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of entering into holy orders, when Sir Jonas wrote to him to come to London, where he had an appointment for him very different from that of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. But as he found that nothing could make him abandon the resolution he had formed, he obtained a situation for him which was perfectly consistent with the character of a clergyman. This was the new office of astronomer to the king, with a salary of £100 per annum. He received ordination at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> by Bishop Gunning, in Easter 1675; and on the 10th of August in the same year the foundation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of the royal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> was laid, which received the designation of Flamsteed house, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the first astronomer royal. Till this edifice was erected, he made his observations in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s house at Greenwich, and in 1681 his Doctrine of the Sphere was published by Sir Jonas Moore in his System of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>. Notwithstanding his extraordinary merit, he never rose higher in the church than to the living of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BURFORD">Burford</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, although he was deservedly esteemed by the greatest men in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. He corresponded with the great Newton, Dr Halley, Mr W. Molyneux, Dr Wallis, and many others; and M. Cassini and he imparted their discoveries to each other with the utmost confidence and cordiality. But none of his works contributed so much to render his fame immortal as his "Historia Caesarea Britannica," in three volumes folio. Mr Flamsteed was suddenly carried off by a strangury on the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1719; and notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> delicacy of his constitution and incessant labours, he reached the 73rd year of his age.

FLANDERS

Pages 711-711

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, bounded by the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and the United Provinces on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the province of Brabant on the east, by Hainault and Artois on the south, and by another <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Artois and the German sea on the west; being about 60 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 50 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Flanders is a perfectly champaign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with not Flanders, a rising ground <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hill in it, and watered with many Flanel, fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodities are fine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>. In this country some important arts were invented and improved. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">Weaving</a> in general was greatly improved, and that of figures of all sorts in linen was invented; also the art of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> cloths and stuffs, and of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> colours; the curing of herrings, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this country are not now in the flourishing state they were formerly; yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, cotton, and woollen stuffs, brocades, camlets, tapestry, lace, and linen, are still manufactured here in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities. This province had counts of its own from the ninth century to the year 1369, when it went by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>; and afterwards from them, by marriage also, to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. France, in 1667, seized the southern part; and the states general obtained the northern, partly by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, and partly by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> treaty of 1715. For a more particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Flanders, with a continuation <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the present times, see the article NETHERLANDS.

FLANEL

Pages 711-712
or FLANNEL, a kind of flax, loose, woollen stuff, composed of a woof and warp, and wove on a loom with two treadles, after the manner of baize. Dr Black assigns as a reason why flannel and other substances of the kind keep the body warm, that they compose a rare and spongy mass, the fibres of which touch each other so lightly, that the heat moves slowly through the interfaces, which being filled only with air, and that in a stagnant state, give little affluence in conducting the heat. From the experiments of Count Rumford, it appears, that there is no relation betwixt the power which the substances usually worn as clothing have of absorbing moisture, and that of keeping the body warm. Having provided a quantity of each of these substances mentioned below, he exposed them, spread out upon clean china plates, for the space of 24 hours to the warm and dry air of a room which had been heated by a German stove for several months, and during the last five hours had raised the thermometer to 85° of Fahrenheit; after which he weighed equal quantities of the different substances with a very accurate balance. They were then spread out upon a china plate, and removed into a very large uninhabited room upon the second floor, where they were exposed 48 hours upon a table placed in the middle of the room, the air of which was at 45° of Fahrenheit. At the end of this space they were weighed, and then removed into a damp cellar, and placed on a table in the middle of the vault, where the air was at the temperature of 45°, and which by the hygrometer seemed to be fully saturated with moisture. In this situation they were suffered to remain three days and three nights; the vault being all the time hung round with wet linen cloths, to render the air as completely damp as possible. At the end of three days they were weighed, and the weights at the different times were found as in the following table. On these experiments our author observes, that though linen, from the apparent ease with which it receives dampness from the atmosphere, seems to have a much greater attraction for water than any other; yet it would appear from what is related above, that those bodies which receive water in its unelastic form with the greatest ease, or are most easily wet, are not those which in all cases attract the moisture of the atmosphere with the greatest avidity. "Perhaps (says he), the apparent dampness of linen to the touch, arises more from the ease with which that substance parts with the water it contains, than from the quantity of water it actually holds: in the same manner as a body appears hot to the touch, in consequence of its parting freely with its heat; while another body which is really at the same temperature, but which withholds its heat with great obstinacy, affects the sense of feeling much less violently. It is well known that woollen clothes such as flannels, &c., worn next the skin, greatly promote insensible perspiration. May not this arise principally from the strong attraction which subsists between wool and the watery vapour which is continually issuing from the human body? That it does not depend entirely on the warmth of that covering, is clear; for the same degree of warmth produced by wearing more clothing of a different kind, does not produce the same effect. The perspiration of the human body being absorbed by a covering of flannel, it is immediately distributed through the whole thickness of that substance, and by that means exposed, by a very large surface, to be carried off by the atmosphere; and the loss of this watery vapour which the flannel sustains on the one side by evaporation, being immediately restored from the other, in consequence of the strong attraction between the flannel and this vapour, the pores of the skin are disencumbered, and they are continually surrounded by a dry and salubrious atmosphere."

FLANK

Pages 712-712

in Fortification, is a line drawn from the extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> towards the inside of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a>, flank is that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a bastion which reaches from the curtain to the face, and defends the opposite face, the flank, and the curtain. See FORTIFICATION. Oblique or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Flank, or Flank of the Curtain, is that part of the curtain from whence the face of the opposite bastion can be seen, being contained between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> rafant and fichant, or the greater and less lines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; or the part of the curtain between the flank and the point where the fichant line of defence terminates. Covered, Low, or Retired Flank, is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of the casement which lies hid in the bastion; and is otherwise called the Orillon. Fichant Flank, is that from whence a cannon playing, fires directly on the face of the opposite bastion. Rafant or Rozant Flank, is the point from whence the line of defence begins, from the conjunction of which with the curtain, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> only rafant the face of the next bastion, which happens when the face cannot be discovered but from the flank alone.

FLAT

Pages 712-712

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground lying at a small depth under the surface of the sea, and is also called a shoal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shallow. Flat-Bottomed Boats are such as are made to swim in shallow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and to carry a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of troops, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, ammunition, &c. They are constructed with a 12 pounder, bow-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, and an 18 pounder, stern-chase; their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> is from 90 to 100 feet, and from 12 to 24 feet beam: they have one mast, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> main-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and a jib-fall; are rowed by 18 or 20 oars, and can carry 400 men each. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> takes up one bow, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> the other, over which the troops are to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>. Those that carry horses have the fore-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> made to open when the men are to mount and ride over a bridge.

FLATUS

Pages 712-713

FLATULENCE, in Medicine; vapours <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the stomach and intestines, chiefly occasioned by a weakness of these parts. They occasion distensions, uneasy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, and sickness, and often a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of pain. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FLAVEL

Pages 713-713

JOHN, an eminent non-conformist minister, was educated at University-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and became minister first of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, and afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, where he resided the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, much respected and admired for his preaching; although he was persecuted on account of his principles, when in 1685, several of the aldermen of the town, attended by the rabble, carried about a ridiculous effigy of him, to which were affixed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">Bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">Exclusion</a> and the Covenant. Upon this occasion, he thought it prudent to withdraw from the town; not knowing what treatment he might meet with from a riotous mob, headed by magistrates who were themselves among the lowest of mankind. Part of his Diary, printed with his Remains, must give the reader a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> idea of his piety. He died in 1691, aged 61; and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his works, which consisted of many pieces of practical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, were printed in two volumes folio. Among these, the most famous are his "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a> Spiritualized, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a New Compass for seamen, consisting of 32 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of pleasant observations and serious reflections," of which there have been several editions in 8vo; and his "Husbandry Spiritualized," &c., with occasional meditations upon beasts, birds, trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and several other objects," of which also there have been many editions in 8vo.

FLAX

Pages 713-724

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See LINUM, BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The following particulars with regard to the manner of raising flax, have been some years past warmly recommended by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and improvements in Scotland. Of the choice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">Soil</a>, and preparing the ground for FLAX. A skilful flax-raiser always prefers a free open deep loam; and all grounds that produced the preceding year a good crop of turnip, cabbage, potatoes, barley, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> clover, or have been formerly laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> rich, and kept for some years in pasture. A clay soil, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or third crop after being limed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> answer well for flax; provided, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ground be still stiff, that it be brought to a proper mould, by tilling after <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> to expel it to the winter frosts. All new grounds produce a strong crop of flax, and pretty free of weeds. When a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> heaps appear upon new ground, it answers the better for flax, after one tilling.
