Fletcher, though rigid in the duties of morality, having been accustomed to foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> both by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, in which he had acquired <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the honour of a soldier and a gentleman, and of the affront of a cane, pulled out his pistol, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> him dead on the spot. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was unpopular in countries where such refinements were not understood. A clamour was raised against it among the people of the country: in a body they waited upon the duke with their complaints; and he was forced to desist the only soldier, and almost the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of parts, in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, to abandon him. With Fletcher all Monmouth's chance of success in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> left him." But, in a manuscript memoir belonging to the family, we have the following notice concerning Mr Fletcher's connection with Monmouth, in which his separation from that prince is very differently accounted for: "To Lord Marischal Mr Fletcher explained the motives which first induced him to join, and afterwards abandon, the duke of Monmouth. The former he ascribed to the duke's manifesto in Scotland relating to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and in England to liberty. For the latter he accounted by the disgust produced in his own mind and that of his associates, when the duke declared himself <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and broke <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> with all who embarked with him on his principles. He complained heavily of the account <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the mayor of Lynne: and mentioned to Lord Marischal, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the contrary, that he did not leave the duke till he came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a>, where he was proclaimed king, several weeks after the death of the mayor of Lynne." Seeing all the efforts of himself and his friends in favour of liberty frustrated at Taunton, he endeavoured to secure his own personal freedom by taking his passage in the first ship bound to a foreign country. It was his misfortune to land in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; where he was immediately arrested, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into prison, and guarded by three Fletcher, three different bands of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, till a vessel should be prepared to carry him a victim in chains to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. But on the morning before the ship could sail, whilst he looked pensively through the bars that secured the window of his room, he was hailed by a venerable personage who made signs to speak with him. The prison doors he found open; and whilst his friendly conductor waved to him to follow him, he passed through three different guards of soldiers all fast asleep. Without being permitted to offer his thanks to his deliverer, he found himself obliged to prosecute with all speed the journey, in which he was directed by a person concerning whom he could never collect any information; and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> he proceeded in safety through Spain. He felt a peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in relating to his friends instances of the care of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> which he had experienced during his exile; and entertained them often with narratives of this kind, which he always mingled with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> reflections. Of these, another may be here mentioned. Happening in the evening to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the skirt of a wood at a few miles distance from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> where he intended to lodge, he came to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> met. After he had entered upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, he was accosted by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> of a respectable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, who warned him to turn back, and take the road on the left; for that in the other there was danger which he could not escape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to proceed. His friendly monitor suddenly retired into the wood, out of which she had issued no less unexpectedly. Having arrived at the city, the inhabitants were soon after alarmed by an account of the robbery and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of several travellers who that evening had fallen into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a banditti upon the very way in which he had intended to travel. From these and other instances of preservation from dangers, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of his mind, habituated from his infancy to an intercourse with heaven, led him to conclude that he was in a peculiar manner the care of Providence, and that in critical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> his understanding received its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> from a supernatural impulse. During his exile, he maintained a frequent and extensive correspondence with the friends of liberty at home; and he partly employed himself in making a curious collection of books, which compose the best private library in Scotland. But his genius also prompted him to engage in more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> employments. He repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and served several campaigns as a volunteer under the duke of Lorraine with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. At length, understanding that the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> then projected in Holland, and upon the issue of which he considered the liberties of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> to be suspended, had attained a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of maturity, he hastened thither; where his councils and addresses were of eminent service. He came over with King William; and in zeal, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, penetration, and political skill, proved superior to none of the leaders in the Revolution. Such, however, was his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, that from a survey of King William's papers, it appears that while others laboured to turn this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> event to the advantage of themselves and the aggrandisement of their family, Mr Fletcher asked nothing. His estate had been forfeited, and his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> abandoned to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>; his fortune was greatly shattered, and his family reduced to circumstances of distress. Nothing was given him in recompense of all his sufferings. On the contrary, he, together with the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, was distinguished by marks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> and ministerial dislike. Still, whatever private resentment he might entertain, it appeared that his ruling principle was the good of his country; and that to this grand object of his heart he was willing to sacrifice all personal considerations. For when, in 1692, the abdicated king meditated an invasion, Mr Fletcher addressed a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> (preserved in Sir John Dalrymple's collection) to the duke of Hamilton, in which every argument is employed with skill and energy to engage his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> to forget his injuries, and in the present crisis to employ the extensive influence and authority he then possessed in the cause of freedom and of his country. This letter produced its full effect; and the duke returned to his duty, from which he had in part begun to deviate. To follow our author through all the mazes of his political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> subsequent to the Revolution, is beyond our purpose, and would exceed our limits. One or two circumstances more shall therefore suffice. Being elected a member for the parliament 1683, he showed an uniform zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his country. The thought of England's domineering over Scotland was what his generous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> could not endure. The indignities and oppression which Scotland lay under galled him to the heart; so that in his learned and elaborate discourses, he exposed them with undaunted courage and pathetical eloquence. In that great event, the Union, he performed essential service. He got the act of security passed, which declared that the two crowns should not pass to the same head till Scotland was secured in her liberties civil and religious. Therefore Lord Godolphin was forced into the Union, to avoid a civil war after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a>. Although Mr Fletcher disapproved of some of the articles, and indeed of the whole frame of the Union; yet, as the act of security was his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he had all the merit of that important transaction. We must not omit mentioning, that in the ardour of his political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> Mr Fletcher forgot not the interests of the place that gave him birth. He esteemed the education of youth one of the noblest objects of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. On this subject he wrote a treatise, still extant, most characteristic of himself; and he established at Salton a foundation for the same purpose, of great utility while it lasted. This great man died at London 1716, aged 66. His remains were conveyed to Scotland, and deposited in the family vault at Salton. That Mr Fletcher received neither honours nor emoluments from King William, may perhaps be in part attributed to himself; a circumstance, however, which must add greatly to the lustre of his character. His uncompromising virtue, and the sternness of his principles, were ill calculated to conciliate courtly favour. He was so zealous an adherent of the liberties of the people, that he was too jealous of the growing power of all princes; in whom he thought ambition so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, that he was not for trifling the best of kings with the power which ill ones might make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of against their subjects; he was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that all princes were made by, and for the benefit of, the people; and that they should have no power but that of doing good. This, which made him oppose King Charles and invade King James, led him also to oppose the giving so much power to King William, whom he would never serve after his establishment. So we are told by the author of Short Political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">Characters</a>, a MS. in the library of the late T. Rawlinson, Esq.—Mr Lockhart, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, p. 72, expresses a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that his aversion to the English and to the Union was so great, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> to them, he was inclined to side with the abdicated family: "But (adds he) as that was a subject not fit to be entered upon with him, this is only a conjecture from some innuendos I have heard him make; but so far is certain, he liked, commended, and conversed with high-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Tories, more than any other set of men; acknowledging them to be the best countrymen, and of most honour, integrity, and ingenuity." It seems difficult to reconcile this with Mr Fletcher's avowed principles and the general tenor of his conduct. May we suppose, that chagrin, if not at the neglect or the ill treatment which he had himself received from government since the Revolution, yet at the public measures relating to his native country, might have occasioned him to relent in his sentiments with regard to the exiled family?—In the family memoirs already quoted, we are informed, That, "Lord Marischal held Mr Fletcher's character in high admiration;" and that, "when governor of Neufchatel, where Rousseau resided about the year 1766, he prevailed with this very extraordinary genius to write the life of a man whose character and actions he wished to have transmitted to posterity with advantage. For this purpose his lordship applied to an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> relation of Mr Fletcher's for materials: which by him were transmitted to Lord Marischal; but the design failed through Rousseau's defultory and capricious disposition." This anecdote must appear incompatible with the known loyalty and attachments of the Earl Marischal, unless we suppose him to have been privy to some such sentiments of Mr Fletcher as those alluded to by Mr Lockhart; for how could we suppose him anxious to promote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in which the talk would be to celebrate principles diametrically opposite to his own, and to applaud actions subversive of that royal family in whose cause he had ventured his life, and forfeited his fortune, and forsook his country!—But however these circumstances may be reconciled, as the integrity, disinterestedness, and public spirit of Mr Fletcher, have been universally acknowledged, there is reason to believe, that all his sentiments and actions were founded in honour, and that he never once pursued a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> further than he judged it to be for the interest of his country. Mr Fletcher was master of the English, Latin, Greek, French, and Italian languages; and well versed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the civil law, and all kinds of learning. In his travels, he had not only acquired considerable knowledge in the art of war, but also became versant in the respective interests of the several princes and states of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In private life, he was affable to his friends, and free from all manner of vice. He had a penetrating, clear, and lively <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>; but is said to have been too much wedded to opinions, and impatient of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>.—He possessed an uncommon elevation of mind, accompanied with a warmth of temper, which would suffer him to brook from no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among men, nor in any place, an indignity. Of this Fletcher he exhibited a singular proof in the Scots parliament. The earl of Stair, secretary of state and minister for Scotland, having in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of debate used an improper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> against Mr Fletcher, he seized him by his robe, and inflicted upon public and immediate satisfaction. His lordship was obliged instantly to beg his pardon in presence of parliament. Mr Fletcher was by far the finest speaker in the parliament of Scotland; the earl of Stair alone rivalled him. The latter was famed for a splendid, the former for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and nervous, eloquence. He formed his style on the models of antiquity; and the small volume of his works, Sir John Dalrymple observes, though imperfectly collected, is one of the very few classical compositions in the English language.

FLETEWOOD

Pages 727-727

WILLIAM, an eminent English lawyer and recorder of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. He was very zealous in suppressing masshouses, and committing popish priests; but once rushing in upon mats at the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, he was committed to the Fleet for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of privilege, but soon released. Mr Wood says, "He was a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and a good antiquary, but of a marvellous merry and pleasant conceit." He was a good popular speaker, and wrote well upon subjects of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Annalium tam regum Eduardi V. Ricardi III. et Henrici VII. quam Henrici VIII. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Reports of Edmund Plowden. 3. The Office of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> of Peace. He died about the year 1593.

FLEURI

Pages 727-727
CLAUDE, an able French critic and historian, was born at Paris in 1640. He applied himself to the law, was made advocate for the parliament of Paris, and attended the bar nine years; he then entered into orders, and was made preceptor to the princes of Conti. In 1689, the king made him sub-preceptor to the dukes of Burgundy, Anjou, and Berry; and in 1706, when the education of these young princes was completed, the king gave him the priory of Argenteuil belonging to the Benedictines in the diocese of Paris. In 1716, he was chosen councillor to Louis XV. and died in 1723. He was the author of a great number of esteemed French works; the principal of which are, 1. An ecclesiastical history, in 20 volumes, the last of which ends with the year 1414. 2. The manners of the Israelites and Christians. 3. Institutions of ecclesiastical law. 4. An historical catechism. 5. On the choice and method of study. 6. The duties of masters and servants, &c.

FLEVILLEA

Pages 727-727

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FLEXIBLE

Pages 727-727

in Physics, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to bodies capable of being bent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> diverted from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>.

FLEXOR

Pages 727-727

in Anatomy, a name applied to several muscles, which are so called from their office, which is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the parts to which they belong; in opposition to the extensor, which open <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stretch them. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

FLIGHT

Pages 727-728

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the manner, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, &c. thereof. Almost every kind of bird has its particular flight; the eagle's flight is the highest; the flight of the sparrow-hawk and vulture is noble, and fit for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> enter- FLIGHT. In melting the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ore in the works at Mendip, there is a substance which flies away in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> which is called the flight. The workmen find it sweetish upon their lips, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their faces happen to be in the way of the smoke, which they avoid as much as possible. This, falling on the grass, kills cattle that feed thereon; and, being gathered, and carried home, kills rats and mice in their houses; that which falls on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, they gather and melt upon a flat hearth into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> and sheet lead.

FLINT

Pages 728-728

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. It is commodiously seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>; and is but a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, though it sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It was formerly noted for its castle, where Richard II. took shelter on his arrival from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; but having quitted it, he was taken prisoner by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>. The castle now is in a ruinous condition. This castle stands <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on a rock, which in various parts forms several feet of its foundation. It covers about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>. The assizes are still held in the town. It is 195 miles north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.

FLINTS

Pages 728-728

in the glass trade. The way of preparing flints for the nicest operations in the glass trade is this. Choose the hardest flints, such as are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> resist the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and will grow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> when calcined in the fire. Cleanse these of the white crust that adheres to them, then calcine them in a strong fire, and throw them while <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; wash off the ashes that may adhere to them, and powder them in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and sift them through a very fine sieve; pour upon this powder some weak aquafortis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the phlegm of aquafortis, to dissolve and take up any particles of iron it may have got from the mortar; stir this mixture several times, then let it rest, and in the morning pour off the liquor, and wash the powder several times with hot water and afterwards dry it for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. You will thus have a powder for making the purest glass as perfectly fine and faultless as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you had used rock-crystal itself. The washing off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> particles with aquafortis is not necessary when the glass intended to be made is to be tinged with iron afterwards; but when meant to be a pure white, this is the method that will secure success.

FLINTSHIRE

Pages 728-728

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded on Flintshire the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east and east by an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which is properly the mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>; on the north-west by the Irish sea; and on the south-west and west by Denbighshire. It is the least of all the counties in Wales, being but 33 miles in length and 9 in breadth. It is divided into five <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>; in which are two market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and 28 parishes, with 32,400 inhabitants. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this county lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of St Asaph, and the rest belongs to that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, one for the county and one for Flint; and pays one part of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but healthful. It is full of hills, intermixed with a few valleys, which are very fruitful, producing some wheat and plenty of rye. The cows, though small, yield a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> in proportion to their size, and are excellent beef. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are well stored with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, coal, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>. This county also produces good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, cheese, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; of which last the natives make <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAD">mead</a>, a wholesome liquor much used in these parts.

FLOAT

Pages 728-728

a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> bound together with rafters athwart, and put into a river to be conveyed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the stream; and even sometimes to carry burdens down a river with the stream. FLOAT Boards, those boards fixed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of under-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, serving to receive the impulse of the stream, whereby the wheel is carried round. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> WHEEL and MILL. It is no advantage to have too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of float-boards; because, when they are struck by the water in the best manner that it can be brought to come against them, the sum of all the impulses <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be but equal to the impulse made against one float-board at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, by all the water coming out of the penstock through the opening, so as to take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the float-board. The best rule in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is to have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> so many, that each of them may come out of the water as soon as possible, after it has received and acted with its full impulse. As to the length of the float-board, it may be regulated according to the breadth of the mill. See MILL. FLOATS for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>. See FISHING Floats.

FLOATAGES

Pages 728-732

all things floating on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; a word much used in the commissions of water bailiffs. FLOATING BODIES are those which swim on the surface of a fluid, the most interesting of which are ships and vessels employed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. It is known to every seaman, of what vast moment it is to ascertain the stability of such vessels, and the positions they assume when they float freely on the surface of the water. To be able to accomplish this, it is necessary to understand the principles on which that stability and these positions depend. This has been done with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ingenuity by Mr Atwood, of whose reasoning the following is a summary account, taken from the Philosophical Transactions for 1796. A floating body is pressed downwards by its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in a vertical line passing through its centre of gravity; and it is supported by the upward pressure of a fluid, which acts in a vertical line that passes through the centre of gravity of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which is under the water; water; and without a coincidence between these two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, in such a manner as that both centres of gravity may be in the same vertical line, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn on an axis, till it gains a position in which the equilibrium of floating will be permanent. From this it is obviously necessary to find what proportion the part immersed bears to the whole, to do which the specific gravity of the floating body must be known, after which it must be found by geometrical methods, in which positions the solid can be placed on the surface of the fluid, so that both centres of gravity may be in the same vertical line, when any given part of the solid is immersed under the surface. These things being determined, something is still wanting, for positions may be assumed in which the circumstances now mentioned concur, and yet the solid will assume some other position wherein it will permanently float. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the specific gravity of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> be to that of the fluid on which it floats as 3 to 4, and its axis to the diameter of the base as 2 to 1: if it be placed on the fluid with its axis vertical, it will sink to a depth equal to a diameter and a half of the base; and while its axis is preserved in a vertical position by outward force, the centres of gravity of the whole solid and immersed part will remain in the same vertical line; but when the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force is removed, it will deviate from its upright position, and will permanently float with its axis <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>. If we suppose the axis to be half the diameter of the base, and placed vertically, the solid will sink to the depth of three-eighths of its diameter, and in that position it will float permanently. If the axis be made to incline to the vertical line, the solid will change its position till it permanently settles with its axis perpendicular to the horizon. Whether a solid floats permanently, or overflows when placed on the surface of a fluid, provided the centre of gravity of the solid and that of the immersed part be in the same vertical line, it is said to be in a position of equilibrium, of which there are three kinds; the equilibrium of stability, in which the solid permanently floats in a given position; the equilibrium of instability, in which the solid spontaneously overflows, if not supported by external force; and the equilibrium of indifference, or the indifferent equilibrium, in which the solid rests on the fluid indifferent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, without tendency to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> itself when inclined, or to incline farther. If a solid body floats permanently on the surface of a fluid, and external force be applied to turn it from its position, the resistance opposed to this inclination is termed the stability of floating. Some ships at sea yield to a given impulse of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and suffer a greater inclination from the perpendicular than others. As this resistance to heeling, duly regulated, has been considered of importance in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of vessels, many eminent mathematicians have laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> rules for attaining the stability of ships from their known dimensions and weight, without recurring to actual experiment. Bouguer, Euler, Chapman, and others, have laid down theorems for this purpose, founded on the supposition that the inclinations of ships from their quiescent positions are evanescent, or very small in a practical point of view. But ships at sea have been found to heel 10°, 20°, or 30°, and therefore it may be doubted how far such rules are applicable in practice. If <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATICS">statics</a> can be applied to naval <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, it seems necessary that the rules should be extended to those <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of inclination are of any magnitude, likely to occur in the practice of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. A solid body placed on the surface of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> fluid, at such a depth as corresponds to the relative gravities, cannot alter its position by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of its own weight and the pressure of the fluid, except by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on some horizontal axis passing through the centre of gravity; but, as many axes may be drawn through this point of the floating body, in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, and the motion of the solid regards only one axis, this must be determined by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the body and the particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. When this axis of motion is ascertained, and the specific gravity of the solid found, the positions of permanent floating will be determined, by finding the several positions of equilibrium through which the solid may be conceived to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, while it turns round the axis of motion; and by determining in which of these positions the equilibrium is permanent, and in which of them it is momentary. The whole of Mr Atwood's valuable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> relates to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of naval architecture, in so far as it is dependent on the laws of pure <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. If the proportions and dimensions adopted in the construction of individual vessels are obtained by exact geometrical measurement, and observations are made on the performance of these vessels at sea; a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments of this nature judiciously varied, are the proper grounds on which theory may be effectually applied, in reducing to system those hitherto unperceived causes, which contribute to give the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of excellence to vessels of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Naval architecture being reckoned among the practical branches of science, every voyage may be viewed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of an experiment, from which useful truths are to be deduced. But inferences of this nature cannot well be obtained, except by acquiring a thorough knowledge of all the proportions and dimensions of each part of the ship, and by making a sufficient number of observations on the qualities of the vessel, in all the varieties of situation to which a ship is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> subject in the practice of navigation. The following is an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the same subject by Mr English, which we give in his own words. "However operose and difficult (says he) the calculations necessary to determine the stability of nautical vessels may, in some cases, be, yet they all depend, says this author, upon the four following simple and obvious theorems, accompanied with other well known stereometrical and statical principles. "Theorem 1. Every floating body displaces a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the fluid in which it floats, equal to its own weight; and consequently the specific gravity of the fluid will be to that of the floating body, as the magnitude of the whole is to that of the part immersed. "Theorem 2. Every floating body is impelled downward by its own essential power, acting in the direction of a vertical line passing through the centre of gravity of the whole; and is impelled upward by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> of the fluid which supports it, acting in the direction of a vertical line passing through the centre of gravity of the part immersed; therefore, unless these two lines are coincident, the floating body thus impelled must revolve round an axis, either in motion or at rest, until the equilibrium is restored. "Theorem 3. If by any power whatever a vessel be deflected..." Floating bodies. Theorem 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre of gravity of any system of bodies being given in position, if any one of these bodies be moved from one part of the system to another, the corresponding motion of the common centre of gravity, estimated in any given direction, will be to that of the aforementioned body, estimated in the same direction, as the weight of the body moved is to that of the whole system. From whence it is evident, that in order to ascertain the stability of any vessel, the position of the centres of gravity of the whole, and of that part immersed, must be determined; with which, and the dimensions of the vessel, the line of floatation, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of deflection, the stability or power either to right itself or overturn, may be found. In ships of war and merchandise, the calculations necessary for the purpose become unavoidably very operose and troublesome; but they may be much facilitated by the experimental method pointed out in the New Transactions of the Swedish Academy of Sciences, first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the year 1787, page 48. In river and canal boats, the regularity and simplicity of the form of the vessel itself, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> disposition and homogeneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the burden, render that method for them unnecessary, and make the requisite calculations become very easy. Vessels of this kind are generally of the same transverse <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> throughout their whole length, except a small part in prow and stern, formed by segments of circles or other simple curves; therefore a length may easily be assigned such, that any of the transverse sections being multiplied thereby, the product will be equal to the whole solidity of the vessel. The form of the section ABCD is for the most part either rectangular, as in fig. 1. Plate CCXVIII., trapezoidal as in fig. 2, or mixtilinear as in fig. 3. In all which MM represents the line of floatation when upright, and EF that when inclined at any angle MXE; also G represents the centre of gravity of the whole vessel, and R that of the part immersed. If the vessel be loaded quite up to the line <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, and the specific gravity of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> and burden be the same, then the point G is simply the centre of gravity of the section ABCD; but if not, the centres of gravity of the boat and burden must be found separately, and reduced to one by the common method, namely, by dividing the sum of the momenta by the sum of weights, or areas, which in this case are as the weights. The point R is always the centre of gravity of the section MMCD, which, if consisting of different figures, must also be found by dividing the sum of the momenta by the sum of the weights as common. These two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> being found, the next thing necessary is to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of the two equal triangles MXE, MXF, their centres of gravity o, o, and the perpendicular projected distance n n of these points on the water line EF. This being done, through R and parallel to EF draw RT = a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the whole area MMCD, either triangle MXE or MXF, and the distance n n; through T, and at right angles to RI or EF, draw TS meeting the vertical axis of the vessel in S the metacentre; also through the points G, R, and parallel to ST, draw NGW and BV; moreover through S, and parallel to EF, draw WSV, meeting the two former in V and W; then SW is as the stability of the vessel, which will be positive, nothing, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, according as the point S is above, coincident with, or below, the point G. If now we suppose W to represent the weight of the whole vessel and burden (which will be equal to the section MMCD multiplied by the length of the vessel), and P to represent the required weight applied at the gunwale B to sustain the vessel at the given angle of inclination; we shall always have this proportion: as VS : SW :: W : P; which proportion is general, whether SW be positive or negative; it must only in the latter case be supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upward to prevent an overturn. In the rectangular vessel, of given weight and dimensions, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is so evident, that any farther explanation would be unnecessary. In the trapezoidal vessel, after having found the points G and R, let <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">AD</a>, BC be produced until they meet in K. Then, since the two sections MMCD, EFDC are equal; the two triangles MMK, EFK are also equal; and therefore the rectangle EK × KF = KM × KM = KM²; and since the angle of inclination is supposed to be known, the angles at E and F are given. Consequently, if a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> proportional be found between the sines of the angle at E and F, we shall have the following proportions: As the mean proportional thus found: sine ∠F :: KM : KF, and in the said mean proportional: sine ∠F :: KM : KE; therefore ME, MF become known; from whence the area of either triangle MXE or MXF, the distance n n, and all the other requisites, may be found. In the mixtilinear section, let AB = 9 feet = 108 inches, the whole depth = 6 feet = 72 inches, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of MM the line of floatation 4 feet or 48 inches; also let the two curvilinear parts be circular quadrants of two feet, or 24 inches radius each. Then the area of the two quadrants = 904.7808 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inches, and the distance of their centres of gravity from the bottom = 13.8177 inches very nearly; also the area of the included rectangle abie = 1440 square inches, and the altitude of its centre of gravity 12 inches; in like manner, the area of the rectangle ABe c d will be found = 5184 square inches, and the altitude of its centre of gravity 48 inches: therefore we shall have Momentum of the two quads. = 904.7808 × 13.8177 = 12501.9866016 Moment of the rectan. abie = 1440 × 12 = 17280 Moment of the rectan. ABe c d = 5184 × 48 = 248832 Now the sum of the momenta, divided by the sum of the areas, will give \( \frac{278613.9866016}{75287808} = 37.006 \) inches, the altitude of G, the centre of gravity of the section. section ABCD above the bottom. In like manner, the altitude of R, the centre of gravity of the section MMCD, will be found to be equal \[ \frac{12393^9896616}{4936788} = 24'934 \text{ inches}; \] and consequently their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, or the value of GR \(= 12'072\) inches, will be found. Suppose the vessel to heel \(15^\circ\), and we shall have the following proportion; namely, As radius : tangent of \(15^\circ :: MX = 54\) inches : \(14'469\) inches \(= ME\) or \(MF\); and consequently the area of either triangle \(MXE\) or \(MXF = 390'663\) square inches. Therefore, by theorem 4th, as \(4936'7808 : 390'663 :: 72 = n = \frac{3}{4} AB : 5'6975\) inches \(= RT\); and, again, as radius: fine of \(15^\circ :: 12'072 = GR : 3'1245\) inches \(= RN\); consequently \(RT - RN = 5'6975 - 3'1245 = 2'573\) inches \(= SW\), the stability required. Moreover, as the fine of \(15^\circ\): radius :: \(5'6975 = RT : 22'013 = RS\), to which if we add \(24'934\), the altitude of the point R, we shall have \(46'947\) for the height of the metacentre, which taken from \(72\), the whole altitude, there remains \(25'033\); from which, and the half width \(= 54\) inches, the distance BS is found \(= 59'520\) inches very nearly, and the angle SBV \(= 80^\circ - 06' - 42'\); from whence SV \(= 58'645\) inches. Again: Let us suppose the mean length of the vessel to be 40 feet, or 480 inches, and we shall have the weight of the whole vessel equal to the area of the section MMCD \(= 4936'7808\) multiplied by 480 \(= 23696'547'84\) cubic inches of water, which weighs exactly 85708 pounds avoirdupoise, allowing the cubic foot to weigh 62.5 pounds. And finally, as \(SV : SW (i.e.)\) as \(58'645 : 2'573 :: 85708 : 3760\), the weight on the gunwale which will sustain the vessel at the given inclination. Therefore a vessel of the above dimensions, and weighing 38 tons 5 cwt. 28lbs. will require a weight of one ton 13 cwt. 64lbs. to make her incline \(15^\circ\). In this example the deflecting power has been supposed to act perpendicularly on the gunwale at B; but if the vessel is navigated by sails, the centre velique must be found; with which and the angle of deflection, the projected distance thereof on the line SV may be obtained; and then the power calculated as above, necessary to be applied at the projected point, will be that part of the wind's force which causes the vessel to heel. And conversely, if the weight and dimensions of the vessel, the area and altitude of the sails, the direction and velocity of the wind be given, the angle of deflection may be found.* *Phil. Mag. i. 393. Floating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>. See Bridge. Flocking Paper. See Paper. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">Flood</a>, a deluge or inundation of waters. See Deluge. Flood is also used in speaking of the tide. When the water is at lowest, it is called ebb; when rising, young flood; when at highest, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> flood; when beginning to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, ebb water. Flood mark, the mark which the sea makes on the shore at flowing water and the highest tide, it is also called high water mark. Flook of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. See Anchor. Flooding, among miners, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express a peculiarity in the load of a mine. The load or quantity of ore is frequently intercepted in its course by the crossing of a vein of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or some different metallic substance; in which case the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> is moved to one side, and this transient part of the load is called a flooding. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">Floor</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the underside of a room, or that part we walk on. Floors are of several sorts; some of earth, some of brick, others of stone, others of boards, &c. For brick and stone Floors, see Pavement. For boarded Floors, it is observable that the carpenters never floor their rooms with boards till the carcass is set up, and also enclosed with walls, lest the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> should injure the flooring. Yet they generally rough-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> their boards for the flooring before they begin anything else about the building, that they may let them by to dry and season, which is done in the most careful manner. The best wood for flooring is the fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> well seasoned, which when well laid, will keep its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> while; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fir becomes <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> by often washing, and looks very bad. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the boards are commonly made plain, so as to touch each other only; but, when the fluff is not quite dry, and the boards shrink, the water runs through them whenever the floor is washed, and injures the ceiling underneath. For this reason they are made with feather edges, so as to cover each other about half an inch, and sometimes they are made with grooves and tenons: and sometimes the joints are made with dove tails; in which case the lower edge is nailed down, and the next drove into it, so that the nails are concealed. The manner of measuring floors is by squares of 10 feet on each side, so that taking the length and breadth, and multiplying them together and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off two decimals, the content of a floor in square will be given. Thus 18 by 16 gives 288 or 2 squares and 88 decimal parts. Earthen Floors, are commonly made of loam, and sometimes, especially to make malt on, of lime, and brook <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> dust, or anvil dust from the forge. Ox blood and fine clay, tempered together, Sir Hugh Plat says, make the finest floor in the world. The manner of making earthen floors for plain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> habitations is as follows: Take two-thirds of lime and one of coal ashes well sifted, with a small quantity of loam clay; mix the whole together, and temper it well with water, making it up into a heap: let it <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> or ten days, and then temper it over again. After this heap it up for three or four days, and repeat the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERING">tempering</a> very high, till it becomes smooth, yielding, tough, and gluey. The ground being then levelled, lay the floor therewith about 2½ or 3 inches thick, making it smooth with a trowel: the hotter the season is the better; and when it is thoroughly dried, it will make the best floor for houses, especially malt houses. If any one would have their floors look better, let them take lime made of rag <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, well tempered with whites of eggs, covering the floor about half an inch thick with it, before the under-flooring is too dry. If this be well done, and thoroughly dried, it will look when rubbed with a little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> as transparent as metal or glass. In elegant houses, floors of this nature are made of stucco, or of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> beaten and sifted, and mixed with other ingredients. FLOOR of a Ship, strictly taken, is only so much of her bottom as she rests on when <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>. Such ships as have long, and withal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> floors, lie on the ground with most security, and are not apt to heel, or tilt on one side; whereas others, which are narrow in the floor, or in the sea phrase, cranked by the ground, cannot be grounded without danger of being overturned. FLOOR Timbers, in a ship, are those parts of a ship's timbers which are placed immediately across the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and upon which the bottom of the ship is framed; to these the upper parts of the timbers are united, being only a continuation of floor timbers upwards.

FLORA

Pages 732-732

the reputed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, was, according to Laclantius, only a lady of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, who having gained <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> by prostituting herself, made the Roman people her heir, on condition that certain games called Floralia might be annually celebrated on her birthday. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> afterwards, however, such a foundation appearing unworthy the majesty of the Roman people, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> to ennoble the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, converted Flora into a goddess, whom they supposed to preside over flowers; and so made it a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to render her propitious, that it might be well with their gardens, vineyards, &c. But Vossius (de Idol. lib. i. c. 12.) can by no means allow the goddess Flora to have been the courtezan above mentioned: he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> rather have her a Sabine deity, and thinks her worship might have commenced under <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>. His reason is, that Varro, in his fourth book of the Latin tongue, ranks Flora among the deities to whom Tatusius <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Sabines offered up vows before he joined <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Add, that from another passage in Varro it appears, that there were priests of Flora, with sacrifices, &c. as early as the times of Romulus and Numa. The goddess Flora was, according to the poets, the wife of Zephyrus. Her image in the temple of Caflor and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a> was dressed in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and she held in her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> the flowers of peace and beans; but the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> poets and painters have been more lavish in setting off her charms, considering that no parts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> offered such innocent and exquisite entertainment to the sight and smell, as the beautiful variety which adorns, and the odour which embalms, the floral <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>.

FLORALES LUDI

Pages 732-732
or FLORAL GAMES, in antiquity, were games held in honour of Flora, the goddess of flowers.—They were celebrated with shameful debaucheries. The most licentious dissolutures were not enough, but the courtezans were called together by the sound of a trumpet, made their appearance naked, and entertained the people with indecent shows and postures: the comedians appeared after the same manner on the stage. Val. Maximus relates, that Cato being once present in the theatre on this occasion, the people were ashamed to ask for such immodest representations in his presence; till Cato, apprised of the reservedness and respect with which he inspired them, withdrew, that the people might not be disappointed of their accustomed diversion. There were several other sorts of shows exhibited on this occasion; and, if we may believe Suetonius in Galba, c. 6. and Vopiscus in Carinus, these princes presented elephants dancing on ropes on these occasions. The ludi florales, according to Pliny, lib. xviii. c. 29, were instituted by order of an oracle of the Sibyls, on the 28th of April; not in the year of Rome 1396, as we commonly read it in the ancient editions of that author; nor in 1394, as F. Hardouin has corrected it, but, as Vossius reads it, in 513: though they were not regularly held every year till after 580. They were chiefly held in the night time, in the Patrician street: some will have it there was a circus for the purpose on the hill called Hortulorum.

FLORALIA

Pages 732-732

in antiquity, a general name for the feasts, games, and other ceremonies, held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Flora. See FLORA and FLORALES LUDI.

FLORENCE

Pages 733-733

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> piece of English <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of standard gold was to be coined into 50 Florences, to be current at six shillings each; all which made in tail 15 pounds; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> into a proportionate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of half Florences, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> pieces, by indenture of the mint: 18 Edw. III.

FLORENTIA

Pages 733-733

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Etruria, on the Arno; of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in Sylla's wars. Now called Firenze <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Firenza by the Italians; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in English. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. Lat. 43. 30. FLORENTINE MARBLE. See CITADINESCA. FLORESCENTIA (from floresco, "to flourish or bloom"); the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of flowering, which Linnaeus and the sexualists compare to the act of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> in animals; as the ripening of the fruit in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> resembles the birth. See FLOWER. FLORID style, is that too much enriched with figures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>.

FLORIDA

Pages 733-734

the most southerly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the British empire in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> before the last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, bounded on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Appalachian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, on the east by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, and on the west by the river <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>. It was first discovered, in 1497, by Sebastian Cabot, a Venetian, then in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; whence a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was claimed by the kings of England; and this province, as well as Georgia, was included in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> granted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. to Carolina. Florida. In 1512, however, Florida was more fully discovered by Ponce de Leon, an able Spanish navigator, but who undertook his voyage from the most absurd motives that can be well imagined.—The Indians of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> had among them a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that somewhere on the continent there was a fountain whose waters had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of restoring youth to all old men who tasted them. The romantic imaginations of the Spaniards were delighted with this idea. Many embarked in voyages to find out this imaginary fountain who were never afterwards heard of. Their superstitious countrymen never imagined that these people had perished. They concluded that they did not return, only because they had drunk of the immortalizing liquor, and had discovered a spot so delightful, that they did not choose to leave it. Ponce de Leon set out with this extravagant view as well as others, and fully persuaded of the existence of a third world, the conquest of which was to immortalize his name. In the attempt to discover this country, he rediscovered Florida; but returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from whence he came, visibly more advanced in years than when he set out. For some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> this country was neglected by the Spaniards, and some Frenchmen fitted in it: But the new colony being neglected by the ministry, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> having accustomed himself to think that he was the sole proprietor of America, fitted out a fleet at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a> to destroy them. His orders were executed with barbarity. The French intrenchments were forced, and most of the people killed. The prisoners were hanged on trees; with this inscription, "Not as Frenchmen, but as Heretics." This cruelty was soon after revenged by Dominic de Gourgues, a skilful and intrepid seaman of Gascony, an enemy to the Spaniards, and passionately fond of hazardous expeditions and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. He sold his estate; built some ships; and with a select band of adventurers like himself embarked for Florida. He drove the Spaniards from all their posts with incredible valour and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>; defeated them in every encounter; and by way of retaliation, hung the prisoners on trees, with this inscription, "Not as Spaniards, but as Assassins." This expedition was attended with no other consequences; Gourgues blew up the forts he had taken, and returned home, where no notice was taken of him. It was conquered in 1539 by the Spaniards under Ferdinand de Soto, not without a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of bloodshed; as the natives were very warlike and made a vigorous resistance. The settlement, however, was not fully established till the year 1665; when the town of St Augustine, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the colony while it remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Spaniards, was founded. In 1586, this place was taken and pillaged by Sir Francis Drake. It met with the same fate in 1665, being taken and plundered by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Davis and a body of buccaneers. In 1702, an attempt was made upon it by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> More, governor of Carolina. He set out with 500 English and 700 Indians; and having reached St Augustine, he besieged it for three months; at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which, the Spaniards having sent some ships to the relief of the place, he was obliged to retire. In 1740 another attempt was made by General Oglethorpe; but he being outwitted by the Spanish governor, was forced to raise the siege with loss; and Florida <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the hands of the Spaniards till the year 1763, when it was ceded by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> to Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.—During the American war, which terminated in 1783, it was again reduced by his Catholic majesty, and was guaranteed to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Spain at the peace.

FLORILEGE

Pages 734-734

is also particularly used for a kind of breviary, in the Eastern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, compiled by Arcadius, for the conveniency of the Greek priests and monks, who cannot carry with them, in their travels and pilgrimages, all the volumes wherein their office is performed. The florilegium contains the general rubrics, psalter, canticles, the horologium, and the office of the feria, &c.

FLORILEGIUM

Pages 734-734

FLORILEGE, a name the Latins have given to what the Greeks call ἀνθολογίας, anthology; viz. a collection of choice pieces, containing the finest and brightest things in their kind.

FLORIN

Pages 734-734

is sometimes used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, and sometimes for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account. Florin, as a coin, is of different values, according to the different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> and different countries where it is struck. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> florins are most of them of a very coarse alloy, some of them not exceeding thirteen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fourteen carats, and none of them seventeen and a half. See MONEY <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. Florin, as a money of account, is used by the Italian, Dutch, and German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, but admits of divisions in different places. Ibid.

FLORINIANS

Pages 734-734
or FLORIANI, a sect of heretics, of the second century, denominated from its author Florinus, or Florianus, a priest of the Roman church, deposed along with Blasius for his errors. Florinus had been a disciple of St Polycarp, along with Irenaeus. He made God the author of evil; or rather asserted, that the things forbidden by God are not evil, but of his own appointing. In which he followed the errors of Valentius, and joined himself with the Carpocratiens. They had also other names given them. Philastrius says, they were the same with the Carpophorians. He adds that they were also called soldiers, miletes, quia de militariibus fuerunt. St Irenaeus calls them Gnostics; St Epiphanius Phibionites; and Theodoret, Barborties, on account of the impurities of their lives. Others call them Zaccheans; others Coddians, &c. though for what particular reasons, it is not easy to say, nor perhaps would be worth while to inquire.

FLORIS

Pages 734-734

FRANCIS, an eminent historical painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1520. He followed the profession of a lawyer till he was twenty years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; when preferring <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, he entered the school of Lambert Lombard, whose manner he imitated very perfectly. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and completed his studies from the most eminent masters. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress he made in historical painting, at his return procured him much employment; and his countrymen complimented him with the flattering appellation of the Flemish Raphael. He got much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and might have rendered his acquaintance more worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the great, had he not debauched himself by frequent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>. He died in 1570, aged 50.

FLORIST

Pages 734-735

a person curious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>: their kinds, names, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, culture, &c. It is also applied to an author who writes what is called the flora Flora of any particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that is, a catalogue of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and trees which are found spontaneously growing there.

FLORUS

Pages 735-735

Lucius Annaeus, a Latin historian, of the same family with Seneca and Lucan. He flourished in the reigns of Trajan and Adrian; and wrote an abridgement of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, of which there have been many editions. It is composed in a florid and poetical style; and is rather a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on many of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> actions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, than a faithful and correct recital of their history. He also wrote <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and entered the lists against the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian, who satirically reproached him with frequenting taverns and places of dissipation.

FLORY

Pages 735-735

Flowery, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fleury**, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> that has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> at the end circumflex and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; different from the potence, in as much as the latter stretches out more like that which is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATE">pate</a>.

FLOTA

Pages 735-735
or Flotta, fleet**; a name the Spaniards give particularly to the ships which they send annually from Cadiz to the port of Vera Cruz, to fetch thence the merchandises gathered in Mexico for Spain. It consists of the captains, admiral, and patch, or pinace, which go on the king's account; and about 16 ships, from 400 to 1000 tons, belonging to particular persons. They set out from Cadiz about the month of August, and are 18 or 20 months before they return. Those sent to fetch the commodities prepared in Peru are called galeons. The name *flotilla* is given to a number of ships which get before the rest in their return, and give information of the departure and cargo of the flota and galleons.

FLOTSON

Pages 735-735
or Flotsom**, goods that by shipwreck are lost, and floating upon the sea; which, with jetton and lagan, are generally given to the lord admiral; but this is the case only where the owners of such goods are not known. And here it is to be observed that *jetson* signifies any thing that is cast out of a ship when in danger, and afterwards is beat on the shore by the water, notwithstanding which the ship perishes. *Lagan* is where heavy goods are thrown overboard, before the wreck of the ship, and sink to the bottom of the sea.

FLOUNDER

Pages 735-735

Fluke, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> But.** See Pleuronectes, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flounders may be fished for all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, either in a swift stream, or in the still deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but best in the stream, in the months of April, May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>; the most proper baits are all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, wafps, and gentles.

FLOUR

Pages 735-735

the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> of wheat-corn, finely ground and sifted. See Meal. The grain itself is not only subject to be eaten by insects in that state; but, when ground into flour, it gives birth to another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of destroyers, who eat it voraciously, and increase so fast in it, that it is not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before they wholly destroy the substance. The finest flour is most liable to breed these, especially when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STALE">stale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ill prepared. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be examined in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be observed to be in continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and on a nicer inspection there will be found in it a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little animals of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the flour, and very nimble. If a little of this flour is laid on the plate of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, the insects are very distinctly seen in great numbers, very brisk and lively, continually crawling over one another's backs, and playing a thousand antic tricks together; whether in diversion, or in search of food, is not easy to be determined. These animals are of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> and slender form; their heads are furnished with a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> or hollow tube, by means of which they take in their food, and their body is composed of several rings. They do vast mischief among magazines of flour laid up for armies and other public uses. When they have once taken possession of a parcel of this valuable commodity, it is impossible to drive them out; and they increase so fast, that the only method of preventing the total loss of the parcel is to make it up into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> as soon as can be done. The way to prevent their breeding in the flour is to preserve it from damp: nothing gets more injury by being put up damp than flour; and yet nothing is more frequently put up so. It should be always carefully and thoroughly dried before it is put up, and the barrels also dried, into which it is to be put; then, if they are placed in a room tolerably warm and dry, they will keep it well. Too dry a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> never does flour any hurt, though one too moist almost always spoils it. Flour, when carefully analysed, is found to be composed of three very different substances.
