The first and most abundant is pure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fecule, insoluble in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but soluble in hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of mucous substances; which, when dissolved, form water glues. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the gluten, most of whose properties have been described under the article Bread. The third is of a mild nature, perfectly soluble in cold water, of the nature of saccharine extractive mucous matters. It is susceptible of the spiritous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and is found but in small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the flour of wheat. See Bread, Gluten, Starch, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FLOWER

Pages 735-739

Flos**, among botanists and gardeners, the most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, containing the organs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> parts of fructification. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">Flowers</a>, designed for medical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, should be plucked when they are moderately <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and on a clear <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> before noon: for conserves, roses must be taken in the bud. Flowers, in antiquity. We find flowers in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> request at the entertainments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, being provided by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the feast, and brought in before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> course; or, as some are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, at the beginning of the entertainment. They not only adorned their heads, necks, and breasts, with flowers, but often befriended the beds whereon they lay, and all parts of the room with them. But the head was chiefly regarded. See Garland. Flowers were likewise used in the bedecking of tombs. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">Burial</a>. Eternal Flower. See Xeranthemum. Everlasting Flower. See Gnaphalium. Flower-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">Fence</a>. See Poinciana, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>-Flower. See Helianthus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>-Flower. See Cyamus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">Trumpet</a>-Flower. See Bignonia, <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a>-Flower. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANEMONE">Anemone</a>, Flower-de-lis, or Flower-de-luce, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> representing the lily called the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of flowers, and the true hieroglyphic of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> majesty; but of late it is become more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, being borne in some coats one, in others three, in others five, and in some fesse or spread all over the escutcheon in great numbers. The arms of France are, three flowers-de-lis or, in a field azure. Flower-de-Luce. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">Iris</a>, Botany Index. Flowers, in Heraldry. They are much used in coats of arms; and in general signify hope, or denote <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frailty and momentary prosperity. Flowers, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>. By this name are generally understood bodies reduced into very fine parts, either spontaneously, or by some operation of art; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly applied to volatile <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substances, reduced into very fine parts, or into a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> by sublimation.—Some flowers are nothing else than the bodies themselves, which are sublimed entire, without suffering any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> or decomposition; and other flowers are some of the constituent parts of the body subjected to sublimation. Colours of Flowers. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a> (of Plants.) Colours extracted from Flowers. See Colour-Making. Preserving of Flowers. The method of preserving flowers in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> through the whole year has been much sought after by many people. Some have attempted it by gathering them when dry and not too much opened; and burying them in dry sand; but this, though it preserves their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> well, takes off from the liveliness of their colour. Muntingius prefers the following method to all others. Gather roses, or other flowers, when they are not yet thoroughly open, in the middle of a dry day; fill the vessel up to the top with them; and when full sprinkle them over with some good French wine, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in it; then set them by in a cellar, tying <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the mouth of the pot. After this they may be taken out at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and, on setting them in the sun, or within reach of the fire, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> open as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> growing naturally; and not only the colour, but the smell also will be preserved. The flowers of plants are by much the most difficult parts of them to preserve in any tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection; of which we have instances in all the collections of dried plants, or herbaria. In these the leaves, stalks, roots, and seeds of the plants, appear very well preserved; the strong texture of their parts making them always retain their natural form, and the colours in many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> naturally remaining. But where these fade, the plant is little the worse for use as to the knowing the species by it. But it is very much otherwise in regard to flowers; these are naturally by much the most beautiful parts of the plants to which they belong; but they are so much injured in the common way of drying, that they not only lose, but change their colours one into another, by which means they give a handle to many errors; and they usually also wither up, so as to lose their very form and natural shape. The primrose and cowslip kinds are very eminent instances of the change of colours in the flowers of dried specimens; for those of this class of plants easily dry in their natural shape; but they lose their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and, instead of it, acquire a fine green colour, much superior to that of the leaves in their most perfect state. The flowers of all the violet kind lose their beautiful blue, and become of a dead <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>: so that in dried specimens there is no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the blue-flowered violet and the white-flowered kinds. Sir Robert Southwell has communicated to the world a method of drying plants, by which this defect is proposed to be in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> remedied, and all flowers preserved in their natural shape, and many in their natural colours.—For this purpose two plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> are to be prepared of the size of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> half sheet of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or larger, for particular occasions; these plates must be made so thick as not to be apt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>; and there must be a hole made near every corner for receiving a screw to fasten them <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together. When these plates are prepared, lay in readiness several sheets of paper, and then gather the plants with their flowers when they are quite perfect. Let this be always done in the middle of a dry day; and then lay the plant and its flower on one of the sheets of paper doubled in half, spreading out all the leaves and petals as nicely as possible. If the stalk is thick, it must be pared or cut in half, so that it may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> flat; and if it is woody, it may be peeled, and only the bark left. When the plant is thus expanded, lay round about it some loose leaves and petals of the flower, which may serve to complete any part that is deficient. When all is thus prepared, lay several sheets of paper over the plant, and as many under it; then put the whole between the iron plates, laying the papers smoothly on one, and laying the other evenly over them; screw them close, and put them into an oven after the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> is drawn, and let them lie there two hours. After that, make a mixture of equal parts of aquafortis and common brandy; shake these well together, and when the flowers are taken out of the pressure of the plates, rub them lightly over with a camel's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipped in this liquor; then lay them upon fresh brown paper, and covering them with some other sheets, press them between this and other papers with a handkerchief till Flowers, the wet of these liquors is dried wholly away. When flowering, the plant is thus far prepared, take the bulk of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> dragon; put this into a pint of fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and let it stand 24 hours; it will in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> be wholly dissolved; then dip a fine hair pencil in this liquor, and with it daub over the back sides of the leaves, and lay them carefully down on half a sheet of white paper fairly expanded, and press them down with some more papers over these. When the gum-water is fixed, let the presser and papers be removed, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is finished. The leaves retain their verdure in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and the flowers usually keep their natural colours. Some care, however, must be taken, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the oven be not too great. When the flowers are thick and bulky, some art may be used to pare off their backs, and dispose the petals in a due order; and after this, if any of them are wanting, their places may be supplied with some of the supernumerary ones dried on purpose; and if any of them are only faded, it will be prudent to take them away, and lay down others in their stead: the leaves may be also disposed and mended in the same manner. Another method of preserving both flowers and fruit found throughout the whole year is also given by the same author. Take <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>; Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a>, two pounds; clean common sand, three pounds: mix all well together. Then gather fruit of any kind that is not fully ripe, with the stalk to each; put these in, one by one, into a wide-mouthed glass, laying them in good order. Tie over the top with an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-cloth, and carry them into a dry cellar, and set the whole upon a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the prepared <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of four inches thick in a box. Fill up the remainder of the box with the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>; and let it be four inches thick all over the top of the glass, and all round its sides. Flowers are to be preserved in the same sort of glasses, and in the same manner: and they may be taken up after a whole year as plump and fair as when they were buried. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Flowers of the Chinese. See TONG-TSAO. Flowers, in the animal economy, denote women's monthly purgations or menstres.—Nicod derives the word in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, from fluere, q. d. flows. Others will have the name occasioned hence, that women do not conceive till they have had their flowers; so that these are a sort of forerunners of their fruit. Flowers, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, are figures or ornaments of discourse, by the Latins called floculi. FLOWERING of Bulbous PLANTS. These plants will grow and flower in water alone, without any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and make a very elegant appearance. We daily see this practised in single roots; but there is a method of doing it with several roots in the same vessel. Take a common small garden pot; stop the hole at the bottom with a cork, and lute in the cork with putty that no water can get through; then fit a board to the top of the pot, and bore six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> holes in it at equal distances, to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the bulbs in; and as many smaller ones nearer them to receive sticks, which will serve to tie up the flowers. Then fill up the pot with water to the board; and place tulips, jonquils, narcissuses, and the like plants in the root upon the holes, so that the bottom of the roots may touch the water: thus will they all flower early in the season, and be much more beautiful than any pot of gathered flowers, and will last many weeks in their full perfection. After the season of flowering is over, the roots will gradually shrink through the holes of the board, and get loose into the water: but, instead of being spoiled there, they will soon increase in size; so that they cannot return through the holes, and will produce several offsets. It is natural to try from this the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of keeping the roots under water during the whole time of their blowing; and in this way they have been found to succeed very well, and flower even stronger and more beautifully than when in the ground. They may thus, also, with proper care in the degree of heat in the room, be kept flowering from before Christmas till <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> or April. It is not easy, in this last manner, to manage the keeping the boards under water, for which reason, it is better to procure some sheet-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> of about four pounds to the foot, and cut this to the size of the mouth of the pot. In this there should be bored holes for the bulbs, and other holes for the sticks; and, in order to keep the sticks quite firm, it is proper to have another plate of lead shaped to the bottom of the pot, with holes in it, answering to those of the upper plate made for the sticks. The sticks will by this means be always kept perfectly steady; and the roots, being kept under water by the upper plate of lead, will flower in the most vigorous and beautiful manner imaginable. Some have thought of adding to the virtues of the water by putting in nitre in small quantities, and others have added earth and sand at the bottom; but it has always been found to succeed better without any addition. It may be more agreeable to some to use glass jars in this last method with the leads, instead of earthen pots. The bulbs succeed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as well in these; and there is this advantage, that the progress of the roots is seen all the while, and they are managed better as to the supply of water. By repeated experiments in this way on dried bulbs, and on those taken fresh out of the ground, the former have been found to succeed the best. For those taken fresh out of the ground being full of moisture, will not, to soon, upon changing their element, be nourished fully by a new one; and the fibres which they had struck in the ground, always rot when put into the water, and new ones must be formed in their places; so that it requires more time for them to come to flowering. The bulbs themselves will not rot in this manner; but they will never be so strong as those which were put into the water dry, which gradually fill themselves with moisture from it, and regularly plump up. The best method of managing the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is this: Place the bulbs at first only on the surface of the water; for thus they will strike out their fibres most strongly. When they have stood thus five weeks, pour in the water so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to cover them entirely, and keep them thus till they have done flowering. Sometimes the roots will become mouldy in several parts while they stand above the water, and the cleansing them of it is to no purpose; for it will eat and spread the farther, and frequently eat through two or three of their coats. In this case they must be immediately covered with water; when the mould will be stopped, Flowering stopped, and the roots become found, and flower as well as those which never had any such distemper. If the roots are suffered to remain in water all the year, they will not decay; but will flower again at their proper season, and that as vigorously as those which have been taken out and dried. The old fibres of those roots never rot till they are ready to put forth new ones. It is found by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that the hyacinth, and many other plants, grow to a greater degree of perfection when thus in water than when in the ground. There is a peculiar species of hyacinth called Keyser's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a>; this never, or very rarely, produces seed-vessels in the common way of flowering in the ground; but it will often produce some pods when blown in water. Mr Miller has intimated, in the Philosophical Transactions, that bulbs set in glases grow weaker, and should be renewed every other year: but it is found, that, when managed in this manner, and kept under water, at the time of taking them up, they are as large, and some of them larger, than when planted; and if these be dried at a proper season, they will flower, year after year, as well as fresh ones. Ranunculus and anemone roots have been found to shoot up their stalks very well in this way; but the flowers are usually blasted, which seems to arise from want of free <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Pinks will flower very well in this manner; auriculas also may, with care, be brought to flower, but not strongly. Roses, jessamines, and honeysuckles, may also be made to flower this way, and will thrive and send out suckers; the best pieces to plant, are suckers cut off about three inches under ground, without any fibres. The succulent plants may also be raised this way; for instance, the opuntia or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> fig. If a fragment of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of this plant be cut, and laid by to dry for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> till it is an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> skin, as soon as it is put in this manner into water, it begins to plump up, and soon sends out <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots, and produces new leaves as quickly as it would do in the ground. This is the more singular in these sort of plants, because in their natural state in the ground, they cannot bear much water. This method of growing in water is not peculiar to the bulbous-rooted ones, but others may even be raised from seed by it. A bean or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, set in this manner, will grow up to its proper standard, and will flower and produce pods which will <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> their seed. The smaller seeds may be also raised in this manner, by the help of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> to support them. No vegetable transplanted out of the earth into water will thrive kindly; but any plant, whether raised from the root or seed in water, may be transplanted to the earth, and will succeed very well. It may be possible, therefore, from this method of raising plants in water, to come at a better way than is usually practised of raising some roots in the earth which are subject to rot there; such as anemones, ranunculuses, and hyacinths. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> dropped by chance upon the ground, will strike out both stronger and more numerous fibres than those which are planted in the usual way in the ground. On this principle, it may be proper to take out the earth of the bed where the bulbs are to stand at the time of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> them, to such a depth as they are to be placed under it when let for flowering. The bulbs are then to be set in their places, on the surface of this low ground; and to stand there till they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out their fibres and their head: then the earth is to be added over them by degrees, till they are covered as high above the head as they are in the usual manner of planting them; thus they would be preserved from the danger of rotting; and their fibres would be much stronger, and consequently they would draw more nourishment, and flower better than in the common way. The common method of planting these roots renders them liable to be destroyed by either <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of a wet or a dry season. In the first case, they immediately rot by the abundance of moisture they receive; and, in the second, they become dry as a stick and mouldy, so that they are infallibly rotted by the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> that falls afterwards. The directions necessary to the success of the bulbs planted in water are these. When the leaden false bottoms are fixed down tight within two or three inches of the bottom of the vessel (which is only designed to hold the sticks steady which are to support the leaves and stalks), then lay on the lead upon which the bulbs are to rest, placing the notched part opposite to that in the false bottom, as near as the sticks, when placed, will suffer it; then place the bulbs one in each hole, and fill up with water to the upper lead. The bottom of the bulb will then touch the water; and as the water diminishes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, keep it supplied with more up to the same height for a month or six weeks; in which time the bulbs will have shot strong fibres. Then fill up the water about half an inch above the surface of the lead; and by degrees, as the fibres strengthen, and the plume shoots from the head, keep the water higher and higher, till at length the whole bulb is covered. The water is to be kept at this standard till the season for drying them returns.—At the time of planting the bulbs, they must be carefully cleaned from any foulness at the bottom by scraping them with the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> till the found part of the bulb appears; clear them likewise from any loose skins, and even take off their brown skin till they appear white; otherwise this brown skin will tinge the water, and the growth will not succeed so well. The notches in the side of each lead are intended to give easy passage to the water, that, if there should be any foulness or sediment in it, on shaking it a little it may all run through, and fresh water be put in its place. But this shifting the water need not be done more than once or twice in a winter, as there may be occasion from the foulness; and when this is done, the sides of the vessel should be cleaned with a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, and rinsed out again, and the bulbs themselves washed, by pouring water on them at a little distance. At any time when the outer skins of the bulbs dry, they are to be peeled off, that they may not occasion foulness in the water; and if any dust or foul matter be at any time observed floating on the surface, the method is to fill up the pot or vessel to the rim, and let it run over: this will carry off that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> foulness, and the water may afterwards be poured away to the proper standard. Bulbs of equal size should be planted together in the same pot, that they may all have the same benefit of the water. Narcissiuses and hyacinths do well together; as also tulips and jonquils, and crocuses and snowdrops.

FLUDD

Pages 739-739

Robert, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and physician of some celebrity in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was the son of Sir Thomas Fludd, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; and was born at Milgate in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in the year 1574. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and afterwards spent six years in travelling through <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He acquired a strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Rosicrucian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which chiefly consisted of mysticism and jargon, and such as were admitted among them had certain secrets analogous to those of free masonry. On his return home, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.D. settled in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and was chosen a fellow of the college of physicians. His piety was of an enthusiastic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and the seeming depth of his knowledge procured him much admiration, and gave him a temporary fame. It is said that he employed a kind of unintelligible cant when speaking to his patients, which sometimes contributed to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, as it operated on their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. He is chiefly known as a seer in philosophy, and not as a physician. He blended the incomprehensible reveries of the Cabalists and Paracellians, forming a new physical system replete with mystery and absurdity. He believed in two universal principles, the northern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> condensing, and the southern or rarefying power. Innumerable geniuses he conceived to preside over these, and committed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of diseases to legions of spirits collected from the four winds of heaven. In his estimation, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> subsisted between the macrocosm and the microcosm, or the world of nature and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. All his fancies and whims it is impossible to enumerate, yet they attracted the notice of the philosophers of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, being supported by mysterious gravity and the shadow of erudition. Even Kepler himself thought his extravagant jargon worthy of refutation, and Gassendi for this purpose wrote his Examen Philosophiae Fluddiana. One of Fludd's performances, entitled Nexus utrinque Cosmi, is illustrated by some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> of a very singular and extraordinary nature.

FLUENT

Pages 739-739
or Flowing Quantity, in the doctrine of fluxions, is the variable quantity which is considered as increasing and decreasing: or the fluent of a given fluxion, is that quantity whose fluxion being taken, according to the rules of that doctrine, shall be the same with the given fluxion. See Fluxions.

FLUID

Pages 739-740

an appellation given to all bodies whose particles easily yield to the least partial pressure, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> force impressed. For the Laws and Properties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, see <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">Hydrodynamics</a>. There are various kinds of animalcules to be discerned in different fluids by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. Of many remarkable kinds of these, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is given under the article Animalcule. All of these little creatures are easily destroyed by separating them from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> element. Naturalists have even fallen upon shorter methods. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> point, dipped in spirit of vitriol, and then immersed into a drop of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, readily kills all the animalcules: which, though before frisking about with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> liveliness and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, no sooner come within the influence of the acid particles, than they spread themselves, and tumble <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to all appearance dead. The like may be done by a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; only with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that, by the latter application, they seem to grow vertiginous, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round and round till they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down. Tincture of salt of tartar, used in the same manner, kills them still more readily; yet not so, but there <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be apparent marks of their first being sick and convulsed. Inks destroy them as fast as spirit of vitriol, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood produces the same effect. Urine, faeces, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> all destroy them, though not so fast; besides, that there is some diversity in their figures and appearances, as they receive their deaths from this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> or that. The point of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> dipped in spittle, prettily killed all the kinds of animalcules in puddle water, as Mr Harris supposes it will other animalcules of this kind. All who are acquainted with microscopic observations, know very well, that in water, in which the best glasses can discover no particle of animated <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, after a few grains of pepper, or a fragment of a plant of almost any kind, has been some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in it, animals full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> are produced; and those in such numbers, as to equal the fluid itself in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>.—When we see a numerous brood of young fishes in a pond, we make no doubt of their having owed their origin to the spawn, that is, to the eggs of the parents of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. What are we then to think of these? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we will consider the progress of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the insect tribes in general, and especially in such of them as are most analogous to these, we shall find it less difficult to give an account of their origin than might have been imagined. A small quantity of water taken from any ditch in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months, is found to be full of little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, seeming in nothing so much as in size to differ from the microscopic animalcules. Nay, water, without these, exposed in open vessels to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, will be always found to abound with multitudes of them, visible to the naked eye, and full of life and motion. These we know, by their future changes, are the fly worms of the different species of gnats, and multitudes of other fly species; and we can easily determine, that they have owed their origin only to the eggs of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> fly there deposited. Nay, a closer observation will at any time give ocular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this; as the flies may be seen laying their eggs there, and the eggs may be followed through all their changes to the fly again. Why then are we to doubt but that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> abounds with other flies and animalcules as minute as the worms in those fluids; and that these last are only the fly worms of the former, which after a proper time spent in that state, will suffer changes like those of the larger kinds, and become flies like those to whose eggs they owed their origin? Vid., Reaumur, Hist. Insect. vol. iv. p. 431. The differently medicated liquors made by infusions of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, afford a proper matter for the worms of different species of these (small flies; and there is no reason to doubt, but that among these some are viviparous, others oviparous; and to this may be, in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, owing the different time taken up for the production of these insects in different fluids. Those which are a proper matter for the worms of the viviparous fly, may be soonest found full of them; as, probably the liquor is no sooner in a state to afford them Fluid. them proper nourishment, than their parents <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> them there; whereas those produced from the eggs of the little oviparous flies, must, after the liquor is in a proper state, and they are deposited in it in the form of eggs, have a proper time to be hatched, before they can appear alive. It is easy to prove, that the animals we find in these vegetable infusions were brought thither from elsewhere. It is not less easy to prove, that they could not be in the matter infused any more than in the water in which it is infused. Notwithstanding the fabulous accounts of salamanders, it is now well known, that no animal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> or small, can bear the force of fire for any considerable time; and, by parity of reason, we are not to believe, that any insect, or embryo insect, in any state, can bear the heat of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water for many minutes. To proceed to inquiries on this foundation: If several tubes be filled with water, with a small quantity of vegetable matter, such as pepper, oak bark, truffles, &c., in which, after a time, insects will be discovered by the microscope; and other like tubes be filled with simple water boiled, with water and pepper boiled together, and with water with the two other ingredients all separately boiled in it; when all these liquors come to a proper time for the observation of the microscope, all, as well those which have been boiled as those which have not, will be found equally to abound with insects, and those of the same kind, in infusions of the same kind, whether boiled or not boiled. Those in the infusions which had sustained a heat capable of destroying animal life, must therefore not have subsisted either in the water or in the matters put into it, but must have been brought thither after the boiling; and it seems by no way so probable, as by means of some little winged inhabitants of the air depositing their eggs or worms in these fluids. On this it is natural to ask, how it comes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, that while we see myriads of the progeny of these winged insects in water, we never see themselves? The answer is equally easy, viz. because we can always place a drop of this water immediately before the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of the microscope, and keep it there while we are at leisure to examine its contents; but that is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with regard to the air inhabited by the parent flies of these worms, which is an immense <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> in proportion to the water proper for nourishing these worms; and consequently, while the latter are clustered together in heaps, the former may be dispersed and scattered. Nor do we want instances of this, even in insects of a larger kind. In many of our gardens, we frequently find vessels of water filled with worms of the gnat kind, as plentiful, in proportion to their size, as those of other fluids are with animalculæ. Every cubic inch of water in these vessels contains many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of animals: yet we see many cubic inches of air in the garden not affording one of the parent flies. But neither are we positively to declare that the parent flies of these animalculæ are in all states wholly invisible to us; if not singly to be seen, there are some strong reasons to imagine that they may in great clusters. Every one has seen in a clear <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when looking steadfastly at the sky, that the air is in many places disturbed by motions and convolutions in certain spots, These cannot be the effects of imagination, or of faults in our eyes, because they appear the same to all; and if we consider what would be the case to an eye formed in such a manner as to see nothing smaller than an ox, on viewing the air with a marsh fully peopled with gnats, we must be sensible that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of these insects, though to us distinctly enough visible, would appear to such an eye merely as the moving parcels of air in the former instance, do to us: and surely it is thence no rash conclusion to infer, that the case may be the same, and that myriads of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> insects, too small to be singly the objects of our view, yet are to us what the clouds of gnats would be in the former case. Nervous Fluid. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">Elastic</a> Fluids. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index.

FLUIDITY

Pages 740-741

is by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton defined to be, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of bodies by which they yield to any force impressed, and which have their parts very easily moved among one another. To this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> some have added, that the parts of a fluid are in a continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is supported by the solution of salts, and the formation of tinctures. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a small bit of saffron is thrown into a phial full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> tincture <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon be communicated to the water to a considerable height; though the phial is allowed to remain at rest; which indicates a motion in those parts of the fluid which touch the saffron, by which its colouring <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is carried up. With regard to water, this can scarce be denied; the constant exhalations from its surface show, that there must be a perpetual motion in its parts from the ascent of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> through it. In <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, where insensible <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> does not take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it might be doubted; and accordingly the Newtonian philosophers in general have been of opinion, that there are some substances essentially fluid, from the spherical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of their constituent particles. The congelation of mercury, however, by an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, demonstrates that fluidity is not essentially inherent in mercury more than in other bodies. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> have vacuities in their substance is evident, because they may be made to dissolve certain bodies without sensibly increasing their bulk. For example, water will dissolve a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; after which it will receive a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and after that a little <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, without increasing its first dimensions. Here we can scarce suppose any thing else than that the saline particles were interposed between those of the fluid; and as, by the mixture of salt and water, a considerable degree of cold is produced, we may thence easily see why the fluid receives these substances without any increase of bulk. All substances are expanded by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and reduced into less dimensions by cold; therefore, if any substance is added to a fluid, which tends to make it cold, the expansion by the bulk of the substance added will not be so much perceived as if this effect had not happened; and if the quantity added be small, the fluid will <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> as much, perhaps more, from the cold produced by the mixture, than it will be expanded from the bulk of the salt. This also may let us know with what these interfaces between the particles of the fluid were filled up; namely, the element of fire <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> heat. The saline particles, up- on their solution in the fluid, have occupied these spaces; and now the liquor being deprived of a quantity of this element equal in bulk to the salt added, feels sensibly colder. As, therefore, there is scarce any body to be found, but what may become <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> by a sufficient degree of cold, and none but what a certain degree of heat will render fluid; the opinion naturally arises, that fire is the cause of fluidity in all bodies, and that this element is the only essentially fluid substance in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Hence we may conclude, that those substances which we call fluids are not essentially so, but only assume that appearance in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an intimate union with the element of fire; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> assume a fluid appearance on being dissolved in spirit of wine, or salts in water. Upon these principles Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> mentions fluidity as an effect of heat. The different degrees of heat which are required to bring different bodies into a state of fluidity, he supposes to depend on some particulars in the mixture and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of the bodies themselves: which becomes extremely probable, from considering that we change the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state of bodies in this respect, by certain mixtures; thus, if two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are compoundcd, the mixture is usually more fusible than either of them separately. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. It is certain, however, that water becomes warmer by being converted into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a>; which may seem contradictory to this opinion. To this, however, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> replies, that fluidity does not consist in the degree of sensible heat contained in bodies, which will affect the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or a thermometer; but in a certain quantity which remains in a latent state. This opinion he supports from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> required to melt ice; and to ascertain the degree of heat requisite to keep water in a fluid state, he put five ounces of water into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> flask, and converted it into ice by means of a freezing mixture put round the flask. Into another flask of the same kind he put an equal quantity of water cooled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> nearly to the freezing point, by mixing it with snow, and then pouring it off. In this he placed a very delicate thermometer; and found that it acquired heat from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the room in which it was placed: <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> degrees of heat were gained the first half <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The ice being exposed to the same degree of heat, namely, the air of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> room without fire, it cannot be doubted that it received heat from the air as fast as the water which was not frozen; but, to prevent all possibility of deception, he put his hand under the flask containing the ice, and found a stream of cold air very sensibly defending from it, even at a considerable distance from the flask; which undeniably proved, that the ice was all that time absorbing heat from the air. Nevertheless, it was not till 11 hours that the ice was half melted, though in that time it had absorbed so much heat as ought to have raised the thermometer to 140°; and even after it was melted, the temperature of the water was found scarce above the freezing point: so that as the heat which entered could not be found in the melted ice, he concluded that it remained concealed in the water, as an essential ingredient of its composition.

FLUKE

Pages 741-741
or FLounder. See Pleuronectes, Ichthyology Index. FLUKE Worm. See Fasciola, Helminthology Index. FLUKE of an Anchor, that part of it which fastens in the ground. See Anchor.

FLUMMERY

Pages 741-741

a wholesome sort of jelly made of oatmeal. The manner of preparing it is as follows. Put three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handfuls of finely ground oatmeal to steep, for 24 hours, in two quarts of fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; then pour off the clear water, and put two quarts of fresh water to it; strain it through a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> sieve, putting in two spoonsful of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> flower water, and a spoonsful of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>: boil it till it is as thick as a hasty pudding, stirring it continually while it is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, that it may be very smooth.

FLUOR

Pages 741-741

in Physics, a fluid; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, more properly, the state of a body that was before hard or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, but is now reduced by fusion or fire into a state of fluidity. FLUOR Acid. See Fluoric Acid, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FLUOR Albac, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> incident to women, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of whites. See Medicine Index. FLUOR <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">Spar</a>, or Blue John, called also fluxing spars, vitreous or glass spars, are minerals composed of calcareous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> united with fluoric acid. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

FLUSHING

Pages 741-741

a handsome, strong, and considerable town of the United Provinces, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALCHEREN">Walcheren</a>, with a very good harbour, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> foreign trade. It was put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, for a pledge of their fidelity, and as a security for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> she advanced. It is one of the three places where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. advised <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. to preserve with care. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 32. N. Lat. 51. 26.

FLUTE

Pages 741-743

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music, the simplest of all those of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind. It is played on by blowing it with the mouth; and the tones <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> notes are changed by stopping and opening the holes disposed for that purpose along its side. This is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> instrument. It was at first called the flute à bec, from bec an old Gaulish word signifying the beak of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> or fowl, but more especially of a cock; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> flute à bec must therefore signify the beaked flute; which appears very proper, comparing it with the traverso or German flute. The word flute is derived from fluta, the Latin for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMPREY">lamprey</a> or small eel taken in the Sicilian seas, having <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> holes immediately below the gills on each side, the precise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the flute. By Mersennus this instrument is called the flûte dulcis seu Anglica; the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, according to him, for the treble flute, is C fa ut, and the compass of the instrument 15 notes. There is, however, a flute known by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> flute, the lowest note of which is F. Indeed, ever since the introduction of the flute into concerts, the lowest note of the instrument, of what size forever it is, has been called F; when in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> its pitch is determinable only by its correspondence in respect of acuteness or gravity with one or other of the chords in the scala maxima or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> system. Besides the true concert flute, others of a less size were soon introduced into concerts of violins; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the method was to write the flute <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> correspondent... correspondent to its pitch. This practice was introduced in 1710 by one Woodcock, a celebrated performer on this instrument, and William Babell organist of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of All-hallows, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a> Street, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. They failed, however, in procuring for the flute a reception into concerts of various instruments; for which reason one Thomas Stanely, a very curious maker of flutes and other instruments of the like kind, about the year 1732, adverting to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of Mercennus, in which the lowest note was C, invented what he called the new system; in which, by making the flute of such a size as to be a fifth above concert pitch, the lowest note became C sol fa ut. By this contrivance the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of transposing the flute part was taken away; for a flute of this size, adjusted to the system above mentioned, became an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> to the violin. To further this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Stanely's, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Merci, an excellent performer on the flute, published about the year 1735, six solos for this instrument, three of which are said to be accommodated to Mr Stanely's new system; but the German flute was now become a favourite instrument, and Stanely's ingenuity failed of its effect. One great objection indeed lies against this instrument, which, however, equally affects all perforated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>; namely, that they are never perfectly in tune, or cannot be made to play all their notes with equal exactness. The utmost that the makers of them can do is to tune them to some one key; as the hautboy to C, the German flute to D, and the English flute to F; and to effect this truly, is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of no small difficulty. The English flutes made by the younger Stanely came the nearest of any to perfection; but those of Bredan, though excellent in their tone, are all too flat in the upper octave. For these reasons some are induced to think, that the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of proficiency on any of those instruments is not worth the labour of attaining it. German Flute, is an instrument entirely different from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> flute. It is not, like that, put into the mouth to be played; but the end is stopp'd with a stopper or plug, and the lower lip is applied to a hole about two inches and a half or three inches distant from the end. This instrument is usually about a foot and a half <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; rather bigger at the upper end than the lower; and perforated with holes, besides that for the mouth, the lowest of which is stopp'd and opened by the little finger's pressing on a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or sometimes a silver key, like those in hautboys, bassoons, &c. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is exceeding sweet and agreeable; and serves as a treble in a concert. Flute, or Fluyt, is a kind of long vessel, with flat ribs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> timbers, round behind, and swollen in the middle; serving chiefly for the carrying of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in fleets or squadrons of ships; though it is often used in merchandise. The word flute, taken for a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or vessel, is derived, according to Borel, from the ancient flote, a little boat. In the verbal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of St Catharine of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in the 12th century, we read Unus equum suum una cum mercurio magni ponderis introduxit super instrumentum de lignis fabricatum, vulgariter dictum flota. Upon which the Bollandists observe, that in some copies it is read flotta, an instrument called by the Latins ratis; and that the word flotta or flota arose from flotten or voloten, "to float." Flutes, or Flutings, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, are perpendicular channels or cavities cut along the shaft of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> or pilaster. They are supposed to have been first introduced in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the plaiting of women's robes; and are therefore called by the Latins fringes and rugae. The French call them corniches, as being excavations; and we, flutes or flutings, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to the musical instrument so called. They are chiefly affected in the Ionic order in which they had their first rise; though they are also used in all the richer orders, as the Corinthian and Composite; but rarely in the Doric, and scarcely ever in the Tuscan. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">Flux</a>, in Medicine, an extraordinary illuse or evacuation of some humour. Fluxes are various, and variously denominated, according to their seats or the humours thus voided; as a flux of the belly, uterine flux, hepatic flux, salival flux, &c. The flux of the belly is of four kinds, which have each their respective denominations, viz. the lienery, or fluxus lieniericus; the caeciac, or fluxus chylotus; the diarrhoea; and the dysenteric, or bloody flux. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flux, in Hydrography, a regular periodical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, happening twice in 24 hours; wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is raised and driven violently against the shores. The flux or flow is one of the motions of the tide; the other, whereby the water sinks and retires, is called the reflux or ebb. There is also a kind of rest or cessation of about half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> between the flux and reflux; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the water is at its greatest height, called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water. The flux is made by the motion of the water of the sea from the equator towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>; which, in its progress, striking against the coasts in its way, and meeting with opposition from them, swells, and where it can find passage, as in flats, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, &c., rises up and runs into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. This motion follows, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; as it loses or comes later every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> by about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an hour, or more, precisely by 48 minutes; and by so much is the motion of the moon slower than that of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. It is always highest and greatest in full moons, particularly those of the equinoxes. In some parts, as at Mount St Michael, it rises 80 or 90 feet, though in the open sea it never rises above a foot or two; and in some places, as about the Morea, there is no flux at all. It runs up some rivers above 120 miles. Up the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> it only goes 80, viz. near to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>. Above London <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> the water flows four hours and ebbs eight; and below the bridge, flows five hours and ebbs seven. Flux, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, is sometimes used synonymously with fusion. For instance, an ore, or other matter, is said to be a liquid flux, when it is completely fused. But the word flux is generally used to signify certain saline matters, which facilitate the fusion of ores, and other matters which are difficultly fusible in effays and reductions of ores; such are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, nitre, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, tartar, and common <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. But the word flux is more particularly applied to mixtures of different proportions of only nitre and tartar; and these fluxes are called by particular names, according to the proportions of these ingredients, as in the following article. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Flux, is made with equal parts of nitre and of tartar detonated together, by which they are alkali- The residuum of this detonation is an alkali composed of the alkalies of the nitre and of the tartar, both which are absolutely of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. As the proportion of nitre in this mixture is more than is sufficient to consume entirely all the inflammable matter of the tartar, the alkali remaining after the detonation is perfectly white, and is therefore called white flux; and as this alkali is made very quickly, it is also called contemporaneous alkali. When a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> only of white flux is made, as a few ounces for instance, some nitre always remains undecomposed, and a little of the inflammable principle of the tartar, which gives a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> or even a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to some part of the flux; but this does not happen when a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of white flux is made; because then the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is much greater. This small quantity of undecomposed nitre and tartar which remains in white flux is not hurtful in most of the metallic fusions in which this flux is employed: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the flux be required perfectly pure, it might easily be disengaged from those extraneous matters by a long and strong calcination, without fusion. Crude Flux. By crude flux is meant the mixture of nitre and tartar in any proportions, without detonation. Thus the mixture of equal parts of the two salts used in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of the white flux, or the mixture of one part of nitre and two parts of tartar for the preparation of the black flux, are each of them a crude flux before detonation. It has also been called white flux, from its colour; but this might occasion it to be confounded with the white flux above described. The name, therefore, of crude flux is more convenient. Crude flux is detonated and alkalized during the reductions and fusions in which it is employed; and is then changed into white or black flux, according to the proportions of which it is composed. This detonation produces good effects in these fusions and reductions, if the swelling and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRAVASATION">extravasation</a> of the detonating matters be guarded against. Accordingly, crude flux may be employed successfully in many operations; as, for instance, in the ordinary operation for procuring the regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>. Black Flux. Black flux is produced from the mixture of two parts of tartar and one part of nitre detonated together. As the quantity of nitre which enters into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of this flux is not sufficient to consume all the inflammable matters of the tartar, the alkali which remains after the detonation contains much black matter, of the nature of coal, and is therefore called black flux.

FLUXIONS

Pages 772-791

Ex. 3. Let the curve be an ellipse. Put \( AB = x \), \( BP = y \), AC the semi-transverse axis \( = a \), CH the semi-conjugate axis \( = b \). The nature of the curve is such, that \[ AC^2 : CH :: AB \times BE : BP^2 \] or \( a^2 : b^2 :: (2a-x)x : y^2 \) Hence \( a^2y^2 = b^2(2a-x)x \), and taking the relation of the

FLUXIONS

Pages 790-809

fluxions as contain the irrational function \( \sqrt{A + Bx + Cx^2} \), and which have necessarily one or other of these forms. \[ X \cdot \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} = \frac{X}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \] \( X \) being put for any rational function of \( x \); and it may be remarked, that the latter form comprehends the former, which may be written thus: \[ \frac{X \cdot \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} = \frac{X(A + Bx + Cx^2)}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \] and here the numerator of the fluxion is a rational function of \( x \). Before we transform the expression \( \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} \) into another that is rational with respect to the variable quantity it contains, we shall put the quantity \( A + Bx + Cx^2 \) under this form, \[ C \left( \frac{A}{C} + \frac{B}{C} x + x^2 \right) \] and, in order to abridge, we shall put \[ C = c^2, \quad \frac{A}{C} = a, \quad \frac{B}{C} = b, \] then we have \[ \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} = c \sqrt{(a + bx + x^2)} \] Let us now assume \( \sqrt{(a + bx + x^2)} = x + z \), then, squaring both sides of the equation, we find \( a + bx = 2xz + z^2 \), hence we get \( x = \frac{a - z^2}{2z - b} \) and consequently \[ \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} = c (x + z) = c \left( \frac{a - z^2}{2z - b} \right) \] \[ \dot{x} = \frac{2(a - bx + z^2)}{(2z - b)^2} \] By means of these values the fluxion \( \frac{X}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \) is transformed into another fluxion \( Z \dot{x} \), where \( Z \) denotes a rational function of \( z \), which is real when \( C \) or \( c^2 \) is positive; but as when \( C \) is negative \( c \) becomes imaginary, the fluxion \( Z \dot{x} \) which involves \( c \) becomes also imaginary. In this case we have to consider \( \sqrt{(A + Bx - Cx^2)} \), and making \[ C = c^2, \quad \frac{A}{C} = a, \quad \frac{B}{C} = b, \] it becomes \( c \sqrt{(a + bx - x^2)} \). The quantity \( x^2 - bx - a \) may always be decomposed into real factors of the first degree; let us represent these factors by \( x - \alpha \) and \( x - \alpha' \), then it is evident that \[ a + bx - x^2 = (x - \alpha)(x - \alpha') \] Let us now assume \[ \sqrt{(x - \alpha)(x' - x)} = (x - \alpha)x, \] then squaring both sides of the equation it becomes divisible by \( x - \alpha \), and we have \( \alpha' - x = (x - \alpha)x^2 \), from which we find \[ x = \frac{a + z^2}{z^2 + 1}, \quad (x - \alpha) = \frac{(a - z^2)}{z^2 + 1}, \] \[ \dot{x} = \frac{2(a - z^2)z}{(z^2 + 1)^2} \] values which render the proposed fluxion \( \frac{X}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \) rational. Let us now take for example the fluxion \( \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \); by applying to it the first of the preceding transformations it becomes \( \frac{-2z}{c(2z - b)} \), the fluent of which is \( \frac{1}{c} \ln(2z - b) + \text{const} \). Substituting now for \( z \) its value \( x + \sqrt{(a + bx + x^2)} \), and for \( a, b, \) and \( c \), the quantities they severally represent, the fluent becomes \[ \frac{-1}{\sqrt{C}} \left[ \frac{B}{\sqrt{C}} - \frac{2x}{\sqrt{C}} \right] + \text{const} \] a result to which we may also give this form, \[ \frac{-1}{\sqrt{C}} \left[ \frac{B}{\sqrt{C}} - \frac{2x}{\sqrt{C}} \right] + \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} + \text{const} \] +1. \( \frac{2}{\sqrt{C}} + \text{const} \) By uniting the constant quantities into one, and observing that the radical quantity \( \sqrt{C} \) may have the sign prefixed to it, we have at last \[ \int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \text{ equal to } \frac{1}{\sqrt{C}} \left[ \frac{B}{\sqrt{C}} + \frac{2x}{\sqrt{C}} + \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} \right] + \text{const} \] Let us take for the second example \( \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A + Bx - Cx^2)}} \). By employing the latter transformation of § 126, we have \( \frac{-2z}{c(z^2 + 1)} \), of which the fluent is \[ - \frac{2}{c} \arctan(x) + \text{const} \] Substituting now instead of \( z \) its value \( \frac{\alpha' - x}{\sqrt{(x - \alpha)}} \) deduced from the equation \( \alpha' - x = (x - \alpha)x^2 \), \[ 5B \dot{x} \] and putting \( \sqrt{C} \) for \( c \), we get \[ \int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A+Bx-Cx^2)}} \] equal to \[ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{C}} \arctan \left( \frac{\sqrt{a'} - x}{\sqrt{(x-a)}} \right) + \text{const}. \] \( a \) and \( a' \) being the roots of the equation \[ x^2 - \frac{B}{C} x - \frac{A}{C} = 0. \] Let us suppose that \( A = C = 1 \) and \( B = 0 \), then the proposed fluxion becomes in this particular case \[ \int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} \] and the preceding formula gives for its fluent \[ -2 \arctan \left( \frac{\sqrt{1-x}}{\sqrt{1+x}} \right) + \text{const.} \] for \( a \) and \( a' \) being the roots of the equation \( x^2 - 1 = 0 \), we must take \( a = -1 \), and \( a' = 1 \). We may, however, give this fluent another form by proceeding thus: Let \( v \) be the arch whose tan. \[ = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}}{\sqrt{1+x}} \] then \( \tan^2 v = \frac{1-x}{1+x} \), and \( x = \frac{1 - \tan^2 v}{1 + \tan^2 v} \) \[ = \frac{2}{1 + \tan^2 v} - 1 = \frac{2}{\sec^2 v} - 1 = 2 \cos^2 v - 1, \] but \( 2 \cos^2 v - 1 = \text{cof. } 2v \) (Algebra, § 358.), therefore, \[ x = \text{cof. } 2v. \] Put \( s \) for the arch whose sine is \( x \), and \( \pi \) for half the circumference, then \( x = \text{cof. } (\frac{\pi}{2} - s) \), therefore \( 2v = \frac{\pi}{2} - s \), and since it has been shewn that \[ \int \frac{\dot{s}}{\sqrt{(1-s^2)}} = -2s + \text{const.} \] therefore \[ \int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} = -\frac{\pi}{2} + \text{const.} \] or, by including the arch \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) in the constant quantity, \[ \int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} = s + \text{const.} \] This conclusion agrees with what has been shewn in § 59. Instead of finding the fluent of \[ \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A+Bx-Cx^2)}} = c \sqrt{(a+bx-x^2)} \] by first transforming it to a rational expression, we may reduce it directly to an arch of a circle by proceeding as follows. Put \( x = \frac{b}{2} \), then \( \dot{x} = \dot{s} \), and the fluxion is transformed to \[ \frac{\dot{s}}{\sqrt{(a+\frac{b^2}{4}-x^2)}} \] again, put \( a + \frac{b^2}{4} = g^2 \), and \( x = g u \), then \( \dot{x} = g \dot{u} \), and this last fluxion is transformed to \[ \frac{\dot{u}}{\sqrt{(1-u^2)}}, \] the fluent of which is \[ \frac{1}{2} \arctan (u) + \text{const.} \] Of the Fluents of Binomial

FLUXIONS
