fluxions to mathematical enquiries. To find the Lengths of Curves. 161. It has been shown in § 63, that if the abscissa of a curve be denoted by $x$, the ordinate by $y$, and the curve line by $z$, then $z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$, hence the general formula for finding the length of a curve is $$z = \int \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}.$$ Therefore, if from the equation expressing the nature of a curve we find the value of $y$ in terms of $x$ and $x$, or else the value of $x$ in terms of $y$ and $y$, and substitute the one or the other in the above general formula, we shall obtain a fluxion the fluent of which will be the length of the curve. Ex. 1. Suppose the curve to be a parabola, and that $AB = x$, $BP = y$, the arch $AP = z$, the parameter $= a$, then the equation of the curve being $ax = y^2$, we have $x = \frac{2yy}{a}$, and $$z = \int \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \int \sqrt{\left(\frac{4y^2}{a^2} + y^2\right)}.$$ By comparing this expression with formula (B) in § 131, we find $$\int \sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)} = \frac{1}{2} y \sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)} + \frac{1}{2} a^2 \int \frac{y}{\sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)}};$$ again by § 127, $$\int \frac{y}{\sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)}} = \frac{1}{2} \left\{ 2y + \sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)} \right\};$$ therefore $$z = \frac{y \sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)}}{2a} + \frac{a}{4} \left\{ 2y + \sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)} \right\} + C.$$ To determine the value of $C$, we must consider that when $y = 0$, then $z = 0$, so that then the general formula will become simply $$C = \frac{a}{4} \left\{ 2y + \sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)} \right\}.$$ Ex. 2. Suppose the curve to be a circle, and that $C$ Fig. 20. is its centre, and $AE$ a quadrant of the circle. Put $CB = x$, $BP = y$, the arch $EP = z$, the radius of the circle $= a$, then $x^2 + y^2 = a^2$, and $y = \sqrt{(a^2 - x^2)}$, and $y = \frac{-ax}{\sqrt{(a^2 - x^2)}}$, hence $$z = \int \sqrt{(x^2 + y^2)} = \int \sqrt{(x^2 + \frac{x^2}{a^2 - x^2})}.$$ This fluent can only be expressed by an infinite series, under which form it has been already exhibited in § 140, the radius being there supposed unity. Ex. 3. Let the curve be an ellipse, and let it be required to find the length of the curve between $E$ the vertex of the lesser axis, and $P$ any point in the curve. To simplify the calculation, let us suppose that the semi-transverse axis $AC = 1$; put the semi-conjugate axis $CE = b$, the eccentricity (that is $\sqrt{(1 - b^2)} = e$, the abscissa $CB = x$, the ordinate $PB = y$, the arch $LP = z$; then, the equation of the curve being $y^2 = b^2(1 - x^2)$, we have Inverse Method. have \( y = b \sqrt{1-x^2} \), and \( \dot{y} = -\frac{b x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \), and therefore \[ z = \int \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \int \sqrt{\frac{b^2 x^2}{1-x^2}} \] This fluent can only be expressed by means of an infinite series, and it has been already given in this form in § 141. If we take \( x = 1 \), then all the quantities in that series which are multiplied by \( \sqrt{1-x^2} \) will vanish, but in this particular case \( z \) is the elliptic quadrant \( EA \), and \( A \) is a quadrant of the circumscribing circle, or \( \frac{\pi}{2} \), therefore the elliptic quadrant is equal to \[ \frac{\pi}{2} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{2.2} e^2 - \frac{1.1.3}{2.2.4.4} e^4 - \frac{1.1.3.3.5}{2.2.4.4.6.6} e^6 - \ldots \right) \] This series converges very fast if \( e \) be a small fraction. Ex. 4. Suppose the curve to be a cycloid. Let a circle be described on its axis meeting the ordinate \( PB \) in \( Q \), and draw \( CQ \) to the centre of the circle. Put \( AB=x \), \( BP=y \), the cycloidal arch \( AP=z \), the radius \( AC=a \), the angle \( ACQ=v \), then \( AB=a(1-\cos v) \), \( BQ=a \sin v \), the circ. arch \( AQ=a v \), so that \( x=a(1-\cos v) \), and from the nature of the curve \( y=a(\sin v+\text{fin. } v) \), therefore (\$ 59.) \[ \dot{x} = a \sin v \cdot \text{fin. } v, \quad \dot{y} = a \cos v (1+\text{cof. } v), \] \[ \dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 = a^2 \left[ \sin^2 v + (1+\text{cof. } v)^2 \right] = a^2 \left( 2+2\text{cof. } v \right); \] but \( 2+2\text{cof. } v=4\text{cof. }^2 \frac{v}{2} \) (\textit{Algebra}, § 356.) therefore \[ z = \int \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = 2a \int \text{cof. } \frac{v}{2} \] \[ = 4a \text{fin. } \frac{v}{2} + C, \quad (\$ 145.) \] but as when \( v=0 \), then \( z=0 \), therefore \( C=0 \), and \( z=4a \text{fin. } \frac{v}{2} \); but if the chord \( AQ \) be drawn, \( 2a \text{fin. } \frac{v}{2} = \text{chord } AQ \), therefore \( z=2 \text{ chord } AQ \). 162. The formula \( z=\int \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \) not being applicable in its present form to curves of the spiral kind, we shall here investigate another suited to that particular class of curves. Let \( APR \) be a curve of such a nature that the position of any point \( P \) in the curve is determined by \( PF \), its distance from a given point \( F \), and by the angle which \( PF \) makes with \( AF \) a line given in position. We shall employ the same construction and notation here as in § 154, with the addition of drawing the chords \( DD', PQ, PP' \), and putting the arch \( AP=z \); then it is manifest that the simultaneous increments of \( v, z, \) and \( r \) will be the arches \( DD', PP' \), and the straight line \( P'Q \) respectively. Hence \[ \frac{z}{v} = \text{limit of } \frac{\text{arch } PP'}{\text{arch } DD'} \] but it is evident from § 62, that the limiting ratio of these arches must be the same as that of their chords, therefore, \[ \frac{z}{v} = \text{limit of } \frac{\text{chord } PP'}{\text{chord } DD'}; \] now the limit of the angle \( PQD \) being evidently a right angle, we have \[ \lim_{DD'} \frac{PP'}{DD'} = \lim_{DD'} \frac{\sqrt{(PQ^2 + QP'^2)}}{DD'} \] \[ = \lim_{DD'} \sqrt{\frac{PQ^2}{DD'^2} + \frac{QP'^2}{DD'^2}} \] but \( \frac{PQ^2}{DD'^2} = \frac{FP'^2}{FD'^2} = r^2 \), and \( \lim_{DD'} \frac{QP'^2}{DD'^2} = \frac{r^2}{v^2} \) therefore \[ \frac{z}{v} = \sqrt{\left( r^2 + \frac{r^2}{v^2} \right)}, \quad \text{and } \dot{z} = \sqrt{\left( r^2 + \frac{r^2}{v^2} \right)}. \] Let us apply this formula to the spiral of Archimedes, Fig. 27, the equation of which (\$ 155.) is \( am=n r \), and therefore \[ v=\frac{n r}{a m}, \quad \text{and } \dot{v}=\frac{n^2 r^2}{a^2 m^2}; \quad \text{hence} \] \[ z=\int \sqrt{\left( r^2 + \frac{r^2}{v^2} \right)} = \frac{1}{a} \int \dot{r} \sqrt{\left( a^2 + \frac{r^2}{m^2} \right)}. \] This fluent may be found by formula B, § 131, and it is worthy of remark that the fluxion has the same form as that which we have found in § 161 for an arch of a parabola; thus the length of any portion of the spiral of Archimedes may be exhibited by means of an arch of a parabola. To find the Contents of Solids: 163. If \( AD \) the abscissa of a curve be denoted by \( x \), Fig. 44 and \( PD \) the ordinate by \( y \), and the solid generated by the revolution of the curve \( APD \) about \( AD \) as an axis by \( s \), it has been shewn, in § 64, that \( s=\pi y^2 \cdot x \), therefore the general formula for finding the content of a solid is \[ s=\pi \int y^2 \cdot x. \] Ex. 1. Suppose the solid to be a paraboloid, or that which is generated by the revolution of a parabola about its axis; in this case \( y^2=ax \), and taking the fluent so that when \( x=0 \), then \( s=0 \), \[ s=\pi \int y^2 \cdot x = \pi \int x \cdot \frac{1}{2} \pi ax^2, \] or \( s=\frac{1}{2} \pi ax^3 \); but \( \pi ax^3 \) is the content of a cylinder having \( y \) for the radius of its base and \( x \) for its altitude, therefore the content of a paraboloid is half that of a cylinder having the same base and altitude. Ex. 2. Suppose the solid to be a parabolic spindle, which is generated by the revolution of \( APB \) an arch of a parabola about \( AC \) an ordinate to its axis. In this case let \( AD=x, DP=y, AB=b \), the parameter of the Inverse Method. axis \(=a\), then from the nature of the parabola \(AD \times DB = a \times PD\), that is \(x(b-x)=ay\), hence \(y=\frac{(b-x)x}{a}\), and taking the fluent, so that \(s\) and \(x\) may vanish together; \[ s = \int y^2 \dot{x} = \frac{\pi}{a^2} \int x^2 (b-x)^3 \dot{x} \] \[ = \frac{\pi}{a^3} \left( \frac{b^3 x^3}{3} - \frac{b^2 x^4}{2} + \frac{x^5}{5} \right) \] or, since \(a^2 = \frac{(b-x)^2 x^2}{y^2}\), \[ s = \frac{\pi y^2}{(b-x)^3} \left[ \frac{b^3 x}{3} - \frac{b^2 x^2}{2} + \frac{x^3}{5} \right], \] which expression (by supposing \(x=AC=x b\), and putting \(d\) for \(CE\), the greatest value of \(y\)) gives \(\frac{4\pi d^3 b}{15}\) for the content of half the solid generated by the curve \(AEB\), therefore the entire spindle is \(\frac{8\pi a^2 b}{15}\), or (by observing that \(\pi d^2 b\) is the content of a cylinder having \(d\) for the radius of its base and \(b\) for its length) it is \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) of the circumfering cylinder. Ex. 3. Suppose the solid to be a spheroid produced by the revolution of an ellipse about either of its axes; put \(a\) for \(\frac{1}{2}AB\) the axis round which the curve revolves, \(b\) for \(\frac{1}{2}EF\) the other axis, \(x\) for \(AD\) the height of any segment made by a plane perpendicular to the axis of the solid, \(y\) for \(PD\) the radius of its base, and \(s\) for its content. Then from the nature of the curve \(y^2 = \frac{b^2}{a^2} (2ax-x^2)\), therefore taking the fluent upon the supposition that \(s\) and \(x\) vanish together, \[ s = \int y^2 \dot{x} = \frac{\pi b^2}{a^2} \int (2ax-x^2) \dot{x} \] \[ = \frac{\pi b^2}{a^2} \left( ax^3 - \frac{x^4}{3} \right). \] To find the content of the whole spheroid, we have only to take \(x=2a\), thus the formula becomes \[ s = \frac{4\pi b^2 a}{3}, \] and as \(2\pi b^2 a\) expresses the content of a cylinder having \(2b\) for the diameter of its base, and \(2a\) for its height, it follows that the contents of a spheroid is \(\frac{4}{3}\) that of its circumscribing cylinder. It is obvious that what has been found for the spheroid will apply also to the sphere, by supposing the axes equal, or \(a=b\). Fig. 4. If instead of supposing the solid \(APQ\) to be formed by the revolution of a curve round its axis (in which case it is called a solid of revolution) we had supposed it to have any figure whatever, then by referring the solid to some straight line \(AC\), given by position, as an axis, and in which \(A\) is a given point, and supposing \(PQ\) to be a section of the solid made by a plane perpendicular to that axis, meeting it in \(D\), and putting \(AD=x\), and the variable solid \(APQ\) (considered as a function of \(x\)) \(=s\), by proceeding as in § 64, we would have found the limit of \(\frac{\text{increment of } s}{\text{increment of } x}\), and consequently \(\frac{s}{x}\), equal to the area of the section of the solid made by the plane \(PQ\); therefore putting \(V\) for that function of \(x\) which expresses the area of the section, we have \(s=Vx\), and \(s=\int Vx\). Let us suppose for example that \(AEFG\) is a solid Fig. 34, bounded by any plane figure \(EFG\) as a base, and by the surface which will be generated if we suppose a straight line drawn from \(A\) any given point above that plane to revolve in the circumference of the base. Let \(AC\) be a perpendicular drawn from the vertex of the figure to its base, and let \(PQ\) be a section of the solid by a plane parallel to the base, meeting the perpendicular in \(D\). Put \(a=\) the area of the base of the solid, \(V=\) the area of the section \(PQ\), \(b=AC\) the altitude of the whole solid, \(x=AD\) the altitude of the part cut off by the plane \(PQ\), and \(s=\) the content of that part; then, as from the nature of the solid it is pretty evident that the part of it cut off by the plane \(PQ\) is similar to the whole, and as the bases of similar solids are as the squares of their altitudes, we have \[ a : V :: b^2 : x^2, \] hence \(V=\frac{ax^2}{b^2}\), and \[ s=\int Vx = \frac{a}{b^2} \int x^2 \dot{x} = \frac{ax^3}{3b^2}, \] this expression for \(s\) does not require the addition of any constant quantity, for by putting \(s=0\) as it ought to be. Suppose now \(x=b\), then \(s=\frac{ab^3}{3b^2}=\frac{1}{3}ab\), from which it appears that the content of the whole solid is \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the product of the base by the perpendicular. It is evident that pyramids and cones are solids of the kind we have been considering. To find the Surfaces of Solids. 165. The altitude \(AD\) of a solid, generated by revolution of a curve about \(AD\) as an axis, being as before denoted by \(x\), and \(PD\) the radius of its base by \(y\), let us now put \(s\) to denote the curved surface of the solid, then, as it has been shewn, § 65, that \(s=2\pi y \sqrt{(x^2+y^2)}\), we have \[ s=2\pi \int y \sqrt{(x^2+y^2)} \] as a general formula for the surface of a solid. Ex. 1. Suppose the solid to be a sphere, generated by the revolution of a circle about its diameter \(AB\), put the radius of the sphere \(=a\), then \(AD\) being denoted by \(x\), and \(PD\) by \(y\), we have from the nature of the curve \(y^2=2ax-x^2\), therefore \[ y=\sqrt{2ax-x^2}, \] and \[ \dot{y}=\frac{(a-x)\dot{x}}{\sqrt{2ax-x^2}}, \] and \[ \dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 = \dot{x}^2 + (a - x)^2 \] \[ \frac{a^2 \dot{x}^2}{2a - x} = \frac{\dot{x}^2}{y^2}, \] therefore, \( y \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = ax \), and taking the fluent, so that when \( x = 0 \), then \( s = 0 \), \[ s = 2\pi \int y \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = 2\pi ax; \] now if it be considered that \( 2\pi a \) is the circumference of a great circle of the sphere, it will immediately appear that the surface of a segment of a sphere is equal to the circumference of a great circle of the sphere multiplied into the height of the segment. Hence it follows that the whole surface of the sphere is equal to four times the area of one of its great circles. **Ex. 2.** Suppose the curve to be a parabola, then putting \( AD = x \), \( DP = y \), the parameter of the axis \( = a \), we have (\$161, example 1.) \[ \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \frac{1}{a} y \sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)}, \text{ therefore} \] \[ s = 2\pi \int y \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \] \[ = \frac{2\pi}{a} \int y \sqrt{(a^2 + 4y^2)} \] \[ = \frac{\pi}{6a} (a^2 + 4y^2)^{\frac{3}{2}} + C, \text{ by } \$108. \] To discover the value of the constant quantity \( C \), we must observe that when \( x = 0 \), then \( y = 0 \), and \( s = 0 \), therefore putting 0 instead of \( x \) and \( y \), the above equation becomes \( 0 = \frac{\pi a^3}{6} + C \), hence \( C = -\frac{\pi a^3}{6} \), and \[ s = \frac{\pi}{6a} \left( (a^2 + 4y^2)^{\frac{3}{2}} - a^3 \right). \] **To find the Centre of Gravity of any Line, Surface, or Solid.** 166. It belongs to the theory of Mechanics to explain what is meant by the centre of gravity, and to demonstrate its general properties, and here it is only necessary to shew how the method of

fluxions we get \( yy = ax - x \dot{x} \), and hence \( \frac{xx}{y} = \frac{a \dot{x}}{y} - y = \dot{x} - y \), therefore \( \dot{x} = a(\dot{x} - y) \); substituting now the values of \( \dot{x} \) and \( \dot{y} \) in the formula of §167., we have \[ X = \int \frac{x}{z} = \frac{a}{z} \int (\dot{x} - \dot{y}) \] \[ = \frac{a}{z}(x - y + c) \] \[ Y = \int \frac{y}{z} = \frac{a}{z} \int \dot{x} \] \[ = \frac{a}{z}(x + c'). \] To discover the values of the constant quantities \( c, c' \), we have from the equations in which they occur, \[ ac = Xz - ax + ay, \quad ac' = Yz - ax; \] but when \( z = 0 \), then \( x, y, X \) and \( Y \) are each \( = 0 \), therefore \( c = 0 \), and \( c' = 0 \), thus we have simply \[ X = \frac{a(x - y)}{z}, \quad Y = \frac{ax}{z}. \] Ex. 2. Let it be required to find the centre of gravity of APB an area bounded by AP an arch of a circle and PB, BA its fine and verified line. Let \(a\) denote the radius, and let the remaining notation be as in § 168. Then, because \(y = x\), we have \(x = y \cdot x\), but from the equation \(y^2 = 2ax - x^2\) (which expresses the nature of the curve), we find \[x = ax - y \cdot y,\] therefore \[x = ay - y^2 = ax - y^2.\] We have also \(y = y' \cdot x = (2ax - x^2) \cdot x\); therefore, \[X = \int \frac{x}{s} \cdot \int \frac{(a - y^2)}{s}\] \[= \frac{1}{x} (a - \frac{1}{3} y^3 + c)\] \[Y = \int \frac{y}{2s} \cdot \int \frac{(2ax - x^2)}{2s}\] \[= \frac{1}{2s} (ax^2 - \frac{1}{3} x^3 + c').\] By proceeding as in the last example we find \(c\) and \(c'\) each \(= 0\), thus we have \[X = \frac{a}{3}, \quad Y = \frac{3ax^2 - x^3}{6s}.\] Ex. 3. Suppose now the figure to be the surface generated by the revolution of AP an arch of a circle about the diameter AB, and that the centre of gravity of the generated surface is required. Then because from the nature of the circle \(x = ax\) we have \(y = ax\), and \(xy = ax \cdot x\), therefore, substituting these values in the formula of § 169, it becomes \[X = \int \frac{xy}{s} \cdot \int \frac{x}{a \cdot s}\] \[= \frac{1}{x} (a^2 + c).\] To find the values of the constant quantities \(c, c'\), we have \[c = X (x + c') - \frac{1}{4} x^2,\] \[c' = \frac{\frac{1}{2} x^2 + c}{X} - x,\] but as when \(x = 0\), then \(X = 0\), it is manifest that \(c\) and \(c'\) are each \(= 0\), thus we have \[X = \frac{1}{2} x.\] Ex. 4. Let us now suppose that it is required to find the centre of gravity of the solid generated by the revolution of AP an arch of a circle about the diameter. In this case, because \(y^2 = 2ax - x^2\), we have from § 170, \[X = \int \frac{y^2}{s} \cdot \int \frac{x}{s} \cdot \int \frac{(2ax - x^2)}{s}\] \[= \frac{3}{4} ax^3 - \frac{1}{4} x^4 + c\] \[= \frac{a}{x} - \frac{1}{3} x^3 + c'.\] and reasoning as in the last example, we find \(c = 0\), and \(c' = 0\), and therefore \[X = \frac{8}{12} ax - \frac{3}{4} x^2.\] If the segment be a hemisphere, in which case \(x = a\), then \(X = \frac{8}{12} a\). Sect. III. Of Fluxional Equations. 172. It has been shewn (§ 49), how, from an equation being given, expressing the relation between \(x\) a variable quantity, and \(y\) a function of that quantity, we may deduce the equation that expresses the relation of their fluxions. We are now to show how from the latter, or fluxional equation, we may return to the equation of the fluents, which, relatively to the other, may be called its primitive equation. 173. As any primitive equation and the fluxional equation derived from it both hold true at the same time, and as the constant quantities which enter into the former retain the same values in the latter, it follows that by means of the two equations we may extinguish any one of the constant quantities, and thus from any proposed primitive equation deduce a fluxional equation, in which one of the constant quantities contained in that primitive shall not at all be found. For example, let the primitive equation be \(y + ax + b = 0\), by taking the fluxions we have \(y + ax + b = 0\), a fluxional equation in which \(b\) is not found; if, however, it be required to find an equation in which \(a\) shall be wanting, we have only to eliminate \(a\) by applying the common rules of Algebra (Algebra, Sect. vii.) to the two equations \[y + ax + b = 0, \quad y + ax = 0;\] and hence we have \(y - xy + b = 0\), thus it appears that from the primitive equation \(y + ax + b = 0\) we may deduce a fluxional equation which may be expressed under either of these forms, \[y + ax = 0, \quad y - xy + bx = 0;\] these hold true at the same time as the primitive equation, they are alike related to, and any two of the three being given the other necessarily follows from them. As a second example, suppose the primitive equation to be \(x^2 - 2ay - ax^2 - bx = 0\), by passing to the fluxions we immediately find \(x - ax - ay = 0\), an equation in which \(b\) is not found. If, however, it be required that the fluxional equation shall want \(a\), we have only to apply the common rules of elimination to the two equations; thus from the second we get \(a = \frac{x}{y}\), and this being substituted in the first it becomes... from which we have \[ (x^2 - b) \dot{y}^2 + 2xy \dot{x} \dot{y} = x^2 \dot{x}^2 = 0 \] and taking the square root, having previously reduced the equation to a proper form, \[ \dot{y} \sqrt{(x^2 + y^2 - b)} = x \dot{x} = 0. \] 174. It is evident that by proceeding in this manner we shall, in some cases, arrive at a fluxional equation involving the second and higher powers of \( \frac{y}{x} \), and when this happens we can only find the value of \( \frac{y}{x} \) by the resolution of an equation; but this may be avoided by preparing the primitive equation in such a manner, that the constant quantity to be eliminated may be entirely separated from the variable quantities, so as to form one of the terms of the equation, then, upon taking the fluxions, this term being constant will vanish, and thus we shall obtain an equation entirely free from the constant quantity contained in that term. Thus the primitive equation \( y + ax + bx = 0 \) has already such a form that by taking the fluxions we get \( \dot{y} + a \dot{x} = 0 \) an equation in which \( b \) is not found. If it be required, that upon taking the fluxions, \( a \) shall vanish; we must put the equation under this form \( \frac{y + b}{x} + a = 0 \), and then taking the fluxion, we find immediately \[ \frac{x \dot{y} - (y + b) \dot{x}}{x^2} = 0, \] an expression in which \( a \) is not found, and which by rejecting the divisor \( x^2 \) becomes \( y \dot{x} - w \dot{y} + b \dot{x} = 0 \), and these two forms of the fluxional equation are the very same as have been found in the last §. In the second example, viz. \( x^2 + 2ay - a^2 - b = 0 \), the equation has already the form suited to the elimination of \( b \); for the fluxional equation is \( x \dot{x} - ay = 0 \), but in order that \( a \) may vanish, we must resolve the equation with respect to \( a \), so as to give it this form \[ y = \sqrt{(x^2 + y^2 - b)} + a = 0; \] passing now to the fluxional equation, \( a \) disappears, and we have \[ \dot{y} \sqrt{(x^2 + y^2 - b)} = y \dot{x} - x \dot{y} = c. \] It is evident that we have only to reject the denominator to give the equation this form \[ \dot{y} \sqrt{(x^2 + y^2 - b)} = y \dot{x} - x \dot{y} = 0 \] the same as was found in the conclusion of last §. 175. From what has been now shewn we may infer that as from any proposed primitive equation we can deduce a fluxional equation that shall contain one constant quantity less than the primitive contains, so on the contrary any fluxional equation being given, its primitive equation may contain one constant quantity more than the fluxional equation, but it can contain only one, for no more than one constant quantity can be made to disappear by returning from the primitive to its fluxional equation. 176. The fluxional equation expressing the value of \( \frac{y}{x} \), which is derived from any primitive equation involving \( x \) and \( y \) a function of \( x \), may be called a fluxional equation of the first order; and as from this equation considered as a primitive, we may in like manner derive an equation that shall involve \( \frac{y}{x} \) (\$ 50.), this last may be called a fluxional equation of the second order, and the fluxional equation from which it is derived may be called its primitive equation of the first order, to distinguish it from the absolute primitive equation, from which all the others are conceived to be derived. A similar mode of definition is to be applied to the higher orders. 177. As any primitive equation and the fluxional equations of the first and second orders derived from it must all hold true at the same time, it is evident, that by means of the three equations, we may exterminate any two of the constant quantities contained in them that we please, and thus produce a fluxional equation of the second order that contains two constant quantities less than the primitive equation. There are however two other ways by which we may arrive at the very same fluxional equation of the second order. For as from the given primitive equation we may deduce two different fluxional equations of the first order, one of which shall contain one only of the two quantities to be eliminated, and the other shall contain the other quantity only, we may consider each of these equations in its turn as a primitive, and, by proceeding in the manner explained in § 173 and § 174, derive from it a fluxional equation, in which that particular constant quantity which remained in its primitive, but which was to be finally eliminated, shall not be found; thus, from each of these primitives we shall deduce the very same fluxional equation of the second order, that shall be freed from two of the constant quantities contained in the absolute primitive equation. Let us take for example the equation \[ x^2 - 2ay + b = 0; \] by proceeding as explained in § 173, or § 174, we find these two fluxional equations of the first order, \[ x \dot{x} - ay = 0, \quad (x^2 + b) \dot{y} - 2xy \dot{x} = 0, \] in the one of these the constant quantity \( a \) is wanting, and in the other \( b \) is wanting. Taking the first equation \( x \dot{x} - ay = 0 \), and proceeding as in § 50 (observing that \( x \) is constant) we find \( \dot{x} - ay = 0 \), if from this equation we now eliminate \( a \) by putting instead of it \( \frac{x}{y} \) (deduced from the equation \( x \dot{x} - ay = 0 \)) we find after proper reduction Now the fluent of \( \frac{m}{x} \) is \( m.l.x + c' \) (\$103.), and in like manner the fluent of \( \frac{n}{y} \) is \( n.l.y + c'' \), therefore \[ m.l.x + n.l.y + c' + c'' = 0, \] or, transposing \( c' + c'' \), and putting a single constant quantity for their sum, which, to be homogeneous with the logarithmic quantities, may be \( -\log_c \), or \( -l.c \), \[ m.l.x + n.l.y = l.c, \text{ or } l.(x^n) + l.(y^n) = l.c, \] or \( l.(x^n y^n) = l.c \), and hence \( x^n y^n = c \), which last is the primitive equation required. 178. When a primitive equation is homogeneous, that is, when the sum of the exponents of the variable quantities \( x \) and \( y \) is the same in each term, as in this example, \[ ax^2 + bx + dy + ey + fy = 0, \] or \( (ax + bx) + (dy + ey) = 0, \) in which the variable part of each term is of the first degree, as also in this equation \[ (ax^2 + bx + dy^2) + (ex^2 + fy + gy^2) = 0, \] in which the variable part of each term is of the second degree, such an equation may be always transformed into another which will admit of the variable quantities being separated. To take a particular example, let us suppose the equation to be \( x + y = n y x \), or \( (x - ny) x + y = 0 \). We assume \( y = x z \) (and the same assumption is to be made for any other homogeneous equation), then \( y = x z + x z \), thus the equation becomes transformed to \[ (x - nz) x + x z (z + x z) = 0, \] but as the terms of this equation have a common factor \( x \), by leaving out that factor, it becomes \[ (1 - nz) x + x z (z + x z) = 0, \] which also admits of being expressed thus \[ (1 - nz + z^2) x + x z z = 0, \] and, by division, \[ \frac{x}{x} + \frac{z z}{1 - nz + z^2} = 0, \] and taking the fluents \[ \int \frac{x}{x} + \int \frac{z z}{1 - nz + z^2} = C, \] where \( C \) denotes a constant quantity, or, since \( \int \frac{x}{x} = l.x, \) \[ l.x + \int \frac{z z}{1 - nz + z^2} = C, \]

FLY

Pages 824-829

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> order of insects, the distinguishing characteristic of which is, that their wings are transparent. By this they are distinguished from beetles, butterflies, grasshoppers, &c. Flies are subdivided into those which have four, and those which have two wings. Of those with four wings there are several genera <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> kinds; as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a>, the ichneumon, &c. Of those with two wings, there are likewise several kinds, as the gad-fly, gnat, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-fly, &c. For their classification and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, see Entomology. House Fly. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSCA">Musca</a>. Pelluculent Fly. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>. Fly, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> with leaden weights at its ends; or rather, a heavy wheel at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to the axis of a windlass, jack, or the like; by means of which, the force of the power, whatever it is, is not only preserved, but equally distributed in all parts of the revolution of the machine. See Mechanics. FLIES for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>. See Fishing Fly. Vegetable Fly, a curious natural production chiefly found in the West Indies. "Excepting that it has no wings, it resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRONE">drone</a> both in size and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> more than any other British insect. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May it buries itself in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and begins to vegetate. By the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the tree is arrived at its full growth, and resembles a coral branch; and is about three inches <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and bears several little pods, which dropping off become <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and from thence flies, like the British caterpillar." Such was the account originally given of this extraordinary production. But several boxes of these flies having been sent to Dr Hill for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, his report was this: "There is in Martinique a fungus of the clavaria kind, different in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> from those hitherto known. It produces foiboles from its sides; I call it therefore clavaria foibolifera. It grows on putrid animal bodies, as our fungus ex pede equino from the dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s hoof. The cicada is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Martinique; and in its nympha state, in which the old authors call it tettigometra, it buries itself under dead leaves to wait its change; and when the season is unfavourable, many perish. The seeds of the clavaria find a proper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> on this dead insect, and grow. The tettigometra is among the cicade in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>; the clavaria is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now known. This is the fact, and all the fact; though the untaught inhabitants suppose a fly to vegetate, and though there is a Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of the plant's growing into a trifoliate tree, and it has been figured with the creature <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> with this tree upon its back." See Edward's Gleanings of Natural History. Fly-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">Boat</a>, or Flight, a large flat-bottomed Dutch vessel, whose burden is generally from 690 to 1200 tons. It is distinguished by a very high stern, resembling a Gothic turret, and by very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> buttocks below. Fly-Catcher, in Zoology. See Muscipara. Venus's Fly-Trap, a kind of sensitive plant. See Dionaea Muscipula, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fly-Tree, in Natural History, a name given by the common people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> to a tree, whose leaves, they say, at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the year produce flies. On examining these leaves about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the time at which the flies used to be produced, there are found on them a sort of bags of a tough <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, of about the size of a filbert, and of a dusky greenish colour. On opening one of these bags with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, there is usually found a single full-grown fly, of the gnat kind, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small worms, which in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two more have wings, and fly away in the form of their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. The tree is of the mulberry kind, and its leaves are usually very largely stocked with these insect bags; and the generality of them are found to contain the insects in their worm state; when they become winged, they soon make their way out. The bags begin to appear when the leaves are young, and afterwards grow with them; but they never rumple the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> or injure its shape. They are of the kind of leaf-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, and partake in all respects, except size, of a species we have frequent on the large maple, or, as it is called, the sycamore.

FLYERS

Pages 829-830

the performers in a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> among the Mexicans, which was made on certain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> festivals, and is thus described by Clavigero in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of that people. "They fought in the woods for an extremely lofty tree, which, after stripping it of its branches and bark, they brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and fixed in the centre of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. They cased the point of the tree in a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, which, on account of some resemblance in its shape, the Spaniards called a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. From this cylinder hung four strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, which served to support a square frame. In the space between the cylinder and the frame, they fixed four other thick ropes, which they twisted as many times round the tree as there were revolutions to be made by the flyers. These ropes were drawn through four holes, made in the middle of the four planks of which the frame consisted. The four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> flyers, disguised like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, herons, and other birds, mounted the tree with great agility, by means of a rope which was laced about it from the ground up to the frame; from the frame they mounted one at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> successively upon the cylinder, and after having danced there a little, they tied themselves round with the ends of the ropes, which were drawn through the holes of the frame, and launching with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from it, began their flight with their wings expanded. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of their bodies put the frame and the cylinder in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; the frame by its revolutions gradually untwisted the cords by which the flyers swung; so that as the ropes lengthened, they made so much the greater circles in their flight. Whilst these four were <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, a fifth danced upon the cylinder, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> a little drum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> waving a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, without the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the danger he was in of being precipitated from such a height. The others who were upon the frame (10 or 12 persons generally mounted), as soon as they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the flyers in their last revolution; precipitated themselves by the same ropes, in order to reach the ground at the same time amidst the acclamations of the populace. Those who precipitated themselves in this manner by the ropes, that they might make a still greater display of their agility, Flyers, frequently passed from one rope to another, at that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> where, on account of the little distance between them, it was possible for them to do so. The most essential point of this performance consisted in proportioning so justly the height of the tree with the length of the ropes, that the flyers should reach the ground with 13 revolutions, to represent by such <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> their century of 52 years, composed in the manner we have already mentioned. This celebrated diversion is still in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; but no particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to the number of the revolutions of the flyers; as the frame is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> hexagonal or octagonal, and the flyers five or eight in number. In some places they put a rail round the frame, to prevent accidents, which were frequent after the conquest; as the Indians became much given to drinking, and used to mount the tree when intoxicated with wine or brandy, and were unable to keep their station on so great a height, which was usually 60 feet.

FLYING

Pages 830-831

the progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other winged animal, in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The parts of birds chiefly concerned in flying are the wings and tail; by the first, the bird sustains and wafts himself along; and by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, he is assisted, in ascending and descending, to keep his body poised and upright, and to obviate the vacillations thereof. It is by the size and strength of the pectoral muscles, that birds are so well disposed for quick, strong, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> flying. These muscles, which in men are scarcely a tenth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the muscles of the body, in birds exceed and outweigh all the other muscles taken together; upon which Mr Willoughby makes this reflection, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be possible for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to fly, his wings must be so contrived and adapted, that he may make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his legs, and not his arms, in managing them. The tail, Messrs Willoughby, Ray, and many others, imagine to be principally employed in steering and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the body in the air, as a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>; but Borelli has put it beyond all doubt, that this is the least use of it, which is chiefly to assist the bird in its ascent and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> in the air, and to obviate the vacillations of the body and wings; for as to turning to this or that side, it is performed by the wings and inclination of the body, and but very little by the help of the tail. The flying of a bird, in effect, is quite a different thing from the rowing of a vessel. Birds do not vibrate their wings towards the tail, as oars are struck towards the stern, but waft them downwards; nor does the tail of the bird cut the air at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> as the rudder does the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but is disposed horizontally, and preserves the same situation whatever way forever the bird turns. In effect, as a vessel is turned about on its centre of gravity to the right, by a brisk application of the oars to the left; so a bird, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the air with its right wing alone towards the tail, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn its fore part to the left. Thus pigeons changing their course to the left, would labour it with their right wing, keeping the other almost at rest. Birds of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> neck alter their course by the inclination of their head and neck; which altering the course of gravity, the bird will proceed in a new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The manner of FLYING is thus. The bird first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> his legs, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> with a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> from the ground; then opens and expands the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of his wings, so as to make a right line perpendicular to the sides of his body: thus the wings, with all the feathers therein, constitute one continued lamina. Being now raised a little above the horizon, and vibrating the wings with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force and velocity perpendicularly against the subject air, that fluid resists those succussions, both from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> inactivity and elasticity, by means of which the whole body of the bird is protruded. The resistance the air makes to the withdrawing of the wings, and consequently the progress of the bird, will be so much the greater, as the waft or stroke of the fan of the wing is longer; but as the force of the wing is continually diminished by this resistance, when the two forces continue to be in equilibrio, the bird will remain suspended in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; for the bird only ascends so long as the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of air the wing describes makes a resistance equal to the excess of the specific gravity of the bird above the air. If the air, therefore, be so rare as to give way with the same velocity as it is struck withal, there will be no resistance, and consequently the bird can never mount. Birds never fly upwards in a perpendicular line, but always in a parabola. In a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> ascent, the natural and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> tendency would oppose and destroy each other, so that the progress would be very slow. In a direct ascent they would aid one another, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> would be too precipitate. Artificial FLYING, that attempted by men, by the assistance of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. The art of flying has been attempted by several persons in all ages. The Leucadians, out of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, are reported to have had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of precipitating a man from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> cliff into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, first fixing feathers, variously expanded, round his body, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the fall. Francis <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, who lived near 500 years ago, not only affirms the art of flying possible, but affirms us, that he himself knew how to make an engine wherein a man fitting might be able to convey himself through the air like a bird; and further adds, that there was then one who had tried it with success. The secret consisted in a couple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> thin hollow <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> globes, exhausted of air; which being much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than air, would sustain a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> whereon a person might sit. Father Francisco Lana, in his Prodromo, proposes the same thing as his own thoughts. He computes, that a round vessel of plate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, 14 feet in diameter, weighing three ounces the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> foot, will only weigh 1848 ounces; whereas a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of air of the same bulk will weigh 2153½ ounces; so that the globe will not only be sustained in the air, but will carry with it a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of 373½ ounces; and by increasing the bulk of the globe, without increasing the thickness of the metal, he adds, a vessel might be made to carry a much greater weight.—But the fallacy is obvious: a globe of the dimensions he describes, Dr Hook shows, would not sustain the pressure of the air, but be crushed inwards. Besides, in whatever ratio the bulk of the globe were increased, in the same must the thickness of the metal, and consequently the weight be increased: so that there would be no advantage in such augmentation. See AEROSTATION. The same author describes an engine for flying, invented by the Sieur Beffier, a smith of Sable, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>. Vid. Philosoph. Collect. No. 1. The philosophers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the second's reign were mightily busied about this art. The famous Bishop Wilkins was so confident of success in it, that he says, he does not question but in future ages it will be as usual to hear a man call for his wings, when he is going a journey, as it is now to call for his boots. FLYING <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>. See BRIDGE. FLYING Fish, a name given to several <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fish, which, by means of long fins, can keep themselves out of the water for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. See EXOCETUS, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FLYING <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">Pinion</a>, is part of a clock, having a fly or fan whereby to gather air, and so <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> the rapidity of the clock's motion, when the weight descends in the striking part.

or Foe; an idol of the Chinese. He was originally worshipped in the Indies, and transported from thence into China, together with the fables with which the Indian books were filled. He is said to have performed most wonderful things, which the Chinese have described in several volumes, and represented by cuts. Set of Fo. See CHINA, No 104. Fo-Kien. See FORKIN.

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">Conic Sections</a>, is applied to certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in the parabola, ellipse, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a>, where the rays reflected from all parts of these curves concur and meet. among miners, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> containing 22 hundred and a half <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> the fodder is only 20 hundred weight. FOENUS NAUTICUM. Where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to a merchant to be employed in a beneficial trade, with condition to be repaid with extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> such voyage was safely performed, the agreement was sometimes called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> nauticum, sometimes ujura maritima. But as this gave an opening for furious and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> contracts, 19 Geo. II. c. 37, enacts, that all money lent on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTTOMRY">bottomry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at respondentia, on vessels bound to or from the East Indies, shall be expressly lent only upon the ship or merchandise; the lender to have the benefit of salvage, &c. Blackf. Com. ii. 459. Mol. de Jur. Mar. 361.

FOETUS

Pages 831-831

the young of all viviparous animals whilst in the womb, and of oviparous animals before being hatched: the name is transferred by botanists to the embryos of vegetables. Strictly, the name is applied to the young after it is perfectly formed; previous to which it is usually called EMBRYO. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> fetus are several peculiarities not to be found in the adult; some of them are as follow. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> of the navel string, which are continuations of the hypogastrics, are, after the birth, shrivelled up, and form the ligamenta umbilic. infer. 2. The veins of the navel string are formed by the union of all the venous branches in the placenta, and passing into the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> become the falciform ligament of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>. 3. The lungs, before being inflated with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> and heavy, but after one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> they become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and as it were spongy; and it may be noted here, that the notion of the lungs sinking in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> before the child breathes, and of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> after the reception of air, are no certain proofs that the child had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had not breathed, much less that it was murdered: for the uninflated lungs become specifically <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than water as soon as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in them; and this soon happens after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the child; besides, where the utmost care hath been taken to preserve the child, it hath breathed once or twice and then died. 4. The thymus gland is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in the fetus, but dwindles away in proportion as years advance. 5. The foramen ovale in the heart of a fetus, is generally closed in an adult.

FOG

Pages 831-831
or MIST, a meteor, consisting of gross vapours, floating near the surface of the earth. Mists, according to Lord Bacon, are imperfect condensations of the air, consisting of a large proportion of the air, and a small one of the aqueous vapour; and these happen in the winter, about the change of the weather from frost to thaw, or from thaw to frost; but in the summer, and in the spring, from the expansion of the dew. If the vapours which are raised plentifully from the earth and waters, either by the solar or subterraneous heat, do at their first entrance into the atmosphere meet with cold enough to condense them to a considerable degree, their specific gravity is by that means increased, and so they will be stopped from ascending; and either return back in form of dew or of drizzling rain, or remain suspended some time in the form of a fog. Vapours may be seen on the high grounds as well as the low, but more especially about marshy places. They are easily dissipated by the wind, as also by the heat of the sun. They continue longest in the lowest grounds, because these places contain most moisture, and are least exposed to the action of the wind. Hence we may easily conceive, that fogs are only low clouds, or clouds in the lowest region of the air; as clouds are no other than fogs raised on high. See CLOUD. When fogs stick, then the vapours are mixed with sulphureous exhalations, which smell so. Objects viewed through fogs appear larger and more remote than through the common air. Mr Boyle observes, that upon the coast of Coromandel, and most maritime parts of the East Indies, there are, notwithstanding the heat of the climate, annual fogs so thick, as to occasion people of other nations who reside there, and even the more tender sort of the natives, to keep their houses close shut up. Fogs are commonly strongly electrified, as appears

FOGAGE

Pages 831-832

in the forest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> grass not eaten up in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>.

FOIBLE

Pages 832-832

a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, frequently used also in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. It literally signifies weak; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is applied to the body of animals and the parts thereof, as foible reins, foible sight, &c., being derived from the Italian fievole, of the Latin flebilis, to be "lamented, pitied." But it is chiefly used with us substantively, to denote a defect <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flaw in a person or thing. Thus we say, Every person has his foible; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> secret consists in hiding it artfully: Princes are gained by flattery, that is their foible. The foible of young people is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; the foible of old men is avarice; the foible of the great and learned is vanity; the foible of women and girls, coquetry, or an affection of having gallants: You should know the forte and the foible of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> before you employ him: We should not let people perceive that we know their foible.

Pages 832-832

among glafs-grinders, a sheet of tin, with quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, hempen cloth, calico, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and all sorts of utensils wrought to the greatest perfection. From other countries they have cloves, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a> wood, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, coral, and many other things. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is Fou-tcheou Fou; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as others would have it written, Fucherofu. But as for Fokien, which most geographers make the capital, Grofier informs us there is no such <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

FOLARD

Pages 832-833
Charles, an eminent Frenchman, famous for his skill and knowledge in the military art, was born at Avignon in 1669, of a noble family, but not a rich one. He discovered an early turn for the sciences, and a strong passion for arms; which last was so inflamed by reading Caesar's Commentaries, that he enlisted at 16 years of age. His father got him off, and shut him in a monastery; but he made his escape in about two years after, and entered himself a second time in quality of cadet. His inclination for military affairs, and the great pains he took to accomplish himself in that way, recommended him to notice; and he was admitted into the friendship of the first-rate officers. M. de Vendome, who commanded in Italy in 1702, made him his aide-de-camp, having conceived the highest regard for him: and soon after sent him with part of his forces into Lombardy. He was entirely trusted by the commander of that army; and no measures were concerted, or steps taken, without consulting him. By pursuing his plans, many places were taken, and advantages gained; and such, in short, were his services, that he had a pension of 400 livres settled upon him, and was honoured with the cross of St Louis. He distinguished himself greatly, August 15, 1703, at the battle of Caffano; where he received a wound upon his left hand, which deprived him of the use of it ever after. It was at this battle that he conceived the first idea of the system of columns, which he afterwards prefixed to his Commentaries upon Polybius. The duke of Orleans sending De Vendome again into Italy in 1706, Folard had orders to throw himself into Modena to defend it against Eugene; where, though he acquitted himself with his usual skill, he was very near being assassinated. The description which he has given of the conduct and character of the governor of this town, may be found in his Treatise of the Defence of Places, and deserves to be read. He received a dangerous wound on the thigh at the battle of Malplaquet, and was some time after made prisoner by Prince Eugene. Being exchanged in 1711, he was made... made governor of Bourbourg. In 1714, he went to Malta, to assist in defending that island against the Turks. Upon his return to France, he embarked for Sweden, having a passionate desire to see Charles XII. He acquired the esteem and confidence of that famous general, who sent him to France to negotiate the re-establishment of James II. upon the throne of England; but that project being dropped, he returned to Sweden, followed Charles XII. in his expedition to Norway, and served under him at the siege of Fredrikshall, where that prince was killed, Dec. 11, 1718. Folard then returned to France; and made his last campaign in 1719, under the duke of Berwick, in quality of colonel. From that time he applied himself intensively to the study of the military art as far as it could be studied at home; and built his theories upon the foundation of his experience and observations on facts. He contracted an intimacy with Count Saxe, who, as he then declared, would one day prove a very great general. He was chosen a fellow of the Royal Society of London in 1749; and, in 1751, made a journey to Avignon, where he died in 1752, aged 83 years. He was the author of several works, the principal of which are; 1. Commentaries upon Polybius, in five volumes, 4to. 2. A Book of New Discoveries in War. 3. A Treatise concerning the Defence of Places, &c. in French. Those who would know more of this eminent soldier, may consult a French piece, entitled, Memoires pour servir à l'Histoire de M. le Chevalier de Folard, Ratibone, 1753, 12mo. FOLC.LANDS, (Sax.) copyhold lands so called in the time of the Saxons, as charter-lands were called boc-lands, Kitch. 174. Folkland was terra vulgi or popularis; the land of the vulgar people, who had no certain estate therein, but held the same, under the rents and services accustomed or agreed, at the will only of their lord the thane; and it was therefore not put in writing, but accounted praedium rusticum et ignobile. Spelm. of Feuds, c. 5.

FOLCMOTE

Pages 833-833
or FOLCMOTE, (Sax. Folcomote, i.e. conventus populis), is compounded of folk, popularis, and mote, or gemonie, consenire; and signified originally, as Sommer in his Saxon Dictionary informs us, a general assembly of the people, to confer of and order matters of the commonwealth. And Sir Henry Spelman says, the folcmote was a sort of annual parliament or convention of the bishops, thanes, aldermen, and freemen, upon every May day yearly; where the laymen were sworn to defend one another and the king, and to preserve the laws of the kingdom; and then consulted of the common safety. But Dr Brady infers from the laws of the Saxon kings of England, that it was an inferior court, held before the king's reeve or fleaward, every month, to do folk right, or compose smaller differences, from whence there lay appeal to the superior courts; Glo's. p. 48. Squire seems to think the folcmote not distinct from the fibremote, or common general meeting of the county. See his Angl. Sax. Gov. 155. n. Manwood mentions folcmote as a court holden in London, wherein all the folk and people of the city did complain of the mayor and aldermen, for misgovernment within the said city; and this word is still in use among the Londoners, and denotes celebrem ex tota civitate conveniunt. Stow's Survey. According to Ken- net, the folcmote was a common council of all the inhabitants of a city, town, or borough, convened often by found of bell, to the Mote Hall or House; or it was applied to a larger congress of all the freemen within a county, called the fibremote, where formerly all knights and military tenants did fealty to the king, and elected the annual sheriff on the 1st of October; till this popular election, to avoid tumults and riots, devolved to the king's nomination, anno 1315, 3 Edw. I. After which the city folkmote was swallowed up in a select committee or common council, and the county folkmote in the sheriff's town and assizes. The word folkmote was also used for any kind of popular or public meetings; as of all the tenants at the court leet, or court baron, in which signification it was of a less extent. Paroch. Antiq. 120.

FOLENGIO

Pages 833-833

THEOPHILUS, an Italian poet, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>. He was known also by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Merlin Cocciaye, a name which he gave to a poem, and which has been adopted ever since for all trifling performances of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, consisting of buffoonery, puns, anagrams, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and humour without good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. His poem was called The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MACARONI">Macaroni</a>, from an Italian cake of the same name, which is sweet to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, but has not the least alimentary virtue, on the contrary palls the appetite and clogs the stomach. These idle poems, however, became the reigning taste in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and in France; they gave birth to macaroni <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, and reaching England, to macaroni clubs; till, in the end, every thing insipid, contemptible, and ridiculous, in the character, dyes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> behaviour, of both men and women, is now summed up in the despicable appellation of a macaroni. Folengio died in 1544.

FOLIA

Pages 833-833

among botanists, particularly signify the leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> being expressed by the word petals. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>.

FOLIAGE

Pages 833-834

a cluster <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> assemblage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, leaves, branches, &c. Foliage, is particularly used for the representations of such flowers, leaves, branches, rinds, &c. whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, as are used for enrichments on capitals, friezes, pediments, &c. FOLIATING of LOOKING-GLASSES, the spreading the plates over, after they are polished, with quicksilver, &c. in order to reflect the image. It is performed thus: A thin blotting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> is spread on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> and sprinkled with fine chalk; and then a fine lamina or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of tin, called foil, is laid over the paper; upon this is poured <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, which is to be distributed equally over the leaf with a hares foot or cotton; over this is laid a clean paper, and over that the glass plate, which is pressed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the paper gently drawn out with the left: this being done, the plate is covered with a thicker paper, and loaded with a greater <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, that the superfluous mercury may be driven out and the tin adhere more closely to the glass. When it is dried, the weight is removed, and the looking-glass is complete. Some add an ounce of marcasite, melted by the fire; and, lest the mercury should evaporate in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, they pour it into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and when cooled, squeeze through a cloth, or through <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. Some add a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an ounce of tin and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the marcasite, that the glass may dry the sooner. Foliating of Globe looking-glasses, is done as follows: Folioting lows: Take five ounces of quicksilver, and one ounce of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>; of lead and tin, half an ounce each: first put the lead and tin into fusion, then put in the bismuth; and when you perceive that in fusion too, let it stand till it is almost cold, and pour the quicksilver into it: after this, take the glass globe, which must be very clean, and the inside free from dust: make a paper funnel, which put into the hole of the globe, as near the glass as you can, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a>, when you pour it in, may not splash and cause the glass to be full of spots; pour it in gently, and move it about, so that the amalgam may touch everywhere: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you find the amalgam begin to be curdly and fixed, then hold it over a gentle fire, and it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> easily flow again; and if you find the amalgam too thin, add a little more lead, tin, and bismuth to it. The finer and clearer your globe is, the better will the looking-glass be. Dr Shaw observes, that this operation has considerable advantages, as being performed in the cold; and that it is not attended with the danger of poisonous fumes from arsenic, or other unwholesome matters usually employed for this purpose: besides, how far it is applicable to the more commodious foliating of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> looking-glasses and other speculums, he thinks, may deserve to be considered.

FOLIO

Pages 834-834

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> books, denotes a page, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather both the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, these being expressed by the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and corresponding to each other. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOOK_KEEPING">Book-keeping</a>. Folio, among printers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a>, the largest form of books, when each sheet is so printed that it may be bound up in two leaves only. FOLIS. See FOLLIS.

FOLKES

Pages 834-834

MARTIN, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and antiquarian of considerable eminence, was born in Wellsminster in the year 1690. A Mr Cappel, once professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>, was his private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. When 17 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he successfully applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and when only twenty-three years of age he was chosen a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. His ingenious communications acquired him so much applause, that he was frequently chosen into its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. He was in habits of friendship with the illustrious Newton, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and by his influence was elected one of the vice-presidents in the year 1723. Mr Folkes became a candidate for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton; but the superior <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Sir Hans Sloane rendered his application ineffectual. In 1733 and the two subsequent years, his residence was for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with the view of improving himself in the knowledge of classical antiquities. To ascertain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and value of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> coins, he carefully consulted the cabinets of the curious; and on his return home he presented to the Antiquarian Society, of which he was a member, a dissertation on this subject. He read before the same learned body, a dissertation on the measurement of Trajan's and Antonine's pillar, together with other remains of antiquity. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his observations he presented to the Royal Society; and, in particular, "Remarks on the standard <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> preserved in the Capitol of Rome," and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of an ancient globe in the Farneian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. He visited <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1739, where he was received with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect, and honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the most eminent literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. This respect indeed he was entitled to by his unwearied application to many branches of knowledge which were both curious and useful. His valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled "A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of English silver coins, from the Norman Conquest to the present time, with their weights, intrinsic values, and some remarks upon the several pieces," was printed in the year 1745. Among the many honours conferred upon Mr Folkes, he was created <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws by both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and chosen president of the Antiquarian Society. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to furnish the Philosophical Transactions with many learned papers, till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> was stopped by a paralytic stroke, which terminated his useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the year 1754. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of very extensive knowledge and great accuracy; but the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> benefit to science which resulted from his labours, was his treatise on the intricate subject of coins, weights, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. His cabinet and library were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and valuable, and exposed to public <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> after his death. His private character was distinguished for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, generosity, and friendship.

FOLKESTONE

Pages 834-834

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-HYTHE">Hythe</a>, 72 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, appears to have been a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, from the Roman coins and British bricks often found in it. Stillingfleet and Tanner take it for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a> Tituli of Nennius. It was burnt by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Godwin, and by the French in the reign of Edward III. It had five churches now reduced to one. It is a member of the town and port of Dover; and has a weekly market and an annual fair. It is chiefly noted for the multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> boats that belong to its harbour, which are employed in the season in catching mackerel for London; to which they are carried by the mackerel boats of London and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARKING">Barking</a>. About Michaelmas, the Folkestone-barks, with others for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, go away to the Suffolk and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> coasts to catch herrings for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> and Lowestoft.—Folkestone gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Viscount to William Henry Bouverie, whose grandfather, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, was created in 1747. It has been observed of some hills in this neighbourhood, that they have visibly sunk and grown lower within <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.

FOLLICULUS

Pages 834-834

(from follis, "a bag"), a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of seed-vessel first mentioned by Linnaeus in his Deliciosa Plantae, generally consisting of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>, which opens from bottom to top on one side, and has no fixture for fastening <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> attaching the seeds within it. FOLLICULI are likewise defined by the same author to be small glandular vessels diffused with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which appear on the surface of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; as at the foot of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-milfoil, and on the leaves of aldrovanda. In the former the leaves in question are roundish, and furnished with an appearance like two horns; in the latter, pot-shaped, and semicircular.

FOLLIS

Pages 834-835
or Folis, anciently signified a little bag or purse; whence it came to be used for a sum of money, and very different sums were called by that name: thus the scholiast on the Basilics mentions a follis of copper which was worth but the 24th part of the millarenis; the gloriae nomiae, quoted by Gronovius and others, one of 125 millarenes, and another of 250 denarii, which was the ancient sestertium; and three different sums of eight, four, and two pounds of gold, were each each called follis. According to the account of the scholiast, the ounce of silver, which contained five milliareses of 60 in the pound, was worth 120 folles of copper. The gloffographer, describing a follis of 250 denarii, says it was equal to 312 pounds 6 ounces of copper; and as the denarius of that age was the 8th part of an ounce, an ounce of silver must have been worth 120 ounces of copper; and therefore the scholiast's follis was an ounce of copper, and equal to the gloffographer's nummus. But as Constantine's copper money weighed a quarter of a Roman ounce, the scholiast's follis and the gloffographer's nummus contained four of them, as the ancient nummus contained four asses.

FOLLY

Pages 835-835

according to Mr Locke, consists in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of false conclusions from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> principles; by which it is distinguished from madness, which draws just conclusions from false principles. But this seems too confined a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>; folly, in its most general acceptation, denoting a weakness of intellect <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, or some partial absurdity in sentiment or conduct.

FOMAHAUT

Pages 835-835
