in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the first magnitude in the constellation <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUARIUS">AQUARIUS</a>.

FOMENTATION

Pages 835-835

in Medicine, is a fluid externally applied, usually as warm as the patient can bear it, and in the following manner. Two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> cloths are dipped into the heated liquor, one of which is wrung as dry as the necessary speed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit, then immediately applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> affected; it lies on until the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> begins to go off, and the other is in readiness to apply at the instant in which the first is removed; thus these flannels are alternately applied, so as to keep the affected part constantly supplied with them warm. This is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 15 minutes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and repeated as occasion may require. Every intention of relaxing and soothing by fomentations may be answered as well by warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> alone as when the whole tribe of emollients are boiled in it; but when disinfectants or antiseptics are required, such ingredients must be called in as are adapted to that end. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat should never exceed that of producing a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heat produces effects very opposite to that intended by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of fomentation.

FONG-YANG

Pages 835-835

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of KIANG-NAN. It is situated on a mountain, which hangs over the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-YELLOW_RIVER"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">Yellow</a> river, and encloses with its walls several fertile little hills. Its jurisdiction is very extensive: for it comprehends 18 cities; five of which are of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and 13 of the third class. As this was the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Hong-you, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the preceding dynasty, this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of rendering it a famous and magnificent city, in order to make it the seat of empire. After having expelled the Western Tartars, who had taken possession of China, he transferred his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> hither, and named the city Fong yang; that is to say, "The Place of the Eagle's Splendour." His intention, as we have said, was to beautify and enlarge it; but the inequality of the ground, the scarcity of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and above all the vicinity of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, made him change his design. By the unanimous advice of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers, this prince established his court at NAN-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">KING</a>, a more beautiful and commodious place. When he had formed this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, a Fong-Yang flop was put to the intended works: the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> which was to have been enclosed by a triple wall, the walls of the city to which a circumference of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> leagues were assigned, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> that were begun, all were abandoned; and nothing was finished, but three monuments that still remain. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and magnificence of these sufficiently show what the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of this city would have been, had the emperor pursued his original design. The first is the tomb of the father of Hong-you, to decorate which no expense was spared; it is called Hoan-lin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Tomb. The second is a tower built in the middle of the city, which is of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form, and 100 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The third is a magnificent temple erected to the god Fo. At first it was only a pagod, to which Hong-you retired after having lost his parents, and where he was admitted as an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>; but having soon become weary of this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he enlisted with the chief of a band of banditti, who had revolted from the Tartars. As he was bold and enterprising the general made choice of him for his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; soon after he was declared his successor by the unanimous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the troops. This new chief feeling himself at the head of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> party, had the presumption to carry his views to the throne. The Tartars, informed of the progress of his arms, sent a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> into the field; but he surprised and attacked them with so much impetuosity, that they were obliged to fly; and, though they several times returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, they were still defeated, and at length driven entirely out of China. As soon as he mounted the throne, he caused the superb temple which we have mentioned to be raised out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to the Bonzes, who had received him in his distress, and assigned them a revenue sufficient for the maintenance of 300 persons, under a chief of their own feet, whom he constituted a mandarin, with power of governing them, independent of the officers of the city. This pagod was supported as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the preceding dynasty lasted; but that of the Eastern Tartars, which succeeded, suffered it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to ruin. FONG-Choui, the name of a ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> among the Chinese. See CHINA, No 105.

FONTAINBLEAU

Pages 836-836

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, and in the Gatinois, remarkable for its fine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which has been the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the kings of France used to lodge when they went a hunting. It was first embellished by Francis I, and every succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> has added something to it; so that it may now be called the finest <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the world. It stands in the midst of a forest, consisting of 26,424 arpents of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, each containing 100 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> perches, and each perch 18 feet. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 33. N. Lat. 40. 22.

FONTAINE

Pages 835-836

JOHN, a celebrated French poet, and one of the first-rate geniuses of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at Chateau-Thierry in Champagne, the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1621, of a good family. At the age of 19 he entered amongst the Oratorians, but quitted that order 18 months after. He was 22 years of age before he knew his own talents for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; but hearing an ode of Malherbe read, upon the assassination of Henry IV., he was so taken with admiration of it, that the poetical fire, which had before lain dormant within him, seemed to be enkindled from that of the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> poet. He applied himself to read, to meditate, to repeat, in fine to imitate, the works of Malherbe. The first essays of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> he confined to one of his relations who made him read the best Latin authors, Horace, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Terence, Quintilian, &c., and then the best Fontaine, best compositions in French and Italian. He applied himself likewise to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Greek authors, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and Plutarch. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> afterwards his parents made him marry a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general, a relation of the great Racine. This young lady, besides her very great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, was remarkable for the delicacy of her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and Fontaine never composed any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> without consulting her. But as her temper was none of the best, to avoid dissension, he separated himself from her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> as often as he well could. The famous duchess of Bouillon, niece to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarine, being exiled to Chateau-Thierry, took particular notice of Fontaine. Upon her recall, he followed her to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of one of his relations, he got a pension settled upon him. He met with great friends and protectors amongst the most distinguished persons of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, but Madame de la Sablière was the most particular. She took him to live at her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and it was then that Fontaine, divested of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> concerns, led a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> conformable to his disposition, and cultivated an acquaintance with all the great men of the age. It was his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, after he was fixed at Paris, to go every year, during the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September, to his native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Chateau-Thierry, and pay a visit to his wife, carrying with him Racine, Defreux, Chapelle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other celebrated writers. When he has sometimes gone thither alone by himself, he has come away without remembering even to call upon her; but seldom omitted setting some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his lands, by which means he squandered away a considerable fortune. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Madame de la Sablière, he was invited into England, particularly by Madame Mazarine, and by St Evremond, who promised him all the sweets and comforts of life; but the difficulty of learning the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and the liberality of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, prevented his voyage. About the end of the year 1692 he fell dangerously ill: and, as is customary upon these occasions in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he made a general confession of his whole life to P. Poquet, an Oratorian; and, before he received the sacrament, he sent for the gentlemen of the French Academy, and in their presence declared his sincere compunction for having composed his Tales; a work he could not reflect upon without the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> and detestation; promising that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it should please God to restore his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he would employ his talents only in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> upon matters of morality or piety. He survived this illness two years, living in the most exemplary and edifying manner, and died the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1695, being 74 years of age. When they stripped his body, they found next his skin a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> shirt; which gave room for the following <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the younger Racine: Et l'Auteur de Jaconde est orné d'un Cilice. Fontaine's character is remarkable for a simplicity, candour, and probity, seldom to be met with. He was of an obliging disposition; cultivating a real friendship with his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> poets and authors; and what is very rare, beloved and esteemed by them all. His conversation was neither gay nor brilliant, especially when he was not amongst his intimate friends. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> being invited to a dinner at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> general's, he ate a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, but did not speak. Rising up from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> very early, under <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of going to the academy, one of the company represented to him that it was not yet a proper time: "Well (says he), if it is not, I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> stay a little longer." He had one son by his wife in the year 1665. At the age of 14, he put him into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of M. de Harley, the first <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, recommending to him his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and fortune. It is said, that having been a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time without seeing him, he happened to meet him one day visiting, without recollecting him again, and mentioned to the company that he thought that young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had a good deal of wit and understanding. When they told him it was his own son, he answered in the most tranquil manner, "Ha! truly I am glad on't." An indifference, or rather an absence of mind, influenced his whole conduct, and rendered him often insensible to the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Madame de Bouillon going one morning to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him, abstracted in thought, sitting in an arbour; returning at night, she found him in the same place, and in the same attitude, although it was very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and had rained almost the whole day. He carried this simplicity so far, that he was scarcely sensible of the bad effects some of his writings might occasion, particularly his Tales. In a great fickleness, his confessors exhorting him to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and alms deeds: "As for alms deeds (replied Fontaine), I am not able, having nothing to give; but they are about publishing a new edition of my Tales, and the bookeller owes me a hundred copies; you shall have them to sell, and distribute their amount amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>." Another time P. Poquet exhorting him to repent of his faults, "If he has committed any (cried the nurse), I am sure it is more from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> than malice, for he has as much simplicity as an infant." One time having composed a tale, wherein he made a profane application of those words of the Gospel, "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, five talents thou didst deliver to me," he dedicated it, by a most ingenious prologue, to the celebrated Arnauld, telling him, it was to show to posterity the great esteem he had for the learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>. He was not sensible of the indecency of the dedication, and the profane application of the text, till Boileau and Racine reprehended it to him. He addressed another, by a dedication in the same manner, to the archbishop of Paris. His Fables are an immortal work, exceeding every thing in that kind, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the learned. People of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the oftener they read them, will find continually new beauties and charms, not to be met with elsewhere. The descendants of this great poet are exempted in France from all taxes and impositions; a privilege which the descendants of Soisson to this day think it an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to confirm to them.

FONTAINES

Pages 836-837
Peter Francis, a French critic, was born of a good family at Rouen in 1685. At 15, he entered into the society of the Jesuits; and at 30, quitted Fontaines quitted it, for the sake of returning to the world. He was a priest, and had a cure in Normandy; but left it, and was, as a man of wit and letters, some time with the cardinal d'Auvergne. Having excited some attention at Paris by certain critical productions, the Abbé Bignon in 1724 committed him the Journal des Savants. He acquitted himself well in this department, and was peaceably enjoying the applause of the public, when his enemies, whom by critical strictures in his Journal he had made such, formed an accusation against him of a most abominable crime, and procured him to be imprisoned. By the credit of powerful friends, he was set at liberty in 15 days; the magistrate of the police took upon himself the trouble of justifying him in a letter to the Abbé Bignon; and this letter having been read amidst his fellow labourers in the Journal, he was unanimously re-established in his former credit. This happened in 1725. But with whatever repute he might acquit himself in this Journal, frequent difficulties made him frequently abandon it. He laboured meanwhile in some new periodical works, from which he derived his greatest fame. In 1731, he began one under the title of Nouvelliste du Parnasse, ou Réflexions sur les Ouvrages nouveaux: but only proceeded to two volumes; the work having been suppressed by authority, from the incessant complaints of authors ridiculed therein. About three years after, in 1735, he obtained a new privilege for a periodical production, entitled, Observations sur les Ecrits Modernes; which, after continuing to 33 volumes, was suppressed again in 1743. Yet the year following, 1744, he published another weekly paper, called, Jugements sur les Ouvrages nouveaux, and proceeded to 11 volumes: the two last being done by other hands. In 1745, he was attacked with a disorder in the breast, which ended in a dropy that proved fatal in five weeks. "He was (says M. Freron) born a sentimental person; a philosopher in conduct as well as in principle; exempt from ambition; and of a noble firm spirit, which would not submit to sue for preferments or titles. In common conversation he appeared only a common man: but when subjects of literature, or any thing out of the ordinary way, were agitated, he discovered great force of imagination and wit." Besides the periodical works mentioned above, he was the author of many others: his biographer gives us no less than 17 articles; many of them critical, some historical, and some translations from English writers, chiefly from Pope, Swift, Fielding, &c. The Abbé de la Porte, published, in 1757, L'Esprit de l'Abbé des Fontaines, in 4 vols. 12mo; prefixed to which is the Life of Fontaines, a catalogue of his works, and another catalogue of writings against him.

FONTANELLA

Pages 837-837

in Anatomy, imports the quadrangular aperture found betwixt the os frontis and os sincipitis, in children <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> born; which is also called fossa pufatilis.

FONTARABIA

Pages 837-837

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>, and in the territory of Guipuscoa, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the sea shore, and on the river Bidafoa. It is small, but well fortified both by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art; and has a good harbour, though dry at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is built in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, on the declivity of a hill, and surrounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> side by the lofty Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It is a very important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, being accounted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of Spain on that side. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. i. 43. N. Lat. 43. 23.

FONTENELLE

Pages 837-838

Bernard le Bovier de, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters, born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in 1657, the most universal genius of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV, in the estimation of Voltaire. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Jesuits at Rouen, where the quickness of his parts became conspicuous at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. He was capable of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> Latin verses when only 13, which were deemed worthy of being published. He studied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> at the desire of his father; but as he lost the very first cause in which he was employed as an advocate, he became disgusted with his profession, and devoted himself entirely to literature and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He composed a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the operas of Pyche and Belleroche, which were printed under the name of his uncle Thomas Corneille. He wrote a tragedy called Aspar; but as it did not succeed, he consigned the manuscript to the flames, and never afterwards attempted that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. His Dialogues of the dead were published in the year 1683, which were well received, as a specimen of elegant composition, combining morality with the charms of literature. His Lettres du Chevalier d'Her, published in 1685 without his name, discovered much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and ingenuity, but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> no small share of affectation. His Entretiens sur la Pluralité des Mondes, has been regarded as one of his ablest performances, combining science and philosophy with vivacity and humour, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> which may be said to belong almost exclusively to the French. It was perused by all, and translated into several foreign languages. In his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">Oracles</a>, he supported the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that oracles were forgeries, in opposition to those who contended that they were supernatural operations of evil spirits, put to silence by the appearing of Christ, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> he exposed himself to clerical animadversion. His Pastoral Poems appeared in the year 1688, with a discourse on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the eclogue, which were very much admired for their delicacy of sentiment, as was also his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> of Thetis and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a>; but his Æneas and Lavinia was not so successful. In the year 1699, Fontenelle was chosen secretary of the Academy of Sciences, which office he held during the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> period of 42 years. He published a volume annually of the history of that learned body, filled with analyses of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, and eulogiums on deceased members. As a poet, he did not rise above elegance and ingenuity; as a man of science, he rather excelled in throwing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on the inventions of others, than in discovering any new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> himself, and as a general writer, he united <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> with the delicacy and refinement of a man of wit. He studied his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> as much as most men, but he never sacrificed to the promotion of it, the duties of a man of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and virtue. He had many friends, and towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, scarcely a single enemy. He was never married, and for a man of letters he acquired considerable influence. Although of a delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he reached the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> age of 90 without any complaint but dulness of hearing. He died on the 9th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1757, being almost a hundred years of age. When asked by a certain person Fontenelle person how he could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> so easily through the world, he replied, "by virtue of these two axioms; All is possible, and every one is in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>."

FONTENOY

Pages 838-838

a village of France, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, remarkable for a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought there in 841, between the Germans and the French, in which were killed above 100,000 men; and the Germans were defeated. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 48. N. Lat. 47. 28.

FONTEVRAUD

Pages 838-838
or **FRONTENVAUX**, Order of, in ecclesiastical history, a religious order instituted about the latter end of the 11th century, and taken under the protection of the holy see by Pope Pascal II. in 1106, confirmed by a bull in 1113, and invested by his successors with very extraordinary privileges. The chief of this order is a female, who is appointed to inspect both the monks and nuns. The order was divided into four provinces, which were those of France, Aquitaine, Auvergne, and Bretagne, in each of which they had formerly several priories.

FONTICULUS

Pages 838-838
or **FONTANELLA**, in Surgery, an illuse, feton, or small ulcer, made in various parts of the body, in order to excite irritation, or to produce the discharge of matter.

FONTINALIA

Pages 838-838
or **FONTANALIA**, in antiquity, a religious feast held among the Romans in honour of the deities who presided over fountains or springs. Varro observes, that it was the custom to visit the wells on those days, and to cast crowns into fountains. Scaliger, in his conjectures on Varro, takes this not to be a feast of fountains in general, as Festus infinuates, but of the fountain which had a temple at Rome, near the Porta Capena, called also Porta Fontinalis: he adds, that it is of this fountain Cicero speaks in his second book De Legibus. The Fontinalia were held on the 13th of October.

FONTINALIS

Pages 838-838
Water-moss, a genus of plants belonging to the cryptogamia clas, and to the order of mucil. See Botany Index.

FOOD

Pages 838-843

in the most extensive signification of the word implies whatever aliments are taken into the body, whether <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fluid; but in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, it is generally used to signify only the solid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our aliment. We are told, that in the first ages men lived upon acorns, berries, and such <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> spontaneously produces; then they proceeded to eat the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of wild animals taken in hunting: But their numbers decreasing and mankind multiplying, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> taught them the art of cultivating the ground, to sow corn, &c. By and by they began to assign to each other, by general consent, portions of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> to produce them their supply of vegetables; after this, reason suggested the expedient of domesticating certain animals, both to assist them in their labours and supply them with food. Hogs were the first animals of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> kind that appeared upon their tables; they held it to be ungrateful to devour the beasts that assisted them in their labours.—When they began to make a free <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of domestic animals, they roasted them only: <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> was a refinement in cookery which for ages they were strangers to; and fish living in an element men were unused to, were not eaten, till they grew somewhat civilized. Menelaus complains, in the Odyssey, that they had been constrained to feed upon them. The most remarkable distinction of foods, in a medical view, is into those which are already assimilated into the animal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and such as are not. Of the first kind are animal substances in general; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not entirely similar, are nearly so, to our nature. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> comprehends vegetables, which are much more difficultly assimilated. But as the nourishment of all animals, even those which live on other animals, can be traced originally to the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, it is plain, that the principle of all nourishment is in vegetables. Though there is perhaps no vegetable which does not afford nourishment to some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of animals or the Med. able distinction is to be made. Those vegetables which are of a mild, bland, agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, are proper nourishment; while those of an acid, bitter, and nauseous nature, are improper. We use, indeed, several acid substances as food; but the mild, and agreeable, are in the largest proportion in almost every vegetable. Such as are very acid, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of an aromatic nature, are not used as food, but as spices or condiments, which answer the purposes of medicines rather than any thing else. Sometimes, indeed, acid and bitter vegetables seem to be admitted as food. Thus celeri and endive are used in common food, though both are substances of considerable acrimony; but it must be observed, that when we use them, they are previously blanched, which almost totally destroys their acrimony. Or if we employ other acid substances, we generally, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, deprive them of their acrimony by boiling. In different countries, the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> grow with different degrees of acrimony. Thus garlic here seldom enters our food; but in the southern countries, where the plants grow more mild, they are frequently used for that purpose. The plant which furnishes <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CASSAVA">cassava</a>, being very acrimonious, and even poisonous, in its recent state, affords an instance of the necessity of preparing acid substances even in the hot countries; and there are other plants, such as arum root, which are so exceedingly acrimonious in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, that they cannot be swallowed with safety; yet, when deprived of that acrimony, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> afford good nourishment. The most remarkable properties of different vegetable substances as food, are taken notice of under their different names: here we shall only compare vegetable foods in general with those of the animal kind. 1. In the Stomach, they differ remarkably, in that the vegetables always have a tendency to acidity, while animal... animal food of all kinds rather tends to alkaleficiency and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. Some animal foods, indeed, turn manifestly acid before they putrify; and it has been asserted, that some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of acelfency takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in every kind of animal food before digestion. This acelfency of animal food, however, never comes to any morbid degree, but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> is always on the side of putrefaction. The acelfency of vegetables is more frequent, and ought to be more attended to, than the alkaleficiency of animal food; which last, even in weak stomachs, is seldom felt; while acelfency greatly affects both the stomach and system. With regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of solution:—Heaviness, as it is called, is seldom felt from vegetables, except from tough farinaceous paste, or the most viscid substances; while the heaviness of animal food is more frequently noticed, especially when in any great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. Difficulty of solution does not depend so much on firmness of texture (as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, from fish of all kinds, is more oppressed than from firmer substances), as on viscidity; and hence it is more frequent in animal food, especially in the younger animals. With regard to mixture:—There is no instance of difficult mixture in vegetables, except in vegetable oils; while animal foods, from both viscidity and oiliness, especially the fatter meats, are refractory in this respect. Perhaps the difference of animal and vegetable foods might be referred to this head of mixture. For vegetable food continues <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the stomach, giving little stimulus: Now the system is affected in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of this stimulus, which is incomparably greater from the animal viscid oily food, than from the vegetable, firmer, and more aqueous. However, there are certain applications to the stomach, which have a tendency to bring on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> fit of fever, independent of stimulus, merely by their refrigeration: and this often arises from vegetables; as we see, in those hot countries where intermittents prevail, they are often induced from a surfeit of vegetable than of animal food. A <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this is, that when one is recovering of an intermittent, there is nothing more apt to cause a relapse than cold food, especially if taken on those days when the fit should return, and particularly acelfcent, fermentable vegetables, as salads, melons, cucumbers, &c., acido-dulces, &c., which, according to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a>, are the most frequent causes of epidemics; therefore, when an intermittent is to be avoided, we then vegetable diet, and give animal foods, although their stimulus be greater. II In the Intestines. When the putrefaction of animal food has gone too far, it produces an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> stimulus, causing diarrhoea, dysentery, &c. But these effects are but rare; whereas from vegetable food and its acid, which, united with the bile, proves a pretty strong stimulus, they more frequently occur; but luckily are of less <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, if the refrigeration is not very great. In the autumnal season, when there is a tendency to dysentery, if it is observed that eating of fruits brings it on, it is rather to be ascribed to their cooling than stimulating the intestines. As to stool:—Wherever neither putrefaction nor acidity has gone a great length, animal food keeps the belly more regular. Vegetable food gives a greater proportion of succulent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and, when excreted by the stomach and intestines, is more apt to stagnate, and produce slow belly and costiveness, than animal stimulating food; which, before it comes to the great guts, where stoppage is made, has obtained a putrefactive tendency, and gives a proper stimulus: and thus those who are coltive from the use of vegetables; when they have recourse to animal food are in this respect better. III. In the blood-vessels. They both give a blood of the same kind, but of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Animal food gives it in greater quantity, being in great part, as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> is, convertible in succum et sanguinem, and of easy digestion; whereas vegetable is more watery, and contains a portion of unconquerable feline matter, which causes it to be thrown out of the body by some excretion. Animal food affords a more dense stimulating <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> blood than vegetable; stretching and causing a great resistance in the solids, and again exciting their stronger <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. It has been supposed that acelfency of vegetable food is carried into the blood-vessels, and there exerts its effects; but the tendency of animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> is so strong to alkaleficiency, that the existence of an acid acrimony in the blood seems very improbable. Animal food alone will soon produce an alkalefcent acrimony; and if a person who lives entirely on vegetables were to take no food for a few days, his acrimony would be alkalefcent. IV. We are next to take notice of the quantity of nutriment these different foods afford. Nutriment is of two kinds: the first repairs the waste of the solid fibres; the other supplies certain fluids, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Now, as animal food is easier converted, and also retained longer in the system, and as it contains a greater proportion of oil, it will afford both kinds of nutriment more copiously than vegetables. V. Lastly, As to the different degrees of perspirability of these foods. This is not yet properly determined. Sanctarius constantly speaks of mutton as the most perspirable of all food, and of vegetables as checking perspiration. This is a consequence of the different stimulus those foods give to the stomach, so that persons who live on vegetables have not their perspiration so suddenly excited. In time of digestion, perspiration is stopped from whatever food, much more so from cooling vegetables. Another reason why vegetables are less perspirable is, because their aqueo-feline juices determine them to go off by urine, while the more perfectly mixed animal food is more equally diffused over the system, and so goes off by perspiration. Hence Sanctarius's accounts may be understood; for vegetable aliment is not longer retained in the body, but mostly takes the course of the kidneys. Both are equally perspirable in this respect, viz., that a person living on either returns once a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to his usual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and if we consider the little nourishment of vegetables, and the great tendency of animal food to corpulence, we must allow that vegetable is more quickly perspired than animal food. As to the question, Whether man was originally designed for animal or vegetable food, see the article Carnivorous. With regard to the effects of these foods on men, it must be observed, that there are no persons who live entirely on vegetables. The Pythagoreans themselves ate <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and those who do so mostly, as these Pythagoreans, are weakly, sickly, and meagre, labouring Food. ing under a constant diarrhoea and several other dif- ficulties. None of the hardy, robust, live on these; but chiefly such as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a livelihood by the exertion of their mental faculties, as (in the East Indies) factors and brokers; and this method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is now confined to the hot climates, where vegetable diet, without incon- venience, may be carried to great excess. Though it be granted, therefore, that man is intended to live on these different foods prolifically, yet the vegetable should be in very great proportion. Thus the Lap- landers are said to live entirely on animal food: but this is contradicted by the best accounts; for Linnaeus says, that besides milk, which they take four, to ob- viate the bad effects of animal food, they use also cala- menyantes, and many other plants, copiously. So there is no instance of any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> living entirely either on vegetable or animal food, though there are indeed some who live particularly on one or other in the great- est proportion. In the cold countries, e.g. the inhabi- tants live chiefly on animal food, on account of the rigour of the season, their smaller perspiration, and little tendency to putrefaction. Of more importance, however, is the following than the former question, viz. In what proportion animal and vegetable food ought to be mixed? 1. Animal food certainly gives most strength to the system. It is a known aphorism of Sanctarius, that "pondus addit robur;" which may be explained from the implication of the blood-vessels, and giving a proper de- gree of tension for the performance of strong oscillations. Now animal food not only goes a greater way in supplying fluid, but also gives the fluid more dense and elastic. The art of giving the utmost strength to the system is best understood by those who breed fighting cocks. These people raise the cocks to a certain weight, which must bear a certain proportion to the other parts of the system, and which at the same time is so nicely proportioned, as that, on losing a few ounces of it, their strength is very considerably im- paired. Dr Robinson of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> has observed, that the force and weight of the system ought to be deter- mined by the largeness of the heart, and its proportion to the system: for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heart will give large blood- vessels, while at the same time the viscera are less, par- ticularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>; which last being increased in size, a greater quantity of fluid is determined into the cel- lular texture, and less into the sanguineous system. Hence we see how animal food gives strength, by fill- ing the sanguineous vessels. What pains we now be- low on cocks, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> did on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol2.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a>, by proper nourishment bringing them to a great degree of strength and agility. It is said that men were at first fed on figs, a proof of which we have from their nutri- tious quality: however, in this respect they were soon found to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of animal food; and thus we see, that men, in some measure, will <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in proportion to the quality of their food. The English labour more than the Scots; and wherever men are exposed to hard labour, their food should be animal.—Animal food, although it gives strength, yet loads the body; and Hip- pocrates long ago observed, that the athletic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, by a small increase, was exposed to the greatest haz- ards. Hence it is only proper for bodily labours, and entirely improper for mental exercises; for who- ever would keep his mind acute and penetrating, will exceed rather on the side of vegetable food. Even the body is oppressed with animal food; a full <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> al- ways produces dullness, laziness, and yawning; and hence the feeding of gamesters, whose mind must be ready to take advantage, is always performed by avoiding a large quantity of animal food. Further, With regard to the strength of the body, animal food, in the first stage of life, is hardly necessary to give strength; in manhood, when we are exposed to active scenes, it is more allowable; and even in the decline of life, some proportion of it is necessary to keep the body in vigour. There are some diseases which come on in the decay of life, at least are aggravated by it; among these the most remarkable is the gout. This, when it is in the system, and does not appear with in- flammation in the extremities, has pernicious effects there, attacking the lungs, stomach, head, &c. Now, to determine this to the extremities, a large proportion of animal food is necessary, especially as the person is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> incapable of much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. Animal food, although it gives strength, is yet of many hazards to the system, as it produces plethora and all its consequences. As a stimulus to the stomach and to the whole system, it excites fever, urges the circula- tion, and promotes the perspiration. The system, however, by the repetition of these stimuli, is soon worn out; and a man who has early used the athletic diet, is either early carried off by inflammatory diseases, or, if he takes exercise sufficient to render that diet salutary, such an accumulation is made of putrefied fluids, as in his after life lays a foundation for the most in- terested chronic distempers. Therefore it is to be ques- tioned, whether we should define this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of bo- dily strength, with all the inconveniences and dangers attending it. Those who are chiefly employed in mental researches, and not exposed to too much bodily labour, should always avoid an excess of animal food. There is a disease which seems to require animal food, viz. the hysterical or hypochondriac; and which appears to be very much akin to the gout, affecting the alimentary canal. All people affected with this disease are much disposed to accretion: which sometimes goes so far, that no other vegetable but <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> can be taken in, without occasioning the worst consequences. Here then we are obliged to prescribe an animal diet, even to those of very weak organs; for it generally obviates the symptoms. However, several instances of fever in ex- cess have been produced by a long-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> use of this diet, which it is always unlucky to be obliged to pre- scribe; and when it is absolutely necessary to prescribe, it should be joined with as much of the vegetable as possible, and when a cure is performed we should gradu- ally recur to that again. 2. Next, let us consider the vegetable diet. The chief inconvenience of this is difficulty of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSIMILATION">assimilation</a>; which, however, in the vigorous and exercised, will not be li- able to occur. In warm climates, the assimilation of ve- getable aliment is more easy, so that there it may be more used, and when joined to exercise gives a pretty tolerable degree of strength and vigour; and though the general rule be in favour of animal diet, for giving strength, yet there are many instances of its being re- markably produced from vegetable. Vegetable diet has this advantage, that it whets the appetite, and that we can hardly suffer from a full meal of it. Besides the disorders it is liable to produce in the prime vize, and its falling short to give strength, there seem to be no bad consequences it can produce in the blood vessels; for there is no instance where its peculiar acrimony was ever carried there, and it is certainly less putrefiable than animal food; nor, without the utmost indolence, and a sharp appetite, does it give plethora, or any of its consequences: so that we cannot here but conclude, that a large proportion of vegetable food is useful for the generality of mankind. There is no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> more dangerous, or more common, than the neglect of bread: for it is the safest of vegetable aliments, and the best corrector of animal food; and, by a large proportion of this alone, its bad consequences, when used in a hypochondriac state, have been obviated. The French apparently have as much animal food on their tables as the Britihs; and yet, by a greater use of bread and the dried acid fruits, its bad effects are prevented; and therefore bread should be particularly used by the English, as they are voracious of animal food. Vegetable food is not only necessary to secure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, but long life: and, as we have said, in infancy and youth we should be confined to it mostly: in manhood, and decay of life, use animal food; and, near the end, vegetable again. There is another question much agitated, viz. What are the effects of variety in food? Is it necessary and allowable, or universally hurtful? Variety of a certain kind seems necessary; as vegetable and animal foods have their mutual advantages, tending to correct each other. Another variety, which is very proper, is that of liquid and solid food, which should be so managed as to temper each other; and liquid food, especially of the vegetable kind, is too ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> off before it is properly assimilated, while solid food makes a long stay. But this does not properly belong to the question, whether variety of the same kind is necessary or proper, as in animal foods, beef, fish, fowl, &c. It does not appear that there is any inconvenience arising from this mixture, or difficulty of assimilation, provided a moderate quantity be taken. When any inconvenience does arise, it probably proceeds from this, that one of the particular substances in the mixture, when taken by itself would produce the same effects; and indeed it would appear that this effect is not heightened by the mixture, but properly obviated by it. There are few exceptions to this, if any, e.g. taking a large proportion of acetic substances with milk. The coldness &c. acidity, flatulency, &c. may appear; and it is possible that the coagulum, from the aceticity of the vegetables, being somewhat stronger induced, may give occasion to too long retention in the stomach, and to acidity in too great degree. Again, the mixture of fish and milk often occasions inconveniences. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of this is difficult, though, from universal consent, it must certainly be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>. Can we suppose that fish gives occasion to such a coagulum as rumen? If it does so, it may produce bad effects. Besides, fishes approach somewhat to vegetables, in giving little stimulus; and are accused of the same bad effects as these, viz. bringing on the cold fit of fever. Thus much may be said for variety. But it also has its disadvantages, provoking to gluttony; this, and the art of cookery, making men take in more than they properly can digest; and hence, perhaps very justly, physicians have universally almost preferred simplicity of diet; for, in spite of rules, man's eating will only be measured by his appetite, and satiety is sooner produced by one than by many substances. But this is so far from being an argument against variety, that it is one for it, as the only way of avoiding a full meal of animal food, and its bad effects, is by presenting a quantity of vegetables. Another <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of preventing the bad effects of animal food, is to take a large proportion of liquid; and hence the bad effects of animal food are less felt in Scotland, on account of their drinking much with it, and using broths, which are at once excellent correctors of animal food and preventives of gluttony. With regard to the difference between ANIMAL FOODS, properly so called, the first regards their solubility, depending on a lax or firm texture of their different kinds. I. SOLUBILITY of animal food seems to deserve less <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> than is commonly imagined; for there are many instances of persons of a weak stomach, incapable of breaking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the texture of vegetables, or even of dissolving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pudding, to whom hung beef, or a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">ham</a>, was very grateful and easily digested. None of the theories given for the solution of animal food in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> stomach seem to have explained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> sufficiently. Long ago has been discarded the supposition of an active corrosive menstrum there; and also the doctrine of trituration, for which, indeed there seems no mechanism in the human body; and, till lately, physicians commonly agreed with Boerhaave in supposing nothing more to be necessary than a watery menstrum, moderate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and frequent agitation. This will account for solution in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, but not entirely. Let us try to imitate it out of the body with the same circumstances, and in ten times the time in which the food is dissolved in the stomach we shall not be able to bring about the same changes. Take the coagulated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, which almost every body can easily digest, and yet no artifice shall be able to dissolve it. Hence, then, we are led to seek another cause for solution, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>; a notion, indeed, formerly embraced, but on the introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, industriously banished, with every other supposition of that process taking place at all in the animal economy. Many of the ancients imagined this fermentation to be putrefactive. But this we deny, as an acid is produced; though hence the fermentation might be reckoned the vinous, which, however, seems always to be morbid. Neither, indeed, is the fermentation purely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACETOUS">acetous</a>, but modified by putrefaction; for Pringle has observed, that animal matters raise and even excite the acetous process. The fermentation, then, in the stomach is of a mixed nature, between the acetous and putrefactive, mutually modifying each other; though, indeed, in the intestines, somewhat of the putrefactive seems to take place, as may be observed from the state of the feces broke down, and from the little disposition of such substances to be so, which are not liable to the putrefactive process, as the firmer parts of vegetables, &c. Upon this view solution seems to be extremely easy, and those substances to be most easily broke down which which are most subject to putrefaction. See ANATOMY, and GASTRIC Juice. But solution also depends on other circumstances, and hence requires a more particular regard. 1. There is a difference of solubility with respect to the manducation of animal food, for which bread is extremely necessary, in order to keep the more slippery parts in the mouth till they be properly comminuted. From want of proper manducation persons are subject to eructations; and this more frequently from the firm vegetable foods, as apples, almonds, &c., than from the animal, though, indeed, even from animal food, very tendinous, or swallowed in unbroken masses, such sometimes occur. Manducation is so much connected with solution, that some, from imperfectly performing that, are obliged to belch up their food, remanducate it, and swallow it again before the stomach can dissolve it, or proper nourishment be extracted. Another proof of our regard to solubility, is our rejecting the firmer parts of animal food, as bull beef, and generally carnivorous animals. 2. Its effects with regard to solubility seem also to be the foundation of our choice between fat and lean, young and old meats. In the lean although perhaps a single <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a> might be sufficiently tender, yet these, when collected in fasciculi, are very firm and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and of difficult solution; whereas in the fat there is a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vessels, a greater quantity of juice, more interposition of cellular substance, and consequently more solubility. Again, in young animals, there is probably the same number of fibres as in the older, but these more connected; whereas, in the older, the growth depending on the separation of these, and the increase of vessels and cellular substance, the texture is less firm and more soluble; which qualities, with regard to the stomach, are at that time too increased, by the increased alkalescence of the animal. To this also may be referred our choice of castrated animals, viz. on account of their disposition to fatten after the operation. 3. It is with a view to the solubility, that we make a choice between meats recently killed, and those which have been kept for some time. As soon as meat is killed, the putrefactive process begins; which commonly we allow to proceed for a little, as that process is the most effectual breaker down of animal matters, and a great assistance to solution. The length of time during which meat ought to be kept, is proportioned to the meat's tendency to undergo the putrid fermentation, and the degree of those circumstances which favour it: Thus, in the torrid zone, where meat cannot be kept above four or five hours, it is used much more recent than in these northern climates. 4. Boiled or roasted meats create a difference of solution. By boiling we extract the juices interposed between the fibres, approximate them more to each other, and render them of more difficult solubility; which is increased too by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of the juices, which are much more alkalescent than the fibres: but when we want to avoid the stimulus of alkalescent food, and the quick solution, as in some cases of diffidence, the roasted is not to be chosen. Of roasted meats it may be asked, which are more proper, those which are most or least roasted? That which is least done is certainly the most soluble: even raw meats are more soluble than drested, as Dr Cullen was informed by a person who from necessity was obliged, for some time, to eat such. But at the same time that meats little done are very soluble, they are very alkalescent; so that, wherever we want to avoid alkalescence in the prime via, the most roasted meats should be chosen. Those who throw away the broths of boiled meat do very improperly; for, besides their supplying a fluid, from their greater alkalescence they increase the solubility of the meat. Here we shall observe, that pure blood has been thought insoluble. Undoubtedly it is very nutritious; and though out of the body, like the white of eggs, it seems very insoluble, yet, like that too, in the body it is commonly easily digested. Moses very properly forbade it the Israelites, as in warm countries it is highly alkalescent; and even here, when it was used in great quantity, the scurvy was more frequent; but to a moderate use of it, in these climates, no such objection takes place. 5. Solubility is varied from another source, viz. viscosity of the juice of aliment. Young animals, then, appear more soluble than old, not only on account of the compaction and firmness of texture in the latter, but also their greater viscosity of juice. And nothing is more common, than to be longer oppressed from a full meal of veal, than from the same quantity of beef, &c. Upon account, too, of their greater viscosity of juice, are the tendinous and ligamentous parts of animals longer retained than the purely muscular, as well as on account of their firmness of texture. Even fishes, whose muscular parts are exceedingly tender, are, on account of their gluey viscosity, longer of solution in the stomach. And eggs, too, which are exceedingly nourishing, have the same effect, and cannot be taken in great quantity: For the stomach is peculiarly sensible to gelatinous substances; and by this means has nature perhaps taught us, as it were by a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, to limit ourselves in the quantity of such nutritive substances. 6. With regard to solution, we must take in the oils of animal food; which, when tolerably pure, are the least putrefactive part of it, and, by diminishing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of the fibres, render them more soluble. On this last account is the lean of fat meat more easily dissolved than other lean. But when the meat is exposed to much heat, this oil is separated, leaving the solid parts less easily soluble, and becoming itself empyreumatic, rancid, and of difficult mixture in the stomach. Fried meats, from the reasons now given, and baked meats, for the same, as well as for the tenacity of the paste, are preparations which diminish the solubility of the food. From what has been said, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of food by fattening it, and keeping it for some time after being killed, although it may administer to gluttony, will yet, it must be confessed, increase the solution of the food. II. The second difference of animal food is with regard to ALKALESCENCE. Of this we have taken a little notice already under the head of Solubility. 1. From their too great alkalescence we commonly avoid the carnivorous animals, and the ferc; and choose rather the granivorous. Some birds, indeed, which live on insects, are admitted into our food; but no man, without nausea, can live upon these alone for any length of time. Fishes, too, are an exception to this rule, living almost universally on each other. But in these the alkalineficiency does not proceed so far; whether from the viscidity of their juice, their want of heat, or some peculiarity in their economy, is not easy to determine. 2. Alkalineficiency is determined by difference of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The older animals are always more alkalineficient than the young, from their continual progress to putrefaction. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a> always found in his endeavours to extract an acid from human blood, that more was obtained from the young than from the old animals. 3. A third circumstance which varies the alkalineficiency of the food, is the wildness or tamehood of the animal; and this again seems to depend on its exercise. Dr Cullen knew a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who was fond of cats for food; but he always used to feed them on vegetable food, and kept them from exercise; and in the same manner did the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> rear up their rats, when intended for food. In the same way the flesh of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a> and the hen seems to be much the same; only, from its being more on the wing, the one is more alkalineficient than the other. Again, tame animals are commonly used without their blood; whereas the wild are commonly killed in their blood, and upon that account, as well as their greater exercise, are more alkalineficient. 4. The alkalineficiency of food may be determined from the quantity of volatile <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> it affords. The older the meat is, it is found to give the greater proportion of volatile salt. 5. The alkalineficiency of aliment may also, in some measure, be determined from its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, the younger animals being whiter and less alkalineficient. We also take a mark from the colour of the gravy poured out, according to the redness of the juices judging of the animal's alkalineficiency. 6. The relish of food is found to depend much on its alkalineficiency, as does also the stimulus it gives and the fever it produces in the system. These effects are also complicated with the viscidity of the food, by which means it is longer detained in the stomach, and the want of alkalineficiency supplied. Having mentioned animal food as differing in solubility and alkalineficiency, which often go together in the same subject, we come to the third difference, viz. III. Quantity of Nutriments. Which is either <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> or relative: absolute with respect to the quantity it really contains, sufficient powers being given to extract it; relative, with respect to the assimilatory powers of those who use it. The absolute nutriment is of some consequence; but the relative, in the robust and healthy, and except in cases of extraordinary weakness, may, without much inconvenience, be disregarded. In another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is the quantity of nourishment relative, viz. with regard to its perspirability; for if the food is soon carried off by the excretions, it is the same thing as if it contained a less proportion of nourishment. For, giving more fluid, that which is longer retained affords most; and, for the repair of the solids, that retention also is of advantage. Now, gelatinous substances are long retained; and besides, are themselves animal substances dissolved; so that, both absolutely and relatively, such substances are nutritive. Of this kind are eggs, shell fish, &c. In adults, though it is disputed whether their solids need any repair, yet at any rate, at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, fluid is more required; for this purpose the alkalineficient foods are most proper, being most easily dissolved. They are, at the same time, the most preferable; on one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> that alkalineficiency leading to disease, while on the other their perspirability obviates it. Adults, therefore, as writers justly observe, are better nourished on the alkalineficient; the young and growing, on gelatinous foods. All this leads to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of young and old meats; the first being more gelatinous, and the last more alkalineficient. This however, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, is not yet properly ascertained. Mr Geoffroy is the only person who has been taken up with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of foods. See Memoires de l'Academie, l'an. 1731 & 1732. His attempt was certainly laudable, and in some respects usefully performed; but, in general, his experiments were not sufficiently repeated, nor are indeed sufficiently accurate. He has not been on his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against the various circumstances which affect meats; the cow-kind liking a moist succulent herbage, which is not to be got in warm climates; while the sheep are fond of dry food, and thrive best there. Again, some of his experiments seem contradictory. He says, that veal gives more solution than beef, while lamb gives less than mutton, which is much to be doubted. If both he and Sanctorius had examined English beef, the result probably would have been very different as to its perspirability, &c. Besides, Mr Geoffroy has only analyzed beef and veal when raw; has made no proper circumstantial comparisons between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> and birds; and has examined the last along with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and not their muscles, &c., by themselves, as he ought to have done, &c. If a set of experiments of this kind were properly and accurately performed, they might be of great use; but at present, for the purpose of determining our present object, we must have recourse to our alkalineficiency, solubility, &c. IV. The fourth difference of animal food is, The Nature of the Fluids they afford. The whole of this will be underlaid from what has been said on alkalineficiency; the fluid produced being more or less dense and stimulating, in proportion as that prevails. V. The fifth difference of animal foods is with respect to their Perspirability. The sum of what can be said on this matter is this, that such foods as promote an accumulation of fluid in our vessels and dispose to plethora, are the least perspirable, and commonly give most strength; that the more alkalineficient foods are the most perspirable, though the viscid and less alkalineficient may attain the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> by long retention in the system. The authors on perspirability have determined the perspiration of foods as imperfectly as Mr Geoffroy has done the solubility, and in a few cases only. We must not lay hold on what Sanctorius has said on the perspirability of mutton, because he has not examined in the same way other meats in their perfect state; far less on what Keil says of oysters, as he himself was a valetudinarian, and consequently an unfit subject for such experiments, and probably of a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>. As to the effects of Food on the Mind, we have already hinted at them above. It is plain, that deli-

FOOSHT

Pages 844-844

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>; situated, according to the observations of Mr Bruce, in N. Lat. 23° 59' 43". It is described by him as about five miles in length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, though only <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in circumference. It is low and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> in the southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, but the north rises in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> hill of inconsiderable height. It is covered with a kind of bent grass, which never arises at any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length by reason of want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and the constant browsing of the goats. There are great appearances of the black hill having once been a volcano; and near the north <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> the ground founds hollow like the Solfaterra in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. There are a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of beautiful fish met with upon the coasts, but few fit for eating; and our traveller observed, that the most beautiful were the most noxious when eaten; none indeed being salutary food excepting those which resembled the fish of the northern seas. There are many beautiful shell-fish, as the concha veneris, of several colours and sizes; sea urchins, &c. Sponges are likewise found all along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. There are also pearls, but neither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> nor of a good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they fell at no great price. They are produced by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of bivalve shells. Several large shells, from the fish named bitter, are met with upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of ten <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twelve tons <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> along the coast. They are turned upon their faces and sunk into the stones, as into a paste, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> being raised all about them in such a manner as to cover the edge of the shell; "a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> (says Mr Bruce) that this stone must some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> lately have been soft or liquefied: for had it been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> would have worn the surface of the shell; but it seems perfectly entire, and is set in that hard <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> rock as the stone of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> is in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> chafing."—The water in this island is very good. The inhabitants of Foolst are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> fishermen of a swarthy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; going naked, excepting only a rag about their waist. They have no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> but what they procure in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for the fish they catch. What they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> in this manner is called seigian. But besides this they catch another species, which is flat, with a long tail, and the skin made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHAGREEN">shagreen</a>, of which the handles of knives and swords are made. There is a small town on the island, consisting of about 30 huts, built with faggots of bent grass or spartum, supported by a few sticks, and thatched with grass of the same kind of which they are built.

FOOT

Pages 845-846
Commissary, The Devil upon Two Sticks, The Lame Lover, The Maid of Bath, The Nabob, The Cozeners, The Capuchin, The Bankrupt, and an unfinished comedy called The Slanderer. All these works are only to be ranked among the petit pieces of the theatre. In the execution they are somewhat loose, negligent, and unfinished; the plots are often irregular, and the catastrophes not always conclusive: but, with all these deficiencies, they contain more strength of character, more strokes of keen satire, and more touches of temporary humour, than are to be found in the writings of any other modern dramatist. Even the language spoken by his characters, incorrect as it may sometimes seem, will on a closer examination be found entirely dramatical; as it abounds with those natural minutiae of expression which frequently form the very basis of character, and which render it the truest mirror of the conversation of the times in which he wrote. In the year 1766, being on a party of pleasure with the late duke of York, Lord Mexborough, and Sir Francis Delaval, Mr Foot had the misfortune to break his leg, by a fall from his horse; in consequence of which he was compelled to undergo an amputation.
