This accident so sensibly affected the duke, that he made a point of obtaining for Mr Foot a patent for life; whereby he was allowed to perform, at the little theatre in the Haymarket, from the 15th of May to the 16th of September every year. He now became a greater favourite of the town than ever; his very laughable pieces, with his more laughable performance, constantly filled his house; and his receipts were some seasons almost incredible. Parsimony was never a vice to be ascribed to Mr Foot; his hospitality and generosity were ever conspicuous; he was visited by the first nobility, and he was sometimes honoured even by royal guests. The attack made upon his character by one of his domestics, whom he had dismissed for misbehaviour, is too well known to be particularized here. Suffice it to say, he was honourably acquitted of that charge: but it is believed by some, that the shock which he received from it accelerated his death; others pretend, that his literary altercation with a certain then duchess, or rather her agents, much affected him, and that from that time his health declined. It is probable, however, that his natural volatility of spirits could scarcely fail to support him against all impressions from either of these quarters. Mr Foot, finding his health decline, entered into an agreement with Mr Colman, for his patent of the theatre; according to which, he was to receive from Mr Colman, 160l. per annum, besides a stipulated sum whenever he chose to perform. Mr Foot made his appearance two or three times in some of the most admired characters; but being suddenly affected with a paralytic stroke one night whilst upon the stage, he was compelled to retire. He was advised to bathe; and accordingly retired to Brighthelmstone, where he apparently recovered his former health and spirits, and was what is called the fiddle of the company who resorted to that agreeable place of amusement. A few weeks before his death, he returned to London; but, by the advice of his physicians, set out with an intention to spend the winter at Paris and in the south of France. He had got no farther than Dover, when he was suddenly attacked by another stroke of the palsy, which in a few hours terminated his existence. He died on the 21st of October 1777; in the 56th year of his age, and was privately interred in the cloisters of Westminster abbey.

SAMUEL, Esq. the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRURO">Truro</a>, in Cornwall; and was descended from a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family. His father was member of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for Tiverton, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> office and fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>. His mother was heiress of the Dinely and Goodere families. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a fatal misunderstanding between her two brothers, Sir John Dinely Goodere, Bart. and Samuel Goodere, Esq. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of his majesty's ship the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUBY">Ruby</a>, which ended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of both, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Goodere estate, which was better than 500l. per annum, descended to Mr. Foote. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, which owed its foundation to Sir Thomas Cookes Winford, Bart. a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> of our author's. On leaving the university, he commenced student of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the Temple; but as the dryness of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> did not <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the liveliness of his genius, he soon relinquished it. He married a young lady of a good family and some fortune; but their tempers not agreeing, a perfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> subsist between them. He now launched into all the fashionable foibles of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> not excepted, and in a few years spent his whole fortune. His necessities led him to the stage, and he made his first appearance in the character of Othello. He next performed Fondlewife with much more applause; and this, indeed, was ever after one of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> parts. He attempted <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Foppington likewise, but prudently gave it up. But as Mr. Foote was never a capital <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> in the plays of others, his salary was very unequal to his gay and extravagant turn; and he contracted debts which forced him to take refuge within the verge of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. On this occasion, he relieved his necessities by the following stratagem. Sir Fr—s D—l—l had long been his intimate friend, and had dissipated his fortune by similar extravagance. Lady N—f—u P—let, who was likewise an intimate acquaintance of Foote's, and who was exceedingly rich, was fortunately at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> bent upon a matrimonial scheme. Foote strongly recommended to her to consult upon this momentous affair the conjurer in the Old Bailey, whom he represented as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of surprising skill and penetration. He employed an acquaintance of his own to personate the conjurer; who depicted Sir Fr—s D—l—l at full length; described the time when, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where, and the dress in which she would see him. The lady was so struck with the coincidence of every circumstance, that she married D—l—l in a few days. For this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> Sir Francis settled an annuity upon Foote; and this enabled him once more to emerge from obscurity. In 1747 he opened the little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> in the Haymarket, taking upon himself the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> character of author and performer; and appeared in a dramatic piece of his own composing, called the Diversion of the Morning. This piece consisted of nothing more than the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> well known in real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; whose manner of conversation and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> this author very happily <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> off in the diction of his drama, and still more happily represented on the stage, by an exact and most amusing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, not only of the manner and tone of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, but even of the very persons, of those whom he intended to take off. In this performance, a certain physician, Dr L—n, well known for the oddity and singularity of his appearance and conversation, and the celebrated Chevalier Taylor, who was at that time in the height of his popularity, were made objects of Foote's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; the latter, indeed very deservedly; and, in the concluding part of his speech, under the character of a theatrical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>, Mr. Foote took off, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> humour and accuracy, the several styles of acting of every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> performer on the English stage. The performance at first met with some opposition from the civil magistrates of Westminster, under the sanction of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament for limiting the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of playhouses, as well as from the jealousy of one of the managers of Drury-lane <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a>: but the author being patronized by many of the principal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and other persons of distinction, this opposition was overruled; and having altered the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his performance, Mr. Foote proceeded, without further molestation, to give <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">Tea</a> in a Morning to his friends, and represented it through a run of 40 mornings to crowded and splendid audiences.—The ensuing season he produced another piece of the same kind, which he called An Auction of Pictures. In this performance he introduced several new and popular characters; particularly Sir Thomas de Veil, then the acting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace for Westminster, Mr. Cock the celebrated auctioneer, and the equally famous Orator Henley. This piece also had a very great run.—His Knights, which was the production of the ensuing season, was a performance of somewhat more dramatic regularity: but still, although his plot and characters seemed less immediately personal, it was apparent that he kept some particular real persons strongly in his eye in the performance; and the town took upon themselves to fix them where the resemblance appeared to be the most striking. Thus Mr. Foote <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from time to time to select, for the entertainment of the public, such characters, as well general as individual, as seemed most likely to engage their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. His dramatic pieces, exclusive of the interlude called Piety in Patterns, are as follows: Tafe, the Knights, The Author, The Englishman in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, The Englishman returned from Paris, The Mayor of Garat, The Liar, The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">Patron</a>, The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, The Orators, The

FORAMEN

Pages 846-846

in Anatomy, a name given to several apertures <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perforations in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of the body; as, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> and internal foramina of the cranium or skull. 2. The foramina in the upper and lower jaw. 3. Foramen lachrymale. 4. Foramen membranae tympani. FORAMEN Ovale, an oval aperture or passage through the heart of a fetus, which closes up after birth. It arises from the coronal vein, near the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> auricle, and passes directly into the left auricle of the heart, serving for the circulation of the blood in the fetus, till such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as the infant breathes, and the lungs are open; in this the fetus differs from the adult; although almost all anatomists, Mr Cheselden excepted, assure us, that the foramen ovale has sometimes been found in adults. See FOETUS.

Pages 846-846

DUNCAN, Esq. of Culledon, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of session in Scotland, was born in the year 1685. In his early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he was brought up in a family remarkable for hospitality; which, perhaps, led him afterwards to a freer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> in social pleasures. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> disposition inclined him to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but, as he soon discovered a superior genius, by the advice of his friends he applied himself to letters. He directed his studies particularly to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; in which he made a quick progress, and in 1709 was admitted an advocate. From 1722 to 1737, he represented in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> the boroughs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, Fortrose, Nairn, and Forres. In 1725, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s advocate; and in 1737 lord president of the court of session. In the rebellions which broke out in Scotland in 1715 and 1745 he espoused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> cause; but with so much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and moderation did he conduct himself at this delicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>, that not a whisper was at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> heard to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> he acquired in advancing the prosperity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and in contributing to re-establish peace and order, was the only reward of his services. He had even impaired, and almost ruined, his private fortune in the cause of the public; but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> did not make him the smallest compensation. The minister, with a meanness for which it is difficult to account, desired to have a state of his disbursements. Shocked at the incivility and rudeness of this treatment, he left the minister without making any reply. Throughout the whole course of his life he had a lively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, without the least taint of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> was extended to every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> and denomination of religionists indiscriminately. He was well versed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and wrote in a flowing and oratorical style, concerning religion natural and revealed, some important discoveries in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and concerning the sources of incredulity. He died in 1747, in the 62nd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and his works have since been published in two volumes octavo.

FORCE

Pages 846-847

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, denotes the cause of the change change in the state of a body, when, being at rest, it begins to move, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> which is either not uniform or not <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>. While a body remains in the same state, either of rest or of uniform and rectilinear motion, the cause of its remaining in such a state is in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the body, and it cannot be said that any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRINSIC">extrinsic</a> force has acted on it. This internal cause or principle is called <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-INERTIA">inertia</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">Mechanical</a> forces may be reduced to two sorts: one of a body at rest, the other of a body in motion. The force of a body at rest, is that which we conceive to be in a body lying still on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, or hanging by a rope, or supported by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, &c. and this is called by the names of pressure, tension, force, or vis mortua, solicitation, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONATUS">conatus</a> movendi, conamen, &c. To this class also of forces we must refer centripetal and centrifugal forces, though they reside in a body in motion; because these forces are homogeneous to weights, pressures, or tensions of any kind. The force of a body in motion is a power residing in that body so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it continues its motion; by means of which it is able to remove obstacles lying in its way; to lessen, destroy, or overcome the force of any other moving body which meets it in an opposite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; or to surmount any dead pressure or resistance, as tensility, gravity, friction, &c. for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be lessened or destroyed by such resistance as lessens or destroys the motion of the body. This is called moving force, vis motrix, and by some late writers vis viso, to distinguish it from the vis mortua spoken of before; and by these appellations, however different, the same thing is understood by all mathematicians; namely, that power of displacing, of withstanding opposite moving forces, or of overcoming any dead resistance, which resides in a moving body, and which, in whole or in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, continues to accompany it, so long as the body moves. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>. We have several curious as well as useful observations in Defaguliers's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">Experimental Philosophy</a>, concerning the comparative forces of men and horses, and the best way of applying them. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> draws with the greatest advantage when the line of direction is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; in such a situation, he is able to draw 200lb. eight hours a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, walking about two miles and a half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the same horse is made to draw 240lb., he can <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> but six hours a day, and cannot go quite so fast. On a carriage, indeed, where friction alone is to be overcome, a middling horse will draw 1000lb. But the best way to try a horse's force, is by making him draw up out of a well, over a single pulley or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>; and, in such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, one horse will; another will draw 200lb. as already observed. Five men are found to be equal in strength to one horse, and can, with as much ease, push round the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> beam of a mill, in a walk 40 feet wide; whereas three men will do it in a walk only 19 feet wide. The worst way of applying the force of a horse, is to make him carry or draw up hill; for if the hill be steep, three men will do more than a horse, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> climbing up faster with a burden of 100lb. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, than a horse that is loaded with 300lb.; a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> which is owing to the position of the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body being better adapted to climb than those of a horse. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the best way of applying the force of a horse, is in a horizontal direction, wherein a man can exert least force; thus a man weighing 140lb., and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> along by means of a rope coming over his shoulders, cannot draw above 27lb., or exert above one-seventh part of the force of a horse employed to the same purpose. The very best and most effectual posture in a man, is that of rowing, in which he not only acts with more muscles at once for overcoming the resistance, than in any other position; but as he pulls backward, the weight of his body assists by way of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>. See Defaguliers, Exp. Phil. vol. i. p. 241. where we have several other observations relative to force acquired by certain positions of the body, from which that author accounts for most feats of strength and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. See also a Memoire on this subject by M. de la Hire, in Mem. Roy. Acad. Sc. 1629; or in Defaguliers, Exp. &c. 267, &c. who has published a translation of part of it, with remarks. Citizen Regnier has invented an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for ascertaining the relative strength of men and animals, for an account of which, see Dynamometer; and for a fuller <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, the reader may consult the original <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the subject in Jour. de l'Ecole Polytechn. vol. ii. or the translation in Phil. Mag. vol. i. Force, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies any unlawful violence offered to things or persons, and is divided into simple and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>. Simple force is what is so committed, that it has no other crime attending it; as where a person by force enters another's possession, without committing any other unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Compound force, is where some other violence is committed, with such an act which of itself alone is criminal; as if one enters by force into another's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and there kills a person, or ravishes a woman. There is likewise a force implied in law, as in every trespass, refuse, or difficilin, and an actual force with weapons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons, &c.—Any person may lawfully enter a tavern, inn, or victualling-house; so may a landlord his tenant's house to view repairs, &c. But if, in these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the person that enters commits any violence or force, the law will intend that he entered for that purpose.

FORCEPS

Pages 847-847

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, &c. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scissors for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dividing, the fleshy membranous parts of the body, as occasion requires. See Surgery.

FORCER

Pages 847-847

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, is properly a piston, without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>. For by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up such a piston, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is drawn up, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> follows; then pushing the piston <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> again, the water, being prevented from descending by the lower valve, is forced up to any height above, by means of a pipe branch between the two.

FORCIBLE ENTRY

Pages 847-848

is a violent and actual entry into houses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lands; and a forcible detainee, is where one by violence withholds the possession of lands, &c. so that the person who has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of entry is barred, or hindered, therefrom. At <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, any person that had a right to enter into lands, &c. might retain possession of it by force. But this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> being abused, to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the peace, it was therefore found necessary that the same should be restrained: Though, at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he Forcible who is wrongfully dispossessed of goods may by force retake them. By statute no person shall make an entry on any lands or tenements, except where it is given by law, and in a peaceable manner, even though they have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of entry, on pain of imprisonment; and where a forcible entry is committed, justices of the peace are authorized to view the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and inquire of the force by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, summoned by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and they may cause the tenements, &c., to be restored, and imprison the offenders till they pay a fine. Likewise a writ of forcible entry lies, where a person feigned of freehold, is by force put out thereof. **FORCIBLE <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a>**, of a woman of estate, is felony. For by the statute 3 H. VII. c. 2, it is enacted, "That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any persons shall take away any woman having lands or goods, or that is heir-apparent to her ancestor, by force and against her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and marry or defile her; the takers, procurers, abettors, and receivers, of the woman taken away against her will, and knowing the same, shall be deemed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> felons; but as to procurers and accessories before the fact, they are to be excluded the benefit of clergy, by 39 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, c. 9. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> on the statute Hen. VII. is expressly to set forth, that the woman taken away had lands or goods, or was heir apparent; and also that she was married or defiled, because no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is within the statute; and it ought to allege that the taking was for lucre. It is no excuse that the woman at first was taken away with her consent; for if the afterwards refuse to continue with the offender, and be forced against her will, she may from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> properly be said to be taken against her will; and it is not material whether a woman so taken away be at last married or defiled with her own consent or not, if she was under force at the time; the offenders being in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> equally within the words of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Those persons who, after the fact, receive the offender, are but accessories after the offence, according to the rules of common law; and those that are only privy to the damage, but not parties to the forcible taking away, are not within the act H. P. C. 119. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may be indicted for taking away a woman by force in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; for the continuing of the force in any country, amounts to a forcible taking there. Ibid. Taking away any woman child under the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16 years and unmarried, out of the custody and without the consent of the father or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, &c., the offender shall suffer fine and imprisonment; and if the woman agrees to any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> of matrimony with such person, she shall forfeit her estate during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, to the next of kin, to whom the inheritance should descend, &c. Stat. 4 & 5 P. & M. c. 8. This is a force against the parents; and an information will <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> for feeding a young man or woman from their parents, against their consents, in order to marry them, &c. See Marriage.

FORCING

Pages 848-848

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a method of producing ripe <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> from trees before their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> season, See Gardening <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Forcing**, in the wine trade, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the wine cooperers, for the fining <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> wines, and rendering them fit for immediate draught. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inconvenience of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of fining down the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wines with isinglass, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> with whites of eggs, is the slowness of the operation; these ingredients not performing their office in less than a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sometimes a fortnight, according as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> proves favourable, cloudy or clear, windy or calm: this appears to be <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of constant observation. But the wine merchant frequently requires a method that shall, with certainty, make the wines fit for tasting in a few hours. A method of this kind there is, but it is kept in a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> a valuable secret. Perhaps it depends upon a prudent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a tartarised spirit of wine, and the common forcing, as occasion is, along with gypsum, as the principal; all which are to be well stirred about in the wine, for half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> before it is suffered to rest.

FORDOUN

Pages 848-848

JOHN OF**, the father of Scottish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, flourished in the reign of Alexander III. towards the end of the 13th century. But of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> there is nothing known with certainty, though there was not a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> that possessed not copies of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The first five books of the history which bears his name were written by him: the rest were fabricated from materials left by him, and from new collections by different persons. There is a manuscript in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a> of Fordoun's History, in the library of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>.

FORDWICH

Pages 848-848

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, called in Doomsday Book "the little borough of Fordwich," is a member of the port of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, and was anciently incorporated by the style of the barons of the town of Fordwich, but more lately by the name of the mayor, jurats, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>, who enjoy the same privileges as the cinque ports. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is famous for excellent trouts in its river Stour,

HISTORY OF ENTOMOLOGY

Pages 250-261

THOUGH the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> must have been attracted by the vegetables and animals with which he found himself surrounded, and by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and minerals on which he trod, even at the very earliest periods of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, yet a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> must have elapsed before any attempts were made at arrangement <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> classification. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> was the first (as far as we know) who deserved the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> historian; his arrangement of animals was the only one followed for many centuries. He divided all animals into viviparous and oviparous; the first contained <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> birds, fishes, and insects. Under insects were comprehended all small animals whose bodies were divided into segments. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of insects was followed by all natural historians <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the time of Linnaeus. Theophratus, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Aristotle, the only other person among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks who deserves the name of natural historian, bestowed the most of his attention on vegetables and minerals. Pliny has given us an account of all that was known in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> down to his own times. Though he has mentioned many insects, owing to his want of method little is to be learnt from him respecting entomology. Dioscorides, who was nearly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Pliny, has confined himself chiefly to natural history connected with medicine. He has given an enumeration of all the natural bodies which entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>. On the revival of learning in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, writers on natural history seemed to have confined themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> commentaries on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and nothing was done in entomology till the times of Gesner, who was the greatest naturalist the world had seen from the time of Aristotle, and who was the first who made a collection of the objects of natural history, and formed a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a> in 1516, and died in 1565. Aldrovandus lived nearly about the same time with Gesner, and, like him, formed a museum which served for the foundation of the public museum at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, where many specimens may be still seen marked with the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the first collector. Gesner formed his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a> on the principles of Aristotle: his history of animals is very voluminous. Aldrovandus made a collection of all that had been written on natural history before his own time, without discriminating <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> from fiction. He has given a methodical arrangement of insects in the seventh book of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> published in 1602. He followed nearly the same arrangement with Gesner. Gesner, in conjunction with some other natural historians, wrote a treatise on insects, which was published by Moufflet, Mouffet, an English physician. About this time our countryman, the illustrious Harvey, ventured to controvert Aristotle's erroneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> with respect to equivocal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. Though his aphorism, omnia ex ovo, at first met with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> opposition, it was at last established by his own experiments and those of Rheldi and Malpighi. From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the writers on entomology have been numerous; we shall content ourselves here with giving little more than an enumeration of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works on the subject. Agricola, in a work entitled de Animalibus Subterraneis, published in 1549, has given a methodical arrangement of insects; he divides them into, 1. Creeping insects; 2. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">Flying</a> insects; and 3. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">Swimming</a> insects. After giving this arrangement, he proceeds to give an account of each <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. A work entitled Theatrum Insectorum Thomae Mouffeti <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> concinnatum, Lond. 1634, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> labour of several of the most eminent natural historians who lived about the middle of the sixteenth century, though not published till 1734, about 30 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mouffet, by whose care the work had been abridged, and prepared to meet the public eye, is the next worthy of notice. It is divided into two books; the first treats of winged insects; the second of insects without wings: these two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> divisions are subdivided into several families characterized by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and position of the legs. There is but little method displayed in the arrangement of the insects which compose the different families. Aldrovandus divides insects into terrebrica et aquatica (<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> insects, and aquatic insects). The different orders and subdivisions of these two classes, are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> determined by the number, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and position of their wings and legs. He calls his first order Favifera, (those which form combs). As to the rest, according to his own <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, he follows Aristotle. Wolfgang Frenzius, in his Historia Animalium Sacra, published in 1612, has divided insects into three classes, viz. 1. Aeria, (such as fly); 2. Aquatica, (such as inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>); 3. Terrea et Reptentia, (such as creep about, or are lodged in the earth). His descriptions are much more accurate than those of any of the authors who preceded him. John Johnston has borrowed freely from his predecessors, in his Historia Naturalis Insectorum, published in 1653. He divides insects into terraglia and aquatica, (into land and aquatic insects): the land insects he divides into three orders; 1. Such as have wings and legs; 2. Such as have legs without wings; and 3. Such as have neither wings nor legs. These three orders occupy his three first books; his fourth contains aquatic insects. Walter Charleton follows the system of Aldrovandus in his Onomasticon Zoicon, published in 1668. Jo. Goodart published Metamorphosis et Historia Naturalis de Insectis, 8vo. Mediol. 1667. Likewise in 1675, a work of his appeared, de Insectis in Methodum reductis, opera Mart. Lister. Ebor. In this work insects are divided into ten families: the first includes butterflies with erect wings; 2d, Butterflies with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> wings; 3d, Butterflies with deflected wings; 4th, Libellulae, (dragon-flies); 5th, Apes, (bees); 6th, Coleopterous insects; 7th, Locusts, and Grasshoppers; 8th, Flies corresponding to the order diptera of Linnaeus; 9th, Millepedes; and 10th, Spiders. This work is full of typographical errors and mistakes in natural history. The discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> in 1618, tended greatly to the advancement of entomology, as by means of it the most minute parts of insects could be viewed, and their organization examined. Naturalists were much engaged in making microscopic discoveries, particularly Borel, Rheldi, Swammerdam, Bonanni, Bonomo, Leeuwenhoek and Joblot. John Swammerdam, in his Biblia Naturae, published in 1669, has divided insects into four classes. John Ray published his Historia Insectorum. Lond. 1710. This work was properly the joint production of J. Ray and Francis Willoughby. These illustrious friends laboured together with uncommon ardour in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of nature. Death carried off Willoughby in the prime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, before he had properly digested what the industry of his early years had collected; and his labours would have been lost to the world, and his name might have sunk in oblivion, but for the friendship of Ray. So <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> was the intercourse between these two naturalists, and so intimately were their labours blended together, that it is not easy to assign each his due share of merit. Indeed Ray has been so partial to the fame of his departed friend, and has cherished his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> with such affectionate care, that we are in danger of attributing too much to Mr Willoughby, and too little to himself. Though what Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> affirms be not correct, that Mr Willoughby had taken the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> for his task, and Mr Ray the vegetable one, yet it is generally agreed, that the Historia Insectorum is principally to be ascribed to Willoughby. In that work insects are divided into Transmutabilia et Intransmutabilia, (those which undergo a metamorphosis, and those which undergo none). These two grand divisions are subdivided into several orders, which are ascertained by the number of their legs, or total want of legs; by the places which they inhabit; by their size; by the configuration of the various parts of the body; by the smell which they diffuse, &c. The transmutabilia are divided into four orders. 1. Vaginipenners, (those which have their wings covered with a sheath). 2. Papilioners, (lepidopterous insects). 3. Quadripenners, (those which have four wings); and 4. Bipenners, (those which have two). The papilioners, quadripenners, and bipenners are again subdivided into families, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are taken, either from the appearance and conformation of their larva, or from the form, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and different properties of the perfect insect. Eleazar Albin published a natural history of English insects in 1720. He likewise published the Natural History of Spiders in 1736. Antony Valfinieri, in his work entitled Esperienze e Osservazioni intorno agli Insetti, published in 1730, has divided insects into four orders, according to the situation in which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> their lives. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Sybelle Merian, published in 1730, Histoire d'Insectes d'Europe et de Surinam. She likewise published in 1705, Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> vivum picta et descripta; and in 1717, Erucarum Ortus. George Bernard Rhump published in 1705, and again in 1741, a work entitled Ambonische Ravituikamer. Hans Sloane, in the years 1707 and 1725, published a Voyage to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, Barbadoes, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a>, Saint Christophers and Jamaica. Henry Ruiisch in 1710 and 1718 published Theatrum Universale omnium Animalium. J. Petiver published in 1715 his Icones et Nomina Aquatilium Animalium Ambiense. Richard Bradley published in 1721 his Philosophical Account of the Works of Nature. Linnaeus, the most celebrated natural historian the world ever produced, in his first edition of the Systema Naturae, published in 1735, divided insects into four orders, from the number and different appearances of their wings; 1. Coleoptera; 2. Hemiptera; 3. Hymenoptera; and 4. APTERA. This was but an imperfect sketch, a first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a>. In the subsequent editions of the System of Nature which he published, to the number of twelve, he completed the arrangement of insects, of which we need say nothing here, as we have followed it in preference to all others; and most authors who have written on the subject for more than half a century past have either followed it closely, or with very slight alterations. His extensive genius embraced all the three kingdoms of nature. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> and entomology in particular he far excels all who went before him, and as yet remains unrivalled. Writers on entomology became so numerous after Linnaeus had published his System of Nature, and established entomology on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundation, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> enumeration of their names and titles of their books would occupy more room than we can afford to bestow on this article; we shall therefore only notice a few of the most remarkable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Degeer, in his Memoires pour servir à l'Histoire des Insectes, in 1752, has arranged insects into fourteen orders, distinguished by the different appearances of the various parts which compose their bodies, particularly the elytra, wings, and most remarkable parts of the head. He published again in 1778. M. de Reaumur published his Memoires pour servir à l'Histoire des Insectes at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1737. No one has paid so much attention to the habits of insects, and to every thing that concerns them, as Reaumur. He ought to be read by every student of entomology. John Retzius, has simplified the arrangement of Degeer, in a small work entitled Genera et Species Insectorum. But although in this arrangement he has followed the method of Degeer, the terms he has made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of are principally those of Linnaeus. His 14 orders are, 1. Lepidoptera. 2. Aliquanta. 3. Neuroptera. 4. Hymenoptera. 5. Siphonata. 6. Dermaptera. 7. Hemiptera. 8. Coleoptera. 9. Haeterata. 10. Proboidea. 11. Suctoria. 12. Ancenata. 13. Atracheia. 14. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRUSTACEA">Crustacea</a>. M. Geoffroy, in his Histoire Abrégée des Insectes, published at Paris in 1762, has divided insects into six orders; Coleopteres, Hemipteres, Tetrapteres ailes fari-neuses, Tetrapteres ailes nus, Dipteres, and Apteres. He determined his families by the number of the articulations of the feet, and his genera by characters drawn from all the parts of the body. He has formed a great number of new genera. John Antony Scopoli, in his Entomologia Carniolica, published in 1762, has followed the arrangement of Linnaeus, and only changes the names of some of the orders; e.g., Proboidea, instead of Hemiptera; Aculeata, instead of Hymenoptera; Halterata, instead of Hiflory, Diptera; and Pedetria, instead of Aptera. J. C. Schaeffer published in 1766, Elementa Entomologica, 135 tabulae are excussae; he follows in many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> the method of Linnaeus. He divides insects into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> classes. 1. Coleoptero-macroptera. 2. Coleoptero-microptera. 3. Hemiptera. 4. Hymeno-lepidoptera. 5. Hymeno-gymnoptera. 6. Diptera; and 7. Aptera. His first and second classes correspond with the Coleoptera of Linnaeus; the fourth with the Lepidoptera, and the fifth with the Hymenoptera. John C. Fabricius is the founder of a new system of Entomology, which he published in his Systema Naturae 1775. He discriminates his orders and genera, by the parts of the mouth, (infrumenta cibaria). He afterwards published Species Insectorum, Entomologia Systematica, and Manuifa Insectorum. The arrangement of Fabricius has acquired great reputation, especially on the continent. It may not therefore be amiss to give a slight view of it. He divides insects into eight classes. Class I. Eleutherata. Mouth armed with jaws, and four or six feelers. The jaws naked and free. Class II. Ulanata. The jaws covered with an obtuse <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>. Class III. Synistata. The jaws united with the lip. Class IV. Agonata. The under jaw wanting. Class V. Unogata. Mouth armed with jaws and two feelers; the under jaw generally furnished with a small unguis or nail. Class VI. Glossata. Mouth furnished with feelers, and a spiral tongue. Class VII. Rhyngota. Mouth furnished with a stout, and an articulated sheath. Class VIII. Antliata. Mouth furnished with a haustellum and a sheath not articulated. In a supplement to his Entomologia Systematica, he has divided insects into thirteen orders. 1. Eleutherata. 2. Ulonata. 3. Synitata. 4. Piczata. 5. Odorata. 6. Mitofata. 7. Unogata. 8. Polygonata. 9. Kleitagnatha. 10. Exochnata. 11. Glofiata. 12. Rhyngota. 13. Anthiliata. He has lately published a work entitled Systema Eleutheratorium, no more than two volumes of which have as yet made their appearance. Moses Harris published an Exposition of English Insects, &c. with coloured plates, 1776. Jo. Christ published Philosophia Entomologica sistens scientiae fundamenta, &c. Hamb. 1778, 8vo. Archiv. der Insektengegeschichte herausgegeben von Joh. Capf. Fueilly, Zurich, 1781. Fr. Paulia, v. Schrank; Enumeratio Insectorum Austriae indigenorum. Aug. Vindel. 1781. P. Sim. Pallas; Icones Insectorum. Hamb. 1781. A. W. Knock; Beytraege zur Insektengegeschichte, 1781. James Barbut published the Genera Insectorum of Linnaeus, exemplified by various specimens of English insects drawn from nature. Lond. 1781. John Nepomuk de Laicharting, has divided insects into ten orders, characterized by the configuration of various parts of the body. He adheres pretty closely to the Order I. Coleoptera. Fig. 16. Scarabaeus <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. Hercules Beetle. Fig. 18. Buprestis Guttata. Spotted Cow burner Fig. 19. Carabus Vulgaris. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> Carabus. Fig. 19. Carabus Coriaceus. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHAGREEN">Shagreen</a> Carabus. Fig. 17. Planus Fatidicus. Death watch. the method of Linnæus. His orders are, 1. Scarabæoidea. 2. Grylloidea. 3. Cimicoides. 4. Papilionoides. 5. Libelluloides. 6. Vespoides. 7. Mulcoides. 8. Cancrioides. 9. Aranoides, and 10. Onicoides. Olivier, in 1780, published Entomologie, ou Histoire Naturelle des Insectes, in 3 vols. 4to. Paris. In 1790, in the Dictionnaire des Insectes, forming a part of the Encyclopédie Méthodique, he has given an arrangement of insects little different from that of Linnæus. He has added one order which he calls Orthopteres, distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of folding the lower wings, and a part on the head, which he terms galea. He has likewise subdivided the order Aptera, into Arachnides and Crustaces. Latreille in 1795, in a work entitled Precis du Caractère des Genres, divides insects into two grand divisions, viz. infètes ailées, et infètes aériennes (winged insects, and insects without wings). These two grand divisions he subdivides into 14 orders. 1. Coleoptères. 2. Orthoptères. 3. Hemiptères. 4. Neuroptères. 5. Lepidoptères. 6. Succures. 7. Thysanures. 8. Pauropites. 9. Acéphalés. 10. Entomotriches. 11. Crustacés. 12. Myriapodes. Since that he has published a more detailed account of this method in a work entitled les Genres et les Familles des Insectes. Clairville in 1795, in the introduction to his Entomologie Helvétique, has given an arrangement of insects, in which he differs from Linnæus almost in nothing, except in the names of his orders, viz. Elytropteres, Dictyopteres, Thlebopteres, Haltipteres, Lepidopteres, Heminopteres, Rophoteires, and Pododuneres. Link, in his Magazin für Thiergeschichte, has divided insects into eleven orders; he follows de Laicharting almost in every thing, even in the names of his orders; he has indeed added an order which he calls Pediculoïdes. Cuvier and Dumeril, in their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPARATIVE_ANATOMY">Comparative Anatomy</a>, have very nearly followed the method of Linnæus; they have however divided the order Aptera into two, viz. Gnathaptera and Aptera; they have likewise altered the arrangement of the orders, and have placed those first which contain insects furnished with jaws, viz. Gnathaptera, Neuroptera, Hymenoptera, Coleoptera, and Orthoptera; and have thrown those last which are destitute of jaws, viz. Hemiptera, Lepidoptera, Diptera and Aptera. We shall refrain from noticing those authors who have written partial treatises; though there are several works of that kind which the entomologist might peruse with advantage, such as the Fauna Suecica, published in 1761 by Linnæus, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>. Fauna Germanica, by Panzer. La Faune Parisienne de Walknair. Kirby's Monographia apum Anglicæ. Latreille's treatise on Ants.

IX. Exchange with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> and the West Indies. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America and the West Indies, accounts, as in Britain, are kept in pounds, shillings, and pence. In North America they have few coins circulating among them, and on that account have been obliged to substitute a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> currency for a medium of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; which having no intrinsic value, is subjected to many disadvantages, and generally suffers a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a>. In the West Indies coins are more frequent, owing to their commercial intercourse with the Spanish settlements. Exchange betwixt Britain and America, or the West Indies, may be computed as in the following examples: 1. The neat proceeds of a cargo from Britain to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a> amount to 845l. 17s. 6d. currency: How much is that in sterling money, exchange at 80 per cent.? If 180 : 100 18 : 10 L. s. d. 9 : 5 :: 845 17 6 9)845 17 6 L. 469 18 7\(\frac{1}{2}\) Ster. Ans. 2. Boston remits to Britain a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of 469l. 18s. 7\(\frac{1}{2}\)d. sterling: How much currency was paid for the bill at Boston, exchange at 80 per cent.? If 100 : 180 L. s. d. 5 : 9 :: 469 18 7\(\frac{1}{2}\) 9)469 18 7\(\frac{1}{2}\) 845 17 6 currency. Ans. 3 How much sterling money <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> 1780l. Jamaica currency amount to, exchange at 40 per cent.? Bills of exchange from America, the rate being <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, is an expensive way of remitting money to Britain; and therefore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> in Britain generally choose to have the debts due to them remitted home in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, rum, or other produce. X. Exchange with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, and all over Ireland, books and accounts are kept in pounds, shillings, and pence, as in Britain; and they exchange on the 100l. sterling. The par of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> sterling is one shilling and one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> Irish; and so the par of 100l. sterling is 108l. 6s. 8d. Irish. The course of exchange runs from 6 to 15 per cent. Exchange betwixt London and other places in Britain. The several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in Britain exchange with London for a small premium in favour of London; such as, Exchange, 1, 1\(\frac{1}{2}\), &c., per cent. The premium is more or less, according to the demand for bills. Examp. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> draws on London for 860l. exchange at 1\(\frac{1}{2}\) per cent.: How much money must be paid at Edinburgh for the bill? \[ \begin{array}{c|c} \text{L.} & \\ \hline 860 & \\ \text{per cent.} & \\ \hline 1 = \frac{1}{100} & 8 12 \\ \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} & 2 3 \\ \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{8} & 1 1 6 \\ \end{array} \] \[ 11 16 \text{ 6 premium.} \] \[ 871 16 \text{ 6 paid for the bill.} \] To avoid paying the premium, it is usual practice to take the bill payable at London a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of days after <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>: and in this way of doing, 73 days is equivalent to 1 per cent. XII. Arbitration of Exchanges. The course of exchange betwixt <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> and nation naturally rises or falls according as the circumstances and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of trade happen to vary. Now, to draw upon and remit to foreign places, in this fluctuating state of exchange, in the way that will turn out most profitable, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of arbitration. Which is either simple or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>. I. Simple Arbitration. In simple arbitration the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> or prices of exchange from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another two are given; whereby is found the correspondent price between the said two places, called the arbitrated price, or par of arbitration; and hence is derived a method of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and remitting to the best advantage. Examp. 1. If exchange from London to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> be 33s. 9d. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> sterling; and if exchange from London to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> be 32d. per crown; what must be the rate of exchange from Amsterdam to Paris, in order to be put on a par with the other two? \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Ster. Flem. Ster.} & \\ \hline \text{s. s. d. d.} & \\ \hline \text{If } 20 : 33 9 :: 32 & \\ 12 12 & \\ \end{array} \] \[ 230 \quad 405 \] \[ 32 \] \[ 810 \] \[ 1215. \] \[ 240 \times 12960 = 304 \text{ Flem. per crown. Ans.} \] 2. If exchange from Paris to London be 32d. sterling per crown; and if exchange from Paris to Amsterdam be 54d. Flemish per crown: what must be the rate of exchange between London and Amsterdam, in order to be on a par with the other two? From these operations it appears, that if any sum of money be remitted, at the rates of exchange mentioned, from any one of the three places to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and from the second to the third, and again from the third to the first, the sum so remitted will come home entire, without increase or diminution. From the par of arbitration thus found, and the course of exchange given, is deduced a method of drawing and remitting to advantage, as in the following example. 3. If exchange from London to Paris is 32d. sterling per crown, and to Amsterdam 40½d. Flemish per pound sterling; and if, by advice from Holland to France, the course of exchange between Paris and Amsterdam is fallen to 52d. Flemish per crown; what may be gained per cent. by drawing on Paris, and remitting to Amsterdam? The par of arbitration between Paris and Amsterdam in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> by Ex. 1. is 54d. Flemish per crown. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">Work</a> as under. \[ \begin{align*} & \text{d. St. Cr. L. St. Cr.} \\ & \text{If } 32 : 1 : 100 : 750 \text{ debit at Paris.} \\ & \text{Cr. d.Fl. C. d.Fl.} \\ & \text{If } 1 : 52 : 750 : 39000 \text{ <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> at Amsterdam.} \\ & \text{d.Fl. L.St. d.Fl. L. s. d. Ster.} \\ & \text{If } 405 : 1 : 39000 : 96 5 11\frac{1}{2} \text{ to be remitted.} \end{align*} \] But if the course of exchange between Paris and Amsterdam, instead of falling below, rise about the par of arbitration, suppose to 56d. Flemish per crown; in this case if you propose to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> by the negotiation, you must draw on Amsterdam, and remit to Paris. The computation follows: \[ \begin{align*} & \text{L.St. d.Fl. L.St. d.Fl.} \\ & \text{If } 1 : 405 : 100 : 40500 \text{ debit at Amsterdam.} \\ & \text{d.Fl. Cr. d.Fl. Cr.} \\ & \text{If } 56 : 1 : 40500 : 723\frac{1}{4} \text{ credit at Paris.} \\ & \text{Cr. d. St. Cr. L. s. d. Ster.} \\ & \text{If } 1 : 32 : 723\frac{1}{4} : 96 8 6\frac{5}{7} \text{ to be remitted.} \end{align*} \] In negotiations of this sort, a sum for remittance is afforded out of the sum you receive for the draught; and your credit at the one foreign place pays your debt at the other. II. Compound Arbitration. In compound arbitration the rate or price of exchange between three, four, or more places, is given, in order to find how much a remittance passing through them all will amount to at the last place; or to find the arbitrated price, or par of arbitration, between the first place and the last. And this may be done by the following RULES. I. Distinguish the given rates or prices into antecedents and consequents; place the antecedents in one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, and the consequents in another on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, fronting one another by way of equation. II. The first antecedent, and the last consequent to which an antecedent is required, must always be of the same kind. III. The second antecedent must be of the same kind with the first consequent, and the third antecedent of the same kind with the second consequent, &c. IV. If to any of the numbers a fraction be annexed, both the antecedent and its consequent must be multiplied into the denominator. V. To facilitate the operation, terms that happen to be equal or the same in both columns, may be dropped or rejected, and other terms may be abridged. VI. Multiply the antecedents continually for a divisor, and the consequents continually for a dividend, and the quot will be the answer or antecedent required. Example. 1. If London remit 100l. sterling to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, by way of Holland, at 3½s. Flemish per pound sterling; thence to France, at 38d. Flemish per crown; thence to Venice, at 100 crowns per 60 ducats; and thence to Spain, at 360 mervadies per ducat; how many piafres, of 272 mervadies, will the 100l. sterling amount to in Spain? \[ \begin{align*} & \text{Antecedents. Consequents. Abridged.} \\ & \text{1l. Sterling = 35s. or 420d. Fl.} \\ & \text{58d. Flemish = 1 crown France} \\ & \text{100 crowns France = 60 ducats Venice} \\ & \text{1 ducat Venice = 360 mervadies Spain} \\ & \text{272 mervadies = 1 piafre} \\ & \text{How many piafres = 100l. sterling} \end{align*} \] In order to abridge the terms, divide 58 and 420 by 2, and you have the new antecedent 29, and the new consequent 210; reject two ciphers in 100 and 1000; divide 272 and 360 by 8, and you have 34 and 45; divide 34 and 60 by 2, and you have 17 and 30; and the whole will stand abridged as above. Then, \(29 \times 17 = 493\) divisor; and \(210 \times 30 \times 45 \times 10 = 2835000\) dividend; and, \(493)2835000(5750\frac{1}{2}\) piafres. Ans. Or, the consequents may be connected with the sign of multiplication, and placed over a line by way of numerator; and the antecedents, connected in the same manner, may be placed under the line, by way of denominator; and then abridged as follows: \[ \begin{align*} & \frac{420 \times 60 \times 360 \times 100}{58 \times 100 \times 272} = \frac{210 \times 60 \times 360 \times 10}{29 \times 1 \times 272} \\ & \frac{210 \times 60 \times 45 \times 10}{29 \times 34} = \frac{210 \times 30 \times 45 \times 10}{29 \times 17} \\ & \frac{2835000}{493}, \end{align*} \] And, \(493)2835000(5750\frac{1}{2}\) piafres. Ans. The placing the terms by way of antecedent and consequent, change frequent working as the rules direct, saves so many flattings of the rule of three, and greatly shortens the operation. NEW ENGLAND

Pages 136-141

New ENGLAND, late a province of the British empire in America, is bounded on the north by Canada, on the east by Nova Scotia and the Atlantic ocean, on the south by the Atlantic and Long Island sound, and on the west by New York. It lies in the form of a quarter of a circle. Its west line, beginning at the mouth of Byram river, which empties into Long Island sound at the south-west corner of Connecticut, latitude 41°, runs a little east of north, until it strikes the 45th degree of latitude, and then curves to the eastward almost to the gulf of St Lawrence. This country was discovered in the beginning of the 16th century, and called North Virginia; but no Europeans settled there till the year 1608. The first colony, which was weak and ill-directed, did not succeed; and, for some time, there were only a few adventurers who came over at times in the summer, built themselves temporary huts for the sake of trading with the savages, and, like them, disappeared again for the At last some Brownists, headed by Mr Robinson, whom Neal styles the Father of the Independents, who in 1610 had been driven from England by persecution, fled to Holland, and settled at Leyden; but in 1621 determined, with Mr Brewster affiant-preacher to Mr Robinson, to found a church for their sect in the new hemisphere. They therefore purchased, in 1621, the charter of the

OUR AUTHOR

r author expresses his surprise, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of wearing <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> next the skin should not have prevailed more universally. He is confident it would prevent a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of diseases; and he thinks there is no greater <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> than the comfortable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> which arises from wearing it, especially after one is a little accustomed to it. "It is a mistaken notion (says he), that it is too warm a clothing for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. I have worn it in the hottest climates, and at all seasons of the year; and never found the least inconvenience from it. It is the warm bath of perspiration confined by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> shirt, wet with sweat, which renders the summer heats of southern climates so unsupportable; but flannel promotes perspiration, and favours its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>; and evaporation, as is well known, produces positive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. It has been observed that new flannel, after some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> wearing, acquires the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of shining in the dark, but loses it on being washed.
